PREFACE t 

The first edition of this work was published in 1934. 

The second edition appeared in 1938. A second edition, partially revised, was published in the early part of 1943. The work was interrupted at that time by military service, after but four chapters had been completed. ASH The Third Edition, as now published, is a complete revision. Many new subjects have been explored, and the entire work has been revised in a manner which seems best adapted to the scholarship and attainments of the general academic student. The scope of this revision has been determined in part by the educational needs of accountants as indicated in recent years by the Pennsylvania State Board for the Examination of Accountants and the American Institute of Accountants.

The statutes cited in this volume are those of the Legislature of Pennsylvania and the Congress of the United States. Unless quoted or made the subject of discussion, the cases cited in the brief excerpts from the opinions of the courts have been omitted, with few exceptions, inasmuch as they disturb the continuity of reading and would unduly lengthen the book.

Many of these lectures were originally published by the Temple Law Quarterly, Current Legal Thought, Journalism Quarterly, University of Pittsburgh Law

Review, Dickinson Law Review, the Pennsylvania Joint

State Government Commission, and the Bureau of Business Research of The Pennsylvania State College. Banking Institutions," published by the American Law

CHAPTER I  Part 1. Common Law Sec. 1. Function of Law. Law is the keystone of human experience, wisdom, and civilization itself, interwoven in all branches of learning and affecting the whole of human endeavor. It enters into nearly every relation of social and economic life, and is fundamental in the enjoyment of civil and political freedom. The importance of the study of law is two-fold. It not only affords an incomparable intellectual training, but its practical aspects are apparent in rules of civil conduct governing the acquisition of wealth. Every man should know, and is presumed to know the accepted codes of human behavior, not only for his own protection, but that of society in which he lives. Blackstone's first lecture at Oxford on the common law of England, October 25, 1758, contains the injunction that as every "subject is interested in the preservation of the laws, it is incumbent upon every man to be acquainted with those at least with which he is immediately concerned; lest he incur the censure, as well as inconvenience, of living in society without knowing the obligations which it lays him under." 1 What was true then must, with added force and persuasion be so in the highly industrialized world of today, and equally so as long as man is concerned with his civil liberty. 

Sec. 2. Definition of Law. Law is the aggregate of acceptable legal standards of human behavior. It is defined in the commentaries of Blackstone as "A rule of civil conduct, prescribed by the supreme power in a state, commanding what is right and prohibiting what is wrong.". Like most words of general import, law as a concept is not always confined to rules of civil conduct, 2

CHAPTER I  Part 1. Common Law Sec. 1. Function of Law. Law is the keystone of human experience, wisdom, and civilization itself, interwoven in all branches of learning and affecting the whole of human endeavor. It enters into nearly every relation of social and economic life, and is fundamental in the enjoyment of civil and political freedom. The importance of the study of law is two-fold. It not only affords an incomparable intellectual training, but its practical aspects are apparent in rules of civil conduct governing the acquisition of wealth. Every man should know, and is presumed to know the accepted codes of human behavior, not only for his own protection, but that of society in which he lives. Blackstone's first lecture at Oxford on the common law of England, October 25, 1758, contains the injunction that as every "subject is interested in the preservation of the laws, it is incumbent upon every man to be acquainted with those at least with which he is immediately concerned; lest he incur the censure, as well as inconvenience, of living in society without knowing the obligations which it lays him under." 1 What was true then must, with added force and persuasion be so in the highly industrialized world of today, and equally so as long as man is concerned with his civil liberty. 

Sec. 2. Definition of Law. Law is the aggregate of acceptable legal standards of human behavior. It is defined in the commentaries of Blackstone as "A rule of civil conduct, prescribed by the supreme power in a state, commanding what is right and prohibiting what is wrong." Like most words of general import, law as a concept is not always confined to rules of civil conduct, 2 

1 Intro. Black. Com. 6. 

2 Intro. Black. Com. 41. 

1

but may be used to describe such things as laws of God, of nature, of health, of logic, of strategy, and of eco- Lomics. In the same broad sense it is used to denote "the laws of motion, of gravitation, of optics, or mechanics, as well as the laws of nature and of nations." Such use not only denotes different things, but different kinds of things, and for this reason it is necessary to distinguish between law in its general sense and law in its strict legal sense. Montesquieu said of the former: "In the largest sense, laws are the necessary relations which arise from the nature of things; in this sense, all beings have their laws, God has his laws, the material universe has its laws, intelligences superior to man have their laws, animals have their laws, man has his laws." Law in its strict legal sense is confined to rules of civil conduct. "This is the origin of law," said Demosthenes, "which for various reasons all are under an obligation to obey; but especially because all law is the invention and gift of heaven, the sentiment of wise men, the correction of every offense, and the general compact of the state; to live in conformity with which is the duty of every individual in society." 5 The sources of law are custom, adjudication, and legislation. 

Sec. 3. Common Law and Civil Law Countries. 

The several countries of the world are usually classified as common law or civil law states. If a particular state is governed in part by the common law and in part by statutory codes, it is called a common law country. If it is governed altogether by statutory codes it is called a civil law country. Code law had its origin in a compilation by Theodosius the Younger (438 A. D.), and by 

Justinian (533 A. D.). As said by Blackstone: "These form the body of Roman law, or corpus juris civilis, as published about the time of Justinian; which, however, fell soon into neglect and oblivion, till about the year 1130, when a copy of the digests was found at Amalfi, in Italy; which accident, con- 

Intro. Black. Com. 38. 

Esprit des Lois, 1. 

51 Shar. Black. Com. 30.

curring with the policy of the Roman ecclesiastics, suddenly gave new vogue and authority to the civil law, introduced it into several nations, and occasioned that mighty inundation of voluminous comment, with which this system of law, more than any other, is now loaded."

Sec. 4. Common Law in the New World. Civil codes, having their institution and authority in written or statutory form, as distinguished from the general principles of the common law, form the basis of law in countries of Latin influence-continental Europe, Latin America, Scotland, South Africa, and because of the influence of the French, in the Province of Quebec and the State of Louisiana. The common law prevails in 

England, Ireland, Canada (except for the Province of 

Quebec), Australia, Porto Rico, the Philippines, and in the United States except for the State of Louisiana. 

Aside from complete written codes which characterize civil law countries, and the doctrine of stare decisis which governs the application of the common law, the chief distinction between the two systems is in the use of the jury. In civil law countries the jury functions only in criminal trials, while in common law countries it functions in civil as well as in criminal matters, except for suits in equity, where a jury may be used to enlighten the conscience of the chancellor. This is discretionary with the court, and where the right of jury trial is not expressly given by statute the verdict is merely advisory. Where an issue is directed to the law side of the court, however, to settle preliminary questions of fact, the verdict is binding on the parties. 

Sec. 5. Influence of the Roman Law. Many com mon law institutions owe their origin to the civil law, principally because on two separate and distinct occasions England was subjected to Latin invasion. The first occurred by the Romans under Julius Caesar and his successors from approximately 50 B. C. to 500 A. D.

The Roman Law being extended to the upper classes it did not gain sufficient foothold, and when the Romans 

6 Intro. Black. Com. 81.

withdrew to defend Rome against the Goths, the civil or Roman Law disappeared. For the succeeding five centuries England was subjected to invasion by the Jutes, Angles, Saxons, and Danes from the western borders of the northern mainland of Europe. The Britains having been practically exterminated, these tribes adhered to their own tribal customs. The more serious invasion of Latin influence occurred in the Norman Conquest in 1066 A. D. The discovery of the Justinian 

Pandects popularized the civil codes on the continent. 

They were studied by the Popish clergy and were introduced into many of the universities on the continent. "But it did not meet with the same easy reception in England, where a mild and rational system of laws had been long established, as it did upon the continent; and though the monkish clergy, devoted to the will of a foreign primate, received it with eagerness and zeal, yet the laity, who were more interested to preserve the old constitution, and had already severely felt the effect of many Norman innovations, continued wedded to the use of the common law.” 7

Sec. 6. Origin of Common Law. The common law may be defined as a collection of unwritten maxims and customs which have existed immemorially, handed down by tradition, use, and experience, and which have the force of law. It "always has reason as its foundation." 8 

Prior to the establishment of courts of justice in the twelfth century, the laws of England consisted of a few ordinances of the kings who reigned during the first two centuries after the Norman Conquest. The English 

Parliament had not yet been established when the King's judges, who were originally a part of the King's personal retinue, set out to administer justice. They had no statutes to guide them, and were undoubtedly influenced by the Roman Law. In the reign of Henry II periodical circuits were established, and in the twelfth and thir- 

7 Intro. Black. Com. 18. 

8 Bagley v. Reno Oil Co., 201 Pa. 78 (1904).

teenth centuries a system of trial by jury. This was an innovation of the Dukes of Normandy. By first hearing the facts, and having them determined with the aid of a jury, the judges then determined which of the parties had violated the customs and traditions of the realm, and by reasoning and judgment gradually established a series of precedents or judiciary law, in which is reflected the customs and usages of the English people, the reasoning of her judges, and in part the Roman Law, the Canon Law, and the Law Merchant, eventually to become the common or unwritten law of England. The following colloquy was incident to the trial of William

Penn, who had been charged with treason for having corresponded with the exiled monarch, Charles II. 

Penn: "I desire you would let me know by what law it is you prosecute me and upon what you ground your indictment." Recorder: "Upon the common law." 

Penn: "Where is that common law?" Recorder: "You must not think that I am able to run up so many years and over so many adjudged cases which we call common law to answer your curiosity." Penn: "This answer I am sure is very short of my question for if it be common law, it should not be so hard to produce." " 

Sec. 7. Blackstone on Common Law. 

"When I call these parts of our law leges non scripta, I would not be understood as if all those laws were at present merely oral, or communicated from the former ages to the present solely by word of mouth. It is true indeed that, in the profound ignorance of letters, which formerly overspread the whole western world, all laws were entirely traditional, for this plain reason, because the nations among which they prevailed had but little idea of writing. 

Thus the British as well as the Gallic Druids committed all their laws as well as learning to memory. . . . But, with us at present, the monuments and evidences of our legal customs are contained in the records of the several courts of justice in books of reports and judicial decisions, and in the treatises of learned sages of the profession, preserved and handed down to us from the times of highest antiquity. However, I therefore style these parts of our 

Loyd, "Early Courts of Pennsylvania," 46. 2

law leges non scripta, because their original institution and authority are not set down in writing, as acts of parliament are, but they receive their binding power, and the force of laws, by long and immemorial usage, and by their universal reception throughout the kingdom." 10

Sec. 8. The Law Merchant. The Law Merchant, or lex mercatoria, is a part of the common law. It had its origin in the Roman Law, but lost its original authority with the disintegration of the Roman Empire. It was revived in the fifteenth century, coincident with the extension of commerce and trade, and was accepted as the common law of Western Europe. As a body of doctrine it consisted of the customs of merchants with respect to bills of exchange, bills of lading, freight, average (loss less than the total to cargo or ship which was shared ratably), demurrage (charge for detention of ship or transportation equipment), insurance, bottomry (hypothecation of the ship as security for a loan or for repairs or supplies), letters of credit, charter parties (contract for an entire ship or principal part thereof), partnerships, trade-marks, and salvage claims. Blackstone describes it as different from the general rules of the common law, yet "ingrafted into it, and made a part of it: being allowed, for the benefit of trade", and of the "utmost validity in all commercial transactions." ¹¹ The 

Law Merchant was originally administered in special courts and by special judges, at ports of import and export, and at fairs and market places. In the eighteenth century the courts of England took judicial notice of the Law Merchant, ousting such quasi-foreign tribunals of that jurisdiction, and in this manner it was absorbed into the common law. The Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act of 1901 12 states: "In any case not provided for in this act, the rules of the Law Merchant shall govern." A similar provision appears in the Uniform Partnership Act of 1915. 13

Sec. 9. Canon Law and Christianity. A discus sion of the antecedents of the common law would be incomplete without mention of the influence of the Canon Law and the general principles of Christianity. When 

William the Conqueror was about to set out on his conquest of England, he received the Papal blessing upon the condition that he permit the establishment of ecclesiastical courts, a promise which he faithfully redeemed."

These courts administered the principles of the Canon Law with respect to such secular matters as marriage, legitimacy, wills, and the distribution of decedents' estates, until the nineteenth century, when this jurisdiction was transferred to the King's Courts by an act of Parliament. The influence of general principles of 

Christianity was early acknowledged by the Supreme 

Court of Pennsylvania. "Christianity, general Christianity, is and always has been a part of the common law of Pennsylvania; Christianity, without the spiritual artillery of European countries; for this Christianity was one of the considerations of the Royal Charter, and the very basis of its great founder, William Penn; not

Christianity with an established Church, and tithes and spiritual courts; but Christianity with liberty of conscience to all men. 99 15

Sec. 10. Common Law Commentators. The writ ings of the early common law commentators have had considerable influence in perpetuating this branch of the law. These were early English jurists who clarified and recorded the customs, usages and traditions of 

England. In 1481, Sir THOMAS DE LITTLETON, Judge of the Common Pleas, wrote a "Treatise on Tenures."

In 1554, RANULF DE GLANVILL, Chief Justiciar of Eng land, wrote his "Forms of Procedure", the first coherent code of law compiled in England. In 1569, HENRY DE 

BRACTON, Judge of the King's Bench, wrote a "Treatise on the Laws and Customs of England." In 1628, Sir

"Institutes", the first volume being known as "Coke upon Littleton."

The most widely known of the Eng lish commentaries is that of Sir WILLIAM BLACKSTONE, first Viner Professor at Oxford, who published his "Commentaries on the Laws of England" in 1765. These were the first lectures delivered at Oxford on the common law. To these may be added the "Commentaries on American Law" by JAMES KENT, Professor of Law in Columbia College, in 1836. In these commentaries, as well as legal reports, digests, encyclopedias, dictionaries, annotations, legal periodicals and texts, will be found the principles of the common law. 17 

Sec. 11. Common Law of Pennsylvania. The Su preme Court of Pennsylvania has observed in recent years that the "foundations of jurisprudence" are in the common law,10 and that "Pennsylvania is still and it is hoped always will be a common law State", although, "of course, the legislature may change the common law." 1 The Act of 1777 18 abrogated all colonial laws in effect at that time, but revived in general those acts and that part of the common law which were not repugnant to the new form of government, including such of the statute laws of England as were previously in force which did not require a declaration of allegiance or fidelity to the King of Great Britain. In 1782 the Supreme 

Court rejected the application of English statutes, other than those which were convenient or adapted to the circumstances of the people,¹º and on April 7, 1807, the General Assembly authorized the judges to examine and report on specific statutes that were in force or which ought to be incorporated into the statute laws of the commonwealth. On December 14, 1808, the Supreme 

Court filed its report, listing 172 statutes or parts of statutes of the English Parliament which were to con-

C. J. "Every country has its common law. Ours is composed partly of the common law of England and partly of our own usages. When our ancestors emigrated from England, they took with them such of the English principles as were convenient for the situation in which they were about to place themselves. It required time and experience to ascertain how much of the English law would be suitable in this country. By degrees, as circumstances demanded, we adopted the English usages, or substituted others better suited to our wants, till at length, before the time of the Revolution, we had formed a system of our own, founded in general on the English Constitution, but not without considerable variations."

Sec. 12. Stare Decisis. The common law would be unworkable without some degree of stability. This is accomplished under the doctrine of stare decisis. 

Broadly stated, this doctrine imposes a duty on all judges who administer the common law to stand by decided cases, uphold precedents, and maintain former adjudications where the "very point" is again in controversy. On March 19, 1810, the legislature made it unlawful to read or quote in any court of Pennsylvania any British precedent or adjudication made subsequent to July 4, 1776, but this was repealed on March 29, 1836. 

If the question is settled in the constitution or statutes the courts will stop there, but if not, recourse must be had to the body of law as previously declared within the same jurisdiction, and if that fail, then to the decisions in other jurisdictions. It should be remembered, however, that except for the powers delegated to the federal government, each state is sovereign and each determines

its own law. While there is a good deal of uniformity in the decisions of the highest courts of record of the several states, it does not follow that the courts of one state are bound to follow the decisions of another. If the search for a precedent should fail, the court then draws from the decided cases nearest in their circumstances, consonant with acceptable standards of right conduct. In a sense this is law-making by the judiciary, but if so by a subtle process. "For it is an established rule to abide by former precedents, where the same points come again in litigation: as well to keep the scale of justice even and steady, and not liable to waver with every new judge's opinion; as also because the law in that case being solemnly declared and determined, what before was uncertain, and perhaps indifferent, is now become a permanent rule, which it is not in the breast of any subsequent judge to alter or vary from according to his private sentiments: he being sworn to determine, not according to his own private judgment, but according to the known laws and customs of the land; not delegated to pronounce a new law, but to maintain and expound the old one.' "20 

Sec. 13. Validity of Precedents. It is seldom that a court will dishonor its own decisions, but this should not be taken too literally. A precedent may become obsolete by lapse of time. And if it is not clear, or is founded on wrong reasoning, insufficient argument, or peculiar circumstances, it may be modified and if necessary overruled. It has been said that the fundamental principles of the common law are in essence unchangeable, but liable to expansion; and that their application to given conditions necessarily varies according to changes wrought by usage or statutory enactment.21 Mr. 

Justice KEPHART, later Chief Justice, observed with respect to the problems created by the introduction of the automobile, that the common law "is not a fixed, unyielding set of principles of a certain standard applying only as conditions warranted a century ago, but adapts itself to changing conditions as marked by the progress of public, material, and social affairs." 22

158 (1919). 

22 Nesbit v. Riesenman, 298 Pa. 475

Sec. 14. Interpretation of the Constitution. A num ber of important landmarks of the past have been overruled by the courts in recent years, but most of these cases have dealt with the interpretation of the federal constitution, in the light of changing social and economic institutions, rather than with the principles of the common law. The constitution consists for the most part of an enumeration of powers, with a paucity of definition or explanation, and it has been incumbent upon the Supreme Court to supply that defect. It is hardly to be expected that such decisions in a dynamic society would be uniform throughout the years, some of which were decided by a bare majority of the court. In a famous case, Hammer v. Dagenhart, 23 decided in 1918, the majority held that the power to regulate commerce among the several states did not justify the exclusion of the products of oppressive child labor from the channels of interstate commerce, but this interpretation was overruled in 1941.24 In an equally famous case, Adkins v. Children's Hospital,25 decided in 1923, the majority held that the provisions of the constitution were not sufficiently broad to sanction minimum wage legislation for women and children, but this decision was overruled in 1937.26 Such a law was then promptly enacted in

Pennsylvania," and it has since been sustained by the 

Supreme Court of Pennsylvania.28 The most important of these cases will appear throughout the text.

The criminal part of the law deals with offenses against society. Equity is associated only with the civil part of the law. It is explained by Sir Henry Maine as "any body of rules existing by the side of the original civil law, founded on distinct principles, and claiming to supersede the civil law in virtue of a superior sanctity inherent in those principles." 38

Grotius defines it as "the correction of that wherein the law (by reason of its universality) is deficient." As said by Blackstone, "since in laws all cases cannot be foreseen or expressed, it is necessary that, when the general decrees of the law come to be applied to particular cases, there should be somewhere a power vested of defining those circumstances, which (had they been foreseen) the legislator himself would have expressed." " Broadly stated, it is the function of equity to afford relief in unusual circumstances from the oper ation of the common law, or afford a remedy which the common law failed to provide, in much the same sense as judges may, by way of probation, and executive officers of the state by way of parole and pardon, afford relief in unusual circumstances from the operation of the criminal law. 31 

Sec. 16. Origin of Equity. Equity is commonly said to have originated in the King's conscience, on the theory that the King "is the fountain of justice" in whom all judicial power is derived. The justification for relief of this sort was occasioned by the slow development of the common law, and the limited number of common law writs available for the redress of civil wrongs. Parliament authorized the Chancellor (the 

Royal Secretary and Keeper of the Seal) to issue these writs, but if he attempted to issue a writ not then authorized by the common law courts it was usually quashed. 

30 "Ancient Law," 27. 

81 Intro. Black. Com. 61.

33 Hence numerous appeals were made to the King, directly or in council, praying for relief "for God and in way of Charity." As a consequence the Chancellor, who had also been delegated with the King's prerogative, disregarded the statute and granted relief for certain grievances not provided for by the common law.32 These were cases requiring relief by way of injunction, or which involved two or more antagonistic parties in what would otherwise have resulted in a multiplicity of suits, or in which a judgment for damages was inadequate, and also cases in which one of the parties had a just defense but was unable to present it under current rules of pleading. The Chancellor also enjoined the common law courts in some instances from entertaining inequitable suits. This conflict finally resulted in a pitched battle between the Chancellor and the common law courts, which was finally resolved by the decree of James I, that where the two came in conflict, equity should prevail. Equitable rules have since crystallized into a definite body of legal doctrine--of principles, procedures, and remedies-in which the theory of judicial precedent is firmly entrenched. 

Sec. 17. Equity in Pennsylvania. There has never been a distinct court of chancery in Pennsylvania, except from 1720 to 1726, when a separate court was conducted by Governor Keith, and by Governor Gordon until his death in 1737. It was then discontinued due to the opposition of the assembly, which resolved on 

March 27, 1736, "That the court of chancery as it is at present established is contrary to the charter of privileges granted to the freemen of the province." This antagonism was mainly due to primitive social conditions, friction between the governors and the assemblies, and because the chancellorship was identified with the crown. The necessity of enforcing equitable principles and remedies eventually led to various devices in which 

32 Jenks, "Book of English Law," 41. 

33 Robinson, "Elementary Law," 385.

www the courts "asserted in themselves" the right to grant equitable relief through the medium of common law actions and the intervention of the jury. 

Seitzinger v. Ridgway, 9 Watts 496 (1840). KENNEDY, J. "Having no court of chancery in this state, and it being conceived that justice could not be administered in all cases without recourse to those principles which have been adopted and maintained in courts of equity in England, with a view to mitigate the extreme rigor of the common law in some instances, and again in others to prevent a failure of justice, our courts of law, with a like view, adopted in similar cases the principles which had governed courts of equity in England, so far as it was found practicable through the medium of common-law forms of action and the intervention of a jury to do so. Equitable principles have thus become, and are regarded in Pennsylvania as part of the common law of the state."

Sec. 18. Powers in Equity. The state constitutions of 1776 and 1790 provided that the legislature might confer the powers of equity on the courts of the commonwealth, but the legislature was slow to exercise this authority. From the very earliest times it had assumed quasi-judicial functions of administering a sort of equitable relief by way of special legislation, until this practice was curtailed in the constitution of 1874.34 This legislation dealt for the most part with the release of debtors from prison, upon making an assignment of their property for the benefit of creditors, reformation of lost deeds, enforcement of contracts of deceased persons, permission to sell real estate in which minors and others laboring under disability had an interest, acquisition and disposition of land by the clergy in the interest of schools and churches, and control over guardians and trustees. The first statute delegating equity powers to the courts was enacted in 1836. This statute was limited to Philadelphia County, in deference to the prejudices of the interior counties, until 1857, when such laws were made uniform throughout the commonwealth. 

The principal delegations of power from that date to the

It should be obvious from the foregoing that the courts of Pennsylvania do not possess general chancery powers, and for this reason he who asserts an equitable remedy must "point to the statute giving it." 30

Sec. 20. Maxims of Equity. Common law remedies are a matter of right. But the origin of equity was the 

King's favor, and a favor cannot be demanded as of right. For this reason relief in equity is a matter of grace, and all equitable remedies are discretionary, although the courts are bound to exercise a reasonable discretion. In so doing they are governed largely by all the circumstances of the case, and by reference to what are known as maxims of equity, namely: (1) He who seeks equity must do equity. (2) One who comes into equity must come with clean hands-He who does iniquity shall not have equity. (3) Equity aids the vigilant. (4) Equity follows the law-As between equal equities the law will prevail. (5) Where there are equal equities the first in order of time shall prevail. (6) Equity regards as done that which ought to have been done Equity abhors a forfeiture. (7) Where one of two innocent persons must suffer from the fraud of a third, he who furnished the means of perpetrating the fraud must bear the loss. (8) Equality is equity. 

Palmer v. Harris, 60 Pa. 156 (1886). Plaintiff was the manufacturer of a cigar known as the "Golden Crown," and had devised a trade-mark which he used in its sale. He alleged that the defendant, who was a printer by trade, counterfeited this mark and sold copies of it to other manufacturers. Defendant admitted 

38 Hawthorn v. Bronson, 16 S. & R. 269 (1827). 

30 Act of June 7, 1907, P. L. 440, 12 

PS 1228.

these allegations, but replied that the cigars sold by the plaintiff were manufactured in the city of New York, while the trade-mark in question stated that they were the product of a "factory of cigars from the best plantations de la Vuelta Abajo, Calle Del 

Agua, Habana." The chancellor dismissed the bill and plaintiff appealed. SHARSWOOD, J. "The party who attempts to deceive the public by the use of a trade-mark, which contains on its face a falsehood as to the place where his goods are manufactured, in order to have the benefit of the reputation which such goods have acquired in the market, is guilty of the same fraud of which he complains in the defendant. He certainly can have no claim to the extraordinary interposition of a tribunal, constituted to administer equity, for the purpose of securing to him the profits arising from his fraudulent act." 

Sec. 21. Decrees in Equity. A judgment at law is ordinarily satisfied by sheriff's sale of the property of the judgment debtor. Much greater latitude is allowed in the enforcement of a decree in equity. A right in rem is any right which may be asserted against all persons or against all but certain determinate persons. A right in personam is a right which may be asserted against a particular person. A judgment at law acts in rem, or against the property of the debtor. A decree in equity acts in personam, or against the person of the defendant, although it has the same qualities as a judg ment in so far as it operates as a lien against real estate owned by the debtor.40 

Butler County v. P. H. B. & N. C. Ry. Co., 298 Pa. 347 (1929). 

KEPHART, J. "The customary processes of a chancery court to enforce the performance of a decree are a mandatory injunction, attachment for contempt, writ of sequestration, or writ of assistance; relief may also be had by a writ or writs of execution analogous to those used in law in actions of the same general character (Equity Rule 86), or the court may designate an individual to perform its order: Equity Rule 87." (1) Injunctions. Injunctions are of two sorts, mandatory and prohibitory. A mandatory injunction requires the performance of a specific act. A prohibitory injunction prohibits the doing of something which is deemed to be injurious and improper. The 

Act of 1836, supra, authorizes the courts to prevent or restrain "the 

40 Act of March 29, 1859, P. L. 289, 12 PS 1225.

commission or continuance of acts contrary to law and prejudicial to the interests of the community or the rights of individuals." 

Subsequent statutes modify this power with respect to labor disputes. The Pennsylvania statute 41 is modeled after the federal 

Norris-LaGuardia Act.42 

(2) Attachment for Contempt. This remedy may be resorted to where there is disobedience of a decree. The Act of 1836 43 provides that imprisonment for contempt shall extend only to such contempts as shall be committed in open court, and that all other contempts shall be punished by fine only. The courts have long held, however, that this statute "has no application to cases of attachments to enforce civil remedies, where the object is to secure compliance with a decree of court." 44 The Act of 1842,45 which abolished imprisonment for debts arising from contract, etc., expressly excepts from its provisions "proceedings as for contempt to enforce civil remedies." An attachment may not be employed, however, to enforce a decree for the payment of money due on a contract or for breach of contract. As said by the Chief Justice in 1855, "In favor of liberty, and in view of the chief object of the Act of 1842, I feel bound to adopt the construction, that the power to imprison for the purpose of enforcing a decree for the payment of money due on a contract, no longer exists." 46 (3) Writ of Sequestration. A writ of sequestration may be used where an attachment cannot be served, or where the defendant persists in his disobedience and chooses to remain in prison. 

Its purpose is to attach the property of the defendant until he complies with the decree. (4) Writ of Assistance. A writ of assistance calls for the specific performance of a particular act. The circumstances under which the courts will grant the specific performance of contacts, in lieu of monetary damages, will be considered in a subsequent chapter.

Pennsylvania has taken a leading part in the adoption of these statutes, although occasionally with some variation. Part 4. Trial by Jury Sec. 24. Qualifications of Jury. The earliest modes of trial were by oath, ordeal, and battle. All have long been abolished in England, the latter in 1819. The modern method of trial in both civil and criminal actions, is by a jury of twelve disinterested persons, summoned from the county where the court is held, who are duly sworn to determine disputed issues of fact. An objection to the whole body of jurors, because of some defect in the venire or partiality of the sheriff by whom it was summoned, is called a challenge to the array. An objection to an individual juror, because of some legal disqualification or probable bias, is called a challenge to the polls. In civil suits the plaintiff and defendant are each allowed four pre-emptory challenges for which no reason need be assigned.5¹ In criminal prosecutions the parties are allowed six, eight, or twenty preemptory challenges, according to the degree of the alleged crime.52 

Jurors receive a fee of four dollars per day and six cents per mile for actual travel.53 Witnesses receive a fee of three dollars per day and five cents per mile for actual travel.54

Expert witnesses may be paid more, but such

This was made effective by the Act of 1874.59 In the Municipal Court of Philadelphia and the Allegheny County Court, a jury trial must be demanded either in the statement of claim or affidavit of defense or it will be deemed to have been waived. A trial by jury is not afforded in contempt cases, except in two instances involving indirect criminal contempt.

The first was allowed a century ago, and constitutes one of the most interesting chapters in the juridical history of Pennsylvania. In 1788 an action involving an alleged libel was pending before the Supreme Court. The defendant, a newspaper publisher, appealed to public sentiment and held himself up as being persecuted. He was cited for contempt on the ground that he had attempted to raise a prejudice against his opponent in a pending action, and summarily fined and imprisoned. In 1802 the same situation arose again. The defendant in the second case was involved in an action to recover on a policy of insurance in an action pending before the Supreme Court, and finding himself annoyed at the legal tactics of his opponent, published a report to the effect that his opponent had sworn falsely and had delayed the disposition of the case. He, too, was summarily fined and imprisoned.65 The defendants in both cases presented memorials to the General Assembly, suggesting that the judges had made themselves the proper object of impeachment. On the second occasion the judges were impeached by the House of Representatives, except one judge who had been ill and had not participated in the alleged grievance, but he asked to be included. The action by the judges was in strict conformity with the common law and they were eventually acquitted by the Senate, although strangely enough, thirteen out of twenty-four Senators voted for conviction."6

Sec. 27. Indirect Criminal Contempt. After the com motion had subsided the legislature removed the cause of complaint by affording a trial by jury where publications out of court are involved. While this privilege accrues largely to the newspaper fraternity, it is available to others as well. In a case decided in 1930 the defendant was accused, among other things, of having published and circulated a libelous cartoon involving one of the judges of Schuylkill County. He was cited for contempt and summarily fined $2,500, but the Supreme Court, on appeal, called attention to the provisions of the statute, which had not been obeyed, and set the fine aside. In 1931 the legislature granted the same privilege to a person accused of violating a restraining order or injunction in connection with a labor dispute, where the act complained of is not committed in the presence of the court or so near as to interfere directly with the administration of justice." The constitutionality of this act was sustained by the Supreme Court in 1935.70 Pennsylvania in this respect is one of the most progressive states in the union.

Sec. 28. Lex Fori. Each state is sovereign, and each generally insists upon the application of its laws to persons and property within its jurisdiction. Perplexing questions arise, however, when the residents of one state own property in another, or when the courts of one state are called upon to enforce obligations created in another, 67 Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 784, 17 PS 2044. es Snyder's Appeal, 301 Pa. 276 (1930). 

00 Act of June 23, 1931, P. L. 925, 17 PS 2047. 

70 Penn Anthracite Mining Co. v. 

Anthracite Miners of Pa., 318 Pa. 401 (1935).

or when a contract is made in one state which is to be performed in another. To add to the confusion, the federal government is also sovereign to the extent of the powers delegated to it. The first principle to be observed with respect to such problems is the lex fori. This is the law of the forum. It is applied to questions of practice and procedure, pleading, evidence, the statute of limitations, and all matters relating to the remedy." In other words, if the resident of one state institutes a civil action in another, he is expected to observe the proprieties under which the courts of that state are authorized to function.

Sec. 29. Lex Domicilli. The lex domicilli is the sub stantive law of one's domicile. Generally, questions pertaining to such matters as rights of citizenship, rights in movable property, domestic relationships, and the distribution of estates, are determined by reference to the place where a person has his legal residence. Residence is the same as domicile, and "means the place where a man establishes his abode, makes the seat of his property, and exercises his civil and political rights."72 Some people move about a good deal, but "if the intention of permanently residing in a particular place exists, a residence in pursuance of that intention, however short, will establish a domicile."73 The fact of one's residence may also be important in meeting the qualifications for public office, in disposing of the application of certain kinds of taxes, in exercising the franchise, and attending a public institution without payment of a non-resident fee, in which various common law and statutory requisites may be imposed. It was decided in 1872 that a student who moves into a college community, for the purpose of attending an institution of learning, does not thereby become a legal resident of that community, whether he is an adult or not and whether he is self-supporting or not. 

71 Continental Ill. Nat. Bank & 

Trust Co. v. Holmes, 21 F. Supp. 309 (1937). 

72 Chase V. Miller, 41 Pa. 403 (1862). 

73 Price (1893). 

V. Price, 156 Pa. 617

His domicile will continue to be that of his parents until he has established a legal residence for himself."4

Sec. 30. Lex Situs. The lex situs is the law of the place where the property subject to determination is situated. The lex domicilli and the lex situs are not always in harmony. At common law a person could have but one legal domicile, but there is a growing tendency to disrespect this principle with respect to property which may become a source of revenue to the state. The 

Supreme Court of the United States has recently sanctioned the right of two states, Tennessee and Alabama, to impose an inheritance tax upon the same propertyintangibles-which were located in Alabama but owned by a deceased resident of Tennessee.75 In the following case Pennsylvania" and New Jersey" claimed the decedent as a legal resident, and exacted an inheritance tax, and in both cases the Supreme Court of the United States refused to intervene. This is a matter which has recently provoked the attention of the legislature. The Act of 

194178 provides that where a reasonable doubt exists as to the domicile of a decedent, the Department of Revenue may, with the approval of the Department of Justice, enter into an agreement with the representatives of such an estate to accept a certain sum in full payment of the tax imposed by Pennsylvania, if said agreement also fixes the amount to be paid to any other state in full payment of death taxes.

When either he or the members of his family went away on vacations they started from 'Woodcrest' and returned there afterwards. Practically his entire time, except when absent on vacations, was spent there. His friends and acquaintances considered it his home. Indeed we may readily believe that in his heart Dr. Dorrance knew 'Woodcrest' to be his true and only home, but for personal reasons he preferred to state in public that it was not his home when every fact and circumstance pointed to the contrary." 

Sec. 31. Doctrine of Comity. Comity in law means courtesy. The doctrine of comity is a rule of courtesy with respect to the laws of other states, and not a rule of law. Broadly stated, where a civil cause of action arises in some other state whose laws may differ, the law of such other state will usually be applied by the courts of this state, as a matter of deference and respect, if such law is not contrary to the public policy of this state. 

Where a wrongful death occurs in some other state, of a resident or non-resident of this state,so and a civil action is instituted in this state, the law of the state 

79 Dickinson v. Jones, 309 Pa. 256 (1932). 

80 Knight v. West Jersey R. R. Co., 108 Pa. 250 (1885).

where the wrong occurs will be accorded recognition though it may be at variance with the law of this state. 

The same observation applies to such ordinary civil obligations as deeds and trusts which have been executed in some other state.81 In about one-third of the states, though not in Pennsylvania, girls attain their majority at eighteen. Under this doctrine the obligation of such a person, executed in some other state, will be enforced in this state.82 A gambling obligation, though recoverable under the law of some other state, is sufficiently against public policy in this state as not to be actionable. The same may be said of corporate obligations which, though legal under the laws of some other state, are in violation of the constitution of this state.84 A marriage contract, if valid where executed, is generally valid everywhere, but not when incestuous, as where an uncle and niece who married in Russia cohabited in this state in violation of the penal laws.85 The marriage of first cousins, though forbidden in this state, is not so objectionable.86 It should be noted, also, that a common law marriage, though defective where executed, is susceptible of ratification in this state."7

Sec. 32. Lex Delicti. The lex delicti means the law of the place where a wrong is committed. Where a resident of one state goes into another state, presumably he agrees to conform to the standards of legal conduct which prevail in such other state. A more difficult question is presented whenever a resident of one state sets in motion a force which results in injury to a legally protected interest in another state. In a recent case a resident of Pennsylvania owned a dog which apparently contracted rabies. The dog wandered to the City of

Trenton, and there bit the plaintiff. The action was in-

New York has an unusual, and perhaps salutary rule, under which absolute liability is imposed upon the owner of an automobile who lends it to another. Such liability is not imposed in this and other states in the absence of a master-servant relationship. In reaching this conclusion the court applied the law of the place of the wrong, under which the driver alone would be liable, and then shifted such liability to the owner under the

Sec. 33. Lex Contractus. Quite frequently a con tract which is made in one state, is to be performed in another. If there is any difference between the law of the state where the contract is made, and the law of the state where the contract is to be performed, the law of the place of performance will generally govern the rights of the parties. Where, however, a contract is to be performed in several states, whose laws may differ, there seems to be no alternative but to apply the local contract rules, or the law of the place where the contract is made. The conflict of laws doctrine applies, strictly speaking, only to transactions of an interstate character. 

It is closely allied to the good faith clause in the federal constitution. Thus, if a judgment is obtained against a married woman resident of this state, in a court of some other state, it will be given effect though the transaction

is unenforceable under the laws of this state.92 Prior to the Act of 1939, the law of another state had to be proved as facts, and in the absence of such allegation or proof was presumed to be the same as that of the forum." 93 The Act of 1939 94 provides that the courts of the commonwealth shall thereafter take judicial notice of the common and statutory laws of other states, and that the determination of such laws shall be a function of the court and not of the jury. The laws of a foreign country must still be specially pleaded, but the determination of such laws, under this statute, is now for the court rather than for the jury. The Act of 19415 invokes the san doctrine of judicial notice with respect to the ordinances of cities and other governmental units. 

Burnett v. Pennsylvania R. R. Co., 176 Pa. 45 (1896). Plaintiff received a pass in New Jersey for transportation from the station in Trenton directly across the Delaware River into this state. It contained a stipulation, in consideration of free transportation, that he should assume the risk of accident. Such a stipulation is valid in New Jersey, but would not absolve the company of liability arising from its negligence in Pennsylvania. This was an action in trespass for negligent injury while using the pass in Pennsylvania. 

In sustaining the action it was said by FELL, J. "The service was to be rendered here; this was the place of performance. Generally as to its formalities and its interpretation, obligation and effect, a contract is governed by the laws of the place where it is made, and if it is valid there it is valid everywhere; but when it is made in one state or country to be performed in another state or country its validity and effect are to be determined by the laws of the place of performance." 

Sec. 34. Federal Rules of Decision. In 1789 Con gress provided that in actions instituted in the federal courts, "The laws of the several States, except where the 

Constitution, treaties, or statutes of the United States otherwise require or provide, shall be regarded as rules of decision in trials at common law, in the courts of the United States, in cases where they apply."98 In a famous

case, decided in 1843, Mr. Justice STORY declared that federal courts were not bound by the pronouncements of the state courts on the common law.⁹7 The courts substituted, in lieu thereof, what was called federal general common law. In an equally famous case, decided in 

1938, the former decision was overruled. Plaintiff, a citizen of Pennsylvania, was injured while walking along a much used stretch of the right of way of the Erie Railroad Company at night, near Hughestown. He was struck by an open door swinging from the side of a car in a train going in the opposite direction. He brought suit against the defendant, a New York corporation, in the federal court for Southern New York. Defendant contended that under the common law of Pennsylvania, the only duty owed to the plaintiff was to refrain from willful or wanton injury. The trial court refused to ascertain the common law of Pennsylvania, and substituted general federal common law. In deciding that this was error, it was said by Mr. Justice BRANDEIS: "Except in matters governed by the federal Constitution or by acts of Congress, the law to be applied in any case is the law of the state. And whether the law of the state shall be declared by its Legislature in a statute or by its highest court in a decision is not a matter of federal concern. 

There is no federal general common law."98 Both cases are landmarks in the history of federal jurisprudence. 

Sec. 35. Full Faith and Credit. Thus far we have been concerned with the law to be applied to a pending action, rather than with the validity of a decided case. 

The federal constitution provides that, "Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and Judicial Proceedings of every other State"; also, that "Congress may by general laws prescribe the Manner in which such Acts, Records and Proceedings shall be proved, and the Effect thereof."99 In the exercise of this power, Congress has provided that judgments 

09 Article IV, section 1. 

97 Swift v. Tyson, 16 Pet. 3 (1842). 

98 Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U. S. 64 (1938).

"shall have such faith and credit given to them in every court within the United States as they have by law or usage in the courts of the State from which they are taken." 100 These provisions have not occasioned much difficulty, except in the matter of divorce. In a famous case, Haddock v. Haddock, decided in 1906,101 a wife brought suit for separation and alimony in New York. 

The husband offered in defense a divorce decree which he had obtained in Connecticut. It was held that New 

York, the matrimonial domicil and where the wife still resided, was not required to give full faith and credit to the Connecticut divorce, since it was obtained by a husband who had wrongfully left his wife, service on her having been obtained by publication and she not having entered an appearance in the action. In a recent case before the Superior Court of Pennsylvania,102 the defendant had moved from Pennsylvania to Illinois. His wife and their two children remained in Pennsylvania. After residing in Illinois for four years he applied for and was granted a divorce on grounds of desertion, and remarried in Illinois. One child was born to this union in 

Illinois. After a continuous residence in Illinois for a period of seven years he returned with his family to Pennsylvania, where another child was born, and because of which, he was convicted of adultery. The legal effect of this conviction, as observed by President Judge 

KELLER, was to brand the woman he married as his mistress and their second child illegitimate. The judgment of conviction was reversed and the defendant discharged. 

Following is the first of two appeals in an important case before the Supreme Court of the United States. 

Williams v. State of North Carolina (1), 63 Sup. Ct. 205 (1942).

O. B. Williams and Carrie Wyke were married in North Carolina in 1916. Four children were born to this union. Another couple, Thomas Hendrix and Lillie Shaver, were married in North Carolina in 1920. In 1940 Mr. Williams and Mrs. Hendrix went to

Nevada, and after six weeks residence in an auto court, each obtained a divorce under the laws of Nevada. They immediately intermarried in Nevada and returned to North Carolina, where they lived as husband and wife. They were then convicted of bigamous cohabitation in North Carolina and sentenced to a term of years in prison. The conviction was sustained by the Supreme Court of 

North Carolina on the authority of the Haddock Case, the jury having handed down a general verdict without a specific finding as to whether defendants had established a legal domicil in Nevada. 

In reversing the judgment, and remanding the case for further proceedings, it was said by DOUGLAS, J.: "Under the circumstances of this case, a man would have two wives, a wife two husbands. 

The reality of a sentence to prison proves that that is no mere play on words. Each would be a bigamist for living in one state with the only one with whom the other state would permit him lawfully to live. Children of the second marriage would be bastards in one state but legitimate in the other. . . . Haddock v. Haddock is overruled." 

Sec. 36. Need of Uniform Legislation. In the meantime a case arose in Pennsylvania which may have had some bearing in the second appeal in the Williams Case. 

A husband and wife were married in Pennsylvania in 1899, and separated in 1919. In 1922 the wife obtained a support order. On two occasions the husband attempted unsuccessfully to obtain a divorce in Pennsylvania. 

In 1941 he obtained a divorce in Nevada, and immediately thereafter took up his residence in Cleveland. In 

1943 he filed a petition in the Pennsylvania courts requesting that the support order be revoked by reason of the Nevada divorce. The denial of this request, on the ground that he had not established a legal domicil in Nevada, was subsequently affirmed by the appellate courts of Pennsylvania, and by the Supreme Court of the United States.108 On the same day the latter court decided the second appeal in the Williams Case. 

Williams v. State of North Carolina (II), 65 Sup. Ct. 1092 (1945). At a retrial, in which the jury considered the legal domicil which defendants claimed to have established in Nevada, the defendants were again convicted of bigamous cohabitation. This

conviction was again affirmed by the Supreme Court of North Carolina. In affirming the judgment, it was said by FRANKFURTER, J. "This is merely one of those untoward results inevitable in a federal system in which regulation of domestic relations has been left with the States and not given to the national authority." 

MURPHY, J., concurring: "It is unfortunate that the petitioners must be imprisoned for acts which they probably committed in reliance upon advice of counsel and without intent to violate the

If the right of collateral attack upon such a divorce were always limited to the property rights of the injured spouse or those claiming under the injured spousewhich induced property settlements in appropriate cases -perhaps the American people would be content to blunder along with the problem as it has in the past. 

It is a matter of public concern, however, when it appears that a spouse who has obtained such a divorce and remarries, may be convicted and imprisoned for bigamy or adultery, and the children of such remarriage bastardized by such proceedings. It is not likely that this problem will be solved by the voluntary adoption of a uniform divorce law. Some states are as unreasonable in their opposition to the granting of a divorce, as are other states in the opposite extreme, and it is unlikely that the latter would voluntarily relinquish what has become a lucrative enterprise. There are other obstacles in the path of such voluntary state legislation. Pennsylvania, for example, is just as positive in its opposition to alimony.104 The solution to this problem may be found

in an effort by Congress, under the present constitution, to more clearly prescribe the legal effect of judgments obtained in the several states, or in a constitutional amendment which would authorize the Congress either to adopt a uniform divorce law, or establish standards for the basis of state legislation.

CHAPTER II  Part 1. Minor Judiciary 

Sec. 37. Philadelphia Magistrates. Courts having the least civil jurisdiction in Pennsylvania are presided over by magistrates in the City of Philadelphia. The constitution authorizes a magistrate's court for each thirty thousand inhabitants, of police and civil causes, with jurisdiction in civil cases not exceeding one hundred dollars, each court to be presided over by a magistrate whose term of office shall be six years.¹ The Act of 19272 established twenty-eight such courts, the location of each to be fixed by the City Council. Under this act magistrates are ex-officio justices of the peace and enjoy all the jurisdiction vested in such office, except that civil jurisdiction is limited to cases not exceeding one hundred dollars instead of three hundred dollars. Each magistrate receives an annual salary of $5,000, the chief magistrate $6,000. A certain number are designated as committing magistrates at the several police stations in the city, but without additional compensation.

Sec. 38. Reform Measures. In years past the Phil adelphia magistrates have periodically fallen into disrepute. Various shameful practices in these courts having come to the attention of the legislature in 1937, a reform measure was adopted establishing from ten to fifteen divisional police courts, and one court of civil causes to be composed of three magistrates sitting as a civil division at City Hall. The provision for but one civil court for the entire city was found to be unconstitutional, but the sections of the statute dealing with criminal reform were upheld. Sec. 39. Justices of the Peace. The next courts of rank exercising civil jurisdiction are presided over by justices of the peace. As authorized by the constitution, these officers are elected in the various political units and commissioned by the Governor for a term of six years.' 

The Act of 18398 provides that two such officers shall be elected for each township, each borough not divided into wards, and each ward in a borough. The same act also authorizes the election of two aldermen for each ward in a city, but the office of alderman in the City of Philadelphia was abolished by constitutional amendment in 1909. The Act of 187410 abolished the office of justice of the peace in cities of the third class, and substitutes one alderman for each ward, with the same jurisdiction as justices of the peace. Each justice must reside within the district for which he is commissioned," but has jurisdiction throughout the county.

Sec. 41. Criminal Jurisdiction. The jurisdiction of justices of the peace varies somewhat in the several counties, and this discussion will be limited to such regulations as are uniform throughout the commonwealth. A summary offense is an offense which is punishable without a jury trial. The Act of 192916 provides that where an act of assembly defines an offense and renders it punishable upon summary conviction, but without conferring jurisdiction upon any court, such jurisdiction shall be exercised by any magistrate, alderman, or justice of the peace within the county in which any such offense is committed. Justices also exercise the same jurisdiction in all actions of debt or penalty for the breach of ordinances and regulations of cities, townships or boroughs," and in suits for such penalties.18 In all other criminal

Sec. 42. Appeals from Convictions. An appeal from the conviction of a summary offense is not a matter of right. The constitution provides that in all cases of summary conviction either party may appeal to such court of record as may be prescribed by law, but only upon an allowance of the court upon cause shown.19 The legislature has designated the court of quarter sessions to entertain appeals from summary convictions, and the court of common pleas in suits for penalties.20 The constitution confers upon the latter court the power to issue a writ of certiorari, commanding the lower court to remit the record for review.21 In an appeal upon cause shown, or where a case is removed to the court of quarter sessions under the Motor Vehicle Code, the court hears the case de novo (on its merits) and enters such judgment as may be proper and right.22 Where a case is reviewed by the court of common pleas on a writ of certiorari, the court determines the regularity of the proceedings before the justice of the peace and may sustain or set aside the judgment.23

Sec. 44. Uniform Responsibility Act. Pennsylvania adopted the Uniform Motor Responsibility Act in 1945.25 

While this act falls short of a requirement of financial responsibility prior to the happening of an accident, it is a decided improvement on earlier legislation. The social implication of the act is the catastrophe of having one's automobile registration and driver's license suspended upon the happening of an accident, pending satisfaction of damages that may be voluntarily acknowledged or established through litigation. Following is the substance of this legislation: (1) No suspension is authorized where the owner or operator carries a policy of liability insurance of not less than $5,000 covering bodily injury or death of any one person, and a total of not less than $10,000 covering two or more of such persons, and not less than $1,000 covering the destruction of property of others (or 

24 Act of April 28, 1943, P. L. 111, 75 PS 741. 

25 Act of June 1, 1945, P. L. 1340, 75 PS 1277.1.

any other form of liability insurance policy or bond sufficient to cover damages resulting from an accident), or who is a qualified self-insurer, or who is the only person injured or damaged in such accident, or whose automobile was legally parked at the time of the accident, or was being operated without his permission. (2) Otherwise, within 60 days after a report of an accident which has resulted in bodily injury or death or damage to property of any one person in excess of $50, the Secretary of Revenue shall suspend the license of each operator, and the registration of each owner, upon ten days notice, unless such operator or owner or both shall deposit security in a sum sufficient in his judgment to satisfy any judgment for damages resulting from such accident. This security may be $11,000 in cash or in legal investment securities, or the bond of a surety company, or the bond of two individual sureties owning real estate having equities equal in value to twice the amount of the bond, the real estate to be approved by a judge of a court of record. (3) The license will be restored upon the filing of such security, or if, within a period of one year, no action for damages has been instituted. Otherwise the suspension will continue unless a person who would otherwise have to file security, has been released from liability, or has been finally adjudicated not to be liable, or has executed a warrant for confession of judgment payable when and in such instalments as the parties have agreed to, or has executed a duly acknowledged written agreement providing for the payment of an agreed amount in installments with respect to all claims for injuries or damages resulting from the accident, or is authorized to pay a judgment by instalments as approved by the court. The act contemplates that there shall be no default in the payment of such instalments. (4) A discharge in bankruptcy does not relieve the judgment. debtor from any of the requirements of the act. (5) Where a suspension results from a conviction of any laws of the commonwealth, proof of financial responsibility is required before the license may be renewed, and not then until permitted under the motor vehicle laws of the state.

Sec. 46. Civil Jurisdiction-Torts. The nature of. 

torts will be considered in the following chapter. The 

Motor Vehicle Code provides that an action for damages arising from the operation of a motor vehicle may be brought before a justice of the peace, if the damage is not more than $100, and if the plaintiff has had the damage repaired and produces a receipted bill properly sworn to by the party making the repairs.28 Plaintiff must show that the damage resulted from defendant's negligence, and that he was free of contributory negligence. More broadly, the Act of 1879, supra, provides that justices of the peace shall have jurisdiction of all actions of trespass and trover, wherein the sum demanded does not exceed $300. An earlier statute provided that justices of the peace should not exercise civil jurisdiction in actions of ejectment or replevin, or actions of trespass for slander, personal assault and battery, wounding or maiming, or for false imprisonment."

Some confusion has resulted, but it has been held in recent years that the Act of 1879 is broad enough to include actions in trespass for injury done or committed on real or personal estates, and for personal injuries where the injury is direct and immediate. 29 Knautt v. Sec. 47. Qualities of Civil Judgments. A judgment of a justice of the peace is final where the amount is not more than $5.33.31 Such a judgment, or a judgment unappealed from, has all the qualities of a judgment of a court of record, and becomes a lien against the real estate of the defendant when filed in the office of the prothonotary.32 It may also be transferred to a county where the defendant may reside or can be found. If the judg ment debtor enters bail absolute, he is entitled to a stay of execution of three months where the judgment is not more than $20; six months where the judgment is not more than $60; and nine months where the judgment is not more than $300; except judgments obtained for wages of manual labor. A stay of execution, however, may be waived by contract.35

Sec. 51. Judicial Districts. In order to carry out the formal administration of the law, the entire state has been apportioned into judicial districts. The constitution provides that whenever a county shall contain forty thousand inhabitants, it shall constitute a separate district and that other counties may be formed into a single district or attached to contiguous districts.59 

Fifty-eight such districts have been established. There are sixty-seven counties in the commonwealth. As a consequence, two and in one instance three counties have been placed within one judicial district. Pursuant to the provisions of the constitution, the legislature has established a court of common pleas," a court of quarter sessions, a juvenile court, a court of oyer and terminer, 65 and an orphans' court,66 for each county. In

Philadelphia County there are seven courts of common pleas. The constitution requires the election of at least one president judge for each district, who shall be learned in the law, and who shall preside over all of the foregoing courts, so that in a district having but one judge learned in the law, he journeys from one county to another within the district, and convenes all of these courts within each county. 63 64 67 68 69

Sec. 53. Lay Judges. A century ago an associate judge for each county, not learned in the law, was found to be quite useful where the law judge had to travel from one county to another on circuit. As indicated in the reports, "their local knowledge has been found to be an essential aid in adjusting questions relating to the value of property, to appointments of minor officers, to bail, and to the selection of viewers, appraisers and inquests in the orphans' court and in the court of quarter sessions." 7 The Act of 1834" authorized one law judge and two associate judges for each court of common pleas except Philadelphia. Under the present constitution the office is abolished in counties forming separate judicial districts,75 and by amendment in 1909 the term of office is six years. The salary is $5 per day, but not less than $600 per annum, and mileage." The chief function of associate judges is to act in an advisory capacity. They may not decide questions of law,78 but may outvote the president judge on questions of fact." 73

It derived its name by hearing the causes of "common people" according to the principles of the common law, but as noted heretofore it now enjoys certain prescribed powers in equity. It has jurisdiction of "all pleas, actions and suits, and causes, civil, personal, real and mixed," in law or in equity, under the constitution and

Sec. 56. Suits against the Commonwealth. It is elementary that a sovereign state may not be sued by one of its citizens without its consent. This does not mean that the commonwealth may never be sued. The consti tution provides that, "Suits may be brought against the commonwealth in such manner, in such courts, and in such cases as the legislature may by law direct." Before

Sec. 57. Political Subdivisions. What has been said of the Commonwealth applies generally to its political subdivisions such as counties; townships, and school districts, and even municipal corporations such as cities and boroughs, in the discharge of purely governmental functions which the sovereign state has imposed upon them, unless some duty or obligation has been authorized by statute. Municipal corporations are liable "for wrongful acts done in what is termed their private or corporate character, and from which they derive some special or immediate advantage or emolument, but not as to such acts done in their public capacity as governing agencies, in the discharge of duties imposed for the public or general (not corporate) benefit." 88 Counties may be sued in the name of the county, but only where 

86 Collins V. Com., 262 Pa. 572 (1919). 

87 Act of June 26, 1939, P. L. 1081, 72 PS 4651-1. 

88 Kelley v. Cumberland County, 229 

Pa. 289 (1910).

this liability has been imposed. In 1929, plaintiff and his wife brought suit against Lackawanna County for personal injuries and for the loss of an automobile, alleged to have been caused by the negligent operation of a truck by an employee of the county. The trial court was obliged to enter a compulsory nonsuit because such liability had not been imposed at that time.90 Such liability is now imposed by the Act of 193791 upon every county, city, borough, incorporated town, or township, in the operation of a motor vehicle or fire department equipment, including fire department equipment used by or belonging to a volunteer fire company. 

Hartness v. Allegheny County, 349 Pa. 248 (1944). Plaintiff, a pedestrian on the sidewalk in front of the County Court House in Pittsburgh, was struck by a mass of snow and ice which fell from the roof of that building, and brought suit against Allegheny County to recover damages for the injuries he sustained. In approving a compulsory non-suit, it was said by STERN, J.: "The immunity from liability which exists when governmental functions are exercised is especially proclaimed and enforced in the case of such quasi-corporate entities as poor districts, school districts, and counties. The Commonwealth itself is not liable for the torts of its employes in the absence of a statute expressing or implying such liability, and counties are largely invested with the same immunity because they are practically nothing more than administrative units which constitute parts of the machinery making up the public system; they are political subdivisions of the State, not municipal corporations. It is true that, although the construction and maintenance of bridges and public roads is a governmental function, counties are held liable for accidents resulting from negligence in repairing and maintaining them. This exception to the general rule has been ascribed to the existence of statutory mandates which impose upon counties the duty to keep their bridges and roads in repair. . .

The primary function of the court of quarter sessions is to serve as a judicial agency in the administration of the regulatory and criminal laws of the commonwealth. In other words, it was established by the state for its own purposes, and not for the use of private litigants. It has jurisdiction to take recognizances and obligations in the name of the commonwealth; to hear and determine violations of the regulatory laws of the commonwealth and impose the fines, penalties, or punishments therefor; and to adjudicate all crimes, misdemeanors and offenses except where the court of oyer and terminer has been given exclusive jurisdiction. Sec. 60. Court of Oyer and Terminer. The court of oyer and terminer has exclusive jurisdiction to try and punish all persons charged with murder, manslaughter, treason, sodomy, buggery, rape, robbery, arson, mayhem, burglary, a woman charged with concealing the death of an illegitimate child, persons charged with the second or subsequent offense of receiving, harboring or concealing any robber, burglar, felon or thief, or with receiving or buying any goods or chattels knowing the same to have been stolen ;95 and kidnapping with intent to extort money." The constitution provides that judges of the Supreme Court shall, by virtue of their office, be justices of oyer and terminer, but the jurisdiction is seldom exercised. 96 97

Part 4. State Appellate Courts 

Sec. 63. Superior Court. Pennsylvania has two appellate courts whose jurisdiction extends throughout the commonwealth. The Superior Court was created by the legislature in 1895.110 It is composed of seven judges, elected for a term of ten years, four of whom constitute a quorum.¹¹¹ The judges receive an annual salary of $18,000, the president judge $18,500.112 The court has authority to hold its sessions at Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Harrisburg, Scranton, or Williamsport.113 The office of president judge is determined by continuous .length of service on the court, and if two members have the same priority they must cast lots.114 The Act of 

1941115 confers upon the court power to issue writs of mandamus and prohibition to courts of inferior jurisdiction, in addition to the writ of habeas corpus, within the scope of its appellate jurisdiction. The primary function of the court is to assist the Supreme Court in the disposition of the less important cases. It has final appellate jurisdiction in civil controversies of less than $2,500, exclusive of costs, except cases authorized or defended by the Attorney General;116 judgments of the courts of quarter sessions except cases involving the right to public office;117 judgments of the courts of oyer and terminer except cases of felonious homicide;118 proceedings for divorce and joint appeals by labor claimants;

Sec. 64. Supreme Court. The constitution provides that the Supreme Court shall consist of seven members, to be elected for a term of twenty-one years, who shall not be again eligible, and that the senior member in point of service shall be chief justice.122 If two judges are elected at the same time they must cast lots for priority of commission.123 All other judges in Pennsylvania are eligible for reëlection. The justices receive an annual salary of $20,000, the chief justice $20,500.124 

A majority constitutes a quorum.125 For purposes of administration the counties are apportioned among three districts, eastern, middle and western.126 The constitution confers original jurisdiction on the court in cases of injunction where a corporation is a party defendant, of habeas corpus, of mandamus to courts of inferior jurisdiction, and of quo warranto as to all officers whose jurisdiction extends over the state. 127 The court exercises appellate jurisdiction in civil controversies involving more than $2,500, exclusive of costs; cases authorized or defended by the Attorney General;128 cases involving the right to public office;129 cases involving felonious homicide;130 and cases of disbarment.131 Unless waived by agreement,' an appeal may be taken from the Superior to the Supreme Court where the jurisdiction of the Superior Court is in issue, or if the case involves the construction or application of the state or federal constitution, or if an appeal is specially allowed by the Superior Court or by any one justice of the Supreme Court.133 132
