Sec. 133. Double Jeopardy. The constitution of 

Pennsylvania provides that "No person shall for the same offense, be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb... " 132

In giving effect to this prohibition the legislature has defined the circumstances under which a defendant in a criminal prosecution may appeal from the evidence or rulings of the trial court, subject to the possibility of another trial, and has sharply limited the right of appeal by the commonwealth, including convictions of summary offenses, a matter which greatly enlarges the responsibility of the trial judge. 

Com. v. Obenreder, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 253 (1941). Three defendants were tried and acquitted in the Court of Quarter Sessions on charges of unlawful speeding under the Motor Vehicle Code. 

The commonwealth then attempted to appeal on the ground that the trial judge had erred in refusing to receive certain evidence relative to the accuracy of the speedometer used to time the speed of the defendant's respective motor vehicles. KELLER, P. J. "It is well settled in this State that the Commonwealth cannot appeal from a judgment of acquittal in criminal prosecutions, except in cases of nuisance, forcible entry and detainer, and forcible detainer. And this is so whether the prosecution be by indictment; or by summary proceeding. And if the former, it does not matter whether the verdict be rendered by the jury of its own accord or by direction of the court. Such a verdict or judgment of acquittal is not to be confused with the quashing of an indictment, or an 

131 Act of June 24, 1939, P. L. 872, 18 PS 4101. 

132 Article 1, section 10.

arrest of judgment following a verdict of guilty, or a judgment sustaining a demurrer to the evidence, which raise only questions of law and do not result in a verdict of not guilty or judgment of acquittal, and accordingly in those cases, the Commonwealth may appeal."

Sec. 134. Parole and Probation. There is a dis tinction between parole and probation, although the two are sometimes confused. A parole is a conditional release from actual imprisonment. Probation is a conditional release after the determination of guilt but before imprisonment. It is, in effect, a suspension of the sentence. The Act of 1911 133 provides that when any person has been convicted in any court of any crime, except murder, administering poison, kidnapping, incest, sodomy, buggery, rape, assault and battery with intent to ravish, arson, robbery, or burglary, and has never been imprisoned for crime (detention in a juvenile institution, and summary offenses excluded), and where the court believes that the public good does not require imprisonment, the court may suspend the sentence and place the defendant on probation upon such terms and conditions as may be right and proper. While this statute does not employ the words "court of record," the practical effect of the statute, in conjunction with the appointment and compensation of probation officers, is to confine the probationary power to courts of quarter sessions, oyer and terminer, the Municipal Court of Philadelphia, and the Allegheny County Court. The minor judiciary have occasionally placed defendants under the supervision of social agencies. The power of the minor judiciary to suspend sentence under this statute does not appear to have been decided by the appellate courts. 

133 Act of June 19, 1911, P. L. 1055, 19 PS 1051.

CHAPTER IV  

Seriousness of Intent

Part 1. 

Sec. 135. Function of Court and Jury. The making of a contract is the act of the parties to it, not of the law. "It is but to repeat a legal aphorism to say that it is primarily the object of our laws and of the courts who administer them, not to make contracts for individuals who are sui juris, but to interpret and enforce those which such individuals make for themselves." ¹ 

In the absence of ambiguity the legal effect of a contract is always a question for the court. It is the function of the jury to resolve disputed questions of fact. It has been said that if no such dispute exists, "there is nothing for them to do." 2 On the other hand if there is competent evidence to sustain a finding of fact which must necessarily be determined by the jury, it is not within the province of the court to decide otherwise. 

Briefly, the court decides questions of law. The jury decides questions of fact. 

Theiss v. Weiss, 166 Pa. 9 (1895). GREEN, J. "The defendant in this case unfortunately and most unwisely put his name to a written proposition, and while it is manifest that he did so while considerably under the influence of liquor, it is very plain that he knew perfectly well what he was doing, and that he was not impelled to affix his signature by any act of fraud, deceit, imposition, mistake or undue influence. . . . But of course all of these things were matters for the consideration of the jury, and it is out of our power to change the verdict, no matter what we may think of the effect of the testimony." 

Sec. 136. Jests and Banter. The first principle in the making of contracts is that of seriousness of intent. 

An apparent agreement may be defective in this respect for various reasons. "A man is not to be snapped up for an unintended proposition made when he has no 

1 Rogers v. Toland, 43 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 248 (1910). 

2 Elliott v. Wanamaker, 155 Pa. 67 (1893). 107

reason to suppose anybody wants to accept what he pro poses. When people meet to do business they are presumed to mean what they propose, and expect to be taken up; but a proposition made and accepted where no expectation of contracting exists" should be "carefully weighed with all the circumstances when the question of assent at the time comes to be questioned." " 3 Armstrong v. McGhee, Addison 261 (1795). Armstrong appearing disgusted with a valuable horse that after a hard ride seemed jaded and lame, offered him for sale to several persons for a trifle, and to McGhee for five pounds. McGhee agreed, and by Armstrong's direction took the horse home his stable. At the time some supposed Armstrong in jest. He said so himself afterwards, and demanded the horse back, as supposing McGhee understood him to have been in jest. Upon McGhee's refusal, the jury awarded eight pounds damages. In sustaining the verdict, it was said by the PRESIDENT JUDGE: "If McGhee gave Armstrong ground to believe that he considered this contract-which, to all appearance, is a complete one as a mere sham or jest, conveying no right, he must take it as he then gave signs that he understood it, and remain a mere trustee to Armstrong, and bound to deliver up the horse when required." 

Sec. 137. Explosions of Wrath. For the same reason expressed above, an explosion of wrath is not to be understood as a manifestation of assent to enter into an enforceable contract. 

Higgins v. Lessig, 49 Ill. App. 459 (1893). Defendant was the owner of a set of old double harness, worth perhaps $15, which had been carried away by a man named Red John Smith, who had been adjudged insane. The evidence showed that he was much excited at the time. Plaintiff's version of what he said was, "I will give $100 to any man who will find out who the thief is, and I will give a lawyer $100 for prosecuting him," using rough language and epithets concerning the thief. He also asserted that he would not have a second-class lawyer. Plaintiff brought himself within the terms of the so-called offer. CARTWRIGHT, J. "This language was in the nature of an explosion of wrath against some supposed thief who had stolen the harness, and was coupled with boasting and bluster about the prosecution of the thief. It was indicative of a state of excitement so out of proportion to the supposed cause of it, that it should be regarded rather as the ex- 

3 Brown V. Finney, 53 Pa. 373 (1866).

travagant exclamation of an excited man than as manifesting an intention to contract." Gratuities. 

Sec. 138. Gratuities. A gratuity, without condition, and in the absence of circumstances indicating a fraudulent design on the part of the beneficiary, imposes no obligation on either party, and particularly where services are voluntarily performed without a view or expectancy of compensation. Members of society are constantly performing favors, social work, and help in times of emergency, but these, and so-called gentlemen's agreements, are social and not contractual obligations. 

To such persons the law applies the term "volunteer." 

Bartholomew v. Jackson, 20 Johns. 28 (1822). Plaintiff was desirous of burning the stubble on his wheat field, on which was a stack of wheat belonging to the defendant. The latter was away from home, but his son said that the wheat would be removed by ten o'clock the next morning. When that time arrived plaintiff set fire to the stubble at the far end of the field, but it spread rapidly, and in order to save the wheat the plaintiff removed it himself. He instituted this action to recover for this work. 

PRATT, J. "The plaintiff performed the service without privity or request of the defendant, and there was in fact no promise, expressed or implied. If a man humanely bestows his labor, and even risks his life in voluntarily aiding to preserve his neighbor's, house from destruction by fire, the law considers the service rendered as gratuitous and it therefore forms no ground of action." 

Sec. 139. Nature of Estoppel. Under some circum stances a person will be held to the obligations of a contract whether he entered into a contract or not. Such a situation would arise whenever one party is led to give valuable services, or part with valuable property, in the belief that the other party is in earnest. Conduct of this sort raises what is called an estoppel. 

Hill v. Epley, 31 Pa. 331 (1858). STRONG, J. "The general principle now is, that where the conduct of a party has been such as to induce action by another, he shall be precluded from afterwards asserting, to the prejudice of that other, the contrary of that of which his conduct has induced the belief. The primary ground of the doctrine is, that it would be a fraud in a party to assert what his previous conduct had denied, when on the faith of

that denial others have acted. The element of fraud is essential, either in the intention of the party estopped, or in the effect of the evidence which he attempts to set up." 

It has been said more recently that, "An estoppel exists where one by his words or conduct causes another to believe in the existence of a state of facts, inducing reliance thereon in some act of mutual concern, and the inducing person wishes to assert, prejudicially, facts in opposition to those first held out to be true, on which action was taken." This may not be done.* 

This may not be done.* "All estoppels," said SHARSWOOD, "shut the mouth of the party, because it would be a fraud in him to speak, whether his original act or declaration was intended to deceive or not.” 5

Waters' Appeal, 35 Pa. 523 (1860). WOODWARD, J. "Estoppels are sustained to exclude the truth. It is called an estoppel or conclusion, says Lord COKE, because a man's own act or acceptance stoppeth or closeth up his mouth to allege the truth."

Sec. 140. Elements of Estoppel. It is an essential element of equitable estoppel that the person invoking it has been influenced by and has justifiably relied on the representation or conduct of the person sought to be estopped." 

Plate v. Durst, 42 West Virginia 68 (1898). When plaintiff was about twelve years of age she went to live in the home of her brother-in-law. She assisted in the home, helped the defendant in his store, attended to customers, and did whatever else the exigencies of the business and her own capacities from time to time suggested. She never received or demanded any pay for her services, but sometime prior to her majority the defendant, influenced by a transient feeling of gratitude, promised her that when she had been with him ten years he would give her $1,000. His defense was, when called upon to meet this obligation, that he was not in earnest, but jesting. DENT, J. "It must be admitted, in any view of the matter, that thi was jesting on a very serious subject to this unfortunate and parentless young girl,-still in the eyes of the law, an infant,-engaged early and late, weekdays and Sundays, 4 Fedas v. Insurance Co. of Pa., 300

5 Kirk v. Hartman & Co., 63 Pa. 97 (1869). 

Gianni v. Union Bank & Trust Co., 311 Pa. 121 (1933).

at home and abroad, actively, earnestly, and faithfully endeavoring to promote the worldly interests of the defendant. Jokes are sometimes taken seriously by the young and inexperienced in the deceptive ways of the business world, and if such is the case, and thereby the person deceived is led to give valuable services in the full belief and expectation that the joker is in earnest, the law will also take the joker at his word, and give him good reason to smile."

Part 2. Certainty of Contracts Sec. 141. Executory Agreements. In addition to seriousness of intent, contracts must be sufficiently definite in terms so that the promises and performances to be rendered are reasonably certain. An executory agreement must be certain and explicit, either within itself or by reference to some other agreement or matter. The following precedent has been cited in this and in other jurisdictions. 

Raffles v. Wichelhaus, 2 Eng. Rep. 375 (1864). Defendant agreed to purchase 125 bales of Surat cotton to be shipped from Bombay to Liverpool on the "Peerless." There were two ships bearing the same name, one of which sailed from Bombay in October and the other in December. Defendant refused to accept the cotton which arrived on the latter, and his counsel argued on demurrer, "There is nothing on the face of the contract to show that any particular ship called the "Peerless" was meant, but the moment it appears that two ships called the "Peerless" were about to sail from Bombay there is a latent ambiguity, and parol evidence may be given for the purpose of showing that the defendant meant one "Peerless" and the plaintiff another. That being so, there was no concensus ad idem, and therefore no binding contract." He was then stopped by the Court, saying, PER CURIAM, "there must be judgment for the defendants."

Sec. 142. Ambiguous Agreements. The following promises have been held to be too indefinite to be enforced: A promise made by a decedent in his lifetime, in consideration of services to be rendered, to provide at his death for the person rendering such services, and to give her "a portion of his estate."" A promise by a 

7 Wall's Appeal, 111 Pa. 460 (1886).

landlord to reduce the rent without naming the amount of the reduction." A promise made by a heavy stockholder to an officer of a corporation that if any profit was made out of the business he would divide it upon a very liberal basis. A promise to repurchase certain shares of stock where no price was fixed at which the shares were to be repurchased.10 A promise by a street railway company to employ a disabled employee the rest of his life at $1.50 per day. As observed by the Court, "employed at what?" ¹¹

Seiss v. McClintic-Marshall Corp., 324 Pa. 201 (1986). Plaintiff was injured while in the employ of the defendant as a fitter, and was confined in a hospital for several weeks. This was prior to the effective date of the Workmen's Compensation Act. He alleged that in consideration of his refraining from bringing suit against his employer to recover damages for his injuries, the defendant agreed to employ him at suitable employment, or such work as he was able to do, for the rest of his life. He continued to work for the defendant as a fitter until 1929, when he alleged the work became too hard and defendant refused him suitable employment. SCHAFFER, J. "The contract here set up is so lacking in precision, so indefinite and vague that nothing certain about it can be formulated. . . . What is 'suitable employment'? Who is to determine what it is? What is implied by 'any employment that I was able to do'? Without more, these words are too indefinite to predicate anything upon with certainty. . . In any employment contract if the rate of pay is uncertain it will not be enforced."

Sec. 144. Future Contingencies. There are many circumstances, of course, where the consideration, as measured in terms of money, may be contingent upon the happening of future events, or costs to be incurred. 

Such agreements are enforceable on the basis of the standard which the parties have agreed upon. 

Compton's Estate, 30 Pa. Superior Ct. 605 (1906). Two sons agreed that if one of them would take their aged father into his home, the other would pay his share of support and maintenance. 

HENDERSON, J. "It is evident that it might have been in the contemplation of the parties that the sum would vary with the age and physical condition of the father. Medical services and nursing might be required at times and not at other times and the amount was not improperly left for determination according to the varying conditions. The pith of the contract is the agreement to pay and in the absence of a sum named the value of the thing rendered will be implied."

In a contract of hiring, where no definite period has been agreed upon, it will be presumed that the employment may be terminated by either party at any time. 

This is known as a hiring at will. But it has been held that where the contract fixed a stated salary per year, 12 Weaver V. Wood, 9 Pa. 220

Sec. 145. Conditional Promises. Many business men, manufacturers in particular, contract for supplies in advance, leaving the amounts to be purchased open for future determination, in order to contract for future sales of the finished product. A conditional agreement of this sort may be enforced if it is reasonably certain and imposes a mutuality of obligation. A promise by one party to buy from another all of a certain material that he may want, order or desire during the year, at a fixed price per unit, is defective for lack of mutuality. 

He may want nothing at all. 

Bailey v. Austrian, 19 Minn. 535 (1873). BERRY, J. "... the engagement of plaintiffs was to purchase all of said pig iron, which they might want in their said business during the time specified; but they do not engage to want any quantity whatever. They do not even engage to continue their business. If they see fit to discontinue it on the very day on which the supposed agreement is entered into, they are at entire liberty to do so at their own option, and, whatever might have been defendant's expectation, he is without remedy."

But a like promise to buy all such material that one party might need in his business is enforceable, if the need can be objectively ascertained. As said by our 

Supreme Court: ""That a contract for the sale or purchase of a commodity, the quantity to be delivered or received to be measured by the output or requirements of an established place of business, is not void for indefiniteness or lack of mutuality, is too well settled to be open to serious question.' " 17

Sec. 146. Executed Contracts. In all executory contracts for the sale of goods or the rendition of services, a reasonably definite understanding as to the consideration to be paid, whether it be money or anything else, is essential. But where such contracts are exe.

Co., 223 Pa. 160 (1909).

cuted, if the consideration agreed upon is too indefinite to be enforced, the parties are relegated to a recovery in quantum valebant, for as much as the goods are reasonably worth, or in quantum meruit, for as much as the services are reasonably worth. Compensation was not denied in the following case, inasmuch as valuable services had been rendered under a promise that such services should be compensated. This would justify a recovery in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of the services, although the consideration agreed upon was so indefinite as to be unenforceable. 

Sherman v. Kitsmiller, 17 S. & R. 45 (1827). George Sherman, deceased, promised the plaintiff, his niece, that if she would keep house for him until his death he would give her one hundred acres of land. DUNCAN, J. "One hundred acres on the Rocky Mountain, or in the Conestoga Manor-one hundred acres in the mountain of Hanover County, Virginia, or in the Conewango rich lands of Adams County-one hundred acres of George Sherman's mansion place at eighty dollars per acre, or one hundred acres of his barren lands at five dollars? This vague and void promise, incapable of specific execution, because it has nothing specific in it, would not prevent the plaintiff from recovering in a quantum meruit for the value of this young woman's services. . .”

Part 3. The Offer 

Sec. 147. Offeror and Offeree. In order to constitute a contract there must be an offer and an acceptance, express or implied. The person who makes an offer is called the offeror. The person who accepts the offer without qualification is called the offeree. If the person to whom an offer is made replies with a counteroffer, or modifies the offer by suggesting new terms, he becomes the offeror. In other words, this title shifts between the parties until some proposition has been finally accepted as made. In other branches of the law the parties are designated as the promisor and promisee, vendor and vendee, grantor and grantee, lessor and lessee, mortgagor and mortgagee, payor and payee, endorsor and endorsee, transferor and transferee, assignor

and assignee, and obligor and obligee, by reference to the subject under consideration. This also serves as an additional convenience by designating the person who initiates or does a thing from the person who accepts or acquiesces in what is proposed or done. 

Sec. 148. Preliminary Negotiations. Preliminary negotiations, indefinite in character, should be distinguished from offers. A man has a right to make inquiry, or to ask a question, without subjecting himself to liability if his question is answered. If he is indebted to a bank and writes to the board of directors, asking them whether they would permit him to surrender enough of his stock to pay the debt, an affirmative reply would be an answer to his inquiry. It would not create a contract. Some one has to open the negotiations, and unless both parties are sufficiently well informed with respect to the business practices of each other, it is seldom that either one of them has sufficient information in his possession to formulate a definitive offer. 

Upsal Street Realty Co. v. Rubin, 326 Pa. 327 (1937). Plaintiff received from the defendant an application, on the usual form, for the lease of a certain apartment. The term applied for was twentyone months at a total rental of $3,465. The application stated that the apartment was to be redecorated throughout to tenants selection, the selection of colors to be made after the lease was signed. Plaintiff accepted this application and had a lease prepared, but defendant changed his mind and refused to sign it. In sustaining the conclusion that these negotiations did not constitute a contract, it was said by MAXEY, J. "Practically all the terms customarily found in leases, except the tenure and rental, were omitted from the application. . . It is not unusual for persons to agree to negotiate with the view of entering into contractual relations and to reach an accord at once as to certain major items of the proposed contract and then later find that on other details they cannot agree. In such a case no contract results." 

Sec. 149. Window Displays. It is commonly supposed that the display of an article in a show window with the price attached is an offer. That is a mistake.

It would be incongruous that several persons should

enter the store and demand it from as many clerks, or subject the proprietor to as many law suits for his failure or inability to meet the demand. A window display of this sort is merely informative, and is designed to solicit offers from those who might be interested in the purchase of the goods at the prices indicated. The fact that such displays are nearly always made in good faith is immaterial. It is elementary that a person may determine with whom he will contract.

Sec. 150. Business Circulars. Business circulars are likewise informative and are not intended to be more than preliminary negotiation leading to the formation of contracts. 

Moulton v. Kershaw, 59 Wisconsin 316 (1884). Defendants wrote as follows: "In consequence of a rupture in the salt trade, we are authorized to offer Michigan fine salt, in full car-load lots of eighty to ninety-five bbls., delivered at your city at 85c per bbl., to be shipped per C. & N. W. R. R. Co. only. At this price it is a bargain, as the price in general remains unchanged. Shall be pleased to receive your order." Plaintiff replied, ordering two thousand barrels. TAYLOR, J. "The only question presented is whether the appellants' letter, and the telegram sent by the respondent in reply thereto, constitute a contract for the sale of 2,000 barrels of Michigan fine salt by the appellants to the respondent at the price named in such letter. . . The language is not such as a business man would see in making an offer to sell to an individual a definite amount of property. . . It is clearly in the nature of an advertisement or business circular, to attract the attention of those interested in that business to the fact that good bargains in salt could be had by applying to them, and not as an offer by which they were to be bound, if accepted, for any amount the persons to whom it was addressed might see fit to order. We think the complaint fails to show any contract.

Sec. 151. Advertisements. The great bulk of adver tising matter has no more significance than business circulars. An offer may be advertised, but other than offers of reward it would have to be distinguished from the great bulk of advertising matter. If a merchant advertised a sale of men's suits and offered them at half price to the first ten persons entering his store on the

~^^~ day of the sale, this would probably be construed as an offer, but not so a mere announcement of a sale at half price. Offers of reward for the return of lost property and the like are frequently definite enough to be accepted without further negotiation. 

Carlill v. The Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., (1893) 1 Q. B. 256. The following advertisement appeared in the Pall Mall Gazette: "£100 reward will be paid by the Carbolic Smoke Ball Company to any person who contracts the increasing epidemic influenza, colds, or any disease caused by taking cold, after having used the ball three times daily for two weeks according to the printed directions supplied with each ball. £1000 is deposited with the Alliance Bank,

Regent Street, shewing our sincerity in the matter." Defendant contended that this was a mere puff or proclamation. LINDLEY, L. 

J. "It seems to me that in order to arrive at a right conclusion we must read this advertisement in its plain meaning, as the public would understand it. . . And it seems to me that the way in which the public would read it would be this, that if anybody after the advertisement was published, used three times daily for two weeks the carbolic smoke ball, and then caught cold, he would be entitled to the reward." 

Sec. 152. Quotations. What has been said of business circulars and advertisements applies to quotations unless, of course, the quotation is in a context which indicates that it may be acted upon by the other party, and identifies with sufficient certainty the subject to which it applies. 

Boyers & Co. v. D. & R. Duke, (1905) 2 Irish Rep. 617. Plaintiff requested a quotation for 3,000 yards of canvas. Defendant quoted a price. Plaintiff then ordered 3,000 yards at the price quoted. O'BRIEN, L. C. J. "It is a matter of common knowledge that quotations of prices are scattered broadcast among possible customers. Wholesale dealers have not in stock an unlimited supply of the articles the prices of which they quote to the public at large... These observations seem to apply with special force to a quotation furnished by a manufacturer, in the position of the defendants, stating the terms on which he is prepared to work, as to price and time for completion. He may receive and comply with many applications for quotations on the same day. If his reply in each case can be turned into a contract by acceptance, his loom might be burdened with an amount of work which would render it impossible for him to meet his engagements."

Sec. 153. Communication of Offer. There can be no valid contract without a communication of the offer. The method employed is not important. The exercise of dominion over things that are offered for sale, accompanied by a tender of the purchase price, is a communication. The other party may accept the tender, or he may protest against the intrusion if he has not invited it. A memorandum of an offer, not communicated to another or seen by him, is of no legal significance. An offer has been communicated, however, when it is received and accepted with knowledge that an offer was intended, even though the person who receives it does not make himself acquainted with its terms. Many contracts in common use, such as deeds, mortgages, leases, judgment notes, bonds, and the like, are frequently printed in blank form. A person may not take time to read all the provisions of such a contract, and may not understand the full legal significance of all such provisions if he did, but if he signs it without reading it, or having it read to him if he himself is unable to read, or making due inquiry of any such provision which he does not fully understand, he is guilty of negligence and is bound, in the absence of fraud, by its terms. 

Com. v. Gudaitis, 323 Pa. 110 (1936). Defendant sought to avoid liability on a bond on the ground that he thought he was signing a paper relating to some stock he was purchasing. He testified that he could not read, but could sign his name. He admitted that he did not ask that the bond be read to him. 

SCHAFFER, J. "As long ago as when Shepard's Touchstone was written (1648), the law was as follows (page 56): 'If a party that is to seal the deed can read himself and doth not, or being illiterate or blind, doth not require to hear the deed read or the contents thereof declared, in these cases albeit the deed is contrary to his mind, yet it is good and unavoidable." " 

Sec. 154. Knowledge of Reward. The necessity of a communication of the offer is applied to offers of reward. Pennsylvania has a special statute directing the counties to pay a reward of $20 for the apprehension of

19 horse thieves.18 Under this statute the courts may determine who is entitled to the reward, and may single out a person who was not acquainted with its provisions. The problem of communication is not involved, however, inasmuch as all persons are presumed to know the law. In contract cases the offeree should have knowledge of the offer before performing the condition.20 

Fitch v. Snedaker, 38 New York 248 (1868). Defendant published a reward of two hundred dollars for the apprehension of the perpetrator of a crime. Plaintiffs, without knowledge of the reward, apprehended the offender and secured his conviction. 

WOODRUFF, J. "I perceive. no reason for applying to an offer of reward for the apprehension of a criminal any other rules than are applicable to any other offer by one accepted or acted upon by another, and so relied upon as constituting a contract. . . The offer could only operate upon the plaintiffs after they heard of it. . ." ... 

Sec. 155. Termination of Offer. An offer may be withdrawn at any time before it has been accepted. It will lapse if not accepted within a reasonable time, and it terminates upon the destruction of the subject matter, or insanity or death of either the offeror or the offeree, or by change of law which would render the transaction illegal, and whenever it has been rejected by the offeree. 

Beach v. First M. E. Church, 96 Illinois 177 (1880). In 1874

Dr. Lorenzo Beach signed a subscription agreement for the construction of a church. In 1875 he was adjudged insane. In 1876 the church began the construction of the building. In deciding that the offer had lapsed, it was said by DICKEY, C. J. “The insanity of Dr. Beach rendered him, in law, as incapable of making a contract, or of continuing or repeating an offer to the church, as if he had been actually dead."

Acceptance of an application for life insurance is in the actual or constructive delivery of the policy, but if the application contains a provision that the policy shall not take effect until the first premium is paid in full, delivery of the policy, without payment of the first premium, is insufficient to make the policy effective.22 

In a few states an insurance company is liable for its nepi gent delay in acting upon an application for insurance, but not in Pennsylvania.

Zayc v. John Hancock Mutual Life Ins. Co., 338 Pa. 426 (1940). 

Decedent made application with defendant for a life insurance policy in the sum of $2,000, and paid four dollars as a deposit on the first premium. He was interviewed by agents of other insurance companies, but refrained from making any other application, relying upon the promptness of defendant in accepting or rejecting the application he had made. He was accidentally killed two months later. Defendant had failed to act upon the application and no policy had been issued. This was an action in trespass by deceased's administrator, based upon the failure of defendant to act upon the application within reasonable time. PATTERSON, J. "It is the established rule in Pennsylvania, as in most jurisdictions, that mere delay, however great, in passing upon an application for insurance cannot be construed as an acceptance thereof by the insurer which will support an action ex contractu, notwithstanding payment of the premium at the time application is made. . . . It is fundamental that negligence and liability therefor cannot be predicated upon a state of facts which does not impose any legal duty."

Sec. 157. Refusal to Accept. The acceptance of an offer is entirely optional with the offeree. He may refuse to accept for any reason satisfactory to himself, or for no reason at all. It is a well established principle that as long as any condition is not agreed to by both the offeror and the offeree, the negotiations between them may be terminated by either party while they are still pending.28 Cases arise in which the offeree ac- 

21 Wilson v. McKee & McDanel, 110 

Pa. Superior Ct. 544 (1933). 

22 Shook v. New York Life Ins. Co., 

343 Pa. 185 (1941). 

23 Rich v. G. W. Pifer Sons, 100 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 483 (1930).

knowledges his inability to accept, but suggests that new terms might possibly be arranged. A communication of this sort is neither an offer nor an acceptance. It is merely an invitation to the offeror to try again. 

Slaymaker v. Irwin, 4 Wharton 369 (1839). Plaintiff sent in an order for the purchase and delivery of pig metal. Defendant explained his inability to accept the order, and suggested prices and conditions under which future deliveries could be made, but without anything specific in the nature of a counter-offer. Plaintiff sent in a second order in response to defendant's suggestions, but defendant concluded not to accept it. In deciding that these communications fell short of a contract, it was said by SARGEANT, J. "If a proposition be made by one man to another to purchase an article from him, at a certain price and on certain terms, which is accepted as offered, there is then an agreement or contract. But if, instead of accepting it, the party declines so doing, and then new terms of purchase are offered, the assent is yet to be given by the other to the terms thus varied. It is not a contract-it is the suggestion or proposal of a new subject of contract, on which the first party has again a right to pause, to consider, to accept, to reject, to suggest new terms; and all is in the meantime merely negotiation." 

Sec. 158. Qualified Acceptance. A qualified accept ance is no acceptance at all. It is well established that an acceptance must be unconditional and absolute.24 

Purported acceptances which introduce new elements, such as credit, security, price, quantity, time, and place of performance, are all counter-propositions which may be accepted or rejected by the person to whom they are made. This is one of the most important principles in the law of contracts, and it appears to be of universal application. 

Cohn v. Penn Beverage Co., 313 Pa. 349 (1934). Defendant offered to sell certain shares of stock at a fixed price, a satisfactory agreement to be executed within ten days. Plaintiff replied that he would be willing to pay ten per cent cash and the balance in sixty days. In concluding that a contract had not yet been made, it was said by FRAZER, C. J. "Of numerous reasons compelling this conclusion, it will suffice to discuss but one. The so-called acceptance materially differs from the offer as to the mode of pay- 

24 Empire Paper Box Corp. v. Hazleton Baking Co., 318 Pa. 522 (1935).

ment. No qualifications having been placed on the price named in the offer, it is presumed a cash transaction was intended. The reply, instead of agreeing unequivocally to defendant's proposition, offered to pay ten per cent cash and the balance in sixty days." 

Sec. 159. Unqualified Acceptance. It is possible for the offeree to accept an offer without qualification, and at the same time propose a more satisfactory arrangement, provided the acceptance is unconditional and absolute. 

The parties to a contract may always modify it by mutual consent,25 and a communication of this sort, if carefully drawn, would constitute an acceptance concluding the contract, and a subsequent offer to modify it. The acceptance, however, would have to be unconditional. A mere counter-offer would not accomplish that result. 

The offeree is likely to answer in this manner if he would prefer a contract on the terms originally proposed, rather than risk having no contract at all. Or if the offeror is the party who is not altogether satisfied, the offeree, in his acceptance, may suggest that if circumstances warrant, a change may be made in the future. 

Such a suggestion, however, is merely extrinsic, and has no bearing on the contract as the parties have made it 

F. A. Ames & Co. v. Pierson, 174 Pa. 597 (1896). Plaintiff ordered 3,000 sets of wheels for the year 1891. Defendant replied that the order was too big and suggested 100 sets per month. Plaintiff entered its order for that amount, whereupon defendant replied: "I will enter your order for 100 sets wheels per mont for the coming year, and if I can add to my facilities so as to enable me to do better than that, will do so." The lower court held this not to be a contract. In deciding otherwise, it was said by Mc- 

COLLUM, J. "A construction of the correspondence which denied the existence of any contractual relation between the parties appears to us to have been unwarranted and to have given to the words, 'I will do my best to serve you' an effect which was not intended or contemplated by either of them." 

Sec. 160. Effect of Counter-Offer. An offer which is refused, or which is met with a counter-offer, is at an end, unless, of course, it is subsequently reinstated by 

25 Shaffer v. Scharding, 348 Pa. 423 (1944).

the person who made it. The following is a leading 

English decision. 

Hyde v. Wrench, 49 Eng. Rep. 132 (1840). Defendant offered to sell an estate for £1,200. Plaintiff declined. Defendant then offered the estate for £1,000. Plaintiff replied offering to pay £950. Defendant refused to sell at that price. Plaintiff then agreed to pay £1,000, but the defendant concluded not to accept. 

LORD LANGDALE. "Under the circumstances stated in this bill, I think there exists no valid binding contract between the parties for the purchase of the property. The defendant offered to sell it for £1,000 and if that had been at once unconditionally accepted, there would undoubtedly have been a perfect binding contract; instead of that, the plaintiff made an offer of his own, to purchase the property for £950, and he thereby rejected the offer previously made by the defendant. I think that it was not afterwards competent for him to revive the proposal of the defendant, by tendering an acceptance of it; and that, therefore, there exists no obligation of any sort between the parties." 

The same situation appears in the following decision by the Supreme Court of the United States, except that plaintiff attempted to justify his belated acceptance on the ground that it was made within the time specified in the original offer, but this did not change the result. 

Minneapolis & St. Louis Ry. Co. v. Columbus Rolling Mill Co., 119 U. S. 149 (1886). Defendant offered to sell from 2,000 to 5,000 tons of rails at specified prices, in which plaintiff was given until the 20th of the month to accept. Plaintiff ordered 1,200 tons on the 16th. It was rejected on the 18th. He then ordered 2,000 tons on the 19th, which would have conformed to the original offer, but this was also rejected. GRAY, J. "The other party, having once rejected the offer, cannot afterwards revive it by tendering an acceptance of it. On December 18th, the defendant by telegram declined to fulfill the plaintiff's order. The negotiations between the parties were thus closed, and the plaintiff could not afterwards fall back on defendant's original offer."

Sec. 161. Statements on Letterheads. The "Re statement of the Law" acknowledges the principle that an offer on a letterhead on which is printed, "All our contracts are subject to strikes," is sufficient to make that declaration a part of the offer." It would be ad- 

20 Contracts, section 70, illus. 4,

visable to refer to it in the body of the letter in order to avoid misunderstanding and unnecessary litigation. 

It does not follow, however, that an unqualified acceptance of an offer will be nullified or construed as a counter-offer, merely because it is written on a letterhead containing that or similar expressions. 

Summers v. Hibbard, Spencer, Bartlett & Co., 153 Illinois 102 (1894). BAKER, J. "The mere fact that appellants wrote their acceptance on a blank form for letters, at the top of which were printed the words 'All sales subject to strikes and accidents,' no more made those words a part of the contract than they made the other words there printed, 'Summers Bros. & Co., Manufacturers of Box-Annealed Common and Refined Sheet-Iron,' a part of the The offer was absolute. The written acceptance which they themselves wrote was just as absolute. The printed words were not in the body of the letter or referred to therein. The fact that they were printed at the head of their letter-heads would not have the effect of preventing appellants from entering into an unconditional contract of sale." contract.

Sec. 162. Time for Acceptance. Whenever time of acceptance is made an integral part of the offer, and such is quite common, the acceptance must be made within the time specified, otherwise the offer will lapse.

If the offeror sends a telegram and requests an immediate answer, a reply two days later is too late.27 If he sends a letter and requests an answer by return mail, the acceptance must be sent by the next convenient mail. 

Groskin v. Bookmyer, 310 Pa. 588 (1933). Plaintiff entered into an agreement to purchase Florida real estate, "subject to the written approval of the owner, which must be obtained within ten days." Defendant put in evidence his copy of the original agreement, which bore his signature under date of August 18th, but admitted that he had never communicated his approval to the plaintiff. This was an action by the plaintiff to recover the hand money he had paid. In granting this relief it was said by DREW, J. "For ten days this offer was to be open, and by its terms it was to expire unless accepted within that time." 

Where no time is designated, the acceptance must be communicated within a reasonable time. This must be 

27 Childs v. Gillespie, 147 Pa. 173 (1892).

determined by the circumstances and situation of the parties. In one of the early cases decided by the Supreme Court of the United States, the defendants despatched an offer to the plaintiff for the purchase of flour, sending it by wagon from Harper's Ferry to the plaintiff at Mill Creek, and requested an answer by return wagon. Plaintiff accepted by mail, which was delayed several days. In holding that the acceptance came too late it was said by Mr. Justice WASHINGTON: "They (the defendants) could easily calculate, by the usual length of time which was employed by this wagon in traveling from Harper's Ferry to Mill Creek and back again with a load of flour, about what time they should receive the desired answer, and therefore it was entirely unimportant whether it was sent by that or another wagon, or in any other manner, provided sent to Harper's Ferry, and was not delayed beyond the time which was ordinarily employed by wagons engaged in hauling flour from the plaintiff's mill to Harper's Ferry." 28 

Huber Mfg. Co. v. Smithgall, 19 Pa. Superior Ct. 641 (1902). 

An offer for the lease of a threshing machine, made on June 10th, was accepted on July 16th. PORTER, J. "It may be said generally that an offer without more, is an offer in the present, to be accepted or refused when made. There is no time which a jury may consider reasonable or otherwise, for the party to whom it is made to consider it, except by the agreement or concession of the party making it." 

Sec. 163. Determination of Reasonable Time. What ever time is allowed for the acceptance of the offer will be governed largely by the subject of the offer and the situation of the parties. In the case of stocks and other securities, the value of which may fluctuate during any minute of the day, the time allowed for deliberation will be relatively short. In the case of real estate, which 

Blackstone indicates is the most serious of all contracts, considerable latitude is allowed for deliberation. In addition, the opportunity for speculation, in the case of real estate, is not so apparent. Goods and merchandise 

28 Eliason v. Henshaw, 4 Wheaton 225 (1819).

which are currently offered in the market, fall somewhere between these two extremes. If the parties are dealing with a commodity, the price of which changes in the market from day to day, the offeree should accept during the same business day, if the offer is received by mail, and if not, at the time the offer is made. Otherwise he would be permitted to take advantage of a change in the market price and speculate at the expense of the other party. The agency used by the parties in their communications, e. g., the telegraph, is some evidence of the urgency of the market and the necessities of the case. 

Minnesota Linseed Oil Co. v. Collier White Lead Co., 4 Dill. 

431 (1876). Plaintiff brought an action against defendant for goods sold. Defendant did not deny the obligation, but set up a counter-claim based upon a subsequent alleged contract, which he contended resulted from the following communications: On the evening of July 31, plaintiff despatched an offer by telegram. The offer was received on the morning of August 2. Defendant remained silent during that day. The subject was linseed oil, the price of which was fluctuating in the market. On the morning of 

August 3, defendant despatched a telegram of acceptance, and shortly thereafter, on the same day, received a telegram revoking the offer. NELSON, D. J. "The delay, here, was too long and manifestly unjust to the plaintiff, for it afforded the defendant an opportunity to take advantage of a change in the market and to accept or refuse the offer as would best subserve its interests." 

In an early case before the Superior Court of Pennsylvania,20 an offer for the sale of 1,000 bags of peanuts was mailed from Norfolk on April 17th. The acceptance was posted at Philadelphia on the 20th. No evidence was offered as to the time when the offer was received, or as to the frequency and time occupied in the transmission of mails between Norfolk and Philadelphia, and for this reason the agreement was upheld. 

The case announces an important principle, in substance, as follows:

What is a reasonable time for the acceptance is a question of law for the court in such commercial transactions as happen in the same way, day after day, and present the question upon the same 

29 Boyd v. Merchants' & Farmers' Peanut Co., 25 Pa. Superior Ct. 199 (1904).

data in constantly recurring instances; but where the answer to the question is one dependent on many different circumstances, which do not continually recur in other cases of like character, and with respect to which no certain rule of law could be laid down, the question is one of fact for the jury. 

Sec. 164. Time in Unilateral Contracts. An offer may be conditioned for its acceptance upon a promise to be made by the offeree, or by the performance of an act. 

If it is directed toward the performance of an act, notice of an intention to perform is not enough. There must be performance. An offer of reward for the return of lost property is a familiar illustration. The resulting obligation is unilateral, and hence it is called a unilateral contract. Many such offers are of a continuing nature, and may be accepted within a reasonable time after they have been announced, or last recognized as continuing in effect. In Shaub v. Lancaster City,30 the defendant offered a reward for the arrest and conviction of incendiaries. It was held that an acceptance after the expiration of seventeen years from the resolution of council and ten years from the last proclamation under it, was not a reasonable time. The following is a leading American decision. 

Loring v. City of Boston, 7 Metc. 409 (1844). Defendant offered a reward of $1,000 for the arrest and conviction of incendiaries. 

Plaintiff brought himself within the terms of the offer three years and eight months later. SHAW, C. J. "In that length of time, the exigency under which it was made having passed, it must be presumed to have been forgotten by most of the officers and citizens of the community, and cannot be presumed to have been before the public as an actuating motive to vigilance and exertion on this subject; nor could it justly and reasonably have been so understood by the plaintiff."

Where the transaction is involved and considerable delay must be encountered, the time may be extended accordingly. The following precedent is, we think, fully as far as the cases have gone. 

30 156 Pa. 362 (1893). 173 1

Hoffman v. Bloomsburg & Sullivan R. R. Co., 157 Pa. 174 (1893). Plaintiff offered a right-of-way of lawful width through his land. It was accepted by construction at that point after a lapse of three years. THOMPSON, J. "The company began its work upon the right of way through his farm and made considerable expenditure of money. It did so in pursuance of the right of way granted by the agreement, without any objection or dissent on the part of the appellant, and was a clear manifestation to appellant that his contract had been accepted by it. . . . Such acceptance was not too late by reason of the delay of over three years. No time was specified in the agreement, and from the nature of the work to be done, the time required to organize the company, and raise the money necessary for the enterprise, it was not intended that it should in any manner be of the essence of the contract."

Sec. 165. Communication of Acceptance. An ac ceptance, to be complete, must be communicated to the offeror, either directly or by some definitive act. In 

Cedar Rapids Lumber Co. v. Fisher, the plaintiff submitted a bid for the construction of a school house, and was advised by telegram that he was low bidder and to come on the morning train. It was held that the telegram could not be permitted to control the situation, and amounted to no more than a conclusion to accept, which was never in fact communicated to the plaintiff. 

In Leskie v. Haseltine,32 a statement to the lowest bidder that he was "the lucky man" was held to have no effect. 

Munhall v. Travelers' Ins. Co., 300 Pa. 327 (1930). On January 14, 1927, Munhall signed an application for life insurance.

The application was sent in to the company on January 20th, the premium was paid on January 26th, and the applicant died on 

January 29th. No policy had been delivered. The statement of claim set forth that defendant's physician reported the deceased as fit to be insured, and that shortly after the premium was paid he became suddenly sick with pleurisy and pneumonia. SCHAFFER, J. "As to the averments that defendant prepared and executed a written policy, and fraudulently refused to issue and deliver it, there is no legal significance in them. As the application was but an offer, the company was free to accept or reject it. The mere execution of the policy is not an acceptance; an acceptance, to be complete, must be communicated to the offeror, either directly, 31 129 Iowa 332 (1906). 

22 155 Pa. 98 (1893).

or by some definitive act, such as placing the contract in the mail. 

The test is not, as appellant seems to think, intention alone." 

Sec. 166. Method of Acceptance Expressed. Where the offeror and the offeree bargain with each other in person, each is informed at the same time of the consummation of their agreement. This result is impossible when they correspond by mail, or through some other agency. 

If the offeror designates the agency to be used in communicating the acceptance, compliance therewith is sufficient to complete the contract. If the offer calls for the posting of a letter, the contract is made when the letter of acceptance is posted. If it calls for the sending of a telegram, the contract is made when a telegram of acceptance is filed. A special problem is presented whenever the offeree uses some agency other than that designated or used by the offeror. The acceptance under these circumstances must be received by the offeror while the offer is still outstanding. There appear to be no Pennsylvania precedents on the subject.

According to the "Restatement of the Law," an acceptance, despatched through some other agency, is effective if it is received within the time in which an acceptance sent in an authorized manner would probably have been received.33 

Lucas v. Western Union Telegraph Co., 131 Iowa 669 (1906).

Plaintiff received a letter from Sas on the evening of the 11th, proposing the exchange of certain real estate, in which the latter indicated that he wanted an early reply. At 9:10 o'clock on the following morning, plaintiff filed a telegram of acceptance. It was delayed in the telegraph office until 4: 41 P. M., and did not reach Sas until 6:03 P. M. Sas sold the property to another at 

3:30 P. M., and plaintiff sued the telegraph company for negligence in transmitting the telegram. The lower court held that the contract between plaintiff and Sas was completed notwithstanding the delay of the telegraph company. In approving this conclusion, it was said by LADD, J. "It is very evident on authority and principle that, in the absence of any suggestion, one transmitting an offer by mail cannot be bound by an acceptance re- 

33 Contracts, section 68.

turned in some other way until it is received or he has notice thereof. The plaintiff, then, did not accept the offer of Sas until the telegram was received by the latter. There was no evidence of the time a letter, if promptly mailed, might have reached Sas. He had indicated in his letter that he was contemplating another deal, and we think ordinary minds fairly differ as to whether in these circumstances, an acceptance twenty-three or twenty-four hours after the letter had been received was in time to bind the party making the offer, and the issue was for the jury to determine."

Sec. 167. Method of Acceptance Implied. When ever the offeror does not specially designate the agency to be used in communicating the acceptance, he impliedly authorizes the use of the same agency which he has selected through which to conduct the negotiations. 

If he sends an offer through the mail and does not designate any agency through which to communicate the acceptance, the posting of a letter of acceptance, properly addressed, will complete the contract. The offeror may not, and usually does not have actual knowledge of the time of the acceptance, but he is held to have constructive knowledge that his offer has been accepted. 

Taylor v. Merchants Fire Ins. Co., 9 Howard 390 (1850). Plaintiff applied to defendant's agent for a policy of fire insurance. The agent replied, advising him of the terms, and added, "Should you desire to effect the insurance, send me your check payable to my order for $57.00 and the business is concluded." This letter reached the plaintiff on the 20th. He posted an acceptance on the 

21st. His dwelling was destroyed by fire on the 22nd. The letter of acceptance was received on the 31st. NELSON, J. "It is obviously impossible, therefore, under the circumstances stated, ever to perfect a contract by correspondence, if a knowledge of both parties at the moment they become bound is an essential element in making out the obligation. And as it must take effect, if effect is given at all to an endeavor to enter into a contract by correspondence, in the absence of the knowledge of one of the parties at the time of its consummation, it seems to us more consistent with the acts and declarations of the parties, to consider it complete on the transmission of the acceptance of the offer in the way they themselves contemplated; instead of postponing its completion till notice of such acceptance has been received and assented to by the company."

Sec. 168. Method of Acceptance not Indicated. 

Occasionally the agency through which to communicate the acceptance is not designated, either expressly or by implication. The offeror may hand a written offer to the offeree. If the offer does not require an immediate response and the parties do not reside in the same community, is the offeree justified in mailing a letter of acceptance, and if so is the contract complete when the letter is posted? According to the "Restatement of the

Law," the acceptance may be despatched by means customary in similar transactions, at the time and place where the offer is received.34 

Henthorn v. Fraser, (1892) 2 Chan. Div. 27. Defendant handed a note to the plaintiff offering to sell a certain property within a period of fourteen days. Plaintiff took the offer to his home and within the time specified mailed a letter of acceptance. On the same day the defendant mailed a letter revoking the offer. The letters crossed in the mails. In deciding that the contract was completed upon the posting of the letter of acceptance, it was said by LORD HERSCHELL: "I should prefer to state the rule thus: 

Where the circumstances are such that it must have been within the contemplation of the parties that, according to the ordinary usages of mankind, the post might be used as a means of communicating the acceptance of an offer, the acceptance is complete as soon as it is posted."

Sec. 169. Effect of Acceptance. An unqualified acceptance of an offer imposes mutual obligations upon the parties which may not be changed without mutual consent. If a contract is completed through the posting of a letter of acceptance, it may not be defeated by the withdrawal of the letter from the mail, or by its loss in transit, or by a retraction before it has been received by the offeror, any more than the offeree may countermand his words of acceptance after they have once issued from his lips. A further principle should be noted. 

There is an essential difference in permitting an offer to remain outstanding for a definite number of days, and a requirement that the acceptance must be received 

34 Contracts, section 66. 

~~3

within the same length of time. Let us assume that the negotiations are carried on by mail. If the offeror allows ten days for the acceptance of his offer, a letter posted on the tenth day would create a contract, even though it is not received until the eleventh day. But if he states that he must receive an answer to his proposition within ten days, a letter, posted on the tenth day, would be ineffective unless it is received by the offeror on that day.

Sec. 170. Notice in Guaranty Cases. Acceptance in unilateral contracts is by performance of an act. The problem of communicating the acceptance is not involved, inasmuch as the contract is made when the act is performed.35 Notice of performance is essential, however, where credit is to be extended under a continuing contract of guaranty. So.

Kay v. Allen, 9 Pa. 320 (1848). Plaintiff received from the defendant the following letter of credit: "I would recommend Mr. 

P. M. Martin, and would go security for him to any reasonable amount; so you can fill his orders, and feel yourself as secure as when I was doing business with you." Plaintiff then sold goods to Martin, but without notifying the defendant that he had done The lower court instructed the jury that plaintiff could not recover from the defendant. Plaintiff appealed. BELL, J. "There is no principle of the law of contracts more firmly settled than that a guarantor of future credit or advancing, is entitled to notice from the party giving the credit, of his acceptance of the guaranty, unless, indeed, the agreement to accept be contemporaneous with it. . . . Without such notice there is no contract, for a party giving a letter of guaranty has a right to know whether the person to whom it is addressed means to hold him ultimately responsible, inasmuch as his own caution and vigilance may, in a great measure, be regulated by his knowledge of the fact." 

Sec. 171. Notice in Reward Cases. In the usual advertisement of an offer of reward for the apprehension of the perpetrator of a crime, or for the return of lost property, notice of performance is not contemplated by the offeror, and may be dispensed with altogether. 

35 Lamb v. Prettyman, 33 Pa. Superior Ct. 190 (1907). 10

As said in Carlill v. The Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., supra, "If I advertise to the world that my dog is lost, and that anybody who brings the dog to a particular place will be paid some money, are all persons to be expected to sit down and write me a note saying that they have accepted my proposal? Why, of course, they at once look for the dog, and as soon as they find the dog, they have performed the condition." 

Sec. 172. Knowledge of Acceptance. In other cases, notice of performance is not necessary if the offeror may inform himself by reasonable inquiry, or has adequate means of ascertaining whether the required act is being performed. In Patton's Executor v. Hassinger,36 the offeror declared, in his lifetime, that whoever took care of his son, John, would be well paid. Plaintiff, with knowledge of the offer, furnished the son with meat, drink, washing, lodging, attendance and funeral expense without communicating with the offeror, but it was said: "There is nothing more significant of the acceptance of a proposition than compliance with it, especially where notice of acceptance is not required." In recent years the Supreme Court has accepted the view that performance, in all cases, is sufficient to conclude the contract, but that liability under it may be defeated under certain circumstances if the offeror is unable to inform himself of such performance. As a matter of business courtesy, such notice should be given. Otherwise, as a matter of law, recovery under such a contract may be denied. 87 circum- 

Ross v. Leberman, 298 Pa. 574 (1930). SADLER, J. "The principle would seem to be properly stated in Hare on Contracts, page 

332: 'When, what the promisor stipulated for is performance, the contract is complete as soon as the act is done, whether it be or be not known or communicated to the promisor. If th stances are such that he cannot inform himself by inquiry, it may be requisite to give him notice; but this is a condition subsequent that will annul the contract if unfulfilled, and not a step that must 

36 69 Pa. 311 (1871). 37 Emerson 

v. Graff, 29 Pa. 358

be taken to call it into being.' It is not the notice which creates the contract, but a lack of it may constitute an excuse from liability."

Sec. 173. Implied Acceptance. Generally speaking an offeree has a right to make no reply to offers, and his silence or inaction may not be construed as a manifestation of assent. In one case it was said of the plaintiff: "When he asked the question whether defendant would bind or renew the policies and obtained no answer, what was his duty? Undoubtedly to repeat his question until he obtained an answer. For his request was that the defendant should make a contract with him, and the defendant says nothing. Certainly such silence is not an assent in any sense." 38 Where goods are received without solicitation, the recipient is under no moral or legal obligation to the sender, and is under no duty to act, much less to act within the time specified by the latter as constituting an acceptance. The dominion over the goods, however, may be construed as an intention to accept and also where services are accepted under circumstances that would indicate that compensation is expected, or where a course of dealing imposes upon the offeree a positive duty to act. These cases are quite unusual. 

Hobbs v. Massasoit Whip Co., 158 Mass. 194 (1893). Plaintiff had sent eel skins to the defendant on several occasions, and they had been accepted by the latter and used in its business. On this occasion plaintiff sent in a shipment, which defendant kept for some months, until they were destroyed. HOLMES, J. "In such a condition of things. . . sending them did impose on the defendant a duty to act about them; and silence on its part, coupled with a retention of the skins for an unreasonable time, might be found by the jury to warrant the plaintiff in assuming that they were accepted, and thus to amount to an acceptance." 

Sec. 174. Mutuality of Obligation. It is sometimes said that unless both parties are bound, neither is bound. 

Such a doctrine may be acceptable in equity. As it has been recently expressed, "where a contract is incapable as The Royal Ins. Co. v. Beatty, 119 Pa. 6 (1888).

of being specifically enforced against one party to it, that party is incapable of enforcing it against the other." 39

But it is objectionable as a rule of law. It will be observed hereafter that the same contract may be enforced against an adult and not against an infant, and that an executory contract for the sale of goods of the value of $500 or upwards may be enforced against a party who has signed a written memorandum but none other. The rule is expressed in the following case as a legal conclusion resulting from the failure of acceptance. 66 

Prescott v. Jones, 69 New Hamp. 305 (1898). Plaintiff's fire insurance policy lapsed on February 1st. He was informed by the insurance company that it would be renewed for an additional year unless he gave notice to the contrary. He remained silent. During the course of the year his buildings were destroyed by fire, and this action followed to recover on the policy. BLODGETT, J. if the plaintiff was not bound by the offer until he accepted it, the defendants could not be, because 'it takes two to make a bargain,' and, as contracts rest on mutual promises, both parties are bound or neither is bound. . . . All the plaintiff did was merely to determine in his own mind that he would accept the offer, for there was nothing whatever to indicate it by way of speech or other appropriate act. Plainly, this did not create any rights in his favor as against defendants."

Part 5. The Revocation 

Sec. 175. Seal and Option. The offeror may withdraw his offer at any time before it has been accepted, even though he has agreed to keep it open for a definite length of time.40 

Bosshardt & Wilson Co. v. Crescent Oil Co., 171 Pa. 109 (1895).

On July 31, plaintiff offered to sell to defendant certain crude oil, and agreed to keep the offer open for sixty days. On September 

25, plaintiff withdrew the offer. On September 27, defendant accepted it. In denying the idea of a contract, it was said by Mc- 

COLLUM, J. "There being no consideration for the offer in this case the defendant had a clear right to withdraw it at any time before there was an acceptance of it." 

30 Heights Land Co. v. Swengel's 

Estate, 318 Pa. 298 (1935). 

40 Rich v. G. W. Pifer Sons, 100 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 483 (1930).

An offer under seal, however, may not be withdrawn, inasmuch as the seal imports a legal obligation. In addition, the parties may enter into a collateral agreement under the terms of which a certain offer is to remain outstanding for a definite length of time. This is known as an option. An option, of course, is a contract. An offer is not. 41 

Sec. 176. Notice of Revocation. A revocation, to be effective, must be received by the offeree. The theory of constructive communication does not apply, except in a few states where the civil codes so provide. In Owen 

M. Bruner Co. v. Standard Lumber Co.,¹¹ a revocation was despatched shortly after a letter of acceptance had been posted. It was said by Judge TREXLER that "while an acceptance is complete where a letter is deposited in the mail, a retraction of an offer can have no effect until it is communicated to the person to whom the offer is made and the revocation can take effect only if it is communicated to the other party before its acceptance." 

Brauer v. Shaw, 168 Mass. 198 (1897). Negotiations between the plaintiffs and defendants involved the letting of cattle carrying space on the Warren Line of steamships for the May sailing from Boston to Liverpool. The communications were in the following order: 

Offer despatched 

Offer received 

Acceptance despatched 12: 28

HOLMES, J. "At the time when the acceptance was received, even the revocation of the offer had not been received. It seems to us a reasonable requirement, that to disable the plaintiffs from accepting their offer, the defendant should bring home to them actual notice that it had been revoked." 

4163 Pa. Superior Ct. 283 (1916). 

Revocation despatched 1:00 

Acceptance received 1:20 

Revocation received 1:42 

Sec. 177. Place of Revocation. A revocation ad dressed to one's place of business, if some person is in charge, would probably be sufficient even though the offeree is not there to receive it, but a revocation addressed to one's residence, in his absence, would not likely have

that effect. Where there is a conflict in the evidence as to whether a revocation has been received by the offeree, the question should be resolved by the jury, or if the parties elect, by a court sitting without a jury. 

Toledo Computing Scales Co. v. Stephens Bros., 96 Arkansas 

606 (1910). Defendant ordered certain scales on December 9. 

The order was accepted at plaintiff's factory on December 15. The question involved was whether the order had been withdrawn before it was accepted. Plaintiff denied that it had received any revocation of the order. A finding in favor of the defendant was based substantially upon the following evidence. HART, J. “Appellee adduced evidence tending to show that they countermanded the order by telegraph on the night following the day they gave the order, and at the same time sent to appellant, properly addressed, a letter countermanding the order; that such letter in the ordinary course of mail should have reached appellant two days after it was sent. They also testified that in a few days after the countermand they telephoned to the agent who received the order, telling him that they countermanded it." 42 

Sec. 178. Indirect Communication. If the offeror makes an offer to one person, and in his presence repeats the same offer to another, is the first offer automatically revoked by the latter? In a famous English case, Dickinson v. Dodds, it was decided that a revocation need not be communicated directly by the offeror to the offeree, but is sufficiently communicated if the offeree has knowledge of the former's change of intention. In other words, knowledge that the offeror has contracted with another concerning the same subjectmatter is a sufficient revocation. This principle has been generally accepted in this country, and is in accord with the "Restatement of the Law." 43 

Coleman v. Applegarth, 68 Maryland 21 (1887). During a thirtyday period in which an offer was to remain open, defendant sold the property to another. Plaintiff had knowledge of this transaction, but nevertheless attempted to accept the offer. ALvey, C. 

J. "In this case, the plaintiff admits that, at the time he proffered to Applegarth acceptance of the previous offer to sell at the price named, he was aware of the fact that the property had been 

42 (1876), 2 Chan. Div. 463. 

43 Contracts, section 42. 

44 Achenback v. Kurtz, 306 Pa. 384 (1932).

sold to Bradley. It was, therefore, too late for him to attempt to accept the offer, and there was not, and could not be made by such proffered acceptance, any binding contract of sale of the property." 

Sec. 179. Advertisement. Where an offer has been made to the public by advertisement or general notification, it may be revoked by equal publicity, inasmuch as it would be impossible for the offeror to ascertain who had knowledge of the offer, and because it would be impracticable to withdraw it in any other manner. 

Shuey v. United States, 92 U. S. 73 (1876). On April 20, 1865, the Secretary of War announced reward of $25,000 for the apprehension of John H. Surratt, one of Booth's accomplices, and a reward for any information that should result in the arrest of either Surrett or Booth, or their accomplices. This offer was made to the public at large by means of newspapers. On November 24, 1865, the President of the United States revoked the offer by publication in the same manner. STRONG, J. "The same notoriety was given to the revocation that was given to the offer; and the findings of fact do not show that any information was given by the claimant, or that he did anything that would entitle him to the reward offered, until five months after the offer had been withdrawn. True, it is found that then, and at all times until the arrest was actually made, he was ignorant of the withdrawal; but that is an immaterial fact. The offer of the reward not having been made to him directly, but by means of a published proclamation, he should have known that it could be revoked in the manner in which it was made."

Sec. 180. Death of Offeror or Offeree. The death of either the offeror or the offeree will cause the offer to lapse. It is well settled that the representatives of either are not qualified to carry on the negotiations."*

Where the offer is directed toward a unilateral contract in the nature of a gift, and has not been acted upon during the lifetime of the offeror, it is too late to do so after his death.45

Pratt v. Baptist Society, 98 Illinois 475 (1879). The Baptist 

Society obtained judgment against Mary L. Pratt as administratrix of the estate of P. B. Pratt, on two promissory notes executed by the deceased. They had been given to enable the Society to 

45 Helfenstein's Estate, 77 Pa. 328 (1875).

purchase a bell. It was shown at the trial that a bell was procured, and probably upon the faith of the notes, but it appeared with reasonable certainty that this had been done since Pratt's death. 

In disapproving the idea of a contract under these circumstances, it was said by SCHOLFIELD, J. "It is the expending of money, etc., or incurring of legal liability on the faith of the promise, which gives the right of action, and without this there is no right of action. Being but an offer, and susceptible of revocation at any time before being acted upon, it must follow that the death of the promisor, before the offer is acted upon, is a revocation of the offer. 

This is clearly so upon principle. The subscription or note is held to be a mere offer until acted upon, because until then there is no mutuality." 

In the following case it was held that promissory notes, not under seal, and without consideration, given by a father to his children, could not be collected from the father's estate after his death.

Tissue's Estate, 64 Pa. Superior Ct. 141 (1916). HENDERSON, J. 

"Natural love and affection is a good consideration for an executed contract or gift, but is not sufficient to support a promise to make a gift. Authorities are abundant to the effect that the delivery of a promissory note or check is not an executed gift of the money represented by it. Such a note is a promise to make a gift in the future, and having no consideration to support it, is not enforceable against the promisor nor against his estate."

Part 6. Selected Contracts Sec. 181. The General Auction Sale. If a contract is shown to exist it is possible to analyze its constituent parts and to detect the offer, the acceptance, or any other element essential to the obligation. In auction sales the announcement is considered as preliminary negotiation. The bid is the offer, and under the principles heretofore considered, it may be withdrawn at any time before the falling of the hammer, or any other act indicative of an acceptance. 

Fisher v. Seltzer, 23 Pa. 308 (1854). Defendant bid seven thousand dollars for a certain property, thinking that it was to be sold free of a mortgage of six thousand dollars. He discovered his error and retracted his bid before the sheriff had knocked down

the property. At a resale the property brought fifteen hundred dollars. This was an attempt to hold him for the difference. 

LEWIS, J. "A bid at auction, before the hammer falls, is like an offer before acceptance. In such case there is no contract and the bid may be withdrawn without liability or injury to anyone.

The brief interval between the bid and its acceptance is the reasonable time which the law allows for inquiry, consideration, correction of mistakes, and retraction. A bidder at sheriff's sale has a right to withdraw his bid at any time before the property is struck down to him, and the sheriff has no authority to prescribe conditions which deprive him of that right." • • • 46 

Sec. 182. Auction Sale Without Reserve. The fore going precedent has been cited in connection with the · supplementary principle that a bid, or offer, need not be accepted by the auctioneer.* Where an auction sale is advertised to be without reserve, however, the owner or auctioneer may not withdraw the goods from the sale, or refuse to accept the highest bid. This is a statutory requirement. The law with respect to auction sales in general, as it is expressed in the Uniform Sales 

Act," may be summarized as follows: 47 A sale by auction is complete when the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer, or in other customary manner. Until such announcement is made, any bidder may retract his bid; and the auctioneer may withdraw goods from the sale unless the auction has been announced to be without reserve. A right to bid may be expressly reserved by or on behalf of the seller, but unless such notice is given it is unlawful for the seller to bid himself, or to employ or induce any person to bid on his behalf, or for the auctioneer to employ or induce any person to bid.
