Any sale contravening this rule may be treated as fraudulent by the buyer. 

46 McPherson Bros. v. Okanogan Co., 45 Wash. 285 (1907).

Sec. 183. Building Contracts. What has been said of auction sales applies to construction bids. The notice or advertisement of the owner is merely preliminary negotiation. The bid is the offer, and this may be accepted or rejected. The offeree is not obliged to accept the lowest bid-he may determine with whom he will contract-unless it be in the case of municipalities when 

47 Act of May 19, 1915, P. L. 543. 

69 PS 161.

public policy, as expressed by statute, requires the acceptance of the lowest responsible bid as a necessary protection to the public.

Leskie v. Haseltine, 155 Pa. 98 (1893). PER CURIAM. "The plaintiff was admittedly the lowest bidder for the erection of defendant's building. It does not follow, however, that because he was the lowest bidder the defendant was bound to award him the contract. After the bids had been opened, it was the right of the defendant to inquire into the fitness and ability of the respective bidders to fulfill the contract. He was not bound to award it to a bidder who lacked either the skill, experience, or ability to properly perform the contract." ...

Part 7. Reduction of Contract to Writing Sec. 184. Condition Precedent. As a general rule contracts need not be expressed in writing. A few exceptions are made by statute, not only that the agreement be reduced to writing, but in other cases that the party sought to be charged shall have signed a written memorandum. These requirements are the exception and not the rule, and will be discussed more fully in a subsequent chapter. We are here concerned with the stipulation of either of the contracting parties that before a contract between them shall become effective, it must be reduced to writing and signed by both. The reason for this requirement is not important from an academic point of view, except to say that a writing greatly facilitates proof of the execution of the contract and of the matters therein set forth. As a condition precedent the rule is this: Where the parties to an intended contract understand that a formal instrument in writing is to be executed before it shall be considered in force, there is no contract so long as one of them withholds his signature from the writing.18 

Sec. 185. Change or Modification. Sometimes the parties stipulate that any change or modification of a contract in writing must also be expressed in writing. 

48 Northwestern Consolidated Milling Co. v. Campbell & Campbell, 78 Pa.

Superior Ct. 96 (1921).

They could, of course, modify the contract by parol, and if there was no dispute about it the oral modification would govern their relations. But allowing the parties full freedom of contract, by parol or otherwise, an alleged modification is difficult to establish in the face of a contractual requirement that any such change shall be reduced to writing and signed by the parties. 

Gross v. Exeter Machine Works, Inc., 277 Pa. 363 (1923). The contract entered into by the parties contained the following provision: "It is understood and agreed that all previous communications, either verbal or written, with reference to the subject matter of this agreement, are hereby withdrawn and annulled, and this contract shall be modified only by written agreement between the parties hereto." Defendant alleged a contemporaneous parol agreement changing the written contract, on the faith of which it executed the written agreement. WALLING, J. "Where the parties, as here, have deliberately put their agreement in writing stipulating therein that it contains the entire contract and shall be modified only by the parties' written agreement, such stipulation forms a material part of the contract and is enforceable as such. Parties having taken the precaution to put their agreement in writing may further safeguard their rights by such a stipulation as above quoted, otherwise a contracting party is powerless to protect himself against parol modifications of his solemn contract."

Sec. 186. Condition Subsequent. Occasionally an oral contract may be enforced notwithstanding an agreement that the contract is to be reduced to writing. The parties may stipulate, in a completed oral contract, that it "shall" be reduced to writing and signed by them.

This principle has been stated, in substance, as follows: 

If it appears that the minds of the parties have met, that a proposition for a contract has been made by one and accepted by the other, that the terms of the contract are in all respects definitely understood and agreed upon, and that a part of the mutual understanding is that a written contract embodying these terms shall be drawn and executed by them, this is an obligatory agreement, which dates from the making of the oral agreement and not from the date of the subsequent writing.¹9 49 

49 Taylor v. Stanley Co. of America, 305 Pa. 546 (1932).

Ketchum v. Conneaut Lake Co., 309 Pa. 224 (1932). Plaintiffs were partners engaged, inter alia, in procuring conventions in behalf of resorts. Defendant was a corporation conducting an amusement resort at or near Lake Conneaut. According to the pleadings they entered into an oral contract whereby plaintiffs were to secure a certain convention for the defendant. It was to be followed by a written contract embodying the same terms. 

Plaintiffs prepared it, but defendant's vice president stated that he could not get it executed forthwith because of the absence of certain of defendant's officials, but that he had talked to one or two of them and that it was all right to go ahead. Plaintiffs did so and the convention was obtained. Defendant denied liability under the oral agreement. The trial court sustained this objection, and entered a compulsory non-suit. Plaintiffs appealed. In setting aside the non-suit it was said by SIMPSON, J. "... where the parties have agreed orally to all the terms of their contract, and a part of the mutual understanding is that a written contract embodying these terms shall be drawn and executed by the respective parties, such oral contract may be enforced, though one of the parties thereafter refuses to execute the written contract." 

Sec. 187. Waiver of Written Contract. Sometimes the parties proceed under an oral contract, with the understanding that a written agreement is to be executed as a convenient memorial. Under these circumstances the oral contract will be enforced, notwithstanding the written agreement is never executed. 

Smith v. Kaufman, 30 Pa. Superior Ct. 265 (1906). Plaintiff, having submitted the lowest bid for the construction of a factory, was awarded the contract with the understanding that a formal contract and bond would be prepared and signed by the parties. 

He completed the building before this had been done. HENDERSON, J. "If it anywhere appeared in the case that the preparation of a written agreement and its execution by the parties was made a condition precedent to the vitality of the contract, no contract would, of course, exist without such writing. Where, however, all the terms of the contract are agreed upon and its reduction to writing is provided for, merely for facility of proof as to its terms, such provision for a contract in writing, is not inconsistent with a present contract, and this is especially true in a case when the things to be done are provided for in written plans and specifications."

Part 8. Implied Contracts Sec. 188. Nature of Implied Contracts. An implied contract arises by implication of law from the voluntary acceptance of valuable services or of the property of another. We utilize the street cars, cabs, and many public conveniences without express agreement, and yet it is too clear for any argument that we are expected to pay the usual and customary charges in so doing. It is not so important that a person rendering services for another expects to be paid, but it is important that the beneficiary knows that payment is expected, for he is then put to an election to ratify or disaffirm the obligation while it is still pending. If he remains silent when he has the option to accept or reject, even if there is no distinct proof that the services were rendered by his authority or at his request, a promise to pay may be inferred.50 

Austin v. Burge, 156 Mo. App. 286 (1911). Plaintiff was the publisher of a newspaper. Defendant's father-in-law subscribed for it, to be sent to the defendant, and paid for it for two years. 

Plaintiff continued to send it for several years more. On two occasions defendant paid the bill, and alleged that he asked that the paper be discontinued. Notwithstanding, he continued to receive and read it. Plaintiff denied having received a stop order. ELLI- 

SON, J. "In this case defendant admits that, notwithstanding he ordered the paper discontinued at the time when he paid a bill for it, yet plaintiff continued to send it, and he continued to take it from the post office to his home. This was an acceptance and use of the property, and, there being no pretense that a gratuity was intended, an obligation arose to pay for it." 

Sec. 189. Special Agreements. A special agreement will seldom be implied, but it may be where unusual circumstances appear. Such cases usually arise where one of the parties has died. An oral or implied contract is difficult to establish, under such circumstances, in view of the statutory mandate that where any party to a contract is dead, a surviving party, whose interests are antagonistic to the decedent's estate, shall not be a 

50 Home Protection Bldg. & Loan Assn. Case, 143 Pa. Superior Ct. 96 (1940).

competent witness to any matters occurring before the death of the deceased.51 

Montgomery's Estate, 299 Pa. 452 (1930). Two brothers, Marshall and Henry, procured a joint life insurance policy in the sum of $20,000, payable to the survivor of either. The yearly premium was $1,540.80, less earned dividends. From 1912 to 1919 each of them paid one-half of the premium. Henry then failed to pay his half until his death in 1927, and the entire amount was paid by Marshall. He sought to be reimbursed. FRAZER, J. "The annual premiums were not trifling in amount, being over $1,500; the insurance money to be paid to the survivor was considerable. It was in fact a matter of large mutual importance, and the nature of these facts alone certainly permits the inference that they must have had, following the ordinary course of financial transactions generally, a compact with each other as to the mutual making and carrying out of all arrangements necessarily attendant upon their contract with the insurance company. We think the evidence sustains the claim of appellee that there was such compact between them."

Sec. 190. Nature of Recovery. If a person works for another without any understanding as to the amount he is to be paid for his services, he will be entitled to receive as much as his labor deserves. If the parties cannot agree, this must necessarily be determined by the jury after a consideration of all the evidence tending to show the extent and value of the services rendered. On the other hand, if the consideration is agreed upon, no other compensation need be paid. 

Johnson v. Wanamaker, 17 Pa. Superior Ct. 301 (1901). PORTER,

J. "The law implies a promise to pay what services are worth, when they are upon request performed and the parties have not expressly agreed upon a rate of compensation; but if the amount of compensation has been agreed upon, or a rule adopted by which it is to be ascertained, the law lets the contract stand as the parties have made it." Where services are gratuitously rendered under the mere expectation of a legacy, there can be no recovery, for in such case there is no contract at all." And when a considerable period of time lapses after services have 52 

1 Act of May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, 28 PS 322. 

52 Thompson v. Stevens, 71 Pa. 161 (1872).

been rendered, without demand for compensation, it is presumed that they were rendered without expectation of payment from motives of benevolence or affection.53

Furthermore, the lapse of time raises a presumption of payment. Where, however, compensation is to be provided for in a will, and no will is made, a recovery may be permitted.55 54 

Sec. 191. The Family Association. There is this refinement to be made of the law of implied contracts, that where persons related by consanguinity or affinity are residing in the same household as members of a family, the family association is sufficient to account for reciprocal acts of kindness and good will. 

Smith v. Milligan, 43 Pa. 109 (1862). STRONG, J. "For the boarding and necessaries furnished to a parent, the law implies no promise to pay. But this is an exceptional case. It springs from the intimate relationship of the parties. . . . The relationship of a father-in-law to his son-in-law is not so intimate." 

A parent or a child may recover for taking care of the other, but only upon an express contract certain and definite in its terms, and proven by direct and positive testimony. It has been said many times that mere loose declarations are not sufficient.56 It should be observed in the following case that the family association did not exist between the parties, but even so it marks a clear trend in judicial opinion. 

Lambert v. Barry, 96 Pa. Superior Ct. 221 (1929). Plaintiff and his wife were injured in an automobile collision as the result of defendant's negligence. The wife required considerable attention and her mother was called to the home to help nurse her daughter and do the housework. Defendant objected to an allowance for these services because of the absence of any specific contract. TREXLER, J. "However, the family relation did not exist at the time. . . . It would seem that the husband was liable to pay her for her services and that therefore in turn the value of such services would form a part of the damages to which he would be entitled to by reason of the injury inflicted." 

53 Johnson's perior Ct. 526 (1933). 

54 Swieczkowski v. Sypniewski, 294 

Pa. 323 (1928). 

Estate, 108 Pa. Su- 

Schoenbachler's Estate, 310 Pa. 396 (1933). 

50 Myers' Estate, 103 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 249 (1931).

Sec. 192. Family Employment. As long as the fam ily association continues there appears to be no necessity for the inference of a contract of employment unless the circumstances are quite unusual. 

Hertzog v. Hertzog, 29 Pa. 465 (1857). LoWRIE, J. "But if we find a son in the employment of his father, we do not infer a contract of hiring, because the principle of family affection is sufficient to account for the family association, and does not demand the inference of a contract. And besides this, the position of a son in a family is always esteemed better than that of a hired servant, and it is very rare for sons remaining in their father's family even after they arrive at age, to become mere hired servants. If they do not go to work or business on their own account, it is generally because they perceive no sufficient inducement to sever the family bond, and very often because they lack the energy and independence necessary for such a course; and very seldom because their father desires to use them as hired servants. Customarily no charges are made for boarding and clothing and pocket money on one side, or for work on the other; but all is placed to the account of filial and parental duty and relationship."

Sec. 193. Remote Relationship. Any other relation except that of parent and child tends to rebut the inference of a gratuity. As said in Smith v. Milligan, supra : "In all other cases there must be evidence beyond the relationship that the creation of no debt was intended. 

If there be such evidence, it must be submitted to the jury, and it will be for them to find whether the presumption is overcome." 

Kerr v. Wilson, 284 Pa. 541 (1925). Eleven years prior to his death decedent went to live with his nephew. He was an invalid during the last eight years of his life. After his death the nephew brought this action to recover for services rendered during the six years immediately preceding decedent's death. The six-year period was probably marked out in view of the statute of limitations. In affirming judgment for the plaintiff it was said by FRAZER, C. J. "The mere relationship of nephew and uncle does not in itself create a presumption of gratuitous service. Consequently an implied promise existed to pay for services rendered and accepted, and the burden devolved upon the person denying such liability to show that no debt was in fact intended."

CHAPTER V  Part 1. The Seal Sec. 194. Necessity of Consideration. The prom ise of a gratuity is not a contract. It is merely a promise to give, without any equivalent. It is not supported by what is called a legal consideration. Sometimes people enter into gratuitous undertakings without realizing that they do not constitute legal obligations such as the law would enforce. And sometimes they desire to create legal obligations out of purely gratuitous undertakings. If so, this purpose may be accomplished in two ways. The addition of a seal, by the promisor, would change a purely gratuitous promise into a legal obligation. This is known as a voluntary bond. The addition of the seal is an ancient device, and has long been known to the law. At mediaeval common law, "The contract under seal was the only purely consensual contract.” ¹ Or the promisor could, if he so desires, transform a gratuitous undertaking into a legal obligation by the expedient of declaring in writing that it is his intention to be legally bound. 

This is a modern innovation of the law. It was accomplished by the Uniform Written Obligations Act. This act provides that a written release or promise shall not be invalid or unenforceable for lack of consideration, if the writing contains an additional express statement, in any form of language, that the signer intends to be legally bound. Otherwise, an offer and an acceptance, such as were considered in the previous chapter, do not in themselves create an enforceable contract. It is also essential that such an agreement be supported by a consideration. 2 

Richards' Executor v. Richards, 46 Pa. 78 (1863). The decedent, Daniel Richards, encouraged his nephew, Samuel Richards, to pur- 

1 Holdsworth, "History of the English Law," Vol. VIII, p. 50. 

2 Act of May 13, 1927, P. L. 985, 33 PS 6. 11 149

chase a farm, with the assurance that he would furnish his nephew with the balance of the purchase money. LOWRIE, C. J. "Assurances of assistance accompanying kind advice are never intended as contracts. And conformance to advice is never intended to stand as a legal consideration for the kind assurances that accompany the advice, though it is a motive for their fulfillment. It would be exceedingly hurtful to the freedom of social intercourse to create even a suspicion in the public mind, that those kind offers of advice and assistance, which take place among friends and kindred, could be converted into contracts which the law would enforce."

Sec. 195. History of the Seal. The seal was used in ancient times because of the almost universal inability to write, and consequently as a means of identification. 

It also added a certain solemnity to the making of a contract.

Cooper v. Rankin, 5 Binn. 613 (1813). BRACKENRIDGE, J. "The use of the seal was originally the distinguishing the person; for every individual was supposed to have his peculiar seal. The act of impressing with a seal, importing greater deliberation, might also be considered as adding to the evidence of its being the act of the party. It was a symbol of solemnity, which gave a greater effect to the instrument."

Many references to the seal will be found in the Old Testament. In the eighth chapter of Esther it is said, "the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse." And in the thirty-second chapter of Jeremiah it is said that, "Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe evidences, and seal them." A reference to Job would indicate that the seal might have been a dab of clay. In the course of time it became an impression of an individual mark or device upon wax or wafer, or upon the parchment. Waxed impressions were followed by gummed discs, pictures, ribbons, flourishes, the expression "locus sigilli" or "L. S.," meaning the place of the seal, and today, the simple word "Seal" is quite sufficient. Even a small dash would suffice if it is intended as a seal.³ 

Hacker's Appeal, 121 Pa. 192 (1888).

Sec. 196. Individual and Corporate Seal. "One is not obliged to exercise his immemorial right to have a distinctive and identifying seal of his own. Any kind of flourish or mark will be sufficient if it be intended for a seal. Writing the word 'seal' or the letters 'L. S.' 

(the place of the seal) after the signature or signing opposite these or similar devices in the printed form, characterize the writing a sealed instrument." * In 

1931 the Superior Court observed that the letters "L. S." or any other substitute should not be used as a corporate seal, but in 1941 it was held that this was not obligatory "in the absence of a statute to the contrary." 

As said by Judge HIRT, "There are many small corporations which rarely have need for a seal. And if the corporation intends to seal an instrument, it should not be permitted to avoid its obligation when the time arrives for performance, merely because it has not adopted and used a corporate seal of its own." " In most legal forms, such as deeds, mortgages, leases, judgment notes, bonds, and other instruments used in recurring business transactions, the seal is incorporated as a part of the instrument. 

Lorah v. Nissley, 156 Pa. 329 (1893). The defendant signed a judgment on which the word "Seal" had been printed beforehand. 

Plaintiff entered the note as of judgment. The lower court opened the judgment on the theory that the instrument had not been properly sealed, and permitted the defendant to interpose the statute of limitations. Plaintiff appealed. MITCHELL, C. J. "Does alter the case any that it was not written by him, but printed beforehand? We cannot see any good reason why it should. Ratification is equivalent to antecedent authority, and the writing of his name to the left of the printed word, so as to bring the latter into the usual and proper place for a seal, is ample evidence that he adopted the act of the printer in putting it there for a seal. . . . The pressure of business life and the subdivision of labor in our day, have brought into use many things ready-made by wholesale which our ancestors made singly for each occasion, and among others the conveniences of printed blanks for the common forms of written instruments." 

4 Collins v. Tracy Grill & Bar Corp., 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 440 (1941). 

5 Huron Leather Co., Ltd. v. Sklar, 101 Pa. Superior Ct. 534 (1931). 

Note 4 supra.

Sec. 197. Modern Function of Seal. In a slight majority of the states the distinction between a sealed and an unsealed contract has been abolished. In some states a contract under seal is presumed to be supported by a consideration; in New York the seal is neither conclusive nor presumptive evidence of consideration; while in New Jersey it is conclusive. These distinctions are all statutory. Pennsylvania still follows the common law. In this state the use of the seal has been retained for three primary reasons: First, it will support a voluntary bond. Second, it may be used as a substitute for a consideration in releasing various claims and obligations arising in contract and in tort. Third, and most important, it will remove the contract from the operation of the statute of limitations. The Act of 1713, which provides that an action on a contract should be brought within six years, expressly exempts instruments under seal. Undoubtedly the seal performs a useful function if it makes people more conscious of the solemnity of their contractual obligations.

This is not the reason, however, that prompts the use of this device in a busy, workaday world, or that accounts for the continued presence of the seal in obligations that are dependent for their validity upon the consideration expressed in the instrument. It is rather the accident of the Act of 1713, and the practical advantage that results from the removal of the obligation from the operation of the statute of limitations. Occasionally a distinction is made between a written contract under seal, a written contract not under seal, and an oral contract, but this is technically inaccurate. 

Rann v. Hughes, 7 Term Reports (Eng.) 350 (1797). The ad ministratrix of an estate promised in writing to assume personal liability for one of the obligations of the estate. The agreement was not under seal, and no consideration was shown. In deciding that such a promise was not enforceable, it was said by LORD CHIEF 

BARON SKINNER: "All contracts are by the law of England dis tinguished into agreements by specialty and agreements by 

Act of March 27, 1713, 1 Sm. L. 76, 12 PS 31.

parol; nor is there any such third class as counsel have endeavored to maintain as contracts in writing. If they are merely written and not specialties they are parol and a consideration must be proved."

Sec. 198. Voluntary Bond. As noted heretofore, a voluntary bond is an obligation under seal, which is executed and delivered without any consideration to support it. It is elementary that a bald promise to make a gift is unenforceable. 

In re Campbell's Estate, 7 Pa. 100 (1847). GIBSON, C. J. "A gift is a contract executed; and, as the act of execution is delivery of possession, it is of the essence of the title. It is the consummation of the contract which, without it, would be no more than a contract to give, and without efficacy for the want of consideration." 29 8 But it is equally well settled that an undertaking under seal, if no consideration is to be received in return, may be enforced. Under these circumstances the seal is more than mere presumptive evidence of consideration. The "seals of the parties in themselves import a consideration and save their covenants from falling within the class of nude facts at law and in equity."

A parol unexecuted promise to make a gift is defective for want of consideration to support it, but an agree ment under seal to do so will be enforced as a legal obligation. It has recently been held that the provisions of the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act do not destroy the significance of the seal, and that the payee of a negotiable note under seal, delivered as a gift, may recover thereon despite the absence of consideration.⁹

Candor & Henderson's Appeal, 27 Pa. 119 (1856). A voluntary bond was given by a father to a trustee for the use of his minor child. Payment was resisted for lack of consideration. LEWIS, C. J. "It is under seal, and is found expressly to be a 'voluntary' bond. 

The seal imports a consideration, and creates a legal obligation. 

In a 'voluntary' bond no consideration is contracted for or expected. The absence of one is therefore no ground for equitable relief from a contract conceded to be good at law without it." 

8 Yard v. Patton, 13 Pa. 278 (1850). 

Balliet v. Fetter, 314 Pa. 284 (1934).

Sec. 199. Failure of Consideration. A different problem is presented whenever a consideration is to pass between the parties, even though the undertaking is under seal. Assume that a contract under seal requires the delivery of certain goods, to be paid for thirty days after delivery. The obligation to pay, as expressed under seal, would not arise if the goods were never delivered. As it is frequently said, there is a well settled distinction between cases in which a valuable consideration was intended to pass, and therefore furnished the motive for entering into the contract, and cases in which such consideration was not contemplated by the parties.10 Whenever the instrument is silent on the question, the burden of proving that a consideration was intended to pass between the parties is upon him who asserts it. 

Killeen's Estate, 310 Pa. 183 (1932). Killeen executed a nonnegotiable note under seal, naming his father as beneficiary. He died four years later, leaving to survive him a minor son. If the note was valid the son would get nothing. The lower court required the holder to submit evidence of consideration. In awarding a new trial it was said by KEPHART, J. "Want of consideration is no defense, as this would contradict the terms of the instrument, while failure of consideration does not contradict the terms of the instrument, but shows that the consideration contemplated was never received. . . . The court was in error in requiring the heirs to prove consideration before the appellee had produced evidence of its own to rebut the presumptions of consideration and delivery raised by the appellant's prima facie case." 

Sec. 200. Meaning of "Value Received." Whenever a person signs an instrument which contains the words "value received," he admits that he has received a consideration, and he is bound by that admission unless he is able to disprove it. The burden of disproving what one has already admitted is not infrequently a difficult thing to do. 

Royer's Estate, 217 Pa. 626 (1907). Decedent handed a note to the claimant, saying as he did so that his financial affairs were 

10 Meek 

V. Frantz, 171 Pa. 632 (1934).

somewhat tied up at that time and that it would suit him better to give her the note. He asked her whether it would do just as well. The claimant accepted it, saying, "That is quite nice," in a laughing way. The note had on it the statement, "for value received." The note was presented at the audit of the estate. The defense was failure of consideration, although no proof was offered. 

The lower court sustained that contention. In overruling this conclusion it was said by BROWN, J. "If the note was a mere gift from the decedent, he would hardly have felt himself called upon to make excuse for not having the money to give to her in its stead. 

He said just about what is frequently said when a debtor, not having ready funds at his disposal, asks his creditor to take his obligation, and her reply in accepting it, in view of the admittedly friendly relations existing between them, is not to be construed as an admission by her that she received it as a gift." 

Part 2. 

Consideration

Sec. 201. Promisor and Promisee. The person who makes a promise is called the promisor. The party to whom it is made is called the promisee. An offer, as has been pointed out, may exact performance of an act, or the making of a promise. If it is directed toward a unilateral contract there is but one promisor and one promisee. If the contract is bilateral there must be two promisors and two promisees, inasmuch as each party is the promisee with respect to the promise of the other. 

A little thought should make this clear. 

Sec. 202. Consideration Defined. A consideration is any detriment sustained by the promisee. This detriment may be (1) the doing, or a promise to do, something that one is not legally bound to do, or (2) abstaining, or a promise to abstain, from the exercise of a legal right. As said by Blackstone: "The civilians hold, that in all contracts, either express or implied, there must be something given in exchange, something that is mutual or reciprocal. This thing, which is the price or motive of the contract, we call the consideration. A consideration of some sort or other is so absolutely necessary to the forming of a contract, that a nudum pactum, or agreement to do or pay any thing on one side, without any compensation on the other, is totally

void in law; and a man cannot be compelled to perform it. As if one man promises to give another £100, here there is nothing contracted for or given on the one side, and therefore there is nothing binding on the other." " 11 Some of the older cases define a consideration as a benefit to the promisor or a detriment sustained by the promisee, but the promisor, presumably, would not make a promise unless he was to derive some benefit from the other party. The modern view is that a person who seeks to enforce a promise should show that he has furnished some consideration for it. Whether the promisor has received a benefit is immaterial. "If the promisee has suffered any detriment, however slight, or, though he has suffered no real detriment, if he has done what he was not otherwise bound to do, in return for the promise, he has given a consideration and the court will not ask whether the promisor was benefited." 12 The following definition is frequently cited in the cases. 

Board of Missions v. Smith, 209 Pa. 361 (1904). THOMPSON, J. "A test of good consideration is whether the promisee at the instance of the promisor, has done, forborne or undertaken to do anything real, or whether he has suffered any detriment or whether in return for the promise he has done something that he was not bound to do or has promised to do some act or has abstained from doing something."

Sec. 203. Nudum Pactum. An agreement without any consideration to support it is called a nudum pactum. If a promise is made to contribute toward the extinguishment of a church mortgage, and the expense of building the church has already been incurred, what consideration is there to sustain the promise? 13 The congregation, as the promisee, would have to show that it has done something that it was not legally bound to do, or has abstained from doing something on the faith of the promise. Undoubtedly every man is bound by the law of nature to fulfill his engagements, but there must be a consideration in order to create a legal duty. 

11 2 Black. Com. 444-445. 

12 Mikos V. Kida, 314 Pa. 561 (1934). 

13 First Congregational Church V. 

Gillis, 17 Pa. C. C. 614 (1896).

It has always been the rule that natural love and affection will not support an executory promise.¹¹ 

Stelmack v. Glen Alden Coal Co., 339 Pa. 410 (1940). Plaintiffs owned a surface lot in the city of Scranton, upon which was a store and apartment. Defendant owned the mineral estate beneath the surface, under deeds which reserved the surface support and which absolved it from liability caused by the subsidence of the surface. Plaintiffs alleged an oral agreement under the terms of which the defendant promised to prop up the building to prevent its collapse, and to make all repairs necessary to restore the property to its original condition. Plaintiffs permitted ties and supports to be erected about the building, which rendered it unsightly and which resulted in some loss of rents. Defendant made repairs to the property from time to time, as damage was caused by subsidence of the surface, but later refused to restore it to its previous condition. In deciding that the alleged promise was not supported by a legal consideration, it was said by BARNES, J. "The interest of plaintiffs alone was served by the defendant's efforts to prevent the collapse of the structure and to minimize the damages resulting from the mining operations. As this was done at the expense of the defendant, and solely for the protection of the plaintiffs, we are unable to see how it could have constituted a consideration for . the defendant's promise, and converted a purely gratuitous undertaking into a binding contract."

Sec. 204. Meaning of Detriment. The theory of detriment has a wider significance than the definition of the word, or its synonyms (loss, damage, disadvantage, prejudice) would imply. The promisee may be benefited by complying with the promise of another, and yet if he has done something that he was not bound to do, or has abstained from doing something, he has furnished a sufficient consideration for the promise. The following case is a leading American decision, and was cited in this jurisdiction in 1936.15 

Pa. 445 

14 Kennedy V. Ware, (1845). 

15 Goodbody v. Margiotti, 323 Pa. 

529 (1936). The Penal Code of June 

24, 1939, P. L. 872, 18 PS 4101, makes it unlawful to furnish any tobacco to infants under the age of sixteen, and any cigarettes or cigarette paper to infants under the age of twenty-one. Any infant who refuses to disclose from whom such cigarette or cigarette paper was obtained, may be punished by fine not exceeding $5 or imprisonment not exceeding five days, or both. Any infant who knowingly and falsely represents himself to be twenty-one years of age for the purpose of procuring any intoxicating liquors, may be punished by fine not exceeding $50 or imprisonment not exceeding sixty days, or both.

Hamer v. Sidway, 124 New York 588 (1891). Story promised his nephew in writing that if the latter would refrain from drinking, using tobacco, swearing, and playing cards or billiards for money until he became twenty-one years of age, he would pay him the sum of $5,000. The money was set aside for that purpose, but 

Story died and his executor declined to make payment, alleging no consideration. PARKER, J. "The defendant contends that the contract was without consideration to support it, and therefore invalid. He asserts that the promisee by refraining from the use of liquor and tobacco was not harmed, but benefited; that that which he did was best for him to do independently of his uncle's promise, and insists that it follows that unless the promisor was benefited the contract was without consideration. . . . Such a rule could not be tolerated and is without foundation in the law. 

We need not speculate on the effort which may have been required to give up the use of those stimulants. It is sufficient that he restricted his freedom of action within certain prescribed limits upon the faith of his uncle's agreement, and now, having fully performed the conditions imposed, it is of no moment whether such performance actually proved a benefit to the promisor. . . ." 

Sec. 205. Forbearance as Consideration. A trifling . inconvenience is sufficient to sustain a promise if the promisor is not at the time under the influence of any fraud, imposition or mistake.16 It has been held that a promise by a childless widower, made to the parents of a newly born babe, that if the parents would give the child his name he would execute a note of $10,000 as an endowment for the child, was supported by a good consideration, inasmuch as the parents relinquished the right of designating the name of the child." It has also been held that the forbearance of an attorney to discontinue his services, which were not of a character making it professionally improper for him to withdraw, was a sufficient consideration to support a promise.' 18 

De Cicco v. Schweizer, 221 New York 431 (1917). Defendant's daughter was engaged to one, Count Gulinelli. He executed a contract whereby he bound himself to pay $2,500 yearly as an endowment for herself and family, in which the marriage was cited as the consideration. Payments were made for a period of ten 

16 Russell V. Henry C. Patterson 

Co., 48 Pa. Superior Ct. 571 (1912). 

17 Wolford v. Powers, 85 Indiana 294 (1882). 

18 Tomlinson v. Wilson, 310 Pa. 41 (1933).

years and then discontinued. The reason assigned was lack of consideration, inasmuch as the daughter was under a contractual obligation to marry prior to the making of the promise. CAR- 

DOZO, J. "They were free by common consent to terminate their engagement or to postpone the marriage. If they forbore from exercising that right and assumed the responsibilities of marriage in reliance on the defendant's promise, he may not now retract it. . . . He offered this inducement to both while they were free to retract or to delay. That they neither retracted nor delayed is certain. It is not to be expected that they should lay bare all the motives and promptings, some avowed and conscious, others perhaps half-conscious and inarticulate, which swayed their conduct."

Sec. 206. Forbearance of Litigation. The actual forbearance, or the promise to forbear to prosecute a supposedly just claim on which one has a right to sue, is universally held to be a good consideration.19 So, too, is the discontinuance of pending litigation, or the abandonment of an appeal. But there is no consideration for a threatened suit for which there is not the least foundation. As said in the following case, one might as well be allowed to recover upon a promise not to 

Islander another as to make a false clamor in court against him. The real question in cases of this sort is the bona fides of the proposed litigation. 

Bryant v. Bryant, 295 Pa. 146 (1929). Plaintiff alleged that defendant promised to reward him in a certain amount if he would refrain from contesting his uncle's will. SADLER, J. "No averment was made that he had any ground for believing in its invalidity, and, as noted, he knew of no reason for such complaint in 1923, and later so swore in the orphans' court proceedings instituted by other relatives. . . . The mere promise not to institute legal proceedings, when there is no bona fide foundation for the same, gives no right of action on a contract to pay in consideration of refraining from so acting. No proceeding had been begun, or threatened, in good faith. Release from mere annoyance, unfounded, or unjustified litigation, does not furnish valuable consideration."

Sec. 207. Performance as Consideration. A consid eration more frequently consists in doing something, or promising to do that which one is not legally bound to 

19 York Metal & Alloys Co. v. Cyclops Steel Co. 280 Pa. 585 (1924).

do. A consideration of this sort may require the payment of money, the transfer of property, or the rendition of services, as long as a person is under no legal duty to do any of these things. Money and property are so usually the consideration that little need be said about them. When we consider the rendition of services, it is necessary to determine, first, whether a person has been or is being fully compensated before it can be determined whether a promise of additional compensation may be enforced. 

Bentley v. Lamb, 112 Pa. 480 (1886). An employer executed a written agreement, reciting that a certain employee had been in his service as a saleslady for a period of twenty-three years, and wishing to give her additional compensation, agreed to and did give her a due bill for $3,000 payable by his executors within one year from the date of his death. His executor refused to honor it, alleging no consideration. GREEN, J. "The writing not only recognizes but declares that the due bill shall be given as compensation for services rendered-additional compensation it is true -but compensation nevertheless. To what it was additional we do not know. Whether it was additional to full or only partial compensation previously paid is only a matter of conjecture. There is no inference of law that the previous compensation was in full, and the inference of fact would rather be that it was partial only, simply because the decedent himself so treats and declares it." 

Sec. 208. Promise of Additional Compensation. If it can be shown that a person is under a contract to perform certain services for a fixed price, a promise of addional compensation would not be supported by a consideration. The following case is a leading American decision. It should be observed that no change was made in the services to be performed. 

Davis & Co. v. Morgan, 117 Georgia 504 (1903). Morgan was employed by Davis & Company for one year at $40 per month. 

After the contract had been in force for some time, Morgan received an offer from another party at $65 per month, and communicated this fact to his employer. His employer then promised him that if he would stay for the balance of the term he would receive $120, at the end of the term, at the rate of $10 per month additional compensation from the beginning of the term. A few weeks before the end of the term a dispute arose between them,

and Morgan was discharged. He instituted this action to recover the additional compensation he had been promised. LAMAR, J. "Had there been a rescission or formal cancellation of the old contract by mutual consent, and if a new contract with new terms had been made; or if there had been any change in the hours, services, or character of work, or other consideration to support the promise to pay the increased wages, it would have been enforceable. But, as it was, Morgan proved that Davis promised to pay more for the performance of the old contract than he had originally agreed. Such a promise was not binding."

Sec. 209. Scope of Employment. It is also neces sary to distinguish sharply between those acts which fall within and without the scope of an existing employment and for which compensation is claimed. An employee may abandon his employment, and if he does so his employer is under no legal obligation to him, not cven to compensate him for his injuries. 

An employee may leave his regular working place, go to a distant section of the mine in which he is working, and there cause an explosion of gas;20 or he may go to a distant section of the mine, where he has no duty to perform, and die of mine gas poisoning.21 An employee has not abandoned his employment, however, by helping a fellow employee in an adjoining working place, 22 or while going from his place of work to some other part of the premises of his employer to get his dinner pail during the lunch hour.23 The same is true of an employee who disobeys instructions incident to his employment.24

A person who is not momentarily in the employ of one employer, may contract with another. If a fireman should be ordered out of a burning structure about to collapse, and reënters the structure at the instance of a stranger, for a consideration, in an effort to retrieve valuable property, there would appear to be no reason why he should not be compensated for his services. 

Reif v. Paige, 55 Wisconsin 496 (1882). Plaintiff was a paid officer and member of the fire department of Oshkosh. During the course of a fire, defendant made the following offer: "I will give

24 Karchut v. Helvetia Coal Mining 

Co., 110 Pa. Superior Ct. 200 (1933).

$5,000 to any person who will bring the body of my wife out of that building, dead or alive." Plaintiff, with knowledge of the offer, rescued the body of Mrs. Paige, but only at the imminent hazard of losing his own life. This action followed. The defense was failure of any legal consideration. LYON, J. "It follows . . . that inasmuch as the plaintiff could not rescue the body of Mrs. 

Paige from the burning building without imminent peril of losing his own life, and inasmuch as it was not his duty as a paid officer and member of the fire department to do so, he is in a position to claim the reward alleged to have been offered by the defendant for such rescue."

Sec. 210. Duties of Public Officers. There is, how ever, a very definite objection whenever the service rendered falls within the scope of one's duties, and particularly where public employees are involved. 

Smith v. Whildin, 10 Pa. 39 (1848). COULTER, J. "It would open a door to profligacy, chicanery, and corruption, if the officers appointed to carry out the criminal law were permitted to stipulate by private contract; it would open a door to the escape of offenders by culpable supineness and indifference on the part of those officers, and compel the injured to take upon themselves the burden of public prosecutions. It ought not to be permitted. Constables must do their utmost to discover, pursue, and arrest offenders within their township, district, or jurisdiction, without other fee or reward than that given by the law itself." 

The Act of 1937 25 provides that no police or peace officer shall perform, directly or indirectly, any official service or duty for any person, or receive, directly or indirectly, any compensation, gifts or gratuities from any person, "during the period of his official services." 

If the legislature had intended this to mean "during the term of one's office," it would undoubtedly have said so. 

Heretofore if a police officer has worked during his off hours in the solution of a crime for which an award is outstanding, and with which his duties do not connect him, he has been rewarded for his effort. 

Hennig v. Glen Alden Coal Co., 117 Pa. Superior Ct. 307 (1935). 

The defendant offered a reward of $2,500 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the persons responsible for blowing

VONN

up a pay car and killing four of its employees. Plaintiff, a police officer of the Lehigh Valley Railroad Company, brought himself within the terms of the offer. Defendant resisted payment of the reward on the ground that it had agreed to pay and did pay the expenses incurred by the railroad company's police officers in working on the case. It was not shown, however, that plaintiff knew anything about this agreement. More important, as said PER 

CURIAM: "The plaintiff's efforts in the detection of the criminals were made after his usual working hours for the railroad company, and it was not shown that the payments to the railroad company included any of the expenses incurred by this plaintiff in his search for the perpetrators of the crime."

Construction Contracts. 

Sec. 211.

Cumulative promises more frequently arise in connection with construction contracts, under circumstances rendering performance more difficult than had been anticipated when the contract was made. The tendency of the courts is to uphold such promises wherever possible. The "Restatement of the Law" acknowledges the principle, with certain exceptions, that facts existing when a bargain is made or occurring thereafter, making performance more difficult or expensive, do not prevent a duty from arising or discharge a duty that has arisen.20 In a few states a mutual rescission of the old agreement seems to be implied.27 The rule has been frequently expressed in Pennsylvania, that where a legal obligation exists, a cumulative promise to perform it, unless upon a new consideration, is a nullity; such promise adds nothing to and takes nothing from the original obligation. A promise cannot be conditioned on a promise to do a thing to which a party is already legally bound.28 In 

Moyer & Morgan v. Kirby," a contractor agreed to build a private dwelling for $1,520. It was blown down shortly before completion, and he was promised additional compensation in the sum of $300. In passing on this claim it was said by the court of common pleas of Dauphin County, that the contractor "claimed the addi-

27 Linz v. Shuck, 104 Maryland 229 (1907). 

28 Wimer v. Worth Township, 102 

Pa. 317 (1883). 

20 2 Pears. 64 (1869).

tional sum not as a right, but because he was poor, 'a new beginner,' and could not afford to bear the loss. 

However this court might feel disposed to divide the loss between the parties, or hold (the promisor) to his promise as a matter of honor, we cannot enforce it as a matter of law."

Sec. 212. Modification of Existing Duties. It should appear, in all of these cases, that the old contract has been mutually rescinded, or something additional required of the promisee other than the duties imposed by the original agreement. A slight advantage, or trifling inconvenience, would be sufficient. It is well settled in 

Pennsylvania that mutual unexecuted undertakings of an existing contract are a sufficient consideration for the cancellation of such a contract and the substitution of a new one with different terms, and it is immaterial if, for a moment during the interval, there is technically a breach of the old agreement, since by the new agreement both parties treat the old one as an existing contract and mutually agree to a rescission of it. Thus it has been held that where one of two parties to a written contract failed in his obligation to deliver merchandise as provided, and the other party, desiring the merchandise and not desiring a suit for damages, agreed to accept a fixed quantity and quality of merchandise at fixed time and prices different from those of the original contract, the old contract would be deemed to have been cancelled by the parties and a new agreement substituted.30 An agreement to an extension of time for performance by one is also sufficient to support a supplemental understanding.³¹ 

Sec. 213. Promises by Third Parties. There is a considerable conflict of opinion as to whether a promise made by a third party to induce performance is sup- 

30 Dreifus v. Columbian Exposition 

Salvage Co., 194 Pa. 475 (1900). 

31 York Metal & Alloys Co. v. Cy clops Steel Co., 280 Pa. 585 (1924).

ported by a consideration. If a stranger should promise a jockey an additional sum if the jockey should succeed in winning an impending race, it is doubtful whether he could recover. Such is the weight of authority in this country, unless the consideration is executed by the payment of a sum of money as an inducement to perform. It is clear, however, that a promise made by a third party will be enforced whenever the promisee has furnished a consideration by doing something that he was not required to do.

Whitehouse v. Green, 81 Pa. Superior Ct. 386 (1923). LINN, J. 

"Plaintiff was a brick subcontractor under contract with one, Bernstein, to do certain brick work on premises owned by defendant, Green. During the progress of the work, the bricklayers struck. 

Before the strike was settled, defendant proposed to plaintiff to pay him $350 in addition to what he was to receive from the general contractor, Bernstein, under the subcontract if plaintiff would pay the bricklayers employed by him the increased rate of wages demanded by them (and for which they struck) and have them start work immediately. Plaintiff accepted the proposal and performed, but defendant refused to pay. . . . As plaintiff was not bound to perform for defendant, but only to perform his subcontract with Bernstein, there was consideration for the agreement with defendant to pay the increased wages and start the bricklayers immediately, something he was not bound to do for the general contractor. 

Having performed, he should have judgment."

Sec. 214. Options and Deeds. Options and deeds must be considered in a class by themselves.

In an option, if the consideration named is one dollar, it is not a matter of inquiry that it was never paid.32 The mere expression of a bona fide consideration is sufficient to sustain a deed. 

Okison v. Patterson, 1 W. & S. 395 (1841). A deed from Gray and his wife to Edmiston contained the following statement: "For a valuable consideration, we the subscribers have bargained and sold," etc. It was objected to on the ground that it contained no other consideration. PER CURIAM: "To raise a use by deed of bargain and sale, a valuable consideration must be expressed; but, as the smallest is sufficient, the amount of it need not be stated."

Part 3.. Promissory Estoppel Sec. 215. Gratuitous Promises. Gratuitous prom ises are not enforceable. This is because society does not impose legal sanctions upon them. Such promises rest for their performance upon the honor and good faith of the parties. The following case was cited approvingly by the Superior Court in 1932.33 

Kirksey v. Kirksey, 8 Alabama 131 (1845). Defendant wrote to his sister-in-law, the plaintiff, saying, inter alia: "Much to my mortification, I heard that brother Henry was dead, and one of his children. I know that your situation is one of grief, and difficulty. 

If you will come down and see me, I will let you have a place to raise your family and I have more open land than I can tend; and on account of your situation and that of your family, I feel like I want you and the children to do well." Plaintiff left her home and moved her family a distance of sixty miles to the residence of the defendant, who gave her a house and land to cultivate for a period of two years. He then requested her to leave. 

ORMOND, J. "The inclination of my mind is, that the loss and inconvenience, which the plaintiff sustained in breaking up, and moving to the defendant's, a distance of sixty miles, is a sufficient consideration to support the promise, to furnish her with a house, and land to cultivate, until she could raise her family. My brothers, however, think that the promise on the part of the defendant, was a mere gratuity, and that an action will not lie for its breach." 

Sec. 216. Nature of Estoppel. There is a limit to the inconvenience to which one man may subject another. 

A promissory estoppel arises from a promise to do something in the future which may lead another to change his position for the worse. It has been called a "substitute for consideration," or "the equivalent of consideration." 34 The following case has been repeatedly cited in this jurisdiction, in cases of promises without consideration, where injustice could only be avoided by the enforcement of the promise.35 

Ricketts v. Scothorn, 57 Nebraska 51 (1898). Plaintiff was a working girl earning the sum of $10 per week. Her grandfather 

33 Langer v. Superior Steel Corp., 

105 Pa. Superior Ct. 579 (1932). 

34 Volkwein v. Volkwein, 146 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 265 (1941). 

35 Langer v. Superior Steel Corp., 

105 Pa. Superior Ct. 579 (1932); 

Fried v. Fisher, 328 Pa. 497 (1938)

handed her a note in the sum of $2,000, saying, "I have fixed out something that you have not got to work any more. None of my grandchildren work and you don't have to." He did not ask her to give up her employment, but merely promised that she would not have to work unless she wanted to. She stopped working. The court admitted that there was no consideration for the promise, but enforced it because it had misled the plaintiff in such a way that it would have been unfair to do otherwise, saying, through 

SULLIVAN, J. "Having intentionally influenced the plaintiff to alter her position for the worse on the faith of the note being paid when due, it would be grossly inequitable to permit the maker, or his executor, to resist payment on the ground that the promise was given without consideration."

In the following case the Supreme Court subsequently held that the president of the corporation had no authority to bind the corporation by the promise of a pension for life, but the decision of the Superior Court has since been cited by the Supreme Court as an apt illustration of the doctrine of promissory estoppel." 36 37 Langer v. Superior Steel Corp., 105 Pa. Superior Ct. 579 (1932). 

Plaintiff retired from active duty as superintendent of the annealing department of the defendant company, and received the following communication from its President, inter alia: "The directors have decided that you will receive a pension of $100 per month as long as you live and preserve your present attitude of loyalty to the company and its officers and are not employed in any competitive occupation." Payments were made for approximately four years, and then discontinued. BALDRIGE, J. "There is nothing appearing of record, except the condition imposed by the defendant, that would have prevented this man of skill and experience from seeking employment elsewhere. By receiving the monthly payments, he impliedly accepted the conditions imposed and was thus restrained from doing that which he had a right to do. This was a sufficient consideration to support a contract." 

Sec. 217. Voluntary Subscriptions. The necessity of a consideration applies to voluntary subscriptions to various religious and charitable objects. As said by

A payment of $400 had been subsequently made on account. The lower court sustained the validity of the obligation without further inquiry. TREXLER, J. However, it was asserted at the argument that there would be no trouble to prove that others had subscribed to this common object and that money had been expended in its prosecution. We are compelled to reverse the case, but will give the claimant an opportunity of producing further proof."

Sec. 218. Consideration for Subscription. The ma jority of American courts enforce such a promise on grounds of promissory estoppel, and there is dictum to that effect by the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania.39 A few American courts infer a consideration in such cases from the mutual promises of the subscribers, and there are cases to that effect in Pennsylvania.10 In recent years, however, the elements of estoppel, usually found in such cases, are construed as a legal consideration in this Commonwealth, the consideration being the obligations assumed on the faith of the promise. 

University of Pennsylvania Trustees v. Coxe's Executors, 277

Part 4. 

Adequacy of Consideration 

Sec. 219. Quantum of Consideration. Adequacy of consideration is a legislative," as well as a judicial problem. For most contracts, as the law is at present established, it is not essential that consideration should be adequate in point of value, or that one party to a contract should derive as much benefit as any other party to the transaction. Goods have different utilities to different persons in altogether different circumstances. 

Thus far individual price-fixing has been one of the principal characteristics of American industrial life. There is, of course, no duty to buy, but we need not quibble. 

The ethicist is inclined to say: Is it not unethical to drive an unconscionable bargain, or, what amounts to the same thing, to exact a price for our merchandise that is disproportionate to its cost? The answer is not so simple as the ethicist would have us believe. If we overlook the question of utility, what is an unconscionable bargain? And if we overlook losses sustained in previous transactions, does this relation of cost to price refer to the cost or expense incurred by the vendor, his most favored or least favored competitor, that of the representative firm, or does it bear some relation to the prevailing market price as determined by the forces of supply and demand. The common law doctrine involved in this conflict is one of relative indifference. As expressed a century ago: "The law does not weigh the quantum of consideration, having no means of deciding on that matter; and it would be unwise to interfere with the facility of contracting, and the free exercise of the judgment and will of the parties. The law allows them to be the sole judges of the benefits to be derived from their bargains, 41 Act of May 24, 1945, P. L. 944, 20 PS 818, provides that inadequacy of consideration shall not relieve a fiduciary of his obligation.

provided there be no incompetency to contract, and the agreement violates no rule of law." 42

In simple language, "Every man must bear the loss of a bad bargain legally and honestly made: If not, he could not enjoy in safety the fruits of a good one." 43

Honesty as here used has a peculiar legal connotation, but the rule itself is not without some justification. If it appears to be a license for much of the selfishness and greed which seems to be inherent in human nature, the answer is that law is merely a reflection of acceptable standards of human conduct, and I am not so sure but that a majority of us would still sympathize with the man who has cause to rejoice at having derived the best of the bargain, at least we would congratulate ourselves. 

The cynicism of Bernard Shaw is not without its point. "You can not believe in honor until you have achieved it." 

Sec. 220. Equitable Relief. It is quite correct to say that "Inadequacy of price, improvidence, surprise and mere hardship, none of these, nor all combined, furnish an adequate reason for a judicial rescission of a contract." 44 The following statement, however, is open to some criticism: "If it be said that the contract, thus read, bears hardly on the defendant, the reply is that courts do not sit to relieve suitors from the results of improvident agreements, nor the consequences of bad bargains." "

Relief is an equitable prerogative, and there are a number of cases similar to that in which the court was "impressed with the fact that if specific performance is decreed here the net result would be that plaintiffs will get property worth in excess of $11,000 for a consideration of approximately $7,000," and that "it is mainly on the ground, therefore, that this contract is an unconscionable one, and would be a gross imposition on 

42 Hind v. Holdship, 2 Watts 104 (1833). 

43 Harris V. Tyson, 24 Pa. 347 

44 Nunge v. Crawford, 88 Pa. Superior Ct. 516 (1926). 

45 Owens v. Wherle, 14 Pa. Superior

Ct. 536 (1900).

29 46 defendants, that the chancellor deems it proper to restore the parties to their former positions.' In addition, an inadequate consideration is often treated in equity as corroborative evidence of fraud, and it is well established that a failure of consideration entitles one to relief in equity, in whole or in part, from his written obligation." A party claiming under a sealed covenant may also be required to give full proof of consideration if there be any evidence, however slight, to impeach the bona fides of the transaction.48

Part 5. Past Consideration 

Sec. 221. Lack of Antecedent Benefit. As a general rule, a past consideration is insufficient to support a present promise. The consideration must be coextensive with it. The following case was cited in this jurisdiction in 1845.49 

Mills v. Wyman, 2 Pick. 207 (1825). Levy Wyman fell sick among strangers and died. His father, upon being informed of this event, promised to reimburse Daniel Mills for his expenditure in this behalf. His defense was no consideration. PARKER, C. J. "General rules of law established for the protection and security of honest and fair-minded men, who may inconsiderately make promises without any equivalent, will sometimes screen men of a different character from engagements which they are bound in foro conscientioe to perform.... The promise declared on in this case appears to have been made without any legal consideration. The kindness and services toward the sick son of the defendant were not bestowed at his request. The son was in no respect under the care of the defendant. He was twenty-five years old, and had long left his father's family. On his return from a foreign country, he fell sick among strangers, and the plaintiff acted the part of the good Samaritan, giving him shelter and comfort until he died. The defendant, his father, on being informed of this event, influenced by a transient feeling of gratitude, promises in writing to pay the plaintiff for the expenses he had incurred. But he has determined to break this promise, and is willing to have his case appear on record as a strong example of particular injustice some- 

46 Rupniewski v. Miazga, 299 Pa. 190 (1930). 

47 Feuerstein V. New Century 

Realty Co., 304 Pa. 271 (1931).

times necessarily resulting from the operation of general rules. . . . 

What a man ought to do, generally he ought to be made to do, whether he promise or refuse. But the law of society has left most of such obligations to the interior forum, as the tribunal of conscience has been aptly called.”

Sec. 222. Post-Contract Promises. It is not un common for a party to a contract, to request some promise from the other party after the bargain has been made. 

The difficulty with such a promise is the lack of a new consideration to support it. It is in this respect that the doctrine of past consideration operates with all its vigor. In Roscorla v. Thomas,50 a vendor undertook to warrant the soundness of a horse after the bargain had been concluded. As said by Lord DENMAN, the "precedent sale, without a warranty, though at the request of the defendant, imposes no other duty or obligation upon him." 

Cleaver v. Lenhart, 182 Pa. 285 (1897). Lenhart sold a creamery to Cleaver. When this contract was made no restriction was placed upon Lenhart not to engage in the same business at any time or place. Subsequently he agreed not to compete with 

Cleaver. His defense was no consideration. GREEN, J. "He (Lenhart) did not become subject to any duty or obligation to abstain from carrying on the same business thereafter, and hence he was at perfect liberty to do so if he chose. It cannot, therefore, be said that it was any part of the consideration of the contract that Lenhart should not engage in the same business in the future. That contract was consequently completely performed when the conveyances were made and delivered, and money paid according to its terms. It necessarily follows that when the second agreement was made there was nothing left of the first agreement which could operate as a consideration of the second." 

Sec. 223. Moral Consideration. All American states. 

recognize the validity of a moral consideration under some circumstances, if it is supported by a present, express promise. Before exploring this subject, it is well to mark the path as laid down by Lord MANSFIELD. 

Hawkes v. Saunders, 98 Eng. Rep. 1091 (1782). Lord MANS- 

"Where a man is under a moral obligation, which no Court

FIELD. 

77777

of Law or Equity can inforce, and promises, the honesty and rectitude of the thing is a consideration. ... As if a man promises to pay a just debt, the recovery of which is barred by the Statute of Limitations: or if a man, after he comes of age, promises to pay a meritorious debt contracted during his minority, but not for necessaries; or if a bankrupt, in affluent circumstances after his certificate, promises to pay the whole of his debts; or if a man promise to perform a secret trust, or a trust void for want of writing, by the Statute of Frauds. In such and many other instances, though the promise gives a compulsory remedy, where there was none before either in law or equity; yet as the promise is only to do what an honest man ought to do, the ties of conscience upon an upright mind are a sufficient consideration." 

Sec. 224. Past Cohabitation. Pennsylvania is undoubtedly the leading exponant of the idea that a moral obligation is a sufficient consideration to sustain an express promise. The validity of an express promise, based on past cohabitation, has been denied in England,¹ and in the majority of American states, but such a promise, if accompanied by seduction, has always been upheld in this state. 

Shenk v. Mingle, 13 S. & R. 29 (1825). DUNCAN, J. "Dismissing the questions of mere form, what would be the substantial cause for reversal? It would be, that either the promise is a nudum pactum, or made on an illegal consideration. If it so appears on the declaration, no verdict could cure the defect, as the consideration is the gist of the action. That it is an illegal consideration, is denied by the counsel in error, and I think with good reason. This is not a contract to tempt a woman to transgress the law, nor wages of iniquity. It is a promise in consideration of past cohabitation, not prostitution. . . . The man who has thus humbled an honest woman, if he will not marry her, is in honour and conscience bound to make some provision for her.

The duty of provision was a moral one; and where a party is under a moral obligation to do a thing, a promise made to do it will not be considered a nudum pactum, though no other immediate consideration appears."

Sec. 225. Promises of Married Women. Prior to the Act of 1945,52 Pennsylvania did not permit a married woman to become an accommodation endorser, 52 Act of May 17, 1945, P. L. 625, 48 PS 31.

maker, guarantor or surety for another, including her husband, or to mortgage her real estate unless her husband joined in the mortgage.58 Such restrictions, or the practical effect of such restrictions, may have been responsible, in part, for the development of the principle, that the promise of a married woman to pay a valid debt of her husband, out of her separate estate, creates a moral obligation of sufficient potency to support an express obligation for the same debt, executed after her husband's death.54 Of other cases of like effect, it has been held that while a married woman was not liable on a promise to pay for work done for her son, such liability was imposed by reason of a new promise made after she had been divorced.55 There are a number of cases which hold that the obligations of married women, incurred under a rule of law that absolved them from lia bility, will be enforced by reason of an express promise made after the disability had been removed.56 

Vineland National Bank & Trust Co. v. Kotok, 129 Pa. Superior

Ct. 309 (1937). Kotok executed and delivered two notes to plaintiff bank, both signed by an accommodation endorsor. The accommodation endorsor having become bankrupt, Kotok executed a new note which his wife signed as an accommodation endorsor. 

This endorsement was not binding upon her. Kotok died, however, and the wife executed a new note at the instance of the bank. 

The bank then instituted this action to recover on the note. The defense was lack of consideration. KELLER, P. J. "Whatever may be the rule in other jurisdictions, in this state it has been held for many years that a woman, after the death of her husband, may legally bind herself by a note given in renewal of a note, on which she was accommodation maker or endorsor, and which was during her coverture legally invalid as to her the moral consideration being sufficient to support the renewal note made after her husband's death."

Sec. 226. Pecuniary or Material Benefit. A present, express promise, supported by a past pecuniary or material benefit-as where the promisor received something 

53 Act of June 8, 1893, P. L. 344, 48 PS 21-32.

55 Hemphill v. McClimans, 24 Pa. 367 (1855).
