of value under circumstances which did not create a legal obligation-rests on surer grounds. It is this view of the law that has gained favor in American states. 

Such a rule was recognized in Pennsylvania as early as 1809. "When the interest of a man is promoted, though not at his request, and he deliberately after engages to pay for it, the law very properly says, he shall fulfill his promise." 57 If a man derives a benefit from the unsolicited services of another, the moral obligation is sufficient to sustain an express promise, but not an implied one. If a person plows the land of another, thinking it to be the land of the party who has engaged his services, or drills a well on the land of another under similar circumstances, and the owner is benefited, the consideration, while past, will support an express promise. As a general rule, circumstances which would not be sufficient to raise an implied contract, but which benefit the promisor, will sustain an express promise. 

Sutch's Estate, 201 Pa. 305 (1902). DEAN, J. "The son had remained working for him without wages for fifteen years after he became of age; the daughter had performed without help all the household duties; had faithfully nursed her invalid sister and mother through years of illness until their death; both had done all they could to save their father's heavily encumbered property.

They thought their father indebted especially to them; they saw the new wife step into their mother's place, and a possible new family about to enjoy the fruits of their labor. Of course they expressed to their father a desire for compensation; he, conscious of their deserts, conceded the justice of their claim. He was not legally bound to pay them anything, but if he chose to consider that he in conscience owed them, the moral debt was a good consideration for the legal promise expressed in the notes." 

Sec. 227. Prior Legal Obligations. The validity of an express promise, based on some prior legal obligation, is almost universal. The principle is recognized, in other states as well as in Pennsylvania, that where a prior legal obligation cannot be enforced by reason of the intervention of some positive law, such as the statute 

57 Greeves v. M'Allister, 2 Binn. 590 (1809).

of limitations, the operation of a judgment, or a dis. charge in bankruptcy, the moral obligation is sufficient to sustain an express promise. Such a promise requires no consideration. The new promise couples itself with the prior legal consideration, and will be enforced as a legal obligation. Concerning the debts of a bankrupt, as said by Lord MANSFIELD, "they are due in conscience, notwithstanding he has obtained his certificate; and there is no honest man who does not discharge them, if he afterward has it in his power to do so. Though all legal remedy may be gone the debts are clearly not extinguished in conscience." 58

Kirstein v. Belsinger, 30 Pa. D. R. 180 (1920). HARGEST, P. J. 

"A discharge in bankruptcy wipes out a preexisting debt, but after such discharge there still remains a moral obligation to pay it. If the debtor, after the discharge in bankruptcy, makes a new promise in clear, distinct and unequivocal terms to pay such preexisting debt, the moral obligation is sufficient consideration to sustain the new promise. . . . This seems to be the universal rule in this country." 

Part 6. Liquidated Obligations

Sec. 228. Unequal Sums of Money. Money is the measure of value. It is a rule of the common law, which had its origin in the days when money was regarded as having a fixed and unchangeable value, that a contract for the bare exchange of unequal sums of money, without more, is without consideration. There is nothing of value that would act as a consideration for the difference.

It is now well known that a fixed quantity of gold, or gold coins, fluctuates in purchasing power with a rise or fall in prices, and does not have an unchangeable value in terms of other commodities, but this is an economic phenomenon which the federal government has sought to obviate in its monetary policy of changing the gold content of the money unit. The legal rule is still the same. 

Trueman v. Fenton, 2 Cowp. 544 (K. B. 1777).

1 

Schnell v. Nell, 17 Indiana 29 (1861). Out of regard for the wishes of his deceased wife, defendant promised to give to three persons $200 each. The consideration recited in the agreement was one cent, the past services of his wife, and the love and affection he had borne her. In deciding that the promise was not supported by any legal consideration, it was said by PERKINS, J. "The consideration of one cent will not support the promise of Schnell. It is true, that as a general proposition, inadequacy of consideration will not vitiate an agreement. But this doctrine does not apply to a mere exchange of sums of money, of coin, whose value is exactly fixed, but to the exchange of something of, in itself, indeterminate value, for money, or, perhaps, for some other thing of indeterminate value."

Sec. 229. Part Payment of Debt. A liquidated obli gation is an obligation or indebtedness which is fixed and certain in amount, and which is neither honestly nor reasonably in dispute. A contract compromising an obligation is called an "accord and satisfaction." An accord and satisfaction is an agreement between the debtor and creditor in which the creditor agrees to accept some other performance as payment in full, and which, when accepted, discharges the claim or abolishes the right. It is, in effect, a compromise agreement in ' which the creditor agrees to accept something else in satisfaction of his claim. Such a compromise, when executed, wipes out the original obligation. It must, however, be supported by a consideration in order to be enforceable. Most of the disputes that arise in this connection involve the payment of a smaller sum of money as payment in full of a larger liquidated amount. 

If the creditor agrees to accept a smaller sum, all is well that ends well. But any such agreement between debtor and creditor for the acceptance of part of a liquidated debt in satisfaction of the whole, is void for want of consideration.50 As said by Mr. Justice MITCHELL, "The reason that payment of money in discharge of a larger amount presently due is not a good accord and satisfaction is that the debtor gives nothing that he was not already bound to give, and the creditor receives nothing 

50 Brockley v. Brockley, 122 Pa. 1 (1888).

he is not already entitled to receive, and there is, there fore, no consideration." 60 

Pinnel's Case, 5 Coke 117 (1602). "Resolved by the whole Court that payment of a lesser sum on the day in satisfaction of a greater cannot be any satisfaction for the whole because it appears to the judges that by no possibility a lesser sum can be a satisfaction to the plaintiff for a greater sum, but the gift of a horse, hawk, or robe, etc., in satisfaction is good. For it shall be intended that a horse, hawk, or robe might be more beneficial to the plaintiff than the money, in respect of some circumstance, or otherwise the plaintiff would not have accepted of it in satisfaction. But when the whole sum is due, by no intendment the acceptance of a parcel can be a satisfaction to the plaintiff."

Sec. 230. History of the Rule. This rule is a puzzle to the layman. If a creditor promises to accept a smaller sum in relief of an insolvent or embarrassed debtor, why should he not be bound? A century ago he would have been. In 1815 the Supreme Court held, in Wentz v. Dehaven, that the release of a debt, not under seal, was a good discharge. The promise was: 61 "This is to certify, that I have a bond and mortgage from Matis 

Wentz, which I intend to give up to them, as I never intend to demand it from them, nor any part of the interest due, or to become due at any time."

The same problem was before the court again in 1829. 

The case involved the question whether an agreement to accept part of a liquidated debt in satisfaction of the whole, not under seal, should be binding on the promisor. This question was answered in the affirmative. 

Milliken v. Brown, 1 Rawle 391 (1829). HUSTON, J. "It has, alas, become too common for men of good character and principles, but who trade on borrowed capital, to fail, and their creditors are glad to receive fifty cents in the dollar, and give a discharge in full; and I do not know the lawyer who would be hardy enough to deny the validity of such a discharge, although given after the money was due, and although the discharge was not under seal, or although it might be doubtful whether it could more properly be called a receipt, or a release, or a covenant never to sue. if the 

60 Fowler v. Smith, 153 Pa. 539 (1893). 01 1 S. & R. 312 (1815).

meaning can be certainly ascertained, and no fraud, concealment, or mistake at the giving it, it is effectual." 

The rule was short lived. In 1845 the Supreme Court declared: "Wentz v. Dehaven is not to be sustained on any ground." 62

Still later it was said that Milliken v. 

Brown "must fall with Wentz v. Dehaven. It is too clear for argument, that if a release of a debt not under seal must have a consideration to support it then payment of part of an acknowledged indebtedness can be no consideration." 63 

Sec. 231. Reinstatement of the Rule. We can only speculate as to why the old rule was reinstated by the courts. It is fairly certain, however, that the primary difficulty was one of proof. If a debtor is unable to discharge an indebtedness on the day it falls due, he does the next best thing by endeavoring to presuade his creditor to accept a part payment and the balance in installments. If the creditor consents to an arrangement of this sort the debtor is in a position, if he finds himself unable to make further payment, to swear falsely that his creditor agreed to accept the payment he had made as payment in full. This raised a question of credibility which had to be submitted to a jury. If insolvent debtors were all scrupulously honest, there would appear to be no sound reason why an oral agreement should not be established by the testimony of the parties to it. An agreement in writing would have overcome the difficulty, but this was a matter for later consideration by the legislature. 99 64 

Sec. 232. Payment by Third Party. The "rule it self never had any application to a payment by a third party.' As said by President Judge KELLER, "While it is the law in this State that ordinarily an agreement by a creditor to accept from his debtor less than the amount due him in satisfaction of the debt is without

64 Ebert V. Johns, 206 Pa. 395 (1903).

consideration and void, it is not applied to a case where the payment was made by a third party under an agreement, accepted by the debtor, that it would be received by the creditor in satisfaction of the debt." 65 This is because a third party, in paying any sum to the creditor of another, has done something that he, the third party, was not legally bound to do. Even a note for a less sum, endorsed by a third person, would accomplish the same purpose." 66 

Sec. 233. Methods of Discharge. Following are the methods by which payment of a lesser sum, in discharge of a larger liquidated amount, could be made effective: (1) The creditor may give his debtor a release under seal for the balance of the debt. As said by Mr. Justice TRUNKEY, “A sealed instrument is presumed to be for good consideration, and therefore, upon part payment of a debt, a release under seal is valid." 99 67 OS (2) Under the Uniform Written Obligations Act, the creditor may give the debtor a statement in writing, stating, in express language, that it is his intention to be legally bound by partial payment in satisfaction of the whole. (3) The debtor may add some additional consideration to the smaller sum, the acceptance of which would constitute an accord and satisfaction. Such additional considerations are indicated in the following section.

Sec. 234. Additional Consideration. Following are additional considerations which may be added to a lesser sum, and which, if accepted by the creditor under an agreement to that effect, will constitute an accord and satisfaction of a larger liquidated debt: (1) Payment of a lesser sum before the debt is due, or at a different place than that agreed upon. In either case the debtor, in addition to paying the lesser sum, would have done something that he was not legally bound to do. As said by Mr. Justice 

MITCHELL, "any circumstance of variation such as payment at a different place or before the debt is due has been held sufficient to take a case out of the rule." "D

(2) Payment of a lesser sum, with the addition of some other economic good. As said in Hoover v. Pursel," "Deckert, in addition to giving the check for $250, conveyed some equities in property in Scranton to the trustee for the banks to which he was liable on various endorsements and if any money could be collected on these the People's Bank would be entitled to a pro rata share. This was sufficient consideration to support the agreement." (3) Payment of a lesser sum, together with the relinquishment of a legal right. As said in Melroy v. Kemmerer:" "In the present case the debtor, being in failing circumstances and contemplating bankruptcy, offered the plaintiffs 30 per cent of his debt as a settlement in full. The plaintiffs dissuaded him from going into bankruptcy, accepted his alternative offer, received the money, and closed the account. They have now brought this suit for the balance. In the absence of any express decision in this state on this point, the learned judge below did not feel at liberty to depart from the general rule. We have no such hesitation. The exact point is whether the debtor's relinquishment of his intention to seek a discharge in bankruptcy, and his payment of 30 per cent instead, constitute a sufficient consideration to bind the creditor to the agreement. On that point we have no doubt. A valuable consideration may consist in some right, interest, or benefit to one party, or some loss, detriment, or responsibility resulting, actually or potentially, to the other."

Sec. 235. Common Law Composition. Two or more creditors may join in an agreement to accept less than is due from their common debtor. Each creditor would furnish a consideration for the promise of every other creditor to the agreement, inasmuch as he refrains from insisting upon the payment of more than is agreed upon. 

In other words, the consideration runs not between a creditor and his debtor, but between two or more creditors. This is known as a common law composition. 

Laird v. Campbell, 92 Pa. 170 (1880). STERRETT, J. "The consideration which supports the agreement of each creditor, in such cases, is the undertaking of the other compounding creditors to release their common debtor from a portion of their respective claims. The agreement of each creditor with the others and the debtor constitutes a good and valid consideration. After a creditor has thus agreed to relinquish part of his claim and induced others to become parties to a composition, it would be a fraud on 

70 67 Pa. Superior Ct. 130 (1917). 

71 218 Pa. 381 (1907). 13

them to permit him to ignore the agreement, and collect the full amount of his claim."

Sec. 236. Effect of Composition. So scrupulous are the courts in compelling creditors to the observance of good faith toward one another, that any security taken for an amount beyond the composition agreed upon, or even for that sum, better than that which is common to all, if unknown at the time to the other creditors, is void and inoperative, and no contract to pay money or to do any other valuable thing, and no security upon such promise, may be enforced.

Robert v. Barnum, 80 Kentucky 28 (1882). Two remaining creditors to a composition agreement, observing a sufficient balance, demanded payment in full. PRYOR, J. "It is argued that this is a controversy between the creditor and debtor only, as all his other creditors are satisfied, and the debtor is able to pay them. The inquiry at once arises, what placed the debtor in a condition by which his ability to pay these two debts is unquestioned?" 

Sec. 237. Voucher Check-Liquidated Debt. 

voucher check is a check which contains a statement of the account being paid, or a statement that the amount of the check is offered as full payment of a certain account. It is an offer by a debtor to his creditor. If the creditor cashes such a check, he promises to accept it on the terms on which it was sent. If it is a part payment of a liquidated debt which is certain and definite in amount, he promises to accept it as payment in full. 

If there were any consideration to support this promise if the debtor had done anything that he was not legally bound to do, or had abstained from the exercise of a legal right-the promise would, of course, be binding upon the creditor. No such consideration appears. 

A voucher check is merely another way of inducing a creditor to make a promise. It must have some consideration to support it. 

Lovekin v. Fairbanks, Morse & Co., 282 Pa. 100 (1925). Plaintiff claimed $9,614.83 for certain materials delivered to the defendant. The defendant alleged that the goods were not of the quality contracted for, and claimed a deduction of $2,920. No agreement

of settlement or compromise was made, but defendant sent to the plaintiff a check for $6,694.83, the amount which was undisputed, together with a statement of the account in the form of a voucher check. On the same paper, below the check, was printed: "Note: if amount is not satisfactory, return without alteration or correction." On the back of the check appeared the words: "By the endorsement of this voucher check the payee accepts the amount of same in payment of account as per statement within." Plaintiff endorsed the check and received the money, but it was held that this did not preclude him from recovering the balance of any just claim he may have had.

Part 7. Unliquidated Obligations Sec. 238. Implied Contracts. A compromise agree ment disposing of unsettled and unliquidated demands is very much to be desired, and will be upheld unless there is a total failure of consideration. A valid claim may be uncertain and unliquidated for various reasons. 

Goods may be sold, or services may be rendered, without any understanding as to the price to be paid. If so it is incumbent upon the parties to liquidate the amount by an agreement among themselves, and if they cannot agree, then have it liquidated by legal tribunals provided for that purpose. 

Donahue v. Woodbury, 6 Cush. 148 (1850). Plaintiff had a claim against the defendant for labor. After a dispute as to the exact amount he accepted $35.00 as a full accord and satisfaction. This was an action to recover an additional amount. SHAW, C. J. "Originally, the present was a claim for services, and was for unliquidated damages. Some services were admitted to have been rendered, but the amount was denied; and an offer was made of a less sum than that claimed. The case was open to two inquiries, first, as to the time of service, and second, as to the rate. The offer therefore of $35 was both to liquidate the claim and pay that sum in satisfaction; the acceptance of the offer fixed and liquidated the sum . . . and . . . discharged it."

Sec. 239. Express Contracts. An obligation is more frequently in dispute when goods are sold at a fixed price and there is a breach of warranty, or otherwise a breach of the contract. An offer of settlement should be accompanied by acts and declarations amounting to express notice that the payment tendered is conditional

and if accepted must be received in satisfaction. "Subsequent payment of money on the claim of the creditor constitutes no estoppel except as the creditor was given to understand, at the time of his acceptance, that the money was paid in full discharge of his cause of action." 72 73 

Sec. 240. Voucher Check-Unliquidated Debt. 

Where a check is offered in full payment of an honestly and reasonably disputed claim upon certain terms and conditions, and it is retained and cashed, there is an acceptance of the terms upon which it is sent, even though the offeree expresses an intention not to assent to the offeror's proposition. In Herzog v. Vozzy," a check for part of a disputed claim was sent "in full settlement." Plaintiff's attorney wrote back that it would not be accepted in full settlement of the account. 

No reply was made by defendant, and about two months later plaintiff deposited the check and received the proceeds. It was held that there was an accord and satisfaction which barred plaintiff from recovering the balance of the disputed claim. 

Barron Co. v. Fox & Co., 84 Pa. Superior Ct. 46 (1924). Defendant ordered a carload of choice Mississippi wrapped tomatoes, and finding them defective, sought to make an adjustment. Plaintiff refused. Defendant then sold them in the open market for various prices, and wrote the plaintiff as follows: "We attach our check together with account sales, which check is in full settlement of this shipment, which we think is fair and right and we believe you will agree with us when you look over government inspection report on this car." With the letter was a check, on the face of which were endorsed the words, "paid in full to date." Plaintiff received the check, endorsed it and deposited it for credit, and brought suit for the balance of the claim. HENDERSON, J. "If he is not willing to accept the check in full payment it is his duty to return it without using it: 1 Corpus Juris 562. Where money is sent by a debtor to a creditor to apply on a disputed claim with a notice that it is to be in settlement of a larger demand, the debtor will be discharged if the creditor receive the money." 

72 Foye v. Lilley Coal & Coke Co., 251 Pa. 409 (1916). 

73 Blaisdell Filtration Co. v. Bayard & Co., 311 Pa. 6 (1933). 

74 44 Montg. L. R. 53 (1928), cited in the preceding case.

CHAPTER VI CONTRACTUAL CAPACITY Part 1. Infants 

Sec. 241. Legal Disability. In addition to the requisites heretofore considered, it is essential that the parties to a contract have contractual capacity, or at least the capacity to incur voidable contractual duties. A person who has full power to contract is said to be sui juris. Capacity to contract is the general rule, but certain qualifications are imposed for the protection of infants, the insane, the intoxicated, and until recently, married women. The contracts of each may be valid, voidable, or void. Those which are voidable differ according to the circumstances which give rise to the defect. In addition to the foregoing, certain restrictions exist where estates are owned by two or more persons, and aliens in Pennsylvania do not have unlimited power to contract. The status and incidents of each of these persons will form the basis of this and the following chapter. 

Sec. 242. Period of Infancy. All members of society are classified as infants or adults. An infant is any person under the age of twenty-one. The period of infancy extends from the time of conception to the first hour of the day immediately preceding the twenty-first birthday. Many men are killed in industry or die before their children are born. A child in ventra sa mere has a legal existence, and enjoys the same status as an infant in esse, provided it be born alive and after such foetal existence that its continuance in life may be reasonably expected. Such a child may not maintain an action for injuries sustained while in ventra sa mere.¹ But it may participate in the benefits of the Workmen's Compensation Act,2 and it also enjoys the same right of inheri-

Sec. 243. Illegitimate Children. An illegitimate child may inherit its mother's, but not its father's estate. Under the laws of Pennsylvania, the marriage of the parents at any time will restore to it all the legal rights of a child born in lawful wedlock." The rule of the common law required the marriage of the parents prior to the birth of the child. Blackstone explains this stigma upon the innocent by saying: "For, if a child be begotten while the parents are single, and they will endeavour to make an early reparation for the offence, by marrying within a few months after, our law is so indulgent as not to bastardize the child, if it be born though not begotten, in lawful wedlock; for this is an incident that can happen but once, since all future children will be begotten, as well as born, within the rules of honour and civil society."" Sec. 245. Custody of Infants. While the father of a child is ordinarily entitled to its custody, service, and earnings, a mother who contributes toward its support now enjoys the same right. If either parent abandons a child, this right accrues to the other. If there is any dispute between them the court may decide which parent, if either, should prevail, "regard first being had to the fitness of such parent and the best interest and permanent welfare of said child." A child of tender years is usually awarded to the mother,15 while an older child is usually given to the father, inasmuch as he is primarily responsible for its support. The right in either case is not absolute. A mother may forfeit this privilege if her associations, surroundings and environment are not conducive to the best interests of the child.10 

In the case of a deep seated enmity between the mother and the child, induced by continued mistreatment, the child may be awarded to the father, notwithstanding an occasional moral lapse, or even a conviction of adultery, if he is otherwise qualified. "A child needs to feel that he belongs to some one in a family relationship.” 17 If neither parent qualifies, the child may be awarded to others. 13 

Commonwealth v. Cook, 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 397 (1936). A boy, eleven years of age, had been reared by his mother's stepfather for ten of those years. His mother had since died and his foster parent and foster sisters, all of whom were of excellent character, lavished upon him the attention and affection of a parent. 

The boy's father made no effort to visit his son during that period. 

His conduct was characterized by "indifference, neglect and abandonment of his offspring." A contest then arose and the lower court awarded the child to his father. This order was set aside by the Superior Court until the boy attained. the age of fourteen, when he might indicate his own wishes in the matter. The father

Sec. 246. Maintenance of Infants. Apparently the common law of England never imposed upon a father a legal duty to support his minor children, it being thought best to entrust this responsibility to the instincts of nature. Blackstone describes this duty as a "natural law." His discussion follows the Statute of Elizabeth: 

"The municipal laws of all well-regulated states have taken care to enforce this duty: though Providence has done it more effectually than any laws, by implanting in the breast of every parent that natural, or insuperable degree of affection, which not even the deformity of person or mind, not even the wickedness, ingratitude, and rebellion of children, can totally suppress or extinguish." Curiously enough, however, the father might be indicted under the common law for failure to provide for his minor children. The American states have generally recognized this duty as a principle of the common law, even though a child has an estate of his own sufficient for that purpose. The common law duty, in strict theory, ought to be enforceable at the instance of an infant, but this is not generally conceded. Third parties are usually required to rest their case on contract, although the parent's assent may be implied under slight circumstances. In some states the parent may be held under "just and reasonable" circumstances, independently of contract, where the parent has abandoned a child. 18 

Fitler v. Fitler, 33 Pa. 50 (1859). WOODWARD, J. "There is no duty more clear and imperative than that of a father to support his children during their minority. And though we have no statute enforcing it, except in case of pauperism, I hold it to be a legal obligation. He is absolutely bound to provide reasonably for their maintenance and education, even though they have property of their own; and if he neglect this duty, he may be sued for necessaries furnished and schooling given, under just and reasonable circumstances." 

18 1 Black. Com. 447.

Sec. 247. Public Support Law. The Act of 1937, as amended in 1945,19 provides that the husband, wife, child, and father and mother of every indigent person shall, if of sufficient financial ability, maintain such indigent person at such rate as the court of the county may direct. 

In 1941 the Superior Court ruled that to be entitled to this relief a person must actually become a public charge,20 but a subsequent Act of 1945 21 requires the support of such person "whether a public charge or not." Any person who wilfully neglects or refuses to comply with the order may be committed to the county jail for a period not exceeding six months. Under this statute a mother may be compelled to contribute toward the support of a child in case of the death or inability of the father. This was not required under the common law. The fact that she has no property or income is not conclusive. She may not abandon a child if she is physically able to obtain suitable employment. Relief under this statute is discretionary with the courts, although the courts are bound to exercise a reasonable discretion. At common law the father was excused whenever a child voluntarily left his father's house, especially to avoid the consequence of a crime, or where the child was wrongfully taken from his custody. 

Angel v. McLellan, 16 Mass. 28 (1819). Defendant's son had fallen into distress in a foreign country, to which he had fled to avoid the consequence of a crime. He was an infant without property. The plaintiff, knowing his father to be a reputable merchant, paid his board and supplied him with necessaries, relying upon the father to reimburse him. The father refused to do 

So. In justifying the father's refusal, it was said by PARKER, C. J. "Could a refractory or vicious son leave his father's house without being exposed to want, carrying with him a credit on his father wherever he might wander, the motive for submitting to authority might be materially impaired, and a great diminution of parental influence might ensue. One of the greatest restraints upon the bad passions and vicious propensities would be removed, if young

Sec. 248. Discipline of Infants. A parent has a right to discipline a child. While the exercise of this power is discretionary, and considerable latitude is allowed as long as the parent acts conscientiously and from motives of duty, nevertheless a child will be protected against the brutality of a barbarous parent. “For error of opinion he ought to be excused, but for malice of heart he must not be shielded from the just claims of the child." 22 A parent who fails to curb a vicious child, may be held responsible for injuries inflicted by such a child upon other children. "A parent who knows of his child's vicious and reckless disposition is under a duty to exercise the control which he has over the child when he knows, or in the exercise of due care should know, that injury to another is a natural and probable consequence of the failure to exercise such control.” 23

The Act of 1911 24 provides that every teacher in the public schools shall have the right to exercise the same au thority as to conduct and behavior over pupils attending his school, during the time they are in attendance, including the time required in going to and from their homes, as the parent. The authority of a teacher, however, does not extend beyond matters of conduct and discipline "there is no implied delegation of authority to exercise her lay judgment, as a parent may, in the matter of the treatment of injury or disease suffered by a pupil." 25 If necessary, a teacher may inflict corporal punishment, if reasonable and confined within the bounds of moderation.26 

Harris v. Galilley, 125 Pa. Superior Ct. 505 (1987). Defendant, a high school principal, appealed from a judgment against him in the sum of $721. He testified that he slapped the plaintiff, a student, on the back of the neck with the open palm of his hand.

Sec. 250. College Education. There is a conflict of opinion as to the duty of a parent, who is financially able, to provide his child with a college education. The question usually arises in connection with orders of support and maintenance where the parents are separated. 

In 1844 the Supreme Court of Vermont held, in Middlebury College v. Chandler,29 that a college education was not a necessary, but in 1926 it was said by the Supreme Court of Washington: "The rule in Middlebury College v. Chandler, supra, was clearly based upon conditions that existed at that time. An opportunity at that early date (1844) for a common education was small; for a high school education less, and for a college education was almost impossible to the average family. . . . Where the college graduate of that day was the exception, today such a person may almost be said to be the rule." 30

Commonwealth v. Binney, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 374 (1941). 

Appellant, who was separated from his wife and two sons, appealed from a support order which required him to pay to his wife and younger son, $50 per week, and to contribute $1,500 per year to maintain his 19 year old son at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. His wife occupied the home owned by them by the entireties. He was a business man of moderate means. He stated at the hearing before the lower court that he intended to keep his son in college as long as he was able to do so, which the lower court apparently construed as consent to the order. In reducing the support order to $40 per week and eliminating the compulsory allowance for the boy in college, it was said by RHODES, J. "To hold that the circumstances of this father require him to furnish 2016 Vermont 683 (1844). 

30 Esteb v. Esteb, 138 Wash. 174 (1926).

his son with a college education would be an unwarranted conclusion. Hence in such a matter he is entitled to a measure of discretion, and must be allowed to exercise his own judgment." 

Sec. 251. Negligent Injuries. Both the parent and the child have a right to recover for negligent injuries inflicted upon the child by third parties. The rights of both, however, must be redressed in but one action.³¹ 

Separate verdicts must be rendered. If the parents are living apart, the action may be brought by the parent having custody of the child. Each parent is the agent of the other, in the care of a child, and the contributory negligence of one will defeat a recovery by the other. In other words, each becomes responsible for the acts of the other. Such "implied authority does not rest upon the legal fiction of the unity of husband and wife but is founded upon the family relation." 83 This principle has also been applied where a child has been placed in the custody of an older sister, who was contributorily negligent, on the theory that the older sister was the agent of the parents.34 While a recovery by the parent may be defeated on grounds of contributory negligence, such negligence does not bar the child. He may recover in his own right, "and no action has failed because of the negligence of the parent or guardian being imputed to the child." 35

Sec. 252. Actions between Parent and Child. The common law did not prevent suit by an unemancipated minor against his parent for injuries resulting from the negligence of the parent. The child is precluded from the exercise of this right in Pennsylvania on grounds of public policy.36 For the same reason, an unemancipated child is not liable to the parent for negligent injuries inflicted by him upon his parent, even though the minor is indemnified against loss or damage by a casualty insurance company.

Sec. 253. Earnings of Infants. The emancipation of an infant means to be free of parental control. An infant is emancipated at common law upon attaining his majority, or upon being abandoned by the parent, or upon marriage. Emancipation may also be temporary, and it may be partial only. An emancipated infant may seek his own employment, and is entitled to recover his earnings in his own right. The parent is entitled to the services of an unemancipated minor, and if the parent obtains employment for such children he is entitled to their earnings.

Kauffelt v. Moderwell, 21 Pa. 222 (1858). An infant, by his next friend, sought to recover wages due. His father had procured the employment, and testified that he informed his son that all he earned should be his own, but he also testified that he never told this to his son's employer. LoWRIE, J. "When a minor is permitted, by his father, to make his own contract for service, it is fair to presume that he is allowed also to receive the wages for himself, and so the law implies the contract until a contrary purpose appears. But it is not so when the father himself makes the contract. He has a right to command the services and receive the wages of his minor son. 

Sec. 254. Guardians of Infants. There are five kinds of guardians who may be interested in vindicating the rights of an infant, or who may be charged with the administration of an infant's estate. These are designated as (1) natural guardian, (2) next friend, (3) guardian ad litem, (4) testamentary guardian, and (5) legal guardian. (1) A natural guardian is the parent, the adoptive parent, or the person who stands in locus parentis to an infant. The natural

38 guardian may act as "next friend" in instituting a legal action on behalf of the infant. The Act of 1917, as amended in 1939, provides that the orphans' court shall not appoint the father or mother of a minor as guardian of the estate of the minor. Where, however, the estate is $500 or less, the court may in its discretion authorize payment to the natural guardian, or person by whom the minor is maintained, or to the minor, without the appointment of a guardian or the entry of security. And if the minor's interest in real estate is not more than $200, the court may authorize the natural guardian to convey or mortgage such property without the appointment of a guardian or the entry of security. (2) A "next friend" is a person who undertakes to institute a legal action on behalf of an infant, and who assumes to be liable for the costs. The Rules of Civil Procedure provide that "An action in which a minor is plaintiff shall be entitled 'A, a Minor, by B, his Guardian,' against the party defendant."

Such a guardian may be the legal guardian, or "a person in the nature of a next friend selected to represent a minor plaintiff in an action."""" 

The minor may select such a guardian to represent him, but subject to removal by the court for cause." A "next friend" or other guardian is not liable on a judgment against the infant, but the Rules of Civil Procedure continue such liability for costs, and impose a similar liability where the infant interposes a setoff or counter-claim." An action in which an infant is a party may be compromised, settled, or discontinued only with the approval of the court. In personal injury cases it has been held that if the court is not adequately informed with respect to the injuries sustained by the infant, the release may be set aside." Where a judgment in favor of an infant does not exceed $500, the court may authorize payment to the guardian of the person, the natural guardian, the person by whom the minor is maintained, or to the minor.45 43 42 (3) A guardian ad litem is a species of attorney appointed by a court to represent the interests of an infant in litigation then pending before the court. The Rules of Civil Procedure provide that "If a minor party to an action is not represented, the court shall appoint a guardian for him either upon its own motion or upon the petition of (1) the minor party, (2) a guardian of the minor appointed by any court of competent jurisdiction, or by a will duly probated, (3) any relative of the minor, or (4) any other party

Such a guardian may be appointed to defend a minor in a legal action brought against him, and also to represent a minor in the settlement of an account in which an infant has an interest. The Act of 1925 provides that a surviving parent may appoint a testamentary guardian of the person or property of a minor child, and if both parents are living, each of them may exercise this power with respect to the property which he or she may leave to the child. The privilege of appointing a testamentary guardian does not extend to a father who has wilfully neglected or refused to provide for a child, or to a mother who has failed to perform her parental duties. The Act of 1945 50 extends the same privilege to the donor of inter vivos gifts of insurance or other property. (5) A legal guardian is a person appointed by a court to administer the estate of an infant. Guardians who administer such estates are subject to the jurisdiction and control of the orphans' courts of the several counties. Such courts will appoint legal guardians when and as often as there shall be occasion, and may permit infants over the age of fourteen to make their own choice, preference in all cases being given to persons of the same religious persuasion as the parents. In addition to the administration of the estate of an infant, a legal guardian is competent to represent an infant in any litigation in which the infant may be a party, or in which the infant may have an interest. 51 

Part 2. 

Contracts of Infants Sec. 255. Power to Contract. It is a popular mis conception that an infant does not have power to contract. Except for a few contractual undertakings that are void, an infant enjoys the same legal right to contract as an adult. Other than for necessaries, and con-

In other words, an infant may enforce his contract against an adult, even though the contract could not be enforced against the infant.52 The adult is bound, notwithstanding the infant may not be.53 An infant's privilege of avoidance may well cause an adult to hesitate to enter into a contract with an infant, but an adult has no ground to complain if the infant elects to enforce the contract against him. Sec. 256. Void Contracts. A void contract is a non existent contract. At one time in the history of the law it was probable that all contracts of an infant were void. But few are so held at the present time. A contract that is entirely prejudicial to the interests of an infant is void, and so is a contract of marriage when either party is under the age of seven. A warrant of attorney to confess a judgment, and a judgment confessed by a minor, are absolutely void.55 Nor is a minor qualified to make a will.56 Other contractual undertakings by an infant are voidable only. A judgment obtained against an infant who is not represented by guardian, is voidable, not void. In a recent case a judg ment was obtained against an infant in an action of trespass resulting from the negligent operation of an automobile. The suit was ably defended by an insurance company. Sec. 257. Necessaries. A contract for necessaries is legally binding upon an infant. As said by Blackstone, he may, under the common law, "bind himself to pay for his necessary meat, drink, apparel, physic, and such other necessaries; and likewise for his good teaching and instruction whereby he may profit himself afterwards." 60 

Strong v. Foote, 42 Conn. 203 (1875). PARDEE, J. "The defendant (an infant about fifteen years of age, having an estate of about $60,000) applied to plaintiff for relief from pain and prevention of its occurrence; he, finding the cause in the defendant's decaying and neglected teeth, immediately began the work of relief and repair, and continued the same from time to time during a period of six weeks, until its completion. It was necessary for the preservation of the teeth and the charge therefor is reasonable in amount. In view of the circumstances of this defendant, we have no hesitation in saying that the services are within the legal limitations of the word 'necessaries.'"

Three questions are open in the determination of the validity of a contract for necessaries: first, the circumstances of the infant; second, the actual needs of the infant; and third, the reasonableness of the charge. As to the circumstances of an infant, the fact that he is wealthy, or has been reared in redundance, is merely extrinsic evidence. 

Wharton v. McKenzie, 114 Eng. Rep. 1378 (1844). While attending Oxford an infant of rank and fortune was supplied with meats, fruits, and confectionery for the entertainment of his

58 Guthrie v. Murphy, 4 Watts 80 (1835). 

50 Watson v. Hensel, 7 Watts 344 (1838). 

60 1 Black. Com. 465.

friends. Lord DENMAN, J. "For a young man in some situations in life, not only clothes may be considered neces cessaries, but a watch and like articles, which he is expected to wear in that condition of life; but with respect to the articles here supplied, it is an outrage to common sense to say they can possibly be necessaries." 

Sec. 258. Uniform Sales Act. Necessaries are de fined in the Uniform Sales Act" as "goods suitable to the condition in life of such infant or other person, and to his actual requirement at the time of delivery." This statute is declaratory of the common law. Such goods are not confined to creature comforts, or to elementary physical necessities. It is for this reason that the word "necessaries" is used. Money is not a necessary. In the hands of improvident youth it is the means of extravagance and dissipation. But the better rule seems to be that it becomes clothed with the attributes of its purchase, and hence, if used in the actual purchase of necessaries, it may be recovered.62 An elementary or 

Vocational education is usually classified as a necessary, but not a college, university, or professional education except under most favorable circumstances. The Supreme Court of Texas has held that a married male infant, who purchased a modest home in which to live. could not rescind the contract upon coming of age.

This is probably the extreme to which the courts have gone in defining what may be considered a necessary in a particular case. The standard provided by the statute is variable. It is obvious that what may be a necessary for one infant may not be a necessary for another and that goods which are obvious necessaries when supplied in a reasonable amount, are not necessaries when supplied in an unreasonable degree. 63 

Johnson v. Lines, 6 W. & S. 80 (1843). GIBSON, C. J. "The case of the plaintiffs below is poor in merits. It appears that they supplied a young spendthrift with goods which they called necessaries, but which ill deserve the name. Their account amounts up

They surely could not complacently look upon the ruin of their own sons, brought on by ministering to their appetites, and stimulating them with the means of gratification. Every father has a deeper stake in these matters than the public mind is accustomed to suppose; and it intimately concerns the cause of morality and virtue, that the rule of the common law on the subject be strictly enforced. Judgment reversed and new trial awarded.”

Sec. 259. Commercial Securities. The contracts of an infant are to be distinguished from the contracts made by the guardian of an infant's estate. The latter is authorized by statute to invest the funds of a trust estate in designated legal investments."4 Commercial securities purchased by an infant are not "goods suitable to the condition in life of such infant and to his actual requirement at the time of delivery." The stock market crash in 1929 provoked a number of difficult cases. In one such case, arising in New York, it was held that an infant who ordered a stockbroker to purchase certain shares of stock when the market price was high, could return the stock to the broker and recover what he had paid, notwithstanding the stock had declined in value.65 The significant feature of that case was the liability of an agent who had contracted for an infant. In another case arising in the same jurisdiction 

64 Act of May 28, 1937, P. L. 1037, 20 PS 801. 

65 Shroeder v. Hitt, 266 New York

Supp. 2 (1932).

it was held that an infant who delivered stock worth $3,342.09 to a brokerage firm in which he carried an account, and who rescinded the contract when the equity in the shares had been reduced to $70.99, could only recover the value of his equity as of the date of disaffirmance. These decisions are not altogether consistent. An allowance for ordinary depreciation has long been the settled rule in New York.67 In Pennsylvania, if an infant returns property not a necessary, he may recover what he had parted with, notwithstanding the property may have depreciated in value."S Under these circumstances a disaffirmance speaks as of the date on which the contract was made, rather than the date on which the contract was disaffirmed.

Sec. 260. Trading Contracts. The fact that an in fant is emancipated and entitled to his own earnings, or that he is self-supporting, or that he may engage in business on his own account, does not bring his trading contracts within the classification of necessaries, other than for the simple tools of his trade. 

Ryan v. Smith, 165 Mass. 303 (1896). Plaintiff, an infant, was entirely self-supporting. He purchased a barber shop, chair, and furniture used in furnishing a barber shop, but subsequently rescinded the contract and demanded back what he had paid. KNOWL- 

TON, J. "The law does not contemplate that a minor shall open a shop and become a trader, or the proprietor of a business which involves the making of a variety of contracts. It is clear that the articles in question were not necessaries. If they had been hand tools to a reasonable amount, such as are ordinarily provided by a journeyman and necessary for use in his trade or business, the case would be different." The status of an infant has undoubtedly improved since the law on this subject was formulated. This has resulted in part from compulsory school attendance, visual education, improved transportation facilities, and the dissemination of information concerning local and

Notwithstanding this general improvement, an infant does not have the experience in business affairs, or the seasoned judgment of an adult, and while there is a trend in some states to enlarge upon the concept of necessaries, Pennsylvania deems it best to shield an infant in his business ventures.

Spangler v. Haupt, 53 Pa. Superior Ct. 545 (1913). An infant took charge of his father's lumber business after the latter's death, and ordered a carload of lumber. Upon becoming of age he disaffirmed the contract. RICE, P. J. "His trading contracts are not an exception to the general rule that, except for necessaries, an infant is not competent to bind himself, nor liable on the contracts he has made. . . . The right to replevy the goods so long as they remain in the possession or under the control of the infant does not necessarily imply a right to enforce the infant's contract." 

Sec. 261. Partnerships. An infant who becomes a partner in a business may rescind the partnership agreement, and avoid personal liability for the debts of the partnership, but he may not withdraw his capital contribution to the prejudice of partnership creditors, or shift this burden to his co-partner, by withdrawal of his capital contribution, unless induced to enter into the partnership agreement by the fraud of his co-partner. 

Adams v. Beall, 67 Maryland 53 (1877). An infant invested $2,900 in a partnership business. After an unprofitable continuance of the business for a period of one year, he withdrew from the firm and demanded of his co-partner the amount of his capital contribution. In denying this relief it was said by ROBINSON, J. "And while fully recognizing the privilege which the law accords to minors in regard to contracts made during their minority, yet, in a case like the present, where money is paid by a minor in consideration of being admitted as a partner in the business of the appellant, and he does become and remains a partner for a given time, he ought not to be allowed to recover back the money thus paid unless he was induced to enter into the partnership by the fraudulent representations of the appellant." 

Sec. 262. Executory Contracts. Except for con tractual undertakings authorized by statute, an infant may always avoid an executory obligation.

Derocher v. Continental Mills, 58 Maine 217 (1870). An infant agreed to work for six months at $1.25 per day, and to give two weeks' notice before leaving. He quit after 252 days without giving notice, and instituted this action to recover the wages he had earned. WALTON, J. "Stripped of all its sophistical surroundings, we think the doctrine contended for in defense amounts to simply this, that the minor's contract not to leave without giving two weeks' notice was obligatory, and having violated it, he must pay the damage. Such a doctrine cannot be maintained." 

The Uniform Sales Act, supra, provides that where necessaries are sold and delivered to an infant, "he must pay a reasonable price therefor, or return the goods in substantially the same condition as when received, within reasonable time." The same rule applies to other contracts for necessaries. 

Gregory v. Lee, 64 Conn. 407 (1894). An undergraduate at 

Yale College leased a room for the school year at $10 per week. 

He paid his rent regularly until December 20th, when he repudiated the lease. TORRANCE, J. "So long then as the defendant actually occupied the room as his sole lodging room it was clearly a necessary to him, for the use of which the law would compel him to pay; but as he paid the agreed price for the time he actually occupied it, no question arises about that part of the transaction between these parties. The question now is whether he is bound to pay for the room after December 20th. . . . In this case the defendant gave up the room and repudiated the agreement, so far as it was in his power to do so, in the most positive and unequivocal manner. The plea of infancy, then, under the circumstances, must prevail."

(2) The Act of 1933 70 provides that a building and loan association may issue shares in the name of a minor not less than 16

(4) The Act of 1939,72 as amended in 1945, provides that an infant 16 years of age may enter into agreements under the Work men's Compensation Act.

Sec. 264. Ratification. Upon attaining his majority, an infant may ratify contracts made during his infancy. "If one who has the right to elect does not exercise it within a reasonable time, but with full knowledge of his privilege, omits or neglects to assert it, his omission may fairly be regarded as the equivalent of an act of affirmance, and as amounting in fact and in law to ratification." 74 It is no longer necessary, in Pennsylvania, that when an infant ratifies a contract he should have knowledge that he might have avoided it. If, with full knowledge of the facts he ratifies or affirms, expressly or by implication, being moved by his own sense of right and duty, he should, in law as in morals, be bound by the affirmance. Dealing with the consideration, after majority, will be considered a ratification.75

Sec. 265. Disaffirmance. 

An infant is vested with power to affirm and perform, or to disavow, at his election, all his contracts of imperfect obligation, either before or within a reasonable time after coming of age, except where real property is involved. It is a well established principle that if an infant elects to rescind, he must do so without qualification or reservation. He may not accept that which is beneficial to him and reject the remainder. If, for example, he executes a purchasemoney mortgage to secure the purchase money for land conveyed to him by deed, he may not, after he comes of age, affirm the deed and at the same time disaffirm the mortgage.' The release in the following case had not been ratified by the infant-she had not reached her majority—and consequently was not binding upon her. 76 

Hollinger v. York Railways, 225 Pa. 417 (1909). An infant executed a release in consideration of the sum of $100, and subsequently brought suit for injuries alleged to have been sustained by reason of defendant's negligence. MESTREZAT, J. "Whether or not she signed it was wholly immaterial, as it was not binding upon her. If by the advice of friends she had agreed when first injured to accept a comparatively nominal sum in payment of her damages, it did not debar her from recovering such damages as she could show the jury at the trial she had actually sustained.” 

Sec. 266. Real Estate. An infant may not disaffirm a purchase or conveyance of real estate, during his minority, except by approval of the orphans' court."

He may do so, in his own right, within a reasonable time after attaining his majority. What is a reasonable time within which to disaffirm depends upon the circumstances. In civil war days it was held that a delay of

Wharen v. Funk, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 133 (1943). The plaintiffs, an infant and her husband, contracted to purchase, as tenants by entireties, certain real estate, but defaulted in the payment of installments, whereupon the property was repossessed in an action of ejectment. The infant then disaffirmed the contract, and she and her husband brought this action to recover the consideration paid by them. "The object is obtained by the avoidance of the contract as to the infant and the return of the consideration paid or the amount expended under the contract by such infant. The right is not given to be exercised for the advantage of others—in the instant case the husband."

Sec. 267. Affirmative Actions. The defense of in fancy must be used as a shield and not as a sword. For this reason an infant may not institute an action to recover what he has parted with, unless he restores, or offers to restore, what he has received. 

Friedman v. Huber, 92 Pa. Superior Ct. 245 (1927). HENDER- 

SON, J. "The plaintiff secured a valuable automobile, as shown by the price to be paid. It nowhere appears in the case that he has returned or offered to return the automobile which he secured by the payment of the amount which he seeks to recover. It is not alleged that the contract was unreasonable, or that any advantage was taken of the plaintiff by the defendant in entering into the contract of sale. The plaintiff having received possession of the defendant's property and the enjoyment of it for a considerable time it should appear that he has attempted at least to restore the status quo.

As this was not done the plaintiff is not in a position to enforce a rescission of the contract."

Sec. 268. Depreciation and Damage. When an in fant disaffirms a contract for necessaries, he must, in the language of the Uniform Sales Act, supra, "return the goods in substantially the same condition as when received." In some jurisdictions this rule is applied to other contracts. Thus, it was held, in New York, that where an infant purchased a bicycle for $45, paid $15 down, agreed to pay $1.25 in weekly installments, used it during the summer months, and then disaffirmed the contract, he ought "to account for its reasonable use or deterioration in value." 80 In this Commonwealth an infant does all that is required by returning the property. As observed in the following case, he may not be held for depreciation, or for damage to the property while in his possession. 

Musser v. Schnock, 95 Pa. Superior Ct. 406 (1928). An infant purchased a new automobile for $1,584.00, trading in an old car for $1,100.00. He gave his note for the balance. While in his possession the new car was damaged and he took it to the defendant for repair. When he demanded it back the defendant refused until he paid the note. He then disaffirmed the entire contract and demanded back the old car. Defendant had sold it. Suit for the value of the old car followed. Defendant conceded the right of the infant to disaffirm, but asserted a right of set-off for the repair bill, as well as depreciation. LINN, J. "An infant, in disaffirming in this state, does all that is required by returning to his vendor, or by tendering to him, the object purchased in whatever condition it may be at the time of its return or tender; it need not be in the condition in which it was when received from the defendant, because by delivering it to the infant the defendant must be presumed to have intended, and to have authorized, the use of the article by the infant; to permit a defendant to assert an infant's obligation to restore the property in its original condition, would, to that extent, be permitting the defendant to enforce his contract against the infant, which is the very thing the policy of the law was intended to prevent. This is in accord with the weight of authority of common law." 

Sec. 269. Defense Actions. In defense actions, or where the infant is made the defendant, an adult may replevy what he had parted with so long as it remains 

80 Rice v. Butler, 160 New York 578 (1899).

209 in the possession or under the control of the infant, but if the infant has lost, wasted, or consumed the consideration, he may not be held accountable for the value of it. 

Yubas v. Witaskis, 95 Pa. Superior Ct. 296 (1928). Plaintiff a bill in equity against the defendant, an infant eighteen years of age, to recover a diamond ring, which he delivered into her possession after they had entered into a contract to marry. 

The chancellor found that the value of the ring was $1,350; that it was given to the defendant upon the express condition, assented to by her, that if she broke the engagement she should and would return it to the plaintiff; that she accepted it upon that condition; that she broke the engagement, but refused and failed to return it to him; and that she sold it for $1,100. A decree was entered ordering the defendant to deliver to the plaintiff within thirty days the ring, or the value thereof, $1,350, in money. In setting aside this decree it was said by GAWTHROP, J. "Although we regard the conduct of the defendant in refusing to return the ring as violative of good morals and common honesty, the plaintiff seems to be without remedy. This is but another case falling within the rule stated in Kent's Com., p. 245, that, 'The hardships which may arise in particular cases must yield to the operation of the general rule founded on public policy, intended to protect persons in fact under age from the danger of imprudent contracts.' The decree is reversed and the bill is dismissed at appellee's costs." 

Part 3. Torts and Crimes of Infants 

Sec. 270. Departure from Bailment. In strict theory an infant is responsible from the earliest age for all offenses against the law of torts. In a majority of the states, if an infant receives property under a contract of bailment, and makes an unauthorized use of it, he may be held liable in tort for any damage to the property during such conversion. 

Towne v. Wiley, 23 Vermont 355 (1851). An infant hired a horse to go from Bellows Falls to Brattleboro and back the same day. He returned by a circuitous route, nearly doubling the distance, and stopped at Westminster at eight o'clock, where he remained until four o'clock in the morning. The night being cold and windy and the horse without shelter of any kind, it took sick and died within a few days. REDFIELD, J. "So long as the defendant kept within the terms of the bailment, his infancy was a protection to him, whether he neglected to take proper care of the

horse, or to drive him moderately. But when he departs from the object of the bailment, it amounts to a conversion of the property, and he is liable as much as if he had taken the horse in the first instance without permission." 82 84 

Sec. 271. Pennsylvania Rule. The rule is otherwise in Pennsylvania.81 "The principle is as well established as any rule of the common law, that a plaintiff cannot convert an action, founded on a contract, into a tort, to deprive an infant of the benefit of a plea of infancy." " 

In Penrose v. Curren 83 the statement of claim alleged that an infant hired a horse and a gig to go to Germantown, but drove to Chester instead, and by hard, severe, unnecessary and cruel driving and treatment killed the horse. But it was held that if plaintiff should succeed, there would be no want of pretences upon which infants might be charged, although it was said, obiter dicta, that if the contract came within the exception of necessaries, such as hiring a horse to visit a sick parent, the infant would be liable for his negligence. The Penal 

Code 4 requires that such extended use be promptly reported, and that compensation be paid therefor, but not "in excess of the rate per mile originally charged or agreed upon." In default thereof the penalty, in the case of hired teams and conveyances, is a fine not exceeding $100 and imprisonment not exceeding 30 days, or both, and liability to the owner in double the amount of the injury done to the property. The penalty for the unauthorized use of an automobile under a contract of hire is a fine not exceeding $200, or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both, but civil liability to the owner is not imposed. It would appear, therefore, that an infant who receives possession of an automobile and who makes an unauthorized use of the property, may be punished under the criminal law, but may not be held for damages to the property.

Sec. 272. Misrepresentation of Age. Misrepresen tation of age is one species of tort. The following case is also cited as indicative of the law in some jurisdictions. 

Rice v. Boyer, 108 Indiana 472 (1886). An infant, representing himself to be of age, purchased a buggy and a set of harness. 

Plaintiff brought an action in tort for deceit. ELLIOTT, C. J. “Our judgment is that where an infant does fraudulently and falsely represent that he is of full age he is liable in an action ex-delicto for the injury resulting from his tort." 

This principle has not been accepted in Pennsylvania, although "an infant running about town, taking up goods on credit, on his assertion that he was of full age, may be indicted as a common cheat." 85 In other words he may be held liable under the criminal laws, but not in a civil action for damages.

Spangler v. Haupt, 53 Pa. Superior Ct. 545 (1913). RICE, P. J. 

"The conclusion that he is liable in such case has support in decisions in some of the states of the union and is ery ably maintained in the opinion of Chief Justice ELLIOTT in Rice v. Boyer, 108 Indiana 472; 9 N. E. Rep. 420. But we are of opinion that the learned trial judge was right in concluding that the weight of authority in Pennsylvania is the other way." 

Sec. 273. Liability of Parents. A parent is not liable for the tort of his infant child unless his negligence has made it possible, or he knows that the infant is committing a tort and makes no effort to restrain him, or the infant is acting under the direction of the parent and furthering his interests or those of the family, or the situation is such that the parent is said to participate in the tortious conduct, either by directing the child's act, by giving his actual consent, or by ratifying and accepting the fruits of it. 

Irvine v. Killen, 109 Pa. Superior Ct. 34 (1983). Defendant conducted a hair dressing establishment. Her son, 18 years of age, lived with her and was employed by the Sun Oil Company at its plant about five miles from their home. She received all of 

85 Curtin v. Patten, 11 S. & R. 305 (1824). wit

her son's wages, and furnished him with an automobile in which to drive to and from his work. While driving home from work the son negligently injured the plaintiff. KELLER, J. "By accepting all the fruits of his employment and furnishing him the means to go to and from his work, he so far became her agent, that she cannot escape liability for an accident due to his negligent operation of the car while on his way to or home from work." 

Sec. 274. Dangerous Instrumentalities. A parent may be negligent in entrusting to a child a dangerous instrumentality, but it is well settled in Pennsylvania that an automobile is not an instrument inherently dangerous.86 If the owner permits an incompetent and unauthorized person to drive it, he will be held liable for the negligence of the driver irrespective of the use of the car.87 A driver's license may not be issued to an infant under the age of eighteen, except to an infant sixteen years of age who includes with his application the written consent of his parent or person in loco parentis to him.88. Where the infant is over the age of sixteen and is furthering his own interests and not those of his parent, the mere fact that he is driving an automobile owned by the parent is not sufficient to render the parent liable for the negligent acts of the infant. It must be shown, in such cases, that the relation of master and servant, or principal and agent, exists, and that the servant or agent is engaged in furthering the interests of the master or principal. 

Kunkle v. Thompson, 67 Pa. Superior Ct. 37 (1917). The lower court found the following facts: "The son lived with his father at Royersford, Montgomery County; was competent to drive and was the only driver of his father's car. The car was a pleasure car for the use of the defendant and his family; the son was permitted by his father to drive the car whenever he desired, and if any members of the family chose to enjoy the car, the son drove it for them. The son had been educated at a business college, had had employment with various persons; had received, with his father's consent, the wages he earned, and out of them clothed and partially educated himself. On the day of the accident, desiring to

213 go to Downingtown in response to a letter offering him a position, he requested his father to permit him to take the car for the journey, first advising him of the purpose of his visit. The father. consented. The son drove to Downingtown alone, and on his return while he was driving the car, the collision with the plaintiff's car occurred." HEAD, J. "Under these circumstances we are unable to reach the conclusion the father had any such interest in the business in which the son was engaged, while operating the car, as would or should justify the assumption the relation of master and servant existed." 

Sec. 275. Crimes. An infant under the age of seven years is conclusively presumed to be incapable of committing a crime. Between the ages of seven and fourteen an infant is presumed to be incapable of doing so, but this is not a conclusive presumption. It may be shown that an infant between these ages understands the difference between right and wrong, and is conscious of wrongdoing. If so, he may be punished under the criminal law. Upwards of the age of fourteen, an infant is presumed to be capable of committing a crime, but this presumption is likewise not conclusive. Unless this presumption is overcome, however, an infant who has attained the age of fourteen may be punished under the criminal law. 

Commonwealth v. Cavalier, 284 Pa. 311 (1925). An infant not quite six months past fourteen years of age was convicted of first degree murder for the killing of his grandmother. He had turned his shirt inside out to hide the blood stains, hid his suit in a closet, carried away money which he hid under his pillow, and attempted to fix the blame on an uncle. Seven bullets were found in the body, although the rifle had to be reloaded before each shot. 

SCHAFFER, J. "BLACKSTONE says: by the law, as it now stands, and has stood at least ever since the time of Edward the Third, the capacity of doing ill, or contracting guilt, is not so much measured by years and days as by the strength of the delinquent's understanding and judgment. For one lad of eleven years old may have as much cunning as another of fourteen; . . . one boy of ten, and another of nine years old, who had killed their companions, have been sentenced to death, and he of ten years actually hanged; because it appeared upon their trials, that the one hid himself, and the other hid the body he had killed; which hiding manifested a consciousness of guilt, and a discretion to discern between good ... 15

and evil. ... Thus, also, in very modern times, a boy of ten years old was convicted on his own confession of murdering his bedfellow; there appearing in his whole behavior plain tokens of a mischievous discretion; and, as the sparing this boy merely on account of his tender years might be of dangerous consequences to the public, by propagating a notion that children might commit such atrocious crimes with impunity, it was unanimously agreed by all the judges that he was a proper subject of capital punishment': Blackstone's Commentaries, vol. 4, pp. 23-4.

We have with great care read the entire record, are satisfied that the defendant committed a murder of the first degree and that there were no errors committed which would justify reversal." 

Part 4. Marriage of Infants Sec. 276. Ceremonial Marriage. A ceremonial mar riage is regulated by statute. No license to marry may issue if either applicant is under the age of sixteen, except as authorized by the judge of the orphans' court in special cases.89 Nor may a license be issued except after three days from the day of making the application, unless authorized by the judge of the orphans' court in cases of emergency or extraordinary circumstances."⁰

The Act of 1945 91 provides that no license to marry shall be issued unless, within 30 days prior thereto, the applicant has been certified free of syphilis, or syphilis in a communicable stage, by a Pennsylvania licensed physician, or medical officer of the Army or Navy, or physician of the Public Health Service of the federal government. If either party is under the age of twenty-one, the consent of the parent or guardian must be given before the clerk of the orphans' court, or certified under the hand of such parent or guardian attested by two adult witnesses, the signature of such parent or guardian to be properly acknowledged before a notary public or other officer competent to receive acknowledgments. 

The Penal Code 92 provides that whoever takes a female child under the age of sixteen years for the purpose of

Sec. 277. Common Law Marriage. Some 21 states and the District of Columbia still recognize common law marriages. “The law of Pennsylvania recognizes common law marriages. But they are a fruitful source of perjury and fraud, and, in consequence, they are to be tolerated, not encouraged.. A common law marriage implies that both parties are able and willing to marry and that they solemnly enter into a contract of marriage, in words of the present tense, for the purpose of establishing the immediate relation of husband and wife. 

If any of these essential requirements is lacking, the relation is illicit and meretricious and not a valid com- 

93 mon law marriage." 98 Under the common law any person over the age of seven, capable of intelligent consent, could enter into a contract of marriage. It could be avoided by a female until she reached the age of twelve, and by a male until he reached the age of fourteen. As said by Blackstone, "If a boy under fourteen, or a girl under twelve years of age, marries, this marriage is only inchoate and imperfect; and, when either of them comes to the age of consent aforesaid, they may disagree and declare the marriage void, without any divorce or sentence in the spiritual court.” ⁹4 It has been held, in 

Pennsylvania, that cohabitation upwards of these ages is equivalent to ratification.95 On June 25, 1941, the

Legislature approved a bill abolishing common law marriage in the future, but on July 1, 1941, the Legislature recalled the measure from the Governor. It will be observed from the following decision that while a common law marriage is still valid, the parties are required to obtain a marriage license in the future, the effect of which is to raise the age at which an infant may con-

Claimant filed a petition under the Workmen's Compensation Act.

That is a matter for the legislature to handle. It is within our province, however, to hold that a valid common-law marriage cannot hereafter be entered into in this Commonwealth without first complying with the Act of 1939 and securing a marriage license pursuant to its provisions. And this holding will go a long way towards eliminating the fraud and perjury so often occurring with respect to common-law marriages; for it would establish a present intention on the part of the applicants to be married, and not merely an intent to have sexual relations."

Part 5. The Insane Sec. 278. Insanity. The contracts of a person bereft of reason may be valid, voidable, or void. Sanity and mental capacity are presumed, and the burden is on him who alleges the contrary. Mere mental weakness, not amounting to inability to comprehend a contract, when unaccompanied by evidence of imposition or undue influence, furnishes no ground for equitable interference. In Patterson v. Snider it was held that evidence that an old man was illiterate, unable to transact business, weak in memory and sloven in dress, was much below the legal standard of required proof of contractual incapacity. 96 

96 Graham v. Pancoast, 30 Pa. 89 (1858). 

97 305 Pa. 272 (1931).
