Fidelity Title & Trust Co. v. Weitzel, 152 Pa. 498 (1898). The master found that the decedent was not insane. She was old, illiterate, and full of eccentricities, and dangerously close to the line that divides the sane from the lunatics; yet she was fully competent to recollect her property and the rent days punctually as they came around, and had sufficient mental capacity to make a contract. MITCHELL, J. "Equity intervenes justly and properly to protect the weak and the aged against imposition by designing people, and even against manifest improvidence though there is no actual fraud in the other party. But on the other hand it is not to be forgotten that the free control and disposition of property is often the sole means in the hands of age, to secure kindly care and attention, as well as support, from others, when greedy relations ignore the claims of relationship to the living but devote themselves with persistent assiduity to the estate after death." 

Sec. 279. Valid Contracts. Contracts may be en forced against a lunatic under three circumstances. 

First, the Uniform Sales Act provides that where necessaries are sold and delivered to a person who by reason of mental incapacity is incompetent to contract, he must pay a reasonable price therefor or return the goods in substantially the same condition as when received, within reasonable time.98 Second, if a contract of a lunatic is made during a lucid interval, or concerning some matter in which he is lucid, or ratified during a lucid interval, it will be binding upon him and his estate. 

Third, if a contract is executed and there has been no judicial finding of insanity, and the party dealing with an insane person does so in good faith and for a valuable consideration, it may not be avoided. 

Beals v. See, 10 Pa. 56 (1848). GIBSON, C. J. "Should he have made a wild and unthrifty purchase from a stranger unapprised of his infirmity, who is to bear the loss that must be incurred by one of the parties to it? Not the vendor, who did nothing that any other man would not have done. As an insane man is civilly liable for his torts, he is liable to bear the consequences of his infirmity, as he is liable to bear his misfortunes, on the principle that where a loss must be borne by one of two innocent persons, it shall be borne by him who occasioned it.” 

98 Act of May 19, 1915, P. L. 543, 69 PS 21.

Sec. 280. Voidable Contracts. There can be no bind ing executory agreement where one of the parties is bereft of reason. An executory contract for necessaries has been noted. In all other matters, if the other party has knowledge of the infirmity, or if there is overreaching and fraud, an insane person may avoid his obligation, and unless it be in his possession or under his control, or that of his guardian, heirs, or representative, he need not restore what he has received. Equitable considerations are invoked in these cases. If a lunatic has received nothing that would swell the corpus of his estate he may be excused upon proof of his insanity, even though the other party did not know of his infirmity. 

Thus, an accommodation endorser of a promissory note, who receives no benefit therefrom either to himself or to his estate, may defend against a bona fide holder on the ground that he was non compos mentis at the time of the indorsement." Liability is usually imposed, however, when a lunatic has been benefited by a contract made in good faith.

Lancaster County Nat. Bank v. Moore, 78 Pa. 407 (1875). PAX- 

SON, J. "It would be an unreasonable and unjust rule that such persons should be allowed to obtain the property of innocent parties, and retain both the property and its price. Here the bank in good faith loaned the defendant the money on his note; the contract was executed so far as the consideration is concerned, and it would be alike derogatory to sound law and good morals that he should be allowed to retain it to swell the corpus of his estate." 

Sec. 281. Void Contracts. Except for necessaries, an adjudication of insanity renders a person incompetent to contract altogether.100 An adjudication of insanity, however, is not conclusive of testamentary incapacity. "It does not necessarily follow that one who is insane and confined to an institution is incapable of making a will." 101

Brennan's Estate, 312 Pa. 335 (1933). Testatrix was an aged maiden woman who had supported herself working as a housekeeper for nearly fifty years. She lived most frugally, was uncommunicative, and kept her business and financial affairs to herself. 

Her disposition was to save continuously and she had accumulated, unknown to her friends, a fund of about $60,000. In 1924 she was adjudged insane, primarily for purposes of observation, and was committed to a hospital where she remained two days. 

According to the testimony of the receiving physician, "she was in good condition for one of her age, seemed to be in an upset state of mind because of her then situation, but was friendly, rather jovial, and he could not understand why she had been put in hospital. She realized the nature of the place, oriented herself readily, and protested at being there." After a parole of six months she was discharged by the hospital. Two years after her commitment she executed a will leaving the bulk of her estate to the husband of her niece. A nephew contested the will on grounds of undue influence and lack of testamentary capacity. The will was prepared by a reputable attorney, who testified as to her intelli gence, memory and capacity. KEPHART, J. "An adjudication of insanity is not conclusive of testamentary incapacity. Testatrix may have been insane at the time adjudged so, but that is not conclusive as to her testamentary capacity two years later. She may well have become infinitely worse, had lucid intervals, or wholly recovered by that time."

Sec. 282. Marriage while Insane. Contracts of marriage, while either party is insane and unable to understand the nature of the transaction, are wholly void, even though the other party be unaware of the defect. 

Nonnemacher v. Nonnemacher, 159 Pa. 634 (1894). Nonnemacher died in the Pennsylvania Hospital for the Insane, to which he had been removed nine days prior to his death. Pauline claimed to have married him twelve days before his death, by Rev. Gardner, and that this marriage legitimated a boy, Franklin. The brothers, sister, and father of the deceased sought to have the marriage set aside on grounds of insanity. PER CURIAM. "The learned court below carefully explained to the jury the question in dispute, and instructed them that if, at the time the marriage was contracted, he was of unsound mind, so that he did not understand the nature and obligation of the contract, they should find for the plaintiffs, and if they should find that at the time of the marriage he was of sound mind, and did understand the nature and obli-

gation of the contract, they should find for the defendant. 

The question was one of pure fact, and the jury after considering it returned a verdict in favor of the defendant. There was ample testimony to justify the verdict, and considering all the circumstances of the case it is difficult to believe there ever could be any other."

Sec. 283. The Intoxicated. At common law a per son could not avoid a contract because of intoxication, on the ground that he should not be allowed to stultify himself. In modern times he may be excused if the intoxication is of such a degree as to render him non compos mentis. The Uniform Sales Act, supra, provides that where necessaries are sold and delivered to a person who by reason of drunkenness is incompetent to contract, he must pay a reasonable price therefor or return the goods in substantially the same condition as when received within reasonable time. In addition, such a person may not avoid a negotiable instrument in the hands of an innocent holder for value.102 Intoxication which does not render a person non compos mentis may be corroborative evidence of overreaching and fraud,103 but it is not, per se, grounds for the avoidance of a contract. 

Wright v. Waller, 127 Alabama 557 (1900). The lower court charged the jury as follows: "If the defendant was so much under the influence of strong drink, or intoxicating liquor that his reason was dethroned to an extent that he could not give that attention to the signing of the note that a reasonably prudent man would be able to give, then the note would be void." MCCLELLAN, C. J. ""To render the transaction voidable he should have been so drunk as to have drowned reason, memory and judgment, and impaired the mental faculties to an extent that would render him non compos mentis for the time being.' Bates v. Voll, 72 Ill. 108. . . . Many perfectly sound and sober men could not bind themselves by contract at all, if the rule laid down (by the trial court) is a sound one."

Part 6. Aliens Sec. 284. Friendly Aliens. The incapacity of friendly aliens is for the most part historical. Under the common law an alien could "purchase lands, or other estates; but not for his own use, for the king is thereupon entitled to them." 104 

The Act of 1791 105 provides that aliens may dispose of personalty by will or otherwise, and take, hold, and dispose of real property by devise or descent. The Act of 1861 106 provides that aliens may hold lands but not exceeding 5,000 acres nor of an annual income of $20,000. Otherwise an alien enjoys full power of contract. As said by Mr. Justice 

WILLIAMS, "He may embark in business, become a stockholder in a joint stock association or corporation, become a manager or director, when not expressly made ineligible, and use, enjoy, control, and direct his property, of whatever nature or kind, in the same manner as any natural citizen may do." 107

Sec. 285. Alien Enemies. Contracts with alien ene mies are void. Obligations, private rights and remedies which existed prior to the outbreak of war are merely suspended, however, during the continuance of the war. 

Arnold v. Ellison, 96 Pa. Superior Ct. 118 (1928). Plaintiffs, doing business in Germany, sued defendants, doing business in Philadelphia and London, for goods sold and delivered prior to the outbreak of the First World War. CUNNINGHAM, J. "Obviously, no suit having been brought within six years from the date when the debt became demandable, the statute of limitations (Act of 

March 27, 1713, 1 Sm. 176, Sec. 1) would bar a recovery had it not been for the interruption in the running of the statute resulting from the war between Germany and the United States which began on April 6, 1917. As between the citizens of two belligerent countries, war suspends all rights of action, and during its continuance stays the running of the statute of limitations. When peace is restored, private rights and remedies are revived and the statute of limitations again becomes operative."

CHAPTER VII  Part 1. 

Married Women Sec. 286. Common Law Disabilities. Following are the disabilities of a married woman at common law as described by Blackstone. Real estate owned by her prior to her marriage, or acquired during her coverture, became subject to her husband's interest, which gave him the right to receive the rents and profits absolutely, except real estate which had been settled upon her for her separate use. Her chattels so acquired became his absolutely. He could also liquidate her choses in action. Her earnings, during coverture, belonged to him, and after his death, to his estate. Her prenuptial debts devolved upon him and he assumed exclusive liability for most of her prenuptial torts. Injuries to her person or property were redressed with his concurrence, and in his name, as well as her own. 

She had no power to contract, except as his agent, or for necessaries for which he was obliged to pay. All deeds and acts done by her were void, except it be a fine or like matter of record, as to which she was required to be secretly examined. He could not grant anything to her, for that would suppose her separate existence, or covenant with her, for that would be only to covenant with himself. "The husband also, by the old law, might give his wife moderate correction." This unusual status had its origin in the following legal fiction: "By marriage, the husband and wife are one person in law; that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband: under whose wing, protection, and cover, she performs every thing. . . Upon this principle, of union of person in husband and wife, depend almost all the legal rights, duties, and disability, that either of them acquire by the marriage. so great a favourite is the female sex of the laws of 

England." 1 

11 Black. Com., Chap. 15. ... 222

Sec. 287. Remedial Statutes. The common law dis abilities of married women have, for the most part, been removed by statute and judicial decision. Chronologically, the Act of 18482 provides that the husband shall no longer be liable for his wife's prenuptial debts, and that the wife's estate shall continue to belong to her after the marriage and be subject to her own debts and obligations. The Act of 18513 provides that a married woman may loan money to her husband and take therefrom a judgment or mortgage as security. The Act of 

1872 * provides that a married woman may institute an action to recover her separate earnings and property.

The Act of 1892 5, as amended, provides that a married woman may sue and be sued in all civil actions, but may not sue her husband except in a proceeding for divorce and to recover her separate property. The Act of 1911° provides that she may make a conveyance to her husband. The husband is no longer liable for the torts of his wife, except those committed in his presence or at his command.' It is still the common law of Pennsylvania, however, that a wife may not sue her husband for tortious acts. This principle is based on the "policy of preserving domestic peace and felicity." She may sue her husband's employer if she is injured through his negligence while he is acting within the scope of his employment. She may also prosecute a claim against her husband under the Workmen's Compensation Act.'

Sec. 289. Liability for Necessaries. Unless for feited by her misconduct, a husband is bound to provide for his wife according to his ability. If they are living together there is a prima facie presumption that the wife purchasing necessaries does so with the authority and consent of the husband. The Act of 1848 22 provides that the wife may also be liable for necessaries furnished for the support of the family, but only where she has entered into an express contract to assume this obligation when the goods are purchased.23 The action should be brought against husband and wife jointly, and execution should first issue against the husband.

If the goods are not necessaries and are purchased by the wife on her credit, she alone is liable." If, through his misconduct, he causes her to withdraw from his home, or abandons his family, she may bind him with third parties for the purchase of necessaries. It has been held that this liability "did not cover money horrowed by the wife as that was not an equivalent of the things which a husband was obliged to furnish his wife under the classification of necessaries." 25 

Sec. 290. Forfeiture of Necessaries. If, through no fault of his own, the wife leaves his home and refuses to cohabit with him, the husband is not responsible for debts which the wife may contract in his name, and those who give credit to her do so at their peril. It has been held, however, that the only justification for non-support is such conduct on the part of the wife as would entitle the husband to a divorce.26

Sec. 291. Power to Contract. The Act of 1893,27 

until amended in 1945, provided that a married woman had the same power to contract as an unmarried person, except that she could not become an accommodation endorser, maker, guarantor or surety for another and could not execute or acknowledge a deed conveying or mortgaging her real estate unless her husband joined in the mortgage or conveyance. In discussing this statute it was said by Mr. Justice STERN: "This does not grant her any choice or discretion, but is an absolute interdiction of her acting in any of the capacities referred to. The purpose of the legislation is to prevent her from yielding to the temptation to assist others, especially her husband, with her own financial resources, even though such protection may be unwelcome and run counter to her earnest desires; it represents the remnant of a public policy rooted in an almost immemorial past." 28

As amended in 1945,29 she now enjoys the same power to contract as a married man, except only that she may not execute or acknowledge a deed conveying her real property without the joinder of her husband. 

By this amendment, Pennsylvania finally brought about the contractual emancipation of married women, excepting only the conveyance of real estate. In other words, a married woman may now act as accommodation endorser, maker, guarantor or surety for another, she may mortgage her real estate without the joinder of her hus- 

27 Act of June 8, 1893, P. L. 344, 48 PS 21, 32. 

28 First National Bank v. Walsh, 

20 Act of May 17, 1945. P. L. 625, 48 PS 31.

band, and except for the conveyance of her real estate, she enjoys the same power to contract as a married man. 

The amendment is prospective only.

Sec. 292. Contracts under Act of 1893. The Act of 

1893 has been a prolific source of litigation, and such litigation is likely to continue as to the prohibited transactions which may have been executed prior to the amendment of 1945. For this reason it may be noted that the prohibitions of the Act of 1893 applied only to technical contracts in violation of its provisions.30 It did not prevent husband and wife or a married woman and any other person, from joining in the execution of an obligation in which they both had a pecuniary interest. 31

In a prohibited transaction, the courts looked through all disguises and subterfuges, where the evidence indicated a manifest intention to avoid the provisions of the statute.32 They were void.33 A judgment confessed on such an obligation, however, was voidable only, and unless a married woman petitioned to have such a judgment opened in order to enable her to assert the defense of incapacity without unnecessary delay, she was barred from this relief.34 Many banks in Pennsylvania used a special form in making loans to a married woman. It required her to certify that she did not sign in any of the prohibited capacities, but it proved to be ineffective. As said by the Supreme Court, "A disability created by law cannot be removed by the disabled party's lying about it." 36 The Act of 1893 lost much of its significance, however, when the Supreme Court ruled, in 1939, that a person who loaned money to a married woman, was not required to ascertain whether it was borrowed for or applied to a purpose prohibited by the statute.37 35

Sec. 293. Deeds and Mortgages. A married woman may not convey her real estate without the joinder of her husband. It has been held, however, that she could not repudiate a contract to sell and retain both the land and the purchase money. Thus, where she agreed to sell her real estate and received the purchase price, and the purchaser went into possession and made valuable improvements, she could not repudiate her agreement on the ground that her husband refused to sign the deed, without returning the consideration and accounting for the expenditures.38 She may now mortgage her real estate without the joinder of her husband. Her husband enjoys the same privilege as to property owned by him, and it has been held that if the property is subsequently sold to satisfy the mortgage, her interest is cut off.39 

Husband and wife both enjoy the right to inherit a share of the estate of each other, however, and if no restrictions were imposed upon either party, it would be a simple matter to dispose of real estate without the joinder of the other spouse by the expedient of defaulting on a mortgage. It has been said of the husband that he could "give away or squander his property and thus reduce himself and wife to poverty, according to the authorities; but no case has gone so far as to sustain a voluntary obligation given and received with intent to defraud the wife's rights." 40 In other words, she may defeat a fraudulent scheme to deprive her of the interest to which she would otherwise be entitled. Presumably the same rule will be applied as to a mortgage executed by her, if the intent is to deprive her husband of his inheritable interest in her estate. 

Sec. 294. Feme Sole Trader. The phrase, "feme sole trader," is used to describe a married woman who, notwithstanding her marriage, has the same contractual power as an unmarried woman. There are a number of statutes which confer upon a married woman the status 

38 McCoy v. Niblick & McCormick, 221 Pa. 123 (1908). 

30 Mitchell v. Mitchell, 8 Pa. 126 (1848). 

40 Hummel's Estate, 161 Pa. 215.

of a feme sole trader, or which empower her to dispose of her property as though her husband were legally dead. 

They may be summarized as follows: (1) The wife of an absent mariner is a feme sole trader.¹1 (2) Whenever a married man neglects or refuses to provide for his wife, either because of drunkenness, profligacy or other cause, his wife has all the privileges of a feme sole trader.42 She may petition the court of common pleas for a certificate to that effect, in order to assure others of her right to dispose of her separate property, but the certificate merely acts as judicial recognition of an existing fact.43 (3) Whenever husband and wife reside together under the same roof, and the husband has failed to support his wife or family for a period of five years or more, although there is no desertion; or whenever husband and wife have lived apart for one year or more and all marital relations between them have ceased, and the husband, for one year or more has not supported his wife or their children, in either of these two circumstances the wife may petition the court of common pleas to be decreed a feme sole trader. 

Her separate property is then subject to her free and absolute disposal during her life, she may dispose of it by will, and if she does not do so it will go to her next of kin.44 (4) Whenever husband and wife have entered into articles of separation, and the husband has released all his interest in the real estate of his wife, the agreement, when recorded, empowers the wife to dispose of it without the joinder of her husband.45 (5) Whenever a wife is granted a legal separation from her husband, she may encumber or dispose of her real estate.40 46

Sec. 296. Dower Interest. A married man may convey his real estate without the joinder of his wife. If she signs an agreement with her husband for the sale of his real estate, she may be compelled to join in a deed conveying the estate.¹º Inasmuch as a father may disinherit his children, such children would have no inheritable interest in real property sold by him during his lifetime. The wife has an inheritable interest in the real property of her husband, however, and the Act of 

1917 50 provides that if she survives her husband, and has not joined in the conveyance of such property, she becomes a tenant in common with whoever owns the land at the time of her husband's death, and will be entitled to receive the same proportion of the estate as though her husband had never disposed of it. This is known as a widow's statutory dower interest in the lands of her husband which he has conveyed during his lifetime without her joining in the deed. 

Bridgeford v. Groh, 306 Pa. 566 (1932). Decedent died in 1926, survived by his widow, Mary, to whom he was married in 1893. 

One child was born to this union. In 1914 he and another woman, Helen, obtained a marriage license and went through a marriage ceremony in a Philadelphia church. Two children were born to this union. In 1919 he purchased certain real estate for the sum of $8,000, which was subject to a mortgage of $4,000. He added a second mortgage in the sum of $3,000, and then conveyed the land, subject to the two mortgages, to Helen. His wife, Mary, did not join in the conveyance. In 1921 Helen conveyed the property to the defendants free of encumbrance. Decedent joined with her in this conveyance. Defendants demolished the old structures then on the land and erected a new building. When decedent died his wife, Mary, instituted this action to recover her dower interest in the land. In deciding that she was entitled only to a one-half share in her husband's equity at the time he conveyed the property, rather than the value of the property at the time of her husband's death, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. In the instant case, title came to the defendants from the reputed wife to whom the prior deed had been made and there was nothing to indicate to them that she was not the lawful spouse of her husband; indeed, everything indicated that she was. Part 2. Joint Estates Sec. 297. Kinds of Joint Estates. It is possible to create different kinds of estates between two or more persons. These estates are known as (1) tenancy in common, (2) joint tenancy, (3) tenancy by the entirety, and (4) tenancy in partnership. The peculiarities of partnership property will be pointed out in the chapter on partnerships. The first three of these estates will be referred to throughout the text. 

Sec. 298. Tenancy in Common. A tenancy in common is an estate owned by two or more persons who have a part interest in the whole. This interest may be onehalf, one-third, or any other fraction. "Tenants in common are such as hold by several and distinct titles, but by unity of possession; because none knoweth his own severalty, and therefore they all occupy promiscuously." 51 

This estate, unlike a joint tenancy, does not pass to the survivor. "Tenants in common may sell their respective shares. They are compellable to make partition. They are liable to reciprocal actions of waste and of account; and if one turns the other out of possession, an action of ejectment will lie against him." 52 The share of a tenant in common is subject to the claims of his creditors, and it will pass to his heirs after his death. 

The common law favored joint tenancies over tenancies in common. This rule of the common law was abolished 

51 2 Black. Com. 191. 

52 Stuckey v. Keefe's Executors, 26 

Pa. 397 (1856).

by the Act of 1812.53 Under this statute the co-ownership of real estate is construed to be a tenancy in common and not a joint tenancy, unless the parties expressly create a joint tenancy. 

Sec. 299. Joint Tenancy. A joint tenancy is an estate owned by two or more persons, the whole of which will pass to the survivor. Blackstone calls the right of survivorship the grand incident of joint estates. The characteristics of this estate are unity of interest, unity of title, unity of time, and unity of possession. It is "well settled in this state that a joint tenancy with right of survivorship is severable by the action, voluntary or involuntary, of either of the parties." 55 The interest of each tenant is an equal part in the whole. This interest is subject to the claims of the creditors of each cotenant. The Act of 1936 56 provides that the accrual to a surviving joint tenant of the interest of a deceased joint tenant, shall be taxable under the Transfer Inheritance Tax Act. The fractional part taxable is to be ascertained by dividing the value of the whole property by the number of joint tenants. The constitutionality of this act has been upheld, notwithstanding unequal contributions to the fund.57

Tenancy by entireties is one of the last, and one of the most important, relicts of the common law fiction of the unity of person of husband and wife. As expressed in Bracton's maxim, "Man and wife are as one person, for they are one in flesh and blood." 58 On this point, Pennsylvania accepted the common law as pronounced by Blackstone: 59 "And therefore, if an estate in fee be given to a man and his wife, they are neither properly joint tenants, nor tenants in com-

Sec. 303. Creditors of Tenants. One of the chief characteristics of a tenancy by entireties, is the immunity of such an estate from the claims of the separate creditors of either the husband or the wife. In other words, the property may not be sold in satisfaction of judgments which a creditor may have obtained against the husband and wife separately.si In McCurdy v. Vanning, a creditor who had obtained a judgment against the husband, purchased the husband's interest and brought ejectment against the husband and the wife, but it was held that during their joint lives the estate was immune from the creditors of either. The rule is the same as to the creditors of the husband, though he furnished the purchase price, part of which was a mortgage, and satisfied the remaining payments after becoming insolvent. It has been held that although the husband has been adjudicated a bankrupt, he and his wife could still convey a marketable title.* The Supreme Court has observed, in the case of bank accounts, that to rule otherwise "would cause tens of thousands of deposits, long made in reliance on the established rule of this Court, to be subject to the action of the creditors of either the husband or the wife." 85 The rule is otherwise if the creditor obtains a joint judgment against both husband and wife.86 A mortgage executed by both is a technical conveyance, and they are both bound thereby. A mortgage by one spouse alone would create an enforceable lien only if such spouse were the last survivor. A distinction is also made with respect to partnerships. "There can be no doubt that under existing law in this state a husband and wife may be partners in a business." 88 In such a case, property owned by them and used in the partnership business, becomes the property of the partnership, and is subject to the 87 81 Arch

Sec. 306. Divorce of Tenants. In a majority of states, an absolute divorce causes a tenancy by entireties to revert to a tenancy in common. In 1907 the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania ruled that the same estate should continue in effect,102 although admitting in a later decision that as between the parties, they become "tenants in common so far as the rents are concerned,” each being entitled to an equal share.103 It has also been held that each former spouse is entitled to one-half the fair rental value of the property where the other former spouse continues to reside therein.104 Neither former spouse, however, is entitled to a partition of the property.105

This status continues until either former spouse invokes the Act of 1927.106 Under this statute the property will be sold and the proceeds divided equally between them, subject to any lien entered of record against them jointly. This act is prospective only, and has no application to tenancies by the entirety acquired prior thereto.107

As to such property the tenancy by entireties continues until the death of one of the parties, even though divorced, unless they both join in the alienation of the property.

An estate by entireties which is purchased by a husband with his own funds, is subject to the Federal Gift Tax.110 The amount of the tax is based upon the interest of the donee spouse, both as to the income and as the survivor, in accordance with actuarial tables.111 An estate held by the entireties is also subject to the Federal Estate Tax, less the consideration actually contributed toward the purchase price by the surviving spouse.112

CHAPTER VIII  

Part 1. Caveat Emptor 

Law and Morals. 

Sec. 308. 

Law and morals are relative concepts.¹ Laws are rules of civil conduct. 

Morals are ideal principles of human conduct. The object of law is to regulate human behavior. The object of morals is to perfect human character. "The one aims to prevent and redress actual wrong; the other to regulate those sentiments of the mind which prompt to outward action. Like concentric circles of unequal circumference they embrace ground common to both; but there are sound moral maxims which fall beyond the sphere of jurisprudence."2 Law and morals frequently coincide, but not infrequently are at variance with each other. It is said that they have a common origin, but if so the point of divergence is lost in obscurity. At times they grow in opposition, but ultimately become reconciled. As Dean Pound has said, there is a "constant progression" of moral ideals to legal precepts. "That which started as a moral principle became an equitable principle and then a rule of law." The persistent recurrence of this phenomenon is persuasive of the influence of morality in the development of the law. 

Aside from the concurrence and infusion of moral and legal principles, practical difficulties are involved in the administration of perfect justice. 

Strickland v. Lomm, 70 Fed. 631 (1895). SEYMOUR, D. J. "The law works with blunt tools. Fallible memories, prejudiced statements, intentional falsehood, the bias of self interest, ignorance, and stupidity, are all concomitants of much of the testimony from which she has to make up her judgments. General rules, applicable to the majority of cases, but sometimes having an oppressive bearing upon particular ones, make up the principles upon which, of necessity, she founds her decisions, for the law must be workable." 

1 Tanner, "Law and Morals in Business Transactions," Vol. 8, Am. Law. 

School Rev., May, 1938. 3 

2 Phipps v. Buckman, 30 Pa. 401 (1858). 

3 "Law and Morals," 33. 241

Sec. 309. Meaning of Caveat Emptor. It has been said that the "general rule of law is a requirement of good faith in mutual dealings," and that the maxim caveat emptor, "let the buyer beware," is an exception.*

This maxim is not a rule of good faith, as that expression is commonly understood. In the interpretation of language, good faith means that we conscientiously desire to arrive at the truth, that we honestly use all means to do so, that we strictly adhere to it when known to us, that we shun subterfuges, quibbles, and political shuffling, and that we avoid anything that would render a transaction unconscionable. But caveat emptor is hardly a calamity. Legal principles are not designed to protect a man from his indolence, carelessness or indifference, or from his own overweening confidence and self-delusion. Whatever the maxim may have meant years ago, however, it has now become so hedged about by legal restrictions designed to protect the buyer that it amounts to little more than this: That whenever a person has an opportunity to inspect, or does inspect that which he buys, he is responsible for all that his inspection ought to have revealed." 

Rothermel v. Phillips, 292 Pa. 371 (1928). Plaintiff purchased a small country store from the defendants for the sum of $7,000, after an examination of the stock by two persons selected by him. 

At the conclusion of this appraisement defendant expressed his opinion that it was his belief that the stock was worth $8,000. 

After taking possession the plaintiff discovered many articles not to be in a salable condition. SADLER, J. "If knowledge of the fact, claimed to have been misrepresented, is equally obtainable by either party on inquiry, and the buyer has been given full opportunity to determine the truth for himself, he cannot subsequently complain."

Sec. 310. Appraisal of Caveat Emptor. The prac tical application of the maxim, caveat emptor, allows a wide latitude for the interplay of moral forces. Under many circumstances it tolerates a cunning reserve on 

4 Strickland v. Lomm, 70 Fed. 631 (1895). 

5 Thomas v. Cohen, 275 Pa. 576 (1923).

the part of either party to the contract, or a shrewd acquiescence in another's ignorance or misapprehension. 

There may be, and frequently is, information in the possession of one party to the agreement which, within certain limitations, he is under no legal duty to disclose. "A purchaser is not bound by our laws to make the man he buys from as wise as himself." According to the highest standards of business ethics, "both buyer and seller have the moral right to all the available data upon which an agreement of purchase and sale is based." 

Professor Isaacs has said that in any sense in which caveat emptor "can be taken to indicate any immunity on the part of the seller, it is not law." " Of course not, if this means any sanction for legal misconduct within the existing framework of the law. Caveat emptor is a maxim of indifference, not a rule of positive obligation. 

To the extent that it is not restricted in its application, it not only furnishes an immunity for unethical conduct, but it also tends to establish a double standard of morality. A great many men would welcome an opportunity to conduct business on a higher plane if their competitors were compelled to do likewise. 

Part 2.

Sec. 311. Nature of Express Warranty. The seller is responsible for his warranty, express or implied. According to Professor Williston, "There is no more troublesome word in the law than the word 'warranty.'""

As the law developed in England, and in all the states in this country except Pennsylvania, a warranty is a statement of fact, or, according to the older jurisdictions, an intent to make a statement as a matter of fact, and not as matter of opinion. 

6 Harris V. Tyson, 24 Pa. (1855). Warranties 

Mitchell v. Pinckney, 127 Iowa 696 (1905). The seller of 21 head of cows said that they were sound. In an action for breach 347 

Sharp & Fox, "Business Ethics," 

8 "The Consumer at Law," Annals, May, 1934.

of warranty, he denied liability on the ground, inter alia, that the buyer did not, in so many words, rely upon this statement. 

DEEMER, J. "But it is not necessary that proof of reliance thereon be by the positive testimony of the buyer. It is sufficient if, considering all the circumstances, such fact fairly appears. Indeed, we have held that where the warranty is a part of the contract of sale, and a part of the consideration of the purchase price, the purchaser need not show by direct evidence that he relied upon it, as the law will presume that he did."

Pennsylvania alone insisted upon an agreement to be bound. Professor Williston attributes this to the strong bent given to the law by Chief Justice GIBSON a century ago.10

McFarland v. Newman, 9 Watts 55 (1839). Plaintiff instituted an action for breach of warranty in the sale of a horse. The lower court held that "a positive averment, made by the defendant at the time of the contract," was an express warranty. In overruling this conclusion it was said by GIBSON, C. J. "Though, to constitute a warranty requires no particular form of words, the naked averment of fact is neither a warranty of itself nor evidence of it. In connection with other circumstances, it certainly may be taken into consideration; but the jury must be satisfied, from the whole, that the vendor actually, and not constructively, consented to be bound for the truth of his representation." 

Sec. 312. Express Warranty Defined. 

vania adopted the Uniform Sales Act in 1915." ing to this statute, any affirmation of fact, or any promise by the seller relating to the goods, is an express warranty if the natural tendency of such affirmation or promise is to induce the buyer to purchase the goods, and if the buyer purchases the goods relying thereon. 

But as late as 1929, fourteen years after the Uniform

Sales Act was adopted, the Supreme Court still quoted with approval the doctrine laid down by Chief Justice GIBSON, and asserted that neither a "naked averment of a fact," nor "mere representations," are warranties.¹2

Whether the citizens of Pennsylvania are capable of being bound by the truth of their assertions, would appear

Sec. 313. Statements of Opinion. A statement as to value or prospectus, or any statement purporting to express an opinion, other than the opinion of an expert, is neither a warranty nor fraudulent representation. "The seller extols, and the buyer depreciates the value of the commodity. For everything untruly said or done by either, sound morals will hold him to account; but the law allows the avarice of mankind thus to play in its orbit, until, by falsehood, damage has been done." ¹¹

It is interesting to contrast the law and morals involved in this conflict. The learned Judge HAND has said: "There are some kinds of talk which no sensible man takes seriously, and if he does he suffers from his credulity. If we were all scrupulously honest, it would not be so; but, as it is, neither party usually believes what the seller says about his own opinions, and each knows it." 15 

13 C. D. Brown & Co., Inc. v. Stand ard Hide Co., 301 Pa. 543 (1930). 

14 Note 2 supra. 

18 Vulcan Metals Co., Inc. v. Simmons Mfg. Co., 248 Fed. 853 (1918).

The ethicist is inclined to reply, and not without some justification, that is a legal excuse for plain dishonesty. A lie is immoral, whether it be expressed as an opinion or in a statement of fact which manifestly is a matter of opinion. Whether or not this problem is capable of a more satisfactory solution, there are sound reasons for a higher degree of truthfulness in the business world. As expressed by Professors Sharp and Fox, "Business Ethics." p. 49, "The man who tells the truth is a creator alike of confidence and of morale. He renews our faith in human nature; some of his strength passes over into us; our eyes, which had perhaps become dulled, see in him our deepest admirations incorporated in a living person, and what we admire in him we can not help wishing to possess ourselves; as we tend to pass our resentment at individual ill treatment on to the world about us, so we tend to pass on to others our personal gratitude for his fair treatment of us; as we see him shoulder his share of the burden we become more willing to shoulder our share too; as he makes it easier for those about him to play a straight game he makes it easier for us to play a straight game." 17

Deming v. Darling, 148 Mass. 504 (1889). The vendor of a bond stated that it was "A No. 1," the very best and safest, and that a railroad was good security for it, etc. HOLMES, J. "It is settled that the law does not exact good faith from a seller in those vague commendations of his wares which manifestly are open to difference of opinion. . . . The rule of law is hardly to be regretted, when it is considered how easily and insensibly words of hope or expectation are converted by an interested memory into statements of quality and value, when the expectation has been disappointed." 

Sec. 314. Implied Warranties. An implied war ranty is a warranty which is automatically annexed to a contract, either at common law, or by direction of the legislature. The recognition of implied warranties, as incorporated in the Uniform Sales Act,16 has been one of the most significant developments of the law in modern times. The first of such warranties are called implied warranties of title. Unless a contrary intention appears, there is:- (1) An implied warranty on the part of the seller that in the case of a sale he has a right to sell the goods, and that in the case of a contract to sell he will have a right to sell the goods at the time when the property is to pass. (2) An implied warranty that the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods as against any lawful claims existing at the time of the sale. (3) An implied warranty that the goods shall be free at the time of the sale from any charge or encumbrance in favor of any third person, not declared or known to the buyer before or at the time when the contract or sale is made. (4) This section shall not, however, be held to render liable a sheriff, auctioneer, mortgagee, or other person professing to sell by virtue of authority in fact or law goods in which a third person has a legal or equitable interest. 

Sec. 315. Merchantable Quality. If the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied warranty as regards defects which such examination ought to have revealed. In the sale of goods by description, however, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall correspond with the description. And in a sale by sample, 18 Note 11 supra.

there is an implied warranty that the bulk shall correspond with the sample in quality. The most generally accepted implied warranty at common law was that of merchantable quality where goods were sold by a manufacturer or grower. A significant change appears in the 

Uniform Sales Act. Where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description, whether he be the grower or manufacturer or not, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be of merchantable quality. And in a sale by sample, if the seller is a dealer in goods of that kind, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be free from any defect rendering them unmerchantable which would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. 

The obvious purpose of these provisions is to impose upon merchants, as well as the manufacturer or grower, the warranty of merchantable quality. 

Peerless Electric Co. v. Call, 82 Pa. Superior Ct. 550 (1924).

Plaintiff sold to the defendant certain electric fans, and instituted this action to recover the price. Defendant averred, in the affidavit of defense, that there were latent defects in the fans which caused a general lack of functioning on the part of the motors, so that they did not run at all or with little or no degree of strength. 

The lower court decided that the affidavit was insufficient to prevent judgment. In deciding otherwise, it was said by TREXLER, J. "Certainly when this defendant bought the fans there was an implied warranty that the goods would raise the wind and were adapted for that purpose and merchantable." 

Sec. 316. Sale of Food. In a few states it is held that a sale of food in a restaurant is not a sale of goods within the meaning of the Uniform Sales Act, and not subject to the warranties therein provided, but the rule in Pennsylvania is the other way.

West v. Katsafanas, 107 Pa. Superior Ct. 118 (1932). Plaintiff ordered a pork sandwich, pie, and coffee. After eating a portion of the sandwich, which proved to be not palatable, he became so ill that it was necessary for him to be taken to the hospital, where his symptoms showed that he was suffering from poisoning. The principal question involved was whether the restaurant keeper was liable under an implied warranty that the food he served was fit

for human consumption. BALDRIGE, J. "Undoubtedly, if one purchases a sandwich, or piece of pie, or other food, to be carried away and eaten, it constitutes a sale and the seller is liable. 

To conclude that he is not subject to pay damages if the food is eaten on the premises, but if carried to the pavement and there consumed, he is liable, is inconsistent and not in accord with sound reasoning. The evil consequences in the one case are the same as in the other. To attempt to establish a distinction as to liability is not practicable." 

Sec. 317. Fitness for Purpose. Generally, there is no implied warranty that goods shall be suitable for a particular purpose, but the Uniform Sales Act provides that if the buyer, expressly or by implication, makes known to the seller the particular purpose for which the goods are required, and it appears that the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgment, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be reasonably fit for such purpose. An implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for a particular purpose may also be annexed by the usage of trade. 

Marbury Lumber Co. v. Stearns Mfg. Co., 32 Kentucky 739 (1908). A lumber company needed a locomotive to haul logs to its mill. It ordered a locomotive from a manufacturer, setting forth specifically such items as the gauge of its tracks, the weight of its rails, its steepest grades, its mileage, the weight of its trains, and the fuel it used. The locomotive furnished failed to do the work, whereupon the lumber company gave notice of breach of warranty and offered to return it. The manufacturer refused to accept it and instituted this action to recover the price. HOBSON, J. "We think the case falls within the following rule as laid down by Benjamin on Sales, sec. 988: 'Where a manufacturer or dealer contracts to supply an article which he manufactures or produces or in which he deals, to be applied to a particular purpose, so that the buyer necessarily trusts to the judgment or skill of the manufacturer or dealer, there is in that case an implied term of warranty that it shall be reasonably fit for that purpose to which it is to be applied.'"

Sec. 318. Patent or Trade Name. In the case of a contract to sell or a sale of a specified article under its patent or other trade name, there is no implied warranty as to its fitness for any particular purpose.

Grand Avenue Hotel Co. v. Wharton, 79 Fed. 43 (1897). A 

hotel company at Kansas City, Missouri, ordered two "Harrison

Safety Boilers" with certain specifications as to material and construction. The manufacturer delivered exactly what had been ordered. Upon installation it was discovered that the boilers were not suitable for use at that location due to the sediment in the water taken from the Missouri River. The purchaser then contended that there was a breach of warranty. LOCHREN, D. J. "There is no claim that the boilers did not in every respect conform to this contract and specifications, nor any claim that they were defective, either in respect to workmanship or material. The purchaser did not exact a warranty that the boilers would operate with the muddy waters of the Missouri river, and therefore assumed that risk itself."

Sec. 319. Waiver of Warranties. The parties may waive an implied warranty by contract, but an express warranty does not of itself operate as a waiver of an implied warranty unless it is inconsistent with it. Nor will an implied warranty be set aside by implication. 

An express provision is necessary for that purpose. 

Bekkevold v. Potts, 173 Minn. 87 (1927). This was an action to recover money paid on a Fordson tractor and equipment. According to the evidence there was an implied warranty that the goods were to be suitable for a particular purpose. The contract, however, contained the following provision: "No warranties have been made in reference to said motor vehicle by the seller to the buyer unless expressly written hereon at the date of purchase."

None were written. In holding that this clause did not negative the implied warranty indicated above, it was said by WILSON, C. J. "Defendants' claim does not commend itself to us as consistent with the honesty of purpose with which they are entitled to be credited in their dealings with their customers. The doctrine of implied warranty should be extended rather than restricted." 

Part 3. Actions by the Consumer Sec. 320. Liability of Manufacturer. One of the most interesting developments in modern times has been the recognition of the liability of a manufacturer to the consumer. Historically the consumer was not permitted to recover from the manufacturer, either in contract or in tort. In a famous English case, decided in

1842," the driver of a mail coach, who sustained personal injuries when a defective wheel collapsed, brought an action against the person who had supplied the coaches and who had agreed to keep them in repair. Recovery was denied for lack of privity of contract between the parties to the action. The necessity of privity as a requisite to a recovery in tort is something of an anomaly, but the doctrine became firmly entrenched in this country. In the case of personal injuries, however, three exceptions have since become standard, namely, (1) the distribution of dangerous substances, as in the case of defective or mislabled drugs, contaminated foods and beverages, and poisonous lotions; (2) fraudulent representation by the manufacturer; and (3) negligence in some respect in the construction or sale of a thing not eminently dangerous. 

Kuelling v. Roderick Lean Mfg. Co., 183 New York 78 (1905).

Plaintiff purchased a horse-drawn road roller from an implement dealer. There was a large knot-hole in the underside of the tongue which the manufacturer had concealed by plugging it with wood. 

This and another knot-hole were then covered with putty and paint. While using the roller the tongue broke, the horses ran away, and plaintiff suffered serious injuries. He brought this action against the manufacturer. The trial court granted a nonsuit. In awarding a new trial, it was said by BARTLETT, J. "In the case at bar we have, not only fraudulent deceit and concealment, but what amounts to an affirmative representation that the tongue of the roller was sound, as the manufacturer, by filling the defect with putty and painting the entire surface, so that the eye could not detect any weakness by reason of the knot, knot-hole filled up, the kind of wood employed, and the fact that it was cross-grained, must be held to have represented that the roller as offered for sale was in a perfectly marketable condition."

Sec. 321. Property Damage. In the Restatement of the Law of Torts, the liability of the manufacturer to the consumer is limited to personal injuries.18 A few states permit a recovery for property damage, but this is a recent development. The following case is a land-

He instituted this action against the manufacturer for breach of warranty, based upon its advertisement that its windshield would not "fly or shatter under the hardest impact." "It would be unjust to recognize a rule that would permit manufacturers of goods to create a demand for their products by representing that they possess certain qualities which they in fact do not possess, and then because there is no privity of contract existing between the consumer and the manufacturer deny the consumer the right to recover damages resulting from the absence of those qualities, when such absence is not readily noticeable." 

Sec. 322. Original Package Doctrine. "A manu facturer who puts upon the market food intended for human consumption in a sealed bottle or original package is held to represent to each purchaser, even though the purchase is made through a dealer, that the contents thereof are wholesome and suitable for the purpose for which they are sold." 20 On the other hand, "The rule of non-liability of vendors in 'original package' cases is firmly established in the law." 21 This doctrine originated in 1901,22 in an action for wrongful death against a druggist who sold a proprietary headache powder in an original package to a customer who apparently died from the effects of taking it. The plaintiff was non-suited on the ground that the druggist was not required to analyze the contents of each bottle or package he received. The possibility of an implied warranty apparently was not considered by the court. The manufacturer is liable under such circumstances, and

Sec. 324. Election of Remedies. Some confusion appears in the cases with respect to the remedy. In tort cases the proper action is trespass, while in contract cases the proper action is assumpsit.33 It should be remembered that a warranty is a part of a contract.

This distinction is not always observed, but it may be important where, as under the original package doctrine, the immediate vendor is not liable for defects altogether attributable to the manufacturer, but may be held accountable in an action of assumpsit for breach

Objection to the form of the action will be considered if the complaint is timely. But the right to take advantage of improper form may be waived by a defendant, where the action is in trespass and assumpsit is the proper remedy or where the action is in assumpsit and the remedy in trespass. 99 34

After consuming a portion of it she was conscious of a creeping sensation on her lips, which proved to be due to a worm that had been in the bottle. Part 4. Fraudulent Representation 

Sec. 325. Requisites of Deceit. It was observed in the introductory chapter that the several courts of common pleas have jurisdiction to set aside contracts on grounds of fraud, accident or mistake. Species of fraud are misrepresentation, concealment, duress, and undue influence. Fraudulent representation, or deceit, consists of (1) a misrepresentation by defendant of an existing fact, (2) which is false, (3) made with knowledge (scienter) of its falsehood, or with reckless disregard of its truth, (4) with intent that plaintiff should act upon it, and (5) damage to plaintiff if he does act 

34 Siegel v. Struble Brothers, Inc., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 343 (1942),

upon it.35 A breach of faith or of an agreement, regarding the doing or refraining from doing something in the future, is not fraud, as that word is used in the phrase, "fraud, accident or mistake." 36 As said by Mr. Justice

MAXEY, now Chief Justice, "The essence of fraud is de ceit intentionally and successfully practiced to induce another to part with property or with some legal right.” 37 

Caldwell v. Continental Trust Co., 291 Pa. 35 (1927). SIMPSON,

J. "It is difficult to understand how a trust company could more readily deceive a proposed purchaser of bonds from them, he being ignorant of the value thereof, than to tell him, after a thorough investigation, they had purchased the entire issue, and were keeping half of it as an investment for themselves." 

Sec. 326. Knowledge of Falsehood. If a man knows the truth, he is neither deceived nor defrauded, and any loss he may sustain is in effect self-inflicted. Furthermore, if a person to whom misrepresentations are made is in a position to know or ascertain the facts, his knowledge of them may be inferred. A purchaser of stock, for example, has no right to rely on the representation that the company is a prosperous and self-sustaining commercial enterprise, when he has before him at the time of purchase a financial statement which shows exactly the contrary.38 Furthermore, "No one is deceived by a declaration he disbelieves." 39

Sec. 327. Ratification of Fraud. The rule is well settled that where a transaction is voidable either by reason of any actual fraud or any fraud existing by construction of law, or any mistake of facts, the party having the right to avoid the transaction must assert his rights promptly, without any unnecessary delay, and before the other party has in any manner changed his position.40

215 (1919). Defendant purchased certain stock, giving therefor a promissory note. Soon after the purchase she made an investigation which disclosed facts which led her to believe that plaintiff's agent had made false and fraudulent statements with respect to the assets, financial ability and property of the corporation. 

After receipt of this information, however, she retained the stock and received dividends amounting to hundreds of dollars. This was a suit to recover on the note. WALLING, J. "Conceding, but not deciding, that the evidence was sufficient to take the case to the jury, we are clearly of the opinion that the retention of the stock and the acceptance of dividends thereon with knowledge of all the facts constitute a waiver of the fraud and a ratification of the contracts. The rule is well settled that to rescind a contract for fraud a party must do so promptly on its discovery, otherwise the fraud will be waived and the contract valid." 41 

Sec. 328. Marriage Contracts. The Act of 1929 ¹¹ 

provides that when a marriage has been contracted, it shall be lawful for the injured spouse to obtain a divorce from the bond of matrimony whenever it shall be adjudged that the other spouse, inter alia, "shall have procured the marriage by fraud, force, or coercion, and which has not been subsequently confirmed by the acts of the injured and innocent spouse." It is well settled, however, that a fraudulent representation which would be sufficient to avoid an ordinary contract will not be permitted to vitiate a marriage contract. "The State's interest in marriage rests upon a sound public policy, which is founded not only upon the regulation of the morals of the people but more especially upon the State's basic concern in the rearing of children." 42 

Herr v. Herr, 109 Pa. Superior Ct. 42 (1983). Libellant alleged, as grounds for divorce, his misconduct with the libellee, and that he had been induced to marry her because of her representation that she was in difficulty, which proved to be not so, and her threat to commit suicide. As evidence of some mental disturbance at the time, he introduced the testimony of his landlady that he had walked the floor most of the night, and the testimony of a minister that he had asked the latter to pray for him. Part 5. Insurance Contracts Sec. 329. Misrepresentations. The reports disclose that many life insurance contracts have failed, within the first two years 3 of the life of such policies, because of fraudulent representations appearing in the applications." Prior to 1885, insurance companies commonly required applicants to warrant the statements made by them as true. Inasmuch as a warranty is a part of the contract, the insured was precluded by his answer, whether made in good faith or not, a situation which brought about the failure of a good many policies. In 

1885 45 the Legislature enacted a statute which reduced such warranties to the plane of representations. The purpose of this legislation was to prevent insurance companies from avoiding policies for matters not material to the risk. The Act of 1939 46 provides that statements made by the insured in his application "shall be deemed, in the absence of fraud, to be representations and not warranties." A misrepresentation is antecedent to the contract. It is a statement on the faith of which the contract was executed. It consists of a statement of fact, known to be false, and uttered with knowledge of its falsehood. Specifically, inquiries by an insurance company as to prior medical or hospital attendance of an applicant for life insurance, are material to the risk, and false answers thereto permit the insurance company to avoid the policy. Where the insured must have been aware of the falsity of such answers, the court may

direct a verdict or enter judgment for the insurance company. On the other hand, "where the misstatement has been set forth inadvertently, or the narrative is incomplete in detail, and was made without intention of concealing the truth, a recovery is permissible, the question of good faith being for the jury." 99 48 

Evans v. Penn Mutual Life Ins. Co., 322 Pa. 547 (1936). A 

young man 21 years of age obtained a policy of life insurance on April 29, 1932, naming his mother as beneficiary. The policy was issued without a medical examination. The insured denied in the application that he had had any disease or infirmity, or any medical or surgical treatment, except Bercitis, for which he was housed up for two weeks, and that he knew of no fact that might affect the insurance. His death occurred on August 9, 1932, from a dislocation of the third cervical vertebra while swimming. About five years before he had experienced such a dislocation, and during this period he had been treated by two osteopaths for what appeared to be temporary indispositions, inasmuch as these attacks cleared up within twelve to twenty-four hours. Apparently he thought they were too trivial to be reported in the application. 

The insurance company sought to avoid the policy on grounds of false representations. In deciding that the question of good faith was for the jury, it was said by DREW, J., quoting the court below: "Mere mistakes, inadvertently made, even though of material matters, or the failure to furnish all details asked for, where it appears there is no intention of concealing the truth, does not work a forfeiture, and a forfeiture does not follow where there has been no deliberate intent to deceive, and the known falsity of the answer is not affirmatively shown." 49 

Sec. 330. Condition Precedent. Although not so numerous, the reports disclose that a number of life insurance contracts have been successfully avoided, within the first two years of the effective date of such policies, because of the failure of a condition precedent. A condition precedent is also antecedent to the contract, but stands at the threshhold of it. It is a fact which must exist as a condition to the validity of the contract, as, for example, that the policy must be delivered before it is to become effective, or that the first premium must 

47 Derr v. Mutual Life Ins. Co. of 

New York, 351 Pa. 554 (1945). 

48 Livingood v. New York Life Ins. 

Co., 287 Pa. 128 (1926). 

40 See note 43 supra.

be paid in full, or that the applicant has never been rejected for insurance, or that he was in good health when the policy was issued. In contrast to the misrepresentation of a fact, the distinction is "making the existence of that fact a condition upon which the contract, by its written terms, is dependent." 50 Or to state it another way, facts asserted in the application, and which constitute representations, are to be distinguished from conditions inserted in the policy. "In the latter type of cases proof of the fact or facts constituting a breach of the condition justifies the insurer in declaring the policy void; fraud need not be proven, hence, knowledge of the insured is immaterial." 51 In matters of health, a condition precedent is closely analogous to a warranty.

These cases usually arise, however, where a physical. examination has been waived. The Act of 1921, as amended in 1935,52 provides that if the medical examiner, or agent recording the answers where a medical examination is waived, issues a certificate of health, or declares the applicant a fit subject for insurance, the insurance company shall be estopped from setting up in defense that the insured was not in the condition of health required by the policy, "unless the same was procured by or through the fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation of or on behalf of the insured." It has been held, however, that the effect of this statute may not be extended beyond its provisions. 53

Part 6. Other Types of Fraud Sec. 331. Concealment. As a general rule neither party to a contract is under any legal duty to disclose facts which he knows might possibly influence the action of the other party. 

Harris v. Tyson, 24 Pa. 347 (1855). BLACK, J. "A person who knows that there is a mine on the land of another may nevertheless buy it. The ignorance of the vendor is not of itself fraud on the part of the purchaser. A purchaser is not bound by our laws to make the man he buys from as wise as himself. The mere fact, therefore, that Tyson knew there was sand chrome on Harris' land, and that Harris himself was ignorant of it, even if that were exclusively established, would not be ground for impugning the validity of the deed."

Concealment, which amounts to fraud, is the nondisclosure of facts and circumstances which one party is under some legal or equitable obligation to communicate, and which the other party has a right to know." "+4 

Grigsby v. Stapleton, 94 Missouri 423 (1888). Plaintiff sought to recover for the sale of one hundred head of cattle, known by him at the time of the sale to be diseased with Spanish or Texas fever. An ordinary inspection would not have revealed the dis- 

BLACK, J. "The sale of animals which the seller knows, but the purchaser does not, have a contagious disease, should be regarded as a fraud, when the fact of the disease is not disclosed." ease. 

Sec. 332. Partial Disclosure. A purchaser, when buying on credit, is not bound to disclose the facts of his financial condition. If he makes no misrepresentations and is not asked any questions, and does not give untrue, evasive, or partial answers, his silence concerning his financial condition is not fraudulent. But it is other 

54 Standard Steel Car Co. v. Stamm, 207 Pa. 419 (1904).

wise when there is a suppression of material facts which he is asked to disclose. 

Newell v. Randall, 82 Minn. 171 (1884). Plaintiff inquired of

Bauman concerning his financial status. The latter replied that he had $3,000 in his business, consisting of merchandise and book accounts, and $300 in cash, but he neglected to mention an indebtedness of $2,100. MITCHELL, J. "To tell half a truth only is to conceal the other half. Concealment of this kind, under the circumstances, amounts to a false representation." 

Sec. 333. Suppression of Fact. Fraudulent conceal ment is defined by Chancellor KENT in his Commentaries as follows: "If there be an intentional concealment or suppression of material facts in the making of a contract in cases in which both parties have not equal access to the means of information, it will be deemed unfair dealing, and will vitiate and avoid the contract." 55

Strickland v. Lomm, 70 Fed. 631 (1895). The S. S. Clandeboye was disabled off the Little Bahama Islands. Her mate proceeded to Savannah and communicated with the owners, by whom the tug Morse was chartered at Philadelphia. Captain Lomm, part owner and master of the tug Dauntless, lying at its home port at Brunswick, learning from the Savannah papers of the condition and location of the Clandeboye, telegraphed through his agents to Savannah and received a reply stating that the Morse had been chartered. He concluded that he could beat the latter in a race to the disabled vessel, and weighed anchor at night. After arriving at the scene he entered into a contract with Captain Strickland to tow the ship to Newport News, without disclosing that the Morse had been employed to come to his relief. The Morse arrived at the scene three or four days later. SEYMOUR, D. J. "There was on the part of Capt. Lomm an intentional suppression of a material fact, in relation to which he was informed, while Capt. Strickland had not access to any means of obtaining information of it. . . . 

The parties were not dealing on equal terms, and their contract cannot be enforced."

Sec. 334. Duress at Common Law. Duress is de fined by Webster as a "state of compulsion or necessity in which a person is influenced, whether by the unlawful restraint of his liberty or by actual or threatened 

55 2 Kent Com., 482. 18

physical violence, to incur a civil liability or to commit an offense." Duress also consists of wrongfully seizing or withholding the property of another for the purpose of coercing a settlement. Such conduct virtually amounts to extortion, and where there is neither suit nor legal process of any kind, money paid for the release of goods unlawfully detained, without any color or pretense of right, may be recovered in an action in quasi contract.5 Duress at common law is explained by Blackstone: 

56 "The constraint a man is under in these circumstances is called in law duress, from the Latin durities, of which there are two sorts: duress of imprisonment, where a man actually loses his liberty, of which we shall presently speak; and duress per minas, where the hardship is only threatened and impending, which is that we are now discoursing of. Duress per minas is either for fear of loss of life, or else for fear of mayhem, or loss of limb. . . .

The confinement of the person, in any wise, is an imprisonment; so that the keeping a man against his will in a private house, putting him in the stocks, arresting or forcibly detaining him in the street, is an imprisonment." 57 

Sec. 335. Test of Duress. Under the common law duress had to be of such a character as to induce a wellgrounded fear in the mind of a firm and courageous man, but the doctrine which is now approved is, that any contract produced by actual intimidation ought to be held void, whether arising from a result of merely personal infirmity, or from circumstances which might produce a like effect upon persons of ordinary firmness. A person is supposed to possess ordinary firmness unless it is shown that by reason of age or other sufficient cause he is weak or infirm. The test of duress is not so much the means by which a person is compelled to execute a contract, as it is the state of mind induced by the means employed. The threat must be of such a nature as to constitute a reasonable and adequate cause to control the will of another, and must have that effect. 58

Pa. 162 (1912).
