Нook, C. J. "In the case at bar the plaintiff had no claim against the defendant. The debtor was her husband, who had failed in business. Primarily she was neither legally nor morally responsible. The representatives of the plaintiff sought to obtain her guaranty of his obligations and to bind her separate estate for their payment. She was of Bohemian extraction and apparently ignorant of business affairs. She was the mother of seven children, the eldest of whom was 14 years of age, and was pregnant with an eighth. We must assume from the verdict and evidence that threats were made to have her husband arrested and jailed unless she signed and guaranteed the notes, and we cannot say as matter of law they were insufficient under the circumstances to deprive her of that freedom of will essential to voluntary action. 

All men appreciate how susceptible the mind of a wife and mother is to such influence, and how she may be coerced to give up her property when the liberty of husband and father is believed to be at stake."

Sec. 336. Relief from Duress. The general rule is that the defense of duress is open only to the party upon whom it is imposed, but there are exceptions. These include husband and wife, parent and child, grandmother and grandson, aunt and nephew, sister and brother, brother and brother, and father-in-law and sonin-law. Either party may avoid his contract made to relieve the other.5 59 

Jordan v. Elliott, 12 W. N. C. 56 (1882). Elliott, insolvent, was indebted to Jordan in the sum of $7,419.78, secured by a note and an insurance policy. It was agreed between them that the note would be renewed by Elliott, with his mother, a widow seventyseven years of age, as surety. Jordan procured a note from the mother without the joinder of her son, under the following circumstances as recited by GORDON, J. "The transaction of the preceding day, which produced the note in question, was both scandalous and violent. Jordan's sudden appearance in the hall of Mrs. 

Elliott's house; his tragic exclamation as though in soliloquy, 'Perhaps this bitter cup may pass;' when in the sitting-room, his rapid pacing back and forth with fierce gesticulation. When pressed by the old lady to leave until next day, that she was at that time not fit to do anything, he answered by lifting up his hand and invoking the God of heaven to bear him witness that he would have the 

50 Fountain v. Bigham, 235 Pa. 35 (1912).

matter settled, or forthwith prosecute her son. Then, when this Edward, the son, began to tell Jordan how he might have defeated his collateral by taking his own life, the climax was reached; then it was 'the girls began to weep and cry,' and the old lady now ready, as she says, through terror and alarm to do anything to put an end to this, as it appeared to her, frightful scene, signed the note." 

Sec. 337. Undue Influence. Undue influence consists of unfair persuasion where one party is under the domination of another. Where the relation existing between contracting parties is of such character that they do not deal on equal terms, and that on the one side, from over-mastering influence, or on the other side, from weakness, dependence, or trust, unfair persuasion has been practiced, the transaction may be challenged by the injured party. · 

Worrall's Appeal, 110 Pa. 349 (1885). Plaintiff filed a bill in equity to set aside a deed executed to the respondent for a consideration of $15, for property worth about $13,000, constituting the major part of his estate, made within a few weeks after becoming twenty-one years of age. He was ill at the time, and the deed was to take the place of a will. He subsequently recovered his health. 

In setting aside the conveyance it was said by TRUNKEY, J. "Their correspondence shows that in their relation, while they lived together, hers was the master mind; that she controlled and managed the property left by Dr. Worrall; that the sickly young man had confided in and depended on her, and that she had exercised a motherly care and influence for and over him. At the last, when he demanded a reconveyance, she reminded him of the many weary nights she had carried him while he was choking with croup, of the long years of affection of the only mother he ever knew, which affection would not be buried until the grave should shut up her poor body, and that she had been true to her trust; but she declined to reconvey. "" 

Sec. 338. Execution of Will. Less capacity is neces sary to make a will than to engage in ordinary business transactions, and the tendency of the courts is to uphold the validity of a last will and testament unless some imperative reason is shown for setting it aside. It would require substantial proof to set aside a will on

grounds of undue influence, but such proof may be shown. 

Central Trust Co. v. Boyer, 308 Pa. 402 (1932). Boyer died testate in his sixty-eighth year, leaving to survive him his widow and a son. The chief beneficiary under the will was his housekeeper, a Mrs. Long, who was not related to him in any way. His son filed a caveat against probate of the will. DREW, J. "This will, made less than four weeks after Mrs. Long came into testator's home and during the course of an illicit relationship with her, is so unnatural as to be almost inhuman. The treatment of the wife is particularly harsh. At the time she was an incurable, invalid. . . . The will placed her in the physical control and possession of Mrs. Long for the rest of her life. Its terms are particularly offensive and insulting. 

This will was the result of undue influence."

Part 7. Constructive Fraud 

60 

Sec. 339. Perfect Good Faith. Undue influence, and the necessity of perfect good faith, are two distinct principles, although closely interrelated. The main difference is in the burden of proof. Perfect good faith is required, independently of undue influence, where a fiduciary relation is shown to exist, or where trust and confidence is justifiably reposed in another. Whenever a confidential relation is shown, the requirement of perfect good faith throws upon the beneficiary of the transaction the duty of showing, expressly, that it is fair and conscientious, and beyond the reach of suspicion. In the case of undue influence, the proof thereof rests affirmatively upon those who challenge the transaction on that ground. Where a confidential relation is shown, however, the burden is upon the beneficiary to show that it was not abused.

ESTE 

Greenfield's Estate, 14 Pa. 489 (1850). Mrs. Elizabeth Greenfield, in her lifetime, executed a declaration of trust which reserved to the trustees the sum of $40,000, being $10,000 to each, professedly as compensation for assuming the burden of a trust which might have terminated in a year, and, according to every probability, would not have continued for a very long period. She was 

60 Null's Estate, 302 Pa. 64 (1930).

about eighty-six years of age, hard of hearing, and otherwise infirm. BELL, J. "I can very well imagine how, without a violation of conscience, they might conceive themselves entitled to a princely remuneration, under the circumstances then surrounding the donor. But in spite of this concession, a rule of public policy and pure morals, founded in long experience of the human heart and knowledge of man's cupidity, interposes to forbid an allowance of the claim. In this feature, the case presents what is called a constructive fraud, springing from the confidential relations existing between the parties. This peculiarity, withdrawing it from the operation of ordinary rules, throws upon the beneficiaries the duty of showing expressly that the arrangement was fair and conscientious, beyond the reach of suspicion. In requiring this, courts of equity act irrespective of any admixture of deceit, imposition, overreaching, or other positive fraud."

Sec. 340. Confidential Relation. The confidential relation is not confined to any specific association of parties. It may be found between persons who are related as trustee and cestui que trust, guardian and ward, attorney and client, parent and child, husband and wife, partners, principal and agent, master and servant, physician and patient, or in any other relation of trust and confidence. In Darlington's Estate,¹ a man eighty-four years of age, feeble and infirm, signed a promissory note for $7,000 in favor of his agent. It was not shown that he had read the note or knew the amount of it. The note was claimed to have been given for past services and those to be rendered in the future. There was no evidence that there had been any past service, the amount of the note was clearly in excess of any probable future service the agent might render, and the total value of the estate was but $9,000. In Unruh v. Lukens,82 a deed to the grantor's physician, who was also her attorney-infact, was set aside. There was no consideration for it, and it had never been explained. In Duncan's Appeal 63 it was held that a trust deed executed by a widow two days before her marriage, without the knowledge of her intended husband, was a fraud upon the marriage and void. This was in 1862. Various statutes since that

Sec. 341. Antenuptial Agreements. As indicated heretofore, each spouse has an inheritable interest in the estate of each other. To state it more accurately, if one spouse disinherits the other spouse, the injured spouse may elect to take against the will of the deceased spouse. 

The share of the injured spouse, under such circumstances, is indicated in the chapter on Decedents' Estates. Persons who are betrothed, however, may by con. tract relinquish any inheritable interest in the estate of each other. This occasionally happens when a young man proposes to marry a girl of great wealth, or where the proposed marriage is between a widow and widower, both of whom have children by former marriages, or where an aged widower, who has accumulated some wealth, proposes to marry his secretary. It was decided, in 1868,65 that a confidential relation exists between such persons, and that the concealment by one spouse of his financial circumstances, in entering into such an agreement, was a constructive fraud. In modern times, however, it has been held that, "It is not necessary that there be exact knowledge of the worth of the other contracting party, 966 and that the test of constructive fraud, under such circumstances, is whether or not the provision in favor of the intended spouse is sufficient to enable her to live comfortably, after her husband's death, in the same way as, considering all the circumstances, she had previously lived. 

Clark's Estate, 303 Pa. 538 (1931). Testator married appellant when he was sixty-four years of age. 

At that time he had seven children by a former marriage. Appellant had two children by a former marriage. They entered into an antenuptial agreement

Part 8. Mistake Sec. 343. Mistake of Substance. If the parties have negotiated a contract which, to all outward appearance is complete and self-sustaining, either party may obtain equitable relief on grounds of mistake. A relievable mistake, however, must be material or the moving cause of the action, and mutual or shared in by both parties to the transaction. It must also be unintentional and free from negligence. "A mutual mistake of fact is a clear impression in the minds of the parties as to the existence of a material fact, sufficient in importance to influence and govern a man of ordinary intelligence, and on which both parties relied and acted, which fact did not exist. To show mistake, the fact contrary to the belief of the parties must not only be made to appear definitely but must be shown to have existed at the time the parties had a different impression." "¹ 71

Leisenring afterwards left Philadelphia and his whereabouts became unknown. Riegel died and his wife succeeded to his rights in the policy. She paid the premiums for nine years, and then being unable to keep up the payments, accepted a paid-up policy in the sum of $2,500. She subsequently learned that at the time of this transaction Leisenring had died.

Sec. 344. Misapprehension of Value. A misappre hension as to the value of the subject of a contract, though shared by both parties to the contract, is not ground for equitable relief. 

Plaintiff found an 

Wood v. Boynton, 64 Wisconsin 265 (1885). uncut stone and sold it to the defendant for $1. Both thought it was a topaz. It turned out to be an uncut diamond worth approximately $1,000. Plaintiff then attempted to rescind the contract. 

In deciding for defendant, it was said by TAYLOR, J. "When this sale was made the value of the thing sold was open to the investigation of both parties; neither knew its extrinsic value, and, so far as the evidence in this case showed, both supposed that the price paid was adequate." 

Sec. 345. Unilateral Mistake. The mistake of one party only in the expression of his agreement or as to the subject-matter, not known to the other, does not render the transaction voidable. In Marmon Philadelphia Co. v. Blocksom," the plaintiff agreed to lease certain premises to the defendant upon the terms of an existing lease. This lease required the lessee to pay all increase of taxes upon the premises in excess of the amount paid for the year 1923, but it was not seen by the defendant, and through an oversight of plaintiff's attorney, was not included in the lease to the defendant. 

It was held that as the mistake was not mutual, and was not due to any fault of the defendant, the plaintiff was not entitled to a reformation of the lease. 

Tatum v. Coast Lumber Co., 16 Idaho 471 (1909). Defendant requested a price for certain tools, machinery, and furnishings for a planing mill and sash and door factory. Plaintiff quoted a price of $5,134.80, but a salesman made a mistake in computing the 

72 103 Pa. Superior Ct. 542 (1931).

prices of some of the articles so that, instead of being $5,134.80 it should have been $6,194.80. Defendant accepted the offer, received the goods, and remitted the contract price. Plaintiff discovered the error and brought suit for the difference. AILshie, J. "A purchaser cannot be made to suffer or be made responsible because a vendor has committed an error or mistake in computing the value of his goods or the expected profits to be derived from the sale thereof. A rescission of the contract has sometimes been allowed where the purchaser was informed of the error and mistake prior to receiving and accepting the goods, and prior to his changing his position and attitude with reference to the contract and property so as to injure or prejudice him. No court, however, so far as we are advised, has ever held a contract void or invalid on account of a unilateral mistake of which the other party was not aware, and which did not go to the subject matter of the contract itself." 

Sec. 346. Mistake of Law. In Pennsylvania, ignorance or mistake of law, with full knowledge of the facts, is not, per se, a ground for equitable relief." There are a few cases which hold that if there would be great hardship in enforcing a contract made in ignorance of law, equity may afford relief." It was denied in Clark v. 

Lehigh & Wilkes-Barre Coal Company," but the opinion states that the court was dealing with a mistake of law pure and simple, unaided by any special circumstances or equitable considerations which should move a chancellor to grant it. "The rule expressed in our cases is that such mistake, or ignorance of the law, is no ground for relief from an agreement entered into fairly and with full knowledge of the facts. This doctrine has been strongly criticized." 76

COLERIDGE, C. J. "It must be remembered that all trade is, and must be, in a sense, selfish; trade not being infinite, nay, the trade of a particular place or district being possibly very limited, what one man gains another loses. As expressed by the Supreme Court of Iowa at that time, "if competition be 'war,' in which ‘everything is fair,' or if it be so regarded by those who participate therein, certainly the law will not give that doctrine its sanction." The occasion was the annihilation of a retail distributor who had decided to give his patronage to others. In order to accomplish this result the Standard Oil Company had purposely entered into competition with its rebellious customer, crushed the uprising with a swift price-cutting campaign, and after buying in the remnants of its opponent at fifteen cents on the dollar, retired from the field of battle." 

Tutle v. Buck, 107 Minn. 145 (1909). Plaintiff was the village barber. Defendant was the village banker. For the purpose of driving the barber out of business, the defendant fitted out a barber shop and employed a barber therein for the purpose of carrying out this intent. In deciding that this was not lawful competiti and that defendant was liable for the wrong, it was said by ELLIOTT, J. "To call such conduct competition is a perversion of terms. It is simply the application of force without legal justification, which in its moral quality may be no better than highway robbery."

Sec. 350. Improvement in Business Conduct. Moral standards in business have improved immeasurably during the last quarter of a century. This may be attributed in part to an effort to avoid mandatory rules and legal sanctions. Some such reason may be partly responsible for the declaration of policy that "Business should render restrictive legislation unnecessary through so conducting itself as to deserve and inspire public confidence." 78 The motive, however, is not material. 

One writer has said that "Business ethics is not a problem for the successful firm or individual, because a well established business can afford to observe certain standards which would seriously affect the income of struggling young merchants." 79 Neither is it a problem for 

77 Dunshee v. The Standard Oil Co., 

152 Iowa 618 (1911). 

78 Policies, U. S. Chamber of Commerce, 1937, p. 43. 

79 Taeusch, "Professional and Business Ethics,' "260.

the less successful in business who consistently adhere to the highest standards of morality, but it is essential that they join with others in a program of vigorous selfdiscipline. Reasonable standards of business practice, if they are made effective, would be sufficient to defeat arbitrary measures of political control.

Sec. 351. Conclusion. Laws are a poor substitute for character. They are necessary to curb the unscrupulous, and to condition the competitive struggle, but by and large, none-the-less, they can be no more perfect than the men who make them and who are to be governed by them. Honesty and virtue are not dependent on legal rules for their achievement. Former United States District Attorney, George E. Q. Johnson, who prosecuted 

Al Capone, has made this observation: "I have lectured to students at a number of colleges, and many of the questions they have asked me indicate that the pernicious doctrine of 'getting by' is prevalent. That doctrine is the quicksand of life. Tragedy lies ahead for those who enter their professional lives with such a philosophy. But the doctrine of 'shooting square' holds up under every 99 80 test." Our conclusion is that success in the business world, as elsewhere, is founded on the highest principles of justice and morality. Justice, as here used, is an ideal, and not merely an idea which has its origin in legal institutions. It is this same ideal, as said by Webster, "which holds civilized nations together. 

Wherever her temple stands, and as long as it is duly honored, there is a foundation for social security, general happiness and the improvement and the progress of our race. And whoever labors on this edifice with usefulness and distinction, whoever clears its foundations. strengthens its pillars, adorns its entablatures, or contributes to raise its august dome still higher in the skies, connects himself in name, and fame, and character, with that which is, and must be, as durable as the frame of human society." 99 81 

80 Diary of Alpha Kappa Psi, Nov., 81 Bouv. Law Dict., p. 1796. 1937.

UNENFORCEABLE CONTRACTS Part 1. Written Law Sec. 352. Public Policy. The two preceding chap ters were devoted to contracts which were for the most part voidable. We are here concerned with contracts that are void. "If an agreement binds the parties or either of them to do, or if the consideration is to do, something opposed to the policy of the State or Nation, it is illegal and absolutely void, however solemnly made." This principle has always been the law of 

Pennsylvania. If the formation or performance of a contract is criminal, tortious, or otherwise opposed to public policy, it is unenforceable. 1 

CHAPTER IX 

2 

Holman v. Johnson, 98 Eng. Rep. 1120 (1775). Lord MANS- 

FIELD, C. J. "The objection that a contract is immoral or illegal as between plaintiff and defendant, sounds at all times very ill in the mouth of the defendant. It is not for his sake, however, that the objection is ever allowed; but it is founded in general principles of policy, which the defendant has the advantage of, contrary to the real justice, as between him and the plaintiff, by accident, if I may so say. The principle of public policy is this: ex dolo malo non oritur actio. No court will lend its aid to a man who founds his cause of action upon an immoral or an illegal act." 

Sec. 353. Violation of Statute. A contract that is contrary to written law is void. It is not necessary that a statute expressly declare that all contracts made in violation of it should be unlawful. A prohibition, whether penal or not, is sufficient. The payment of a penalty is not a license for the doing of an unlawful act. 3 

Snaman v. Maginn, 77 Pa. Superior Ct. 287 (1921). HEAD, J. 

"It appears to me that reason alone, without authority, would necessarily lead us to the conclusion that a contract, the making

Ct. 94 (1927).

of which is positively prohibited by a statute, cannot be enforced by the aid of the courts of the state in which the statute has been enacted. In vain would the legislative power thunder its prohibitions against the performance of a given act, if the coordinate branch of the government, the courts, would lend their powerful aid to the transgressor in recovering the fruits of the unlawful transaction." 

Sec. 354. Improper Tendency. It is also important to note that although a contract does not directly require any unlawful or improper act for its performance, yet if the tendency of such a contract is to encourage or hold out a reward for a result which can be brought about only by an unlawful act, the agreement is opposed to public policy. The following case is frequently cited. 

Badgley v. Beale, 3 Watts 263 (1834). GIBSON, C. J. "It is an undoubted rule that a contract growing out of a transaction whose known tendency was to encourage a breach of the laws, is not to be enforced. For this reason it has been held, that an action is not maintainable for the price of drugs purchased by a brewer. avowedly with a design to use them in violation of the provisions of a statute; or by an innkeeper for refreshments furnished to the defendant's voters at an election. So an action has been held not to lie on a contract in reference to an illegal voyage, because the accessory follows the nature of its principal; or for the use and occupation of lodgings let with knowledge that they were to be used for purposes of prostitution. The only apparent exception to this, is the case of an action sustained for washing the clothes of a prostitute, knowing her to be such, on the humane principle that even a prostitute must have clean linen for honest purposes, and that it is impossible to distinguish the articles that are intended to be put to an impure use: but the principle of the exception has been qualified in respect to dresses furnished, by requiring it to appear that they were not delivered with a view to the business of prostitution, or with an expectation that they would be paid for out of the profits for it."

Sec. 355. Liquor Statutes. 

Liquor Statutes. It is common knowledge that agreements were not infrequently made in violation of the state and federal prohibition statutes. These statutes have now been superseded by the Liquor Con trol, the Liquor License, and the Beverage License Laws.

Tucker v. Binenstock, 310 Pa. 254 (1933). KEPHART, J. "Here equity is asked to use its power to distribute the proceeds of a business which was in open defiance of the law, illegally selling liquor without a permit, a product in thousands of gallons that had been libelled by the government, making gross sales of approximately two million dollars; paying $188,000 for police protection; registering their clients on the books by numbers instead of names, and whose properties were finally padlocked by the courts. It is extraordinary, to say the least, to ask a court of justice to encourage and protect such flagrant violators of the law." 

Sec. 356. Usury. A reasonable charge for the use of capital is called interest. An unreasonable charge is usury.

Under the Mosaic Law the taking of interest was prohibited as between the Jews, and it seems that all taking of interest was originally branded a sin by the ecclesiastics, although the rule was considerably modified in the course of time. As said by Blackstone: "... it hath been observed, that the Mosaical precept was clearly a political, and not a moral, precept. It only prohibited the Jews from taking usury from their brethren the Jews, but in express words permitted them to take it of a stranger; which proves that the taking of moderate usury, or a reward for the use, for so the word signifies, is not malum in se: since it was allowed where any but an Israelite was concerned. And as to the reason supposed to be given by Aristotle, and deduced from the natural barrenness of money, the same may with equal force be alleged of houses, which never breed houses; and twenty other things, which nobody doubts it is lawful to make profit of, by letting them to hire." (2 Black. Com. 454). 

Sec. 357. Legal Interest Rate. Technically, usury is exacting a greater profit for the loan of money than is permitted by statute. The Act of 1858 provides that in all cases where no express contract shall have been made for a less rate, the lawful rate for the use of money shall be six per centum per annum. Any amount paid in excess of that rate may be deducted from the principal. 

Mylott v. Skinner, 12 Pa. Superior Ct. 137 (1899). Plaintiff borrowed $10 for one month and gave his note for $11. At the 

Act of May 28, 1858, P. L. 622, 41 PS 3. 19

end of the month he paid defendant $11 and received back $10 and gave a new note for $11. This process was repeated monthly for sixteen months. SMITH, J. "The case thus exhibits a scheme on the part of the lender, to secure interest on the loan at the rate of ten per cent a month." 

Sec. 358. Interest Contracts. The statute does not make the payment of a usurious rate of interest unlawful. A lender may charge and receive excess interest, but he cannot coerce its payment. Furthermore, the borrower may recover any excess interest if an action is brought within six months after payment. The Act may not be waived by contract. Usury arises between borrower and lender, not between successive purchasers of obligations already created. Hence, the sale of commercial paper at a discount in excess of the legal rate is not usurious. Neither is a loan at the legal rate of interest to enable a borrower to purchase goods from the lender.8 It has been held that a note payable one day after date, with four per cent interest, bears that rate even after maturity; but when interest on a note is fixed at less than six per cent "from date until paid," that rate applies up to the maturity of the note, at which time the legal rate will prevail.¹0 Where a loan in excess of six per cent is made in another state, and the contract is to be performed there, the agreement will be enforced by the courts in Pennsylvania.¹¹

Sec. 360. Special Interest Rates. There are several notable exceptions to the Act of 1858. The Act of 

1929 13 provides that it shall be lawful for the parties to agree in writing to pay any rate of interest on advances of more than $5,000 repayable on demand, where such loans are secured by negotiable and other securities. 

The Act of 1933 14 provides that a business corporation may not plead usury as a defense to any of its obligations. It must pay all that it has promised.15 The Act of 1933 16 provides that a building and loan association may charge a premium on loans (if the borrower agrees in writing) of not more than ten per cent per annum of the amount of the loan, but not more than one per cent per annum if the loan is to be repaid in installments; and the Act of 1937 17 authorizes such an association to assess a fine not to exceed one per cent per month for failure to pay dues on installment shares, interest, or premiums.

Sec. 364. Wagering Contracts. Under the common law a wagering contract was no different than any other contract. Most of the states, as well as England, have modified the common law, either by judicial decision or by statute. Wagering contracts have never been recognized by the higher courts in Pennsylvania. As said by the Supreme Court more than a century ago, "though bets were recoverable by the common law of England, it was not a part of the common law introduced into 

Pennsylvania by William Penn." 22 

Phillips v. Ives, 1 Rawle 35 (1828). The parties placed a wager that Napoleon Bonaparte would, within a specified time, be removed or escape from the Island of St. Helena, or would die within a period of two years. Chief Justice GIBSON, with the concurrence of Mr. Justice SMITH, took the position that the policy of the law was "not a subject for our consideration," but the majority decided otherwise, saying through HUSTON, J. "There are many things which politeness would not mention, and charity would conceal; I would not assist folly or malignity in making them public. 

I would not as a man, and I will not as a judge. I hold that no bet of any kind, about any human being, is recoverable in a court of justice."

Sec. 365. Recovery from Stakeholder. Money or property may be recovered from a stakeholder, even after the happening of the event,23 but not if paid over except as authorized by statute. In some states a recovery from the stakeholder is not permitted after the bet has been decided. As to such persons the Supreme

Sec. 367. Life Insurance. It was early decided that an insurance without interest is a wagering policy. "An insurance amongst us, is a contract of indemnity. Its object is, not to make a positive gain, but to avert a possible loss. A man can never be said to be indemnified against a loss which can never happen to him. 

There cannot be an indemnity without a loss, nor a loss without an interest. A policy therefore made without interest, is a wager policy, and has nothing in common with insurance, but name and form." 28 ters.

Sec. 368. Insurable Risks. The Act of 1921 29 au thorizes the following insurable risks:

A person liable for the support of a child may take out a policy of insurance on such child and persons, copartnerships, associations, and corporations may insure the lives and health of officers, directors, principals, partners, and employes, without the signing of a personal application as hereinbefore required. Any person may insure his own life for the benefit of any person, copartnership, association, or corporation,30 but no person shall cause to be insured the life of another, unless the beneficiary named in such policy or agreement of life insurance, whether himself or a third person, has an insurable interest in the life of the insured. The term "insurable interest" is defined as meaning, in the case of persons related by blood or law, an interest engendered by love and affection, and, in the case of other persons, a lawful economic interest in having the life of the insured continue, as distinguished from an interest which would arise only by the death of the insured. 31

Sec. 371. Ratification. Unlike other contracts that are executed in violation of a statute, contracts entered into on Sunday are not void per se, but may be ratified, expressly or impliedly, on a week day. The payment of interest is sufficient.50 If deeds, bonds and notes have been executed on Sunday and are delivered on a subsequent day, this will be construed as a ratification. 

Proof that a chattel is delivered on Sunday does not raise a presumption that the contract was made on that day, but if this be established it will be construed as a valid obligation if it has been executed on a secular day. 

If a negotiable instrument is executed on Sunday and is dated as of a week day, the maker will be estopped from asserting its invalidity if it reaches the hands of a holder in due course. 51

Part 2. Governmental Affairs Sec. 372. Improper Influence. Contracts designed to improperly influence governmental affairs, or which have as their purpose the encouragement of public officials to neglect their duty, agreements to influence legislation or to obtain official appointments, and the buying of elections, are clearly void as against public policy. 

A contract founded upon a promise and engagement to procure signatures and to obtain a pardon from the Governor, for one convicted of a criminal offense, is unenforceable. As said by the Supreme Court, "we do not wish to see advertisements, that pardons will be obtained at the lowest price, nor anything which approaches to it." In Bowman v. Coffroth a member of Congress claimed $500 to secure immunity for his client from the draft during the Civil War, through official influence. In Spalding v. Ewing the defendant promised to pay for services rendered in securing the passage of an act of Congress to require the Postmaster General to make payment of a claim which had been resisted for years as invalid and unlawful. These contracts were declared void as being contrary to public policy and of a type invalid in all jurisdictions. 53 54 55 

Sec. 373. Lobbying. There is a conflict among the states as to whether a contract to use one's influence to secure the passage of law is contrary to public policy. 

It seems that such agreements are upheld in a majority of the states, but it is otherwise in Pennsylvania. In 

Clippinger v. Hepbaugh, plaintiff sought to recover on a promise by defendant to pay $100 if the plaintiff succeeded in procuring a law authorizing the disposition 56

289 57 of certain real estate which had been devised to defendant's wife and her children, but as said by the Supreme Court, "we are clearly of opinion that it would be against sound policy to sanction a practice which may lead to secret, improper and corrupt tampering with legislative action." The Penal Code " provides that whoever practices the occupation of soliciting members of either House of the General Assembly, or other officers of the state, to corruptly influence their official action, shall be punished by fine not exceeding $1,000 or imprisonment not exceeding two years, or both.

Spayd v. Ringing Rock Lodge, 74 Pa. Superior Ct. 139 (1920). 

KELLER, J. "This does not forbid an individual or association, or their attorney or representative, from presenting their views relative to pending legislation to legislative committees and urging its passage or defeat, or undertaking by petition, legitimate argument, and a fair showing of the circumstances to procure such action; it does strike at lobbying, as it is commonly understood, or the solicitation of members of a legislative body with intent to influence their votes by personal agency, and it matters not how this influence is attempted to be exerted, whether by promises, threats or other devious methods. Nor does it matter how meritorious is the end thus sought to be attained; any interference with the creation of laws and their proper enforcement is contrary to the law and public policy of this State." 

Sec. 374. Government Contracts. Agreements to procure contracts from the government to furnish its supplies, or to favor the letting of contracts, or for the location of public facilities, are likewise contrary to public policy.

Providence Tool Co. v. Norris, 2 Wall. 45 (1865). The Provi dence Tool Company entered into a contract with the Secretary of War to deliver to the United States government 25,000 muskets at $20 per musket. The plaintiff had previously agreed with the company to receive compensation for favorably influencing the proper officials. He obtained judgment in his favor in the lower court. 

FIELD, J. "It was not claimed, on the trial, that the plaintiff had rendered any other services than those which resulted in the procurement of the contract for the muskets. We are of opinion, therefore, that the proposition of law is fairly presented by the 

57 Act of June 24, 1939, P. L. 872, 18 PS 4101.

record, and is before us for consideration. The question, then, is this: Can an agreement for compensation to procure a contract from the Government to furnish its supplies be enforced by the courts? We have no hesitation in answering the question in the negative."

Part 3. Administration of Justice Sec. 375. Judicial Process. Contracts designed to improperly influence the administration of justice, such as bribing jurors, stifling prosecutions, compounding felonies, or bargains to pay for or to suppress evidence, or to conceal discreditable facts, or agreements to enforce unfounded claims or to prosecute fictitious litigation, are void. "The law guards with jealousy every avenue to its courts of justice, and strikes down everything in the shape of a contract which may afford a temptation to interfere with its due administration." 58 The 

Act of 1939 59 provides that any person not a member of the bar who solicits for an attorney shall be punished by fine not exceeding $200 or imprisonment not exceeding two years, or both. This is known as barratry. 

Morgan v. Doe, 16 D. & C. 314 (1932). Plaintiff's statement of claim alleged: "That on many occasions prior to and during 1929 the above-named defendant requested the plaintiff to bring to the defendant's office such clients and such legal business as the plaintiff was able to procure, and orally agreed that he, the said defendant, would pay to the plaintiff herein a sum equal fifty per cent (50%) of any earnings and fees secured by the defendant from and through such clients and law business as the plaintiff might influence and bring to the office of the defendant, directly or indirectly." In deciding that this complaint did not disclose a legal cause of action, it was said by STERN, P. J. "Any practice by which 'runners' or agents are employed to procure business for members of the bar degrades and stultifies the profession and reduces it to the level of hucksters in the market place. Lawyers may attract clients, but they must not seek them by methods properly employed in the business world. This is not merely a canon of good taste, but a rule that reaches deeply into the heart of legal ethics, for a violation of it is apt to breed objectionable practices." 

58 Ormerod v. Dearman, 100 Pa. 561 (1882). 

50 Act of June 9, 1939, P. L. 329, 17 PS 1611.

Sec. 376. Maintenance and Champerty. There is a proverb to the effect that he who mixeth with strife which concerneth not himself, is like a person that taketh a dog by the ears. It has always been the rule that third parties must not interfere in lawsuits in which they have no interest, or promote litigation in consideration of a part of the proceeds. Maintenance is the promoting of the litigation of another. Champerty is a division of the proceeds between one of the parties to the action and a stranger supporting the litigation. 

The Supreme Court has held that a bargain to endeavor to enforce a claim in consideration of a promise of a share of the proceeds, or of any other fee contingent on success, is illegal, if it is also part of the bargain that the party seeking to enforce the claim shall pay the expense incident thereto, unless such party already has or reasonably believes he has an interest recognized by law in the claim. On the other hand, an assignment of a claim is not rendered illegal by the fact that litigation is necessary for its collection; nor is such an assignment rendered illegal by the further fact that the assignee promises to endeavor to enforce the claim at his own expense and pay the assignor a share of the proceeds, unless the assignee gives no other substantial consideration.80

Sec. 377. Arbitration. The expense of litigation, the duration of trials, and the impediments and legal intricacies that delay the administration of justice, have caused many persons to seek pre-arranged arbitration on grounds of expediency. The validity of such an agreement has, in years past, been the subject of much judicial discussion and divergence of opinion, as tending to oust the courts of their jurisdiction. For this reason the following statute is of unusual significance.

The Act of 1927 61 provides that an arbitration agreement shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as 

60 Ames v. Hillside Coal & Iron Co., 314 Pa. 267 (1934). 

61 Act of April 25, 1927, P. L. 381, 5 PS 161-179.

exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract. If no arbitrator is agreed upon and no method provided for his appointment, the court of common pleas, upon the petition of either party, must appoint one. The award of the arbitrator is final and without appeal, except where it is procured by corruption, fraud, undue means, or there has been evident partiality or corruption on his part, or he has been guilty of misconduct or other misbehavior, or has exceeded his powers in the reference. The court may, however, modify or correct an award where there is evident miscalculation of figures, or material mistake in the description of person, thing, or property, or where the arbitrator acted upon a matter not submitted to him, or where the award is imperfect in matter of form not affecting the merits of the controversy, or where the award is against the law and such that had it been a verdict of the jury the court would have entered different or other judgment notwithstanding the verdict.

Part 4. Domestic Relations Sec. 378. Marriage Agreements. Unenforceable agreements in derogation of the family institution are bargains not to marry or to prevent marriage, marriage brokerage contracts, bargains for immoral purposes, or for the improper custody of minor children, or to facilitate a divorce.

Braum v. Potter Title & Trust Co., 301 Pa. 365 (1930). An old man, 71 years of age, desired to marry a child, Gertrude, 15 years of age.

He held a mortgage on the home of her parents. He entered into an agreement with them whereby he agreed to assign the mortgage to the child, with the stipulation that it should not be foreclosed, or interest demanded, as long as they lived, if they would consent to the marriage. The parents consented, the bond and mortgage were assigned, and the marriage consummated. After she became of age Gertrude caused judgment to be entered on the bond and levied on the property described in the mortgage. The court below ordered that execution be stayed during the lifetime of the parents, saying: "The plain fact is that these defendants gave or sold their daughter to the old man while she was still a child. 

The situation is abhorrent to decent sensibilities. Nevertheless, we are unable to say that the agreement, if proved rested upon an illegal consideration or one contrary to public policy." SIMPSON,

J. "We are in full accord with the court's characterization of the transaction, but do not agree with its conclusion. Instead of such a contract being enforceable, it was and is wholly and irremediably tainted, incapable of supporting an action or defense."

Sec. 379. Separation Agreements. The parties to a marriage may enter into a valid separation agreement. 

But any agreement which invites a violation of marital duties, or the promotion of domestic discord by appeal to mercenary motives, is unenforceable. 

Reamey v. Bayley, 7 Sadler 239 (1887). The parties entered into a reconciliation agreement under the terms of which the husband executed and delivered to his wife a bond in the sum of $10,000, secured by a mortgage. The agreement provided that if he should behave himself otherwise towards his wife so that her life, by his conduct, should be rendered miserable and intolerable, the bond and mortgage should become immediately due and payable. The wife alone was to determine the existence or happening of such contingency. DEAN, P. J. "We hold that it is clearly against the policy of the law to give effect to such stipulation in this postnuptial contract. It tends directly to discourage that confidence, trust and forbearance on the part of the wife which should be inseparable from the marriage relation." It

Sec. 380. Divorce Agreements. An agreement hav ing as its object the divorce of husband and wife is contrary to public policy. In Mathiot's Estate 62 the question involved was whether decedent's widow could maintain a claim for $15,000 received by him from her, to be used to procure a divorce from his former wife. was said by the orphans' court that it was immaterial whether she, the claimant, "was willing to pay for her husband or whether it was a loan," the mischief being the same. Husband and wife are not permitted to dissolve, of their own accord, a contract which is said to be in its nature indissoluble, and any arrangement tending to facilitate the granting of a divorce is invalid. 

Shannon's Estate, 289 Pa. 280 (1927). Husband and wife entered into a separation agreement which provided that each of them should have the full use and enjoyment of his or her own estate. 

The husband agreed to file an application for divorce within ten days and to prosecute it to judgment. The wife agreed that she would make no defense to this action. The court below held that this last provision rendered the entire contract void. SCHAFFER, J. "We agree with the conclusion reached by the trial judge that the entire contract is void." 68 

62 243 Pa. 375 (1914).

Sec. 381. Custody of Children. An agreement lim iting the relation of parent and.child is subject to judicial review. In Commonwealth v. Manning a separation agreement provided that the father of two minor children should not visit them at any time thereafter. 

In passing upon the validity of this stipulation it was said: "While the agreement gave the custody of the children to their mother, it does not deprive the father of the privilege of seeing and conversing with his children from time to time in such circumstances as the court may deem proper, if the interests and welfare of the children will be promoted by such access. It is against public policy to destroy or limit the relation of parent and child save as provided by law." 64 

Part 5. Good Morals 

Sec. 382. Public Morals. Any agreement that violates the commonly accepted standards of morality and decency, or that is contrary to the first principles of right and duty, is unenforceable. The judges are not arbiters of public morals, and quite properly hesitate to impugn the validity of contracts on that ground, but if the reasons are clear and imperative, and the evidence admits of no other reasonable inference, they do not hesitate to withhold legal sanction from agreements of that sort. All such contracts which have as their object the perpetration of a fraud, or injury to third persons or to the public, or interference with rights belonging to third persons or to the public, are contrary to public policy. So, too, is a contract to indemnify another for a wrongful act. 

Arnold v. Clifford, 2 Sumner's Rep. 238 (1835). Defendant secured the publication of a libel concerning a third person, and agreed to indemnify the publisher. STORY, J. "The man who is hired to publish a libel against another, is guilty of an offense equally reprehensible in morals, although not so aggravated in its character; for the publication may not only be ruinous to the repu- 

04 89 Pa. Superior Ct. 301 (1926).

295 tation of the individual aspersed, but may involve an innocent family in agonizing distress, and, perhaps, destroy its peace forever. 

There is no such right recognized in civil society, or at least in our forms of government, as the right of slandering or calumniating another." 

Sec. 383. Breach of Trust. A contract which has as its object or tendency the breach of trust or duty, is equally objectionable. The Penal Code 65 provides that whoever offers to bribe or bribes any agent, employee, or servant of another, directly or indirectly, without the knowledge and consent of the principal or employer, in return for any favor or disfavor in relation to the affairs or business of the principal or employer, may be punished by fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. This statute expressly excludes the practice of tipping. It has been held many times that the director of a corporation occupies a position of trust as to demand that he participate in the management of the business in such manner as to promote, not his own interests, but the common interests of all the shareholders. 

Dubbs v. Kramer, 302 Pa. 455 (1931). Plaintiff, minority stockholder, director and vice-president of a corporation, entered into a written agreement with the defendant, who was also an officer and the majority stockholder, that at a meeting of the board of directors the board would vote a named salary to the plaintiff. FER- 

GUSON, P. J. "It is the duty of a director to deal with the affairs of a corporation at meetings of the board. Presumably he will discuss with his fellows the business of the corporation and act for its best interests. He cannot contract to use his vote for the benefit of anyone else, or even for the benefit of the corporation. If it were otherwise, a director might for a consideration moving to himself personally sell his vote as a director."

Part 6. Restraint of Trade 

Sec. 384. Agreement not to Compete. Pennsylvania follows the distinction between contracts in general restraint of trade and those in partial restraint. 

The former are void, while the latter will be sustained 

65 Note 57 supra.

if reasonable.66 Combinations in restraint of trade, and price-fixing agreements, are considered in the chapter on Government Regulation of Business. The third type of agreement in restraint of trade is a restriction placed upon the vendor of a business not to compete, or to engage competitively in the same business with the vendee. 

Such contracts tend to deprive society of the services of persons in those capacities in which they are more useful. The criterion of legality is whether the restraint is reasonable with reference to the situation, business, and objects of the parties, and whether it is imposed for a just and honest purpose, for the protection of the legitimate interests of the vendee. The restraint is unreasonable if the protection afforded by the agreement is greater than necessary, or imposes an undue hardship, or tends to create a monopoly. Within recent years the 

Supreme Court has adopted the majority view that a restriction, unlimited in time, may be sustained if the contract is otherwise reasonable."7

Holland v. Brown, 304 Pa. 545 (1931). A merger agreement provided that none of the subscribers should engage in the dairy business within a radius of ten miles of East Pittsburgh, for an indefinite period of time. FRAZER, C. J. "Under the circumstances here presented and established by the evidence, we are of opinion the ten-mile restriction is not objectionable and that defendants' competitive activities within that radius should be enjoined. The area-limiting clause of the merger agreement here in question, having regard to the subject matter of the contract, is not against public policy or unreasonable; it merely affords a fair protection to plaintiffs and does not oppress defendants."

Sec. 385. Interpretation of Agreement. A promise not to engage in the same business at any place within a radius of twenty-five miles from any point or place where the promisee may be engaged in such business, has been construed to apply to the vicinity in which the promisee was established in business at the time the agreement was made, and not to each successive location.68

Johnson v. McIntyre, 309 Pa. 191 (1982). A physician agreed not to reëngage in the practice of medicine and surgery within a radius of fifteen miles from the Borough of Boswell for a period of fifteen years.

The distance by nearest traveled public road from Boswell to an office he had established in Johnstown was 15.4 miles, and by direct line, 12.2 miles. If the defendant, as his argument implies, intended to describe a district irregular in shape and extent, as dependent on accessibility by public roads, he should have said so." 

Sec. 386. National Industries. Many industries are general and not local, and the better opinion seems to be that an area limitation may be coextensive with the interest to be protected.

Diamond Match Co. v. Roeber, 106 New York 473 (1887). De fendant agreed not to engage in the manufacture or sale of friction matches in the United States, except in Nevada and Montana, for a period of ninety-nine years. ANDREWS, J. "There are trades and employments which, from their nature, are localized; but this is not true of manufacturing industries in general. We are unwilling to say that the doctrine as to what is a general restraint of trade depends upon state lines, and we cannot say that the exception of Nevada and Montana are colorably merely. The rule itself is arbitrary, and we are not disposed to put such a construction upon this contract as will make it a contract in general restraint of trade, when upon its face it is only partial." 

Part 7. Relief Sec. 387. Illegality Remote. Where a transaction is illegal, and this fact necessarily appears in the testimony, the courts will lend their aid to neither party. It is not essential that such a defense appear in the pleadings. If a claim can be made out without showing any wrongdoing, or if a new contract has been entered into although having its origin in an inhibited transaction, or if the forbidden act is merely incidental and need not be shown as part of the case, suit may be successfully maintained. There is a distinction between ignorance of the law, and justifiable ignorance of the illegality of a particular transaction. Such situations have been

recognized where a truck was leased without knowledge that it was to be unlawfully used for the transportation of intoxicating liquor," or where a buyer purchased neo salversan without knowledge that it had been smuggled into the United States in violation of the legal rights of the licensed distributor,70 or where an architect was unaware that the proposed construction of a schoolhouse created an excessive indebtedness.71 

Sec. 388. Non Pari Delicto. As a general rule, moneys paid cannot be recovered where illegality appears in the evidence necessary to sustain a judgment,"2 but there are exceptions. Rescission may be permitted, or compelled, where it would otherwise cause harm to parties for whose protection statutes have been enacted. 

This principle is applied to an improper agreement entered into by a trustee in violation of a trust. Or if one of the parties, though blameworthy, is not in pari delicto, or in equal fault, and is not guilty of serious moral turpitude, he may repudiate the bargain and recover what he has parted with." And where an illegal contract is executory, money or goods may be recovered if the illegal part is wholly unexecuted, unless the agreement involves serious moral turpitude. As said in 

Peters v. Grim, in reference to moneys in the hands of a third party which were supposedly to be used in the future in the continuance of gambling transactions: "There is always a locus penitentioe, and just as much in regard to a second act as to a first, if the second is distinct and separate." 74

CHAPTER X  Part 1. General Statutes Sec. 389. English Statute. During the 29th year of 

Charles II, 1676, the English Parliament enacted a comprehensive statute designed to prevent, either by purchase or descent, the fraudulent acquisition of property. This statute is known as the Statute of Frauds.¹ 

Its title is, "An act for prevention of frauds and perjuries." It was enacted "for the prevention of many fraudulent practices, which are commonly endeavoured to be upheld by perjury and subornation of perjury." 3 

Sec. 390. Pennsylvania Statute. Eight sections 2 

of the English statute have been adopted, in whole or in part, and on different occasions, by the legislature of Pennsylvania. The majority of the states have adopted but two. Consequently there is considerable difference between the Pennsylvania Statute of Frauds and that of other jurisdictions. The Pennsylvania statutes, although based on more of the sections of the English code, are limited in their application to three subjects, (1) interests in land, (2) contracts of guaranty, and (3) the sale of goods of the value of $500 or upwards. By adopting two sections of the English statute in their entirety, the Statute of Frauds in other states includes, in addition to the foregoing, (4) agreements made upon consideration of marriage, and (5) agreements not to be performed within the space of one year.

Sec. 391. Purpose of Statute. In order to prevent fraud and perjury the several statutes provide, with certain exceptions to be noted hereafter, that all such transactions should be manifested or established by a written memorandum, rather than by oral testimony. 

1 Robert's Digest of British Statutes, 304. 

2 Sections 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, and 17. 

8 Sections 4 and 17. 

299

They do not disturb or dispense with any other element of a valid contract heretofore considered, but merely add this additional requirement. 

Edgcomb v. Clough, 275 Pa. 90 (1922). SCHAFFER, J. "... It was designed to prevent litigation over oral agreements, where the terms are always dependent upon the uncertain and varying memory of witnesses. This evil was to be remedied by the reduction of the terms of the contract to writing, so that the parties might not misunderstand the particulars of the contract which they were making; that no man might be induced to enter a court of justice to vex the peace of his opponent without clear and definite evidence of the terms of the contract which form the ground of action, equally accessible to both parties and to the court; and that perjury might not be invited to sustain a claim which never had any real existence.' 927 

Sec. 392. The Evidence Act. In addition to the 

Statute of Frauds, there is another important statute which is designed to prevent proof of fraudulent claims. Under the common law of Pennsylvania, all persons were disqualified from testifying in suits in which they had an interest in the subject matter in controversy. This general disability was removed in 1869. It was perpetuated by the Act of 1887,5 although a few exceptions continue to the present day.

The Act of 1887 is called the Evidence Act. It might be prefaced with the scriptural proverb: "Wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together."

It provides that where any party to a contract is dead, a surviving party, whose interests are antagonistic to the decedent's estate, shall not be a competent witness to any matters occurring before the death of the deceased. Such a contract may be proved by a writing, or by the declarations the decedent may have made in his lifetime to others, or by any other legally competent evidence, but not by the testimony of a surviving party. To this extent the death of one party to a contract seals the lips of the surviving party. A 

4 Act of April 15, 1869, P. L. 30. 

5 Act of May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, 28 

PS 314. 

Gest on Wills, 95.

blanket injunction of this sort may, on occasion, defeat an honest claim, but this result is inevitable where general rules are depended upon to work substantial justice. 

Swieczkowski v. Sypniewski, 294 Pa. 323 (1928). Plaintiff re covered a judgment in the lower court for domestic services rendered to her deceased uncle pursuant to the terms of an alleged oral contract. She was permitted by the lower court to testify in detail as to her services in decedent's home, her hours of employment, household purchases made by her, and the expenditure of moneys he gave her, the latter to negative the idea that she received any of it for herself. In setting aside the judgment, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "All of these things were 'matters occurring before the death' of her uncle. About them she was forbidden to testify by the express terms of the act; to permit her to so testify was manifest error. Plaintiff was not only a surviving and remaining party to the contract in action, but she had an interest adverse to the right of the decedent."

The usual mortgage is, in form, a conveyance but with a clause of defeasance which provides that the title shall revert back to the mortgagor upon repayment of the loan. Sec. 394.

The Act of 1772 16 contains the first and part of the second section of the English Statute of Frauds. It provides, in substance, that a lease of real estate, which exceeds a term of three years, must be signed by the lessor or by his agent lawfully authorized in writing. Many of the states have shortened the term to one year, but Pennsylvania still follows the

English law. The following principles may be derived. from this statute: (1) An oral lease for a term of less than three years is valid. (2) A lease for a term of more than three years, in order to be valid for the full term, must be in writing. (3) If it is executed by an agent, the authority of the agent must be in writing. (4) The term of three years begins to run from the date of the agreement,18 and not from the date on which the lessee is to take possession.19 (5) An oral lease for a term of more than three years is not void. It is a lease at will,20 the lease agreement regulating the terms of the tenancy in all other respects.21

Sec. 396. Sale of Land. The remaining part of the 

Act of 1772, supra, is taken from the third section of the English Statute of Frauds. It deals with assignments, to be considered hereafter, and sales of any interest in real estate. It provides that a sale of real estate must be by deed or note in writing, signed by the grantor or by his agent lawfully authorized by writing. The sig nature of the buyer is not essential. The statute was passed for the protection of landowners. A contract is essential, as in all other contracts, but the landowner is the only one who is required to sign the memorandum or agreement. An oral promise may be made good by a subsequent writing, but not by parol.25 A last will and testament may constitute supporting evidence of an oral agreement, if it makes some reference thereto.26 It has recently been held that an agreement of sale, signed by two of three co-tenants, was insufficient to convey the entire fee, and that equity would not decree specific performance, or order a conveyance by those who executed the agreement of their undivided interests in the property.2 If a memorandum or agreement is signed by an agent, his authority to do so must be in writing. A contract signed by an agent not having written authority, however, may be ratified in writing by his principal, 27

Sec. 397. Agreement to Sell. In 1808 the Supreme 

Court observed that "it is one thing to convey an estate, and another and very different thing to make an agreement that you will convey it." 29 The Act of 1772, supra, applies only to the grant or conveyance of the title. The validity of an oral, executory agreement to sell, is disposed of in the fourth section of the English Statute of Frauds. It provides that no action shall be brought upon an oral contract for the sale of land. This clause is in effect in a majority of the states. It was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1856,30 but for some reason it was repealed in 1857.31 If damages were to be awarded for breach of an oral agreement to sell, the effect might be to nullify, by indirection, the requirement of a writing in order to pass the estate. This may account for the ruling of the Supreme Court in modern times, that damages may not be recovered for breach of an oral agreement to sell, unless "it was obtained by fraud." 2 In 

1937 the Supreme Court announced its intention to enforce an oral contract unless timely objection is made at some stage of the proceedings in the trial court. "To permit a party to invoke the statute of frauds for the first time on appeal would be manifestly unfair." 33

Sec. 400. Executed Contracts. In 1807 the Supreme 

Court held that if there had been a partial performance of an oral contract for the sale of land there was "no danger of perjury in proving it," and enforced it on that ground. That was more than a century ago. During the next fifty years the Court built up a series of precedents requiring other equitable circumstances to appear, one of which was the insolvency of the vendor. 43 Jamison v. Dimock, 95 Pa. 52 (1880). Both plaintiff and defendant claimed title to a house and lot under Peter Herdic, the plaintiff by deed and the defendant under an oral agreement. 

Herdic built the home for the defendant, put her in possession, and received the full purchase price. He became insolvent and mortgaged the property. The mortgage was foreclosed and plaintiff purchased at sheriff's sale. In sustaining the oral agreement, it was said by STERRETT, J. "Departures from the strict letter of the Statute of Frauds have been reluctantly sanctioned only on the ground that the statute, enacted for the purpose of preventing fraud and perjury, should not be used as the means of perpetrating fraud. . . . In this case we have the important additional element of complete performance by the vendee, coupled with the insolvency of the vendor and the fact that in violation of his contract, he conveyed the legal title to a stranger, who had notice, however, of the defendant's equitable title." 

Sec. 401. Substantial Improvements. In order to sustain the validity of an oral contract for the conveyance of real estate, a chancellor is required to act, if at all, in the teeth of the Statute of Frauds, and ordinarily will not do so unless the statute is being used as an instrument of fraud. In order to justify equitable relief under these circumstances, the evidence should identify the parties as well as the land, fix the amount of the consideration, and show such performance or part performance as cannot be compensated in damages. Per formance is usually interpreted to mean valuable improvements, such as the construction of buildings upon 

43 Ebert v. Wood, 1 Binn. 216 (1807).

1 the land, although it has been said that "an owner cannot be improved out of his estate," and not after notice by the owner repudiating an oral agreement.*5 A different situation is presented where one of the parties is dead. The chancellor is then aided by the express mandate of the Act of 1917.46 This statute requires specific performance where one of the parties shall have died, "in all cases where such parol contract shall have been so far executed that it would be against equity to rescind the same." Tetlow's Estate" established an oral agreement, identified the land, fixed the amount of the consideration, and put the vendee in possession, but little more than circumstances which made it unfair not to have sustained the agreement. This would not likely have been sufficient if both parties had been living, and if the court had not been aided by statutory authority.

Furthermore, a parol gift of land is invalid under the statute of frauds unless followed not only by change of possession but by the making of such permanent improvements on

Sec. 403. Assignments. The Act of 1772, supra, also applies to the assignment of a lease, or of any other interest in real property. An assignment of such an interest, however, is not void per se. "It has long been established that a contract within the statute of frauds will be accorded full legal effect if those who are entitled to the protection of the statute choose to affirm the existence of the contract and recognize it as binding on them." 49

An oral assignment of a leasehold estate, having more than three years to run, may be accepted or rejected by the owner of the reversion.50 In the following case it was rejected.

Part 3. Guaranty

Sec. 406. Contract of Guaranty. The Act of 1855 55 

is taken from section four of the English Statute of Frauds. It provides that no action shall be brought on a promise to answer for the debt or default of another, unless such promise is in writing, signed by the promisor, or some other person authorized by him.

There are always two separate contracts in an undertaking of this sort. The first is a contract between a creditor and his debtor. This is known as the primary contract. The second is a contract between the creditor and the guarantor. This is the collateral, or contract of guaranty. If the two contracts are made concurrently, as is usually the case, the first contractunder which credit or a loan is to be extended to the debtor-will furnish the consideration for the promise of the guarantor in the second contract. Otherwise, the creditor must show some other consideration to support the promise of the guarantor. It is the second, or contract of guaranty, which must be supported by a written promise on the part of the guarantor. The provision that, "No action shall be brought," is interpreted in this state as a limitation of judicial authority, rather than as a personal defense, and for this reason, "judgment should be entered for the defendant where the evidence shows the contract not to be legally sustainable." 56 In other words, an oral contract of guaranty is not legally enforceable. 

55 Act of April 26, 1855, P. L. 308, 33 PS 3. This act also includes a promise by an executor or administrator to answer damages out of his own estate. Section two expressly excludes any contract, the consideration of which is less than $20. 

50 Bayard V. Pa. Knitting Mills 

Corp., 290 Pa. 79 (1927).

Shannon v. American Iron & Steel Co., 66 Pa. Superior Ct. 211 

(1917). Plaintiff sought to enforce an oral contract of guaranty. 

He sold goods to Weller, relying upon the oral promise of the treasurer of the defendant company: "If there is anything new in the way of tools and machinery that he (Weller) needs to complete the job, don't hold him up. Give it promptly and we will see that you are paid." HENDERSON, J. "The purpose of the promise was to guarantee the payment of the bill which Weller contracted for the goods ordered by him. In such a case the promise is within the statute and not enforceable in an action at law." 31 

Sec. 407. Business Practice. A good many business men, when confronted with a situation of this sort, will convert the proposed guarantor into a debtor by suggesting that the goods be sold to him and charged to his account, and delivered to the person whom he might designate. If this suggestion is accepted the transaction would not constitute a contract of guaranty, and a writing would be unnecessary. Otherwise the creditor should, under the statute, obtain a written promise from the guarantor. 57 

Sec. 408. The Memorandum. A written promise to answer for the debt or default of another should be self sustaining. The endorsement of a negotiable instru ment, such as a promissory note or check, will create a secondary liability, if certain conditions are satisfied, but only as provided by the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act. If the note or check is not a negotiable instrument, such an endorsement does not impose any liability for the payment of the obligation.58 At most it merely operates as an assignment of whatever property right the endorser has in the instrument. In other words, one's signature, standing alone, is not a contract of guaranty. An express undertaking is necessary for that purpose. This is usually accomplished, in the case of commercial paper, by the statement, "I hereby guarantee payment of the within obligation, and all renewals and extensions thereof." 

57 Act of May 16, 1901, P. L. 194, 56 PS 1. 

58 Reardon's Estate, 307 Pa. (1932). 350

Moore v. Eisaman, 201 Pa. 190 (1902). The parties to a con tract obtained the following endorsement from the defendant: "O. K., J. R. Eisaman." Plaintiff contended that the letters, "O.

K." were equivalent to a promise to guarantee payment of the obligation. MESTREZAT, J. "We have examined the evidence with care, and it fails to show that the common acceptation or meaning of the letters written by Eisaman at the end of the contract is that of a guaranty." 

Sec. 409. Personal Interest. Whenever the guaran tor has some personal interest in the transaction, a written memorandum is unnecessary, even though the promise is to answer for the debt or default of another. 

Otherwise the Statute of Frauds could be used as an instrument of fraud.

Mosley v. Massiah, 89 Pa. Superior Ct. 463 (1926). Defendant orally promised certain plasterers who were working on his property under a contractor who had not paid them for their prior week's wages, that if they would continue the work he would see that they were paid. TREXLER, J. "The law is well settled that where the leading object of the promisor is to subserve some interest or purpose of his own, notwithstanding the effect is to pay or discharge the debt of another, his promise is not within the statute." 

Sec. 410. Secondary Liability. The distinguishing characteristic of a contract of guaranty, is the secondary liability of the guarantor. Before the creditor is entitled to recover from him, he must first exhaust all available remedies against the debtor. The guarantor becomes liable only after the debtor has proved to be insolvent and the creditor has used due diligence to obtain payment from him without success. It has been held that a judgment against the debtor, and the return of an execution unsatisfied, would be prima facie evidence of insolvency and of due diligence.50 The liability of a surety, on the other hand, is primary. In a contract of suretyship, it is not necessary to first proceed against the principal debtor in order to hold a surety liable for the payment of the debt," or even against the collateral.61 

50 League Island Com. B. & L. Assn. v. Doyle, 323 Pa. 287 (1936). 

60 Brock's Assigned Estate, 312 Pa. 

7 (1933).

85 Pa. Superior Ct. 480 (1925).

The Act of 1913 62 provides that a contract of guaranty shall subject the promisor to the liabilities of a surety, unless it contains, in substance, the words: "This is not intended to be a contract of suretyship." Some explanation of this unusual situation appears to be justified. 

Part 4. 

Suretyship Sec. 411. Origin of Suretyship. In 1827 the Su preme Court distinguished between the liability of a guarantor and that of a surety, but without mention at that time of either of these terms.63 The liability of the former was conditional upon the exercise of due diligence in an effort to recover from the principal debtor, while the liability of the latter was absolute. By 1863 these two concepts had become recognized as "special" and "general" guaranty." The latter is now identified as a contract of suretyship.65 Difficulty then arose in ascertaining the intent of the parties. The expression used was in some cases held conclusive of absolute liability, but in the course of time the question was made to depend largely upon the character of the obligation. 

If it was indefinite in point of time, or uncertain in its application, it was and may still be construed as a guaranty undertaking. The decisions prior to 1913 are difficult to reconcile. Thus, substantially the same language, which was later held sufficient to create a suretyship when employed in a demand note, was held insufficient when employed in a time obligation.* In 

1880 68 a "guaranty" of "payment of the within note" was held to constitute a secondary obligation, while in 

1893 ** substantially the same expression in a similar obligation was held to create a surety relation. 67 69 64 

62 Act of July 24, 1913, P. L. 971, 8 PS 1. 66

Sec. 413. Unauthorized Change. The distinction between the primary contract, and the surety's collateral obligation, has been pointed out. A surety's obligation is made in reference to the primary contract, and generally, his obligation is to do what he has agreed to do. 

Suppose the parties change or alter or modify or compromise the primary contract without the consent of the surety. At first blush, he would be justified in denounc ing his obligation under the collateral contract. Suppose, however, that he is a paid surety for a public of ficer, that there is a default by such officer, and that instead of first calling upon the surety to make good the loss, the government accepts a note from such officer which proves to be worthless. Is the surety to be relieved, on the ground that he did not concur in this effort to recoup the loss? The answer has been well expressed
