Part 5. Sale of Goods Sec. 414. Uniform Sales Act. The Uniform Sales 

Act," which was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1915, incorporates the seventeenth section of the English Statute of Frauds. It provides that a contract to sell or a sale of any goods or choses in action," of the value of $500 or upwards," shall not be enforceable unless (1) the buyer shall accept part of the goods or choses in action and actually receive the same, or (2) give something in earnest to bind the contract or in part payment, The available without recourse to an action." Black's Law Dict., 324. chose, or thing, which gives rise to the action is usually a contract, note, bond, stock, or other commercial security. 

75 Ten pounds sterling or upwards in the English statute,

or (3) unless some note or memorandum in writing be signed by the party to be charged or by his agent in that behalf. This statute is not a mere rule of evidence, which may be invoked by the defendant at his option, but is a limitation of judicial authority to entertain the suit. Thus, where an action was brought to enforce an oral contract for the sale of tobacco of a value exceeding $500, which was entirely executory, it was said by Judge LINN: "It is well settled that as the statute prescribes that such oral contract is not enforceable, the statute need not be pleaded."" 99 76 

Sec. 415. Acceptance. 

Acceptance. If the statute permitted the buyer to accept part of the goods under an oral contract, and then prohibited the seller from instituting an action against the buyer, the statute would merely sanction a fraud. It is for this reason that an oral contract may be established under such circumstances. It will be ob served in a later chapter that title passes from the seller to the buyer, under certain conditions, when the goods are delivered to a common carrier, but this does not satisfy the statute of frauds." The words "accept" and "actually receive" have distinct meanings, and both are essential.78 

Where there are two or more contracts of sale, and the allotments for delivery are for different quantities to be bought and paid for at different times, the acceptance of one allotment is not an acceptance of the goods as to any other allotment."9 The same is true of a single unit, which is separately sold and paid for.80 

The rule is otherwise where several items are contained in but one contract.

Sec. 416. Parol Modification. Not infrequently the parties to a written contract modify it by a subsequent oral agreement. The acceptance of part of the goods under the subsequent parol agreement is sufficient to satisfy the statute of frauds.

Producers' Coke Co. v. Hoover, 268 Pa. 104 (1920). Plaintiff sought to recover on a written contract which required the delivery of 48,000 tons of coke @ $3.60 per ton, to be delivered at the rate of 4,000 tons per month during the year. Defendant offered to prove a subsequent oral modification which reduced the amount to be delivered, and that deliveries had been made and accepted for seven months thereafter. Plaintiff objected to this testimony on the ground that the alleged modification was not in writing. 

WALLING, J. "Here defendant's offer was to prove, not only that the written contract had been modified by the parol contract, but also that for seven months thereafter the coke had been delivered, accepted, and paid for under the latter; if so, it would be valid, although not in writing." 

Sec. 417. Sale on Option. Where goods are sold and delivered under an oral agreement by the seller to take them back at the option of the buyer, acceptance of the goods is sufficient to sustain the agreement to repur chase. 

Ellis v. Greenbaum Sons Investment Co., 307 Pa. 77 (1932).

KEPHART, J. "It is contended that the oral agreement to repurchase the bonds is within section 4 of the Sales Act of 1915, P. L. 

543, statute of frauds, and should have been in writing. The stipulation for repurchase was made at the time the bonds were sold; it was part of the consideration of the original sale. The statute of frauds was complied with by the delivery of the bonds to the appellee under the original agreement, and the entire transaction, including the agreement to repurchase, thereby rendered valid and binding." 

Sec. 418. Assent to become Owner. The statute expressly recognizes an acceptance "when the buyer, either 1-1

before or after delivery of the goods, or any part thereof, expresses by words or conduct his assent to becoming the owner of those specific goods."

Clegg & Clegg v. Lees & Lees, 82 Pa. Superior Ct. 584 (1924). 

KELLER, J. "There was evidence in the present case, which, if believed by the jury, would justify a finding by them that one of the defendants inspected the very lot of yarn in suit at the plaintiffs' warehouse, drew samples of it and took them to his partner for examination; that after such inspection and examination the other partner, acting on behalf of the defendants, agreed to buy the whole lot of yarn, "As is," at 1712c. per pound, and thereby before delivery expressed defendants' assent to becoming the owners of those specified goods; and that the specific goods thus purchased by them were actually delivered to and received by the defendants. This brings the case squarely within the requirements of the Sales Act and permits the plaintiffs to bring their action to enforce the contract, and a recovery if entitled thereto on the merits." 

Sec. 419. Part Payment. The second condition under which an oral contract may be established, is the giving of something in earnest to bind the contract, or in part payment. The reason for this provision is obvious. If the statute permitted the seller to receive a part payment, without delivery of the goods, and then prohibited the buyer from instituting an action against the seller, it would sanction a fraud. Part payment may consist in the performance of an act, the transfer of something of value, or even applying an existing obligation in part payment, provided it is followed by an actual discharge or cancellation by the giving of a receipt and the entry of credit on the seller's books of account.8 81 

Sec. 420. The Memorandum. In the absence of the acceptance of part of the goods, or the receipt of part payment, a written memorandum is essential in order to sustain a contract for the sale of goods or choses in action of the value of $500 or upwards. The statute does not require that both buyer and seller sign such a memorandum, but only "the party to be charged or his agent 

81 H. Feldman's Sons Co. v. Netsky, 348 Pa. 237 (1944).

84 in that behalf." 82 The authority of an agent need not be in writing.83 An agent may act for both buyer and seller with the full knowledge and consent of both, but if the same person acts in this dual capacity, it is essential that he sign a memorandum in behalf of the principal sought to be charged.85 It is immaterial in what part of the writing the signature appears. A memorandum need not be in any particular form, but it should be self-sustaining. "A memorandum which merely recognizes that there is a contract does not satisfy the requirements of the statute. The note or memorandum must contain all essential terms of the contract, so that it will not be necessary to supply any omissions by parol." 87

Several writings may be used to satisfy the statute if one contains a reference to the other, either expressly or by internal evidence of their relation and connection with each other.88 But this connection must appear on their face, and if it does not, oral evidence may not be used to supply the omissions.89 An oral agreement may be confirmed by a subsequent memorandum," but a letter or telegram repudiating an oral agreement may not be used for that purpose. 

Southern Pine Sales Corp. v. Braddock Lumber Co., 81 Pa. Su perior Ct. 309 (1923). Defendant wrote to the plaintiff stating that he had given an order to plaintiff's agent for certain lumber, but that the acknowledgment did not comply with the terms of the order. For this reason the letter cancelled the order. Plaintiff contended that this letter was a sufficient memorandum to satisfy the statute of frauds. KEller, J. "It was to avoid just such disputes as to the contract entered into between the parties, and the consequent temptation to falsify testimony concerning it, that the provisions of the Statute of Frauds and of our Sales Act, invoked here by the defendant, were enacted." 

82 Franklin Sugar Refining Co. v. 

Howell, 274 Pa. 190 (1922).

Co., 93 Pa. Superior Ct. 227 (1928).

Sec. 421. Special Manufacture. The Statute of 

Frauds has no application to the sale of goods which are to be manufactured by the seller especially for the buyer, and which are not suitable for sale to others the ordinary course of the seller's business. 

American Shirt Co. v. Sapper, 70 P. L. J. 492 (1922). SHAFER,

P. J. "The action is for the price of shirts sold and delivered by plaintiff to defendant. The contention of defendant is that no contract for the purchase of shirts was made and that if such contract was made it was not enforceable because not in writing and for over $500.00 and that there was no evidence that the shirts were made in accordance with the order as claimed by the plaintiff. The jury has found upon sufficient evidence that there was a contract, and that the shirts, being according to the contract marked with the label of the defendant, were not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of seller's business, and that therefore the statute of frauds did not apply."

Part 6. Other Jurisdictions 

Sec. 422. Marriage Settlements. Section four of the English Statute of Frauds requires "any agreement made upon consideration of marriage" to be signed by the party sought to be charged, but while this provision is in effect in a majority of the states, it has never been adopted in Pennsylvania. It was decided very early in other jurisdictions that this clause had no application to mutual promises of marriage, but only to "settlements" in consideration of marriage. Furthermore, "Marriage is not such a part performance of an oral antenuptial contract as to take it out of the operation of the Statute of Frauds." 91

Sec. 423. One Year Agreements. Section four of the English Statute of Frauds also provides that any agreement that is not to be performed within the space of one year from the making thereof, must be signed by the party sought to be charged, but this clause, although in effect in a majority of the states, has never been adopted in this Commonwealth. As interpreted in 

91 Hunt v. Hunt, 171 New York 396 (1902).

other jurisdictions, it applies only to contracts impossible of performance within the space of one year." Complete performance upon the one side at the time of making the contract, has also been held sufficient to take such a case out of the operation of the statute." 

Sec. 424. Conflict of Laws. As a general rule any conflict between the laws of two or more states is determined by the laws of the place of performance. In 

Bernstein v. Lipper Manufacturing Company, however, the contract was to be performed in several states. 

It was made in Pennsylvania, and was one of those oral agreements "not to be performed within one year from the making thereof." It was contended that the invalidity of the agreement in other states made it unenforceable in Pennsylvania. In disposing of this problem it was said by Mr. Justice KEPHART: "The validity of a contract as affected by the statute of frauds is generally to be determined by the law of the place of contract. 

See 12 C. J. 451. The contract in this case was to be performed in various states, and this illustrates the value of the rule above indicated, for, if the place of performance was to control, the law would find itself in a hopeless tangle." 

92 Warner v. Texas & Pac. R. R. 

Co., 164 U. S. 418 (1896). 94 

93 Bowman v. Wade, 54 Oregon 347 (1909). 

94 307 Pa. 36 (1932).

CHAPTER XI  Part 1. Privity of Contract 

99 1 

Sec. 425. Meaning of Privity. Privity of contract is defined by Webster as "a connection, or bond of union, between parties, as to some particular transaction." 

The question presented by this definition is whether a person who is not a party to the making of a contract has the right to enforce it. "The rule of the common law is that no one can maintain an action in his own name upon a contract to which he was not a party." 

This problem has been a prolific source of judicial and academic discussion both here and abroad. In this country the right of a beneficiary to sue on a contract made expressly for his benefit has been recognized, either by judicial decision or by legislation. Following are the circumstances under which this right is recognized in Pennsylvania. 

Sec. 426. Consideration Beneficiaries. The first ex ception is made in favor of a party who has furnished any part of the consideration.2 

Philipsborn v. 17th & Chestnut Holding Corp., 111 Pa. Superior

Ct. 9 (1933). Bonwit Teller & Company agreed in writing, under seal, to pay to Maximilian Philipsborn the sum of $5,000 per annum as long as he lived and after his death, $2,500 per annum to his wife until her death. Included in the same contract was the relinquishment at a fixed price of Philipsborn's interest in the company and in addition, he and his wife were to refrain from engaging in any manner whatsoever in any business similar to that of the company; and they, as well as any of his immediate family bearing it, were not to use the Philipsborn name in such business. 

Payments were made to Philipsborn during his life, and to his widow for a period of fourteen years. The defendant then acquired the personal assets and good will of the Bonwit Teller Company and discontinued further payments. TREXLER, J. "We prefer to place our conclusion on the fact that part of the consider- 

1 Sweeney v. Houston, 243 Pa. 542 (1914). 

2 Bruber's Estate, 27 Pa. D. R. 474 (1917). 322

ation of the contract was that the wife of Philipsborn should abstain from going into business and while strictly she may not be considered a party to the contract, she was specifically named therein and furnished part of the consideration." 

Sec. 427. Novation Beneficiaries. The second ex ception is made against the purchaser of a business who undertakes to take the place, fill the contracts, and assume the business obligations of the seller of the busi- 

This is known as a contract of novation. ness. 

Delp v. Bartholomay Brewing Co., 123 Pa. 42 (1888). In 1887, A purchased the Hotel Albermarle in Pittsburgh from B, and agreed to assume the existing obligations of the business, which included the balance of a claim by C, which was shown to be $351.45, for merchandise previously sold and used in the running of the hotel. 

In sustaining a judgment in favor of the creditor under this agreement, it was said by CLARK, J. "Whether thereby a technical trust was created is not material. It has always been held that the creditor in such a case has a right of action to compel payment in accordance with the agreement. The Act of April 26, 1855, requiring a promise to pay the debt or to answer for the default of a third person, has no application."

Sec. 428. Donee Beneficiaries. The third exception is made in favor of donee beneficiaries. It has long been established that where a person has received money or property which is to be transferred to a third party, the third party may release the promisor or institute an action against him in his own name. The relation between the parties is essentially that of donor, trustee, and donee. Life insurance beneficiaries are included within this exception. 3 

McNally v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 16 Pa. Superior Ct. 111 (1901). Plaintiff, as beneficiary, instituted this action to recover on a policy of life insurance. The insurance company made payment to the administrator of the person it had insured, rather than to the beneficiary named in the policy. ORLADY, J. "The company has nothing to do with determining who is 'equitably entitled' to this money. No discretion is vested in it by the contract, to weigh and decide between conflicting worthiness, and to act as conclusive judge of its own liability." 

8 Wash. Steel Form Co. v. North City Trust Co., 308 Pa. 351 (1932).

Sec. 429. Creditor Beneficiaries. The fourth excep tion is made in favor of creditor beneficiaries. This exception is generally accepted in other jurisdictions, and is recognized in the Restatement of the Law, but except for beneficiaries under a contractor's surety bond, the principle has not been established as a general rule in Pennsylvania. A possible exception is made where a mortgagor takes out a policy of insurance with a fire insurance company for the protection of his creditor, the mortgagee, in which the mortgagee is made a beneficiary, but in Pennsylvania this is construed to create an independent contractual obligation between the insurance company and the mortgagee. The following case, decided more than a century ago, has been consistently followed in this commonwealth. 

Blymire v. Boistle, 6 Watts 182 (1837). A conveyed a lot of ground to B, under an agreement that B would discharge a debt which A owed to C. C attempted to enforce this agreement against 

B. SERGEANT, J. "Where one person contracts with another to pay money to a third, or to deliver over some valuable thing, and such third person is thus the only party in interest, he ought to possess the right to release the demand, or promise by a third person to pay such debt, being for the benefit of the original debtor, and to relieve him from the payment of it, he ought to have a right of action against the promisor for his own indemnity; and if the promisor were also liable to the original creditor, he would be subject to two separate actions at the same time, for the same debt, which would be inconvenient, and might lead to injustice." 

Sec. 430. Surety Beneficiaries. The fifth exception is made in favor of labor and materialmen, under a contractor's surety bond. Such bonds are customary in public building or construction projects, inasmuch as these beneficiaries are unable to perfect mechanics' liens in projects of this sort. This exception was denied by the Supreme Court in 1928,5 but this defect in the law was supplied by the legislature in 1931. In the meantime the Supreme Court, apparently influenced by nu-

merous articles on the subject,' and by the Restatement of the Law, decided to overrule the principle it had announced in 1928, and to permit such beneficiaries to recover on such a bond in private, as well as public" 

projects. 

• .. 

Com. v. Great American Indemnity Co., 312 Pa. 183 (1933). 

SIMPSON, J. "In 44 out of the 48 states of the Union, that rule has long been enforced (Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Connecticut and Michigan being the exceptions), and in the Restatement of the Law of Contracts, it is considered at length and adopted as the true rule. Since the Restatement was adopted, Connecticut has joined with the other 44 states, and those determinations are so equitable and just, and so certainly carry out the intention of the parties, as shown by the contract and bond, that we willingly join with our sister states in their conclusion on this subject, especially as the legislature by the Act of June 23, 1931, P. L. 1181, has now established our public policy in regard to the matter, by expressly providing for such a provision in all future bonds."

Sec. 431. Compromise Beneficiaries. The sixth ex ception is made in favor of beneficiaries under agreements of compromise. The following "decision created a new class of exceptions, and its effect is limited to that class." 10 

It will be observed that the beneficiary is neither a creditor of the promisee nor of the promisor.

Tasin v. Bastress, 284 Pa. 47 (1925). A agreed to discontinue litigation against B in consideration of B's promise to pay an outstanding indebtedness which C owed to D. SIMPSON, J. "Of course, in this class of cases, presumptively the agreement is made for the benefit of the promisee, but if it clearly appears that the beneficiary was the one primarily to be benefited, there is no substantial reason why it should not be so adjudged.”

Sec. 432. Public Policy Beneficiaries. The seventh exception is made "upon the ground of public policy.

Brill v. Brill, 282 Pa. 276 (1925). The mother of a boy and his alleged father entered into an agreement by which the latter was, at intervals, to pay to the former stipulated sums of money, a specific part of which was to be for the mother's benefit, and

Payments in behalf of the boy were to be made to his mother, "as guardian of the person of her son, Edward, through the guardian of the estate of the said Edward." Subsequently, the mother, for a valuable consideration paid to her by the alleged father, executed and delivered to him a release from all liability, as well to the boy as to herself. In deciding that the obligation to the infant's estate could only be compromised with the approval of the orphans' court, and was enforceable by him, it was said by STERN, J. He has a definite, vital interest in the fund created and in the income therefrom, and it would certainly seem that he thereby comes well within the requirement laid down in Klingler v. Part 2. Assignments 

Sec. 433. Common Law. Under the common law a contract was regarded as creating a personal relationship which neither party could transfer or assign. This principle was based upon the supposition that an assignment would tend to stir up litigation, but this view of the law has since been abandoned. As a general rule every demand connected with a right of property, real or personal, may be assigned and thus create an interest in a third party, unless such an assignment is prohibited by statute or by public policy, or unless the parties by their contract provide that it is not to be assigned. 

Lockerby v. Amon, 64 Wash. 24 (1911). A contract for the sale of real estate contained a stipulation that it was not to be assigned. CHADWICK, J. "A vendor may have confidence that his vendee will not use the property to his disadvantage. It is his privilege to decline to deal with strangers. 

Whatever may have been the reasons for reserving the right to decline to deal with an assignee, such reservation contravenes no rule of public policy. and is enforceable." 

Sec. 434. Executory Contracts. As a general rule an executory agreement is assignable unless it would materially vary the duty of the obligor, or increase the risk, or impair his chance of obtaining performance

from the assignor. The parties to an assignment are called assignor, assignee, and obligor. 

Galey v. Mellon, 172 Pa. 443 (1896). Mellon contracted in writing with Galey for the drilling of an oil well. Galey assigned the contract to the firm of Smith Brothers, experts in the drilling of oil. Mellon resisted payment on the ground, inter alia, that the contract was not assignable. FELL, J. "The work of necessity required the labor and attention of a number of men, and it does not appear that because of this knowledge, experience or pecuniary ability, or for any other reason, Galey was especially fitted to carry it on.

There is nothing of a personal nature about it, and its personal performance by him was not the inducement nor of the essence of the contract."

Sec. 435. Test of Assignability. The usual test in ascertaining whether a contract is assignable, is whether it involves personal confidence, professional skill, or commercial credit. Illustrations of agreements of this sort, as noted in Huffman v. Huffman,¹² are contracts by physicians to cure a patient of a particular disease, contracts by teachers and masters to instruct their pupils or apprentices, and promises of marriage. A contract of fire insurance is personal to the insurance company and the assured. If the assured sells the property which is the subject of the insurance, he should assign the contract of insurance if it is important to the buyer. Written consent, however, should be obtained from the company issuing the policy. All money demands are assignable. So, too, are contracts for the purchase of goods to be paid for on delivery, but not to be paid for sometime after delivery. A vendor may not be compelled to accept the credit of another.

Demarest v. Dunton Lumber Co., 161 Fed. 264 (1908). A lum ber company agreed to sell certain lumber to Kelley & Company, to be paid for within ten days from the date of the invoice. Kelley & Company assigned the contract to Demarest. The lumber company resisted the assignment. WARD, C. J. "The contract under consideration is not merely for the sale of personal property for cash, but implies confidence in Kelley & Co., because they were to have 10 days' credit after title to the lumber passed to them..." 

12 311 Pa. 123 (1933).

Sec. 436. Operation of Law. State and federal stat utes authorizing an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or bankruptcy, provide that the assignee, receiver, or trustee shall be vested with the property and assets of the debtor. The primary function of these officers is to liquidate and distribute the estate among those who are entitled to participate. Performance of the executory contracts of the debtor is incidental, and for the most part optional. The principles noted above apply to assignments of this sort. The question involved in the following case was not whether an insurance agency was assignable, but rather whether the earnings of the agent in that employment were assignable. 

In re Wright, Bankrupt, 157 Fed. 544 (1907). The trustee in bankruptcy sought to recover renewal premiums owing to the bankrupt. NOYES, C. J. "The right to receive the renewal commissions under the present contract, which is the right involved in the question certified, seems not to involve personal confidence. The contracts of insurance have already been obtained. The collection of renewal premiums is largely a ministerial act." 

Sec. 437. Decedents' Estates. The same principles of assignability are also applied to decedents' estates. 

To the extent of the assets that come into their hands, the personal representatives of a decedent are responsible on all his contracts, whether named therein or not, or whether the breach occurs in his lifetime or afterwards.13 Where a contract may be performed by an executor or administrator, or where it embodies a property right, performance of the contract, and the succession of the right, are required as matter of law.¹ 

Book's Estate, 297 Pa. 548 (1929). Maria J. Book, an elderly widow, bound herself, her heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, to care for, maintain, provide for, and educate her niece, Eleanore, a child 22 months of age, in a manner suitable to her financial status, until the child could reach legal age. Shortly after the execution of this agreement and the delivery of the child into her possession, Mrs. Book became quite ill and died within a few days. In reasoning that this obligation did not terminate 

13 Stumpf's Appeal, 116 Pa. 33 (1887). 

14 Young v. Gongaware, 275 Pa. 285 (1922). 1

upon her death, it was said by KEPHART, J. "As personal attention is understood in law, Mrs. Book was not required to give it, nor did the personal relation with respect to attention form the basis of the contract. . . . If the agreement, in terms or by necessary implication, contemplated the personal attention of Mrs. Book as to care, education and maintenance, a different question would be before us." ... 

Sec. 438. Terminable Obligations. Where performance of an executory contract will extend beyond the time during which executors and administrators are required, by statute, to settle the estate, or where such a contract is not consistent with their duties as such, or where personal confidence or professional skill were inducements to the making of the contract, or the act could be done only by the party himself, the act of God, producing sickness, insanity, or death, will excuse performance. 15 

Schrum's Estate, 90 Pa. Superior Ct. 554 (1927). An indenture of apprenticeship between the Directors of the Poor of the County of Mercer, and James and Mary Schrum, provided that a poor child nine months of age, was to dwell with and serve them from the day thereof until the full term of 20 years and three months.

The Schrums both died prior to the expiration of that period. The question involved was whether the contract of apprenticeship survived their death. HENDERSON, J. "That the relationship of master and apprentice is personal, we think cannot now be doubted. . . . 

Service by the apprentice, and nurture and instruction from the master are the inducements supporting the agreement, and if by reason of a cause beyond the control of the parties the contract becomes impossible of performance, it is discharged. At common law such an agreement is not assignable." 

Sec. 439. Future Expectancies. At common law there could be no enforceable assignment of an indefinite future expectancy or thing which had no present actual existence and which rested in mere possibility, although it was otherwise where the right or thing would arise in process of time or by operation of law. In Pennsylvania, equity will support a contingent interest or ex- 

16 Scully v. Kirkpatrick, 79 Pa. 324 (1875).

pectancy as a present contract, to take effect and attach as soon as the thing comes in esse.¹ 16 

Philadelphia v. Lockhardt, 73 Pa. 211 (1873). Four days after the execution of a contract for the construction of a schoolhouse for the city of Philadelphia, the contractor, Lockhardt, assigned all moneys and warrants that were to become due. The city challenged the validity of the assignment on the ground that nothing was due at the time it was made. MERCUR, J. "We think this position is not sound. It is well settled that a contract may be assigned so as to vest in the assignee the equitable right to the proceeds, although the money may not have been due or earned at the time of the assignment. It is often done by builders and other contractors to enable them to procure the materials necessary to fulfill their contracts." 

Sec. 440. Company Stores. The validity of an assignment of wages to be earned in the future, was considerably influenced in Pennsylvania by a contest between the legislature and the courts over the subject of company stores.

The Corporation Act of 1874 17 pro vided that a manufacturing or mining company should have no authority to withhold wages due to any of its employees by reason of the sale to them of household goods, wares or merchandise. The Act of 1881 18 made such transactions unlawful, but in 1886 this act was declared unconstitutional in rather forceful language. 

As said by Mr. Justice GORDON, "The Act is an infringement alike of the right of the employer and the employee; more than this, it is an insulting attempt to put the laborer under a legislative tutelage, which is not only degrading to his manhood, but subversive of his rights as a citizen of the United States." 19 The legislature countered with the Act of 1891,20 which required the payment of wages in lawful money of the United States, and which provided that no assignment of future wages should be valid; and with the Act of 1891,21 which made it unlawful for a manufacturing or mining company to

Sec. 441. Future Wages. The rule which is gen erally approved in other jurisdictions, sanctions the assignment of wages to be earned in the future under an existing contract of employment,23 but not under prospective employment." In this Commonwealth, the assignment of future wages, other than for charitable purposes, 25 is prohibited by the Act of 1891, supra, although as noted, this act has been held unconstitutional as applied to the payment of wages partly in goods and partly in cash. In 1913 26 the legislature experienced a change of sentiment and authorized the assignment of future wages, with the written acceptance of the employer, and the written consent of the employee's wife if any, but this act was declared unconstitutional in the 

24 

Foster's Application, 23 Pa. D. R. 562 (1914). SULZBERGER, P. 

J. "The 1st section of the Bill of Rights is still a living force in this Commonwealth. One of the inherent and indefeasible rights thereby guaranteed is the enjoyment and defence of liberty. It is a declaration against slavery in any form, however modified or disguised. The distinction between a man's acquired estate (that is, his property) and his personal earning power by labor (that is, his freedom) is carefully preserved and sedulously guarded. A man may pledge his property, but not his person. . . It is true that the freedom of contract is a great and necessary right, but it has its limit. And this limit is reached and passed when a man's future labor is pledged to pay his past debts, with the consequence that he and his family are rendered liable to fall from the status of free citizenship into the degradation of pauperism."

Sec. 445. Rights of Parties. Unless there is a nova tion, the assignor may not relieve himself from an undertaking by a mere transfer of his agreement to another. "Every man has the right, as far as contracts are concerned, to decide who shall be his debtor or obligor thereunder." 48

The assignor may have an action against the assignee if compelled to make payments which the latter is bound to liquidate."" The assignee may not increase that burden, inasmuch as the assignor neither reaps its benefits nor shares its responsibilities. 48 

44 Draper Paper Mills V. Huff, Barnes & Opie, Inc., 110 Pa. Superior Ct. 336 (1933). 

45 Lancaster County Nat. Bank's Appeal, 304 Pa. 437 (1931).

Pa. Superior Ct. 202 (1927). 49 

Sec. 446. Parties to the Action. Prior to the adop tion of the Rules of Civil Procedure in 1939, an assignee was generally required to bring his suit, as legal plaintiff, in the name of the assignor as use-plaintiff. In 

1939 the Supreme Court adopted a rule which provides that all actions at law shall be prosecuted by and in the name of the real party in interest, except where a statute or ordinance provides otherwise. Under this rule a third party beneficiary, as well as an assignee, may sue in his own name. It will be observed in a subsequent chapter that real estate is frequently sold "under and subject" to a mortgage. Under the Act of 1878,50 an action by the mortgagee against the purchaser of the real estate to enforce such an obligation, must still be brought in the name of the mortgagor to the use of the mortgagee.

Part 3. 

Interpretation Sec. 447. Parol Evidence Rule. Whenever a writing bears evidence of careful preparation, of a deliberate regard for the many questions which would naturally arise out of the subject-matter, and if it is reasonable to conclude from it that the parties have expressed their final intentions in regard to the matters within the scope of the writing, it will be deemed to be a complete and unalterable exposition. But if it does not purport to disclose the entire contract, or if, when read in the light of attending facts and circumstances it is apparent that it contains only a part of the agreement entered into by the parties, parol evidence is admissible to show what the rest of the agreement is, except that such parol evidence must not be inconsistent with or repugnant to that which is in writing. Where the writing does not fully express the agreement of the parties, the same strictness of pleading and proof is not required;5¹ and either party has the right to show what the true facts are regarding the matter thus resting in parol.52 It should be said that the interdiction of parol evidence to vary or contradict written instruments does not apply to mere receipts.53 

Sec. 448. Contemporaneous Parol Agreement. For many years in Pennsylvania, parol evidence was admissible, irrespective of fraud, accident or mistake, to establish the terms of a contemporaneous oral agreement which induced the execution of a written contract, though it varied, changed, or reformed the instrument. 54

In criticising this departure from the English rule, it was said by Mr. Justice KEPHART: "The Parol Evidence 

Rule was steadily widened so that almost any promise was sufficient to invade the security of a written contract. Constructive fraud was created from mild excuses, and it was acknowledged in Fuller v. Law, 207 

51 Federal Sales Co. v. Farrell, 264 

Pa. 149 (1919). 

52 Kerr v. McClure, 266 Pa. 103 

53 Wagner v. Marcus, 288 Pa. 579 (1927). 

54 Potter v. Grimm, 248 Pa. 440 (1915).

Pa. 101, that our efforts to prevent the abuse of the liberality of the Parol Evidence Rule had not met with success. The following is typical of the better of these cases: 9955 

Croyle v. Cambria Land & Improvement Co., 233 Pa. 310 (1912). 

Plaintiff executed a deed of release, granting to the defendant a right of way upon and over his land for a thoroughfare. He alleged and offered to prove, that he refused to execute this agreement as it had been prepared, but that at defendant's suggestion and in order to avoid delay, he did so relying upon the promise that the defendant company would, within a fixed period, so fill the flat or lowlands on plaintiff's lot, at either side of the thoroughfare to be constructed, so as to bring it to a level with the surface of the thoroughfare. Defendant objected to the admission of this evidence. In overruling the objection it was said by STEWART, J. "No case could better illustrate the wisdom of the policy adopted in this state at a very early period, and since steadfastly adhered to, of excepting out of the operation of the English rule excluding parol evidence to vary, contradict, or alter a written contract, cases where a contemporaneous parol promise is proposed to be shown, on the faith of which the contract was executed." 

Sec. 449. New Parol Evidence Rule. In recent years the Supreme Court has repeatedly announced its intention to uphold the integrity of written instruments, and to insist upon rigid adherence to the rule that where the parties have deliberately and formally committed their engagements to writing, they will not be permitted, by parol evidence, to vary or qualify their contract unless, upon averment and proof of fraud, accident or mistake, the terms sought to be introduced were omitted from the writing.56 A statement of the New Parol Evidence Rule, as expressed by the Supreme Court in 1924, may be summarized as follows: 

Where parties, without any fraud or mistake, have deliberately put their engagements in writing, the law declares the writing to be not only the best, but the only, evidence of their agreement; and unless fraud, accident or mistake be averred, the writing constitutes the agreement between the parties and its terms cannot be added to nor subtracted from by parol evidence. If the contract 

55 Speier v. Michelson, 303 Pa. 66 (1931). 

56 Russell v. Sickels, 306 Pa. 586 (1932). 41.

is couched in such terms as import a complete legal obligation without any uncertainty as to the object or extent of the engagement, it is conclusively presumed that the whole engagement of the parties, and the extent and manner of their undertaking, were reduced to writing; and if an oral and a written contract relate to the same subject-matter and are so interrelated that both would be executed at the same time and in the same contract, the scope of the subsidiary agreement must be taken to be covered by the writing.57 

Sec. 450. Customs. When a contract is made in relation to a matter about which there is an established custom, it is to be understood as forming part of it and may be referred to for the purpose of showing the intention of the parties in all particulars which are not expressed in the agreement.

Colonial Iron Co. v. Workmen & Trattner, 81 Pa. Superior Ct. 

51 (1923). A contract dated March 25, 1920, called for the delivery of a quantity of pig iron during the last half of 1920. Plaintiff contended that he was not bound to deliver the iron until December 31, 1920. Defendant contended that there was a general trade custom in the iron business covering shipments under such a contract, requiring equal monthly shipments during the period of the contract. In sustaining this contention, it was said by GAWTHROP, J. "In the case at bar the custom is not repugnant to the terms of the contract nor inconsistent with them, but merely explains a provision as to shipment which is indefinite and uncertain, and gives effect to the intention of the parties by reading into the contract a usage or custom in the light of which they made the contract. It is not unreasonable nor in conflict with law." 

Sec. 451. Essentials of Custom. In order to be admissible, and before it will be permitted to control the rights of the parties, it must be shown that a custom is certain, definite, uniform, notorious, and reasonable. 

Albus v. Toomey, 273 Pa. 303 (1922). Plaintiff, a Philadelphia manufacturer of ladies' dresses, purchased certain merchandise from a New York jobber. Two months after the goods were received and paid for, plaintiff, through his agents, inspected them, and complained that they were not as warranted. He relied on an alleged custom or trade usage as excusing his neglect to have the 

57 Gianni v. Russell & Co., Inc., 281 Pa. 320 (1924).

goods examined within a reasonable length of time, and instituted this action on the warranty. KEPHART, J. "A jury, from the evidence here introduced, could not have found a definite, fixed custom or trade usage good in all its parts, such as is required to control the affairs of men. It was indefinite in extent of territory, uncertain in its terms, indefinable as to the imperativeness of its operation, obedience being more a matter of grace than compulsion; and it was not so universally practiced as to be notorious."

Sec. 452. Warranties. In the interpretation of contracts it is occasionally necessary to distinguish between a warranty of personal satisfaction, and a warranty of commercial quality or mechanical utility. 

Singerly v. Thayer, 108 Pa. 291 (1885). A being engaged in erecting a high building, B proposed in writing to put in a patent passenger elevator, of novel construction, "warranted satisfactory in every respect." A accepted the offer. After use for about two months, A alleged that it was not satisfactory, and after notice to B to take it out at once, dismantled it and placed it in storage. 

The lower court was of the opinion that if the jury thought that A ought to have been satisfied, he was bound to accept it. In deciding otherwise it was said by MERCUR, C. J. "Was it to be satisfactory to the person for whom it was to be made and by whom it was to be used?. . . It would not have been any clearer had it read warranted satisfactory to you in every respect." 

Sec. 453. Personal Satisfaction. It may be a poor business policy to render valuable services, or to part with valuable property, subject to the personal satisfaction of the other party to the agreement, and yet under some circumstances it is difficult to engage in business on any other basis. This is particularly true of the mail order houses. Dissatisfaction, of course, may not be capriciously or dishonestly asserted. In 

Thaler v. Greisser,58 "The trial judge instructed the jury that if the declaration of dissatisfaction by the construction company was made in good faith, it was a sufficient defense and the plaintiffs could not recover; on the other hand, if it was not made in good faith, but was merely an arbitrary expression of dissatisfaction for the pur- 

58 229 Pa. 517 (1911). Yo

pose of avoiding payment of the balance due on the contract, then it would not be a good defense." This instruction was affirmed. 

Randal v. Mitchel Motor Car Co., 263 Pa. 425 (1919). Plaintiff purchased an automobile under an agreement that if it was not satisfactory he could return it and receive his money back, or he could take a new car under the same agreement. The first automobile was not satisfactory and he received a new and more expensive one, paying the difference in the purchase price. Plaintiff claimed that the second car was not satisfactory, and that he was compelled to send it to defendant's shop twenty or twenty-five times for repairs, within the space of some three months. He then instituted this action to recover the purchase price. SIMPSON, J. "In all our cases, from Singerly v. Thayer, 108 Pa. 291, to Williams v. Notopolos, 259 Pa. 469, it has been uniformly held that such objections need only be made in good faith, and not merely capriciously, in order to justify the returning of an article because it violates a contract that it shall be satisfactory." 

Sec. 454. Commercial Quality. While there is a tendency to let the honest judgment of the party to be satisfied control in matters peculiarly the subject of personal taste, fancy, sentiment and judgment, it is otherwise as to commercial quality, workmanship, fitness for use, and salability, of which others can just as well determine, and where the market is made the exclusive judge.5

This is particularly true of warranties concerning the operative fitness or mechanical utility of goods sold for particular purposes.

Lord Co. v. Industrial D. & F. Works, 252 Pa. 422 (1916). Plain tiff agreed to "furnish such chemicals as shall be required for a thorough and satisfactory treatment of this well water, and guarantees that the chemicals furnished will purify the water so as to make it equal to, or better than, Philadelphia water." The lower court was of the opinion that this was a warranty of personal satisfaction. FRAZER, J. "We do not construe the language of the contract now before us to signify that the work should be done to the satisfaction of defendant, but in such manner as to conform to certain standards, the principal requirement being that the water after treatment should correspond with a specified chemical test. There is nothing in the language to indicate that if the 

Jacobs v. Kraft Cheese Co., 310 Pa. 75 (1933).

plaintiff did the work as stipulated, defendant should still retain the option of refusing payment to the contractor by alleging dissatisfaction with either the appliance or the results produced." 

Sec. 455.

Rules of Construction. Neither the courts nor the legislature have undertaken to announce a formal series of rules which should be applied generally in the construction and interpretation of contracts. The following principles will be found scattered throughout the opinions. (1) A contract comprehends only those things in respect to which the parties propose to contract, and will not be extended to cover other matters not thought of or intended to be included."⁰ (2) Contracts should be construed if possible in a manner that will render them valid rather than invalid; legal rather than illegal; possible of performance rather than impossible; reasonable rather than unreasonable; just rather than unjust; and “we ought not to be studious to create a forfeiture." 61 (3) The purpose in construing all contracts is to ascertain the intention of the parties by a general survey of the entire agreement.62 (4) The acts, declarations, and circumstances surrounding the parties at the time the contract is made are to be taken as a guide to their understanding and intention in giving a construction to it, and preliminary negotiations may be considered, if necessary, in arriving at the intent of the parties.63 (5) If an executory agreement is ambiguous and indefinite, the parties themselves are entitled to show by their respective declarations what each understood at the time of its execution.64 (6) Where the parties have construed their own undertaking and have definitely determined their respective rights and liabilities by a sufficient performance or acts directed toward performance, the courts will not then construe its meaning, even though the agreement be susceptible of two different meanings. 

The courts will construe it to mean what they thus determine it 65 means. (7) A provision contained in an agreement which is capable of two or more meanings should be construed most strongly against the person whose undertaking it is, and ambiguous contracts or 

60 Silverthorn V. Silverthorn, 276 

Pa. 579 (1923). 

01 Stafford v. Walker, 12 S. & R. 

190 (1824). 

62 Vulcanite Paving Co. v. Philadelphia, 239 Pa. 524 (1913). 

63 Ruppert's Estate, 9 Berks 98 

64 Rochester & Pitts. Coal & Iron 

Co. v. Makoma Coal Co., 24 Dauphin 135 (1921). 

65 Daub's Estate, 313 Pa. 35 (1933).

parts of contracts are to be construed most strongly against the party who prepared it or who used the ambiguous expressions.66 (8) A broad and all conclusive word or phrase at the end of an enumeration of words or phrases will be limited to the class of words and phrases set out. This is the rule of ejusdem generis (of the same kind).67 (9) The express mention of one or more things belonging to a class, all of which would have otherwise been included, implies the exclusion of those not mentioned. This is the maxim, expressio unius est exclusio alterius (the expression of one thing is the exclusion of another). (10) No word in a contract is to be treated as surplusage or redundant if any reasonable meaning consistent with th other parts can be given to it.68 The standard for the interpretation of words is their natural meaning to the parties who have contracted at the time and place where the contract is made, considering all the circumstances surrounding it. Words are to be construed according to their primary acceptation unless, from the context of the instrument and the intention of the parties to be collected from it, they appear to be used in a different sense.69 (11) Written words are entitled to have greater effect in the interpretation of contracts than those which are printed, for the written words are those selected by the parties, whereas the words of the printed form are of more general use. But printed parts should be reconciled with written words if this can re reasonably be done. (12) Bad grammar, incorrect spelling, improper punctuation, erasures, and clerical errors will not vitiate a contract or destroy its effect.70 (13) Words will prevail over figures. The Uniform Negotiable

CHAPTER XII  Part 1. Rescission Sec. 456. Kinds of Discharge. Discharge means to relieve or acquit an obligation, liability, debt, duty, or burden. A person so discharged may be free of all duty, or a new duty may be substituted, or he may be under a quasi-contractual duty to restore what has been received. Such a status may result by a rescission, performance, waiver, breach, novation, merger, alteration, avoidance, release, accord and satisfaction, and impossibility of performance. Contractual rights may also be barred by a statutory composition agreement, an adjudication in bankruptcy, and by statutes of limitation.

Sec. 457. Mutual Rescission. The parties to a con tract may agree not to do what they have agreed to do. 

In this sense an executory agreement may always be discharged by mutual consent. If no obligation has been incurred, a mutual agreement to rescind is supported by the same consideration that made it enforceable. It is the agreement to do or not to do a certain thing. If the contract calls for the construction of a building, the parties may, by mutual consent, abandon the undertaking. Neither party may add to, subtract from, rescind or abandon it without the consent of the other. If he attempts to do so he makes himself liable to that other for any resulting damage.¹ 

Sec. 458. Option to Rescind. Not infrequently the parties to a contract stipulate that it may be terminated at the option of one or both of the parties, either on a fixed date or by notice given in advance. The criterion for the exercise of this privilege, is the contract. If it is an agency which may be terminated upon thirty days' notice, "with or without cause," the party exercising 

1 Briggs v. Logan Iron & Steel Co., 276 Pa. 326 (1923). 

23 341

such right is "not obliged to assign reasons for cancellation, nor were its motives material." 2 If it is a sale of coal underlying a farm, to be paid for on a royalty basis, which may be rescinded on default after sixty days' written notice, a rescission without giving such notice will subject the grantor to an action for damages,3 unless the injured party ratifies the wrongful act.* It is a cardinal principle of judicial construction that where a contract provides a mode of rescission, it must be strictly followed." 

Central Guarantee Co. v. Union National Bank, 92 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 70 (1927). A contract for a subscription to a bank directory, entered into April 21, 1922, for five years, subject to cancellation by defendant "at the end of the first year," contained the provision that "subscription commences 7-1-22" and "subscription ends 

7-1-27." Defendant attempted to cancel the subscription on July 

11, 1923. GAWTHROP, J. "The privilege to cancel was written into the contract for the benefit of appellee and it was its duty to give appellant notice of its intention to exercise it on or before July 1, 1923, which was the day which the contract fixed as the end of the first subscription year." 

Sec. 459. Implied Rescission. Mutual assent to abandon a contract may be implied. This is largely a matter of intention. A contract complete in itself cannot be altered without another meeting of minds and a new consideration, but it is competent for the parties to show that it was subsequently abandoned in whole or in part. In the absence of an express agreement, the facts should be conclusive of mutual assent.s 

Bordo v. Grayek, 136 Pa. Superior Ct. 124 (1939). Claimant and two other journeyman plasterers entered into a contract to do the lathing and plastering of a theater building. Union difficulties arose concerning the right of union members to act as contractor-employers, whereupon all of them repudiated the contract in order to retain their status in the union. The owner then let

Part 2. 

Performance Sec. 460. Tender of Performance. Fundamental principles with respect to tender of performance may be expressed as follows: (1) If one party offers to perform, but his offer is refused, defeated, or frustrated, he may rescind the contract and sue for damages.⁹ (2) 

If one party refuses to perform, the other party need not offer to perform before instituting an action for damages.10 (3) As between an innocent party and the party at fault, the former is relieved from the conditions imposed by the agreement. For example, if an insurance company disclaims liability, the insured is no longer required to file a proof of loss.11 (4) It is seldom that tender of payment will discharge a money demand.12 It will discharge interest and costs. The sum brought into court becomes the money of the plaintiff, and the verdict goes for the defendant, carrying with it the costs.13

Sec. 461. Inadequate Performance. A contractual duty is discharged by exact performance. The courts are hesitant to sanction any deviation in the prescribed manner of performance, but it is not every deviation that justifies legal complaint. In a recent case, in which the

It was held that such deviation did not justify a forfeiture of compensation for the work done. If the issue is clear cut and unembarrassed by questions of waiver or compromise, no recovery can be had for partial performance of an entire contract, and especially where performance is clearly inadequate.

Performance Sec. 462. Substantial Performance. 

need not be literal and exact. If the major features of a contract have been executed in good faith, a defense of technicality will not avail to defeat remuneration, and if such a defense is made, there may be a recovery on the contract price less whatever loss or damage may have been sustained. As said in the preceding case: "The law calls for honest, substantial performance, regardless of trifling defects, when passing upon that question, and the judgment of men will always determine what will be a sufficiently close compliance with the requirements of the stipulations, to insure substantial justice." 

Wright v. Barber, 270 Pa. 186 (1921). Plaintiff taxpayers filed a bill in equity seeking to enjoin the Borough of Susquehanna 

15 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 233 (1943). 

14 Sgarlat v. Griffith, 349 Pa. 42 (1944).

Depot and its officers from making further payments to a contractor who had been employed to pave, curb and gutter West Main Street and Willow Avenue. The chancellor found that it would cost more than the balance of the contract price to put the work in the condition provided by the contracts. SIMPSON, J. "Under such circumstances it is well settled that a taxpayers' bill to enjoin further payments under the contracts will be sustained; and we need only again repeat the warning that in a proper case public policy requires this remedy shall be unflinchingly applied, since not otherwise can those who contract with the public be taught that it is just as dishonest to wrong the citizens in their governmental as it is in their individual capacities." 

Sec. 463. Wilful Refusal. The equitable doctrine of substantial performance is applied where there has been a bona fide effort to perform the contract in its entirety, and where slight particulars remain unfinished.16 It is not applied where there is fraud, gross negligence, ❝or obstinate and wilful refusal to fulfil the whole engagement, or even a voluntary and causeless abandonment of it." 

Typhoon Air Conditioning Co., Inc. v. Fried, 147 Pa. Superior

Ct. 605 (1942). Plaintiff sought to recover the balance due on a contract to install an air conditioning system in defendants' theatre. The contract price was $8,200, of which $6,440.12 was paid, leaving a balance of $1,759.88. Defendant offered evidence to show that it would cost $1,431 to perfect the system, leaving a balance of $328.88, but that plaintiff's refusal to complete the work was wilful. The jury found for the defendant, and plaintiff appealed. 

KENWORTHEY, J. "Thus, here, a finding by the jury that plaintiff had substantially performed would have entitled it to a verdict for the balance due, less an allowance for the cost of completing the performance, if the jury had not also found its failure was wilful. 

Under the limitation of the rule, its wilfulness prevents recovery." 

Sec. 464. Architect's Certificate. It is customary to provide, in building projects, that final payment is to be made upon a certificate of completion by the architect, although such a requirement may be waived by the parties if they so desire." Where the production of the 18

Zimmerman v. Marymor, 290 Pa. 299 (1927). Plaintiff sought to recover for the construction of a building by producing the certificate of the architect as agreed upon. Defendants' evidence tended strongly to show that much of the work was so defectively done as to be worthless. They employed a new architect and let a new contract to other parties to complete the work at a loss exceeding plaintiff's claim. WALLING, J. Sec. 465. Anticipatory Breach. Where one party repudiates in advance his obligations and refuses to be longer bound, and communicates such repudiation to the other party, the latter is not only excused from further performance, but may, at his option, treat the contract as terminated for all purposes and institute an action against the party at fault, without waiting the time fixed by the contract for performance.

Hochster v. De La Tour, 118 Eng. Rep. 922 (1853). Plaintiff was employed by the defendant as a courier. The defendant repudiated the agreement before the day fixed for the commencement of the work. Plaintiff promptly instituted an action for damages. 

In deciding that this was a renunciation (not merely an intention) on which plaintiff had a right to rely, it was said by CROMP- 

TON, J. "When a party announces his intention not to fulfill the contract, the other side may take him at his word and rescind the contract." 

Sec. 466. Intention to Repudiate. Notice of an in tention not to perform is only a matter of intention, and if it is not accepted by the other party, it may be withdrawn at any time before performance is due. 

Shamlian v. Waxman, 80 Pa. Superior Ct. 73 (1922). Plaintiffs agreed in writing to purchase of the defendant certain real estate for the sum of $18,000, of which $1,000 was paid at the signing of the agreement. It was to be forfeited in case plaintiffs made de-

Part 3. Waiver 

Sec. 467. Estoppel. It has been observed that a rescission abrogates the contract. A waiver, on the other hand, is a voluntary relinquishment or renunciation of some part of it, or the foregoing or giving up of some particular benefit or advantage flowing from it. It is based squarely on the doctrine of estoppel. Waiver may be shown by acts and declarations manifesting an intention not to claim some privilege growing out of the contract, and under some circumstances by mere neglect or failure to act. In order to constitute a waiver the conduct complained of should be sufficient to raise an estoppel, the effect of which is to excuse technical compliance with all the provisions of the contract. In Ger mantown Dairy Co. v. McCallum,20 the plaintiff agreed to sell its business and to assign the unexpired portion of its lease. The defendant thereafter expressed his unwillingness to take over the lease, and it was not assigned. Apparently the defendant decided not to use it, and did not want to be bothered with it. It was held 

20 223 Pa. 554 (1909).

under these circumstances that he should be estopped from asserting the non-performance of this part of the contract as a defense to an action for the purchase money.

Sec. 468. Mutual Indulgence. A waiver more frequently arises in connection with the time of performance of a contract. As it is frequently expressed, where performance is extended from time to time, with no intention manifested to insist upon a literal compliance with the provisions of the contract, and where there has been indulgence on both sides, one party may not suddenly rescind without notice to the other, or without fair warning of an intention to insist upon a literal compliance in the future.21 In Portland Ice Co. v. Connor, it was held that where payments for ice were to be made weekly and there had been a variance for over a year with the assent of the vendor, the latter could not, in view of the previous course of dealing, make a sudden, unconditional and absolute rescission without giving notice to insist on a strict and literal compliance with the terms of the contract as to future payments. 22 

C. Trevor Dunham, Inc. v. Nemitz, 82 Pa. Superior Ct. 382 (1923). Plaintiff delivered to the defendant an automobile on a bailment lease calling for a total rental in the sum of $2,305.80. 

The sum of $922.32 was paid on the execution of the lease. The balance was payable in monthly installments of $115.29. Title was to pass when the full amount had been paid. Monthly payments were made, none on the date when due, but acceptable to the plaintiff without objection. At the expiration of about nine months the plaintiff issued a writ of replevin. HENDERSON, J. "If the position of the (plaintiff) may be maintained a designing person could indulge the lessee up to the time when the last payment became due and then insist on strict performance by which means he would secure practically all the money intended to be the price of the automobile and by a rescission of the contract retake the property itself. Such a forfeiture could not be enforced consistently with equitable principles, especially where, as in this case, the lessee was ready and willing to pay the balance due." 

21 Forsyth v. The North American 

Oll Co., 53 Pa. 168 (1866). 

22 24 Pa. Superior Ct. 493 (1904).

Sec. 469. Time as Essence. Where time of performance is definitely provided for in a contract, it is said to be of the essence of the contract, in actions at law, but not in equity, unless the parties have expressly made it so.

It is difficult to establish a waiver by mere delay in making payment, when time is expressly made material. 23 Shilanski v. Farrell, 57 Pa. Superior Ct. 137 (1914). Plaintiff agreed to purchase two lots of land for $300, payable $25 in cash and $10 per month. The time for each payment was expressly made material, and provision was made for a forfeiture in case of any default. Payments were made substantially but irregularly from March 5, 1910 to June 30, 1912. On November 9, 1912, the defendant sold the lots to another. RICE, P. J. "The purchaser has no right to rest on such indulgence shown on one occasion, or on a number of occasions, as a ground for claiming it on all occasions. . . . There is the bare fact that up to and including June 30, 1912, the defendants accepted payments at irregular intervals and varying in amount. This, we conclude, does not raise a legal implication of waiver of strict performance by the plaintiff of his agreement to pay the balance of the purchase money when it fell due."

Part 4. Merger and Novation Sec. 470. Merger of Contracts. A merger of con tracts is essentially a change in the form of an existing agreement, as distinguished from a change in substance. In a strict legal sense it means the absorption of a thing of lesser importance by a greater, whereby the lesser ceases to exist but the greater is not increased. 

All obligations are not of equal rank. The higher the form of the obligation, the greater are the legal remedies for enforcing it, even though the substance remains the same. Preliminary negotiations will merge in a parol agreement. A parol agreement will merge in an agreement in writing. An agreement in writing will merge in a specialty, and a specialty will merge in a contract of record. A judgment merges the cause of 

23 Smith v. Brown, 10 Illinois 309 (1848).

1 action and extinguishes it. Merger is largely a matter of intention.24

Sec. 471. Merger of Estates. There is another type of merger. 

As expressed by Blackstone, "whenever a greater estate and a less coincide and meet in one and the same person, without any intermediate estate, the less is immediately annihilated; or, in the law phrase, is said to be merged, that is, sunk or drowned in the greater."25 This, too, may be a matter of intention. "The principle of law which provides that where the holder of a mortgage purchases the fee such purchase operates as a payment of the mortgage debt would seem to apply only where it is the intention of the parties that the purchase should so operate." 26 

Sec. 472. Novation. We have used the term "novation" heretofore as indicating a substitution of parties to an agreement. It is also used to indicate any change of substance. The elements of novation are the displacement and extinction of the prior contract, the substitution of a new contract, a sufficient consideration therefor, and the consent of the parties thereto.27 The obligation may remain the same but with a substitution of parties, or the parties may remain the same but with the substitution of a new obligation." 28 

York Metal & Alloys Co. v. Cyclops Steel Co., 280 Pa. 585 

(1924). The parties agreed to the sale of 85,000 pounds of tungsten powder at a fixed price, one-half to be delivered by the first of January following. After more than one-half had been delivered, disputes arose as to the quality of it, and a new contract was executed extending the date of delivery and payment. SADLER, J. "If there is a real contention between the parties, modification of the existing contract, to settle the differences, is supported by the

Backenstoss v. Stahler, 33 Pa.

reciprocal benefits which follow. Parties may at any time rescind their previous understanding and substitute another therefor where some consideration appears, and the new contract will take the place of that formerly entered into." 

Part 5. Compromise Sec. 473. Accord and Satisfaction. "Accord and satisfaction" is the name given to an agreement in which a creditor accepts some other performance as a complete discharge of an existing obligation. An accord is the agreement of settlement. Satisfaction takes place when the accord is performed. The result, as distinguished from a novation, is to relieve the parties altogether from any further obligation. The original obligation continues to exist, however, until the accord has been executed. "The plea must allege that the matter was ac cepted in satisfaction. Mere readiness to perform the accord, or a tender of performance, or even a part performance and readiness to perform the rest, will not do. 

Such is the law between debtor and creditor." 29 There has been no tendency to depart from this principle. In 

Konqueror B. & L. Assn. v. G. R. Kinney Co., Inc.,30 a lessee agreed to pay the lessor the sum of $3,000 as consideration for the cancellation of a lease, but it was held that inasmuch as an accord is revocable at the pleasure of either party, the agreement could not be enforced notwithstanding the offer and acceptance, where the lessee refused to pay over the sum agreed upon and remained in possession of the premises. 

Hosler v. Hursh, 151 Pa. 415 (1892). Defendant entered into an agreement under seal to pay to plaintiff $3,000 cash in fifteen days and $4,000 in securities, in lieu of two notes. The evidence tended to prove that defendant promptly and in good faith tendered performance of everything required of him by the terms of the agreement, but that plaintiff refused to accept. STERRETT, J. "Tender of performance can never take the place of satisfaction, unless accepted. Accord to be good must be in full satisfaction, and must be executed; readiness to perform is not enough." 

29 Hearn v. Kiehl, 38 Pa. 147 (1861). 

80 315 Pa. 318 (1934).

Sec. 474. Release. An obligation may also be compromised by the execution of a release. A release is an act in writing by which some claim or interest is surrendered and discharged. It may yield, discharge, or abandon a right of action arising in tort as well as contract. It is usually under seal, but under the Uniform 

Written Obligations Act of 1927 31 it may be made effective, without other consideration, if the writing contains an additional express statement, in any form of language, that the signer intends to be legally bound. 

Part 6. Alteration and Avoidance Sec. 475. Effect of Alteration. It is well settled, in both English and American jurisprudence, that a material alteration of any contract or commercial paper, without the consent of the party sought to be charged, and without negligence on his part, extinguishes his liability. If its identity has been changed and another agreement with different terms is substituted, there is no longer the necessary concurrence of minds, and in pursuance of a stern but wise policy, there is no longer any obligation. 

Getty v. Shearer, 20 Pa. 12 (1852). LEWIS, J. "The true foun dation of the doctrine on this subject is, the dangerous consequences which would flow from permitting one of the parties to a written contract, without the consent of the other, to make any material change in it whatever. The alteration may be so artfully made as to render it difficult of detection; and if no penalty follows the discovery, every one may be led into temptation to alter the contracts in his possession, so as to make them more conformable to his interests. The law, therefore, in great wisdom, declares that an alteration by the holder of an instrument in a material part, destroys it altogether."

Sec. 476. Material Alteration. Whether an instru ment has been altered is a question of fact for the jury. 

Whether an alteration is material is a question of law for the court. An alteration is material if it changes the date, names, amount, time, place of payment, rate of 

31 Act of May 13, 1927, P. L. 985, 33 PS 6.

interest, or words of negotiation. In 1909 the Supreme 

Court held that the addition of the signature of a witness, made after the execution of the instrument, was sufficient to destroy its validity,32 but in the absence of some prejudice, this ruling has not been consistently followed.33 The Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act³¹ provides that where a negotiable instrument is in the hands of a holder in due course, who is not a party to the alteration, "he may enforce payment thereof according to its original tenor."

Philadelphia National Bank v. Buchman, 314 Pa. 343 (1934). 

This was an action by a holder in due course on three promissory notes, one of which was in the sum of $2,500. A credit of $18.96 had been applied on this note. Defendant alleged a material alteration of this note on the ground that a faint pencil line had been drawn through the figure $2,500, and the sum of $2,481.04 written above. MAXEY, J. "We agree with the court below that 'there is in fact no material alteration and obviously no harm has been done the defendants.' Furthermore, since the appellants did not aver that the appellee was a party to the alleged alteration 'he may enforce payment according to the original tenor.'" 

Sec. 477. Avoidance. Fundamental grounds for the avoidance of a contractual obligation are failure of consideration, lack of contractual capacity, fraud, public policy, lack of formality where a writing is required, and breach. There is a good deal of decisional law involving the right to exercise this privilege on grounds of fraud or any mistake of facts. The person injured must act promptly, without unnecessary delay, and before the other party has in any manner changed his position.³ 

As soon as the fraud is discovered, he must announce his intention and adhere to it.36 Failure to repudiate within a reasonable time may be conclusive of an election to affirm the obligation.37 Where the evidence is not clear as to whether a party has rescinded, he will be
