Part 7. Impossibility Sec. 478. Duties Distinguished. 

Hand v. Baynes, 4 Wharton 203 (1838). ROGERS, J. "When the law creates a duty or charge, and the party is disabled to perform it, without any default in him, and hath no remedy over, then the law will excuse him; but when the party by his own contract creates a duty or charge upon himself, he is bound to make it good, if he may, notwithstanding any accident by inevitable necessity, because he might have provided against it by his contract. 

This distinction is founded in reason and authority." 

Where a duty has been imposed by contract, mere inconvenience, hardship, or increased expense will not excuse performance, inasmuch as the parties might have provided against these contingencies in their agreement. 

One of two innocent persons must suffer, and he who undertakes the risk must bear it on the ground that he might have protected himself, had he so desired, either by a suitable clause in the agreement, or by insuring the risk.

Booth v. Spuyten Duyvil Rolling Mill Co., 60 New York 487 

(1875). On December 27, defendant contracted to sell 100 tons of steel caps for rails, delivery to be made on or before April 1. 

On March 10, defendant's mill was destroyed by fire. In an action for non-delivery, it was said by CHURCH, C. J. "There was no physical or natural impossibility, inherent in the nature of the thing to be performed, upon which a condition that the mill should continue can be predicated."

Sec. 479. Performable Contracts. "A contract to perform an impossible thing may be void; but it never is impossible to procure and deliver an article of commerce which may be had in the market in some quarter of the world." 39 

Holmes v. Cameron, 267 Pa. 90 (1920). On September 28, 1917, defendant contracted to sell to plaintiff 108 bags (10,800) pounds of noils, a by-product of wool, at 48 cents a pound, per defendant's sample No. 492. A week later defendant wrote the plaintiff that it would be impossible to make delivery, as he had made a mistake in the sample and had none of that grade. In the meantime the 

30 Myers v. Drake, 10 Watts 110 (1840).

market price had gone up to 622 cents per pound. In sustaining an action for non-delivery, it was said by WALLING, J. "As the performance here was not impossible, it is unnecessary to consider to what extent and under what circumstances such impossibility would relieve from the obligation of a contract." 

Sec. 480. Construction Contracts. Where a build ing contract provides that a contractor shall erect a building according to certain plans and specifications, and shall deliver it to the owner in a completed condition, the contractor is liable for any damage to the building during the course of construction, and before it is delivered. This principle is limited in its application to those instances where the building, prior to its completion, is under the sole jurisdiction and control of the contractor, and not where possession or control is reserved by the owner, or where the project is merely an addition to an existing structure, or where the contract calls for repairs to a building over which the contractor has no control. In new building projects, the criterion of liability is the contract. As a practical matter the contractor usually insures the risks incident to the proj ect, or requires the owner to provide such insurance. 

Murphy & Hamilton v. Liberty National Bank, 184 Pa. 208 (1898). GREEN, J. "Thus the total collapse of the building from defects in the foundation or from violent tempest, or its destruction by fire while in the course of construction, will not relieve the contractor from his obligation to finish the building and deliver it in completed condition to the owner, unless such contingencies have been specially excepted by the terms of the contract. 

There is no doubt that the rule is well established and is the settled law both in England and in this country, including our own state." 

Sec. 481. Act of God. Occasionally the parties to a contract stipulate that an act of God, rendering performance impossible, shall excuse either of them from liability. It would be conducive to clarity and obviate unnecessary litigation, if the exemption were made more specific. An act of God, as a legal concept, means some contingency which cannot be reasonably foreseen in the

human course of events. Inclement weather during the seasons of the year is readily foreseeable in this climate, but not a flood of unexpected magnitude,"¹ or an unprecedented drought. The following case is made the basis of an illustration in the Restatement of the Law."2 42 40 

Berg v. Erickson, 234 Fed. 817 (1916). Plaintiff was awarded $20,000 for breach of contract by defendant to furnish plenty of good grass to his cattle during the grazing season of 1913. Defendant claimed exemption because of an unprecedented drought, although no such exemption was provided by the contract. In sustaining the award, it was said by SANBORN, C. J. "The proof in this case has satisfied that it was the intention of the parties that Erickson should thereby make, and that he did make, an absolute covenant with Berg to furnish plenty of good grass for the cattle throughout the entire grazing season without exempting himself from liability in case of drought, fire, or other act of God, or accident that might make his performance impossible; that he took the risk of such an event, and that he is not absolved from liability for the damages which Berg sustained by reason of Erickson's failure to perform his covenant, although that failure was caused by the unprecedented drought which made his performance impossible."

Sec. 482. Effect of War. The question of hardship caused by war has been considered both here and abroad. 

In Blackburn, Bobbin Co. v. Allen & Sons, plaintiffs were manufacturers of bobbins for spinning. Defendants were timber merchants. By contract made in the early part of 1914, defendants sold to plaintiffs timber to be imported from Finland. Defendants claimed to be discharged owing to the disorganization of transport caused by the World War. In overruling this contention it was said by the Court: "If I were to hold otherwise, I should create a rule the results of which no man can foresee, and to the operation of which no judge can satisfactorily fix the limit." 

Com. v. Bader, 271 Pa. 308 (1921). Defendant contracted to construct one of the state highways. On suit for non-performance he admitted that he did not complete his contract, but in avoid-

SIMPSON, J. "In considering the alleged impossibility of performance, it is not necessary to differentiate the interesting cases found in the opinion of the court below, and in the paper-books of the respective parties; for it is conceded that difficulty of performance is not a valid excuse, and we are of opinion the affidavits of defense, fairly interpreted, assert nothing beyond this, whether impossibility of performance is construed to mean absolute impossibility, or 'commercial impracticability,' as averred in some of the cases cited." 

Sec. 483. Supervening Impossibility. Where an agreement is of a continuing character, dependent upon the continued existence of the subject-matter, the subsequent destruction of the subject of the agreement will relieve the parties of the duty of further performance. 

Following are obligations which were discharged for this reason: the delivery of coal by a mining company, by the destruction of a canal by which it could only be delivered; the supplying of water from a particular spring, by the drying up of the spring; the use of canal boats, by the abandonment of the canal; and the supplying of bark from a specified tract of land, by the exhaustion of the supply." 45 46 

Dixon v. Breon, 22 Pa. Superior Ct. 340 (1903). Plaintiff, a log jobber, contracted to sell to the defendant a certain quantity of hemlock and hard wood logs, located on certain specified tracts of land, which he was to cut, saw, manufacture into lumber, and deliver to a common carrier. While the work was in progress a forest fire which started at some distant point, and without fault on the part of either party, destroyed the lumber. Plaintiff claimed to be discharged from further performance. In sustaining that contention, it was said by ORLADY, J. "Where a contract is entered into of a continuing character or to be performed at a future time dependent upon the continued existence of a partic-

Sec. 484. Illness or Death. Where an agreement is contingent upon the continued existence of a person, his death, or such illness that further performance would seriously endanger his health, will relieve him or his estate. Following are typical illustrations taken from the cases: the death of a vendor who had agreed to sell all the lumber sawed in his mill; 48 the death of the manager of Sousa's band; and the death of two sons who had received their mother's property under an agreement to live upon and manage the property and maintain a home for her during the balance of her life.50 Where disability complained of is temporary, performance is suspended while the condition exists, but otherwise where it would impose a greater burden on either party than that contemplated in the agreement. 

Sec. 485. Change of Law. Where performance of an executory agreement, which is lawful in its inception, is made unlawful by subsequent enactment of law, the agreement is dissolved. Performance is never required where it would involve a violation of law.51 It has been held, however, that a surety on a completion bond is not to be discharged by reason of impossibility of construction due to building restrictions.52 Where an agreement has been partially executed and the contract becomes illegal by change of law, neither party has a legal right to retain the fruits of his bargain without rendering an equivalent. He must either restore the property or make restitution in damages.

Sec. 488. Toll of the Statute. When the running of time has commenced, there are several circumstances which will toll the statute, or cause the time to run anew.

Sec. 489. Effect of Fraud. Equity frequently adopts the statute of limitation which would apply to an analogous proceeding at law. "This is especially, if not invariably, true if the cause of action is not exclusively cognizable in equity. . "If the circumstances are such that a man's eyes should have been open to what is occurring, then the statute begins to run from the time when he could have seen, but if by concealment, through fraud or otherwise, a screen has been erected by his adversary which effectually obscures the view of what has happened, the statute remains quiescent until actual knowledge arises."79 9978 

Deemer v. Weaver, 324 Pa. 85 (1936). Anna C. Lerch had a life interest in certain real estate. Her nieces were to come into possession of the property at her death. She persuaded them to join in a deed conveying the property, supposedly for $5,000, and agreed as an inducement to them, to add $500 of her own funds, the total to be placed in a trust fund. She actually sold the property for $9,000. The sum of $5,000 was expressed in the deed. 

The balance was paid to her as a bonus. She placed $5,500 in trust with a bank. The conveyance was executed on July 11, 1919. 

She died in 1931. In 1934 her nieces discovered the fraud and instituted this action against her estate. The lower court held that there had been no active concealment of the fraud such as would toll the statute of limitations. BARNES, J. "We are unable to agree with the learned court below that there was here no concealment to toll the running of the statute. By having the deed drawn so as to show the consideration as only $5,000 in accordance with her misrepresentations to plaintiffs, and by having the additional consideration paid to her in a separate transaction, the decedent concealed from plaintiffs all facts which might have put them upon notice that her statements, that the price for which she sold the property was $5,000, were false."

Sec. 490. Appropriation. The statute of limitations, as well as the extinguishment of a debt, may be determined by the manner in which payments are appropri

Pa. 129 (1945).

ated to a number of different obligations. This problem is of especial interest to the accountant. Where a payment is in the exact amount of a particular obligation, there is a strong inference that it is to be applied to that specific debt. It is the privilege of the person paying a debt, however, to stipulate how such payment shall be applied, provided he gives notice to his creditor. Where the debtor does not so stipulate, the creditor may make the application, provided he give prompt notice to the debtor of his purpose.

Page v. Wilson, 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 427 (1942). KELLER, P. J. 

"When no application is made by either party, the law determines how the payments are to be applied in accordance with equitable rules and principles, and primarily, it deems the payments to have been made in discharge of the earliest liabilities of a running account each item of credit is applied in extinguishment of the earliest debit items in the account; in other cases, it will apply the payment, when not appropriated by either party, in the way most beneficial to the creditor, that is, to the debt least secured, unless to the prejudice of a surety."

Sec. 491. Principal and Interest. The allocation of payment, as between principal and interest, is not so difficult. Pennsylvania follows the rule that "A partial payment on a contract bearing interest is to be applied to the interest in the first place and in the second place to the principal. In this way the interest on the principal is settled as it accrues periodically and the principal is diminished by the excess of the payment over the amount of interest due."80

Cusati v. Dellisanti, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 223 (1948). A judgment note for $1,500, payable one day after date, was executed on March 13, 1922. The sum of $800 was paid on September 7, 1927, and $700 on August 27, 1929. The question involved was the balance due as of October 17, 1942. The trial judge applied each payment to principal and interest, making a balance of $1,135.10. 

The lower court en banc applied both payments to principal, making the balance of $576.24 as of August 27, 1929, the date of the last payment. In deciding that the computation by the trial judge was correct, it was said by RENO, J. "Clearly, the trial judge fol-

Sec. 492. Adverse Possession. The Act of 178581 

provides that no person may maintain a writ for the possession of lands than within twenty-one years after entry and retention by the adverse possession of another. 

Llewellyn v. P. & R. C. & I. Co., 308 Pa. 297 (1982). Plaintiff's ancestors leased an anthracite property from 1873 to 1886, during which time they deposited on a coal bank, together with slate and dirt, what was then considered unmarketable coal. They then disposed of the equipment and relinquished the property. During the next forty years it was operated by the defendant, and the coal on the bank, estimated at 1,500,000 tons, of a value of $3,000,000, was salvaged. Plaintiff claimed ownership, but it was held that defendant's continued, open, notorious, and adverse possession during that period of time was sufficient to vest title. 

Sec. 493. Essentials of Possession. In order to establish title by adverse possession, there must be an actual entry and use of the property, such as the true owner might make. It must also be hostile and adverse, continuous and uninterrupted, visible, open, notorious and exclusive. Where the claim extends beyond the limits of the land actually occupied, it must be under color of title. 

Camp Chicopee v. Eden, 303 Pa. 150 (1931). Plaintiff conducted a boy's camp. It owned a tract of land containing fifty acres, some four of which were covered by the waters of a lake. 

Defendant owned a tract of land on the opposite side of the lake which also extended into the pond. He claimed title to all the land under the lake by adverse possession. In deciding otherwise, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "The owner thereof does not have to become amphibious and dwell part of the time in the lake in order to retain his title thereto." 

81 Act of March 26, 1875, 2 Sm. L. 299, 12 PS 72.

CHAPTER XIII  Part 1. Passing of Title 

Sec. 494. Uniform Sales Act. Pennsylvania adopted the Uniform Sales Act in 1915.¹ A similar statute, called the "Sale of Goods Act," was adopted in England in 1893, and subsequently in most of the British dominions. "The purpose of the act was to establish uniformity of usage and customs in trading throughout the United States, so that, where any buying and selling is engaged in, the parties may know their rights and liabilities, no matter where the contract is made. The act embodies simple rules founded on the prevailing trade usages and customs, and is intended to produce certainty in dealing, to promote freedom of exchange and flexibility in all matters pertaining to buying and selling." It is, for the most part, declaratory of existing law. Many of its provisions have been considered elsewhere, and the following discussion will be confined to the remaining important features of the code. It should be observed at the outset that its principles apply only to the sale of goods and choses in action, and not to other contracts.3 

Sec. 495. Contract to Sell. A contract to sell is de fined as "a contract whereby the seller agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a consideration called the price." A contract to sell is an executory contract. It merely creates a right in personam as between the contracting parties, or right to recover damages for breach of such a contract. No property passes in the goods which are the subject of the contract. The title remains with the seller until the contract is executed. There are three important reasons for this distinction: first, the risks of ownership are upon the 

1 Act of May 19, 1915, P. L. 543, 69

PS 1. 

Dolan Mercantile Co. v. Marcus, 276 Pa. 404 (1923). 

3 York Heating Co. v. Flannery, 87 

Pa. Superior Ct. 19 (1926). 364

seller; second, the goods are subject to the claims of the creditors of the seller; and third, the remedy of the buyer, in case of default, is an action for damages, but not for the possession of the property. 

Hamilton v. Gordon, 22 Oregon 557 (1892). Plaintiffs agreed to purchase of defendant all the grain on a certain tract of land. 

Defendant was to harvest the wheat and deliver it to plaintiff's warehouse. He delivered part of it, but wrongfully retained about 

234 sacks. Plaintiffs brought suit to recover possession of it. In deciding that title had not passed as to this part of the wheat, and that plaintiffs were pursuing the wrong remedy, it was said by BEAN, J. “The contract is only a contract for the sale of a certain crop of grain, and if defendant has violated his agreement, by delivering only a part of the grain, and refusing to deliver the remainder, plaintiffs, if damaged, have their remedy, but not by an action to recover possession of the property." 

Sec. 496. Sale. A sale is defined as "an agreement whereby the seller transfers the property in goods to the buyer for a consideration called the price." A sale is an executed contract, in which the property in the goods, or the title, passes from the seller to the buyer. Consequently, a sale creates a right in rem, or property right in the goods, which the buyer may assert as against all the world. There are three important reasons for this distinction: first, the title to the goods immediately vests in the buyer; second, the risks of ownership are upon the buyer; and third, the goods are subject to the claims of the creditors of the buyer. It may be noted at this point that a contract to sell or a sale may be absolute or conditional, and may be made between one part owner and another. The subject of the contract may also be existing goods, or it may be goods to be manufactured or acquired by the seller. Such goods are called "future goods." Goods of this sort may be dependent upon a contingency which may or may not happen. The seller may not then be the owner of the goods which he purports to sell, and this fact may be known to the buyer, but that is immaterial as far as the buyer is concerned. 

Such an agreement operates as a contract to sell.

Sec. 497. Fungible Goods. The subject of a contract to sell or a sale may consist of an undivided share of goods owned by a tenant in common, and in the case of fungible goods, or goods which are identical, there may be a sale of an undivided share of a specific mass. 

Kimberly v. Patchin, 19 New York 380 (1859). "A" owned 6,429 bushels of wheat which were stored in a warehouse. He "sold" 

6,000 bushels of this wheat to B, and then found a buyer to whom he sold the full 6,429 bushels. It was held by COMSTOCK, J., that even though there had been no separation, B had "acquired a perfect title to the 6,000 bushels of wheat." 

Sec. 498. Destruction of Goods. Where the goods have been wholly destroyed before the contract is made, and this fact is unknown to the parties, or before title passes to the buyer, and without any fault on the part of either party to the contract, the agreement is void. 

As noted in Section 343, supra, this principle is common to other contracts. The code provides, in addition, that where the goods have perished in part, or have so deteriorated in quality as to be substantially changed in character, the buyer may, at his option, treat the sale (1) as avoided, or (2) as transferring the property in all the existing goods or in so much as have not deteriorated, and as binding the buyer to pay the full agreed price, if the sale was indivisible, or if it was divisible, then the agreed price for the goods received by the buyer. 1 Sec. 499. The Price. The price to be paid for goods may be fixed by the contract, or in such manner as the parties have agreed, or it may be determined by a course of dealing between the parties. Otherwise, the buyer must pay a reasonable price. It has been held that if a subcontractor is required to purchase his materials from the principal contractor, not to exceed any other price that the subcontractor could obtain elsewhere, the principal contractor "certainly could not ask any more than the highest market prices, and the court below was clearly right in admitting evidence tending to show what

those prices were." Where the price or terms is to be fixed by a third person who cannot or does not act, without the fault of either the buyer or the seller, the contract may be avoided. The rule is otherwise where either party is at fault. If the buyer receives the goods, in whole or in part, and the third party fails or refuses to act, the buyer must pay a reasonable price. 

Sec. 500. Incidents of Ownership. There are many reasons why the question of ownership is important.

The owner, whether it be the seller or the buyer, may exercise the usual incidents of ownership. He may dispose of, assign, or pledge the property, as long as he has title to it, even though he may have to account to the other party for breach of the contract. The question of risk is also involved. Who is to bear the loss caused by theft, damage, or destruction, and who is to have the right to prosecute the wrongdoer, sue for damages, or compel an insurance company to make restitution? The rights of attaching creditors must also be considered, to say nothing of the bankruptcy of the owner, whoever he happens to be, and some one is usually called upon to pay taxes on the property. These contingencies, as a general rule, are not provided for in the contract, but depend, for the most part, on the question of ownership. 

Sec. 501. Passing of Title. Property in specific or ascertained goods is transferred to the buyer when the parties so intend. In ascertaining this intention, regard must be had to the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties, and the circumstances of the case. Unless a different intention appears, if the goods are in a deliverable state, title passes to the buyer when the contract is made, and it is immaterial whether the time of payment or the time of delivery, or both, be postponed. 

Perkins v. Halpren, 257 Pa. 402 (1917). Plaintiff sold goods to the defendant, which were then in a United States bonded ware- 

Van Horn v. Kemena, 281 Pa. 579 (1924). 

---

house, and subsequently forwarded invoices describing the character of the merchandise, and stating the price, terms and date of payment, the price to include the duties and carrying charges. 

This was an action for the price. Defendant contended, inter alia, that as the goods had not been delivered, the sale was not complete. The goods had in the meantime been attached by a creditor of the defendant. In deciding that title had passed, it was said by FRAZER, J. "When the terms of sale are agreed upon, and the bargain is struck, and everything the seller has to do with the goods is complete, the contract of sale, says Chancellor Kent, becomes absolute as between the parties, without actual payment or delivery, and the property, and the risk of accident to the goods, vests in the buyer." 99 

Sec. 502. Duty Unperformed. Unless a different intention appears, if the seller is bound to do something to the goods, for the purpose of putting them into a deliverable state, the property does not pass until such thing be done.

Rochester & Oleopolis Oil Co. v. Hughey, 56 Pa. 322 (1867). 

This was an action in assumpsit to recover the price of a quantity of oil alleged to have been sold and delivered to the defendant. 

The contract called for four barge-loads, about 2200 barrels, at $4.50 per barrel. Defendant furnished the barges. When two barges had been partially filled, the oil took fire and was destroyed, together with the barges. The question involved was whether delivery was complete before the burning. THOMPSON, C. J. "The defendant could not be compelled to take a partly filled barge when he had contracted for full ones, any more than if he had contracted for a barrel of oil could he have been compelled to accept one half or quarter full." 

Sec. 503. Goods Appropriated. Unless a different intention appears, if the contract is to sell unascertained or future goods by description, and goods of that description and in a deliverable state are thereafter appropriated to the contract, the property in the goods passes to the buyer. The appropriation must be unconditional. 

It has been held that where goods selected by the buyer are set aside by the seller in a special compartment on the seller's premises, subject to call at any time, and the goods are charged to the buyer's account and invoices

are sent to the buyer, the appropriation is complete." 

This principle stems from early English cases. 

Rohde r. Thwaites, 6 B. & C. (Eng.) 388 (1827). Plaintiffs owned sugar in bulk. They contracted to fill and sell 20 hogsheads to defendant. Four were filled and delivered, and a few days later the remaining 16 were filled. Defendant agreed to call for them as soon as he could, but neglected to do so. Plaintiffs brought this action to recover the purchase price. BAILEY, J. "I am of opinion, that by reason of that appropriation made by the plaintiffs, and assented to by the defendant, the property in the sixteen hogsheads of sugar passed to the vendee. That being so, the plaintiffs are entitled to recover the full value of the twenty hogsheads of sugar, under the count for goods bargained and sold." 

Sec. 504. F. O. B. Contracts. Goods are frequently ordered F. O. B. seller's place of business. Unless a different intention appears, where delivery is made to a carrier, whether named by the buyer or not, for the purpose of transmission to the buyer, the goods are presumed to have been appropriated to the contract, notwithstanding the buyer is to pay the price before receiving delivery. If the seller uses an order bill of lading, which he sends through commercial channels for collection, the buyer is obliged to pay for the goods before they will be surrendered by the carrier. In F. O. B. contracts, however, the title passes to the buyer when the seller delivers such goods to the carrier for shipment. 

Miller v. Seaman, 176 Pa. 291 (1896). Plaintiff sold to defendant all the lumber contained in certain piles, F. O. B. Williamsport, at $8.25 per 1000 feet. Part of the lumber had been loaded and shipped. The remainder was swept away by a flood. In deciding that the loss should be borne by the plaintiff, it was said by WILLIAMS, J. "The title had left the plaintiff only as orders had been filled and shipped, and, as to all that remained in the yard, it had never left him."

Sec. 505. Bills of Lading. State and federal' stat utes authorize common carriers to issue two kinds of bills of lading, one stating that the goods received will 

5 In re Cope's Estate, 191 Pa. 589 (1899). 

6 Act of June 9, 1911, P. L. 838, 6 

739 Stat. 538 (1916), 49 U. S. C. 81. 

PS 51.

be delivered to a specified person (a straight bill of lading), and the other stating that the goods received will be delivered to the order of a specified person (an order bill of lading). The latter is negotiable and may be sold or transferred by indorsement. It is the duty of the carrier to deliver the goods to the person named in a straight bill of lading. The carrier must deliver the goods to the holder of an order bill of lading, properly endorsed, if the carrier has no notice of irregularity. The purpose of the order bill of lading is to insure payment before delivery. 

Sec. 506. Order Bills. When the seller uses the order bill of lading, he usually consigns the goods to himself or order, and then endorses the order bill for collection, which he discounts at his bank for that purpose. Ordinarily, when a person ships goods to himself or his order, he reserves the title to the goods, but not when he uses an order bill of lading merely for the purpose of securing performance by a buyer of his obligations under a contract. In maritime shipping the parties employ, as a substitute for the F. O. B. contract, what is called the 

C. I. F. (costs, insurance and freight) contract. Where such goods are shipped on an order bill, title passes on delivery to the carrier. 

Smith Co. Ltd. v. Marano, 267 Pa. 107 (1920). Plaintiff, doing business in St. Johns, Newfoundland, sold to defendant, doing business in Philadelphia, a quantity of codfish, "C. I. F. Philadelphia." The goods were shipped by steamer from St. Johns. About two days later the ship was sunk by a German submarine, and the goods were lost. The bill of lading and sight draft were tendered to defendant in Philadelphia and refused. BROWN, C. J. "The bill of lading, made out to (plaintiff) or its order, was endorsed immediately by it in blank and attached to the draft drawn upon the (defendant). This merely meant that the (plaintiff) intended to retain property in the goods to secure performance by the defendant of his promise to pay for them, and did not, by the express words of the Sales Act, relieve (the defendant) from the risk that was upon him from the time the goods were delivered to the carrier." 

8 Utley v. Lehigh Valley R. R. Co., 292 Pa. 251 (1928).

Sec. 507. Duty to Deliver. Many merchants under take to deliver merchandise, especially in the local trade, and in the case of perishable goods, frequently arrange for and pay the cost of delivery as an assurance to the buyer. Unless a different intention appears, if the contract requires the seller to deliver the goods to the buyer, or at a particular place, or to pay the freight or cost of transportation to the buyer, or to a particular place, the property does not pass until the goods have been delivered to the buyer or reached the place agreed upon. 

Pittsburgh Provision & Packing Co. v. Cudahy Packing Co., 

260 Pa. 135 (1918). Plaintiff ordered certain meat from the defendant, guaranteed fresh, cash and freight at Pittsburgh. Defendant shipped the goods from Chicago on an order bill of lading, with a draft which it forwarded to a Pittsburgh bank. Plaintiff paid the draft without waiting the arrival of the shipment. Upon arrival the meat was found unfit for human consumption. In deciding that defendant had title, and that plaintiff was justified in refusing to accept the goods, it was said by FRAZER, J. "Where the contract requires delivery at the place of destination title remains in the vendor until that point is reached and the risks of transportation are assumed by him." 

Sec. 508. Stoppage in Transit. Where the buyer is or becomes insolvent, the seller has a right to stop the goods in transit and to regain possession and title, subject to the rights of an innocent holder of a negotiable document of title. Under the American rule, the seller enjoys a preemptory right of stoppage under such circumstances. As adopted in Pennsylvania, however, the 

Uniform Sales Act requires the seller to give notice to the carrier that the buyer is insolvent and has not paid for the goods. It has been held that if the carrier actually accepts notice which is defective in this respect, and the facts justify the right of the seller to have the goods stopped in transit, the carrier may be estopped from questioning the form of the notice, i. e., notice that the buyer is insolvent and has not paid for the goods." 

Teller & Co. v. American Railway 

Express Co., 78 Pa. Superior Ct. 300 (1922).

Sec. 509. Sale on Approval. Where goods are deliv ered to the buyer on approval, or on trial, or on satisfaction, title passes to the buyer only when he signifies his approval, or retains the goods beyond the time fixed in the contract, or if no time has been fixed, then at the expiration of a reasonable time. 

Pence v. Carney, 78 Arkansas 123 (1906). Plaintiff gave two rings to defendant, with the understanding that if defendant was pleased she would keep them, otherwise return them to plaintiff. 

The rings were lost, without fault, while in defendant's possession. 

In deciding that title had not passed, and that the loss must be borne by the plaintiff, it was said by MCCOLLOCH, J. "Under the contract stated the title remained in the seller and any loss or damage sustained from any cause except negligence of the purchaser fell upon the seller." 

Sec. 510. Sale on Option. Where the contract gives the buyer an option to return the goods instead of paying the price, title passes to the buyer on delivery of the goods to him, but revests in the seller if the goods are returned within the time fixed in the contract, or if no time has been fixed, within a reasonable time. 

Foley v. Felrath, 98 Alabama 176 (1893). Plaintiff, a manufacturer of gold pens, sold a bill of goods to the defendant, with the understanding that defendant might return some of the goods in exchange. The goods were lost by the common carrier while in transit to the buyer. In deciding that title had passed on delivery to the carrier, and that plaintiff was entitled to recover the purchase price, it was said by HARALSON, J. "An option to purchase if the party to whom the goods are transferred should like, is very different from an option to return the goods if he should not like them." 

Sec. 511. Reservation of Title. In the Christmas trade and otherwise, it is quite common for a prospective buyer to make a down payment and request the merchant to set goods aside until the balance of the purchase price has been paid. Under such circumstances the seller may reserve both title and possession, notwithstanding the goods have been appropriated to the contract, or even delivered to a common carrier for transmission to the buyer.

McLaughlin r. Victor Motor Supply Co., 71 Pa. Superior Ct. 

415 (1919). Stetson agreed to sell an automobile to McLaughlin. 

The consideration was $425 and a second-hand car. The contract provided that the new car was to remain in the possession of the seller until the whole of the purchase price had been paid. Me- 

Laughlin surrendered the second-hand car, and sent his agent with the balance of the purchase price. The agent paid but $225 and defaulted in the balance. Stetson, not being fully paid, sold the automobile to Stern. McLaughlin then issued a writ of replevin in an attempt to recover it. HENDERSON, J. "Until he completed the purchase of the car by the payment of the price agreed on, or the tender of the balance due, he had not acquired a title which he could assert against his vendor or the person to whom the latter transferred the property." 

Sec. 512. Title by Estoppel. As a general rule, the buyer of goods can acquire no better title than the seller has, unless the actual owner is estopped by his conduct from denying the seller's authority to sell the goods to the buyer. 

Truck Tractor & Forwarding Co. v. Baker, 281 Pa. 145 (1924).

A tractor company delivered a truck to Baker on a bailment lease, which it assigned to a finance company. Baker defaulted, whereupon the truck was taken back by the tractor company and delivered to Langford on another bailment lease. Langford made payments for six months to the tractor company, at which time the tractor company became insolvent and its manager a defaulter. 

To save itself from loss, the finance company disclosed its ownership and repossessed the truck by writ of replevin. In holding the plaintiff finance company liable for this action, it was said by WALLING, J. "The undisputed facts constitute such laches on behalf of plaintiff as to support the trial court's finding that it was estopped from asserting a claim to the truck as against an innocent purchaser from the tractor company."

Part 2. Rights of the Seller Sec. 513. Lien. Under the Uniform Sales Act, supra, an unpaid seller enjoys rights of two sorts, the first of which may be designated as a right in rem, or right in the nature of a lien which may be asserted against the goods to the exclusion of other creditors of the buyer; and second, a right in personam, or right to hold the 25

buyer personally for damages resulting from breach of the contract, i. e., an action for the price, or for damages for non-acceptance. The former is not exclusive of the latter, for though an unpaid seller exercises the right of a lien holder and disposes of the goods in partial satisfaction of the damages he may have sustained, he may yet hold the buyer personally for the balance of the contract price. The lien may be exercised as long as the goods are in the possession or custody of the seller. 

Arnold v. Delano, 4 Cushing 33 (1849). A seller "sold" 65 cords of wood to the buyer on credit, the buyer to remove the wood from the seller's land within a period of one year. The buyer was adjudicated a bankrupt before any of the wood had been removed. 

This was a contest between the seller and the buyer's creditors in bankruptcy. In deciding that the seller had a lien on the goods for the purchase price, it was said by SHAW, C. J. ". ... the law, in holding that a vendor, who has thus given credit for the goods, waives his lien for the price, does so on one implied condition . . . that the vendee shall keep his credit good." 

Sec. 514. Resale. Where the buyer has been in default for a reasonable time, or when goods sold are perishable, or when the contract so provides, the seller in possession may resell the goods at public or private sale, not as agent for the buyer-otherwise the buyer would be entitled to any profit made upon the resale-but because the statute confers upon him the right to do so. 

The main purpose of a resale is to fix the liability of the buyer, since the buyer may be held liable for any loss occasioned by the breach. Subject to reasonable care and judgment, the seller may resell the goods either at public or private sale. It is not essential that the buyer be given notice of the time and place of the sale, but it would be prudent to give such notice in view of the possibility of a dispute as to whether the buyer had been in default for a reasonable time, and any dispute as to the fairness of the resale and the actual expense involved. 

Sec. 515. Refusal to Accept. Where the buyer refuses to accept the goods, the seller may maintain an

1 action against him for damages for non-acceptance. If the buyer repudiates the contract prior to delivery, the seller may rescind, but he is not required to do so. He may ignore the repudiation and insist upon performance by the buyer. 

Barber Milling Co. v. Leichthammer Baking Co., 273 Pa. 90 (1922). Plaintiff, in Minneapolis, sold to the defendant at Norristown, 400 barrels of rye flour for future delivery. Defendant repudiated the contract. Plaintiff refused to acquiesce in the abrogation of the agreement, and shipped the flour to Norristown. 

Defendant still refused to accept, whereupon the goods were sold in the nearest available market at a loss of $1,660.35. SCHAFFER, J. "Under our decisions, and the weight of authority elsewhere, the vendor was not required, by the vendee's cancellation, to resell it in the Minneapolis market and then sue for the loss, if any; vendor could, as it did, treat the contract as continuing, and, upon actual breach by defendant's refusal to accept at the place named for delivery, establish the loss by a resale in an available market." 

Sec. 516. Action for the Price. Where the goods have been received by the buyer, but he wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay for them, the seller may maintain an action against him for the price. If the goods have not been received by the buyer, and cannot readily be resold by the seller for a reasonable price, the seller may offer to deliver them to the buyer, and upon refusal, may notify the buyer that the goods are thereafter held by the seller as bailee for the buyer. It is unusual for the seller to retain possession, even as custodian or bailee, and recover the full purchase price, and for this reason the buyer is entitled to strict notice of such a status.

Cohen v. LaFrance Workshop, Inc., 112 Pa. Superior Ct. 309 

(1934). Plaintiff received an order from defendant for 50,000 wire frames for lamp shades, of which 40,000 were delivered and paid for. Defendant refused to accept the remainder, averring that the frames were not constructed of tin wire, as was required, but of copper wire. Plaintiff brought this action to recover the price, but neglected to give notice that it held the remaining goods as bailee for the buyer. In deciding that defendant was entitled to binding instructions, it was said by PARKER, J. "We cannot regard.

this provision as anything else than mandatory. It was the apparent purpose of the legislature to require the seller to take a definite position in this respect before starting suit by declaring himself bailee for the buyer."

Part 3. Rights of the Buyer 

Sec. 517. Delivery. Subject to any usage of trade, special agreement, or course of dealing between the parties, where the seller delivers a quantity of goods less than he contracted to sell, the buyer may reject the goods. If he accepts them, knowing that the seller is not going to deliver the balance, he must pay for them at the contract rate, but if he does not have that knowledge, then he is liable only for the fair value to him of the goods so received. Where the seller delivers a greater quantity than is provided for in the contract, the buyer may accept all the goods at the contract rate, or he may accept the quantity provided for in the contract and reject the rest, or he may reject the whole. 

Meyercord Co., Inc. v. P. H. Butler Co., 79 Pa. Superior Ct. 473 (1922). Defendant ordered 200 window signs. Plaintiff delivered 

297 to a common carrier, all of which the defendant refused to accept. In justifying this refusal, it was said by GAWTHROP, J. "A delivery of the exact amount of the contract to the American Express Company would have been a delivery to the buyer, but surely a delivery of a number of signs which he had a right to reject or accept, or partially reject or partially accept, could not be construed to be a delivery to him.'" 

Sec. 518. Examination. Where goods are delivered to the buyer which he has not previously examined, he is entitled to a reasonable opportunity of examining them for the purpose of ascertaining whether they are in conformity with the contract. A "reasonable time" has been defined as the period that suffices for the performance of the required act "if the one whose duty it is to perform uses such diligence in the performance as a person of ordinary diligence and prudence would use under like circumstances." 10 

10 Truscon Steel Co. v. Fuhrmann & 

Brewing Co., 327 Pa. 10

Schmidt (1937).

Crunden-Martin Mfg. Co. v. Turner, 274 Pa. 425 (1922). Plaintiff sought to recover on a sale of paper bags, delivered on March 5. 

Plaintiff had knowledge that they were to be resold in small lots to local merchants in the original packages. They were defective. 

Defendant did not receive complaints from the local merchants until April 29, and on May 11, he notified the plaintiff. The lower court held this delay to be unreasonable. In deciding that the question should be submitted to a jury, it was said by FRAZER, J. "Under the circumstances, a delay of twelve days from the time of receiving the first notice of imperfect construction by defendant in making an investigation and reporting the result to plaintiff could not be said to be so unreasonable as to justify the court in directing a verdict for plaintiff." 

Sec. 519. Notice of Breach, In the absence of an express or implied agreement, the buyer may accept the goods and hold the seller for any breach of contract or warranty. It is essential, however, for the buyer to give notice to the seller within a reasonable time after he knows or ought to know of such breach, otherwise the seller may not be held liable. This provision in the Uniform Sales Act has received a strict interpretation. 

Catalano v. Corcoran, 86 Pa. Superior Ct. 32 (1926). A carload of grapes, ordered by plaintiffs, was delayed in transit, and upon delivery was sold at a regular public fruit auction at a loss. This action followed, alleging breach of warranty. LINN, J. "As notice of a claim for breach of warranty was necessary under section 49, and as there is no evidence that such notice was given, 'the seller shall not be liable therefor." 

Sec. 520. Acceptance. The buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when he intimates to the seller that he has accepted them, or by act which is inconsistent with the ownership of the seller, or when, after the lapse of a reasonable time, he retains the goods without intimating to the seller that he has rejected them. Ordinarily, when a person rescinds a contract he must restore all that he has received. He may not return part and retain part. He may do so under unusual circumstances, however, as where the breach is not discovered until part of the goods have been used or disposed of,¹¹ 11 11 Moskowitz v. Flock & Flock, 112 Pa. Superior Ct. 518 (1934).

or where it is necessary to test part of the goods in order to determine whether they conform to the contract. 

Charles E. Hires Co. v. Stromeyer, 65 Pa. Superior Ct. 241 

(1916). Plaintiff purchased 500 bags of sugar, to be delivered clean and merchantable in lined, jute sacks. It was furnished in unlined sacks. Plaintiff used about six percent in a test to ascertain whether the quantity of fibre and lint would clog its filters. 

Finding it unusable, plaintiff purchased the nearest substitute in the open market, paying a higher price, and brought this action for damages. The lower court ruled the defects to be discernible by ocular inspection, and in any event plaintiff had used too much. 

In deciding otherwise, it was said by TREXLER, J. "He cannot use part and return part. This rule however applies after the vendee has had the chance to inspect it. The use of a portion of the goods is in many cases a prerequisite to a determination of its quality." 

Sec. 521. Remedy Prior to Acceptance. Where the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver the goods, the buyer may maintain an action against him for nondelivery. Where there is a breach of warranty, which is discovered before the property has passed to the buyer, he may rescind the contract and recover what he had paid, or he may refuse to accept the goods and hold the seller liable for damages for the breach. The Uniform 

Sales Act provides that in the absence of special circumstances showing proximate damages of a greater amount, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time when the goods should have been delivered or accepted. It has been held, however, that if the breach is known prior to the date fixed for delivery, and the buyer purchases a substitute before the date of delivery in a rising market, the measure of damages is the difference between the contract price and the price actually paid. 

Morris v. Supplee, 208 Pa. 253 (1904). Plaintiffs bought of defendants, for future delivery, 900 bales of cotton, and brought this action for non-delivery. They admitted that they had purchased substitute cotton prior to the date of delivery, in a rising market, but claimed to recover the difference between the contract price and the market price as of the date fixed in the contract for delivery. In deciding that the measure of damages was the difference

379 

10 in the contract price, and the price actually paid, it was said by MITCHELL, C. J. Plaintiffs "could not charge the defendants with a higher price than that of the market on the contract date, but if they had bought for less, then their loss was less, and they were bound to show how much."

Sec. 522. Remedy after Acceptance. Where a breach of warranty is discovered after the property has passed to the buyer, he may keep the goods and set up the breach of warranty in diminution of the price, or keep the goods and maintain an action against the seller for damages resulting from the breach. 

North Alaska Salmon Co. v. Hobbs, Wall & Co., 159 Calif. 380 (1911). Plaintiff purchased a number of salmon boxes, specifically for the shipment of empty cans to its canneries. The boxes were warranted to be "of dry stock and free from dampness." 

Payment was made on delivery. Inspection on delivery disclosed a number of boxes to be made of damp wood, and prompt notice was given of this condition. It was too late in the season to obtain boxes elsewhere, and plaintiff made an effort to use them. As a result, some of the cans became rusty and unfit for use. This was an action for breach of warranty. Defendant contended that plaintiff had waived the defect when it accepted the goods. In deciding otherwise, it was said by SHAW, J. "If one who buys goods upon an express warranty of quality must refuse to receive them if he knows they are defective at the time, and waives his right of action on the warranty if he accepts them, the warranty would be useless, since he would have the same right if he had not taken the warranty, and his damage for nondelivery of the goods would be practically the same in one case as in the other, except in the one case where greater damages are allowed by the code." 

Sec. 523. Rescission. In one respect the Uniform 

Sales Act enlarges the rights of the buyer. Where there is breach of warranty, the buyer may also rescind the contract, notwithstanding the property may have passed to the buyer. This changed the existing law. Prior to this statute, the buyer could not rescind the contract for breach of warranty after the property had passed, unless the contract so provided, or there was an agreement to take them back, or there was fraud. The Uniform Sales

Act proceeds upon the assumption that it is just as immoral for the seller to take advantage of an innocent

misstatement of fact, as it is of a fraudulent repre sentation. Where there is a breach of warranty, therefore, and the goods have been received by the buyer, he may return or offer to return the goods, and recover what he had paid. He also has a lien on the goods to secure repayment of the purchase price.

Part 4. Damages Sec. 524. Anticipatory Damages. The subject of damages in the sale of goods, and other contracts, is so interrelated, that both will be considered in this discussion. Generally, the parties to a contract may fix beforehand, or at the time the agreement is made, the amount to be paid as damages in the event of a breach, provided the sum agreed upon is compensation and not a penalty. "If the intention is to secure performance of the contract by the imposition of a fine or penalty, then the sum specified is a penalty; but if, on the other hand, the intention is to assess the damages for breach of the contract, it is liquidated damages." 12 In sales of real estate it is customary for the buyer to pay an amount as hand money, and for the parties to agree that this amount is to be forfeited as liquidated damages for failure to tender the balance of the purchase price on delivery of the deed. Damages for breach of these contracts are so difficult of ascertainment that the courts generally sus tain agreements of this sort unless the sum agreed upon is grossly disproportionate to the loss actually sustained. 

Ellis v. Roberts, 98 Pa. Superior Ct. 49 (1929). A contract for the sale of real estate for the sum of $16,800 provided for the payment of $100 in cash and a judgment note in the sum of $2,000 at the signing of the agreement. It provided further that in case the vendees defaulted in performance they should forfeit in liquidated damages "the deposit" together with any moneys paid by them to the vendor. The vendor caused judgment to be entered on the note. Defendants petitioned to have the judgment opened. 

They admitted default in settlement, but alleged that the cash payment and the note constituted an exorbitant penalty and not 

12 Law v. Redditch, (1892) 1 Q, B.127.

liquidated damages. GAWTHROP, J. "In the light of the amount of the purchase price, the knowledge which plaintiff had of defendants' financial condition, the relation which the sum agreed upon as liquidated damages bears to the purchase price and all the other circumstances, we are led to the conclusion that plaintiff intended the provision in the contract for liquidated damages to compel specific performance by defendants. This made it a provision for a penalty and precludes plaintiff from recovering more than just compensation for the breach of the contract by defendants, and requires us to open the judgment."

Sec. 525. Actual Damages. In all actions on con tract, the measure of damages is the loss actually sustained, or naturally resulting in the ordinary course of events from the breach, or which the defendant might have foreseen as the result of the breach when the agree ment was made.

Schmitt v. Republic Collieries Co., 269 Pa. 75 (1920). Plaintiff was employed for one year, and was to furnish two automobile trucks. He was to receive $175 per month for his services and $35 a day for the use of each truck. He was discharged without cause after two months. He instituted this action to recover wages for ten months, and for loss of profits upon his trucks, which the testimony showed to be about $28 per day on each. 

About a month after his discharge he lost his trucks through inability to pay the installments on time. The jury allowed $1,750 for ten months' wages and $5,750 for loss of profits on the trucks. 

PER CURIAM. "Appellant's only complaint is of the refusal of the learned trial judge to instruct the jury that there could be no recovery for loss of the profits plaintiff might have realized from the use of his trucks. The refusal to do so was not error, for if the plaintiff had not been unjustifiably discharged by the defendant he would have been able to pay for the trucks and use them in the performance of his contract."

Sec. 526. Special Damages. Special damages may be recovered only when the circumstances giving rise to such injury are known when the agreement is made. 

The following case was cited in this jurisdiction in 1943.13

Hadley v. Baxendale, Court of Exchequer (1854), 9 Exch. 341. 

Plaintiffs were millers at Glouster. Their mill was stopped by the 

13 Siegel v. Struble Bros., Inc., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 343 (1943).

breakage of a crank shaft, and they employed the defendant to carry it to the manufacturer at Greenwich. It was to serve as a model for a new one. The delivery of the shaft at Greenwich was delayed by the carrier for several days, through negligence, and plaintiffs' mill being idle, they lost profits they would otherwise have received. These special circumstances were not communicated to the defendant when the contract was made. ALDERSON, J. "It follows, therefore, that the loss of profits here cannot reasonably be considered such a consequence of the breach of contract as could have been fairly and reasonably contemplated by both parties when they made this contract." 14 

Sec. 527. Choses in Action. Prior to the Act of 

1929, Pennsylvania followed the rule that the measure of damages for conversion of stocks, bonds, or other like property of fluctuating value was the highest value between the time of conversion and the time of trial.15 This statute limits the amount of recovery to such higher value as the property may have reached within a reasonable time after the owner had notice of the conversion. 

Sec. 528. Punitive Damages. Exemplary or puni tive damages are not awarded in contract actions. "But in torts the rule is different; the motive of the defendant becomes material. In those that are committed through mistake, ignorance, or mere negligence, the ordinary rule is mere compensation; but in such as are committed wilfully, maliciously, or so negligently as to indicate a wanton disregard of the rights of others, the jury are not restricted to compensation merely. They may, if the evidence justifies it, give vindicative or exemplary damages, such as will not only compensate the injured party, but at the same time tend to prevent a repetition of the wrong, either by the defendant or others."16

Stone v. C. I. T. Corp., 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 71 (1986). Plain tiff, a vacuum cleaner salesman, acquired an automobile under a bailment lease. After thirteen payments he defaulted for one month, whereupon the automobile was repossessed by the defendant. Plaintiff made other arrangements to finance the car, tendered 

14 Act of April 10, 1929, P. L. 476, 68 PS 481. 

15 Foley v. Wasserman, 319 Pa. 420 (1935). 

16 Pittsburgh C. & St. L. Ry. Co. v. 

Lyon, 123 Pa. 140 (1888).

the amount demanded by the finance company, and the automobile was delivered to him. Three months later, claiming that it had made a mistake in its calculations, and that plaintiff owed a balance of $44, the finance company again repossessed the automobile without notice to the plaintiff. In an action in trespass for wrongful seizure, plaintiff obtained a verdict of $260 actual damages, $500 for humiliation, and $1,250 as punitive damages. In striking the damages awarded for humiliation, it was said by BALDRIGE, J. "We have been unable to find any case where mental suffering, or humiliation which is a form of mental anguish, unaccompanied by injury to the person, has been allowed as an element of damages. . . No serious difficulty is presented in sustaining the element or the amount of punitive damages. The defendant, instead of resorting to an orderly and legal procedure to enforce its alleged claim, chose, in a despotic way, to oppress and harass this plaintiff. It must bear the consequences of its invasion of the plaintiff's rights."

Sec. 529. Specific Performance. Jurisdiction to award specific performance of contracts was conferred upon the court of common pleas in 1836,17 and upon the orphans' court in 1917.18 Such relief was first decreed in contracts for the sale of land, principally because of the difficulty of ascertaining damages resulting from a breach, but also because land possesses unique value and in many cases has some peculiar use entirely aside from agricultural purposes. Equitable principles are invoked in transactions of this sort. Such relief will not be granted where the conduct of the complainant has been inequitable, or where he has induced the other party to enter into the contract by fraud or misrepresentation, or where the transaction is inequitable or unjust in itself." 

The Uniform Sales Act authorizes relief by way of specific performance, but it is only in rare instances that equity will intervene where chattels are involved.20 This is because monetary damages are usually adequate. "The examples afforded by the English books are usually those cases, where, from the nature of the thing sought after, 17 Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 784, 17 PS 281. 

18 Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, 20 PS 611. 

10 Rupniewski v. Miazga, 299 Pa. 

190 (1930). 

20 Caton V. Wellershouse, 77 Pa.

Superior Ct. 331 (1921).

its antiquity, or because of some peculiarity connected with it, it cannot easily, or at all, be replaced." 21 

Reid v. Rogers Coal Co., 275 Pa. 501 (1923). Before making application for a charter, it was agreed between the three plaintiffs and the defendant that each should own one-fourth of the capital stock of the company. Plaintiffs filed a bill in equity for specific performance on the ground that the shares were without known market value and represented the controlling voice in the management of the company. FRAZER, J. "Ordinarily a court of equity will not take jurisdiction to determine the ownership of stocks or other goods and chattels, for the reason a complete and adequate remedy at law can be had in an action for damages. 

However, it is equally well settled that where stock in question is not purchasable in the market and possesses a peculiar value to the claimant, as, for instance, where its possession is necessary to the control of a corporation, or it is held under such circumstances as to make the legal owner a trustee, the action at law offers no adequate remedy and a court of equity will assume jurisdiction." 

Sec. 530. Injunctive Relief. It would be impractical to attempt to enforce specific performance of contracts requiring personal services. Courts of equity may, however, grant relief in the form of a negative, as well as an affirmative decree, where no other remedy would answer the justice of the case. 

Philadelphia Ball Club, Ltd. v. Lajoie, 202 Pa. 210 (1902). 

Lajoie, considered an immortal in the baseball firmament, repudiated a contract to play with the plaintiff club and arranged to play for a rival organization. The lower court found that he was an expert player, that he had a great reputation, that he would be hard to replace, and that his withdrawal would weaken the team and probably make a difference in the size of the audience attending the game. POTTER, J. "Substantial justice between the parties requires that the court should restrain the defendant from playing for any other club during the term of his contract with the plaintiff."

Sec. 531. New Trial. "An award of a retrial is an inherent power of the court of common pleas and entirely discretionary." "Nor is there any limit on the number of times that a new trial may be ordered." There are 9923

24 many reasons for the granting of a new trial, such as error of the trial court, after-discovered evidence, misconduct of the jury, and misconduct of counsel. A new trial may also be granted where the verdict is against the plaintiff, or where the verdict is excessive, or where it is inadequate.25 It is seldom that a court will award a new trial merely because the verdict is against the plaintiff, but it may do so upon firm conviction that justice demands another trial, or where the trial judge feels that he has improperly instructed the jury and imposed too heavy a burden upon the plaintiff.27 26 Sec. 532. Excessive Verdicts. Not infrequently the court of common pleas is called upon to grant a new trial because of excessive verdicts, although in practice it first gives the plaintiff the option to consent to a lower verdict in lieu of a new trial. This is called a voluntary remittitur. 

Thirkell v. Equitable Gas Co., 307 Pa. 377 (1932). Plaintiff was totally and probably permanently disabled as the result of the explosion of a building, and his wife was killed. He and his wife were an ideal couple, and he had always been a steady worker. 

His earnings during the year previous averaged $170 a month. 

His injuries to the chest resulted in a paralysis of the vocal chords and he was required to use a tube in breathing. An injury to the spine compelled him to wear a steel brace. He walked slowly and did not sleep well. The jury's verdict was $50,845.50. The Supreme Court, on appeal, remitted the record with directions to grant a new trial unless plaintiff would remit all over $33,375. 

This was to cover (1) property loss in the sum of $2,000, and (2) medical and funeral expense in the sum of $1,375. The balance, $30,000, was to cover (3) loss of earning power, (4) loss of his wife's companionship, (5) past and future pain and suffering, and (6) the reasonable and probable future expenses for the balance of his life.

Sec. 34. Reducing Verdict. The Supreme Court alone has power to reduce excessive verdicts absolutely. 

This power stems from the Act of 1891,81 under which the court may "amend or modify" a judgment. While the legislature may have had in mind other situations, the act has been construed to justify a compulsory reduction of an excessive verdict.32 

Koontz v. Messer, 320 Pa. 487 (1986). Plaintiff was a young woman 24 years of age. As the result of an automobile injury, her right leg had become permanently shortened so that she could not bring her heel to the ground, she suffered a permanent loss of about one-third of the normal motion of the hip joint and onehalf of the normal flexion of the knee, and a further limitation in the ankle to the extent of one-third of its normal motion. The trial court sustained a verdict in the sum of $25,875. Defendant appealed. DREW, J. "While we are reluctant to interfere with a jury's award which has been sustained by the trial court, we will do so where the verdict grossly exceeds the amount to which the plaintiff is justly entitled. We think that $15,000 is the largest amount which can be supported as not excessive."

It is a criminal offense for the seller to give a false statement, or for the buyer to obtain a list of creditors for the purpose of injuring the seller in his business. CHAPTER XIV  Part 1. Bailments Sec. 537. Contractual Bailment. The word "bail ment" is the name given to a transaction in which personal property belonging to or in the possession of one party, is temporarily transferred to another person for various purposes, usually for transportation, storage, use, or repair. This transaction is described by Blackstone as a "delivery of goods in trust upon a contract expressed or implied, that the trust shall be faithfully executed on the part of the bailee."¹ It is more accurately defined as "the holding of a chattel by one person under an obligation to return or deliver it to another after some special purpose is accomplished." The bailor is the person who delivers the property in trust to another. The bailee is the person who receives the property and who is bound to return it after the object of the bailment has been accomplished. 

Sec. 538. Constructive Bailment. A bailment may be contractual or constructive. The latter arises by implication of law. As said in the following case, a "constructive bailment arises where the person having the possession of a chattel holds it under such circumstances that the law imposes upon him the obligation of delivering it to another." The following two cases are presented in contrast. 

Gilson v. Pa. R. R. Co., 86 N. J. L. 446 (1914). Plaintiff hung his coat on a clothes tree a few feet from where he seated himself in defendant's restaurant. After he had finished eating he discovered that his coat was missing. TRENCHARD, J. "Clearly he did not thereby transfer the exclusive possession of the coat to the defendant. The defendant had no knowledge of the transaction, and was not in any way apprised that it was to be the bailee of the coat or charged with its safekeeping." 

12 Black. Com. 451. 

2 Gilson v. Pa. R. R. Co., 86 N. J. L. 446 (1914). 26 389

we 

Webster v. Lane, 125 Misc. 868, 212 N. Y. S. 298 (1925). Plaintiff left her fur coat in the reception room of the defendant, a dentist, while undergoing treatment. On returning to the reception room her coat could not be found. PER CURIAM. 66 think we may take judicial notice of the fact that the patients of a dentist are not placed in a dental chair for treatment while they have their overcoats or wraps on. It seems clear, therefore, that defendant undertook voluntary custody of the coat as an accommodation to his patient, and as part of the service for which he was being paid." 

Sec. 539. Consideration. A constructive bailment is not usually sustained by any particular consideration, but rather by some benefit or advantage which the bailee hopes to derive from the transaction with the bailor and others as an incident of trade. 

Woodruff v. Painter & Eldridge, 150 Pa. 91 (1892). Plaintiff removed his coat for the purpose of fitting on some clothing, and was advised by the salesman to place his watch and chain in a drawer. After trying on the garments he returned for his watch, but it was gone. HEYDRICK, J. ". . . while the customer pays nothing directly, or eo nomine, for the safekeeping of his effects, the dealer receives his recompense in the profits of the trade of which the bailment is a necessary incident."

Sec. 540. Risks of Ownership. Occasionally proper ty in the possession of a bailee is injured without the fault of anyone. Contracts of bailment commonly provide that the bailee shall assume the risk of accidental or unavoidable loss or destruction of the property, but otherwise this risk must be borne by the bailor as an incident of his ownership. 

Loeb v. Ferber, 346 Pa. 348 (1943). Plaintiff left three fur coats with a fur dealer for storage, under the following agreement: "In consideration of $25.00 charges I hereby agree to keep the said articles free from damage by moths and to return the said articles in the same condition as when received by me." One of the coats was stolen by a trusted employee, without fault or negligence on the part of the bailee. In deciding that the bailee was not liable for the loss, it was said by PATTERSON, J. "While a bailee may, by special contract, assume the extraordinary liability of an insurer towards the bailed property, a covenant to insure may never be implied and will be imposed only where it is found in the agree ment in clear and explicit language."

Sec. 541. Liability of Bailee. The liability of the bailee for property entrusted to his care is determined by the nature of the bailment. If it is for the sole benefit of the bailor the bailee is liable only for gross negligence, and if it is for the sole benefit of the bailee the latter is required to exercise great diligence." Where the bailment is one of mutual benefit it is the duty of the bailee to exercise reasonable and ordinary care. Failure to return the goods raises a presumption of negligence, which the bailee is required to explain.* 

Smith v. Cohen, 116 Pa. Superior Ct. 395 (1935). Plaintiff stored his automobile in a public garage over night. It was stolen during the early hours of the morning. There was evidence that the attendant of the garage went out for a few minutes to deliver a car. The trial judge, sitting without a jury, found for the plaintiff. In sustaining the judgment, it was said by BALDRIDGE, J. "The plaintiff having stored his car for a consideration with the garage owner, the latter became a bailee, and, as such, it was his duty to exercise reasonable and ordinary care for the safety of the plaintiff's car. Whether he performed that duty was a question of fact for the trial judge."

Sec. 542. Limitation of Liability. The liability of the bailee may be limited by contract, but Pennsylvania and about half the states follow the rule that any attempt on the part of the bailee to limit his liability resulting from his future acts of negligence, is contrary to public policy. 

Wendt v. Sley System Garages, 124 Pa. Superior Ct. 224 (1936).

Plaintiff parked his automobile in an open parking lot operated by the defendant, and received a ticket or check which stated: "Not responsible for fire or theft. All valuables must be checked."

The car was stolen from the lot. It was recovered the following day, but with some of the equipment missing. The trial judge, sitting without a jury, found that defendant was negligent in not exercising due care in safeguarding the car, and entered judgment for the plaintiff. In sustaining the judgment, it was said by 

BALDRIDGE, J. "Whatever construction may be placed on the receipt, however, the appellant is confronted with the well-recognized rule that the right of a bailee to limit his liability by special contract does not go to the extent of relieving him against his own negligence." 

3 Carlisle Bank v. Graham, 79 Pa. 

106 (1875). 

4 O'Malley v. Penn Athletic Club, 

119 Pa. Superior Ct. 584 (1925).

Sec. 543. Misuse. The bailee is liable for misuse of bailed property, independently of the question of negligence. As said in a case involving a deviation in the use of a team and wagon, during which both were accidentally destroyed by fire, "if the thing is used for a different purpose from that which was intended by the parties, or in a different manner, or for a longer period, the hirer is not only responsible for all damages, but if a loss afterwards occurs, although by inevitable casualty, he will generally be responsible therefor." Under such circumstances the liability of the bailee is substantially that of an insurer.

Sec. 544. Conversion, The conversion of bailed property is usually regarded as a more serious breach of trust than a mere deviation in the use of the property. 

Where the bailee asserts dominion over the property, in a manner inconsistent with the property rights of the bailor, the bailee is liable in trespass for the value of the property, and where malice or oppressive circumstances appear, he may be liable for punitive damages." 

Sec. 545. Misdelivery. The duty of the bailee to return the property, is one of the chief characteristics of a bailment. According to the great weight of authority in the American states, misdelivery is the equivalent of conversion, and renders the bailee liable independently of negligence. There is dictum in the cases supporting this doctrine in Pennsylvania, although the decisions appear to rely upon negligence or bad faith as grounds for relief." 

Potomac Ins. Co. v. Nickson, 64 Utah 395 (1924). Wallace stored his automobile in defendant's garage over night. During the night a stranger, Weibers, slipped into the office, obtained a blank claim check, and substituted the stub on the Wallace car. 

As soon as the day shift came on duty he appeared at the garage

Sec. 546. Bailee v. Third Party. Not infrequently, property in the possession of a bailee is injured by the wrongful conduct of a third party. In the ordinary bailment for use, in which the bailee is given the right to the possession and enjoyment of the property for a definite term, the bailee is entitled to an action in his own right against any person who interferes with the possession and enjoyment of the property. He also has the right to recover the full value of the property, "in case of its destruction or conversion by the third party, the bailee being liable over to the bailor for any damage recovered in excess of his interest.' 9910 Some of these cases involve situations where the bailee is legally liable to the bailor for the injury, irrespective of the negligence of the bailee, as in the case of goods in the possession of a common carrier.¹¹

Sec. 547. Bailor v. Third Party. The reversionary interest of the bailor, is his right in the property at the conclusion of the bailment. If this interest is not protected by the bailee, when such property is injured by the wrongful conduct of a third party, the bailor has a right of action against the third party to the extent of his reversionary interest, and also in the case of a gratuitous bailment, where the bailee has no pecuniary interest in the property.12 Where there is a conversion of the property by a third party, the bailor may maintain an
