Sec. 548. Total Destruction. The practice of leasing automobiles with an option to purchase at the end of the term, under the so-called bailment lease, has thrown this problem into bold relief. Where such property is destroyed beyond repair, the courts distinguish sharply between the separate and distinct interests of the bailor and the bailee. Both may sue the wrongdoer concurrently, and recover such damages as each may have sustained.

General Motors Acceptance Corp. v. B. & O. R. R. Co., 97 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 98 (1929). An automobile in possession of a bailee was destroyed in an accident at a railroad crossing. The value of the car new was $887. It was delivered to the bailee in consideration of a down payment of $276, and twelve monthly installments of $50.91 each. At the time of the accident the unpaid rentals amounted to $560.09. Both the bailee and the bailor brought actions against the railroad company. The bailee was denied recovery on grounds of contributory negligence. It was indicated, however, that in a proper case, "his damages could not have exceeded compensation for the injury to his rights under the contract-the right to possess and use the car during the term of the lease and to buy it at its expiration upon the specified conditions." 

The lower court approved a verdict for the bailor for the market value of the automobile. Defendant appealed. CUNNINGHAM, J. 

"In the case of an ordinary bailment the bailor would have a right to recover full damages for the destruction of the property. 

We are not dealing with an ordinary bailment. . . . What this bailor was entitled to recover from the tort feasor was the actual value of its ownership in the property; that value was dependent to a large extent upon the length of time the lease had been running and whether the bailee had paid the rentals therein specified." 

Sec. 549. Release by Bailee. A troublesome question arises whenever the bailee gives a release for the entire damage, and then defaults in his obligation to the bailor. 

It has been held that a release, given for a consideration 

13 Commercial Banking Corp. v. Active Loan Co., 135 Pa. Superior Ct. 124 

(1938).

which is fair and reasonable, is binding upon the bailor where the damage is less than the total value of the property," but not where the consideration is partial and the property is destroyed or damaged beyond repair. 

National Bond & Inv. Co. v. Gill, 123 Pa. Superior Ct. 341 (1936). The interest of the bailor, in an automobile which had been practically destroyed in a collision, was fixed by the jury at $410. The bailee had previously settled his claim against the wrongdoer for the sum of $263, which covered his interest in the car and slight personal injuries. The wrongdoer contended that the settlement made with the bailee constituted a bar to the action by the bailor. There was no evidence that the bailee had acted in any way for the bailor, or that the bailor knew anything about the settlement at the time it was made. The court pointed out that such a rule would be unreasonable and unjust. As said by 

CUNNINGHAM, J., "a bailee threatened with a defense of contributory negligence, or conscious of the fact that he had been even partially responsible for the accident, would naturally settle at a low figure."

Sec. 550. Lien for Repairs. Another troublesome question arises whenever a third party attempts to assert a lien against the property for repairs. No question arises whenever the bailor expressly authorizes the repairs, but when the fact is dependent upon his implied assent, the question is usually for the jury.15 Whether the contract imposes upon the bailor, or the bailee," the duty of keeping the property in repair, such a provision does not raise an implied assent such as would support a lien against the bailor for repairs authorized by the bailee. 16 

Part 2. Common Carriers 

Sec. 551. Common Law. A common carrier, at common law, is any person who "undertakes generally, and for all persons indifferently, to carry goods or persons and deliver them, for hire."18 Such an undertaking is

17 Stern v. Sica, 66 Pa. Superior Ct. 84 (1917).

distinguished because of the high degree of responsibility which is imposed upon it for the protection of the public. 

Any kind of carrier, whether it be railroad, boat, motor vehicle, elevator, and the like, may qualify as a common carrier. The consideration for the undertaking may be contractual, or it may be imputed from the income of the business. 

Petrie v. Kaufmann & Baer Co., 291 Pa. 211 (1927). Plaintiff was riding on an escalator. It momentarily stopped and then started forward with such a sudden and violent jerk as to cause her to fall against the moving stairway. She sustained serious and permanent injuries and recovered judgment in the sum of $15,000. In sustaining the judgment, it was said by WALLING, J. "As an escalator and an elevator perform the like service of conveying people from one elevation to another, they are subject to like duties and responsibilities. The passenger is at least powerless to influence the action of the former as the latter. Hence, the rule that an elevator is deemed a common carrier applies equally to an escalator." 

Sec. 552. Interstate Commerce Act. In 1887 Con gress enacted a comprehensive measure for the regulation of railroads engaged in the transportation of persons or property in interstate or foreign commerce.19 

Jurisdiction to administer the provisions of the act is vested in the Interstate Commerce Commission. In 1935 

Congress enacted a similar measure for the regulation of motor carriers.20 This statute defines a common carrier by motor vehicle, as any person who undertakes to serve the "general public," and a contract carrier as any person who transports passengers or property under "special and individual contracts or agreements." Except in matters of safety, a number of activities are excluded from the operation of the law, such as the transportation of school children, taxicab service and the like, including the casual, occasional, or reciprocal transportation of passengers or property in interstate commerce. The 

Interstate Commerce Commission is authorized to establish reasonable requirements for the regulation of com-

20 49 Stat. 543, 49 U. S. C. 301.

mon and contract carriers generally, and also for private carriers in the interests of safe operation. 

Sec. 553. Public Utility Law. In 1937 the legisla ture enacted a comprehensive measure for the regulation of public utilities, including common carriers, common carriers by motor vehicle, and contract carriers by motor vehicle, in the transportation of passengers or property between points within the commonwealth.21 Jurisdiction to administer the provisions of the act is vested in the Public Utility Commission. Under the provisions of this statute, a common carrier is required to obtain a certificate of public convenience. A contract carrier is required to obtain a permit. The act does not purport to include all motor vehicle transportation. As amended in 1943,22 the following persons or activities are excluded: the lessor of a motor vehicle, school districts in the transportation of school children, farmers and cooperative associations in transporting their own produce, persons using dump trucks in various activities, the transportation of voting machines, and the transportation of property by the owner to himself or to purchasers directly from him, and not otherwise used in the transportation of property for others.

Allaman v. Public Utility Commission, 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 

353 (1942). On the complaint of nine railroads, a bona fide and duly licensed coal dealer at Shippenville was enjoined by the Public Utility Commission from delivering coal from various coal mines to its customers, without first obtaining authority from the commission. In setting aside the order, it was said by KELLER, P. J. "The evidence establishes that the appellants in delivering coal to the Penzoil Company and its other customers are merely transporting their own property to customers who have purchased it directly from them, in vehicles owned and operated by them, as the owners of the coal, and not otherwise used in the transportation of property for compensation for others; and that they are. neither common carriers by motor vehicle nor contract carriers by motor vehicle, within the intendment of the Public Utility Law."

Sec. 554, Warehouseman Liability. The liability of a common carrier may be that of the ordinary bailee, or it may be such as the common law imposes upon the bailee in his capacity as a common carrier. The first is commonly called warehouseman liability, the second, common carrier liability. Where goods are in the custody of a carrier merely as a warehouseman, the carrier is responsible for the exercise of reasonable or ordinary care, as in the case of any other bailment for mutual benefit. Such is the case where baggage or parcels are checked for storage only, or held as a matter of convenience. A much higher degree of liability is imposed upon a common carrier per se. The following opinion is indicative of this trend very early in the history of the common law.. 

Coggs v. Bernard, 2 Ld. Raymond 909 (1708). Lord HOLT. "If a delivery to carry or otherwise manage is made to one that exercises a public employment, and he is to have a reward, he is bound to answer for the goods at all events. The law charges this person thus intrusted to carry goods, against all events, but acts of God, and of the enemies of the King. For though the force be never so great, as if an irresistible multitude of people should rob him, nevertheless he is chargeable."

Sec. 555. Common Carrier Liability Common car rier liability begins when goods have been accepted for transportation, and ends at such time after the goods have arrived at their destination as may be fixed in the bill of lading.

Michigan Central R. R. Co. v. Mark Owen & Co., 256 U. S. 427 

(1921). The bill of lading in this case provided: "Property not removed by the party entitled to receive it, within 48 hours exclusive of legal holidays, after notice of its arrival has been duly sent or given, may be kept, etc., subject to warehouseman liability." 

The shipment was a carload of grapes. While they were being unloaded, during the 48-hour period, some of the goods were stolen. 

MCKENNA, J. "The carrier's liability as a common carrier continues during the 48 hours, unless property is removed within that time, though the car is accepted by the consignee, the seals broken, and unloading commenced. Only a right of access was given."

Where no time has been fixed in the bill of lading, common carrier liability continues in Pennsylvania, "until the consignee of the freight, or the passenger, as the case may be, has had reasonable time to call for and take away his goods or baggage." At the expiration of a reasonable time, liability of the carrier changes to "that of a warehouseman and not a carrier." 23 

Moyer v. Pa. R. R. Co., 31 Pa. Superior Ct. 559 (1906). Plaintiff shipped a trunk from Atlantic City to Lilly on August 11.

On the night of the 12th some thieves broke into the warehouse and removed part of the contents. BEAVER, J. "The delay of the owner of the baggage to claim and remove it having been unreasonable, the liability of the carrier was changed from that of an insurer to that of a warehouseman, which required of him simply ordinary care." 

Sec. 556. Excepted Causes. There are a number of circumstances which will excuse a common carrier from the liability imposed upon it by the common law. These exceptions may be listed as follows: (1) Act of God. 

This is usually an earthquake, an unprecedented flood, or extraordinary weather conditions, such as cyclones, hurricanes, and severe snow storms.24 (2) Act of the public enemy. By public enemy is meant an organized force at war, e.g., seizure by the confederate army,25 and not mobs, rioters or thieves. (3) Loss due to the inherent vice of the goods transported, such as fermentation or evaporation." (4) Act of the law, as where goods are seized under judicial process. (5) Act of the shipper, or fault on his part in loading or unloading,28 even though he uses the equipment of the carrier.29 26 27 

Long v. Pa. R. R. Co., 147 Pa. 343 (1892). Plaintiff sought to recover the value of two trunks and their contents which had been delivered to the defendant for transportation from Cincinnati to

Sec. 558. Duties and Obligations. State and fed eral laws impose upon common carriers the duty to furnish adequate facilities at just and reasonable charges, and to transport persons and property without unreasonable delay. Such laws make it unlawful to discriminate with respect to charges or facilities. The Penal 

Code" prohibits racial discrimination. Where a carrier has made a mistake in charging less than the lawful rate, the shipper is under a duty to refund the difference, even though he was not at fault. In Pa. R. R. Co. v. 

Osborn,38 defendant purchased return trip tickets for himself and family from Uniontown to Butte, and was charged the sum of $277.74. According to the tariffs on file with the Interstate Commerce Commission he should have paid the sum of $451.77. The carrier was permitted to recover the full legal rate. Following are important decisions involving unlawful discrimination in rates and facilities, insofar as they served to clarify the obligations of a common carrier. (1) In Mitchell Coal & Coke Co. v. Pa. R. R. Company,39 plaintiff alleged and proved that defendant required him to pay ten and fifteen cents more per ton than was paid by certain other competitors. Damages were assessed in the sum of $20,883.64. (2) In Sonman Shaft Coal Co. v. Pa. R. R. Company,40 plaintiff was refused cars, notwithstanding defendant had a surplus on hand. Plaintiff was compelled, under these circumstances, to sell its coal to its competitors in private cars furnished by them. Damages were assessed in this case in the sum of $145,830.25. 

Sec. 559. Injury to Passengers. "While a carrier is not an insurer of the safety of the passengers, he is bound to exercise the highest practical degree of care for their safety, and where a passenger is injured through some defect in the means of transportation or the manner of operation, the burden is upon the carrier to show it could not have been prevented by human foresight.""1

Gerlach v. Pittsburgh Railways Co., 94 Pa. Superior Ct. 121 (1928). Plaintiffs, husband and wife, were assaulted by a group of disorderly young men while riding on a trolley car. Both suffered personal injuries. The wife was pushed off while attempting to alight, and suffered the loss of issue. Neither the conductor nor the motorman made any effort to protect them. "Conductors on trains have authority to exercise reasonable control over the passengers and are responsible for the exercise of that authority." 43 

Sec. 560. Injury without Fault. A common carrier is not liable for injuries sustained by a passenger when it is in no way at fault. In Moore v. P. R. T. Co.,2 the conductor attempted to eject an unruly passenger, and in doing so, both of them collided with the plaintiff. It was held that the unruly passenger was the one who should respond in damages under these circumstances, and not the carrier, who was doing what it should have done. In Miller v. P. H. B. & N. C. Rys. Co., plaintiff boarded a crowded car and stood on the first step below the platform. In attempting to recover a coin that had dropped inside the car he stooped over, thus extending a portion of his body beyond the side of the car, which in this manner came in contact with a milk platform. It was held that the carrier was not bound to anticipate this hazard. In Rosen v. P. R. T. Co.," an automobile skidded into a trolley car in which plaintiff was a passenger, resulting in injuries to the plaintiff, but it was not shown that the carrier had caused or contributed to the accident, and judgment against it was set aside. 

Part 3. Negotiable Documents of Title Sec. 561. Purpose of Documents. Negotiable in struments are of two sorts, one of which calls for the payment of a sum certain in money, the other of which represents ownership in personal property. We are here concerned with the latter. It is a document in which it is stated that the goods referred to therein will 

44100 Pa. Superior Ct. 242 (1930). 

42 87 Pa. Superior Ct. 393 (1926). 

43 102 Pa. Superior Ct. 547 (1931).

be delivered to the bearer, or to the order of any person named in the document.* Such documents in this country are confined almost entirely to bills of lading and warehouse receipts. They are issued by common carriers and warehousemen, upon receipt of the goods which they represent, and are used to transfer title in the goods while they are in the course of transit or in the possession of a warehouseman. The method of transfer, or sale by the owner, is by indorsement in blank, or to bearer, or to a specified person. In either case the person to whom such a document is endorsed may negotiate the instrument in the same manner. Each indorsement is, in effect, a transfer of ownership in the goods. 45 46 

Sec. 562. Innocent Purchasers. Negotiable documents of title, prior to 1937, were not as freely negoti able as were instruments requiring the payment of money. Legislation during that year placed both types of instruments on the same footing. The purpose of such legislation is to protect an innocent purchaser for value, even though the instrument is negotiated by a finder or thief, or a person who would ordinarily lack the requisite authority to vest a good title in the purchaser. This is accomplished, as to warehouse receipts, by the Act of April 29, 1937, and as to negotiable documents of title, by the Act of May 28, 1937.47 In brief, the validity of the negotiation of such instrument is not impaired by the fact that the negotiation was a breach of duty on the part of the person making the negotiation, or by the fact that the owner of the document was deprived of the possession of the instrument by loss, theft, accident, conversion, fraud, mistake, or duress, if the person to whom the document is negotiated, or person to whom the document was subsequently negotiated, paid value therefor, in good faith, and without notice of the breach of duty, or loss, theft, accident, conversion, fraud, mistake, or duress.

CHAPTER XV CREDIT DEVICES Part 1. Pledge Sec. 563. Secret Liens. "The law abhors a secret lien." This maxim has been repeated so often, that it is difficult to trace its origin. So deep seated is this prejudice, that the law frowns upon any attempt of the owner of personal property to transfer the title to another, and yet continue to enjoy the possession and use of the property. As observed by the Supreme 

Court more than a century ago, "it is a rule of general policy which declares possession to be evidence of property, the presumption being that every man is trusted according to the property in his possession."'¹

As to creditors, and innocent purchasers for value,³ the party in possession is deemed to be the lawful owner. The following problems are typical of the hostility of the law: (1) A loans money to B, and takes from B an assignment of the title to certain goods, but allows B to retain possession. One of B's creditors levies upon the goods. (2) A leases certain goods to B, but authorizes B to sell the goods. B sells the goods to C, an innocent purchaser for value, but fails to remit to A. In such cases, the claims of the creditor, or an innocent purchaser for value, will prevail over the claims of the legal owner. 

This chapter is a study of the extent to which the law will recognize a separation of the title, and the possession, of personal property. 

Sec. 564. Pledge of Property. A pledge is a trans fer of personal property from one person to another, as security for some obligation, usually a loan of money. The person who pledges the property is called

250 Pa. 194 (1915). 

3 McKee V. Ward, 289 Pa. 414 (1927). 

4 Clow v. Woods, S. & R. 275 (1819). 404

CREDIT DEVICES 

405, 5 the pledgor. The person who receives the property in trust is called the pledgee. In a contract of pledge, title remains in the pledgor, subject to a lien in favor of the pledgee for the amount of the obligation for which the pledge is made. When the obligation has been, satisfied, the pledgor is entitled to the return of the property. Such a transaction is valid as to third parties, if there is a bona fide transfer of possession of the property to the pledgee. 

Wendel v. Smith, 291 Pa. 247 (1927). Blough, an automobile dealer, borrowed money from Wendel in order to purchase certain cars, and transferred the title to Wendel as security for the loan. 

Wendel placed small cards on the instrument board or steering wheel of each car, which stated the car to be his property, but otherwise Blough remained in possession. Blough became bankrupt, and a dispute arose between Wendel and the trustee in bankruptcy over the right to the cars. In deciding in favor of the trustee, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "What was here done, the putting of small tags on the automobiles, was not sufficient to indicate a change of ownership. There must be a change in physical possession if title is to pass against creditors to such things as automobiles, readily movable."

Sec. 565. Pledge of Title. A pledge of title is an assignment of the title to personal property, without a transfer of possession, as security for some obligation, usually a loan. Such a transaction is valid as between the parties to it,' but it is constructively fraudulent as to creditors of the party in possession, and innocent purchasers for value. 

First National Bank v. Parks, 94 Pa. Superior Ct. 570 (1928).

A farmer wanted to borrow some money from a bank. He assigned to the bank the title to certain cattle but remained in possession. 

The bank delivered a conditional sale contract back to the farmer, which was duly recorded. A creditor of the farmer levied upon the cattle. In sustaining his right to do so, it was said by HENDER- 

SON, J. "It is too late now to overthrow the well established doctrine that personal property assigned if susceptible to actual delivery must be so delivered. The change of possession must be both actual and continued."

Part 2. 

Assignment of Accounts Receivable 

Sec. 566. Nature of Pledge. Occasionally a mer chant finds it necessary to make an assignment of an account receivable as security for a loan or the extension of credit. The merchant is called the pledgor. 

The bank or person who receives the assignment is called the pledgee. The debtor under the account receivable will be called the debtor. We have observed that a valid pledge requires delivery of the thing pledged. The common law recognizes, however, an assignment of an account receivable, upon delivery of the original record of the account to the pledgee, accompanied by a written assignment. We have also observed in a preceding chapter that assignments prevail in the order in which notice is given to the debtor." 

Difficulty arises at this point. The reputation of the financial ability of a merchant is not as fragile as that of a banking institution, but it would undoubtedly be injurious to him if such an assignment became known to his debtor or to the public. An assignment of this sort is often understood as a symbol of distress. 

The Act of 194110 provides an alternative. Under this statute, if the pledgor, concurrently with the assignment, makes a record thereof upon his books of account of the name of the pledgee, in such manner as will disclose upon inspection the fact and the date of such assignment, it shall be enforceable against all subsequent assignees, pledgees, and other creditors, notwithstanding notice is not given to the debtor. This statute, in effect, validates a secret lien. 

Sec. 567. Value of Notice." While it may not be practical to give notice of such an assignment, notice is still essential if the utmost security is to be obtained.

Sec. 568. Constructive Fraud. The Uniform Fraud ulent Conveyance Act, as adopted in this commonwealth,¹² and as incorporated in the federal Bankruptcy Act,13 provides that an obligation is deemed fraudulent when made without a fair consideration, or when made to secure an existing obligation in such manner as to unreasonably prefer one creditor over another. 

In Pennsylvania an assignment of an account receivable is deemed fraudulent as to creditors, if the merchant retains such control over the account that he is able to use the proceeds for his own purposes. If he has power to control the lien, or to terminate the lien, it is invalid as to attaching creditors, or a trustee in bankruptcy. 

In re Pusey, Maynes, Breish Co., 122 F. (2d) 606 (1941). In

The bank received an assignment of each new substituted account. The merchant was adjudicated a bankrupt on August 4, 1936. Four months prior thereto, the assigned accounts amounted to $24,640.10. The trustee in bankruptcy sought to avoid the assignments on the ground that they constituted a voidable preference under the federal Bankruptcy Act. Part 3. 

Bailment Lease

Sec. 569. Validity. Prior to the adoption of the 

Uniform Conditional Sales Act in 1925,14 the only way a merchant in Pennsylvania could sell goods on the installment plan and reserve the title until the last installment had been paid, secure of the claims of creditors and innocent purchasers, was to lease the goods at monthly rentals equivalent to the purchase price, and give the lessee an option either to return the goods at the end of the term, or to purchase the goods at the end of the term, usually for one dollar. This simple security device is called a bailment lease. The merchant is the bailor. The customer is the bailee. "Such a transaction includes two distinct, but consistent contracts, the one taking effect, if at all, when the other is spent. The contract of bailment preserves the ownership of the bailor during the particular relation created by it, and the contract of sale which supersedes it, transfers the title as soon as it is called into action, by the payment of the price. "'15 The following case is of particular interest because of the recognition of this practice by the federal courts. 

General Motors Acceptance Corp. v. Horton, 85 Fed. (2d) 452 

(1936). A motor company delivered a car to a business firm under a bailment lease, and assigned the lease to a finance company. 

The bailee paid $268 in cash, and agreed to pay $28 per month until a total of $952 had been paid, at which time the bailee could buy the car for $1. The bailee became bankrupt during the life of the lease, and Horton was appointed trustee in bankruptcy. This was a contest between the finance company under the lease, and the trustee on behalf of the creditors of the bankrupt. In sustaining the right of the finance company to the car, it was said by DAVIS, 14 Act of May 12, 1925, P. L. 603, 69 PS 361. 

15 Myers v. Harvey, 2 P. & W. 478 (1831).

CREDIT DEVICES 

409 C. J. "It must be admitted that this transaction in face, though not in form, amounted to a conditional sale. But to construe such contracts as bailment leases is a policy, regardless of what may be thought of it as a principle of law or business, which has long been pursued in Pennsylvania, and her courts have uniformly sustained them as bailment leases. This court has felt constrained to follow the decisions of the Pennsylvania courts in construing such contracts."

Sec. 570. Reservation of Title. The bailment lease, if properly employed, is not a fraudulent transfer of possession, either as to the creditors of the bailee,¹º or innocent purchasers from the bailee." An exception may be made on grounds of estoppel, as where the bailee, with the knowledge and acquiescence of the bailor, painted the bailee's name and occupation on a wagon, which the bailee subsequently sold to an innocent purchaser.18 Otherwise the bailor's title is good against the world, and without notice. The Uniform 

Conditional Sales Act, as originally drafted, requires the public recording of a conditional sale contract, and the bailment lease, but when this act was adopted in 

Pennsylvania, the bailment lease was excluded. Consequently, bailment leases are not jeopardized by failure to comply with that legislation. 

Stern & Co. v. Paul, 96 Pa. Superior Ct. 112 (1928). Plaintiff leased to two persons a diamond ring for a period of 125 weeks, $50 to be paid on delivery of the ring and $6 per week until $675 had been paid. It was to be returned at the expiration of the term, with an option to purchase it at any time upon full payment of the rental. After the bailees had paid a total of $98, they pledged the ring to a third party for a loan of $175. The lease had not been recorded. In an action of replevin to recover possession it was held, in an opinion by CUNNINGHAM, J., that in adopting the 

Uniform Conditional Sales Act, the legislature "deemed unwise to make any change in the existing law relative to bailment leases," and that the agreement in question was a bailment, beyond the scope and requirements of that act.

Sec. 571. Fictitious Bailments. The use of the bailment lease is never sanctioned except in the case of the bona fide leasing of goods for use by the bailee. 

The bailor may not authorize the bailee to sell the goods, and on default of the bailee to remit the proceeds, dispossess an innocent purchaser.19 Fierce and repeated onslaughts have been made over the years, particularly by lenders of money, to pervert the use of this device, but all such attempts have been just as vigorously defeated by the courts.20 The usual artifice is for the lender of money to require an assignment of the borrower's automobile, and then give the borrower a bailment lease under which the borrower remains in possession. Another stratagem is for an automobile dealer to pledge the title of automobiles to a finance company, without a bona fide surrender of the property, and receive back a bailment lease, or have the finance company deliver a bailment lease to a customer of the dealer.21 In all such cases the courts treat the parties as debtor and creditor, and disregard the bailment. As said in the following case: "Those who buy and sell, bail and loan money on motor vehicles must be given to understand that the realities of their transactions will be sought for by the courts; they will look through the screen of paper titles to ascertain what was the real situation." 

Root v. Republic Acceptance Corp., 279 Pa. 55 (1924). The 

Averill Sales Company borrowed money from a finance company, and delivered to the finance company bills of sale and storage receipts for various automobiles, receiving in return bailment leases. The Averill Company having become bankrupt, this was a contest between the trustee in bankruptcy and the finance company. 

In deciding in favor of the trustee, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "However much appellant desired and endeavored to disguise the transaction between it and the Averill Company by the dressing of the papers which were executed-the bill of sale, the storage receipt and the bailment lease, the real transaction, so far as

Sec. 572. Remedies of Bailor. Property trans ferred to the bailee under a bailment lease belongs at all times to the bailor. The bailee is liable for a conversion of the goods, and may be prosecuted for larceny by bailee. A creditor of the bailee may attach the equitable interest of the bailee, "but no right of the bailor will thereby be extinguished."22 This applies, also, to the bailee's trustee in bankruptcy. Even a repairman may not assert a lien against the property,' unless the circumstances are such that the assent of the bailor for the repairs may be reasonably implied."

If the bailee defaults in any payment or installment, the bailor may repossess the property and retain all that has been paid. He may not use force in retaking the property,26 but may resort to subterfuge," as long as he does not commit a breach of the peace. The right of the bailor to repossess the property on default, and retain all that has been paid, has received just condemnation, particularly since the first installment of rent approximates in most cases about one-fourth the value of the property, but as a practical matter it is rare for the bailee to default after making a number of monthly payments. The penalty is usually sufficient to induce compliance with the contract. 

Sec. 573. Cumulative Remedies. A bailment lease which confers upon the bailor, on default of the bailee, a right to repossess the property, retain all that has been paid, and yet recover the remaining installments of rent, by confessing judgment against the bailee for the full amount of future rentals, presents a serious problem. The use of the bailment lease in itself is

If the right of such cumulative remedies were to be sanctioned by the courts, the legislature might well abolish the use of the bailment lease altogether, and compel the parties to resort to a conditional sale. Fortunately, the decisions of the courts do not appear to sanction any such abuse. If the lease provides for an alternative remedy, such as repossession and rent due at the time of repossession, or a declaration and confession of all rentals under the contract without repossession, the bailor is put to an election which remedy to pursue.28 If it provides for repossession on default, the sale of the property, and confession of judgment for the loss actually sustained by the bailor, the agreement has been sustained.29 This is essentially the remedy authorized by the Uniform Conditional Sales Act upon repossession and resale of the property.

Act was adopted in 1925.30 This statute provides a method for the sale of goods on the installment plan, title to remain in the seller until the last installment has been paid. The purpose of the act is to protect the seller's interest against the creditors of the buyer, or innocent purchasers from the buyer. The contract must be filed in the office of the prothonotary within ten days. The filing fee is fifty cents. Such reservation of title is valid for three years, but it may be extended thereafter from year to year by refiling within thirty days preceding the expiration of each period. The buyer may not remove the property from the county, except for temporary use for a period of not more than thirty days, without giving to the seller ten days

Sec. 575. Risk of Loss. As a general rule, the owner of personal property assumes the risk of unavoidable injury to, or destruction of the property. A different rule appears in the code. The "risk of injury and loss shall rest upon the buyer." As a result, the destruction of the property does not terminate the liability of the buyer to pay the purchase price, and he should, if he deems it advisable, insure the risk. 

Burnley v. Tufts, 66 Miss. 48 (1888). Plaintiff sold a soda water fountain to defendant under a conditional sale contract. Prior to payment of the last installment, the equipment was destroyed without fault on the part of either party to the agreement. In deciding that the loss should be borne by the purchaser, it was said by COOPER, J. “The contract imposed upon the buyer an absolute promise to pay."

Sec. 576. Redemption. When the buyer defaults in his obligations, the seller may retake the property, peaceably if possible, otherwise by legal process. If the seller gives not less than 20 nor more than 40 days notice of an intention to retake the property, and if the buyer does not, prior to the day set for retaking, satisfy his obligations due under the contract, the buyer is not thereafter entitled to redeem the property. If the seller retakes the property on default, but without advance notice to the buyer, he must retain the goods for 10 days thereafter. During this period the buyer may redeem the property upon tender of the amount due under the contract, with interest and the expenses of retaking. The buyer may demand a statement of the amount due. If the seller fails to furnish such statement within a reasonable time after demand, he "shall forfeit to the buyer ten dollars and also be liable to him for all damages suffered because of such failure." 

Sec. 577. Resale. When property is retaken under a bailment lease, the bailor is not required to resell the property, or otherwise account to the bailee, nor is the bailee entitled to redeem the property. It is in these respects that the bailment lease differs sharply from a conditional sale. The Uniform Conditional 

Sales Act provides that if the buyer has paid 50% of the purchase price, the seller must resell the goods at public auction, within thirty days after the retaking, and after not less than ten days written notice to the buyer. The seller must also give the requisite public notice of the sale. If the buyer has not paid at least 

50% of the purchase price, the seller need not resell the goods unless commanded to do so by the buyer. 

Such demand by the buyer must be made within ten days after the retaking. In any event the seller must resell the goods, voluntarily or otherwise, before he may recover damages arising from the default of the buyer. The provisions for redemption and compulsory

CREDIT DEVICES 

415 resale are for the protection of the buyer. If the seller fails to comply therewith, "the buyer may recover from the seller his actual damages, if any, and in no event less than one-fourth of the sum of all payments which have been made under the contract, with interest."

Sec. 578. Distribution. The proceeds of the resale are distributed in the following order: (1) expense of the resale; (2) expense of retaking; and (3) the balance due under the contract. Any sum remaining must be paid to the buyer. Where a resale is not made, the buyer is discharged of any further obligation under the contract. Where a resale is made, either as required by the code or at the election of the seller, the seller may recover any deficiency from the buyer. 

Hare & Chase, Inc. v. Hutchison, 138 Atl. 611 (Del. 1927). Plaintiff sold an automobile to the defendant on a conditional sale contract and received a note in payment. The note not being paid, plaintiff repossessed the car, sold it, applied the proceeds to the note, and brought this action to recover from the buyer he defi ciency of the purchase price. RODNEY, J. "The Uniform Condi tional Sales Act, and especially section 22, substantially adopts the theory that the buyer has the use of the goods until default; that after default they are then retaken, resold, and proceeds credited to account of buyer; that then the seller may recover from the buyer the deficiency of the purchase price, for the buyer has had the entire benefit of the goods which the seller lost by the resale."

Part 5. Title to Motor Vehicles Sec. 579. Certificate of Title. It should be obvious from the foregoing, that merchants in Pennsylvania utilize the bailment lease in preference to the conditional sale. The lack of any public record in the use of the bailment lease proved to be a disadvantage to the public, particularly with respect to automobiles, since a prospective buyer had no notice of the nature of the title, or of any encumbrance against the property. As a result of this and other circumstances, thefts and unauthorized sales became a public nuisance.

In order to correct this situation the legislature, in 1923, first made provision for a certificate of title from the commonwealth. This was a police measure, which was designed primarily to facilitate the recovery of stolen automobiles. It was not intended to "affect in any manner the actual ownership of the vehicle," or "the relations of the persons interested in it," nor did it constitute a "warrant of ownership or muniment of title as usually understood in the law.'' The subsequent Act of 1929 provides that no person shall own a motor vehicle unless a certificate of title is obtained.35 

Sec. 580. Notice of Lien. Vigorous attempts have been made, by money lenders and others, to convert the Commonwealth's certificate of title into an enforceable encumbrance. In 1933, under the title, "Change of Ownership by Operation of Law and Judicial Sale, as by inheritance, bankruptcy or sheriff's sale and the like, the legislature provided that the certificate, "showing a lien or encumbrance shall be adequate notice to the Commonwealth, creditors, and purchasers that a lien against the motor vehicle exists."'36 In 

1936 the Superior Court held that such notice was effective only as to changes of ownership indicated in the statutory title." In 1939 the legislature reënacted the same provision under the title, "Contents, Deliv ery, Effect and Life of Certificate of Title.""38 The legislature may have intended to give the certificate of title the effect of a lien," but the statutory evidence is too inconclusive, and it has been so decided.40 A mere "notice" that a lien exists does not in itself create a lien, if there be none such as the law would en-

Part 6. Chattel Mortgage 

Sec. 581. History. Although common to other states, the chattel mortgage did not receive general recognition in Pennsylvania until 1945. In the past, this commonwealth has always been hostile to such a device. 

As said by the late Judge CUNNINGHAM, "it has long been the settled rule in this state that chattel mortgages generally are contrary to our public policy and will not prevail against claims of bona fide purchasers or creditors. So great was this hostility, that 

Pennsylvania refused to recognize such mortgages when executed in other states, covering property afterwards brought within the state. The change brought about by the legislature in 1945 deserves some explanation. 9941 42

The Contract. In a chattel mortgage, the relation of the parties is that of creditor and debtor. 

The creditor receives from his debtor an assignment of the title to specific goods, under a clause of defeasance which provides that title is to revest in the debtor when the mortgage debt is paid. The purpose of a public recording of the transaction is to give notice, actual or constructive, of ownership in the goods, so that no one who cares to go to the trouble of examining the records may be deceived. The Act of 1945 provides that any person may, for any indebtedness, give a bond, promissory note or judgment note, secured

by a chattel mortgage upon any chattel of any kind, including, but not limited to, livestock, poultry, farm machinery, farm equipment, and crops, including annual or perennial crops, and other plant products, either grown, growing, or to be grown within one year thereafter. Such a mortgage may include additions in kind, replacements, the progeny of animals, and also future advances to be made within a period of five years, not to exceed the amount stated in the mortgage, including advances for taxes, levies, insurance, and repairs. Sec. 584. Recording. The mortgage must be filed in the office of the prothonotary of the county in which the chattel is located. The filing fee is 75c. As between the parties, the lien is valid until paid, but not as to third parties for a longer period than five years, unless renewed for successive five year periods. In the case of motor vehicles, the lien does not operate as notice to the commonwealth, creditors or purchasers, until noted on the certificate of title. When chattels are brought into the state which are subject to a chattel mortgage elsewhere, such mortgage may now be recorded in this state in the manner indicated above. 

The assignment of a chattel mortgage, showing the balance due, may also be recorded. Unless otherwise provided in the contract, the risk of injury or destruction of the property is upon the mortgagor. If the mortgaged chattel is moved to another county without the consent of the mortgagee, the lien follows the property. If written consent is given for such removal, the mortgagee has six months in which to record the mortgage in the county to which the chattel is taken. 

Sec. 585. Remedies. The mortgagee may consent in writing to the sale of any part of the mortgaged

421 property, free of lien, or free of the lien upon condition that the proceeds be paid to the mortgagee. Otherwise the mortgagee has a lien against both the chattel and the proceeds of the sale, and may enforce either one at his option, subject to but one satisfaction. Upon default of any of the terms of the contract the mortgagee may repossess the property, by process of law or otherwise, and sell the same at public or private sale, after ten days notice to the mortgagor, during which period the mortgagor may redeem the property by payment of the indebtedness with interest and costs. Any person who, without the written consent of the mortgagee, wilfully sells, injures, destroys, conceals, abandons, or defaces any marks identifying the property, is punishable by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or fine of double the value of the property, or both.

Part 7. Trust Receipts Sec. 586. Common Law. Another security device used to facilitate credit transactions is called the trust receipt. Heretofore this device has been approved in 

Pennsylvania only in the case of import transactions. in connection with the sale or processing and marketing of goods in bulk. In other states it has also been used in domestic short term transactions, including the marketing of automobiles. It was first associated, however, with importations from abroad. Where this 28

device is used, the foreign seller consigns merchandise to a bank in this country. The bank thereupon surrenders the bill of lading or warehouse receipt to the importer or dealer, as part of the transaction extending credit to the dealer, and receives from the dealer a trust receipt. The trust receipt provides that the dealer shall hold the goods in trust for the bank, but with liberty to sell the same for the account of the bank, and to apply the proceeds toward the extinguishment of the loan. The legal title is in the bank. The dealer in possession is authorized to dispose of the goods in the usual course of trade. When this practice began the courts were called upon to decide whether a trust receipt created a secret lien in favor of the bank, and whether it should prevail over the claims of the general creditors of the dealer. In some states the transaction is designated as a conditional sale, but more commonly a chattel mortgage. In Pennsylvania it was construed to be a bailment. 

Brown Brothers & Co. v. Billington, 163 Pa. 76 (1894). Sweet ing ordered a consignment of bicycles from a concern in England, by means of a letter of credit drawn on Brown Brothers & Company, a Philadelphia bank. The goods were consigned to the bank, which thereupon surrendered the bill of lading to Sweeting and received from him a trust receipt. While the goods were in his possession they were levied upon by one of his creditors. In an interpleader proceeding, in which the bank was the claimant, the lower court held in favor of the attaching creditor. In deciding that the transaction was a bailment, and that the goods were the property of the bank, it was said by GREEN, J. "It will be observed that this was not in any event an undertaking on the part of Brown Bros. & Co. to sell the bicycles to Sweeting. He was not to become the owner of them by purchase or in any other He was to hold the goods in trust for Brown Bros. & 

Co. as their property, with liberty to sell them for their account and pay over to them the proceeds, to be applied to the payment of acceptances given for the price of the bicycles, and was entitled to credit upon any other indebtedness of his to either of the plaintiff's firms." way. ..

Sec. 587. Uniform Trust Receipts Act. When trust receipts were extended to internal transactions, a sub-

CREDIT DEVICES 

423 stantial conflict of judicial opinion arose in the several states as to the status of general creditors of the dealer. 

In Pennsylvania the courts frowned upon an exchange of a bailment lease and trust receipt as between the parties, as inconsistent with the proper use of the bailment lease in domestic transactions.56 Experience indicated the need of some practical device, consistent with established business practice, and in response thereto, the National Conference of Commissioners on

Uniform State Laws prepared the Uniform Trust Re ceipts Act. This act was adopted in Pennsylvania in 

1941.57 The lender in this statute is called the "entruster." The dealer is called the "trustee." The subject of the trust receipt was broadened so as to include not only merchandise and the processing of goods, but also securities, negotiable instruments, and documents of title. 

Sec. 588. Statement of Intention. This statute does not make any provision for the recording of a trust receipt, as in the case of a conditional sale or chattel mortgage. Nor was it intended to cover isolated transactions not constituting a course of business, unless such business is contemplated. It requires that parties who contemplate engaging in financing under trust receipts, shall file a statement of intention with the Department of State and with the prothonotary of the county where the trustee has his principal place of business, defining the parties and their places of business, in conjunction with the statement that the entruster is or is about to engage in financing under trust receipts, and describing the goods to be covered by such financing. Such a statement is effective for one year, but it may be renewed for a like period. It is also retroactive for a period of thirty days. Notice as above operates to preserve the entruster's interest against the creditors of the trustee, an assignee for

the benefit of creditors, an equity receiver, and a trustee in bankruptcy.

Sec. 589. Innocent Purchasers. The act does not affect the rights of purchasers from the trustee, to the extent authorized in the trust receipt, and in the ordinary course of trade. To this extent the entruster is still dependent upon the honesty and integrity of the trustee. A trust receipt has some of the characteristics of a pledge,58 but it does not create a lien which would allow an unpaid entruster to challenge an authorized sale and follow the goods in an effort to realize his claim out of them. He is protected, however, where the sale is unauthorized, or where it is not made in the usual course of trade. The foregoing is a summary of the act. It is too soon to say how these provisions will be interpreted by the courts.

Sec. 590. Consignments. It has long been the rule that a manufacturer or distributor may part with the possession of goods and merchandise and still retain the title, by the delivery of such goods on consignment, but this is not a credit device. It is a strict agency transaction. The consignor is the principal. The consignee is an agent, although often called factor or commission merchant. The principal retains title absolutely. He may retake the goods from his agent at any time, or the proceeds thereof if they can be traced, as against the creditors of his agent or a trustee in bankruptcy,59 and may institute an action on the contract made by the agent in disposing of the goods. 

He also assumes the risk of loss or destruction incident to ownership. The agent is a custodian, and may return the goods at any time. He is authorized to sell the goods for his principal, either in his own or in his

CHAPTER XVI  -Part 1. Kinds of Agency Sec. 591. Agency Defined. Agency is a relationship created by an express or implied contract, or by law, in which one party called the principal delegates the transaction of some lawful business to another. This relationship involves three parties, a principal, an agent, and a third party. Agents and servants are both employees of the principal, but with the following distinction: (1) An agent is a person who has authority to transact business for his principal in such a way as to bring his principal into contractual relations with third parties. It is this characteristic which distinguishes the relation of principal and agent from that of master and servant. (2) A servant is person who is employed to execute the commands of his master, and who is subject to his master's direction and control. A servant may be delegated with authority to negotiate a contract, just as an agent may render acts of service, and if so the two relationships are fundamentally interchangeable. 

Sec. 592 Gratuitous Agency. A person may act gra tuitously as the agent of another. This relationship is characterized by the absence of the usual contract between the principal and the agent, but it is not without legal responsibility. As observed by the Supreme Court of the United States very early in its history, while one person may not be compelled to render a gratuitous service for another, he is legally bound to comply with his instructions if he does.¹ The modern law also imposes legal responsibility upon a gratuitous agent who fails to act, if he knows or has reason to know that his principal will suffer irreparable injury by reason of such failure. The illustrations afforded by the Restatement of the Law are failure of a gratuitous agent to submit what would have been the successful bid for the purchase 1 Walker v. Smith, 4 U. S. 389 (1804). 426

of certain property, which is not discovered until it is too late for the principal to act, or failure to pay a premium due on a policy of insurance, causing the policy to lapse.2 3 

Sec. 593. Independent Contractor. An independent contractor is neither an agent nor a servant. He is a person who contracts to do work for another, and who has the exclusive control of the manner in which it is done. Most building and construction projects are conducted under an arrangement of this sort. A contractor is usually paid a lump sum, but he may be paid on a "cost-plus" or "time and equipment," or "time and material" basis. Whatever the method of payment, if he has a right to control the manner of accomplishing the result, his status is that of an independent contractor. 

It has been suggested, in claims arising under the Workmen's Compensation Act, that "neither the compensation authorities nor the courts should be solicitous to put a claimant in the position of an independent contractor when a reasonable view of the evidence warrants a finding that he was an employee." 994 

McCall v. Bell Telephone Co., 79 Pa. Superior Ct. 505 (1922).

Plaintiff was a teamster who did hauling of various kinds for the defendant and others at a per diem rate which covered his own services as well as the use of his team and other equipment. He had been employed by the defendant from time to time to haul telephone poles from its ware room to points along its lines and to help put them in place. This work was done under the direction of defendant's foreman, who told him what to do from day to day. He was paid for each day or fraction thereof. He was not carried on the pay roll, but rendered his bills at the end of each week. He sustained a fracture of the leg while skidding poles preparatory to loading them on his wagon, and filed a claim petition under the Workmen's Compensation Act. In sustaining the claim, it was said by GAWTHROP, J. "Defendant's foreman had full control over the extent, character and manner of service rendered by plaintiff. The fact that plaintiff was not carried on defendant's pay roll is without significance." 

2 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 278, illus. 1 and 2. 

3 Brooks v. Buckley & Banks, 291

Pa. 1 (1927). 

Mooney v. Weidner, 102 Pa. Superior Ct. 411 (1981).

Sec. 594. Principal and Agent. (1) Principal: Any person who is competent to act in his own right may delegate another to act for him. Incapacity may be natural, as in the case of infants, or legal, as in the case of a judicial finding of insanity. (2) Agent: Less competence is required of an agent, inasmuch as he is not the person to be bound. He may be any person of sound mind, capable of conducting the negotiations. Many persons are competent to negotiate a contract for another, when they could not bind themselves. Infants, slaves or aliens may act as agents, but not imbeciles or infants of tender years.

Sec. 595. Methods of Formation. Agency may be established by (1) express contract, (2) implied contract, (3) ratification, (4) necessity, (5) estoppel, and (6) by operation of law. The burden of proving such an agency, as well as the authority of an agent, is upon him. who asserts it.5

Sec. 596. Express Contract. An express contract of agency may be established by written or parol authority. 

Where an agent is authorized to enter into a contract under seal, the authority itself should be under seal, unless the contract is executed in the presence of and by the direction of the principal. As observed by the 

Chief Justice more than a century ago, "I do not see how the stream can rise higher than its source." Where, however, a contract under seal is not an instrument requiring a seal to insure its validity, the seal may be treated as surplusage and the agreement sustained as one within the power of an agent acting without sealed authority. Blackstone declared that a deed should be under seal, but this requirement was abolished in 1909, although the seal is customarily employed. 

Pore v. Duke, 303 Pa. 528 (1931). 

Cooper v. Rankin, 5 Binn. 613 (1813). 

Dick v. McWilliams, 291 Pa. 165 (1927). 

8 2 Black. Com. 305.

Act of April 1, 1909, P. L. 91. 

and April 30, 1925, P. L. 404, 21 PS 10.

Sec. 597.

Statute of Frauds. It was observed in the chapter on the Statute of Frauds, that an agent may not, without written authority, enter into a number of contracts pertaining to real estate, including an agreement to sell the real estate of his principal.10 Where such authority is required, a subsequent ratification is effective only when it is evidenced in the same way.¹¹ A contract for the sale of real estate, signed by an agent not having written authority, may be ratified by his principal in writing, provided the other party has not repudiated the agreement prior to the ratification.¹2 11 

Sec. 598. Testimony of Agent. An agent's authority may be established by his testimony.13 He is a competent witness, and may testify as to the circumstances surrounding a particular transaction between him and his principal, leaving the fact of agency, as well as the authority of the agent, to be determined by the court.¹4 14 

Isaac v. Donegal & Conoy Mutual Fire Ins. Co., 301 Pa. 351 

(1930). An insurance company authorized an appraiser to adjust a loss, and sought to prove the agency through the testimony of the agent. The trial court sustained an objection to the admission of this evidence. KEPHART, J. "The rule excludes an agent's declarations to prove agency when offered by a third person, but authority may be shown by the agent's own testimony. The authority of an agent can always be proven by the agent himself; he is always a competent witness for his principal. The witness may state the facts from which his right to act for his principal in a given matter may appear." 

Sec. 599. Declarations of Agent. As noted above, declarations of an agent are not admissible in evidence when offered by the person to whom they are alleged to have been made, but this rule is subject to the exceptions disclosed in the following case. 

Campbell v. G. C. Murphy Co., 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 342 (1936).

Plaintiff alleged and the jury found that she contracted food 

10 Humphrey v. Brown, 291 Pa. 53 (1927). 11 Mott (1927). v. Kaldes, 288 Pa. 264 

12 McClintock v. South Penn Oil Co., 146 Pa. 144 (1891). 

13 Hileman V. Falck, 263 Pa. 351 (1919).

Assn., 252 Pa. 587 (1916).

poisoning from eating unwholesome chicken salad sandwiches in the restaurant of defendant's store. Her daughter, who had visited the store, testified that a Miss Calvin, in charge of personnel, admitted that two other girls had been made sick from eating chicken salad sandwiches. An objection to this testimony was overruled. Defendant appealed. STADTFELD, J. "In order to warrant the proof of admissions by an agent, one or more of the following facts must exist: It must appear that the agent was specifically authorized to make them; or his powers must have been such as to constitute him the general representative of the principal, having the management of the entire business; or the admissions must have formed part of the consideration of a contract; or, if they are non-contractual they must have been part of the res gestae.' . . . The situation discloses an entire lack of authority conferred upon Miss Calvin to make admissions binding upon the defendant company as to other persons who became ill from eating chicken salad sandwiches." 

Sec. 600. Implied Agency. Agency may be implied.

The difference between an express agency and an implied agency, is in the method of proof. In the latter, the relation is implied from the words and conduct of the parties and the circumstances of the particular case. 

The fact that a person has acted as an agent for another in previous transactions is evidence tending to prove agency to act in similar transactions. 

Ubaldini v. C. I. T. Corp., 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 428 (1936). 

Ubaldini purchased a Nash sedan from a motor company, turning in an old car and giving a negotiable note for the balance, $500 of which was payable two weeks later. The dealer transferred the note to the C. I. T. Corporation. On the due date Ubaldini paid the $500 to the motor company without the production of the note. 

Some difficulty arose between the motor company and the finance company, as the result of which the motor company did not pay over the amount to the finance company. The latter entered judgment against Ubaldini for the full amount of the note. PARKER, J. "For a period of three years the C. I. T. Corporation had been financing installment sales to customers of the motor company under circumstances identical with that under which Ubaldini dealt with the parties and during that time on an average of 10 or 15 times a week installments had been paid by customers, makers of notes, to the motor company for account of the finance company. 

Not only did the finance company recognize such payments and not disavow the agency, but it was party to the manner in which

receipts were given. With its knowledge receipts were made out in triplicate, one of which was delivered to it and to show that it had actually received the proceeds as between principal and agent it initialed the receipt retained by the motor company. This in our opinion was sufficient to sustain a finding by the jury that the motor company was the implied agent of the C. I. T. Corporation to receive payment of the note in question." Sec. 601. Ratification. A century ago it was said by 

TINDALL, C. J., in a leading English case: "That an act done for another, by a person not assuming to act for himself, but for such other person, though without any precedent authority whatever, becomes the act of the principal, if subsequently ratified by him, is the known and well established rule of law."15 Such approval may be established by a course of action, by a failure to repudiate, by the bringing of a suit as though the act were authorized, or by receiving the proceeds of the transaction. Mere silence under some circumstances is cogent evidence of approval.16 If the principal is ignorant of material facts involved in the transaction when ratified, he may avoid the affirmance, unless he manifests an intention to be bound, as, for example, knowing that he does not possess such knowledge and not caring to make further inquiry." It is well established that when one adopts a contract entered into without his authority, he must adopt it as a whole; he may not ratify the beneficial part and reject the remainder.18 

Dempsey v. Chambers, 154 Mass. 330 (1891). McCollock took it upon himself to deliver defendant's coal as his servant. While unloading the coal he negligently broke a plate glass window. Defendant ratified the delivery of the coal. Plaintiff contended that defendant was thereupon liable for the loss of the window. 

HOLMES, J. "We have found hardly anything in the books dealing with the precise case, but we are of opinion that consistency with the whole course of authority requires us to hold that the defendant's ratification of the employment established the relation of master and servant from the beginning, with all its incidents, including the anomalous liability for his negligent acts."
