Sec. 602. Necessity. The principle has been affirmed, in Pennsylvania, that one will be bound by the acts of a self-constituted agent where his own neglect or the act of God has rendered those acts necessary for his selfpreservation.19 It has also been affirmed, that the emergency of an accident, or an unusual condition which requires prompt action, may invest the representative of an employer, highest in authority, with power to do such things as are reasonable to meet the emergency. 

Jones v. Pennsylvania Coal & Coke Co., 255 Pa. 339 (1917).

MESTREZAT, J. "Carroll was the engineer at the substation, a short distance from the boiler house. After lightning had struck the high-tension wire, he attempted to use the telephone wire which was highly charged by contact with the power wire and received a severe shock. As soon as he recovered from the shock, he went to the boiler house where he discovered Acken's body lying on the floor near the telephone box. He recognized the necessity for immediate medical assistance, possibly from the effects of a like shock received by himself. His experience told him that it would be dangerous to use the telephone in attempting to communicate with the officers of the defendant company or in calling medical assistance for Acken. He then did the only thing he could do, sent a messenger to summon a physician. Can it be doubted that had the president or any other high official of the defendant company, under the circumstances and with Carroll's knowledge of what had occurred, entered the power house and found the body of the company's engineer, as Carroll did, he would not have summoned a physician?" 

Sec. 603. Operation of Law. Agency may result from the operation of the law under a number of circumstances. First, it has been observed that title to pledged property remains with the pledgor. The pledgee in possession, however, has a special interest in the property, which he may exercise on behalf of the pledgor, upon default of the obligation for which the pledge is made. 

Second, it will be observed in the discussion of liens, that repairmen, commission merchants, factors, common carriers, warehousemen, innkeepers, hotelkeepers, and boarding house proprietors may, in certain circum- 

19 Sherman's Estate, 6 Pa. C. C. 225 (1888).

stances, sell goods in their possession, on behalf of the legal owner, to secure their claims. Third, it has been observed that a wife is the agent of her husband, as a matter of law, for the purchase of necessaries which the husband wrongfully fails or neglects to provide. It should be noted that marriage alone does not otherwise constitute the husband or wife the agent of each other. 

Moyer v. Norristown-Penn Trust Co., 296 Pa. 26 (1929). Plaintiff was the owner of 31 bonds, each of the par value of $80, which she kept in a safety deposit box maintained by her husband as a family box to which he had access. The bonds were called for payment in 1923, but the plaintiff did not present them for redemption. In the fall of 1924 her husband presented them for payment, received a check to her order, endorsed her name, credited the same to his account, and checked it out as his own. This was an action against the trustee-bank for the value of the bonds. WALLING, J. "The marriage relation does not constitute the husband an agent for the wife or authorize him to sign her name to obligations relating to her separate estate. One who asserts an agency must prove the authority of the agent to do the act in question. Here the defense fails; for plaintiff positively denies that her husband had any authority, express or otherwise, to dispose of her bonds or to sign her name to the check received therefor and there is no sufficient evidence to the contrary." 

Sec. 604. Estoppel. An agency, as well as the authority of an agent, may be established on grounds of estoppel. Such an agency, however, is presumed rather than · actual. 

Reel v. Adams Express Co., 27 Pa. Superior Ct. 77 (1905). Plaintiff delivered a shipment of fur garments to a person wearing a cap bearing defendant's name, and in a wagon marked with defendant's name, but who proved to be an imposter. In holding the defendant liable, it was said by SMITH, J. "The possibility of a fraudulent use of its name was as apparent to the defendant as to the shipper. By not employing some more certain indicia or evidence of the authority of its drivers, to be brought to the notice of shippers, the defendant led the public to believe that goods might properly be delivered for transportation over its lines to persons whose employment was to be inferred from their uniforms, and its name on wagons and caps. Since a jury may draw this inference, it may well be drawn by a shipper."

Part 2. Authority of Agents 

Sec. 605. Duty to Ascertain. "It is a familiar rule that one dealing with an agent is bound to ascertain the extent of the agent's authority, which is, prima facie, limited to the powers expressly granted, or arising by implication from the character of the grant." 20 He "may not trust to a mere presumption of authority, or to any mere assumption of authority by the agent; but must trace the authority to its source if he would be protected."" This is probably the most important principle in the law of agency. 

Sloan v. Brown, 228 Pa. 495 (1910). Plaintiff authorized his agent, Ward, to sell 261,112 shares of stock at fifty cents per share or better. Ward was unable to obtain that price, and finally sold the stock to defendants for ten cents per share. Defendants relied on the agent's power of attorney to transfer the stock, but made no other inquiry as to the agent's authority. Plaintiff filed a bill in equity to recover the stock. POTTER, J. "The defendants here, having dealt with Ward as an agent, and not as a principal, were bound to inquire into the nature and extent of his authority. 

They did so to a limited extent, and what they admittedly learned, was quite sufficient to put them upon notice of the limitations upon that authority. We are of opinion that under the established rule of law, as applied to the facts of this case, plaintiff is entitled to the relief for which he prays, and that he should have a decree for the restoration of the 261,112 shares of stock, upon the repayment of the amount paid to Ward therefor, with interest." ..

Sec. 606. Kinds of Authority. The authority of an agent may be (1) express, (2) implied, or (3) apparent, or (4) it may arise by necessity, or (5) by ratification, or (6) it may be established on grounds of estoppel. 

Sec. 607. Express Authority. Express authority may be authorized orally or in writing, or even by conduct which leads an agent to believe that his principal desires him to act on the principal's account.22 An authority in writing must be strictly pursued. Letters of 

20 Culbertson v. Cook, 308 Pa. 557 (1932). 

21 Interstate Securities Co. v. Third 

National Bank, 231 Pa. 422 (1911). 

22 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 26.

attorney, especially, are subject to a strict interpretation, and are never extended beyond the authority given in express terms or whatever is necessary and proper to carry into effect that which is expressed.23 

Lewis v. Lewis, 203 Pa. 194 (1902). Plaintiff decided to live apart from his wife, but in discharge of his marital obligations, gave her a power of attorney to dispose of his property for the support and maintenance of herself and children, and also power To dispose of certain real estate. In the exercise of this power she transferred the property to her son, whereupon plaintiff filed a bill in equity to have the conveyance set aside. In granting this relief, it was said by POTTER, J. "In this case Mrs. Lewis undertook to sell her husband's real estate, not for any consideration paid to her in cash at the time of the conveyance, but for past payments of money made to her in small amounts by her son, and used by. her for her own purposes. The conveyance based upon this indebtedness, coupled with an agreement for her future support, was not a lawful execution of the power."

Sec. 608. Limit of Express Authority. As a general legal proposition, the authority conferred on an agent to make a contract, does not carry with it authority to alter its terms, or waive its conditions, or otherwise terminate or discharge it. In the application of this principle, it has been held that a power of attorney authorizing an agent to demand and receive moneys payable to his principal, to institute and prosecute to judgment actions at law necessary for their collection, to give such acquittances and discharges as might be necessary and proper, and to compromise matters in dispute, did not authorize the agent to postpone the lien of a mortgage.24 

Severance v. Heyl & Patterson, Inc., 123 Pa. Superior Ct. 553 (1936). The defendant corporation entered into a lease under seal which contained the following recital: "The Board of Directors of Lessee has by resolution duly adopted directed the execution and delivery of these presents." Under its terms the corporation had a right to terminate liability by surrender of the premises on or before April 30, 1931. Plaintiff alleged, and the jury found, that Mr. Heyl, vice president of the defendant company, entered 

23 Campbell v. Foster Home Assn., 163 Pa. 609 (1894). 

24 Note 20 supra.

into an oral agreement which required one year's notice in advance of an intention to terminate the lease. In deciding that the exercise of such authority was not sustained by the evidence, it was said by PARKER, J. "An officer of a corporation certainly has no power merely by virtue of his office to alter the provisions of a formal agreement under seal made by authority of and for the benefit of the corporation, and no specific authority has been shown. In addition we search the record in vain for a single item of evidence tending to show that Heyl had apparent authority to vary the terms of a written contract entered into by authority of the board of directors." 

Sec. 609. Implied Authority. Implied, or incidental authority, may be defined as authority to perform those supplementary acts which are necessary to accomplish the main objective, or which are usual in transactions of like character. "Every general power necessarily implies the grant of every matter necessary to its complete execution." 25 In the absence of specific instructions, the authority to buy or sell includes authority to agree upon the terms, to make usual representations and warranties, to execute instruments in the usual form, to pay or receive the price, and to part with or receive possession of the subject-matter." "It is undeniable that an agent to whom merchandise has been intrusted, with authority to sell and deliver it, is authorized to receive the price; otherwise the fraud on the purchaser would run into cruelty."27 

Sec. 610. Mortgage Obligations. It has been held many times that the authority of an agent to receive payment of interest due on a mortgage does not give him authority to receive payment of the principal. If it can be shown that an agent has been employed to make investments in mortgages for the same employer on a number of occasions, and collected both interest and principal over a period of years which were accepted by the principal without objection, such proof would be sufficient to show that the agent had authority to collect 

Peck v. Harriott, 6 S. & R. 146 (1820). 

20 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 56. 

27 Seiple (1858). 

V. Irwin, 30 Pa. 513

the principal debt on a particular occasion,28 but the circumstances are unusual and the proof difficult to obtain. 

Judith v. Dicola, 317 Pa. 353 (1935). Plaintiff, holder of a bond and mortgage, entered judgment on the bond against defendants, the mortgagors, for $3,500, the full amount of the bond. The transaction was arranged by Hetrick, an attorney, at the instance of the defendants. Plaintiff authorized Hetrick to collect the interest, but nothing was said as to his collecting the principal. 

Hetrick instructed defendants to make periodic reductions in the amount of the mortgage, and to make all payments, principal and interest, at his office. For over eight years defendants paid him in accordance with these instructions, paying $3,000 in reduction of the principal sum, and all interest due. During all this time 

Hetrick sent to plaintiff his own checks for the amount of the interest, but never informed her in any way of his collections of principal. He then became involved in financial difficulties, and for the first time plaintiff and defendants learned of his embezzlements. DREW, J. "Although the loss was caused by the fault of neither plaintiff nor defendants, it must be borne by one side or the other, and the law is settled beyond question that, under circumstances such as were here present, an attorney authorized to receive payments of interest on a mortgage has thereby no authority, real or apparent, to receive payments of principal." 

Sec. 611. Limit of Implied Authority. The exercise of incidental authority has been narrowly circumscribed by the courts, and the tendency has been to protect the principal. As a general proposition, an agent has no authority to borrow money, or to execute evidences of debt, or negotiable paper, unless such authority is expressly conferred upon him, or is incident to the acts he is expressly delegated to perform. The decided cases usually disclose negations of what is alleged to be incidental authority. An agent who is employed to solicit and send in orders for goods, and to collect outstanding accounts, has no authority to release the debtor and substitute his successor in the business.29 It is ordinarily within the scope of the authority of an attorney to bind his client for the printing of paper-books on an appeal, 28 Dobbs V. Zink, 290 Pa. 243 (1927). 

20 Ludwig v. Gorsuch, 154 Pa. 413 (1893). 29

but a verdict for the client has been sustained where the printer had notice that the attorney prosecuted an appeal on his own responsibility.30

Graham v. U. S. Savings Institute, 46 Missouri 186 (1870). An agent was authorized to make certain collections for his principal. 

He received two checks, both payable to the order of his principal, to which he indorsed his principal's name and presented them for payment at the bank on which they were drawn. He failed to remit the money to his principal. The principal, on learning these facts, brought suit against the bank. In deciding for the principal, it was said by CURRIER, J. "The indorsement of the checks was no necessary incident of the collection of the accounts." 

Sec. 612. Apparent Authority. Apparent authority has been defined to be, "such authority as a reasonably prudent man, using diligence and discretion, in view of the principal's conduct, would naturally suppose the agent to possess. The apparent authority of an agent which will be sufficient to bind the principal for acts done thereunder is such authority as he appears to have by reason of the actual authority which he has." Authority to manage a business includes authority to make contracts which are incidental to the business, to procure equipment and supplies, to make reasonable repairs, to employ and discharge employees, and to direct the ordinary operations of the business. The apparent authority of an agent may also be established by the customs and usages of the business in which an agent is engaged.33 

Brooke v. N. Y., L. E. & W. R. R. Co., 108 Pa. 529 (1885). A freight agent fraudulently issued a negotiable bill of lading for goods which had not been received. It came into the hands of an innocent purchaser for value. STERRETT, J. "It is conceded in this case that the company did not authorize the issuance of bills of lading without receipt of the goods, but it put Weiss in its place to do that class of acts, and it should be answerable for the manner in which he conducted himself within the range of his agency. 

Public policy, as well as the ultimate good of corporations themselves, requires that this should be the rule."

Pa. Superior Ct. 63 (1924).

Winter v. Iron City Stamping Co., 51 Pa. Superior Ct. 11 (1912). 

32 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 73.

Sec. 613. Secret Instructions. "Private instructions to an agent may not empower him to act within the ordinary scope of duties entrusted to him, but the public or an interested person is not always bound by private instructions."84 If such limitation of authority is not known to others, the principal will be bound by the acts of the agent which are performed in the usual and customary mode of conducting it.35 Such situations usually arise where a general agent has been appointed to manage a business. This principle is illustrated in the Brooke case, supra, but more commonly in routine transactions more familiar to the public. What if the manager of a local store, whose instructions are not to employ colored persons, hires a negro janitor, or who, contrary to his instructions, purchases his local supplies on credit? 

Williams v. Getty, 31 Pa. 461 (1858). THOMPSON, J. "If the principal holds out the agent to the world, as a general agent in the transaction of his business, any contract made by him, within the scope of that business, will bind the principal; although there may be, as between the principal and agent, a restriction upon the general authority of the latter; if the person with whom the contract is made has no notice of such restriction." 36 

Sec. 614. Course of Dealing. Apparent authority may be established by a course of dealing. When a general practice has been followed, a third party is justified in assuming a continuance of the authority apparently approved. A word of caution is necessary, however, inasmuch as the principal may negative a course of dealing by an express contract. 

Herman Nelson Corp. v. Welty, 313 Pa. 123 (1983). Plaintiff employed Rinkenberger as its sales agent in western Pennsylvania, under a contract which provided: "you are given no authority to make collection of accounts." Rinkenberger obtained two orders from the defendant, on which was stated: "All payments shall be direct to the Home Office of the Herman Nelson Corporation, Moline, Illinois." The goods were delivered, and Rinkenberger suggested to the defendant that if the latter would pay both ac- 

34 Faiola v. Calderone, 275 Pa. 303 (1923). 

35 Williams v. Cook, 289 Pa. 207 (1927). 

30 Robertson C. & C. Co. v. Rothey, 106 Pa. Superior Ct. 463 (1932).

counts at that time an allowance of six per cent discount would be made instead of five per cent as provided in the contracts, and that if the checks were made payable to him, he would pay certain costs incurred in the installation of the equipment. He received the money under this arrangement, but never remitted to his principal. Plaintiff instituted this action on the ground that Rinkenberger lacked authority to receive payment. Defendant then produced evidence that Rinkenberger, on a number of occasions, had collected money from other parties to whom he had sold goods, and had remitted to the plaintiff by his own check. DREW, J. "The course of dealing between Rinkenberger and his principal in prior transactions with other parties was powerless to expand his authority beyond the limits imposed in this transaction by the parties themselves in their written contracts." 

Sec. 615. Necessity. The authority of an agent may be extended or varied according to the pressure of the circumstances connected with the business with which an agent is entrusted. A freight agent, for example, has extensive power to dispose of perishable goods received in a damaged condition, which a consignee refuses to accept, in such manner as he considers to the best advantage of the company, and may bind his principal by an agreement with the consignee that if the latter will pay the freight due and sell the goods at the best price he can obtain, the company will pay any loss sustained by reason of the condition of the shipment. For the same reason, a shipmaster may buy necessaries on the owner's credit, or sell the cargo, or even the vessel, in case of an emergency. 37 Sec. 616. Ratification. The principal may ratify an act not previously authorized. Otherwise, it is his duty to disavow an unauthorized act within a reasonable time after he has notice of it.38 If he remains silent, with full knowledge of the facts and without sufficient excuse, he makes the act his own. In Smuckler v. Di Napoli,39 an agent secured an order for five barrels of flour, with the understanding that if the flour was satisfactory the 

37 Short v. Del. & Hudson Co., 41 

Pa. Superior Ct. 141 (1909). 

38 Birkle v. Coleman, 50 Pa. Superior Ct. 105 (1912). 

3962 Pa. Superior Ct. 570 (1916).

order would be for one hundred barrels. It was held that the act of the principal, in forwarding the sample order with full knowledge of this condition, was a ratification of the entire agreement. We have already observed that if a principal ratifies an unauthorized act he must accept it in its entirety. Thus, where an agent obtains possession of property by making a stipulation which he is not authorized to make, the principal is required to either return the property or be subject to the condition upon which it was parted with.40 

Sec. 617. Estoppel. The authority of an agent may be established on grounds of estoppel. There are many types of conduct which would accomplish that result. 

Any representation on the part of a principal that an act was in fact done on his account, or was ratified by him, or that the act of an impersonator was done by him, will operate as an estoppel if it is reasonably calculated to mislead another. An estoppel more frequently arises whenever the fraudulent conduct of an agent results in a loss which must be borne by either the principal or by the third party. As it is commonly expressed, where one of two innocent persons must suffer from the fraud of a third, he who makes possible the commission of the fraud must bear it." "This principle has never been carried by the courts to the absurd lengths to which its literal interpretation would logically lead, though it is often oracularly quoted as though it should be taken literally and applied indiscriminately as the touchstone of responsibility wherever fraud appears."42 

Pore v. Duke, 303 Pa. 528 (1931). Tracy, a real estate agent, negotiated the purchase of a house and lot for defendants. They needed $2,000 to complete the purchase, which Tracy secured for them by a loan on the property. This he negotiated through plaintiff's attorney. Defendants paid both principal and interest to 

Tracy. Tracy paid the interest to plaintiff's attorney as it fell due, but absconded with the principal. WALLING, J. "This is a 

40 Mundorff v. Wickersham, 63 Pa. 

87 (1869). 

41 Frolo v. Armstrong, 277 Pa. 18 (1923). 

42 Fifth Street B. & L. Assn. V. 

Kornfeld, 315 Pa. 406 (1934).

hard case, but the question of who must bear the loss is not difficult of solution. Plaintiff never knew Tracy and never constituted him her agent, directly or indirectly. It is the duty of one paying a mortgage or other obligation to ascertain that he is paying the right party. . . He whose agent the defaulter is must bear the loss." 

Part 3. Authority of Particular Agents Sec. 618. Kinds of Agents. The authority of an agent is to be determined in part by the nature of the undertaking in which the agent is engaged. Agents may be classified on a functional basis as (1) special, (2) general, (3) corporate, and (4) professional. Professional agents include such persons as factors, brokers, auctioneers, cashiers, shipmasters, attorneys, and the like.

Sec. 619. Special Agent. A special agent is a per son who is authorized to conduct a single transaction or a series of transactions not involving a continuity of service. He is employed to do one specific act or certain specific acts, with only such powers as are indispensable to a proper execution of the grant. A special agent, in particular, must adhere strictly to his instructions.43 It has been said that the acts of such an agent outside of his authority do not bind the principal,** and that whoever deals with an agent constituted for a special purpose does so at his peril when the agent passes the precise limits of his authority.45 

43 Union Trust Co. v. Means, 201 Pa. 

374 (1902). 

44 Lewis v. Matias, 300 Pa. 238 (1930). 

Hoffman v. Marano, 71 Pa. Superior Ct. 26' (1918). Defendant went to a public sale for the purpose of buying a property in the Italian section of the city. He understood very little English. 

At the sale he authorized a real estate broker to bid for him, subject, however, to a limit of $12,000. The broker made some bids and dropped out. The bidding continued and shortly after the broker, without acquainting the defendant with the last bid, said: "If you want the property, don't lose it for another hundred." Defendant agreed, but when he was about to sign the clerk's sale bid he was informed by the broker that his bid was 

45 Van Pelt v. Spotz, 92 Pa. Superior Ct. 213 (1927).

$14,000. He promptly repudiated the transaction and the property was immediately put up for resale. Plaintiff brought suit for the difference between $14,000 and the resale price, but lost in the court below. This action was affirmed on appeal. 

Sec. 620. General Agent. A general agent is a person who is authorized to conduct a series of transactions involving a continuity of service. He has authority to do any act on behalf of his principal which is usual and necessary in the ordinary course of the business. The fact that he occupies the position of general agent implies, without further proof, his authority to do anything that pertains to the ordinary business of his principal." 

A general agent, however, does not have unqualified authority. The "implied power of any agent, however general, must be limited to such acts as are proper for an agent to do, and cannot extend to acts clearly adverse to the interest of the principal."47 

Sec. 621. Authority to Prosecute. "Generally the duty of superintendence does not carry with it the duty to arrest or prosecute. The inference of authority to do either does not arise from the mere fact of the agency. 

The authority may be implied when the arrest is made by the agent in the absence of the principal for the protection of property that is in danger, or in some cases it has been inferred when the arrest was to recover the property back, or where the crime was at the time being perpetrated. But where the act is done for the punishment of the supposed criminal, or for the vindication of the law, it is not the act of the principal and does not subject him to liability."48 The following is a borderline case. 

Groda v. American Stores Co., 315 Pa. 484 (1934). Plaintiff,

Groda, was employed as meat manager by the American Stores 

Company at Hummelstown. On a Saturday evening when he and another employee left the store to deposit the day's receipts at a bank across the street, they were surrounded by armed men 

46 Long v. Lehigh Coal & Nav. Co., 292 Pa. 164 (1928). 

47 Culbertson v. Cook, 308 Pa. 557 (1932). 

48 Markley v. Snow, 207 Pa. 447 (1904).

and taken into the country several miles away, where the American Stores' money was taken from them. On the following 

Tuesday, Ludwig, manager of the store, filed an information charging Groda and the other employee with the larceny of the money. The real perpetrators of the robbery were subsequently apprehended, and Groda then sued the American Stores Company, alleging that Ludwig had acted with the authority of the defendant in instituting the criminal action against him. The latter denied that Ludwig acted as its agent or within the scope of his authority. MAXEY, J. "There was sufficient evidence to go to the jury on the question of whether or not the act of Ludwig in making these informations was the act of the defendant." 

Sec. 622. Sub-Agents. The principal may authorize his agent to appoint another agent, or to employ subagents. Authority to employ sub-agents may be inferred under many circumstances, as where it is impracticable or impossible for the immediate agent to perform the duties entrusted to him, or where it is customary, or where some contingency makes it necessary for the protection of the interests of the principal. As a general rule, however, an agent may not delegate his authority to perform those duties which require discretion, personal confidence, or skill.40 50 

Sec. 623. Corporate Agents. The board of directors of a corporation "is the central power which authorizes the executive agents of the corporation to transact business for it, enter into contracts and embark upon new adventures.' Agents derive their authority from the board, and it would therefore be prudent for third par ties to ascertain that fact under all circumstances. It has been held, however, that when an officer has been allowed to manage the affairs of a corporation, in the usual course of its business, his authority to represent it may be implied from the manner in which he has been permitted by the directors to transact its business." And when a corporation entrusts an agent with the supervision and management of a particular branch of its 

40 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 78-80. 

50 Severance v. Heyl & Patterson, 123 Pa. Superior Ct. 533 (1936), 51 Robertson C. & C. Co. v. Rothey. 

106 Pa. Superior Ct. 403 (1932).

business, it invests him with authority coextensive with the business entrusted to his care. 52 Eastman has said that corporate officers "have, in general, no powers to contract for the corporation."53 This is perhaps a little too strict. The "chief officer, cashier, or secretary, may do many things to bind the company, in the line of his peculiar duties, and in the course of that part of the transaction of the business intrusted to him, and sanetioned by usage. Otherwise there would be no such thing as getting on with business."54 Officers as such, however, do not have any special authority except that which pertains to the ordinary duties of the office they hold, or the ordinary business of the company. 

Kelly, Murray, Inc. v. Lansdowne Bank & Trust Co., 299 Pa. 

236 (1930). As the result of the merger of separate institutions, the Lansdowne Bank & Trust Company became the owner of two buildings which were no longer required for its corporate purpose. 

The board of directors, which met regularly once a month, and a finance committee which convened weekly, authorized negotiations for the sale of these properties. The jury found, on a conflict of evidence, that the president of the company offered to sell one of these properties, and that the plaintiff had accepted the offer and had secured a client able and willing to buy. The board of directors approved the sale of the property to another party. Plaintiff brought this suit to recover a commission. The defendant contended that its president did not have the authority to bind the corporation without the approval of either the board of directors or the finance committee. In sustaining this contention, it was said by SADLER, J., "Parties, who deal with officers of a corporation, are bound to take note and advise themselves of the extent of their powers to act for the company. . . . It cannot be said that the sale of real estate of the value of $250,000 by a bank with a capitalization of $75,000 was an ordinary routine transaction which an officer, the president, had implied power to consummate without consultation with the other regularly constituted managers of the institution." 

Sec. 624. Notice of By-Laws. For many years Penn sylvania followed the rule that third parties were

CHAPTER XVII  Part 1. Liability of Principal to Third Party Sec. 625. Maxims of Responsibility. The liability of a principal for the acts of his agent is expressed in two legal maxims. The first is qui facit per alium facit per se.

He who acts through another acts for himself. 

The second is respondeat superior. Let the master answer for the wrongful acts of his servant. 

Sec. 626. Unauthorized Contracts. The circumstances under which an agent is authorized to contract on behalf of his principal, are analyzed in the preceding chapter. 

In order to charge a principal on a contract made by an agent, it is encumbent upon the third party to show, in some manner, that the agent was authorized to make it.¹ There are many circumstances which will exclude a principal from liability at the instance of a third party. 

He is not liable where he has been expressly excluded from the agreement, or upon sealed covenants as indicated in the preceding chapter, or on negotiable instruments unless named therein, and he may avoid liability where the third party knows that the authority of the agent is prescribed in writing, if there is any departure therefrom, even though the contract as made by the agent would otherwise have been sustained. 

Sec. 627. Knowledge Acquired by Agent. The liability of a principal to a third party is frequently governed by whatever knowledge is acquired by his agent in the course of his employment. Subject to well defined exceptions, such knowledge will be imputed to the principal. As expressed in a leading English case more than a century ago, "the safety of the public forbids a person 2 

1 American Mailing Device Corp. v. 

Widener, 260 Pa. 375 (1918). 

2 Knowledge acquired by an agent whose interests are antagonistic to those of his principal (First Nat. 

Bank of Bangor v. Bangor Trust Co., 297 Pa. 115 (1927); and knowledge acquired by an agent in independent transactions: Byrne v. Dennis, 308 Pa. 

72 (1931).

447

to deny knowledge while he is so dealing as to keep him. self ignorant, or so as that he may keep himself ignorant, and yet all the while let his agent know, and himself, perhaps, profit by that knowledge." 993 

Sec. 628. Undisclosed Principal. Not infrequently, the identity of a principal is not disclosed. His liability, however, is the same as that of a disclosed principal if his identity is subsequently ascertained.* 

Hubbard v. Tenbrook, 124 Pa. 291 (1889). P employed A to conduct a grocery business in A's name, but with the property and for the benefit of P. There was a secret agreement between them that A should not bind P by any purchases on credit. T, a creditor, discovered the agency and brought suit against P. 

MITCHELL, J. "A man conducting an apparently prosperous business obtains credit thereby, and his creditors have a right to suppose that his profits go into his assets for their protection in case of a pinch or an unfavorable turn in the business. To allow an undisclosed principal to absorb the profits, and then when the pinch comes, to escape responsibility on the ground of orders to his agent not to buy on credit, would be a plain fraud on the public." 

Sec. 629. Doctrine of Election. According to the weight of authority in other states, and as expressed in the Restatement of the Law, if the third party brings suit on a contract and obtains a judgment against the agent, with knowledge of the identity of the principal, the latter is discharged from liability on the contract, but otherwise if the judgment is obtained without knowledge of the identity of the principal. This doctrine does not appear to have been recognized in Pennsylvania, although the third party is entitled to but one satisfaction. 5 

Beymer v. Bonsall, 79 Pa. 298 (1875). Bonsall purchased 5,000 barrels of crude oil from Wagner and Leech, and paid the purchase price. Wagner and Leech failed to make delivery. He brought suit and recovered a judgment against them, but failed to collect anything on the judgment. During this proceeding he 

3 Kennedy v. Green, 40 Eng. Rep. 266 (1834). 

McCracken v. Hamburger, 139 Pa. 326 (1890). 

Agency, A. L. I., sec. 210.

learned that Wagner and Leech were agents, and that the real principal was Beymer. He then instituted a second action against 

Beymer. Beymer protested that Bonsall had elected his remedy by suing the agents, and could not thereafter obtain a judgment against the principal. In overruling this contention, it was said 

PER CURIAM, ". . . the principal has no right to compel the creditor to elect his action, or to discharge either himself or his agent, but can defend his agent only by making satisfaction for him." 

Sec. 630. Torts of Agents. The liability of the prin cipal for the torts of his agent is very much the same as the liability of the master for the torts of his servant. 

A principal is liable for those acts which result from his direction, and for the negligence of an agent who is acting within the scope of his authority. He is also liable for the failure of his agent to act, where the principal is under a duty to third persons, and when he ratifies an act causing injury to third persons. The torts in general for which a principal may be liable are negligence, trespass, conversion, libel and slander, malicious prosecution, false imprisonment, fraudulent representation, and fraudulent acts. If goods are obtained through the false representation of an agent, the third party has a right to rescind the contract and take the goods from the principal, whether the agent had authority to make the representations or not." 

McClung v. Dearborne, 134 Pa. 396 (1890). Because of the failure of payments, defendant's employees forcibly removed an organ from plaintiff's home which had been placed there under a bailment lease. Defendant had instructed his men not to commit an assault or battery, and not to break the law. The lower court held that these instructions were sufficient to exempt him from liability. In deciding otherwise, it was said by WILLIAMS, J., "Servants and employees are often without the means to respond in damages for the injuries they may inflict on others by the ignorant, negligent, or wanton manner in which they conduct the business of their employer. . . The defendant was bound not only to give proper instructions to his servants when sending them on such an errand, but he was bound to see that his instructions were obeyed." 

Meyerhoff v. Daniels, 173 Pa. 555 (1896).

Sec. 631. Unauthorized Acts. The liability of the principal does not extend to injuries resulting from the performance of unauthorized acts by his agent. 

Guille v. Campbell, 200 Pa. 119 (1901). Defendant's employee was dragging bales of cotton from a sidewalk into a warehouse. 

He waved a hook which he was using at some boys who were playing around the bales as if to frighten them. The hook slipped from his hand and struck one of them in the eye, causing the loss of sight. There was no evidence that the boy was making any attempt to trespass upon the property of the defendant. He was not on the bales, but was standing on the sidewalk nearby. In deciding that this was an unauthorized act of the servant, outside the scope of his employment, for which he himself must be responsible, it was said by PoOTTER, J. "Where an injury is caused by a servant in the use of means fairly adapted to accomplish the purposes of his employment, the master is responsible. This is true, even though the act of the servant is wrongful, or unauthorized. But where the act of the servant does not fairly tend to effectuate the discharge of the duty, for which he is employed, the master is not liable."

Sec. 632. Scope of Employment. It is frequently a matter of difficulty to ascertain whether the tortious act of an agent falls within the scope of the agency. The act must be one which an agent has been employed to perform, within reasonable limits of time and space, and with intent to serve the principal. The incidents usually considered are whether the act is authorized or incidental, whether it is commonly done, the purpose to be accomplished, whether it is within the enterprise, the previous relations of the parties, the similarity in quality to those acts which have been authorized, whether the instrumentality has been furnished by the employer, the extent of departure, and whether it is seriously criminal."

Chikowska v. Prado Garage, 349 Pa. 508 (1944). An employee of a public garage, located in the rear of an apartment house, was directed to drive an automobile belonging to a customer of the garage from the front of the apartment house to the garage in the rear, for storage. On his own initiative and without authorization, he drove the car about seven blocks to his home to get his 

7 Agency, A. L. I., sec. 228.

rubbers and gloves which he contemplated wearing, if he later should be called upon to wash cars at the garage. While enroute from his home back to the garage, he negligently struck the plaintiff, at a point about four blocks from the garage. In deciding that the employer was not liable for this injury, it was said by DREW, J. "Considering plaintiff's case in its most favorable light, it is clear that he fell far short of showing any negligence of defendant. He did show defendant's servant negligently caused the accident, but at the same time he showed the servant was then acting outside the scope of his employment." 

Sec. 633. Torts by Automobile. It is difficult at times to prove the agency of a person driving an automobile or truck. It has been held that "a business truck with defendant's name thereon, displayed as business names usually appear, raises a presumption that it belongs to defendant and also that it is being used in his business."8 

The same applies where a dealer permits an employee to use his dealer's plates, although such presumptions are rebuttable. If the agency or employment is established, the principal may be responsible to a third party for the negligence of the driver, but only within the scope of the agency. So it has been held that-where a nine-year old boy climbed on a delivery truck with the consent of the driver, whose express orders were not to permit any persons to ride thereon, and the boy fell off as it was coming to a stop, due to a sudden jerk, and was run over by the rear wheel, no recovery could be had from the driver's employer.10 Many employers warn the public of such lack of authority by "No Rider" signs affixed to the vehicle. 

Zavodnick v. A. Rose & Son, 297 Pa. 86 (1929). Plaintiff's husband was offered a ride by the driver of defendant's truck. 

He stood on the back platform holding on to a stanchion at the side. One of the wheels struck a depression, caused by the settling of a manhole, and he was killed The jury found for the plaintiff in the sum of $10,000, but the lower court set aside the verdict. Plaintiff appealed. WALLING, J. "The unauthorized act

Pa. 21 (1927).

Ct. 404 (1930). 

10 Hartigan v. Public Ledger, 291 

Pa. 588 (1928).

of the servant in suffering a third party to ride upon a truck cannot impose upon the master the duty of safe carriage or make him liable for an injury the party may suffer from the act of the servant unless it. be wilful or wanton, of which there is here neither allegation nor proof. Both defendant's manager and the driver, called by plaintiff, not only say there was no such authority, but that the driver had been forbidden to take any one on his truck, and there was no other proof on the question." 

Sec. 634. Traveling Salesmen. In many cases, the use of an automobile by a traveling salesman while engaged, directly or indirectly, in furthering the interests of the employer, is a matter of indifference to the employer. As said by the Supreme Court: "To hold a master legally responsible for the act of a servant who is engaged in furthering his master's business and who while doing so negligently uses some instrumentality that carries him from place to place, it must either be proved that that instrumentality, or the use of the instrumentality at the time and place of the act complained of must be of such vital importance in furthering the business of the master that the latter's actual or potential control of it at that time and place may reasonably be inferred."11 Such observations are pertinent when the instrumentality is neither owned, furnished, nor required by the employer. 

Sinclair v. Perma-Maid Co., Inc., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 226 

(1942). Plaintiff was injured by the negligent operation of an automobile driven by a salesman employed by the defendant. The employment of the salesman was for the purpose of demonstrating and selling stainless steel cooking utensils. The salesman was required to furnish an automobile, and to conduct his work under the direction and control of the company or its authorized representative. In concluding that the employer exercised at least "potential control" over the means of transportation, and was therefore liable for the injury, it was said by HIRT, J. "In these respects the present case differs from those relied upon by defendant where the use of the instrumentality was a matter of indifference to the employer, or its use was not reasonably necessary to the furtherance of the business of the master and was not controlled by him." 

11 Wesolowski v. Hancock Ins. Co., 308 Pa. 117 (1932).

Sec. 635. Personal Malice. As a general rule the lia bility of a principal does not extend to acts done to gratify the ill will or malice of his agent, even though the agent at the time is in his employ.¹2 

Berryman v. Pa. R. R. Co., 228 Pa. 621 (1910). An officer in the employ of the defendant began shooting at the plaintiff, who had just alighted from a train, and then ran from the scene. Seven bullets entered plaintiff's body. Plaintiff had given no occasion for offense and was behaving in a quiet, orderly way. He had had no altercation with anyone, and had been guilty of no violation of law. STEWART, J. "In such case, where the servant in the discharge of a lawful duty wilfully and maliciously inflicts injury, he alone is responsible for the consequences."

Sec. 636. Wilful Acts. Generally the principal will not be held for the wilful acts of an agent, as distinguished from acts of negligence, although the passing of time has softened the rigor of the rule that a principal is not liable, in any event, for a wilful, wanton trespass. 

In a case before the Supreme Court in 1871, a railway company was charged with liability for injuries inflicted by a conductor on a boy who was a trespasser on the train. The conductor struck him upon the head with an iron switch turner and knocked him over. A recovery was permitted, not because of the act of the conductor in striking the boy on the head, but because of culpable negligence when the car was driven over his feet.13 In a case decided in 1922, it appears that a boy, six and a half years of age, climbed on a wagon with the permission of the driver. After riding for a short distance the driver lashed him with his whip and with an oath ordered him off. In his fright the lad jumped off and his foot was caught in a chain hanging from the tailboard. As a result, he was dragged a considerable distance and seriously injured. It was held that the act of the driver was so wanton and inconsiderate as to render his employer liable,¹4

Pa. 200 (1911). 

13 Pittsburgh, etc. Ry. Co. v. Donahue, 70 Pa. 119 (1871).

Part 2. Liability of Third Party to Principal 

Sec. 637. Disclosed Agency. The principal may enforce a contract made by his agent, as though he had made it himself, unless he is excluded by the terms of the agreement. Where the third party has received goods or property with knowledge that the agent has exceeded his authority, the principal may, at his election, ratify the transaction, or treat the third party as a trustee, or sue on grounds of unjust enrichment. The third party is not liable to the principal in a common law action on a sealed covenant, or negotiable instrument, unless the principal is named therein, although the principal could take an assignment from his agent, or transfer by indorsement. Broadly stated, an assignment is the substitution of parties as to the same right. 

Under the current Rules of Civil Procedure, an assignee may now institute an action on such an assignment in his own name. 15 

Sec. 638. Undisclosed Agency. The mere fact that an agency is not disclosed to a third party does not of itself amount to fraud. "It is textbook law applied and enforced in a long and unbroken line of cases, that where a simple contract, other than a bill or note, is made by an agent in his own name, his undisclosed principal may maintain an action, or be sued, upon it." If the inducement of the contract is by representation that an agent is not acting for another, and the third party would not have dealt with the principal, he may rescind but not otherwise. Where an agent of a corporation secures an option on property, and does not disclose his principal, the owner of the land may not defend in a bill in equity filed against him in the name of the corporation, on the ground that he had been defrauded in not having this information disclosed.¹7 

Guaranty Safe Deposit & Trust Co. v. Liebold, 207 Pa. 399 (1904). Plaintiff obtained an option on a certain hotel property 

15 Pa. R. C. P. No. 2002. 

16 Lancaster v. Knickerbocker Ice 

Co., 153 Pa. 427 (1893). 

17 Standard Steel Car Co. v. Stamm, 207 Pa. 419 (1904).

in Butler. Shortly thereafter the land increased appreciably in value due to the decision of the Standard Steel Car Company to locate its plant in that community. This was an action for specific performance. Defendant complained that plaintiff had knowledge that the Standard Steel Car Company intended to locate its plant in that locality, and wrongfully withheld this information from the defendant. BROWN, J. "When the prospective seller knows as much as the prospective buyer, options can rarely, if ever, be procured, and the rule that counsel for appellant would have us apply would practically abolish them. The prospective buyer seeks an option, instead of at once entering into a contract for the purchase of land, because no matter what information he may possess exclusively, he is unwilling to act upon it until it becomes a certainty. In the meantime, on the contingency of its becoming so, he makes his contingent bargain to purchase. This is fair in law and in morals."

Sec. 639. Rights of Third Party. The law does not extend to an undisclosed principal the right to perform himself the executory contract of the agent which involves personal trust or confidence imposed on the latter; but if such a contract has been executed by the agent there seems to be no reason why an undisclosed principal should not be entitled to enforce it.18 Where the agency is undisclosed, and the third party has no knowledge that the agent has exceeded his authority, the principal must take the contract as his agent made it. 

Eldridge v. Finniger, 25 Okla. 28 (1909). The agent of an un disclosed principal sold a quantity of coal to a tailor for $23.30, and agreed to accept a $23 tailored suit as part payment. The principal then disclosed his identity, and attempted to avoid this method of payment. TURNER, J. "As the principal, by this action, now seeks to enforce said contract, he must take it as the agent and purchaser left it. He must take his pay as the agent agreed to receive it."

Part 3. Agent and Third Party 

Sec. 640. Disclosed Agency. An agent is not personally liable to the third party on a contract which he makes on behalf of his principal, provided he (1) discloses the agency, (2) proves his authority, (3) with- 

18 Sullivan v. Shailor, 70 Conn. 733 (1898).

draws any personal interest he may have in the transaction, and (4) keeps his name from negotiable paper. 

Sec. 641. Lack of Authority. "When a person as sumes to act for another, knowing that he is not authorized to do so, he becomes personally liable to the party with whom he deals for or on account of his alleged principal."1 "Even in a case where the agent honestly believes he has authority to make a contract, but in fact has not, a plain principle of justice requires that if an injury be done to another by the assumption of an unauthorized authority the person occasioning the loss should be responsible rather than the party who was misled to his hurt by the exercise of such assumed power." 20 

Kroeger v. Pitcairn, 101 Pa. 311 (1882). An agent delivered a fire insurance policy containing a stipulation that no petroleum should be kept on the premises. The insured, observing this condition, stated that he was obliged to keep a little petroleum on hand, but the agent replied that it was only when kept in large quantities that it should be noted on the policy, and not when kept in a single barrel. In reasoning that the agent was personally liable for this representation, it was said by STERRETT, J. "This whole doctrine proceeds upon a plain principle of justice; for every person, so acting for another, by a natural if not a necessary implication holds himself out as having competent authority to do the act; and he thereby draws the other party into a reciprocal engagement."" 66 

Sec. 642. Undisclosed Agency. If an agent would avoid personal liability, the duty is upon him to disclose his principal, and not on the party with whom he is dealing to discover it." The mere addition of the word "agent" after one's signature does not establish the agency or relieve the agent from personal liability." 

Neither does the disclosure of the agency after the contract is made.23

Descalzi v. North American Fruit Exchange, 96 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 293 (1929). Plaintiff brought suit against the defendant to recover damages for breach of warranty in the sale of certain cars of fruit. Defendants sought to avoid liability on the ground that they were acting as agents for different sellers. Such information was not disclosed when the contract was made, but was discovered before this action was instituted. In this aspect of the case, it was said by KELLER, J. "If when the orders were placed and the contract was made defendant did not disclose that it was acting as agent only for different sellers, but contracted as a principal in the transaction, the status would not be changed by the fact that later when the drafts were lifted and paid, the invoices disclosed other principals as the sellers of the fruit." 

Sec. 643. Torts of Agent. Where torts have been committed by an agent, it is sometimes said that the relationship of principal and agent does not exist. An agent is generally liable for his own negligent acts and is not relieved from his torts, unless he is exercising a privilege held by him for the protection of his principal's business. He is also liable for an independent fraud, even though he is acting within the scope of his employment, and for conversion and all negligent acts beyond the scope of his authority. 24 25 

Sec. 644. Rights of Agent. The rights of an agent against a third party are confined within narrow limits. 

Unless authorized by his principal, an agent has no authority to institute an action against a third party," unless the contract so provides, or the agent has some property right in the subject-matter of the agreement." 

An agent may be delegated with authority to institute a legal action on behalf of his principal, and he may do so in his own name if the agency is undisclosed. He may also institute an action against a third party who tortiously interferes with the property held by him in behalf of his principal, or for a tort committed against him while acting within the scope of his employment. In suits by an agent, the third party is entitled to whatever set-off he may have had against the principal. 

24 Freeman v. Tabas, 291 Pa. 448 (1928). 

25 Steamboat Co. v. Atkins & Co., 22 

Pa. 522 (1854).

458.  Part 4. Liability of Agent to Principal Sec. 645. General Duties. It is the general duty of an agent to comply with all reasonable directions, communicate all material facts, keep his principal informed of his activities, protect the title to that which has been entrusted to him, account for money and property received and parted with, and yield all profits obtained. 

He should also advise his principal when the undertaking proves to be impossible or impracticable, or subject to unnecessary risk or expense. Negatively, an agent should not conduct himself with impropriety or bring disrepute upon his principal, or use or communicate confidential information-trade secrets, list of names, or confidential matters-acquired by him in the course of his employment, either before or after the termination of his authority, or presume to act after the termination of the agency.

Sec. 646. Specific Duties. It is the primary duty of an agent, whose authority is limited by instructions, to adhere faithfully to those instructions, especially when they are imperative and not discretionary. Where, for example, a bank receives for collection a draft for a definite amount of money, accompanied by a warranty deed and a letter of instructions authorizing the delivery of the deed upon payment of the draft, delivery of the deed without payment of the draft would render the bank liable.26 

Wilson v. Wilson, 26 Pa. 393 (1856). Matthew Wilson, in Pennsylvania, held $300 which belonged to Thomas Wilson, in North Carolina. Thomas instructed Matthew to send it by mail in $50 or $100 notes. Matthew sent $5, $10, and $20 notes, and only one note of $100. The letter was never received. This suit was based on disobedience. LEWIS, C. J. "In sending bank-notes by mail, it is manifest that while a large package would attract the attention and care of honest agents on the route, it might tempt the duplicity of dishonest ones. The party who proposes to take the risk of this method of remittance has a right to weigh the advantages and disadvantages of the money to be remitted in notes of $100 or $50, 20 Stewart v. Penn Argyl Nat. Bank, 307 Pa. 328 (1932).

5 the debtor has no right to increase the size of the package by remitting in notes of $10 or $5." 

Sec. 647. Standard of Care. An agent may be held for the exercise of reasonable care and diligence in transacting the business of his principal, consonant with the nature of the undertaking, and should conform to reasonable standards of business practice. Where, for example, he has authority to sell real estate and accepts bonds which become worthless, he is liable to his principal for the price of the land."7 

Whitney v. Martin, 88 New York 525 (1882). Plaintiff authorized an attorney to invest certain moneys. The attorney invested the funds in second mortgages of inadequate security. This suit was based on the failure of the attorney to exercise ordinary care and diligence in making these investments. MILLER, J. "And as this case is presented upon the evidence, we are brought to the conclusion that the agent exceeded his authority and was chargeable with a want of proper care and skill in making the investment; and for this neglect he is legally liable for the loss sustained."

Sec. 648. Del Credere Liability. An agent may not dispose of his principal's property on credit, unless he is authorized to do so. The agent may agree with his principal to guarantee payment of a credit transaction.28

Such an arrangement is common in foreign trade, and in domestic trade where goods are delivered to a commission merchant on consignment. Under such circumstances the agent may be held liable for the payment of the account, if the third party fails to pay it. 

Sec. 649. Care of Funds. An agent should not commingle the property of his principal with his own. If he does so the principal may reclaim from the admixture an amount equal to his own, although it may not be the same identical property.29 An agent is not under the same duty as a servant to deliver the identical coins, bills or checks received by him within the scope of his

20 Webb v. Newhall, 274 Pa. 135 (1922).

agency. He may deliver an equal sum of money.

3 30 If the agent deposits the moneys of his principal in a bank in his own name, the principal may claim the funds as against an attaching creditor of the agent.³¹ 

Sec. 650. Patents and Inventions. The interest of the employer in a patent obtained by an employee is indicated in an opinion by Mr. Justice ROBERTS of the United 

States Supreme Court: (1) a person employed to make an invention is bound to assign to his employer any patent obtained. (2) If the employment is general, the contract is not so broadly construed as to require such an assignment, although the employee conceived the idea in the performance of his duties. (3) "Recognition of the nature of the act of invention also defines the limits of the so-called shop right, which shortly stated, is that where a servant, during his hours of employment, working with his master's materials and appliances, conceives and perfects an invention for which he obtains a patent, he must accord his master a non-exclusive right to practice the invention."32

Sec. 651. Fiduciary Relation. Agency is a fiduciary relation. For this reason an agent may not compete with his principal within the scope of the agency, except as otherwise understood and agreed upon.

East & West Coast Service Corp. v. Papahagis, 344 Pa. 183

Two weeks prior thereto, defendant secured a lease for himself, by offering $500 more than his principal had been paying. 

Plaintiff thereupon filed a bill in equity for an assignment of the lease and an accounting. In approving this relief, it was said by

Sec. 652. Constructive Fraud. For the same reason, an agent may not make the business of the principal an object of interest to himself.33 Where a real estate agent agrees to sell land for another, he may not sell to a straw man, who thereafter resells at a profit, without accounting for the profit.34 "He cannot buy his principal's property, even from the principal himself, except upon the fullest disclosure of every matter which may affect its value. He is treated by law precisely as trustees are treated who seek to make profit for themselves out of their trust relation."85 

Bachrach v. Fleming, 269 Pa. 350 (1921). Bachrach authorized a real estate agent, Fleming, to offer $90,000 for certain real estate. 

Fleming secretly bought it for $85,000, and then persuaded Bachrach to pay $95,000. These facts being discovered while the contract of sale was being prepared, Bachrach filed a bill in equity praying that it be adjudged that Fleming held title for and should convey the property to him. In approving such relief, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "Mr. Justice STEWART, speaking for the court in Bergner v. Bergner, 219 Pa. 113, summed up the controlling principles of agency in these pregnant words: 'Agency is a recognized fiduciary relation; its vital principle is good faith, without which the relation could not exist.' That case reiterated the established rule: 'An agent to purchase cannot be allowed, except as his principal assents, to purchase for himself. He can acquire nothing by an adverse purchase, even though he contribute of his own means or credit to effect it; the product will belong to the principal exclusively."" 

Sec. 653. Dual Agency.

'No man can serve two masters; for he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one and despise the other.' So, also, is our law."

Sec. 654. Shifting Agency. It is more accurate to say that, "Ordinarily one cannot serve two masters in the same matter." "But this rule has no application where the duties of the agent to the two principals are of such nature that there can be no conflict between his duty of loyalty to the one and his duty of loyalty to the other." An insurance agent is primarily the agent of the insurer. An insurance broker is primarily the agent of the insured. Either one may be authorized to act for the other principal in some phase of the transaction, if there be no conflict in the duty which he owes to them both. Aside from the question of good faith, the criterion to be observed is the identity of the principal, and the appointed duty to be performed. An insurance agent may be authorized to keep property insured, to transmit an offer, or cancel a policy, on behalf of the insured. It may be noted in connection therewith, that a person who signs an application for insurance without reading it, containing statements of fact untrue and a promise that they were true, has no right to rely on the fact that an agent of the insurance company filled it in.38 More commonly, of course, an insurance agent is authorized to countersign, endorse, or deliver the policy, and collect the premium, or cancel the policy, on behalf of the insurer. The Act of 192139 requires the licensing of insurance agents and brokers, and imposes personal liability upon an agent on a contract of insurance unlawfully made by or through him on behalf of any company not authorized to do business in Pennsylvania. For this purpose any person who solicits risks, forwards premiums, or countersigns or delivers policies, is deemed to be the agent of the company. 

Sec. 655. Double Dealing. "No broker, agent or middleman can recover for services which uncover double dealing." It is a rule of public policy that an agent 40

An agent may not set up an unlawful contract to enable him to hold money or property received by him for his principal. Though the contract as between the principal and third party is unenforceable as opposed to public policy, an agent having possession of the property of his principal may not assert such illegality as grounds for retaining it. In 

Smith v. Blackley** a physician, in attendance upon two families, in one of which was a son and in the other a daughter, represented that an illness of the daughter was caused by an abortion, and by falsely representing that a prosecution was imminent, obtained a considerable sum of money to stifle the supposed prosecution.

It was held that he could not, upon discovery of the fraud, retain what he had received, notwithstanding it was paid for an illegal purpose.

Sec. 657. Violation of Duty. A principal may dis charge his agent for a violation of duty, refuse to compensate him for his services, and institute an appropriate action against him.

Part 5.

Liability of Principal to Agent Sec. 658. Duties of Principal. It is the duty of a principal to comply strictly with the contract he has made with his agent, to give the latter whatever notice the principal has of risks of physical harm or pecuniary loss, to refrain from harming his agent's reputation or making it impossible for his agent to perform the duties entrusted to him consistent with reasonable self-respect and personal safety, to reimburse his agent for authorized payments, and to indemnify his agent for losses incurred in authorized transactions.* 45 

Hoggan v. Cahoon, 26 Utah 444 (1903). A principal employed an agent to take possession of certain property, upon the representation that the principal was entitled to possession. The taking constituted a tort, and the agent was personally obliged to answer in damages. He then brought this action against his principal for indemnification. BARTCH, J. ". . . where, as appears from the allegations in this case, an agent acts in good faith for his principal, under the principal's direction, and relies upon his representations that the transaction is lawful, and the same is not manifestly unlawful, the law implies indemnity, for damages of third parties."

Sec. 659. Compensation. It is the duty of the principal to pay his agent for services rendered whenever the law would imply a duty to do so. A principal is not liable for a specified service or result unless it has been performed or accomplished, or unless performance has been substantial. Nor is the principal liable for unauthorized acts. Where the agency has been wrongfully terminated the agent may treat the contract as rescinded and recover damages for its breach, or he may treat the contract as in force and recover his loss at the end of the term. 

45 Bode & Heinz v. Campolo, 99 Pa. Superior Ct. 208 (1930).

Horter v. Walsh, 70 Pa. Superior Ct. 442 (1918). Walsh authorized Horter to obtain a mortgage loan in the sum of $10,000, and agreed to pay the latter $500 as a commission. The loan was accepted by a building association, $3,000 to be paid at once and $7,000 when the building was completed and the liens released. 

Walsh acknowledged his satisfaction with the agreement, accepted the $3,000, and made a part payment of $150 to Horter. Later, however, he released the association from loaning the balance, and refused to pay any further commission to his agent. TREXLER, J. "The conclusion was warranted that the loan had been granted, that the plaintiff had done all that was required of him, and that the failure of the defendant to get the money was due to his own fault. The plaintiff was therefore entitled to his commission." 47 

Sec. 660. Commissions. A volunteer is not entitled to a commission merely because he has brought buyer and seller together and is the efficient means of producing a sale. It is incumbent upon him to establish his employment to do the thing for which a commission is claimed. Where an agent is promised a commission if he secures a purchaser, and he does so and a written agreement of sale is executed, he has earned the commission. But where the commission is to be paid at the time of settlement, the commission has not been earned.48 An insurance agent's commission is earned when he places a policy. The cancellation of the policy during its term does not, in the absence of an agreement to that effect, deprive him of the full benefit of his labor, or deprive him of compensation for his service. The failure or refusal or inability of either the principal or the third party to carry out the contract negotiated by the agent does not defeat the latter's right to compensation for his services, nor is it defeated by the fact that the principal and third party subsequently modify, rescind, or cancel it." 50 

Sec. 661. Exclusive Agency. A sole and exclusive agency for the sale of property entitles an agent to the

Sec. 662. Forfeiture. Inasmuch as agency is a fiduciary relation, a violation of trust is sufficient to warrant the forfeiture of compensation to which an agent would otherwise be entitled to receive. In Shepard & 

Co. v. Kaufman,53 an agent who was authorized to sell real estate conveyed it to his own wife without notify ing his principal prior to the conveyance. It was held that this "was a constructive fraud and destroyed his right to any commissions upon the sale." 

Greene v. Hawtof, 87 Pa. Superior Ct. 479 (1926). Plaintiff was authorized to sell certain real estate. He found a buyer, but because he knew that his principal was not on good terms with the proposed purchaser and would not have approved the sale, he procured a straw man to act in the capacity of purchaser. When this situation was disclosed, the principal refused to proceed further, and plaintiff instituted this action to recover a commission. 

HENDERSON, J. "It is an elementary rule in the law of agency that a broker is to be regarded as an agent of the seller, and that it is his duty in such capacity to act in the utmost good faith towards his principal, and that if he fail to do so, he is not entitled to compensation for service."

Part 6. Termination of Agency Sec. 663. Suspension of Authority. The authority of an agent may be suspended because of the happening of an event, or a change in conditions, if the agent should reasonably infer that his principal would not have con-

Other incidents having that effect are loss of capacity, a change of law rendering the transaction illegal, and the destruction of the subject-matter. 54 

Sec. 664. Revocation of Authority. The principal may revoke the authority of his agent to enter into contracts with third parties. If such a revocation is a breach of contract between the principal and the agent, the agent has his remedy. He may recover in quantum meruit for the expenditures which he has been encouraged to make, as well as compensation for his labor and time. But this does not preclude the right of the principal to decline to deal with third parties. Where the principal has placed documents in the hands of his agent, which authorize the agent to deal with third parties, the principal may not escape liability arising therefrom by secretly revoking the authority of the agent. If he does not recall the documents, or in some way give notice to third parties, he will be estopped to deny his liability to a third party who in good faith deals with the agent on that authority.55 It will be observed that in the following case, the third party had knowledge of the revocation. 

Blackstone v. Buttermore, 53 Pa. 266 (1866). Buttermore executed what was stated to be an irrevocable power of attorney to Davidson to sell certain land within a specified period of time. 

He revoked the power within that period. Within the time specified, and with knowledge of the revocation, Blackstone contracted with Davidson to buy the land and brought this action to recover it. This demand was denied. Concerning the situation of the agent, it was said by AGNEW, J. "The interest of the agent was only in his compensation for selling, and without a sale this is not earned. A revocation could not injure him. If he had expended money, time or labor, or all, upon the business intrusted to him, 54 Jaekel v. Caldwell, 156 Pa. 266 (1893). 

55 Keller v. N. J. Fidelity & Plate 

Glass Ins. Co., 306 Pa. 124 (1932).

the power itself was a request to do so, and on a revocation would leave the principal liable to him on his implied assumpsit. But it would be the heighth of injustice if the power should be held to be irrevocable merely to secure the agent for his outlay or his services rendered before a sale."

Sec. 665. Termination of Agency. An agency may generally be terminated (1) at will by either party. It will also terminate (2) at the expiration of the term, (3) at the fulfillment of the purpose, (4) at the expiration of a reasonable time, (5) upon the incapacity (insanity) of the principal or agent, (6) upon the death of the principal or agent, and (7) it may be terminated upon breach of contract. "Where a continuing relationship is created by a writing, which places no limitation upon the length of time it shall remain in effect, there is a presumption that it is to continue in force for a reasonable time after it was executed and after a date on which it was shown to have been recognized as still in force." In Davidsville First National Bank v. St.

John's Church,57 a church secured a permit from its bishop to contract a debt for the purpose of making repairs and changes to its school and convent. Two and one-half years thereafter the pastor of the church obtained a loan from a bank and absconded with the proceeds. It was held that the age of the permit was such as to require investigation, and that one who gave credit otherwise did so at his peril. 50 

Sec. 666. Death of Principal. Termination of the agency upon the death of the principal is subject to two exceptions. As expressed by the Supreme Court more than a century ago: "In the civil law, the acts of the agent, done bona fide in ignorance of the death of his principal, are held valid and binding upon the heirs of the latter. The same rule holds in the Scottish law, and 

I cannot believe the common law is so unreasonable, notwithstanding the doubts expressed by Chancellor 

KENT in the 2d volume of his Commentaries, 646." 58 

50 Ibid. 

57 296 Pa. 476 (1929). 

58 Cassiday v. M'Kenzie, 4 W. & S. 282 (1842).

Sec. 667. Power Coupled with Interest. Notwith standing the death of the principal, the agency is not revocable where the authority conferred upon the agent is coupled with an interest, as where it is necessary to effectuate a security. Such power, however, must create an interest in the thing itself, or in the property which is the subject of the power. 

Lightner's Appeal, 82 Pa. 301 (1876). Herr pledged certain stock to a bank as collateral security for a loan, and irrevocably constituted and appointed Eberman, the cashier, his attorney to dispose of it, with power of substitution. AGNEW, C. J. "Eberman, the attorney, having died, the question is whether the power given under these circumstances has fallen. We think it has not. 

It was not only by its own terms irrevocable for value received, but it was so by the legal operation of the agreement which induced it. It is a power coupled with an interest, and was made and executed for the very purpose of carrying the agreement into performance."

Sec. 668. Notice to Third Parties. Apparent author ity may exist independently of the termination of an agency, and frequently necessitates notice to third persons, either in person, in writing, by publication, or in some other manner.

Claflin v. Lenheim, 66 New York 301 (1876). The principal in this case terminated the agency of his brother, who had been in charge of his business in Pennsylvania. This was an action for goods sold after the agency was alleged to have been revoked. 

RAPALLO, J. "As to persons who have been previously in the habit of dealing with the firm, it is requisite that actual notice should be brought home to the creditor or at least that the credit should have been given under circumstances from which notice can be inferred." 1371

CHAPTER XVIII PARTNERSHIPS Part 1. Formation of Partnership Sec. 669. Partnership Defined. The Uniform Part nership Act was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1915.¹ 

This statute, which will be referred to in this chapter as the code, defines a partnership as an association of two or more persons to carry on as co-owners a business for profit. It is an unincorporated association, created by the agreement of two or more competent parties, who contribute money, property, skill, labor, or credit, for the transaction of some lawful business.2

A partnership may be formed under an oral agreement. 

In a proper case it may be implied. "As between the parties themselves partnership is a matter of intention, and where they expressly declare that they are not partners this settles the question, for, whatever their obligations may be as to third persons, the law permits them to agree upon their legal status and relationship inter 

Se." 4 

Sec. 670. Not a Legal Entity. A partnership in this commonwealth is not a legal entity. As said in Sumner v. Brown," "it is well known that the act was drawn and enacted to give effect, as its terms indicate, to the common law or aggregate theory that partners are joint principals in partnership transactions, holding property as tenants in partnership, and not to give effect to the theory that the partnership is a legal or fictitious person, which owns the property, and for whom the partners act as mere agents." 3
