Sec. 672. Fictitious Names Act. A different situa tion is presented where a business is conducted under an assumed or fictitious name by a partnership or oth- The Act of 1945 provides that no persons or individuals shall conduct any business under an assumed or fictitious name, without filing with the Secretary of the Commonwealth, and with the prothonotary of the county where the principal place of business is located, a prescribed statement thereof, with proof of publication. The act also requires such a statement upon the dissolution of the business, or whenever a person withdraws from the business. Failure to register does not impair the contracts of such persons, but no legal action may be instituted thereon until the parties register as provided by the act, and pay a license fee or fine of $25. Violation of the act is a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. Sec. 673. Qualifications. As a general rule all persons having contractual capacity may become partners. This would exclude persons under guardianship of the law. Infants may become partners, but subject to the right of rescission. Married women could not become partners under the common law, but this disability has been removed by statute. Alien friends may become partners, but not alien enemies. A corporation has no implied power to enter into a partnership, but it may become a party to, and share in

Partners may, of course, become stockholders in corporations, and there is a tendency for large partnerships to organize corporations for the purpose of conducting certain functions of the partnership enterprise. In some cases corporations have elected to dissolve and to carry on the business as a partnership because of the burden of corporate taxes. 

Sec. 674. Agreement to Form. An agreement to form a partnership does not of itself create a partnership, nor does the advancement by one party of his agreed share of the capital. As said in the following case, persons who have entered into a contract to become partners at some future time, or upon the happening of some future contingency, do not become partners until the agreed time has arrived or the contingency has happened. If the following facts disclosed a partnership from the date of the agreement, as held by the court below, the plaintiff should have filed a bill in equity for an accounting. If, on the other hand, the contract established the relation of master and servant, as held by the Supreme Court, the plaintiff properly instituted an action in assumpsit. 

Coens v. Marousis, 275 Pa. 478 (1928). Defendant secured rooms, furniture, and goods suitable for a shoeshine parlor, and installed the plaintiff as manager, under an agreement that, after the receipts should repay the cost of the original investment, maintenance, and board and room of plaintiff and defendant, plaintiff, who was to receive in the meantime no other compensation, should receive a half interest in the business. After a profitable continuance of the business for two years, plaintiff demanded a half interest in accordance with the agreement, and on refusal, brought this action with a count on a quantum meruit for his services. Sec. 675. Undisclosed Partnership. The burden of proving that two or more persons are associated as partners is upon him who asserts it. This is not infrequently a difficult task. A great many partnerships are not registered. "The articles of co-partnership are perhaps never published. The stipulations they may contain, are to regulate the conduct and rights of the parties, as between themselves." 10 If one partner furnishes the necessary capital and another partner manages the business, without disclosing their relation, how is the public to know that the business is being conducted by a partnership? There is always the temptation, when the pinch comes, for an inactive partner to conceal his identity. If such a situation is disclosed, the mere fact that the partner in charge of the business has agreed to assume the burden of whatever losses might be sustained would not relieve the dormant partner of liability to the creditors of the business. 

Purviance v. McClintee, 6 S. & R. 258 (1820). TILGHMAN, J. "If A and B are about to form a connection in mercantile business, they may, so far as concerns themselves, make what terms they please. If it be agreed that A shall furnish all the stock, and B contribute his services in consideration whereof he shall be entitled to one-half the profits, without being subject to any part of the loss, it is all very fair and very well between A and B. But as to the world, who have no means of knowing the secret arrangements of partners, such a condition is not to be permitted. The partnership creditors trust to the partnership stock, and, therefore, no man shall be allowed to lessen that stock, by taking part of the profits, without incurring the responsibility of a partner. This principle may bear hard upon a man who never intended to assume such responsibility, but it is founded in good policy, and has the effect of preventing fraud."

Sec. 676. Statutory Rules. The rules appearing in the code are not very helpful in determining the existence of a partnership, except in so far as they negative 

10 Hoskinson v. Eliot, 62 Pa. 393 (1869).

the idea of a partnership under many circumstances. 

The code starts out with the declaration that "persons who are not partners as to each other are not partners as to third persons."

Beecher v. Bush, 45 Michigan 188 (1881). COOLEY, J. 

"Beecher furnished the use of the hotel and a clerk to supervise the accounts, and received for so doing one-third the gross returns. 

It was not understood that he was to inter-meddle in any way with the conduct of the business so long as Williams adhered to the terms of his contract. If the business was managed badly Beecher might be a loser, but how could he help himself? He had reserved no right to correct the mistakes of Williams, supply his deficiences or overrule his judgment. . . . Our conclusion is that Beecher and 

Williams, having never intended to constitute a partnership, are not as between themselves partners. There was to be no common property, no agency of either to act for the other or for both, no participation in profits, no sharing of losses. We also think there can be no such thing as a partnership as to third persons when as between the parties themselves there is no partnership and the third persons have not been misled by concealment of facts or by deceptive appearances."

Sec. 677. Joint Ownership. The code then declares that, "Joint tenancy, tenancy in common, tenancy by the entireties, joint property, common property, or part ownership does not of itself establish a partnership, whether such co-owners do or do not share any profits made by the use of the property." This principle has long been recognized in Pennsylvania." A partnership is not implied between a number of such tenants merely because they agree to develop or operate common property, since they may rightfully do this by vir tue of their respective titles as part owners.' 12 ...

Sec. 678. Sharing of Profits. The code further pro vides that, "The sharing of gross returns does not of itself establish a partnership, whether or not the persons sharing them have a joint or common right or interest in any property from which the returns are derived." 

This disposes of the common fallacy that a person who

Sec. 679. Qualifications. The concluding provisions of the code, on this phase of the subject, express an affirmative declaration concerning the receipt of profits, but with a number of qualifications. "The receipt by a person of a share of the profits of a business is prima facie evidence that he is a partner in the business, but no such inference shall be drawn if such profits were received in payment: (a) As a debt by installments or otherwise, (b) As wages of an employee or rent to a landlord, (c) As an annuity to a widow or representative of a deceased partner, (d) As interest on a loan, though the amount of payment vary with the profits of the business, (e) As the consideration for the sale of the good-will of a business or other property by installments or otherwise."

Sec. 681. Profits Paid as Interest. The receipt of profits in lieu of interest does not constitute the creditor a partner if he takes no part in the management of the business and does not hold himself out as a partner. 18

An agreement was made between this firm, known as the Stewart Gas & Oil Company, and others, known as "well beneficiaries," under which the beneficiaries were to make contributions toward the general project and receive a proportionate share of the net income, but they were given no interest in the physical properties or in the management of the business, and were not to be liable for any obligation beyond the amount of their contribution. One of the partners died and the executors of his estate filed a bill for dissolution, the appointment of a receiver, and the distribution of firm assets. This action was resisted because the "well beneficiaries" were not joined as members of the partnership. KEPHART, J. "While the partnership planning included further financing, the scheme set up and the acts thereunder did not make these contributors partners." 

Sec. 682. Essentials of Partnership. From what has been said it should be obvious that there are two essential facts which should be proved if an alleged partnership is to be established, first, co-ownership of the business, and second, the sharing of its profits.19 These facts may be proved by direct or by circumstantial evidence. The incidents to be considered are common ownership of property, joint tenancy and joint enterprise, and the sharing of profits and losses, but no one of these elements in itself is conclusive. The true test of a partnership is the intent of the parties as evidenced by their correspondence, signed papers, agreements to share in the profits, the existence of mutual agency, joint ownership of assets, and the like. This relationship, like any other agency, may be established by the testimony of the partners, or by the admissions of all those who are alleged to compose it, or by the admissions of

Sec. 683. Partnership by Estoppel. The partner ship relation, as well as the authority of a partner, may be established on grounds of estoppel.22 The principles expressed in the code may be summarized as follows: 

If a person falsely represents himself as a member of a partnership, he may be held to the liability of a member of that partnership. He is also the agent of all persons consenting to such a representation, and he may bind them by contract to the same extent as though he were in fact a partner. If all the members of a partnership consent to the representation, a partnership obligation results, but otherwise the obligation is that of the person held out as a partner and those who permit this to be done. Partnership by estoppel is presumed rather than actual. Permitting onesself to be introduced as a partner, and participating in the transaction, is sufficient to carry the case to the jury.23 In Cancelmo v. Tilli,24 plaintiff testified that the defendant introduced him to two other persons, stating: "I wish you to meet my partners." No objection being heard, this was held sufficient to establish the relation, whether in fact it existed or not. It has been said, however, that the use of the word "partner" by a foreigner who speaks English poorly, and is dull of apprehension, is of doubtful import. 25

Sec. 685. Implied Authority. In all partnerships there is an implied power in each partner to bind the firm by any contract necessary to carry out the purpose for which it was formed. Grimaldi v. Martin, 27 Pa. D. R. 734 (1918). Plaintiff alleged that he entered into an agreement with Antonio Martin to purchase a barber shop owned by the latter and John Martin as partners, but that when a bill of sale was prepared, John Martin refused to sign it. The relief sought was a decree of specific performance. VAN SWEARINGEN, P. J. "There is no authority in one partner to sell the entire property of a partnership, when the business of the firm is not that of buying and selling, but is a business to which the continued ownership of the property sold is indispensable. An attempted transfer by one partner of all the property of a partnership, not in the course of trade, especially if it be for the purpose of breaking up the partnership, or under such circumstances that it practically terminates the business, is not binding on a partner not consenting thereto." 

Sec. 687. Trading Partnership. The apparent au thority of a partner is responsive to the nature of the business being conducted by the partnership. In many states a distinction is made between a trading and a non-trading partnership with respect to the power of a partner to borrow money and execute negotiable instruments, "the distinction being that in commercial partnerships the extent of a partner's power to bind the firm is a question of law, while the power of a partner in a non-commercial firm to bind his co-partners is a question of fact." 30 If the partnership is engaged in buying and selling goods and merchandise, each partner is held to have authority to borrow money and issue negotiable instruments as a matter of law. In professional and other non-trading partnerships, a single partner does not have such authority except as it may be authorized by his co-partners. This distinction has become an established tradition in American law, although it has 

30 Judge v. Braswell, 76 Kentucky 67 (1877).

lost much of its significance. This is due to the neces sity of enlarging upon the concept of trading partnerships necessary to make it workable, the need of working capital in non-trading industries, and modern methods of finance. Pennsylvania has long adhered to the rule that such authority may exist in a non-trading partnership, as well as in a trading partnership, within the apparent scope of the business being conducted by the partnership.31

Dowling v. The National Exchange Bank, 145 U. S. 512 (1892). 

Ferry, Dowling and White were partners "for the purpose of carrying on the business of sawing lumber, pickets, and laths" at Montague, "in the steam saw mill lately there erected." Ferry fraudulently executed notes against the partnership in the sum of $15,- 781,38, which were discounted at the National Exchange Bank of Boston. A judgment having been entered against the partnership, a severance was had between the defendant partners so as to authorize a writ of error in the name of Dowling. HARLAN, J. the difficulty in this case is that the jury were not permitted to determine, from a consideration of all the circumstances of the case, what, in view of the admitted nature of the business of F. The judgment is reversed as to the defendant Dowling, who alone prosecutes this writ of error, with directions to grant him a new trial." 66 ... 

Sec. 688. Secret Limitations. A third party is not charged with notice of inconsistent articles of co-partnership of which he has no notice, or secret limitations upon the powers of the partners among themselves, in dealing with a partner within the apparent scope of the partnership business.

Burdsall's Estate, 28 Pa. D. R. 541 (1919). HENDERSON, J. 

This proceeding "relates to the allowance of a claim made by the First National Bank of Media for the sum of $4,765.81, arising out of a loan made by the bank to the firm of Burdsall & Adams, 31 Hoskinson v. Eliot, 62 Pa. 393 (1869).

481 consisting of the decedent, J. Frank Burdsall, and Joseph M. 

Rodgers; and the question raised is as to whether one partner had authority to bind the partnership for this loan. The partnership agreement was offered in evidence, and it appears that under it neither partner could so bind the partnership, and it is needless to add that third parties with notice would be barred from making any claim. The auditing judge, however, has found as a fact that the bank had no notice of the contents of the partnership agreement, and, hence, this agreement cannot be offered in bar of the bank's claim. This question of fact has been found against the exceptant by the auditing judge, and his finding will not be disturbed except for manifest error." 

Sec. 689. Notice of Limitation. A third party in dealing with a partner may be charged with whatever knowledge he has that the partner negotiating a particular transaction does not have authority to act for his co-partners, as well as knowledge of any article of copartnership that is inconsistent with the authority assumed by a partner, notwithstanding the ostensible power of a partner to act within the scope of the partnership business.

Branby Mining & Smelting Co. v. Laverty, 159 Pa. 287 (1893). 

A partnership agreement contained a provision that checks and drafts should be signed by both partners of the business. This information was communicated to the bank where the funds were on deposit. Checks were so drawn down to within about four months of the dissolution of the firm, when a large number of checks aggregating $8,101.63 were signed by one of the partners and paid by the bank. The paying teller refused payment, but his action was overruled by the cashier. The cashier was the father of the partner who drew the checks. A partnership creditor issued an attachment execution against the bank, alleging that the funds noted above were improperly paid. WILLIAMS, J. "Upon these facts the bank took the risk of their being drawn for a legitimate partnership purpose, and is entitled to credit no further than it is able to show that the money drawn upon them was used in the payment of igations for which the firm was legally bound."

Sec. 690. Notice of Irregularity. Some transac tions are so irregular as to carry their own danger signal. Where a partner makes a promissory note in his

own name, payable to the order of his firm, endorses the name of the firm thereon, and requests a bank to discount it and place the proceeds to his personal credit, the bank has notice of such irregularity as imposes upon it the duty to inquire as to the authority of the endorser.32 Many transactions of this same general nature are not so unusual as to challenge the attention of a third party. Where a draft or bill is drawn in the name of the firm by one of the partners, and is offered for discount, the presumption is that the partner is acting within the scope of his authority, even though the instrument is made payable to the order of one of the members of the firm.33

Sec. 691. Statutory Limitations. A few transac tions require the consent of all the members of a partnership. The code provides that unless authorized by all the partners, or they have abandoned the business, one partner may not, without the consent of his copartners, (a) assign the partnership property in trust for creditors or on the assignee's promise to pay the debts of the partnership; (b) dispose of the good will of the business; (c) do any other act which would make it impossible to carry on the ordinary business of the partnership; (d) confess a judgment; or (e) submit a partnership claim or liability to arbitration or reference. Prior to the adoption of this act, one partner could confess a judgment for a partnership debt which would bind his individual property, as well as that of the partnership, but not the separate estates of other partners. 34

Sec. 692. Individual Tort. Where a tort is committed by a partner who is acting in the ordinary course of the business of the partnership, and injury results to

Polis v. Heizmann, 276 Pa. 315 (1923). Plaintiff was the owner of a small farm in an outlying district of Philadelphia, a part of which he leased as a piggery to two persons who were partners in the business. The city thereafter prevented the use of the place for such a purpose, and one of them went upon the premises to remove some lumber. In an altercation over his right to do so, he wilfully and intentionally struck and injured the plaintiff, who brought suit against the partnership. The other partner was not present, and did not authorize or ratify the assault. 

Walling, J. “Knocking a man down, as in this case, with the fist and then again with an automobile, both done wilfully, cannot be said to come within the scope of the business of raising pigs. . 

While here the act of the offending partner in going for the lumber was within the scope of the firm's business, the vicious assault committed by him was not, and for that he alone was liable. The case is different where the master or partner, sought to be charged, was present at the assault and failed to protest." ...

Sec. 693. Admissions. The code provides that admissions and representations by a partner who is at the time acting within the scope of his authority, may be offered in evidence against the partnership. This principle applies in contract as well as in tort. 

Treon v. Shipman & Son, 275 Pa. 246 (1922). Plaintiff was struck by an automobile. Shortly thereafter the driver of the car, who was a member of the defendant partnership, appeared at plaintiff's home and stated that he was on a partnership errand at the time. The partnership objected to the admission of this declaration. KEPHART, J. "If the partner's statements be correct, and it was so determined by the jury, he was doing an act in furtherance of the business of the partnership, and the accident resulted from his careless prosecution of the firm's business." 

Sec. 694. Breach of Trust. The partnership is bound by the act of a partner who receives money or property of a third party while acting within the scope of his apparent authority, and misapplies it, or who appropriates property belonging to a third party while it

is in the possession of the firm. In Blaustein v. Shapiro, a verdict against a partnership was sustained where the evidence tended to prove that a machine was received by one of the members of the firm for the purpose of making repairs thereon, and subsequently the firm, under an invalid claim of title, refused to redeliver it to the plaintiff.

Sec. 695. Liability. The tort liability of partners, within the scope of the partnership undertaking, is both joint and several. In other words, an injured party may institute an action against the partners jointly, or he may institute an action against a single partner and recover from him the full amount of the damage. He may even single out a partner who was not personally involved in the commission of the tort.36 Partners are jointly liable for all other debts and obligations of the partnership, and suit should be brought against them jointly. Under the common law a release given to one partner who is jointly liable with his co-partners, would discharge all other partners, but the Act of 1862, which authorizes a composition or compromise with one or more joint debtors, also applies to partnerships. 35 37 

35 73 Pa. Superior Ct. 235 (1919). 

38 Baxter v. Wunder, 89 Pa. Superior Ct. 585 (1926).

Part 4. Tenancy in Partnership Sec. 696. Partnership Property. The estate of the partners in partnership property is called tenancy in partnership. This estate has some rather peculiar characteristics. The partners as a whole, and not as individuals, are entitled to the possession and disposition of it. It may not be assigned by a partner, it is not subject to attachment except on a claim against the partnership, no part of it may be claimed under the debtor's exemption law, and when one partner dies it automatically passes to the surviving partners for liquidation. It is not subject to dower or allowances to 

37 Act of March 22, 1862, P. L. 167, 59 PS 135.

485 1 E 5 widows, and does not pass to the heirs or next of kin of a deceased partner. 

Wharf v. Wharf, 306 Illinois 79 (1922). Two partners were engaged in the real estate business. Title to lands was taken in the names of both partners individually. One of them died, and there remained, after the settlement of partnership obligations, fiftyeight lots for distribution. The heirs at law of the deceased partner claimed title by descent. In deciding that title vested in the surviving partner, it was said by CARTWRIGHT, J. "It seems that the legislative intention (as expressed in the Uniform Partnership Act) was to adopt the English rule, that real estate which becomes personal property for the purposes of a partnership remains personal property for the purpose of distribution." 39 

Sec. 697. Real Estate. The code provides that real estate may be acquired in the partnership name, and that title so acquired can be conveyed only in the partnership name. More commonly, such real estate is taken in the names of the individual partners, a matter which gives rise to some difficulty. Where real estate is purchased and paid for with partnership funds it is regarded as partnership property, although title is taken in the name of the partners.38 It may be shown by parol evidence or otherwise that it was purchased with partnership funds for partnership purposes, and if so it becomes the personal property of the partnership. It may seem unusual for real property to become personalty when owned by a partnership, but this is an old and well established legal fiction.40 If it is found to be partnership property it may, so far as the partners are concerned, be conveyed by a single partner as personal property, free of dower. The statute provides that if title is in the name of one of the partners and he conveys it without the authority of his co-partners, it may be recovered by the partnership unless the purchaser is a holder for value. Pennsylvania follows the rule that the purchaser may rely on the record title, unless he has notice of the firm's ownership." 41

Sec. 698. Assignment of Interest. While a partner may not, acting for himself, assign partnership property, he may assign his own interest in the profits and surplus of the partnership. This is personal property. 

An assignment of such an interest would not of itself cause a dissolution. The assignee would have no authority, however, to interfere in the management of partnership affairs. The assignment merely entitles the assignee to receive the profits which the assigning partner would otherwise be entitled. 

Herman v. Pepper, 311 Pa. 104 (1933). Herman, Bobb and Raymond J. Pepper were partners engaged in the building and operation of apartment houses. Herman mortgaged his interest to John 

W. Pepper.

Thereafter John W. Pepper took Bobb's place with the consent of all concerned. The partnership then consisted of 

Herman, Raymond J. Pepper, John W. Pepper. Sometime later the latter two partners took the position that because of the mortgage, Herman was no longer a partner and had no interest in the property. DREW, J. "By the execution of a mortgage on his interest, complainant did not cease to be a partner, nor was he deprived of his rights as such." 

Sec. 699. Insolvency of Partner. Occasionally a partner becomes insolvent, although the partnership is a prosperous concern. Such personal insolvency may result from failure to live within one's income, the expense of maintaining children in college, an accident giving rise to personal liability, and the like. In an action by his personal creditors, the partnership may become involved. The code furnishes a solution without being very specific. The judgment creditor may have a charging order. 42 This would entitle him to the insolvent partner's share in the profits of the partnership, and after dissolution his share in the partnership assets. 

The court "may then or later appoint a receiver of his share of the profits, or of any other money due or to fall due to him in respect of the partnership, and make all other orders, directions, accounts and inquiries which the debtor partner might have made, or which the cir- 

42 Northampton Brewery Corp. v. Lande, 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 181 (1938).

PARTNERSHIPS 

487 cumstances of the case may require." If the partnership is at will or the term has expired, the creditor may obtain a dissolution. The interest charged may be redeemed by the other partners, before foreclosure, without causing a dissolution. The use of partnership property for this purpose would automatically reduce the insolvent or debtor partner's interest in the partnership. 

Any one of the partners may redeem such interest with separate property.

Part 5. Change of Partners 

Sec. 700. Incoming Partner. No person may become a member of an existing partnership without the consent of all the partners. A person who is admitted as a member is liable for all the obligations of the partnership arising before his admission, except that this liability may be satisfied only out of partnership property. The reason is, that a new partner was not a party to the contracts under which such obligations were created. This is a statutory rule. An incoming partner may agree to become personally liable for past obligations. This is accomplished by an assignment which expressly constitutes the assignee a member of the firm during the entire period of its previous existence. Under these circumstances, all the incidents of the partnership relation attach to the membership thus created, including not only the right to participate in the profits and the distribution of assets, but also the correlative duty of sharing losses and contributing to the payment of the debts of the firm which had their origin prior to the assignment.43 

Sec. 701. Withdrawing Partner. Sometime prior to the adoption of the Uniform Partnership Act, it was said by the Supreme Court: "It may be considerable inconvenience to the retiring partner, but it is certainly no great hardship, to hold that he shall give actual no- 

43 Earon v. Mackey, 106 Pa. 452 (1884).

tice of withdrawal to all who have trusted the partnership because of his connection with it, otherwise he shall remain answerable to those who have a right to believe him still a member." 44 In a case decided in 1860, notice of the withdrawal of a partner was published in the newspapers of Chambersburg, where the firm had principally transacted its business, but it was held that this publication was not sufficient to preclude a creditor on obligations incurred thereafter, whose place of business was Baltimore, and who had no notice of the withdrawal.45 The code provides that where a third party has extended credit to the firm prior to (and has no knowledge of) the withdrawal of a partner, or where a third party has known of the partnership prior to (and has no knowledge of) the withdrawal of a partner, notice of the withdrawal of a partner should be advertised in a newspaper of general circulation at each place where the partnership business has been regularly carried on, and in the legal periodical, if any, designated by rule of court in such place or places for the publication of legal notices. 

Sec. 702. Notice by Partnership. It is almost as essential for the partnership to give notice of the withdrawal of a member, or of the dissolution of the firm, as it is for a withdrawing member to do so, otherwise the remaining partners might find themselves involved in contracts made between the partner who has withdrawn and others who have had previous dealings with the firm or who have had no notice or knowledge of the withdrawal or dissolution. This notice may be published in the manner indicated above. 

Part 6. Relations between Partners 

Sec. 703. Profits. Partners may agree to share in the profits of the business in other than equal shares. 

Unless they agree otherwise, each partner is entitled to 

44 Robinson v. Floyd, 159 Pa. 178 (1893). 

45 Deford & Co. v. Reynolds, 36 Pa. 325 (1860).

PARTNERSHIPS 

489 share equally in the profits and surplus. It is not unusual for laymen to assume that profits are to be distributed in proportion to the capital contribution of each partner, but if one partner contributes all the capital and his co-partner does all the work, should the partner who contributes all the capital receive all the profits? 

Sec. 704. Losses. Partners may agree to share in the losses of the business otherwise than equally. If they do not so agree, the following rule appears in the code: "Each partner shall be repaid his contributions, whether by way of capital or advances to the partnership property, and share equally in the profits and surplus remaining after all liabilities, including those to partners, are satisfied; and must contribute towards the losses, whether of capital or otherwise, sustained by the partnership, according to his share in the profits." 

Following are applications of this rule: (1) Capital and Surplus. A contributes $10,000 and B contributes $20,000 to the partnership capital. At dissolution the net assets of the firm for distribution amount to $32,000. A's share is his $10,000 capital contribution plus $1,000 (one-half the surplus). B's share is his $20,000 capital contribution plus $1,000 (one-half the surplus.) 46 (2) Capital and No Surplus. A contributes $10,000 and B contributes $20,000 to the partnership capital. At dissolution the net assets for distribution amount to $30,000. A's share is his capital contribution of $10,000. B's share is his capital contribution of $20,000.47 (3) Capital Impaired. A contributes $10,000 and B contributes $20,000 to the partnership capital. At dissolution the net assets for distribution amount to $20,000. A's share is his capital contribution of $10,000 less $5,000 (one-half the loss), or $5,000. B's share is his capital contribution of $20,000 less $5,000 (one-half the loss), or $15,000.48 (4) No Capital or Surplus. A contributes $10,000 and B promises to contribute $20,000 to the capital of the partnership. B

47 See Glenn v. Weill, 319 Pa. 380 (1935).

never makes the contribution. At dissolution the partnership has no assets left to distribute. A is entitled to recover one-half the loss of the partnership capital, or $5,000, from B.49 

Sec. 705. Liabilities. The statute provides that partners shall contribute the amount necessary to satisfy the liabilities. If one of the partners is insolvent, or is not subject to process, the remaining partners must contribute his share of the loss in the same proportion. 

Let us assume that A, B and C are partners. Their agreement provides that A is to receive three-twelfths, B is to receive four-twelfths, and C is to receive fivetwelfths of the profits. The business fails and the loss, after all assets have been exhausted, amounts to $24,000. 

This amount is still owing to the creditors of the business. A should contribute $6,000, B should contribute $8,000, and C should contribute $10,000, inasmuch as they were to receive profits in this same proportion. If 

B is insolvent or is not subject to legal process, A and C must contribute his share of the loss, $8,000, in the same proportion that they were entitled to the profits. If we divide $8,000 into eight parts, A would have to contribute three-eighths, or $3,000, and C would have to contribute five-eighths, or $5,000, in order to make up the amount that B should have paid. Whenever one partner is required to pay more than his proportionate share of the losses, he is entitled to contribution from his co-partners, assuming, of course, he is fortunate enough to be able to recover it. Where the agreement provides that the losses are to be shared equally, but that one partner should in no event be put to a loss of more than a certain amount, he is entitled to recover from his co-partners any payment in excess of that amount.50

Sec. 706. Income During Liquidation. Income re ceived by the partnership during liquidation, but before the assets of the partnership are distributed, is allocated 

40 See Emerick v. Moir, 124 Pa. 498 (1889). 

50 Magilton v. Stevenson, 173 Pa. 560 (1896).

PARTNERSHIPS 

491 to the respective shares of capital to which each partner is entitled as of the date of dissolution.

Wood v. Wood, 312 Pa. 374 (1933). Stuart and Walter Wood were partners. Stuart contributed $726,014.16 and agreed to share 

23/65ths of the profits and losses. Walter contributed $409,813.31 and agreed to share 42/65ths of the profits and losses. After the death of Stuart, and during the period of liquidation, income was received in the sum of $563,079.27 from interest on bonds and dividends on stock owned by the partnership at the time of dissolution. The principal question involved was whether this income should be distributed as capital or profits. LINN, J. "We agree that the decisive date for the purposes in question is the date of dissolution. On that date, March 2, 1914, the relative rights of the partners became fixed, and each partner, or his representative, became entitled to take out his share of the capital, creditors having been paid. If it could not then be delivered because the amount required ascertainment by winding up, he was nevertheless to be treated from that time as owner of it, and, therefore, entitled to receive what it earned from that time until paid or delivered to him. On that date, each partner became a creditor of the capital in the then net value of his contribution." 

Sec. 707. Management. The partners should agree among themselves as to how the partnership should be managed. If they have not done so, "All partners have equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership business." It is a well settled principle that a majority, acting fairly and in good faith, may direct the conduct of a partnership, as long as they keep within the purpose and scope of the partnership business.51 

Clark v. State Valley Ry. Co., 136 Pa. 408 (1890). Two out of three partners authorized a law suit against the defendant on a contract for the construction of a railway. The lower court ruled that such action required the approval of all the partners. In deciding otherwise, it was said by WILLIAMS, J. "In such case, the minority must yield so long as the majority do not transcend or pervert the powers with which the firm has been invested. If the number of partners should in any given case be an even number, and they should be evenly divided in opinion, with no provision for such contingency in their articles, then it may be that, as to that subject, the power of the firm to act is suspended, so long as the even division continues; and if the subject be one upon 

51 Markle v. Wilbur, 200 Pa. 457 (1901).

which action is essential for the purposes of the partnership, such disagreement might work a dissolution by rendering the further prosecution of the common enterprise impossible." 

Sec. 708. Compensation. Unless the partners have agreed otherwise,52 "No partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the partnership business, except that a surviving partner is entitled to reasonable compensation for his services in winding up the partnership affairs." In Herman v. Pepper,53 a partnership was dissolved by judicial decree and a receiver was appointed to operate the business. The receiver retained one of the partners to manage certain apartments. Complaint was made because of the allowance of compensation for his services, but it was pointed out that the partner was retained as an employee of the receiver and was entitled to compensation for acting in that capacity. 

Sec. 709. Partnership Books. The code provides that, "The partnership books shall be kept, subject to any agreement between the partners, at the principal place of business of the partnership, and every partner shall at all times have access to and may inspect and copy any of them." The code also provides that, "Partners shall render on demand true and full information of all things affecting the partnership to any partner, or the legal representative of any deceased partner, or partner under legal disability.” 

Sec. 710. Fiduciary Relation. Each partner is accountable as a fiduciary. This requires the highest degree of integrity and good faith. 

McCutcheon v. Smith, 173 Pa. 101 (1896). Smith and Mc- 

Cutcheon, doing business as George F. Smith & Company, desired to dispose of a certain farm owned by the firm. Smith found a purchaser, Rolshouse, who was willing to pay $8,500. He went to his partner, and without disclosing this information, succeeded in purchasing his partner's interest for $2,500. The sale to Rolshouse followed. Upon discovery of these facts, McCutcheon filed a bill in equity for an accounting. STERRETT, C. J. “In view of the facts 

53 317 Pa. 349 (1935). 

52 Curtis v. Mankus, 295 Pa. 381 (1929).

PARTNERSHIPS 

493 thus conclusively established, the master was fully warranted in his conclusions that Smith's duty in the premises was to fully inform McCutcheon of the Rolshouse contract; that the relation of trust and confidence, which had so long bound them together, could not be severed by the one buying out the other's interest in the farm without first divulging to the fullest extent all the knowledge he possessed concerning their joint enterprise."

Sec. 711. Use of Firm Property. The same rule applies where one partner has made a secret profit in the partnership business by exploiting a by-product of the business, or has used partnership property or funds in separate ventures. 

Bracht v. Connell, 313 Pa. 397 (1934). Three partners associated themselves for the purpose of carrying on a road construction business. Two of them, without the knowledge of the other, with the use of firm funds, bid on and obtained a large contract in West Virginia for building a hard surfaced road. KEPHART, J. "Appellants considered the contract for the construction of the West Virginia road their own. They made it in good faith and the court below was unable to discover bad faith or fraudulent intent in their actions, and we concur in that finding. Appellants were led to the conclusion that they had a right to make this contract, by their conduct in other prior instances when they made similar contracts which had the apparent assent of appellee, though he denied knowing anything about them. Appellants were under the impression they might perform the West Virginia contract as their own. They were mistaken as to the legal aspect of their action in making this contract with the aid of partnership funds as Judge PARKER finds. The result is that the law imposes on the contract a partnership status at dissolution and gives appellee the right at dissolution either to have the contract distributed, that is, lawfully appraised, so that appellee could receive the value of his interest, or, appellee, being denied this, could require appellants to account for his proportion of the profit."

Sec. 712. Right to Account. A partner is entitled to a formal account from his co-partners whenever he is wrongfully excluded from the business, or possession of partnership property, or under the terms of any agreement, or for breach of the fiduciary relation, or whenever other circumstances render it just and reasonable, and notwithstanding the equitable doctrine of clean

hands. "This is so because one partner cannot sue another at law on an unsettled partnership account." 5+ 

Where one partner makes repeated demands of what is due, but is unable to procure a settlement, he may be justified in demanding interest from the time the partnership accounts should have been settled.55 A partner should keep partnership funds unmixed with his own and equally within the grasp of the other partners. If he deposits them in a bank in his own name, to the exclusion of his co-partner, and loss occurs therefrom, he alone must bear it.56 "The general rule is firmly established that one who, while acting in a fiduciary capacity, mixes with his own money the funds under his control, is liable either for interest thereon or a share of the profits in lieu of interest, at the option of the cestui que trust." 57 

Part 7. Actions Involving Partnerships Sec. 713. Actions by Partnerships. The Rules of 

Civil Procedure provide that, "A partnership having a right of action shall prosecute such right in the names of the then partners trading in the firm name, in the following manner: 'A, B and C trading as X & Co.""

Similarly, "An action prosecuted by the liquidator of a dissolved partnership shall be prosecuted in the name of the liquidator in the following manner: 'A, Liquidator of A, B and C, late trading as X & Co.'" 58 This rule is mandatory. If a defect appears, however, it may be cured by amendment of parties.59

Sec. 714. Actions against Partnerships. The Rules of Civil Procedure provide that an action against a partnership may be brought against one or more partners as individuals trading in the firm name, or "against the partnership in its firm name." 60

Aside from the well known grounds for equitable relief, certain broad principles distinguish each jurisdiction. 

It was observed in Section 674 that an action at law is the proper remedy for breach of an executory agreement to form a partnership. Other circumstances may now be considered. 

Sec. 717. Non-Partnership Transactions. There are two circumstances under which a partner may enter into an obligation personal to him. First, the code provides that a partner may enter into a separate obligation to perform a partnership contract. It has been held, accordingly, that where a creditor of a partnership accepted a note of one partner for a firm debt, with full knowledge of the existence of the partnership, he could not, after recovering judgment against him, levy on the partnership goods in satisfaction of the judgment." 

Second, a partner, acting for himself or with others, may enter into a business transaction with the partnership of which he is a member. The remedy for breach of such an agreement is an action at law, whether the action be instituted by the partner or by the partnership. 

Seanor v. Fitt, 263 Pa. 389 (1919). Seanor, Fitt and Hileman were partners. Seanor sold certain goods to the partnership. The other two partners personally agreed to pay one-third of the appraised value of the goods. Seanor brought an action in assumpsit for breach of this agreement. SIMPSON, J. "When the stock was appraised, Hileman paid his one-third, but Fitt paid only a portion of his, and his attempt, at the two trials of the case, was to tangle up the matter with the later affairs of the partnership. In this he was unsuccessful, as he should have been. So far as the duty to pay was concerned, it was an individual and not a partnership transaction." 

Sec. 718. Wrongful Dissolution. An action at law is also the proper remedy to recover damages resulting 

74 White v. Rech, 171 Pa. 87 (1895). 

73 Act of May 14, 1915, P. L. 483, 12 PS 393.

from the dissolution of a partnership wrongfully brought about by one of the partners. 

McCollum v. Carlucci, 206 Pa. 312 (1903). Lord and Carlucci were partners operating a quarry. In order to bring about a wrongful dissolution of the partnership, Carlucci declared the business at an end, notified creditors not to pay partnership obligations to Lord, advised the employees of the partnership to reduce their claims to judgment and sell out the partnership property, which he himself purchased, and obtained an assignment of the lease of the quarry upon which he entered judgment for default in the payment of rent, etc. Lord having died, his executors brought an action in assumpsit for breach of the partnership agreement. Defendant resisted the form of the action. BROWN, J. "The finding of the jury has sustained Lord's contention that the partnership was wrongfully dissolved by Carlucci, and the representatives of his estate are not asking for an accounting, but for damages resulting from Carlucci's broken covenants and wrongful dissolution of the partnership. The remedy for the wrong sued for is neither an action of account nor bill in equity, but is in assumpsit on the broken contract."

Part 8. Termination of Partnerships Sec. 719. Causes of Dissolution. A partnership may be dissolved (1) by the partners themselves, (2) by operation of law, and (3) by judicial decree. As summarized in the code: (1) A partnership may be dissolved by the partners themselves at the end of the term agreed upon, or when the purpose of the partnership has been accomplished, or at will when the partnership is at will, or by the express will of all partners who have not assigned their interests or suffered them to be charged for their separate debts, or by the expulsion of a partner as may be authorized in the articles of copartnership. Dissolution may also be caused, in contravention of the agreement between the partners, by the express will of any partner at any time, but subject to liability for breach of the partnership agreement. (2) A partnership is dissolved by operation of law upon the death of a partner, or upon the bankruptcy of a partner or the partnership, or by war making the partners alien enemies, and by a change of law making the business illegal. (3) A partnership may be dissolved by judicial decree upon the insanity of a partner, or when a partner becomes otherwise incapable of performing his part of the

PARTNERSHIPS 

499 agreement, or when the conduct of a partner tends to effect prejudicially the carrying on of the business, or because of the wilful and consistent breach of the partnership agreement, or when the business can only be carried on at a loss, and when other circumstances render a dissolution equitable. 

The partners may agree upon terms of dissolution different from those provided for in the original agreement.75 A court of equity will not decree a dissolution of a prosperous business except upon substantial grounds. As said by the Supreme Court: "Differences and discord should be settled by the partners themselves by the application of mutual forbearance rather than by bills in equity for dissolution. Equity is not a referee of partnership quarrels. A going and prosperous business will not be dissolved merely because of friction among the partners; it will not interfere to determine which contending faction is more at fault." 76 The code provides that where a partnership agreement is rescinded on grounds of fraud, the injured partner is entitled to a lien on the surplus of partnership property after satisfying partnership liabilities to third parties, for any sum of money paid for the purchase of an interest in the partnership, and to stand in the place of the creditors for payments made by him for partnership liabilities. He is also entitled to be indemnified by the person guilty of the fraud. 

Sec. 720. Liquidation. A partnership is not terminated on dissolution, but continues until the winding up of partnership affairs is completed, including transactions begun but not then finished. Otherwise, dissolution terminates the authority of a partner to act for the partnership, or to bind the partnership with third parties after the fact of dissolution has been properly advertised. It has been held that a creditor who extended credit in new transactions, with notice of dissolution, did so at his peril." Unless the partnership agree-

The expense of liquidation may, according to the equities of the case, be charged to both capital and income.78 During the process of liquidation, it may be necessary to renew a partnership obligation after the death of one of the partners. 

Heller's Estate, 319 Pa. 135 (1935). A partnership, Sol Heller & Sons, executed three notes, which were renewed by the surviving partners after the death of Sol Heller. The latter's executors denied liability on the notes on the ground that the renewals were executed subsequent to his death. This contention was sustained by the lower court. In deciding otherwise, it was said by LINN, J. "During the period necessary to wind up the business, the surviving partners had the same power to bind the partnership and decedent's estate (subject to rights of separate creditors) that they had during his lifetime, provided their acts were directed toward the liquidation of the business."

Sec. 721. Priority of Creditors. The code provides that when partnership property and the individual properties of the partners are in the possession of a court for distribution, partnership creditors should have priority on partnership property, and separate creditors on individual property, except as to the rights of lien or secured creditors. Claims of partnership creditors against partnership property rank in the following order: (1) Those owing to creditors other than partners. (2) Those owing to partners other than for capital. (3) Those owing to partners in respect of capital. (4) Those owing to partners in respect of profits. Where a partner has become bankrupt or his estate is insolvent, the claims of creditors against his separate property rank in the following order: (1) Those owing to separate creditors. (2) Those owing to partnership creditors. (3) Those owing to partners by way of contribution.

Sec. 722. Authorized Continuance. The surviving partner, or the personal representative of a deceased partner, may carry on the business where the partnership agreement so provides, or the deceased partner directs by will that this should be done." No new partnership is thereby created." The primary purpose of such an arrangement is to afford the surviving partners a reasonable time in which to liquidate the interest of the deceased partner. An agreement among partners that the business may be continued after the death of one of the partners, is subject to the right of the surviving spouse of the deceased partner to take against his will.81 It may be more practical for the partners to agree that in case of the death of one partner, his interest may be purchased by the surviving partners at the terms agreed upon. Such an agreement may be specifically enforced." 82 

Sec. 723. Unauthorized Continuance. The code provides that if the business is continued by the surviving partner without any settlement, and unless otherwise agreed, the representative of the deceased partner may have the value of decedent's interest ascertained as of the date of dissolution, and may elect to receive the value of this property with interest, or the profits attributable to the use of the property. "In such case the surviving partner acts at his risk and if no profits are made or if a loss results he must bear the entire deficit and pay to the estate the share to which it is entitled, together with interest." 88 Occasionally a widow takes her deceased husband's place in the formation of a new partnership, without disturbing the partnership capital. It has been held, however, that she may not compromise the inheritance of the children of the deceased partner in so doing."4 Where a widow

Part 9. Special Partnerships 

Sec. 724. Limited Partnership. Pennsylvania adopted the Uniform Limited Partnership Act in 1917.80

The purpose of this statute is to permit an inactive or dormant partner to contribute to the capital of the partnership and participate in the profits, but without subjecting him to the liability of a general partner. An arrangement of this sort is a pure creature of statute. 

It is defined as an association by two or more persons having as members one or more general partners and one or more limited partners. The liability of a limited partner is limited to his capital contribution, or such as he has agreed to make, but this privilege is extended to him provided he takes no part in the control of the business. Because of this circumstance, the public is entitled to know the identity of a limited partner and the contribution he has agreed to make. This is accomplished by filing the certificate of co-partnership in the office of the recorder of deeds of the county in which the principal place of business may be located. 

This certificate must be comprehensive of the details of the partnership. Upon dissolution the assets of such a partnership are distributed first to creditors, second to limited partners, and third to general partners, according to the degree of their respective claims. 

Sec. 725. Partnership Association. In 1874 the legislature authorized a partnership of three or more persons in which the liability of all members should be

The duration of such an association was fixed at twenty years from the date of its organization, or from the date of an amendment to its certificate,88 but the Act of 193189 authorizes a renewal for an additional period of twenty years. A comprehensive certificate must be filed with the recorder of deeds. 

A partnership association has many of the characteristics of a corporation. It may adopt a common seal," as well as by-laws, sue and be sued in the association name, acquire and dispose of real property,⁹¹ and declare dividends in an amount that will not impair its capital stock. It is managed by a board of managers of from three to nine members,92 whose function is similar to that of the board of directors of a corporation. The interests of its members are transferable, except that a transferee may not participate in the business unless elected to membership.93 Upon dissolution the assets of the association are distributed first, to the payment of all debts for wages of labor, second, to the satisfaction of its other liabilities and indebtedness, and third, to its members in proportion to their respective interests.

Sec. 727. Bonus on Capital Stock. The Act of 1927, as last amended in 1945, imposes a bonus of one-fifth of one per centum, for state purposes, upon the amount of the stated capital with which any corporation, partnership association, or registered partnership, will begin business, and upon the amount of actual increase thereof.96 The Act of 1929 provides that the recorder of deeds may not accept articles of partnership or amendments thereto unless a receipt for this tax is recorded therewith, and that if the tax is not paid the articles shall be void and the members held liable as general partners. In addition, the Act of 193198 provides that every limited partnership and joint-stock association shall file a registration statement with the Department of Revenue. 97

Sec. 729. Defective Partnerships. Joint stock com panies were quite common in colonial times owing to the expense and difficulty of obtaining charters of incorporation. They are a curiosity in modern times, and usually result from a failure to comply with statutes designed to limit the liability of partners. 

Fairman Brothers v. Ogden Gas Co., 106 Pa. Superior Ct. 130 

(1932). Ogden was the owner of an oil and gas lease. By his efforts an association was formed to operate the lease, and the name "Ogden Gas Company" was adopted to represent the parties in their operations in this lease. Shares or interest similar to certificates of stock were issued. KELLER, J. "After full consideration

of the evidence taken on the rule to open the above judgment, we are of opinion that the parties composing the Ogden Gas Company were not operating the oil and gas lease as tenants in common but as a joint stock company, and as they had not complied with the provisions of the Act of June 2, 1874, P. L. 271, limiting the liability of the subscribers or contributors for the debts of such association to the capital subscribed, or the acts relating to limited partnerships (April 12, 1917, P. L. 55), or registered limited liability partnerships (May 9, 1899, P. L. 261), that they were liable for such debt as partners. It may be that on the trial of the issue in court other evidence may be introduced that will support a different conclusion, but as now presented our judgment is as above stated."

CHAPTER XIX  Part 1. Nature of Corporations Sec. 730. Business Corporation. The corporate form of business organization had its origin in the trade guilds of the mediaeval period and in joint stock companies for the control of trade, notably the Company of 

Merchants of London Trading to the East Indies. This 

Company was chartered in 1600. The Bank of England received its charter in 1694, but until that time there were few business corporations in existence. One of the first nonprofit corporations chartered in America was the Presbyterian Ministers' Fund, which received its charter from the proprietors of the Province of Pennsylvania in 1759. One of the first business corporations chartered in America was the Philadelphia Contributionship for Insuring Houses from Loss by Fire. This was in 1768. Prior to 1933 corporations in Pennsylvania were divided into two general classes. Nonprofit corporations were then known as corporations of the first class. The business corporation was known as a corporation of the second class. These same corporations are known today as nonprofit and business corporations, both of which are governed by separate codes enacted by the legislature in 1933. 2 

Sec. 731. Corporation Defined. The Business Cor poration Code of 1933¹ "is, in part, a declaration and codification of, and, in part, a supplement to, the prior law on the subject." It will be referred to in this, and in the following two chapters, as the "code." A corporation for profit, as defined in the code, "means a corporation organized for the direct or indirect pecuniary profit of its shareholders." A corporation has been 

1 Act of May 5, 1933, P. L. 364, 15 PS 2852-1. 

2 Bowman v. Gum, Inc., 821 Pa. 516 (1936). 507

defined by the Supreme Court of the United States as "an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of law." 3 

Commonwealth v. Fall Brook Coal Co., 156 Pa. 488 (1893). 

WILLIAMS, J. "The corporation comes into existence, like a natural person, naked. The money furnished by those whose representative it is to be, is its capital stock. The amount that each person contributes to this fund is his share in the venture, and is called his share or shares in the stock. The legal title to the whole sum so contributed is in the corporation, and so is the legal title to all the property real or personal in which it may be invested. The equitable title, that is, the right to the profits from the business done, and to a return of the capital when the corporation is dissolved, is in the stockholders. There is one estate, one business, but the title has been divided, by the separation of the power of control, from the right to receive the profits." 

Sec. 732. Federal Constitution. The charter of a corporation is a contract with the state. Both the state* and the federal constitution prohibit the impairment of contracts. It was early decided that both, as existing when a corporate charter is granted, are a part of that contract, the obligations of which may not be impaired either by the state or by the federal government without the consent of the corporation. 

Dartmouth College v. Woodward, 4 Wheat. 518 (1819). The charter of Dartmouth College provided that it should be governed by a board of twelve trustees, and should "hereafter forever to consist, of twelve and no more." In 1816 the legislature of New 

Hampshire increased the number to twenty-one, and also established a board of twenty-five overseers. The corporation challenged the constitutionality of this enactment. MARSHALL, C. J. "The opinion of the court, after mature deliberation is, that this is a contract, the obligation of which cannot be impaired, without violating the Constitution of the United States." 

Sec. 733. State Constitution. In order to subject corporations to a reasonable degree of public control, the present constitution, as adopted in 1874, contains the following provision:

The foregoing is incorporated in the code." This ex- plains why a charter in Pennsylvania may be granted in perpetuity. The constitution further provides that, "the exercise of the police power of the State shall never be abridged or so construed as to permit corporations to conduct their business in such manner as to infringe the equal rights of individuals or the general well-being of the State." 9

The corporation is as fully controlled by the Constitution and laws pursuant thereto as though incorporated thereunder, provided however such acts do not overthrow its previously granted corporate existence, identity, or the powers necessary to its life. Sec. 735. Shareholders Distinguished. Inasmuch as a corporation is a legal entity it is necessary to distinguish sharply between the identity of the corporation and that of its shareholders. They "are not one and the same. The latter are not owners of the property of the corporation, but the title to the property rests exclusively in the entity called the corporation. 99 12 

Monongahela Bridge Co. v. P. & B. Traction Co., 196 Pa. 25 (1900). Plaintiff instituted this action against the defendant to recover tolls for the use of its bridge. Defendant denied liability on the ground that the City of Pittsburgh had purchased all the stock of the bridge company, and that as a consequence the property was owned by the city. MESTREZAT, J. "It does not follow, however, that the city is the owner of the property of the company because it purchased its stock. We have been referred to no authority, and we know of none, that asserts the doctrine that the purchaser of all the shares of the capital stock of a corporation thereby becomes the owner of its property. On the contrary the principle is well established that the shares of the capital stock of a corporation are essentially distinct and different from the corporate property, and that the owner of all the stock of a corporation does not own the corporate property or become entitled to manage or control it." 

Sec. 736. Officers Distinguished. It is also necessary to distinguish between the separate identity of the corporation and its officers. As said in Magaw v.

Bloomsburg Heating Company,13 "The fact that these two companies had identical officers and stockholders did not affect their legal status as separate and distinct corporations." 

Donaldson v. Andresen, 300 Pa. 312 (1930). Andresen owned the stock of the McCracken-Robinson, Inc., a reorganized concern, and was president and one of its directors. The company published a magazine known as "Motor Coach Transportation." After considerable effort to rehabilitate the business, and at considerable personal expense, he sold his stock to another company and agreed not to engage in the same business for a period of ten years. A creditor of the corporation, not being paid, instituted this action to compel him to account for the amount received for 

12 Puritan Coal Mining Co. v. Pa. 

R. R. Co., 237 Pa. 420 (1912). 

13 117 Pa. Superior Ct. 540 (1935).

his stock. WALLING, J. "It is a novel proposition in Pennsylvania that the owner of corporate stock is precluded from selling it in good faith merely because he happens to be an officer of the corporation. . . . As Andresen owned the stock, the right to its proceeds did not belong to the creditors. He neither sold the corporate assets nor converted them to his own use."

Sec. 737. Liability for Torts. The liability of a corporation for its torts is the same as that of an individual. 

Pa. Iron Works Co. v. Henry Voght Machine Co., 29 Ken tucky 861 (1906). A Pennsylvania corporation opened a branch office at Louisville, Kentucky. It was engaged in the manufacture of ice machines. The corporation made an unsuccessful bid for the installation of machines, whereupon the local manager wrote a libelous letter, on behalf of his company, concerning the successful bidder. In sustaining an action for damages against the corporation, it was said by CARROLL, C. J. "Corporations transact all their business through agents; and when the agent is acting in the course of his business and within the scope of his employment, the corporation will be held accountable for his acts and doings in the same degree as an individual will be held answerable for torts perpetrated by him in his individual capacity. 

When an action will lie against an individual for a tort, it will lie against a corporation, if the tort was committed by its agent or servant in the scope of his employment." 

Sec. 738. Torts of Officers. A corporate officer may not hide behind the cloak of the corporate entity in an effort to escape individual responsibility for his own. tortious wrongs. 

Pearl Assur. Co., Ltd. v. Nat. Ins. Agency, Inc., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 146 (1943). Plaintiff brought an action in trespass against a corporate insurance broker and its president, for net premiums on certain insurance policies wrongfully withheld by defendants. In affirming a judgment against the president of the corporation, as well as against the corporation, it was said by 

KELLER, P. J. "With respect to the question of the defendant

Rovno's personal liability to the appellee company, it should be noted that he was not only the owner of all the stock of the corporate defendant, as well as its president and authorized agent, but he also personally did all the acts involved in the transactions complained of in this action."

Sec. 739. Liability for Crimes. A corporation is amenable to the criminal laws, except felonies and malicious wrongs. It may be held for other crimes, such as assault and battery, obtaining money under false pretense, violation of the child labor laws, and accepting rebates in violation of law, where it can be reached for punishment by fine and seizure of its property. 

New York Central & H. R. R. Co. v. U. S., 212 U. S. 481 (1909). 

A railroad corporation was convicted of granting rebates in violation of the Interstate Commerce Act, and appealed from the conviction, contending that a corporation was incapable of committing a crime. In overruling this contention, it was said by 

DAY, J. "It is true that there are some crimes which in their nature cannot be committed by corporations. But there is a large class of offenses, of which rebating under the federal statute is one, wherein the crime consists in purposely doing the things prohibited by statute. In that class of crimes, we see no good reason why a corporation may not be held responsible for and charged with the knowledge and purposes of their agents acting within the authority conferred upon them." 

Part 2. Corporate Entity Disregarded Sec. 740. Public Policy. The legal entity of a cor poration will be disregarded, generally, where the shareholders are using the corporation as an instrument with which to evade creditors, or defraud the public, or avoid statutory regulations, or create a monopoly, or commit a crime. In the following case it was held that equity would not, as between partners owning all the stock of a corporation, decree an accounting of the profits of the business obtained by conducting an illegal liquor business with the knowledge of the partners. 

Tucker v. Binenstock, 310 Pa. 254 (1933). KEPHART, J. "The fiction of a corporation as an entity distinct from the aggregate of individuals composing it was designed to serve convenience and justice. There is consequently an exception recognized wherever the rule is known, namely, that the fiction will be disregarded and the individuals and corporation considered as identical whenever justice or public policy demand it and when the rights of innocent parties are not prejudiced thereby nor the theory of corporate entity made useless."

Sec. 741. Fraudulent Transfer. A creditor may disregard the corporate entity in order to follow the assets of his debtor into the possession of a corporation, provided the debtors and shareholders are substantially the same, and no discrimination will result between secured and unsecured creditors.15 14 

Kulka v. Nemirovsky, 321 Pa. 234 (1936). Plaintiff obtained judgment against a partnership. One-half of this judgment was paid by an insurance company. The partners then incorporated and transferred partnership assets to the corporation. The lower court found that the partners and the shareholders were the same identical persons, and held that the property transferred to the corporation was liable for the judgment obtained against the partnership. KEPHART, C. J. "When a partnership transfers its assets to a corporation composed of substantially the same members as was the partnership, the creditor cannot be deprived of his prior right against the partnership assets and he may follow these assets into the corporation and enforce payment of his claim therefrom."

Sec. 742. Intercorporate Dealings. Where the shareholders of two corporations are the same, a creditor may also follow the assets of one corporation into the possession of another.16 Creditors may also nullify a fraudulent transfer from one company to another. 

Halpern v. Grabosky, 296 Pa. 108 (1929). KEPHART, J. "Where the sale of corporate assets creates a preference, or is made with intent to defraud creditors, their rights are safeguarded in law. 

Creditors may pursue the assets in the hands of the new company through judgment against the old company, or they may by proper proceedings fasten a constructive trust as to such assets on the new company as trustee, with liability to account for such assets; or the new company may assume payment of the debts. . . 

Sec. 743. Subsidiary Corporation. A more difficult problem is presented with respect to the relation of a parent corporation to its subsidiary. The general rule is that the two corporations are distinct corporate entities, even though the directors are identical and the parent corporation is the sole stockholder." Pennsyl- 

14 Summit Hosiery Co. v. Gottschall, 292 Pa. 464 (1928). 

15 Coaldale Coal Co. v. State Bank, 142 Pa. 288 (1891). 

10 Montgomery-Webb Co. v. Deinelt, 133 Pa. 585 (1890). 

17 Callery's Appeal, 272 Pa. 255 (1922).

vania follows the rule that the parent corporation is not liable for the obligations of its subsidiary, in the absence of fraud or bad faith, unfair dealing, or the commission of unlawful acts on the part of the parent company.' 

In bankruptcy and receivership cases, if the parent corporation is a creditor of its subsidiary, it may have to yield to other creditors if it so dominates and controls the subsidiary that the latter is a mere agent or instrumentality of the former. In tort cases the parent corporation may be held liable for the torts of an employee of the subsidiary if this same situation exists. 

North v. The Higbee Co., 131 Ohio State 507 (1936). The de fendant corporation desired to lease a certain property for a department store, but the only lease available was a 99-year lease which still had 85 years to run. It organized a subsidiary corporation for the sole purpose of taking over this lease, and then took a 10-year lease from its subsidiary. The parent corporation did not renew the lease at the end of the 10-year term, and the subsidiary corporation defaulted in the balance of the 85-year term. An attempt was made to hold the parent corporation liable for the default of its subsidiary. It was held, on appeal, that the parent corporation was not liable. In a dissenting opinion, it was said by WILLIAMS, J. "The subsidiary had no use for the building and did not profit by the getting of the leasehold. All the negotiations and the transaction itself were managed and controlled from beginning to end by the parent." 18

Sec. 745. Corporate Name. The corporate name must be expressed in English letters, and contain the word "corporation," "company," or "incorporated," or an abbreviation thereof, except that the phrase "and company" may not be used unless followed by the word "incorporated." Such name shall not imply that the corporation is a governmental agency of the Commonwealth or of the United States, or is subject to the supe vision of the Department of Banking, the Public Utility

Commission, or of the Insurance Department, a number of words being listed in the code which must not be used for that reason. As amended in 1945, the code provides that the words "State," "Commonwealth," "United 

States," or "Federal" may be used, if such use does not imply that the corporation is a governmental agency of the Commonwealth or of the United States.21 The name may not be deceptively similar to that of any other corporation doing business in the Commonwealth.22 To illustrate what may or may not be deceptive, the Dime 

Savings Bank of Philadelphia received a charter notwithstanding the protest of the Dime Savings Fund and Trust Company,23 but the application of the Gas Company of Altoona was refused at the instance of the Altoona Gas Company. 24

Sec. 748. Advertisement. Notice of an intention to file articles of incorporation with the Department of State should be advertised one time in two newspapers published in the English language, one of them a newspaper of general circulation and the other the legal newspaper designated by rules of court for the publication of legal notices, otherwise in two newspapers of general circulation published in the county in which the initial registered office of the corporation is to be located. If there is but one newspaper of general circulation published in the county, advertisement should appear at least three days prior to the filing of the articles with the Department of State. It should be set forth, briefly, (1) the name of the proposed corporation, (2) a statement that the proposed corporation is to be organized under the provisions of the Business Corporation Code, (3) the purpose of the proposed corporation, and (4) the time when the articles are to be filed with the Department of State.27

Sec. 749. The Charter. The articles and the adver tisement must be filed with the Department of State. If the articles are in accordance with the code, the Department of State will endorse its approval thereon, and when all bonus, fees, and charges have been paid, will file the articles and issue a certificate of incorporation to the incorporators, with a copy of the approved articles of incorporation. The articles then constitute the charter of the corporation. If a license is required to conduct the business, the Department of State must certify the requisite information to the department, board, or commission concerned.28
