Sec. 750. Corporation de Jure. The corporate ex istence begins when the Department of State has issued a certificate of incorporation," but the corporation may not incur any indebtedness or begin the transaction of any business (except such as is incident to its organization, or obtaining subscriptions to, or the payment for, its shares) until (1) the amount of capital with which it will begin business, as stated in the articles, has been fully paid, and (2) there has been filed with the Department of State an affidavit signed by at least a majority of the board of directors, stating that the amount of capital with which it will commence business has been fully paid in. Any officer of the corporation who disregards these requirements may be held personally liable for debts and liabilities arising therefrom.30 Compliance with all statutory requirements will create a corporation de jure.

Sec. 751. Corporation de Facto. "What is a corpo ration de facto? It is an apparent corporate organization, asserted to be a corporation by its members and actually acting as such, but lacking the creative fiat of the law.... Their organization may be imperfect, so that upon a quo warranto they could not show a sufficient compliance with the law to justify the exercise of corporate powers, but, as to the parties dealing with them, and as to each other, they are estopped to deny that they are what they hold themselves out to be." 31 

The recognition of a corporation de facto will excuse the incorporators from personal liability for the acts of the corporation. It is generally held, however, that the following requirements must be satisfied: (1) The existence of some law by which a corporation might be lawfully created; (2) a bona fide attempt to organize a corporation under such statute; and (3) a user of the rights claimed to be conferred under the law. The following case is typical of a procedural defect. 

Prior to the

Business Corporation Code of 1933, Pennsylvania re quired a statement of the place where the business was to be conducted. The Code of 1933 substitutes a statement of the initial registered office.

Eight persons executed articles of incorporation, which were filed in the proper office. They then accepted subscriptions to the capital stock and proceeded to do business in corporate form. The corporation as such became indebted to the plaintiff. Plaintiff sued the incorporators individually, however, on the ground, inter alia, that the place where the business was to be carried on was not stated in the articles. "The omission to state distinctly in the articles the place within which the business is to be carried on, though that might be essential to make it a de jure corporation, would not prevent it becoming one de facto."

Sec. 752. Organization Meetings. "A charter under which no corporate action has ever been taken, after a reasonable time has elapsed, can be avoided by the state at common law." 32 When a charter has been granted there must be an organization meeting of the shareholders, or a majority of them, either within or without the commonwealth. Each shareholder is entitled to at least ten days' written notice of the time, place, and purpose of the meeting. A similar meeting must be held by the board of directors. Each director is entitled to five days' written notice of the time and place of meeting.33

This notice is usually waived. The code provides that whenever written notice is required it may be waived in writing, and that attendance either in person or by proxy is a sufficient waiver.34

Sec. 753. Organization Procedure. The purpose of the organization meeting is to adopt by-laws, unless the articles provide that the by-laws shall be adopted by the board of directors, and to transact any other business stated in the notice. The usual procedure at the shareholders' meeting is to (1) select a chairman and acting

secretary, (2) accept the charter, (3) adopt by-laws or authorize the board of directors to do so, (4) appoint judges of election if they have not already been appointed by the board of directors, (5) nominate and elect officers, (6) accept subscriptions to the stock of the corporation, (7) adopt a form of stock certificate, (8) authorize the board of directors to issue stock and stipulate the consideration to be paid therefor, and (9) adopt a common seal. The board of directors usually meets directly after the shareholders' meeting. The usual procedure at this meeting is to (1) nominate and elect officers, (2) fix the amount of the treasurer's bond, (3) designate how stock should be issued, (4) adopt by-laws if authorized to do so by the shareholders, (5) designate the compensation to be paid to the officers and agents of the corporation, and (6) transact such other business as may be necessary. 

Sec. 754. Contracts of Promoters. It has been said that a promoter may "(1) Take on (the corporation's behalf) an offer from the other, which, being accepted after the formation of the company, becomes a contract. (2) Make a contract at the time binding himself, with the stipulation or understanding that if a corporation is formed it will take his place, and that then he shall be relieved of responsibility, or (3) bind himself personally without more and look to the proposed corporation, when formed, for indemnity." 35 One or two cases have been decided without reference to the principle expressed in the following case, but the principle itself has never been abrogated.

He attended meetings, visited Harrisburg for the purpose of obtaining a charter, assisted in making a preliminary survey, and paid some of this expense. There was no contract with any one for the payment of his services, beyond the statement of two or three of the parties

After the charter had been obtained plaintiff brought suit against the corporation to recover for his services. PAXSON, J. "Such a minority can have no more authority to bind the association or corporation in its incipient or inchoate condition than they would have to bind it if fully organized. In this case the two or three persons who it is alleged promised the plaintiff to see him paid, bound no one but themselves."

Sec. 755. Amendment of Articles. A business cor poration may, from time to time, amend its articles in order to (1) adopt a new name, (2) modify the term of its existence, (3) add to or diminish its powers or purposes, and (4) increase or diminish its capital stock, or change the structure of its shares. Every such amendment must be proposed by the board of directors and approved by the shareholders.37 Ten days' written notice of the meeting should be given to each shareholder. Because of a constitutional requirement, sixty days' notice is necessary where the proposed amendment would involve an increase in the stated capital or paid-in surplus.38 Whenever the proposed amendment would affect adversely the shares of any class, the holders of such shares may vote as a class.39 An amendment must be approved by at least a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote. Whenever the holders of any class are entitled to vote as a class, not only for amendments but for other purposes, a majority of such holders is necessary, in addition to a majority of all shareholders entitled to vote.40 Articles of amendment setting forth the requisite information must be executed under the seal of the corporation and verified by two duly authorized officers of the corporation."1 Advertisement is similar to that prescribed for the original articles.¹² The amended articles, together with proof of advertisement, should be delivered to the Department of State, and if they are in proper form and all bonus and other charges 36 15 PS 2852-801.

Part 4. Merger and Consolidation 

Sec. 756. Combinations Distinguished. A merger is the absorption by one corporation of the rights, franchises, and property of another. One of the combining corporations continues in existence and absorbs the others. A consolidation is an amalgamation or union of two or more corporations so as to form a new body. 

All the combining corporations "are deemed to be dissolved and to lose their identity in a new corporate entity which takes over the properties, powers and privileges, as well as the liabilities, of the constituent companies." 45 46 

Sec. 757. Procedure. A domestic or a foreign corpo ration may merge or consolidate with either a domestic or a foreign corporation, if the laws of the state in which a foreign corporation is organized permit. The proposal, setting forth the terms and conditions, should be approved by a majority of the members of each board, and submitted to the shareholders of each corporation. 

The shareholders should receive ten days' written notice of the meeting. Due to a constitutional requirement, sixty days' notice is required if the plan contemplates an increase in the aggregate capital stock of the constituent companies. The approval of a majority of the shareholders of each corporation is necessary." 47 Arti- cles of merger or consolidation, setting forth the requisite information, must be executed under the seal of each corporation, and signed and verified by two duly author- 43 15 PS 2852-808.

ized officers of each corporation.48 Advertisement is similar to that prescribed for the original articles.¹º 

The articles, together with proof of advertisement, should be delivered to the Department of State, and if they are in proper form and all bonus and other charges are paid, the department will issue a certificate of merger or consolidation.50 The merger or consolidation becomes effective when the department has issued its certificate.51 A Pennsylvania corporation may merge or consolidate with a foreign corporation in any other state by following this procedure. 52 

Sec. 758. Effect of Consolidation. Two important principles are perpetuated in the code. First, the new corporation is subject to all the obligations of the merging or consolidating corporations. 53 Second, liens and 5* claims against the merging or consolidating corporations 55 are not affected:56 As recently expressed by Mr. 

Justice STERN, "a consolidation does not work any change in the assets, rights and liabilities of the constituent corporations or in the status of creditors and shareholders; it rather resembles the flowing together of two rivers the waters of which become mingled in a common stream." 99 57

Part 5. Dissolution Sec. 760. Kinds of Dissolution. A business corpo ration may be dissolved (1) by expiration of its charter, or (2) at the election of the incorporators, or (3) at the election of the shareholders. It may also be dissolved by judicial decree (4) upon petition of a shareholder, or (5) upon petition of a creditor, or (6) upon petition of the Commonwealth.

Sec. 761. Expiration of Charter. Where a business corporation is dissolved by expiration of its charter, the code provides that it shall continue to exist for the purpose of liquidating its affairs, and that the board of directors shall continue to function for that purpose. 59 

Sec. 762. Election of Incorporators. A business corporation that has not commenced business, or which has not issued any shares, may be dissolved at the election of all the incorporators by filing articles of dissolu-

Sec. 763. Election of Shareholders. A business corporation that has commenced business may elect to dissolve by a written agreement signed by all the shareholders, or by resolution of the board of directors approved by a majority of the shareholders entitled to vote.61 A certificate of election to dissolve must be filed with the Department of State. The corporate existence, however, will continue pending liquidation.62 The board of directors has full power to settle the affairs of the corporation. Notice of dissolution should be sent to each creditor, and should be published in the manner prescribed in the code. It is the duty of the board to liquidate all corporate assets, discharge all corporate liabilities, and distribute the surplus to the shareholders according to their respective preferences. The board may, at any time, apply to the court of common pleas of the county to conclude the proceedings under the supervision of the court.63 When liquidation proceedings are completed, articles of dissolution, together with proof of advertisement, are filed with the Department of State, and if the statutory requirements are satisfied, the Department will issue a certificate of dissolution."4

Sec. 767. Liquidation Proceedings. When dissolu tion proceedings are instituted, the code confers upon the common pleas all the ordinary powers of a court of equity to issue injunctions, appoint receivers, and liquidate the business.72 If the suit has been instituted by a shareholder and it is made to appear that the deadlock in the corporate affairs has been broken or the management or control has been changed, or if the suit has been instituted by a creditor and it is made to appear that the debts of the corporation have been paid or provided for, the court may in its discretion dismiss the proceedings. If a proposed compromise or reorganization receives the approval of a majority representing threefourths of the creditors or of the shareholders, as the case may be, or the same proportion of any class of creditors or shareholders, such compromise, if approved by the court, will be binding on all creditors or shareholders, or creditors or shareholders of the class affected, and also on the corporation and its receiver.73 

Sec. 768. Survival of Remedies. The code imposes a statutory period of two years after the dissolution of a corporation for the bringing of any suit against the corporation, its directors or shareholders, for any liability incurred prior to such dissolution, whether such dissolution be accomplished by voluntary or involuntary pro- 

72 15 PS 2852-1108. 78 15 PS 2852-1109.

ceedings, or by expiration of the charter, or by the sale of all its franchises, property and assets to another business corporation."

Merwine v. Mt. Pocono Light & Improvement Co., 304 Pa. 517 

(1981). Plaintiff brought suit against the defendant in trespass, alleging personal injuries as the result of defendant's negligence. 

Defendant thereafter sold its franchise and property to the Pennsylvania Power & Light Co., with the approval of the Public Service Commission. The lower court ruled that plaintiff's action should abate. In deciding otherwise, it was said by FRAZER, C. J. "According to the old settled common law, upon the civil death of a corporation . . . all the debts due to and from it (were) totally extinguished (but) the rule of the common law has become obsolete and odious.' . . . Defendant corporation not having been legally dissolved, its present condition is rather that of an inactive corporation and it is not altogether dead. . . Whatever the liability of the Pennsylvania Power & Light Company may or may not prove to be, we pass that point and note that the proper course at the present state of proceedings requires plaintiff first to proceed to judgment against defendant if she can, and, having secured judgment, to levy where defendant's assets liable for the judgment may be found."

Part 6. Foreign Business Corporations Sec. 769. Constitutional Limitations. The constitu tion of Pennsylvania provides that "No foreign corporation shall do any business in this State without having one or more known places of business and an authorized agent or agents in the same upon whom process may be served." This has been held to require an agent upon whom process might be served in every county of the commonwealth where a foreign corporation carries on its business. The code provides that a foreign corporation, before doing any business in the commonwealth, must procure a certificate of authority from the Department of State, unless the entire operations of the company are within the protection of the commerce clause of the federal constitution." Neither of these propositions can be sustained." 

Sec. 770. Interstate Commerce. Many of the decisions under the commerce clause of the federal constitution involve ordinances passed by boroughs which require peddlers' licenses. These ordinances do not distinguish between state and interstate commerce, or if they do, enforcement officers are frequently unable to comprehend this distinction. If the goods sold are located in the state, interstate commerce is not involved and a peddler's license may be required before the orders are solicited.80 If the goods are located without the state, an ordinance requiring a peddler's license is unconsti tutional.81 Some of the ordinances attempt to make a

Brennan v. Titusville, 153 U. S. 289 (1893). Brennan was a house-to-house salesman who solicited orders for pictures and frames for a Chicago manufacturer. "It is true, in the present case, the tax is imposed only for selling to persons other than manufacturers and licensed merchants; but if the State can tax for the privilege of selling to one class, it can for selling to another, or to all. In either case it is a restriction on the right to sell, and a burden on lawful commerce between the citizens of two States. It is as much a burden upon commerce to tax for the privilege of selling to a minister as it is for that of selling to a merchant. . . . That this license tax is a direct burden on interstate commerce is not open to question." 

Sec. 771. Green River Ordinance. In an effort to prohibit itinerant house-to-house soliciting of orders, many municipalities throughout the United States have adopted an ordinance as first employed by the Town of Green River, Wyoming, and which is known as the Green River Ordinance. The device employed in this ordinance is to make it unlawful for solicitors to go in or upon a private residence without having been requested or invited to do so. The constitutionality of the ordinance was upheld, as a valid local police regulation, by the U. S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and by the Supreme 

Court of Wyoming.85 The facts in those cases disclosed that certain residents of the town did not wish to have this intrusion upon their properties, although other resi- 82 2 D. & C. 739 (1922).

Sec. 772. Isolated Transactions. Under the present code, as well as under the previous Act of 1874,88 a foreign corporation which engages in an occasional transaction in Pennsylvania is not required to register, the reason being that an isolated transaction does not constitute "doing business" within the state. This phrase has received a liberal interpretation." Thus, it has been held that a single loan," purchase,¹ sale,°² or the sale of merchandise by a commission merchant, did not constitute "doing business" in Pennsylvania. 92 93 

Williams v. Golden & Crick, 247 Pa. 397 (1915). Plaintiff, a foreign corporation engaged in the manufacture and installation. of bronze ornamental work, brought suit to recover the balance due under a contract requiring installation of its product in a bank building at Pittsburgh. The manufacturing was performed outside the state. Defendant contended, inter alia, that plaintiff not having registered in Pennsylvania, could not maintain the suit. In overruling this contention, it was said by SHAFER, J. "We are clearly of opinion that this does not show a doing of business in Pennsylvania within the meaning of the registration acts. The plaintiff had not established an office or transferred any part of its capital to the State, nor carried on its ordinary business here. If it had merely taken orders to make and ship to Pittsburgh the ornamental work sued for, there would of course be no doubt that it had a right to do that without registration. 

We are unable to see how the fact that in addition to sending the material it sends its skilled employees to set it up can make any difference."

Sec. 773. Penalty for Non-Registration. The code as amended in 1945, provides that any foreign corporation which is required to procure a certificate of authority and has not done so, or any person, agent, officer or employee who shall transact any business within this Commonwealth for any foreign business corporation which has failed to procure such a certificate, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by imprisonment not exceeding thirty days or by fine not exceeding $1000, or both. The code further provides that failure to register shall not impair the validity of any contract with such corporation, but that no action thereon shall be instituted in any of the courts of the commonwealth until such corporation shall obtain a certificate of authority, and pay to the Department of State a fine of $250. The following case discloses a continuing project, as distinguished from a single transaction. 94 

Hoffman Construction Co. v. Erwin, 381 Pa. 384 (1938). Plaintiff, a New Jersey corporation, brought this action to recover for work done in landscaping, grading, and road construction on defendant's estate in Bucks County. The work was in progress for about four months. Materials were purchased in Bucks County, and a few workmen were hired locally. The equipment was brought from New Jersey, with the exception of several trucks which were hired locally. The gross charge was $4,471.74. Defendant objected to the suit on the ground that plaintiff had not registered to engage in business in Pennsylvania. In sustaining this objection, it was said by DREW, J. "The purpose of the Act of 1933, supra, is to bring foreign corporations doing business in this State within the reach of legal process. The act is for the protection of those with whom such corporations do business or to whom they may incur liabilities by their wrongful acts. It is also to bring such corporations within our tax laws. There is no logical reason why a foreign corporation should be allowed to avoid these requirements, even though it entered the State only to perform one contract."

Sec. 774. Service of Process. An application for a certificate of authority must contain a designation of the Secretary of the Commonwealth upon whom all law-

ful process in any action or proceeding against it may be served.95 Service of process may be issued, in the first instance, by any court having jurisdiction of the subject matter in any county of the Commonwealth in which the corporation shall have its registered office, or in the county in which the right of action arose. Such process upon the Secretary of the Commonwealth is made by the sheriff of Dauphin County." 

Openbrier v. General Mills, Inc., 340 Pa. 167 (1940). Plaintiff was injured by swallowing pieces of broken glass contained in a package of flour, which she bought from a local grocer in Washington, Pa. The latter had purchased it from a wholesale dealer in McKeesport, who in turn purchased it from the defendant company in Buffalo. She instituted this action against the defendant in Washington County. The sheriff of that county deputized the sheriff of Dauphin County to execute the writ, which he did by serving it upon the Secretary of the Commonwealth, who thereupon notified the defendant. Defendant objected to the service on the ground that its registered office was in Philadelphia. 

In sustaining the process, it was said by STERN, J. "Of course, the legislature has the power to determine the venue of suits against a registered foreign corporation, and since it has seen fit to allow such actions to be instituted in the county in which the right arose, the Washington County court clearly had jurisdiction of the present suit."

A registered foreign corporation enjoys the same rights and privileges as a domestic business corporation, including the right to acquire, hold, mortgage, lease, and transfer real property," but no more.98 The authority of a receiver of a foreign corporation, appointed by another state, or ancillary receiver appointed in this state, is subordinate to the claims of the creditors in this state." The code provides that nothing contained therein "shall be construed to authorize this Commonwealth to regulate the organization or the internal affairs of such corporation." 100

CHAPTER XX  Part 1. Corporate Powers Sec. 776. Statutory Powers. A business corporation is governed by (1) the constitution, (2) statutory and common law, (3) its charter, and (4) its by-laws. The 

Business Corporation code confers general powers upon every business corporation, subject to the provisions of its charter, and provides that it shall not be necessary to set forth any of such powers in the articles of the corporation. As summarized, every such corporation shall have power: (1) To continue as a corporation for the time specified in its articles. (2) To sue and be sued in the corporate name. (3) To have a corporate seal. (4) To acquire and dispose of real and personal property. (5) To encumber or dispose of its property and assets. (6) To acquire and dispose of corporate securities of any other corporation and exercise the rights of ownership. (7) To acquire and dispose of its own shares except to reduce its net assets below its stated capital. (8) To borrow money and execute evidences of indebtedness. (9) To invest its surplus funds and hold real or personal property as security. (10) To conduct its business within or without the commonwealth. (11) To make and repeal by-laws. (12) To appoint and remove officers and agents and define their duties and compensation. (13) To enter into any obligation necessary for the transaction of its affairs. (14) To exercise all powers necessary to effectuate the purpose for which it was organized. (15) To dissolve and wind up.¹ 

Sec. 777. Corporate Seal. Under the common law, all acts of the corporation had to bear the corporate seal. 

As said by Blackstone, "it is the fixing of the seal, and that only, which unites the several assents of the individuals who compose the community, and makes one joint assent of the whole." It was decided very early in Pennsylvania that this rule did not apply to contracts executed in the usual course of the business of the cor- 

1 Act of May 5, 1933, P. L. 364, 15 PS 2852-302. 

21 Black. Com. 475. 535

poration. In 1932 the Supreme Court indicated, by way of dictum, that all obligations should bear the corporate seal. In 1941, however, the Superior Court observed, after reviewing the authorities, that there were "many small corporations which rarely have need for a seal," that the code on this point is permissive and not mandatory, that while a corporation should adopt a distinctive seal of its own it was not obliged to do so in the absence of a statute to the contrary, and that a business corporation could lawfully adopt the seal printed on the ordinary judgment note. The court further indicated, by way of dictum, that a corporation could authorize the execution of a judgment obligation without a seal. It would be prudent, of course, for every business corporation to adopt a distinctive seal of its own, and to affix such seal to all of its obligations. 3 

Sec. 778. Statutes of Mortmain. The necessity of express authority, either by charter or by statute, to take and dispose of real estate resulted from the adoption, in Pennsylvania, of the English statutes of mortmain. These statutes prohibited the accumulation of lands for the use of civil and religious bodies corporate, "upon pain that the immediate lord of the fee, or, on his default for one year, the lords paramount, and in default of all of them, the king, might enter thereon as a forfeiture." The Report of the Judges in 1806 on the adoption of British Statutes, ends with the following statement with respect to the statutes of mortmain: "These statutes are in part inapplicable to this country, and in part applicable, and in force. They are so far in force, that all conveyances, either by deed or will, of lands, tenements, or hereditaments, made to a body corporate, or for the use of a body corporate, are void, unless sanctioned by charter or act of assembly." The language used in this summation is too broad. Except as to super-

The constitution provides that no corporation shall hold real estate "except such as may be necessary and proper for its legitimate business."" 

Sec. 779. Acquiring Own Shares. As noted in the code, a corporation may acquire and dispose of its own shares, except to reduce its net assets below its stated capital. There are many legitimate reasons why a corporation may acquire its own shares. It may, for example, exercise the rights of a lien holder for unpaid assessments, or it may buy its own stock in satisfaction of a debt,¹º or if it is solvent, it may dispose of its stock under an agreement of repurchase." There are two claimants, however, to the capital stock of a corporation, namely, its creditors and its shareholders. The claim of creditors is paramount to that of the shareholders, otherwise the latter could turn in their stock and make off with all the assets. "As its capital stock is a trust fund for the payment of its debts, the use of this fund in the purchase of shares, in itself, is destructive of a security intended primarily for the creditors, and a plain misappropriation of it."12 For the same reason it has been held that a corporation may not issue stock to itself for the purpose of pledging it to a bank as collateral security for a loan.13 The following transaction would not have been objectionable if the rights of creditors had not been involved. 

Warren v. Queen & Co., 240 Pa. 154 (1913). Plaintiff brought this action to recover on the following clause in a certificate of preferred stock: "The shares represented by this certificate shall be redeemed by the Company on March 1, 1911, at par." MESTRE-

Sec. 780. Ultra Vires Acts. The constitution pro vides that no corporation shall engage in any business other than that expressly authorized by its charter.¹ 

For this reason it is necessary, as an act of incorporation, to specify the purposes, objects and the powers sought to be exercised. Any act of a corporation which is in excess of its charter powers, or which violates some rule of positive law, is ultra vires, and if the corporation persists in conduct of this sort its charter may be dissolved. The following views were expressed when charters were conferred by acts of assembly, but the principles have been reaffirmed in recent years.' 15 

Com. v. Erie & North-East R. R. Co., 27 Pa. 339 (1856). BLACK,

C. J. "That which a company is authorized to do by its act of incorporation, it may do; beyond that all its acts are illegal. 

And the power must be given in plain words or by necessary implication. All powers not given in this direct and unmistakable manner are withheld. . . . If you assert that a corporation had certain privileges, show us the words of the legislature conferring them. Failing in this, you must give up your claim, for nothing else can possibly avail you. A doubtful charter does not exist; because whatever is doubtful, is decisively certain against the corporation."

Sec. 781. Rule Prior to 1933. Prior to the code of 

1933, it had long been the rule in Pennsylvania that where a corporation accepted the benefits of a transaction and ratified the acts of its representatives, it was estopped from setting up a defense that the contract was entered into without authority, or that it was beyond the power of the corporation to make.18 As said by the 

Supreme Court: "It is repugnant to every sense of justice and fair dealing that a principal shall avail himself of the benefits of an agent's act, and at the same time repudiate his authority. A corporation may not avail

itself even of ultra vires as a defense where a contract has been entered into and executed in good faith by the other party and the corporation has received the benefit of the performance."¹

Wright v. Oil City Pipe Line Co., 101 Pa. 204 (1882). The de fendant company gave its note as the purchase price of certain stock, and attempted to avoid liability on the note on the ground that the transaction was ultra vires. PAXSON, J. "The instances are rare in which a corporation or individual has been permitted to set up its own wrong in order to retain both the property and its price. The defendant corporations have obtained the stock which they now allege they had no right to buy, and propose to retain it without payment. It would be difficult imagine a defense with less merit, and the law would be exceedingly important were it to allow it to succeed." 

Sec. 782. Defense Abolished. The code of 1933 abol ished the defense of ultra vires in all contracts and obligations with third parties.18 This was to be expected.

The ease with which a charter can be obtained requires that a corporation should be held to a high degree of accountability. The code, however, does not purport to authorize ultra vires acts, or to excuse the corporation or its officers from accountability therefor. A single stockholder may restrain the corporation from engaging in ultra vires acts by notice to its officers to desist, and if necessary through equitable proceedings. It is also necessary to determine the legality of the acts of a corporation in suits against its officers, or against the board of directors for exceeding their authority, and also in proceedings by the commonwealth to enjoin the corporation from the transaction of unauthorized acts, or to dissolve the corporation.19 Under all such circumstances it is pertinent to inquire into the legality of corporate conduct.

Sec. 783. Implied Powers. The charter powers of a corporation are express and implied. Those which are implied are such as are necessary to carry into effect 

17 Presbyterian Board v. Gilbee, 212 

Pa. 310 (1905). 18 15 PS 2852-303, 10 Ibid,

those which are expressed, or which are incidental or auxiliary to the principal object for which the charter was obtained.20 In 1931 the Superior Court observed that department stores conducted restaurants, beauty parlors and hair dressing establishments as part of their activities; transportation companies operated restaurants, barber shops, soap and towel cabinets, shoe-shining stands and pay toilet rooms; and hotels had public stenographers, news stands, cigar and tobacco stores, barber shops, and laundries in connection with their main business. Such uses were justified as furthering the comfort and convenience of patrons.21 In Commonwealth v. Philadelphia Electric Company,22 the defendant corporation, which was chartered for the purpose of supplying heat, light and power by electricity, undertook to sell electric refrigerators. The attorney general instituted a quo warranto proceeding. A decision in favor of the corporation was sustained for the reasons expressed in the following case.

Malone v. Lancaster Gas Light Co., 182 Pa. 308 (1897). The defendant corporation was chartered for the purpose of manufacturing and supplying illuminating and heating gas. It undertook to purchase the right to use and deal in a steam heater, radiating mantel, and gas consuming appliances covered by the Backus patents, in order to supply its customers with this equipment. 

Objection was made that this was ultra vires. MITCHELL, J. "It would be of no use to manufacture gas if there were not customers to buy, and hence the company may fairly supply not only the gas itself, but incidentally such appliances and conveniences as will induce new customers to use gas or old ones to use more. 

This is a legitimate mode of extending the company's business, in direct furthering of its charter object." 

Sec. 784. Unauthorized Acts. In addition to abol ishing the defense of ultra vires in actions by third parties, the code provides that no purchase or sale of property shall be invalid because the the board of directors or any of the officers of the corporation, 20 Watts's (1875).

Otherwise, however, a corporation may defend itself against unauthorized acts of its officers or agents, unless it has received and retained the benefits of the transaction.24 It has been repeatedly held that an ordinary business corporation such as a mining concern,25 a lumber company,26 or a railway company," may not divert its capital by guaranteeing the obligations of another. 

If the corporation has general power to issue and endorse negotiable paper for its own benefit, and incidentally becomes accommodation maker or endorser on such paper, it will be liable to a holder in due course, but not where the act is clearly ultra vires and the holder has knowledge of that fact." 28 

Part 2. Corporate By-Laws Sec. 785. Purpose of By-Laws. "A by-law is a rule or law adopted by a corporation or association for the regulation of its own action and concerns and of the rights and duties of its members among themselves." 20 

Bagley v. Reno Oil Co., 201 Pa. 78 (1902). BROWN, J. "The by-laws of a corporation are the rule of its life. It comes into being through some general or special statute, with its charter as the evidence of its existence, and one of its necessary and inseparable incidents is the power to make by-laws which become its private statutes for its own government, unless contrary to the laws of the land. By its by-laws the management of a corporation's affairs is regulated and most frequently, as in the present case, its directors or managers are chosen in accordance with their provisions."

Corporate by-laws should not be repugnant to the constitution and laws of the commonwealth, or of the 23 15 PS 2852-303.

It is a "principle of the common law, running back so far that its origin cannot be found, that the by-laws of a corporation will be set aside by the judicial courts courts when deemed unreasonable.' unreasonable." 31 Those "which are nugatory, vexatious, and oppressive, or manifestly detrimental to the interest of the corporation, are void." 32

Sec. 786. Power to Make By-Laws. At common law, only the shareholders had the right to adopt, amend, or rescind by-laws. The code provides that this right may be expressly vested by the articles or the by-laws in the board of directors, but "subject always to the power of the shareholders to change such action." The code further provides that while the by-laws may be changed by the directors or shareholders at any regular or special meeting, notice should be given that such change is contemplated.38 In Bagley v. Reno Oil Company, it was proposed at the annual meeting of the corporation to amend the by-laws by increasing the number of directors from nine to eleven. No notice had been given of this proposed change, but a vote was taken and the amendment adopted. It was said by BROWN, J., that such action, "being manifestly of great importance, extraordinary and out of the usual business transacted at a regular or annual meeting of the stockholders, the weight of authority seems to be, as it ought to be, that in the absence of notice previously given, it cannot be made."

Sec. 787. Contents of By-Laws. The contents of corporate by-laws vary to some extent, but as a rule they (1) provide for the meetings of the shareholders; (2) also for the meetings of the directors; (3) define the

Part 3. Corporate Duties Sec. 788. Registered Office. Every business corpo ration must have and continuously maintain in the commonwealth a registered office. This office may, but need not be the same as its place of business. A change of location may be authorized by a majority of the board of directors. This change becomes effective when the 

Department of State has been notified. There must be kept at this office a record of the proceedings of the shareholders and of the directors, and a copy of the bylaws to date as certified by the secretary of the corporation. In addition, there must be kept either at this office or at the office of a transfer agent or registrar within the commonwealth, a copy of the share register, giving the names of the shareholders in alphabetical order, and showing their respective addresses, the number and classes of shares held by each, the number and date of certificates issued for the shares, and the number and date of cancellation of every certificate surrendered for cancellation. Books or records of account, which must be appropriate, complete and accurate, may be kept at this office or at the principal place of busi- 38 ness.

Sec. 789. Right to Examine Records. Every share holder has a right to examine, in person or by an agent or attorney, at any reasonable time, and for any reason- 

37 15 PS 2852-307. 

38 15 PS 2852-308.

able purpose, the share register, the books or records of account, and records of the proceedings of the shareholders and directors, and to make extracts therefrom.39 

This is necessary for the protection of stockholders, and may be enforced by mandamus. Such writs have been authorized upon averment of the need of information of mismanagement, to ascertain whether the business is being properly conducted, that it is necessary to a pending suit to see the books and papers in order to correctly state the facts then concealed, that the best interests of the corporation require the election of a new board of directors, and that a list of the stockholders is necessary for that purpose. The stockholders of one corporation also have a right to inspect the books and records of a subsidiary corporation where the two are conducted under the same management and the latter is an instrumentality of the former.40 A foreign corporation, registered and doing business in Pennsylvania, with all or most of its property and assets in the state, is also subject to an order by a court of equity permitting its stockholders to examine its books for a proper purpose. 

The right of a director is superior to that of a stockholder, and all that he need show to entitle him to an inspection is that he is a director of the company, that he had demanded permission to examine the records, and that his demand has been refused.42 41

Sec. 790. Increase of Indebtedness. The passing of time has brought about a diminishing degree of corporate control by shareholders. In order to secure to them some measure of control over the capital structure of the corporation, the constitution provides that the stock and indebtedness of corporations shall not be increased except in pursuance of general law, nor without the consent of the persons holding the larger amount in value of the stock, first obtained at a meeting to be held after sixty days' notice. These provisions are incorporated in the code, with the proviso that they do not apply "to indebtedness contracted in the usual course of corporate business."" This proviso is in response to the decisions of the courts to the effect that the constitutional mandate does not apply to debts and obligations incurred in the usual course of the corporate enterprise. 

The character of such obligations is indicated in the footnotes.44 43 

Sec. 791. Transfer of Assets. A corporation may sell, lease, or exchange all, or substantially all of its corporate property and assets. Such a transfer may be authorized by the board of directors without submission to the shareholders if it is made in the usual and regular course of the business, but otherwise by the holders of at least a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote. These provisions of the code do not authorize the conversion or exchange of assets in fraud of corpo-

Sec. 792. Miscellaneous Powers. A number of mis cellaneous powers are cited in the code. A business corporation may acquire property at a tax or judicial sale on which it holds a mortgage or other lien ;*7 contract with the federal government and assist the state and federal governments in the prosecution of war;18 continue the salaries of such of its employees as may be enrolled in the military service; and pension its employees.50 In addition, a business corporation may, by suitable provisions in its articles, confer voting and other privileges upon the holders of its bonds or debentures, including power to vote with respect to corporate affairs and management.51 

Sec. 793. Financial Report. Unless the by-laws provide otherwise, the directors of a business corporation should cause to be sent to the shareholders, within ninety days after the close of its fiscal year, a financial report as of the closing date of the preceding fiscal year. "Such report shall give a summary of the assets and liabilities of the corporation, the amount of dividends paid or declared during the past year, the condition, as to surplus or deficit and how acquired or created, the number of shares issued and outstanding, 45 15 PS 2852-311. 

46 Peoples Trust Co. v. Consumers

together with any such particulars as are necessary to disclose the general nature of the liabilities and assets of the corporation. 

The report shall also set forth a balance sheet as of the closing date of the preceding fiscal or calendar year, together with a statem of income and profit and loss for the year ended on that date. 

The statement of income and profit and loss shall be prepared in the form ordinarily used by accountants for the particular kind of business carried on by the corporation. Unless the by-laws expressly provide otherwise, all such reports shall be verified by a certified public accountant, who is not a director or full-time employee of the corporation, or by a firm of practicing public accountants at least one member of which is a certified public accountant. The accountant or firm shall be elected by the shareholders of the corporation." 52

Sec. 794. Reorganization. Whenever the property and franchises of a corporation are sold under any judicial process, or by virtue of a power of sale contained in a mortgage or deed of trust, the creditors of the corporation may organize a new corporation. The new or reorganized corporation is then vested with, and is entitled to exercise and enjoy, all the rights, privileges and franchises of the old. The articles of incorporation should set forth, as additional information, the name of the old corporation, the date of the judgment or decree authorizing the sale, and a brief description of the property sold. Considerable latitude is permitted, at or previous to such sale, in readjusting the respective interests of creditors, mortgagees, and shareholders of the old corporation, and for the representation of such interests in the bonds, shares, obligations, or other securities of the new corporation. Such a plan may provide for the regulation of the voting powers of any class or classes of shares, and for the voting privileges of the holders of the bonds of both the old and new corporation. Considerable latitude is also permitted the new corporation, within six months after its organization, in compromising the debts and liabilities of the old corporation." 53 

Sec. 795. Bankruptcy. Whenever a business corporation may be insolvent or in financial difficulty, the

board of directors may, by resolution and without the consent of the shareholders, authorize the officers of the corporation to make an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or otherwise institute or participate in insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings.54 A business corporation may also carry out a plan or reorganization or an arrangement as authorized by the federal courts of bankruptcy.5 55 

Part 4. Directors and Officers Sec. 796. Board of Directors. Every corporation must be managed by a board of at least three directors. 

They must be natural persons of full age. Unless the articles or by-laws provide otherwise, they need not be residents of the commonwealth or shareholders in the corporation. The names and terms of office of the first directors must be stated in the articles. Subsequent directors must be elected by the shareholders.50 Women, married or single, may serve as directors or officers.5

Sec. 797. Powers and Duties. The number, quali fications, terms of office, manner of election, time and place of meeting, compensation, and powers and duties of the board should be prescribed in the by-laws. The code states that if the by-laws do not provide otherwise: (1) A director shall be elected for a term of at least one year. (2) The number of directors shall be the same as that stated in the articles. 

(3) Vacancies in the board of directors shall be filled by a majority of the remaining members of the board though less than a quorum, and each person so elected shall be a director until his successor is elected by the shareholders, who may make such election at the next annual meeting of the shareholders or at any special meeting duly called for that purpose and held prior thereto. (4) The meetings of the board of directors may be held at such place within this Commonwealth, or elsewhere, as a majority of the directors may from time to time appoint, or as may be designated in the notice calling the meeting. 54 15 PS 2852-319. 55 15 PS 2852-320. 

50 15 PS 2852-401. 

57 15 PS 2852-409.

(5) A majority of the directors in office shall be necessary to constitute a quorum for the transaction of business, and the acts of a majority of the directors present at a meeting at which a quorum is present shall be the acts of the board of directors.58 

Sec. 798. Informal Action. The directors of a busi ness corporation may act without the necessity of a formal meeting, if they do so in writing, and if all the members concur therein. Informal action of this sort is more common in the case of close or family corporations. The code provides that "if all the directors shall severally or collectively consent in writing to any action to be taken by the corporation, such action shall be as valid corporate action as though it had been authorized at a meeting of the board of directors." 59 

Sec. 799. Executive Committee. It is customary for large corporations to establish an executive committee, and to authorize such committee to transact the routine business of the corporation in the intervals between the meetings of the board. As authorized in the code, "The board of directors may, by resolution adopted by a majority of the whole board, delegate two or more of its number to constitute an executive committee, which, to the extent provided in such resolution, shall have and exercise the authority of the board of directors in the management of the business of the corporation." 60

Sec. 800. Revolving Board. It is also customary for large corporations to provide for a revolving board of directors. If the articles or by-laws so provide, directors may be classified for that purpose. Each class should be as near equal in number as possible. The members of each class may be elected for a term of from one to four years, in such a way that the term of one class will expire in each year." 61 

Sec. 801. Notice of Meetings. Meetings of the direc tors may be held upon such notice as the by-laws pre- 58 15 PS 2852-402.

Sec. 802. Removal of Directors. The entire board, or an individual director, may be removed from office without assigning any cause, by the majority of the shareholders entitled to vote, and new directors may be elected at the same meeting. The board may vacate the office of a director if he be judicially declared of unsound mind, or is convicted of a felony, or for any other proper cause, or if, within sixty days or such other time as the by-laws may specify, he does not accept the office, either in writing or by attending a meeting of the board. Prior to the adoption of the Business Corporation Code, a court of equity had no power to remove an officer of a private corporation. The code provides that upon the suit of the shareholders holding at least ten per centum of the outstanding shares, the court of common pleas may remove a director "in case of fraudulent or dishonest acts, or gross abuse of authority or discretion with reference to the corporation, and may bar from reëlection any director so removed for a period prescribed by the court."

Markovitz v. Markovitz, 336 Pa. 145 (1939). The Chancellor in the court below removed defendant from the office of director of Markovitz Brothers, Inc., a family corporation, and barred him from reëlection for a period of two years. In sustaining this action, it was said by BARNES, J. "While undoubtedly friction and animosity of a personal nature were present in the relations between the parties, aside from the indignities suffered by other officers at the hands of defendant, there was the serious harm which he caused to the corporation by his unreasonable and unjustifiable abuse of the authority he possessed. As a director he 02 15 PS 2852-404.

It was his duty to coöperate with the other officers of the corporation, that its business might prosper, and not to thwart and obstruct them in the performance of their duties, particularly where they had achieved an excellent record in the management of the company." 

Sec. 803. Joint Boards. Not infrequently, the same person is elected to serve as a director in two or more corporations, and occasionally the identical persons are elected to serve as directors for inter-related corporations. This practice is not objectionable, except to note that directors and officers "shall be deemed to stand in a fiduciary relation as to each corporation.' 99 64 

Mercantile Library Hall Co. v. Pittsburgh Library Ass'n, 173 

Pa. 30 (1896). "The interests of corporations are sometimes so interwoven that it is desirable to have joint representatives in their respective managements, and at any rate it is a not uncommon and not unlawful practice. But the action of such persons should be open, and free from any suspicion of secret dealing in favor of one principal while acting as the representative of the other. Such action is always open to investigation, and the utmost good faith must not only exist but be made manifest."

Sec. 804. Officers and Agents. Every business cor poration must have a president, a secretary, and a treasurer. It may have such other officers and agents as it may authorize. 

Officers need not be directors. The articles or by-laws may prescribe special qualifications. 

Unless the by-laws provide otherwise, two or more offices may be held by the same person, except the offices of president and secretary. The president and secretary must be natural persons of full age. The treasurer may be a corporation, but if a natural person must be of full age. Officers and agents must be elected by the shareholders, or appointed by the board, in either case "at such time, in such manner, and for such terms and compensation as the by-laws may prescribe." The board may secure the fidelity of any officer by an appro- 64 15 PS 2852-408.

priate bond or otherwise. Unless the by-laws provide otherwise, the board may fill any vacancy in any office. 

Officers and agents, as between themselves and the corporation, respectively, have such authority, and may perform such duties, as may be provided in the by-laws, and by resolution of the board of directors.5 

Sec. 805. Removal of Officers. The code provides that any "officer or agent elected or appointed by the board of directors may be removed by the board of directors whenever in its judgment the best interests of the corporation will be served thereby, but such removal shall be without prejudice to the contract rights, if any, of the person so removed." 66

Sec. 806. Salaries of Directors. The code provides that "A business corporation may allow compensation to its directors for their services, and a director may also be a salaried officer of the corporation." 67 Compensation to a director should be prescribed either in the charter or in the by-laws, or should be authorized at a shareholders' meeting.68 It should also be authorized before the service to be compensated has been rendered. In Loan Association v. Stonemetz,69 a director of a loan and saving fund association served as chairman of the committee on short loans. The duties were quite laborious and were well performed. At the expiration of two years the board passed a resolution awarding the sum of $200 annually as compensation for this work, but it was held that antecedent authority was indispensable. The rule is for the protection of the shareholders.

Grafner v. P. N. I. & C. Street Ry. Co., 207 Pa. 217 (1908).

Sec. 807. Salaries of Officers. 

Pennsylvania follows the rule that compensation of corporate officers should be authorized in advance, the reason being that “a corporate officer has ample opportunity to adjust and fix his compensation before he renders his services, and no great mischief is likely to result from compelling them to do so." 99 70 If the board of directors has been given authority to adjust the salaries of its officers and employees, it should not delegate that authority to one of its members. 

Shannon v. Early Foundry Co., 296 Pa. 141 (1929). The bylaws of defendant corporation provided that the board should determine the salary to be paid the president, vice-president, secretary and treasurer. The board adopted a resolution authorizing one of its members to do so, whereupon she adjusted her own salary as secretary from $90 to $150 per week. In answer to the protest of the minority shareholders it was said by MOSCHZISKER, C. J. "Any fixing of salaries had to be done by the board, and not by an individual member of that body, who, as an interested official of the corporation, would personally profit by the readjustment of compensation."

Sec. 808. Disinterested Quorum. If an officer of the corporation is also a member of the board of directors, his salary should be authorized by a disinterested quorum. Where all the members of the board are also paid officers of the corporation, the board may nevertheless act upon the salary of each officer without violating this rule, inasmuch as a disinterested quorum is obtained in each case. 

Schaffhauser v. Arnhold & Shaefer Brewing Co., 218 Pa. 298 (1907). Two members of the board, consisting of five members, voted a salary increase to the president, who was also a member of the board, from $5,720 to $10,400 per annum, and two members voted against it. The president then cast the deciding ballot in favor of the increase. ELKIN, J. "The generally accepted rule applicable to such cases, is that the voting of a salary or compensation to a director, who either is, or is not, an officer of the board, 70 Culp v. Independent Card Corp., 99 Pa. Superior Ct. 275 (1930).

must be entirely free from fraud, actual or constructive, and that the action is illegal, if it is determined by the vote of the director, or officer, whose salary is thus increased." 

Sec. 809. Excessive Salaries. It is possible for the majority shareholders, who elect themselves as directors, and who in turn employ themselves as officers, to appropriate to themselves excessive salaries to the prejudice of the minority shareholders. "While the courts have some measure of supervision over the action of directors in fixing their own salaries as officers or for other services rendered, there should be no judicial interference in that regard unless fraud or overreaching appears." " Where such overreaching appears, a shareholder may, if necessary, appeal to a court of equity for relief,72 and notwithstanding the action of the board in fixing salaries has been ratified at a stockholders' meeting. 73

An officer is not deprived of compensation when the amount is found to be excessive. A reasonable amount will be awarded." The court, however, will not determine upon the value of services to be rendered in the future.75 

Lowman v. Harvey R. Pierce Co., 276 Pa. 882 (1923). During the first ten years of its business the net profits of defendant corporation were slightly less than $39,000. For seven of these years the salaries paid to its three directors amounted to $98,725. A certain proportion was represented by notes. Plaintiff, a minority stockholder, filed a bill in equity, praying that the resolutions. fixing salaries be annulled, and that the notes be surrendered and cancelled. The lower court determined the defendants guilty of overreaching, and fixed the amount of salaries fairly earned during the disputed period. Defendants appealed. SADLER, J. "The findings of fact here made are justified by the evidence, and therefore are to be sustained. In applying the law thereto, many and uniform decisions of this court are to be found justifying supervision of the action of directors of corporations in fixing their own salaries, where fraud or overreaching appears."

Sec. 810. Fiduciary Relation. Inasmuch as direc tors occupy a fiduciary relation to the corporation, they may not make the business of the company one of profit to themselves. In Provident Trust Company v. Geyer, certain directors sold the unissued stock of the company for $64 per share, and after paying the par value, $50 per share, to the corporation, proposed to retain the dif ference, $14 per share, as profit for themselves. In Gilmore v. Gilmore Drug Company," the majority stockholder, who controlled the board, purported to have borrowed $200,000 from the company for the purchase of real estate, which he thereafter sold to the corporation for a price in excess of $400,000. 

Sec. 811. Gratuities and Bribes. "Gifts, gratuities or bribes given to a director to influence his official action, must be accounted for by him and surrendered to the company." 78 The Penal Code 79 provides that whoever bribes or attempts to bribe an officer of a corporation, with respect to any sale of supplies or materials to such corporation, or to influence such officer in the discharge of his official duties, and whoever receives such reward or gratuity, may be punished by fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both, in addition to the forfeiture of the office. 80

The fiduciary rela tion does not prevent the officers or directors from contracting with the corporation.8 Such contracts are subject to close scrutiny, but will be upheld if fair and reasonable.81 Officers and directors, however, must take no unfair advantage of the corporation. Russell v. Rock Run Fuel Gas Co., 184 Pa. 102 (1898). Snee was a large stockholder. He sold certain wells and pipes to the corporation for $53,000, most of which was paid with stock. Sec. 813. Standard of Care. In the management of business corporations, directors and officers are held to "that diligence, care and skill which ordinarily prudent men would exercise under similar circumstances in their personal business affairs." 84 

Loan Society of Philadelphia v. Eavenson, 248 Pa. 407 (1915).

This was a suit by plaintiff corporation against its former directors. The business of the company was to loan money on collateral security. The lower court found, on competent evidence, that the directors were guilty of gross negligence because they knowingly declared dividends which had not been earned, permitted fraudulent transactions with a borrower which resulted in a loss to the society of some $40,000, employed a person in a responsible position who was already under suspicion and which made possible the theft of several thousand dollars, and permitted the overissuance of stock. MESTREZAT, J. "If this were an action by the holders of the stock they could not compel the former directors to replace the part of the capital they had already received by way of dividends. But the corporation is a going concern and is not in liquidation, and hence its right as well as its duty to compel the replacement of its capital. This is necessary for the protection of

Part 5.

Shareholders 

Sec. 814. Meetings. 

Meetings of shareholders may be held within or without the commonwealth, but unless the by-laws provide otherwise, they must be held in the commonwealth at the registered office of the corporation. The by-laws should prescribe the number of meetings to be held. There must be one such meeting in each calendar year for the election of directors, but failure to hold such a meeting will not work a dissolution of the corporation. If the meeting is delayed for more than six months, any shareholder may call one. Special meetings may be called by the president, or the board, or by the holders of not less than one-fifth of the outstanding stock, or as otherwise designated in the by-laws. 

Any meeting may be adjourned, but the meeting for the election of directors may only be adjourned from day to day.8 85 

Sec. 815. Notice of Meeting. Shareholders are en titled to five days' written notice of every meeting, unless a greater period of notice is required in a particular case. (It has been observed that ten days' notice is required for the organization meeting, and that sixty days' notice must be given where the purpose is to increase the indebtedness of the corporation. It has also been observed that notice in any case may be waived in writing, and that attendance is a sufficient waiver.) It is not necessary to give notice of an adjourned meeting, other than by announcement at the meeting adjourned, unless otherwise provided in the by-laws. 86 

Sec. 816. Quorum. A shareholders' meeting may not be organized unless a quorum is present. Unless the articles provide otherwise, "The presence, in person 15 PS 2852-501. 

86 15 PS 2852-502.

or by proxy, of the holders of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote shall constitute a quorum." 

If a meeting has been properly organized, it may continue to transact business until adjournment, notwithstanding the withdrawal of enough shareholders to leave less than a quorum. If a meeting cannot be organized because of the absence of a quorum, it may be adjourned by those present, but if it has been called for the election of directors, those who attend the adjourned meeting, though less than a quorum, may elect directors.87 

Commonwealth v. Vandegrift, 232 Pa. 58 (1911). An annual meeting was called, at which a quorum was present. A chairman was elected by oral vote. Certain stockholders were not satisfied and requested that a chairman be elected by stock vote. The chairman ruled that the request came too late as the meeting had already been organized. The dissenting stockholders then withdrew in order to defeat a quorum for the election of directors, although they were informed that the directors would be elected by stock vote. ELKIN, J. "They should have remained in the meeting to exercise their privileges and perform their duties. When they did not do so but without sufficient cause withdrew, they are not in position to complain about the acts of those who remained and performed their duties in a regular and lawful manner." 

Sec. 817. Voting by Proxy. Except as provided in the charter or as designated in the code, each shareholder is entitled to one vote at every shareholders' meeting for every share standing in his name on the books of the corporation. He may vote either in person or by proxy. Every proxy must be executed in writing and filed with the secretary of the corporation. It is revocable unless coupled with an interest, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, but notice of the revocation must first be given to the secretary. An unrevoked proxy is not valid after eleven months from the date of its execution, unless a longer time is expressly provided, but an unrevoked proxy may not be voted after the lapse of three years unless it is coupled with an interest. A proxy is not revoked by the death or inca- 87 15 PS 2852-503.

pacity of the person giving it, unless written notice to that effect is filed with the secretary before it is exercised. A shareholder may not sell his vote for any sum of money or anything of value.88 89 

Sec. 818. Cumulative Voting. The constitution pro vides that, "In all elections for directors or managers of a corporation each member or shareholder may cast the whole number of his votes for one candidate, or distribute them upon two or more candidates, as he may prefer." ⁹ This provision is incorporated in the code. 

It is designed to permit minority representation on the board of directors. According to a recent decision by the Supreme Court, a by-law which provides that votes for directors can be cast only for persons nominated for the office of director, is a violation of the constitution.90 "The candidates receiving the highest number of votes up to the number of directors to be elected, shall be elected." 91

The 

Commonwealth v. Acker, 308 Pa. 29 (1982). The Presbyterian

Ministers Fund was incorporated in 1759. The corporation accepted the constitution of 1874. At the annual election held in 

1931 certain of the corporators attempted to vote cumulatively for the directors, a thing which had never before been done. ballots cast were rejected, and this proceeding followed. KEPHART, J. "By its plain language, the intent of the Constitution was to give to those who could vote for such executive managers of a corporation the right of cumulative voting. It was intended as a check on majority control. . . . That the members of this fund did not attempt to exercise this right in the past, does not preclude their exercise at this or any time they desire to do so. The right exists and no basis for an estoppel is shown." 

Sec. 819. Shares Held by Others. Shares standing in the name of a trustee appointed by the common pleas, or assignee for the benefit of creditors, or a receiver, may be voted in person or by proxy of the trustee, assignee, or receiver. A pledgor of shares may vote in person or by proxy, until the shares have been transferred on the 88 15 PS 2852-504.

A corporation owning shares in another corporation may vote by its president or by his proxy, unless some other person has been designated by resolution of the board of directors. A corporation may not vote its own shares of stock held by it, unless the shares are held in a fiduciary capacity.94 

Sec. 820. Shareholders of Record. Shares are so frequently bought and sold that it is necessary to determine from time to time who the shareholders are. This is necessary for three very important reasons: first, to determine who are entitled to vote; second, to determine who are entitled to the payment of dividends, allotments of rights, and to the conversion or exchange of shares; and third, to determine the liability of a shareholder to the corporation and others. Unless the by-laws provide otherwise, the board may fix a time, not less than ten or more than seventy days, as a record date for the determination of shareholders of record. The board may close the books against transfers during the whole or any part of this period, upon written or printed notice by mail at least ten days before the closing date, to each shareholder of record, at the address appearing on the records of the corporation. No transfer of shares may be made while the books are closed. If no date has been fixed, holders of shares which have been transferred on the books within ten days preceding the date of a meeting of shareholders are entitled to notice of and to vote at the meeting.' 95 

Sec. 821. Voting Lists. At least five days before each meeting of shareholders, a voting list must be prepared by the officer or agent having charge of the trans-

Sec. 822. Voting Trusts. Two or more shareholders may, by agreement, transfer their shares to any corporation or person for the purpose of vesting in such trustee all voting or other rights pertaining to the shares, for a period of not exceeding ten years, and upon such terms and conditions as may be stated in the agreement. 

The legal owner receives in return negotiable voting trust certificates." A voting trust is not, per se, contrary to public policy, unless, as in the case of any other contract, it is executed for an illegal purpose. As observed by the Supreme Court of Washington, "the object and not the form of the agreement furnishes the test, and where the trust is voluntarily created as a condition precedent to a loan to protect those who have furnished the money that has put the life into a corporation, the courts should not seek further for a consideration." Sec. 823. Judges of Election. 

Judges of election may be appointed by the directors, in advance of any meeting, but if this is not done the chairman of the meeting may do so, and he must do so at the request of any shareholder. The number of judges may be one or three, but no person is qualified who is a candidate for office. It is the function of the judges to determine the number of shares outstanding, the voting power of each, the shares represented at the meeting, the existence of a quorum, the validity of proxies, to receive votes or ballots, to hear and determine all challenges, to count and tabulate all votes, to determine the result, and do

Sec. 824. Informal Action. It is quite common for the shareholders of close or family corporations to dispense with formal meetings. The following provision appears in the code: "Except for the action required by this act for increasing the stated capital or indebtedness of a corporation, any action required by this act to be taken at a meeting of the shareholders of a corporation may be taken without a meeting, if a consent in writing, setting forth the action so taken, shall be signed by all of the shareholders who would be entitled to vote at a meeting for such purpose and shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation." 101 

Sec. 825. Actions by Shareholders. As a general rule a shareholder may not vindicate a corporate right in a legal action, without first making every reasonable effort to prevail upon the board of directors to do so. 

But as said in the following case: "Where it appears that fraudulent acts, prejudicial to the interests of the corporation, have been committed, so interwoven with the conduct of the corporate managers and of such nature that it might be presumed the officers would commit a breach of trust in refusing to proceed, a demand is not necessary, as it would be 'vain and useless." "

Where there is a misappropriation or diversion of corporate funds, an individual stockholder may not sue directly for his proportionate share, but may compel repayment to the treasury of the corporation.102 The Act of 1945 103 provides that in any suit to enforce a secondary right against any officer or director, the plaintiff must have been a shareholder at the time of the transaction of which he complains, and that if the plaintiffs are holders of less than five per centum of the outstanding shares of any class, they may be required to give security for reasonable expenses and attorneys' fees

Wilson v. Brown, 269 Pa. 225 (1920). Plaintiff alleged that defendants, a majority of the board of directors and others, had issued to themselves, some years previous but concealed from her, 340 shares of the stock of the company, without consideration, which stock (of the value of $34,000, upon which dividends were paid amounting to $51,000) had been appropriated to their own use. It was apparently issued for past services, which was illegal, void, and a fraud on other stockholders. The lower court dismissed the bill because no proper effort had been made to get the directors to act. KEPHART, J. "It is admitted that if this complainant went before the board of directors, they would refuse to act. 

What advantage would be gained by dismissing the bill and inferentially directing the stockholder to ask the directors to proceed, when they have already indicated they will not do so?" 

Sec. 826. Power of Expulsion. Very early in the history of the commonwealth it was said, in reference to a nonprofit corporation, that "Every incorporation possesses inherently, the power of expulsion in certain cases." 104

The same purpose may be accomplished in a business corporation by an agreement that if any stockholder ceases to be a desirable associate, either on account of incompetency or personal conduct, the holders of a majority of the stock may thereupon appraise and take his stock at its cash value.105 An agreement among all the stockholders that in the event of the death or withdrawal of any shareholder, the remaining stockholders shall have the option to purchase the stock at its book value, is not contrary to public policy or an improper restraint upon alienation.108 Such an agreement or by-law may be defeated, however, whenever a widow elects to take against her husband's will, and to retain the stock.107
