CHAPTER XXI CORPORATION FINANCE Part 1. Shares of Capital Stock Sec. 828. Classes of Shares. Considerable latitude is allowed a business corporation in the creation of its capital structure. According to the Business Corporation Code, a corporation may issue such kinds or classes of shares of stock, with or without par value, and with full, limited, or no voting rights, and with such other designations, preferences, qualifications, privileges, limitations, options, conversion rights, and other special rights, as may be authorized in the charter. the charter does not provide otherwise, each share of stock is equal in all respects to every other share. The board of directors is authorized to issue, from time to time, the classes of shares designated in the charter, unless the by-laws provide otherwise.¹ If Sec. 829. Shares in Series. It has been customary in the past for a business corporation to classify its stock as common or preferred, and much of the deci sional law is based on this distinction. It is now quite common for a corporation to issue different kinds of shares in series, and to designate each series as class "A," "B," and "C," etc. If the articles authorize the board to do so, the board may determine the relative rights of each series with respect to the rate of dividend, the price at, and the terms and conditions on which shares may be redeemed, the amounts payable upon shares in the event of voluntary or involuntary liquidation, sinking fund provisions for the redemption or purchase of shares, and the terms and conditions on which shares may be converted in the event the shares of any series are issued with the privilege of conversion. 

Act of May 5, 1933, P. L. 364, 15 PS 2852-601. 37 565

The resolution of the board in each case must be approved by the Department of State.2 

Sec. 830. Fractional Shares. A business corporation may also issue fractional shares, or scrip, or other evidence of ownership, which will entitle the bearer or holder to receive a certificate for a full share upon the surrender of the aggregate of a full share, "but which shall not, unless otherwise provided, entitle the bearer or holder to exercise any voting right, or to receive dividends, or to participate in any of the assets of the corporation in the event of liquidation." In a recent decision approving the ouster of directors who had been elected by splitting fractional shares, the Supreme Court observed "that the Legislature may wisely have hesitated to confer upon stockholders the right to vote fractional shares of stock because of the complications and confusion in voting which would inevitably result." 4 5 

Sec. 831. Consideration for Shares. The constitu tion provides that, "No corporation shall issue stocks or bonds except for money, labor done, or money or property actually received; and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void." This requirement is incorporated in the code. It is intended for the protection of the creditors of the corporation. As expressed by the Supreme Court of the United States, "if it be once admitted that a corporation may issue stock without receiving a consideration therefor, and where it does not represent actual or substantial value in corporate assets, there is apparently no limit to the extent to which the original stock may be 'watered,' except the caprice of the stockholders." The code provides that the reasonable charges and expenses of organization, reorganization, or for the sale or underwriting of shares, 2 15 PS 2852-602. 315 PS 2852-608.

Sec. 832. Value of Shares. The value of shares hav ing no par value must be determined by the incorporators prior to incorporation, and thereafter by the shareholders, or by the board acting under the authority conferred by the shareholders or in the charter. The consideration for a share dividend is the surplus transferred to stated capital when the shares are issued. A similar adjustment may be made when an exchange or conversion of shares is authorized. A complaint that stock has been issued in violation of the constitutional mandate should be asserted within a reasonable time. In 

Commonwealth v. Reading Traction Company,10 it was alleged that the officers of the corporation had issued fictitious stock, but the corporation did nothing for several years and in the meantime the stock had reached the hands of innocent purchasers. It was held that, "To bring the shareholders in at this late day would be a hardship upon them which a court of equity is not constrained to commit."

Sec. 835. Post Incorporation. Sec. 837. Preemptive Rights. A preemptive right, in corporation law, means the right of a shareholder to purchase the same proportion of a new issue, as the shares he owns bears to the total number of shares out standing. Prior to the Business Corporation Code of 

1933, shareholders in Pennsylvania had the first right to subscribe to new issues of stock.30 A new rule appears in the code. "Unless otherwise provided in its articles, a business corporation may issue shares, option rights or securities having conversion or option rights, without first offering them to shareholders of any class or classes." 31

Part 3. Liability of Shareholders 

Sec. 838. Corporate Debts. A shareholder is not liable for any debt or liability of the corporation, except for salaries and wages owing to laborers and employees for services rendered to the corporation. Suit must be brought within six months after the salaries or wages become due, and not from the date when the corporation is found to be insolvent.32 The liability of each shareholder is measured by the value of his shares. This is the par value of the shares, or in case of shares without par value, the consideration received by the corporation. 

In an action to enforce this liability, a claimant may include the corporation, as well as one or more shareholders, as defendants, although it has been held that a judg ment against the corporation is mandatory. An execution must first be levied on the property of the corporation, and then against the shareholder for any deficiency. A shareholder is entitled to contribution pro rata from other solvent shareholders.33

Eiffert v. Pa. Central Brewing Co., 141 Pa. Superior Ct. 548 (1940). Plaintiff brought suit against defendant corporation and certain of its shareholders to recover $1,156.76 for wages earned from January 8, 1934 to December 22, 1934. The corporation had 

214 shareholders, 73 of whom were nonresidents of Pennsylvania. 

The suit was filed on March 26, 1935. Plaintiff obtained a judgment for $444.23, the amount earned within six months prior thereto. Both parties appealed. Plaintiff complained that on 

Dec. 8, 1934, in a reorganization proceeding under the federal 

Bankruptcy Act, the U. S. District Court had issued a perfunctory order restraining all persons from suing the corporation, but it was ruled that this did not preclude him from issuing a praecipe against the shareholders, and thereafter joining the corporation as a party to the action. Defendants challenged the constitutionality of the act on the ground that it arbitrarily selected one or more stockholders upon whom to cast the entire wage debt of the corporation, without an effective remedy of contribution from other stockholders. In approving the judgment, it was said by PARKER, J. "While we find no Pennsylvania cases directly in point, the appellants would probably be allowed to recover a ratable proportion from the solvent shareholders within the jurisdiction." 

Sec. 839. Subscriptions. The code provides that a subscriber to the shares of a business corporation, or a holder of such shares, shall not be under any liability to the corporation with respect to such shares, other than the obligation of complying with the terms of the subscription. Persons who hold stock in a fiduciary capacity are exempt from such liability, but not the trust estates. Pledgors of shares are liable, but not the pledgees. 34 

The liability of a subscriber accrues when a call is made, or when the corporation is insolvent. A formal assessment is not necessary when the corporation is insolvent and all the subscriptions are necessary to satisfy the claims of creditors. The statute of limitations begins to run from the date of the assessment or demand, unless as in the case of such contractual liability, the call is unreasonably delayed.36 35

This is for the convenience and protection of the corporation, in order that it may know who "can claim to exercise the rights of a corporator." 37 This does not prevent the record owner from disposing of his stock, but if the transfer is not accepted by the corporation and recorded on the books of the company, he is primarily liable for assessments. 

It has been held that a stockholder, "whether original or holding by transfer, cannot rid himself of his responsibility to creditors after the corporation has become insolvent." 38 

Cook v. Carpenter, 212 Pa. 177 (1905). McCord subscribed for certain stock. The by-laws prescribed that no transfer should be made while the books were closed. While the books were closed for the annual election, and before the insolvency of the company was known, McCord sold the stock to Carpenter. It was contended that McCord was no longer liable for assessments. MITCHELL, C. J. "The principle of the decisions is that the transfer must be complete and in accordance with the by-laws of the corporation to fix the liability of the transferee and release the transferor. To begin the recognition of irregular or incomplete transfers would be to open the door to contests over colorable or disputed facts and subject the rights of creditors to endless litigation." 

Sec. 841. Release of Owner. After a sale has been recorded on the books of the company, or whenever the company has accepted the transferee as a shareholder, the original subscriber is relieved from further assessments.

Schmitt v. Kulamer, 267 Pa. 1 (1920). KEPHART, J. "To be relieved of this continuing liability, the subscriber may transfer his right or interest in the shares subscribed, but such transfer must be made as required by law, subject to such regulations as may be provided by the by-laws. Where such transfer is entered upon the books of the corporation, he ceases to be liable for future calls, the consent of the corporation is in effect a novation, a release of the transferor's liability; and, unless there is some statutory regulation, the assignor is no longer liable for future calls to stock subscribed for him, or held in his name." 

37 Com. v. Watmough, 6 Wh. 116 (1840), 38 Aultman's Appeal, 98 Pa. 505 (1881).

CORPORATION FINANCE 

573 40 Sec. 842. Purchaser. The code provides that a purchaser of shares of stock, in good faith and without knowledge that the full consideration has not been paid to the corporation isssuing the same, shall not be personally liable for any unpaid subscription."9 In French v. Harding, the receiver of an insolvent corporation instituted an action against the purchaser of stock for which the corporation had not been paid, but which defendant purchased through a Philadelphia broker without knowledge of such non-payment. It was held that defendant was not liable. The code protects the pur chaser, however, only where he has no knowledge of such non-payment. Where he purchases stock with such knowledge he may be held liable, either to the corporation or to the shareholder of record from whom he pur chased the stock, if such shareholder of record has been obliged to indemnify the corporation. 

Lichten v. Verner, 8 Pa. D. R. 218 (1899). Lichten subscribed for 100 shares of stock of the par value of $50 each, on which he paid $30 per share. The amount paid appeared on the face of the certificate. Lichten then sold the stock to Verner, who acted for an undisclosed principal. The transfer was never recorded on the books of the company. Calls were made, which Lichten's Estate was obliged to pay, and this suit was brought against Verner to recover the amounts so paid. AUDENREID, J. "The law on the subject is thus expressed in Beach on Private Corporations, par. 570, page 920: 'Where shares of stock have been assigned, but from neglect or omission from any cause the assignor remains the nominal owner on the books of the company, there is an implied obligation on the part of the assignee to reimburse him for moneys paid on calls made by the company on the stock during the time he remains the nominal owner. Part 4. Transfer of Shares Certificates Sec. 843. Stock Transfer Act. The transfer of share certificates may be regulated by such by-laws as are not inconsistent with the Uniform Stock Transfer 30 15 PS 2852-609. 

40 235 Pa. 79 (1912).

Act. This statute provides that title to such certificates may be transferred only: (1) By delivery of the certificate, indorsed either in blank or to a specified person, by the person appearing by the certificate to be the owner of the shares represented thereby, or (2) By a delivery of the certificates and a separate document containing a written assignment of the certificate or a power of attorney to sell, assign or transfer the same or the shares represented thereby, signed by the person appearing by the certificate to be the owner of the shares represented thereby. Such assignment or power of attorney may be either in blank or to a specified person.41 While a certificate may be transferred by indorsement, it is more common to execute an assignment, which is usually printed on the back, together with a blank power of attorney constituting the person named as the attorney for the assignor. 

Hyman v. Gerlach, 153 Pa. 197 (1898). MITCHELL, J. "A certificate of stock with a power of attorney to transfer, duly executed but in blank as to date and name of transferee, is in the position of merchandise prepared for market. That is the way sales and transfers of stock are usually made, and the presumable intent of executing the power to transfer, is to put the holder in position to complete a sale by delivery of the certificate and transfer of the stock."

Sec. 844. Innocent Purchaser. The general purpose of the Uniform Stock Transfer Act is to facilitate the negotiation of corporate securities. A wrongful transfer may be rescinded, unless (1) "The certificate has been transferred to a purchaser for value, in good faith, without notice of any facts making the transfer wrongful," or (2) "The injured person has elected to waive the injury, or has been guilty of laches in endeavoring to enforce his rights." 42

Sec. 845. Purpose of Legislation. In 1941 the leg islature enacted a new and comprehensive statute which is designated as The Pennsylvania Securities Act. This legislation is sometimes referred to as the Blue Sky Law, a term descriptive of "speculative schemes which have no more basis than so many feet of blue sky." " Its purpose, according to one authority, is to curb "sales by unknown and nonresident vendors and sleek peripatetic salesmen, with glib tongues and indurated consciences, of stock and other securities for the purpose of developing wild-cat oil fields in distant states, mythical rubber plantations in Guatemala, or imaginary copper mines in 

Mexico, for extracting gold from sea water, and light from cucumbers, and developing power from the rise and fall of the tides, and for the hundreds of visionary schemes, domestic and foreign, designed to secure a great return from a small investment in a short time. 9945 

Such legislation is unquestionably the product of public demand. It is dictated in part by a desire on the part of the public to. protect itself from its own folly. 

It "burdens honest business, it is true, but burdens it

Sec. 846. Registration of Dealers. The act requires the registration, with the Pennsylvania Securities Commission, of dealers, salesmen of such dealers, investment advisors, and solicitors employed by such advisors. Exceptions to this requirement are indicated in the footnotes.* All registrations expire at the close of the calendar year, but are renewable upon application. The registration of the investment advisor is a new feature of the code. Such an advisor is defined, generally, as any person who engages in the business of advising others as to the value of securities or as to the advisability of purchasing securities, or who engages in the business of managing any investment account in securities, or who issues or promulgates analyses. Only dealers or salesmen may engage in the issuance, underwriting or promotion of securities. An investment advisor may, how ever, sell, underwrite or promote the securities of an investment company if such advisor is engaged principally in the business of rendering investment supervisory services and otherwise satisfies the requirements of the code.

Sec. 847. Registration of Securities. Another fea ture of the code is the registration of securities to be offered to the public. In this respect Pennsylvania joins those states which indirectly qualify the securities to be sold. No security may be sold in the State until notice of such intention is filed with the Commission.

Sec. 848. Pennsylvania Corporations. The same exemptions on behalf of Pennsylvania corporations are made in the following three circumstances: (1) Sales of its own securities by a domestic or foreign corporation which has at least one-half of its paid-in capital invested or employed in Pennsylvania, for the sole account of such corporations, without any commission or fee, and at a total expense of not more than three per centum of the proceeds; (2) Sales of its own securities by a domestic corporation whose authorized capital stock added to its outstanding securities does not exceed $25,000-no-par stock being considered as having a value of $100-which are disposed of in good faith for the sole account of such corporation; and (3) Sales of its own securities in good faith by a domestic corporation and for its own account, so long as the number of stockholders of such corporation does not exceed twentyfive, and the securities are disposed of without the use of advertisements, circulars, agents, salesmen, solicitors or any form of public solicitation. In all such cases, five days' notice of such sale, together with the

facts justifying such exemption, must be filed with the

Part 6. Dividends Sec. 849. Stated Capital. Every business corpora tion must have a stated capital. This consists of the aggregate par value of all shares having a par value, and the aggregate amount of value of the agreed consideration received for shares without par value. When shares are issued for cash, the board may divide the consideration received between stated capital and paid-in surplus, and if shares have been issued for labor or services or for property other than cash, the board may make a similar distribution within a period of sixty days thereafter. In any such determination, the stated capital shall be not less than the aggregate of the par value of the shares, and the aggregate consideration received for shares without par value having a preferential right, in the event of involuntary liquidation. It is the duty of the board to specify, in dollars, the part of such consideration which shall be stated capital. The books of the corporation must also show the allocation between stated capital and paid-in surplus. The stated capital may be increased from time to time by resolution of the board, directing that all or a part of the surplus of the corporation be transferred to stated capital, or stated capital in respect of any designated class of shares.18 

Sec. 850. Paid-in Surplus. Paid-in surplus, as distinguished from earned surplus, is a part of the contributed capital of the corporation. The primary purpose of such a segregation of capital, in a banking or credit institution, is to secure depositors and creditors against any impairment of the capital stock. In a business corporation, paid-in surplus serves primarily as a source of dividends on preferred shares until the earnings of the corporation become available. The fund usually origi 

48 15 PS 2852-614.

CORPORATION FINANCE 

579 nates from the sale of par stock at a premium, or from the consideration received from shares without par value, a part of which is allocated to paid-in surplus. 

The code provides that dividends may be paid out of paid-in surplus only upon shares having a preferential right to receive dividends, and then only when the source of such dividends has been disclosed to the shareholders entitled thereto.49

Sec. 851. Discretion of Directors. The board of di rectors may declare and pay dividends upon the outstanding shares of the corporation, out of its surplus, from time to time and to such extent as the board may deem advisable.50 If the corporation is solvent, and the rights of creditors are not impaired, the earnings of the company may be distributed, notwithstanding the possibility of future losses.51 

McKean v. Biddle, 181 Pa. 361 (1897). An insurance corporation proposed to declare a dividend of ten per cent. At that time the amount of insurance outstanding amounted to $14,573,908, its assets were valued at $4,258,040, and deposits or premiums subject to redemption amounted to $495,659. Plaintiff filed a bill in equity to enjoin the payment on the ground that it would impair the assets available for future losses. ARNOLD, P. J. "This mere possibility is no reason for enjoining the payment of a dividend. 

Every business or trading corporation has a right to declare and pay dividends to its members, and it also has the right to pass its dividends for a time in order to accumulate a surplus and strengthen the company. That is what was done by the defendant corporation in this case. Having accumulated enough, in the judgment of the members, to make it safe and prudent to resume the division of its profits, it has the right to make such division." 

Sec. 852. Abuse of Discretion. Ordinarily the de cision of the board is final unless, on appeal to equity, fraud or abuse of discretion can be shown. The earnings of a corporation belong to its stockholders, and under some circumstances it is an abuse of discretion to 49 15 PS 2852-704. 

30 15 PS 2852-701. 

61 Powers-Buchanan Co. v. Powers, 269 Pa. 388 (1921).

refuse to declare dividends in an appropriate amount. 

The cases are quite unusual. 

Dodge . Ford Motor Co., 204 Mich. 459 (1919). Plaintiffs, minority stockholders, filed a bill in equity to restrain the alleged business policy of the majority stockholder, Henry Ford, and for a decree requiring distribution to stockholders of part of the accumulated cash surplus. When the complaint was made the corporation had assets of more than $132,000,000, a surplus of almost $112,000,- 000, and cash on hand and municipal bonds, $54,000,000. total liabilities, including capital stock, were a little over $20,000,- 000. The alleged business policy of Henry Ford, as it appeared in the public press, read as follows: "My ambition is to employ still more men; to spread the benefits of this industrial system to the greatest possible number, to help them build up their lives and their homes. To do this, we are putting the greatest share of our profits back into the business." OSTRANDER, C. J. "It had been the practice, under similar circumstances to declare larger dividends. Considering only these facts, a refusal to declare and pay further dividends appears to be not an exercise of discretion on the part of the directors, but an arbitrary refusal to do what the circumstances required to be done. . . . There should be no confusion (of which there is evidence) of the duties which Mr. Ford conceives that he and the stockholders owe to the general public and the duties which in law he and his codirectors owe to protesting minority stockholders. A business corporation is organized and carried on primarily for the profit of the stockholders. The powers of the directors are to be employed for that end." 

Sec. 853. Function of Courts. It is seldom that a court of equity will overrule the judgment of the board. 

Each business has its own peculiar needs, and the judges are not business experts. A considerable reserve may be necessary under some circumstances, not only to guard against future losses, but to provide for depreciation of plant and equipment and to allow for the reasonable growth of the business.52 

Jones v. Motor Sales Co., 322 Pa. 492 (1936). Plaintiff, a stockholder, filed a bill in equity to require the corporation to declare a dividend. In 1934 a profit was made and a dividend declared of slightly less than one-half, after deducting the losses of 1932 and 1933. This was in accord with a policy that had been 

52 Pardee v. Hardwood Electric Co., 262 Pa. 68 (1918).

581 adopted some years before. The circumstances of the business indicated the need for a larger amount of capital. Plaintiff may have been prompted by the death of the majority stockholder, Costlow, whose life had been insured in favor of the corporation in the sum of $35,000. With respect to this item it was said by 

LINN, J. "In the consideration of that problem, the directors had now in the treasury the insurance money, $35,000, created and received to tide over its affairs in the event of Costlow's death until, if possible, its effect on the corporation's business had been minimized. The results of the deliberation on this problem were that it was determined to increase the extension of credit to its purchasers to the extent allowed by this accretion to its assets. 

This conclusion was in the interests of the entire shareholding body; if it should turn out to be ill-advised, the shareholders must bear it as an act performed by their representatives; but no court, on this record, can say that it is a business policy that should not have been adopted." 

Sec. 854. Source of Dividends. A corporation may only distribute its earnings and surplus among its shareholders.53 The code provides that dividends may be paid in cash, in property, or in shares of the corporation, but that no corporation shall pay dividends: (1) in cash or property, except from the surplus of the aggregate of its assets over the aggregate of its liabilities, including in the latter the amount of its stated capital, after deducting from such aggregate of its assets the amount by which such aggregate was increased by unrealized appreciation in value or revaluation of fixed assets unless the amount thereof shall have been transferred to, or included in, its stated capital; (2) In shares of the corporation, except from the surplus of the aggregate of its assets over the aggregate of its liabilities, including in the latter the amount of its stated capital."* 

West v. Hotel Pennsylvania, Inc., 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 373 (1942). HIRT, J. "While the capital is impaired the earnings of a corporation belong to its creditors. "This rule effectively prevents payment of dividends on any class of stoc while the corporation is a going concern unless there be earnings from which such declaration can be made': Levin et al. v. Sec. 855. Share Dividends. Share dividends may be paid in shares with or without par value. If a share dividend is paid in shares having a par value, there must be transferred to stated capital an amount of surplus equal to the aggregate par value of the shares. If the dividend is paid in shares having no par value, there must be transferred to stated capital an amount of surplus equal to the aggregate value of the shares as determined by the board of directors.55

Sec. 856. Vesting of Dividends. The declaration of a dividend creates a vested right in the shareholders, and if the action of the board is not unlawful or injurious to the company, it may not be rescinded.56 It is customary for a large corporation to announce a dividend some time in advance, in order to permit its shareholders to record their holdings on the books of the company. Where this is done, the dividend vests in the shareholders of record on the date specified in the declaration, whether payment is to be made on that date or at some later date. Otherwise a cash dividend vests in the shareholders on the date on which it is declared, though payment is to be made at some later date. 

Opperman's Estate (No. 1), 319 Pa. 455 (1935). Testator owned 6,000 shares of corporate stock, constituting the larger part of his estate. On January 24, 1930, the corporation adopted the following resolution: "On motion duly seconded and carried, it was decided to declare a dividend of $90,000, payable quarterly as follows: March 10th, June 10th, Sept. 10th, Dec. 10th." Testator's share of the dividend was $36,000, payable $9,000 on each of the foregoing dates. He died on February 12, 1930. By his will he gave one-half of his residuary estate to his wife and daughter absolutely, in shares of three-tenths and two-tenths respectively.

Co., 167 Pa. 370 (1895).

In disposing of the problem as to whether the above dividend became a part of the trust, and therefore payable to the executor, it was said by KEPHART, J. the dividends having, by the resolution above quoted, been declared generally, during his lifetime, though not payable until a later date, they form part of the corpus of the estate and go to the executor' . . . The court below was right, therefore, in deciding that those four dividends, when and as received, were properly placed in the corpus of the trust." ...

Sec. 857. 

Distribution. 

Distribution. Unless a corporation has notice of the assignment or sale of its stock, it is justified in distributing its earnings to the shareholders as disclosed by its records.57 Where stock is sold after a dividend has been declared, no question as to the right to the dividend is likely to arise. Where such sale is made prior to the declaration of a dividend, the dividend belongs to the purchaser of the shares, though he may not be the shareholder of record, and if it is paid to the shareholder of record by the corporation, it may be recovered by the purchaser of the shares from the shareholder of record. 

Hornblower v. Austin, 112 Pa. Superior Ct. 90 (1934). On May 

10, 1929, plaintiffs purchased from the defendant ten shares of stock. The books of the corporation were closed on May 22, 1929, and the transfer was not recorded. Subscription warrants, having a value of $193.40, were distributed to the defendant on June 15, 1929, and disposed of by him, without remitting to the plaintiff. 

This action followed. STADTFELD, J. "The closing of the books of the company on May 22, 1929, was for the protection of the company, as it necessarily must depend on the record ownership in sending out the warrants for the right to subscribe. But as between the defendant and the persons to whom he had sold the stock, a different question arises. The warrants which he received, and the proceeds thereof when sold, were the property of plaintiffs. 

Defendant was no longer a stockholder and anything which he received was equitably the property of plaintiffs to whom he must account therefor." 

57 Bank of Commerce's Appeal, 72 Pa. 59 (1873).

Sec. 858. Pledge of Shares. It has been observed that the pledgor of shares, is entitled to vote the shares until the shares have been transferred to the pledgee on the books of the corporation. If such a transfer is made, the corporation will pay its dividends to the pledgee, but otherwise to the pledgor. Unless the right to retain the dividend is reserved by the pledgor, an implied trust arises in favor of the pledgee. 

Peoples-Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. Saupp, 320 Pa. 138 (1936).

Plaintiff held 100 shares of corporate stock which defendant had pledged as security for a substantial indebtedness. Subsequently the corporation declared a stock dividend of 6623% on its capital stock, and defendant received a certificate for 663 shares. Plaintiff filed a bill in equity to recover it. MAXEY, J. "It is well recognized that 'a pledgee is entitled to hold the natural increase of the thing pledged. Thus if he has taken in pledge domestic animals, he will hold in pledge the young of such animals afterwards born': Jones on Collateral Securities (Pledges), section 

396.. (Defendant) was under the same obligation to turn over these 663 shares to (plaintiff) as she would have been to turn over a cash dividend which might have been paid her on the stock she had pledged as security." ..

By resolution adopted at a shareholders' meeting, the holders of the preferred stock were to receive a cumulative yearly dividend of five per cent in each year before any dividends should be set apart or paid on the common stock. From 1899 to 1907 the holders of the preferred stock were paid the stipulated five per cent annual dividend, and no more, while all profits above the amount so paid were distributed to the common stockholders. Sec. 861. Distribution of Assets. Preferred shares may not only enjoy a preference in the payment of dividends, but also in the distribution of assets in case of dissolution. 

Petry v. Harwood Electric Co., 280 Pa. 142 (1924). Plaintiffs were the owners of preferred stock which provided: "In case of the dissolution of the company, the preferred stock shall be first paid and redeemed at its par value, in preference to the common stock, out of the property or assets of the company." The defendant company having merged with other companies, plaintiffs contended that the merger worked a dissolution as far as the preferred stockholders were concerned, and that the preferred stock should be redeemed at par. The defendant denied that the merger worked a dissolution, and urged that the preferred shares should be redeemed at their market value. SCHAFFER, J. "Our conclusion is, that the merger worked a dissolution, so far as the preferred stockholders are concerned, and they, therefore, are entitled to receive payment according to the terms of their contract out of the assets of the defendant."

Sec. 862. Changes in Capital Structure. Where a corporation has issued shares which are subject to redemption and cancellation, it may, by resolution of the board, redeem and cancel such shares, and it may use that portion of its stated capital represented by such shares, provided this does not reduce the remaining assets of the corporation below an amount sufficient to pay all debts and known liabilities of the corporation as they mature, except such debts and liabilities as have been otherwise adequately provided for, or reduce the net assets below the aggregate amount payable to the holders of shares having prior or equal rights to the assets of the corporation upon dissolution.62 A corpo- ration may also reduce its stated capital without chang- 

62 15 PS 2852-705.

CORPORATION FINANCE 

587 ing its share structure. 

This change should be authorized by resolution of the board of directors, and approved by a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote.63 In either case a complete statement must be filed with and approved by the Department of State before the change will become effective.

Sec. 863. Unlawful Dividends. The directors of a corporation who declare or pay a dividend, or who authorize the withdrawal or distribution of corporate assets in violation of the provisions of the code, are jointly and severally liable to the corporation. A director who dissents from any such unlawful payment should cause his dissent to be entered on the minutes of the meeting, and if he was not present, he should file a written objection with the secretary of the corporation upon learning of it.64 

Branch v. Kaiser, 291 Pa. 543 (1928). A grocery company was incorporated in 1908. The original capital was $175,000, which was later increased to $1,000,000. Its business was prosperous until 

1920, when it sustained a loss of $1,000,000. This was not due to mismanagement, but because of contracts for future delivery and a subsequent sharp decline in prices. The business was continued, however, until 1925, when the corporation was adjudicated a bankrupt. During this period the defendants, officers of the corporation, adopted a practice of concealment, misrepresentation and fictitious inventories, and distributed the earnings of the corporation in dividends amounting to more than $132,000. The trustee in bankruptcy instituted this action to recover the moneys so paid out. FRAZER, J. "The court below found the disbursements were illegal . and that the directors are personally liable for the dividends so declared. We concur in that judgment.”

Cornell v. Seddinger, 237 Pa. 389 (1912). The board of direc tors declared dividends in the sum of $28,000 in 1901, $28,000 in 1902, and $48,000 in 1903. These payments were made out of capital, and when there were no profits to divide. A receiver, subsequently appointed, filed a bill in equity to compel the directors to replace these amounts. The lower court entered judgment against two of them (the president and the vice president and general manager), but excused the other three on the ground that they were not familiar with the business, a ship building concern, and were excusable for accepting certain reports of the treasurer at their face value. In overruling this conclusion, it was said by POTTER, J. "Mere ignorance of facts which they could easily have ascertained cannot excuse them for the performance of illegal acts, in declaring dividends out of capital. It was the duty of the directors to inform themselves as to the actual condition of the company before declaring dividends. If they had made full inquiry and reasonable examination, and had been misled by erroneous information on which they had the right to rely, that might have served as an excuse for distributing capital instead of profits. But nothing of the kind appears from the evidence." 

Part 7. Trust Estates 

Sec. 865. Principal and Income. Corporate shares are often held in trust for the benefit of a life tenant. 

Such trusts usually provide that income arising therefrom is to be paid to the life tenant, and that at the end of the life estate, the corpus is to be distributed to remaindermen. The intricacies of corporation finance have given rise to an "interminable struggle between life tenants and remaindermen, intact value and income, the primary objects of testator's bounty and those of remoter interest. Judicial opinion may cause the struggle to hesitate, but, as long as trusts continue, these quarrels will not end." Difficulty arises when dividends which accrue during the life of the first tenant are not declared until after the death of the tenant, or 67 

06 Fell v. Pitts, 263 Pa. 314 (1919). 

07 Opperman's Estate (No. 1), 319 

Pa. 455 (1935).

CORPORATION FINANCE 

589 68 when a corporation utilizes its earnings by declaring a share dividend, or when a trustee exercises an option to invest in new shares or conversion rights and realizes a profit from the sale of such shares. In 1945 the legislature sought to clarify the respective rights of successive tenants, life tenants, and remaindermen, through the adoption of a Uniform Principal and Income Act."

Two sections of this statute are of particular interest to the accountant, namely, section four, which governs the apportionment of income as between successive tenants, and section five, which attempts to distinguish between principal and income in reference to corporate dividends. These sections are set forth below:

Section 4. Apportionment of Income. Whenever a tenant shall have the right to income from periodic payments, which shall include rent, interest on loans, annuities and ordinary dividends on corporate shares, and such right shall cease and determine by death or in any other manner at a time other than the date when such periodic payments should be paid, he or his personal representative shall be entitled to that portion of any such income next payable which amounts to the same percentage thereof as the time elapsed from the last due date of such periodic payments to and including the day of the determination of his right is of the total period during which such income would normally accrue. The remaining income shall be paid to the person next entitled to income by the terms of the transaction by which the principal was established. 

But no action shall be brought by the trustee or tenant to recover such apportioned income or any portion thereof until after the day on which it would have become due to the tenant but for the determination of the right of the tenant entitled thereto. The provisions of this section shall apply whether an ultimate remainderman is specifically named or not. Likewise when the right of the first tenant accrues at a time other than the payment dates of such periodic payments, he shall only receive that portion of such income which amounts to the same percentage thereof as the time during which he has been so entitled is of the total period during which such income would normally accrue; the balance shall be a part of the principal.

Section 5. Corporate Dividends and Share Rights. (1) All divi dends on shares of a corporation forming a part of the principal 

88 Act of May 3, 1945, P. L. 416, 20 PS 3471.

which are payable in the shares of the corporation shall be deemed principal. Subject to the provisions of this section, all dividends payable otherwise than in the shares of the corporation itself, including ordinary and extraordinary dividends and dividends payable in shares or other securities or obligations of corporations other than the declaring corporation, shall be deemed income. 

Where the trustee shall have the option of receiving a dividend either in cash or in the shares of the declaring corporation, shall be considered as a cash dividend and deemed income, irrespective of the choice made by the trustee. (2) All rights to subscribe to the shares or other securities or obligations of a corporation accruing on account of the ownership of shares or other securities in such corporation, and the proceeds of any sale of such rights, shall be deemed principal. All rights to subscribe to the shares or other securities or obligations of a corporation accruing on account of the ownership of shares or other securities in another corporation, and the proceeds of any sale of such rights, shall be deemed income. (3) Where the assets of a corporation are liquidated, amounts paid upon corporate shares as cash dividends declared before such liquidation occurred or as arrears of preferred or guaranteed dividends shall be deemed income; all other amounts paid upon corporate shares on disbursement of the corporate assets to the stockholders shall be deemed principal. All disbursements of corporate assets to the stockholders, whenever made, which are designated by the corporation as a return of capital or division of corporate property shall be deemed principal. (4) Where a corporation succeeds another by merger, consolidation or reorganization or otherwise acquires its assets, and the corporate shares of the succeeding corporation are issued to the shareholders of the original corporation in like proportion to, or in substitution for, their shares of the original corporation, the two corporations shall be considered a single corporation in applying the provisions of this section. But two corporations shall not be considered a single corporation under this section merely because one owns corporate shares of or otherwise controls or directs the other. (5) In applying this section the date when a dividend accrues to the person who is entitled to it shall be held to be the date specified by the corporation as the one on which the stockholders entitled thereto are determined, or in default thereof the date of declaration of the dividend.

CHAPTER XXII NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS Part 1. Nature of Negotiable Instruments Sec. 866. Kinds of Instruments. The Uniform Ne gotiable Instruments Act has been adopted in every state in the union. It was adopted in Pennsylvania in 

1901.¹ The instruments governed by the provisions of this act are (1) promissory note, (2) bill of exchange, (3) bank check, (4) trade acceptance,² (5) certificate of deposit, and (6) coupon bond. Each instrument requires the payment of money, as distinguished from shares of stock or documents of title which may also be transferred by indorsement. Negotiable instruments, as used in this chapter, are money obligations. (1) A promissory note is a promise in writing, made by one person to another, signed by the maker, who engages to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time a sum of money to order or to bearer.5 (2) A bill of exchange is an order in writing, addressed by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay on demand or at a determinable future time a sum of money to order or to bearer." (3) A bank check is a bill of exchange drawn on a bank payable on demand." (4) A trade acceptance is "draft or bill of exchange, drawn by the seller on the purchaser of goods sold, and accepted by such purchaser." 8

The drawer and the payee are usually the same person. (5) A certificate of deposit is a written instrument issued by a bank, "acknowledging that the person named has deposited in the bank a specified sum of money, and that the same is held subject to be drawn out on his own check or order, or that of some other person named in the instrument as payee." 9 

1 Act of May 16, 1901, P. L. 194, 56 PS 1. 

2 Traders Securities Co. v. Kalil, 107 Pa. Superior Ct. 215 (1932).

Pa. 323 (1932).

(6) A coupon bond is a bond to which is attached coupons in the nature of promissory notes, which are "designed to be cut off severally and presented for payment as they mature." 10 

Sec. 867. Non-Negotiable Instruments. It is com mon for the layman to assume that all the above instruments are "negotiable instruments" within the meaning of the Negotiable Instruments Act. They may be nothing of the sort. If they do not meet the requirements of the act they are non-negotiable instruments. 

The transfer of a non-negotiable instrument from one person to another is by assignment, as in the case of any other contract. Assignments are governed by principles of the common law. It is said that a negotiable instrument is a "courier without luggage." If so, a non-negotiable instrument is a train loaded with freight. 

It may be transferred by assignment, but it loses none of its impediments. Such an instrument, in the hands of an assignee, is subject to any defense which the maker has against the assignor, including all defenses, set-offs, and counterclaims of the maker against the assignor."

Furthermore, if the maker has no knowledge of the assignment, and no notice is given to him by the assignee, the holder is in "peril of losing the debt, either by a subsequent assignment to another person, or by new defenses arising between the debtor to the assignor." 12

It should be observed at the outset that there is a vast difference between a negotiable and a non-negotiable instrument, and between the transfer of a negotiable instrument by indorsement and the transfer of a nonnegotiable instrument by assignment. 

Sec. 868. Innocent Purchasers. "The purpose of the Negotiable Instruments Law is to enhance the marketability of such securities and to allow bankers, brokers and people generally to trade in them with confidence." 99 13

In order to accomplish this purpose, the 

10 Black's Law Dict., 456.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

593 law accords a higher degree of protection and security to innocent purchasers for value, than to other persons who may acquire the same instruments under different circumstances. An innocent purchaser for value is called a holder in due course. Not every person who comes into possession of a negotiable instrument is a holder in due course, or entitled to the rights of a holder in due course. Nor is the act concerned solely with the rights of a holder in due course. It is also concerned with the rights of an immediate or a remote party who is not able to qualify as a holder in due course. It will be observed in the study of this law that the rights of the holder are governed by the circumstances under which the instrument is acquired. In the discussion that follows, reference will frequently be made to an immediate or a remote party, as well as a holder in due course. (1) An immediate party is a person who takes the instrument in the first instance from the maker or drawer, or any person who subsequently acquires the instrument under agreement with his immediate transferor. The maker and the payee are immediate parties. Two successive endorsers are also immediate parties if one acquires the instrument from the other. (2) A holder in due course is a person who acquires the instrument before maturity, for a valuable consideration, and without notice of any defect. A person who derives his title through a holder in due course is entitled to the same right. (3) A remote party is a party who acquires the instrument after its maturity, and who does not derive his title through a holder in due course.

Sec. 869. Personal Defenses. It has been observed that a holder in due course is entitled to a greater security than any other holder of a negotiable instrument. 

This is accomplished by depriving the principal debtor of certain defenses which may not be asserted against a holder in due course. These are known as personal defenses. Each one deserves some explanation. They are enumerated at this point for the purpose of identifying the peculiar status of a holder in due course. Such

defenses are (1) lack of consideration, (2) failure of consideration, (3) breach of contract, (4) fraud inducing the execution of the instrument, (5) set-off or counterclaim, (6) payment before maturity when such payment is not marked on the instrument or the instrument is not cancelled, and (7) non-delivery of a completed instrument. The principal debtor could assert such a defense against an immediate or a remote party, but not against a holder in due course. 

Sec. 870. Absolute Defenses. It is not the purpose of the Negotiable Instruments Act to so exalt a holder in due course as to deprive the principal debtor of every defense known to the law, otherwise the act would be an intolerable instrument of fraud. Certain defenses are absolute, whether the instrument is in the possession of a holder in due course or not. Such defenses are (1) forgery of signature, (2) material alteration, (3) fraud in the procurement of the instrument, (4) non-delivery of an incomplete instrument, (5) lack of contractual capacity, (6) instruments void as against public policy, and (7) lack of authority of an agent who may execute such an instrument on behalf of the principal debtor.

Part 2. Requisites of Negotiability Sec. 871. Execution. The first requirement of a negotiable instrument is, that it be in writing and signed by the maker or drawer.14 It is not necessary that it be written on paper. It may be inscribed on any substance capable of bearing a writing. Nor is it neces sary that it appear in the handwriting of the maker. 

He may print his signature, or use a rubber stamp containing a facsimile, but if he uses the latter he must take proper precautions to prevent an unlawful use of it.15

Some people are unable to write. In Shemonia v. 14 56 PS 1.

595 Verda,¹ objection was made that a note was signed by mark, as "Z (his 'X' mark) T. Morris," without attesting witnesses, but it was observed that under the common law the mark was sufficient. 

In re Donohoe's Estate, 271 Pa. 554 (1922). Objection was made that the following instrument was not signed at the end thereof: "I, Cecilia W. Donohoe, promise to pay to the order of Richard 

Donohoe, thirteen thousand and seventy dollars and 86/100 dollars with interest at 6%." WALLING, J. "That Mrs. Donohoe's signature appears in the body of the note and not at the end is unimportant, so long as she intended thereby to obligate herself for its payment. There is no law requiring a note to be signed at the end thereof, as in the case of a will; hence, whenever it can be found that the signature, wherever it appears, was intended as an execution of the note, it is sufficient." 

Sec. 872. Sum Certain. A negotiable instrument must be payable in a sum certain in money. The amount payable is certain, within the meaning of the act, although it is to be paid with interest, or by stated installments, or by stated installments with a provision that upon default in payment of any installment or of interest the whole shall become due, or with exchange, whether at a fixed rate or at the current rate, or with costs of collection or any attorney's fee in case payment is not made at maturity." Whether an instrument is uncertain in the amount payable depends upon its provisions. One bank in Pennsylvania includes, as a part of a judgment note otherwise negotiable, an obligation to pay "all taxes or/and premiums paid by said bank.” 

While such an instrument is transferable by assignment it is not a "courier without luggage." 

First National Bank of Miami, Fla., v. Bosler, 297 Pa. 353 (1929). A promissory note, dated at Miami, Florida, stated that the principal sum was to bear interest at 8% per annum from date until fully paid, but also that deferred payments were to bear interest from maturity at 10% per annum, the two clauses being irreconcilable as regards payment after maturity. Plaintiff sought to recover as a holder in due course. The lower court offered leave 

10 24 Ohio App. 246 (1927). 17 56 PS 2.

to amend so that plaintiff might sue as an assignee, but the offer was refused. In sustaining a non-suit, it was said by SIMPSON, J. "It does not contain, therefore, as it 'must,' in order to be negotiable, 'an unconditional promise to pay a sum certain."" 

Sec. 873. Unconditional Promise. The promise to pay must be unconditional,18 It is not unconditional where a "note is given for advancements, and it is the understanding it will be renewed at maturity,' or where it is expressly made subject to the terms or conditions of some other agreement. 99 19 

Klots Throwing Co. v. Manufacturers' Commercial Co., 179 Fed. 

813 (1910). A promissory note in the sum of $3,166, otherwise negotiable, contained the statement: "Value received, subject to a contract between maker and payee of October 25, 1905." It was transferred, for value received and prior to maturity, to the plaintiff. The maker refused to pay it on grounds of breach of the contract for which the note was given. In deciding that the note was not a negotiable instrument, and that plaintiff held the instrument as an assignee, rather than as a holder in due course, it was said by NOYES, C. J. "In our opinion when a note contains special stipulations, and its payment is subject to contingencies, it fails to possess the character of a negotiable instrument, and is subject in the hands of an assignee to any defense which would be available if it were still held by the original payee."

Sec. 877. Contingent Event. The code provides that an instrument payable upon a contingency is not negotiable, and that the happening of the event does not cure the defect.20 Death is certain, and an instrument pay. able on such a contingency, or within a fixed period thereafter, is negotiable." Whether a person will live to reach his majority, however, is a contingency. 

Kelley v. Hemingway, 18 Illinois 604 (1852). A promissory note was made payable when the payee reached the age of twenty-one. 

In commenting on the possibility as to whether the money would ever become payable, it was said by TREAT, C. J. "The fact that the payee lived till he was twenty-one years of age makes no difference. It was not a promissory note when made, and it could not become such by matter ex post facto."

Sec. 879. Confession of Judgment. A negotiable instrument may authorize the confession of judgment if the instrument be not paid at maturity. It is well settled, however, that a note which authorizes confession of judgment prior to the maturity of the obligation is not a negotiable instrument.30 Most banks in Pennsylvania, in making direct loans to borrowers, use judg ment notes on which judgment may be confessed at any time. It has long been the practice in this commonwealth of allowing a judgment to be confessed on an obligation sounding in contract, whether the obligation be then due or not.3 "Execution cannot issue until default and then only for the amount due, but in the meantime the creditor has the right to his judgment as contracted for.... 32 The judgment immediately operates as a lien against the real estate of the defendant which may be located in the county where it is recorded, or to which it may be transferred.³* 

This lien continues for a period of five years, at which time it will terminate unless revived in the manner provided by statute.85

A judgment of this sort is intended to serve as collateral security, and may even cover future advances.36 Such a note is not a negotiable instrument.

It may be transferred by assignment, but the holder could not qualify as a holder in due course. Most banks, however, retain these notes until paid. It is more important, when a merchant accepts a judgment note from his customer, and then discounts it at a bank, to use the negotiable form, i. e., a note which authorizes the confession of judgment only at maturity. The bank could then qualify as a holder in due course. 33

Sec. 883. Negotiability. The written acknowledgment of a debt is not a negotiable instrument. Either the instrument must contain words authorizing its negotiation, such as, "I, we, or either of us promise to pay to the order of," or the instrument must be payable to bearer.

A executed and delivered to B a promissory note properly dated and reading as follows: "Sixty days after date I promise to pay to B the sum of one hundred ($100.00) dollars payable at the 

Second National Bank, State College, Pa." B endorsed the note to C before maturity, and for value. A refused to pay the note on its due date, and defended on the ground that there had been a failure of the consideration for which the note was given. Assuming the validity of this defense, could C compel A to pay the note?

Sec. 884. Payable to Order. "The instrument is payable to order where it is drawn payable to the order of a specified' person, or to him or his order." 51 If an instrument is payable to order and is endorsed in blank (this means the signature of the payee standing alone), it is thereafter payable to bearer and is transferable by delivery, whether it be voluntary or involuntary, intentional or unintentional. If it is lost or stolen, the finder or thief is liable to the lawful owner of it, and if it is converted into money such persons are liable in an action in quasi-contract for money had and received to the use of the rightful owner.5 But an instrument endorsed in blank may be negotiated by a finder or thief without further indorsement, and if it reaches the hands of a holder in due course, such a holder may collect or further negotiate the instrument. 52 

Employers' Liability Assurance Corp., Ltd. v. Greenfield, 316 Pa. 

477 (1934). This was an action in replevin to recover stolen bonds held by the Washington Trust Company as collateral security for a loan. The bonds were acquired in good faith, before maturity, for value and without notice of any infirmity or defect in the title. 

It was not until the bonds matured and were presented for redemption that the bank learned that they had been stolen. PER CURIAM. "There was an abundance of evidence that the bank obtained the instruments in good faith, and nothing to indicate the contrary. 

Consequently, there was no question to leave to the jury." 

Sec. 885. Payable to Bearer. Where an instrument is payable to bearer, it may be negotiated without any indorsement at all.53 The code provides that an instrument is payable to bearer (1) when it is expressed to be so payable; or, (2) when it is payable to a person named therein or bearer; or, (3) when it is payable to the order of a fictitious or nonexisting person, and such fact was known to the person making it so payable; or, (4) when the name of the payee does not purport to be the name of any person; or, (5) when the only or last indorsement is an indorsement in blank.5 The intent of the maker 54

603 of a check, in inserting the name of the payee, is usually the test as to whether the payee is a fictitious person. 

Where the maker believes that the payee is a real person, and intends that he should be paid, and the payee's indorsement is forged, the bank that pays on the forged instrument is liable for the loss.55

Commonwealth v. Globe Indemnity Co., 323 Pa. 261 (1936). The laws of the commonwealth provide for the condemnation and slaughter of tubercular cattle and the payment of compensation to the owner. Thomas, an employee of the commonwealth, fabricated papers showing amounts payable to fictitious or non-existent persons, as payment for the destruction of such cattle. The fiscal officers of the commonwealth executed and mailed the checks, ignorant of the fraud. Thomas went to the post offices to which this mail was sent and obtained the checks. He then endorsed the names of the payees, and in due course the checks were honored by the drawee bank. The commonwealth instituted this action against the surety for the bank. LINN, J. "In drawing the check to the order of the payee the commonwealth was not intending that an imaginary person or a nonexistent person should as the payee take the check. The checks were therefore not payable to bearer. 

The alleged endorsement of the payee's name was a forgery; the drawer had not intended that Thomas should endorse the payee's name." ..

Part 3. Execution and Delivery Sec. 886. Date of Instrument. A negotiable instru ment may be antedated or postdated, if this is not done for an illegal or fraudulent purpose." Where an instrument is payable at a fixed period after date, but is issued undated, the holder may insert the true date."7 But the insertion of a wrong date does not avoid the instrument in the hands of a subsequent holder in due course. to him, "the date so inserted is to be regarded as the true date." 58

The application of this principle should involve no difficulty. If an undated instrument, expressed to be payable six months after date, is delivered on July 1, 1946, and is dated as of Feburary 1, 1946, As

Sec. 887. Incomplete Instrument. Where an incom plete instrument has not been delivered it will not, if completed and negotiated without authority, be a valid contract in the hands of any one.59 This is an absolute defense. But a person who executes a paper in blank and delivers it to another for the purpose of having it filled in as a negotiable instrument, gives such other person prima facie authority to complete the instrument.

If a third party receives it prior to its completion, it must be filled out strictly within the authority given. 

But if it is completed and then negotiated to a holder in due course, he may enforce it as if it had been filled up strictly in accordance with the authority given." 

Where a note is delivered to the payee in blank, the maker makes the payee his agent, and if his agent fills it in for a larger sum than he was authorized to do, an innocent party who parts with his property on the faith of it may look to the maker.61 This is merely an application of the rule that as between two innocent parties, he whose misplaced confidence has caused a loss is required to bear it."2

Sec. 888. Complete Instrument. Non-delivery of a complete instrument is a personal and not an absolute defense. As between immediate or as to remote parties, delivery is essential. In Bean's Estate,63 decedent's housekeeper, during his last illness, saw upon his bureau a pocketbook, and with his consent locked it in her trunk for safekeeping. After his death she opened it and found a note for $3,000 payable to the order of the claimant, a niece who had resided in the family for several years, and delivered it to her. The note was re- 50 56 PS 20. 60 56 PS 19.

The code provides, however, that where a completed instrument is acquired by a holder in due course (in good faith and for value, as distinguished from the gratuitous claimant above), "a valid delivery thereof by all parties prior to him, so as to make them liable to him, is conclusively presumed." 64

A different case would have been presented, therefore, if the note above had been payable to bearer or had been endorsed in blank, and then had reached the hands of a holder in due course.

Sec. 890. Forgery. The forgery of a signature, in the absence of an estoppel, e. g., negligence in the care of a rubber stamp which makes a facsimile," is an absolute defense.67 The act of 1849 68 provides that where a signature is forged, the holder may recover back from the person previously holding the instrument the value or amount that has been paid. It was held that the drawee bank might recover back from the collecting bank. Notice of a forgery within a reasonable time after it should have been discovered is essential. A delay of a few days has been held unreasonable where the drawer was negligent in discovering a forged indorsement," but a delay of twenty-two months has been held not to be unreasonable where the payee whose indorsement was forged was deceived by her agent."2 

Sec. 891. Fraud. Fraud in the inducement of a negotiable instrument, e. g., fraudulent representation, is a personal defense which may be asserted against an immediate or remote party, but not against a holder in due course. Fraud in the procurement of a negotiable instrument, or trickery employed in obtaining one's signature, is a forgery and in the absence of an estoppel may be asserted as an absolute defense to the instrument. In Jensen v. Braslafsky," it was held that where a note formed a part of a printed order for merchandise, which was so cunningly attached to the contract that it could be separated, one part of which with the maker's name constituted a negotiable instrument and the other an unsigned order for the goods, the separation of the formal note from the contract was a forg ery of the writing as it was executed, and that if there was no negligence in the maker, the good faith and absence of negligence on the part of the holder were immaterial.

Sec. 893. Other Defenses. Lack of contractual ca pacity is an absolute defense. The code provides, however, that the "indorsement or assignment of the instrument by a corporation or by an infant passes the property therein, notwithstanding that, from want of capacity, the corporation or infant may incur no liability thereon." 70 In other words, an infant who acquires a negotiable instrument may further negotiate the instrument by indorsement, or transfer the title. He may be permitted to avoid personal liability on his indorsement, but this would not disturb the rights and liabilities of other parties to the instrument. Where an instrument is void on grounds of public policy, such defense is absolute. Sec. 894. Personal Defense. Absence or failure of consideration is a personal defense. The execution, or any negotiation of a negotiable instrument, is presumed to be supported by a valuable consideration,³¹ but as far as immediate and remote parties are concerned, this is a rebuttable and not a conclusive presumption.82 As to such parties, the absence or failure of consideration may be shown, in whole or in part, by the party sought to be charged with liability. If the maker submits testimony showing a want of consideration, the burden then shifts to the holder to prove that a consideration exists. 

When a note is repeatedly renewed there is a strong inference that it is supported by a consideration. In First 

National Bank v. Singer,85 a note was renewed fourteen times. The maker then attempted to prove a failure of consideration, but it was held that such a defense was untenable. 84 

Sec. 895. Estoppel. An exception to the necessity of a consideration, as to immediate and remote parties, may be made on grounds of estoppel. If a person lends his credit to a bank in the form of a promissory note, purely as an accommodation and for the purpose of deceiving the government agencies as to the bank's solvency, he must abide by the consequences of what he does. 88 

Bangor Trust Co. v. Christine, 297 Pa. 64 (1929). Defendant executed and delivered to the president and secretary of plaintiff trust company a promissory note in the sum of $10,000. It was used to cover overdrafts of a construction company in which the two officers of the trust company were largely interested. In holding the defendant liable on the note, it was said by SCHAFFER, J. "He necessarily knew that the transaction was intended to misrepresent something to somebody concerned for the bank's solvency. 61 56 PS 61.

Sec. 896. Holder in Due Course. Absence or failure of consideration may not be asserted against a holder in due course, or against a person who derives his title through a holder in due course.87 It is important to note, however, that a holder in due course is a person who acquires the instrument without notice of any defect. If he knows when he takes the instrument that the maker has a valid defense, he is not a holder in due course. Where, for example, a note is given as consideration for a contract which is broken while it is still in the hands of the payee, the maker may avoid payment as against the person to whom the payee negotiates the instrument with knowledge of the breach.88 This was the situation in Enterprise Manufacturing Company v. 

Moore.89 Moore executed a promissory note to Murphy in the sum of $700 as part payment for the installation of three stokers in a heating plant. Murphy negotiated the note to the plaintiff, but the jury found that the plaintiff had notice when it accepted the note that the stokers had not been installed and that there was a breach of the contract between the maker and the payee. 

Sec. 897. Accommodation Party. The position of an accommodation party is a peculiar one. 

He is a person who lends his name and personal credit to another without receiving any consideration.90 The absence of a consideration is usually known to all parties to the transaction. The person for whose accommodation the instrument is executed would have no claim against the party who signed it purely as an accommodation.º¹ But the code specifies that the accommodation party shall be liable to the holder of the instrument, notwithstanding the holder, in taking the instrument, knows that the accommodation party received no consideration." Part 5. Negotiation 

Sec. 898. Methods of Negotiation. If there is any agreement between the maker and the payee of a negotiable instrument that it is not to be negotiated, it should be expressed on the face of the instrument. said in Levitt v. Johnstown Office Supply Company, if it is "given for value and is an actual obligation of the maker or acceptor, its legal effect cannot be affected or destroyed by an alleged parol agreement not to negotiate it." If the instrument is payable to order, it may be negotiated by indorsement and delivery. If it is payable to bearer, it may be negotiated without indorsement." If it is payable to order and is then endorsed in blank, it is thereafter payable to bearer." As a general rule the person accepting a negotiable instrument will insist upon having the indorsement of the transferor. He may wish to hold the transferor to the liability of an endorser, or otherwise liable if the instrument has been improperly obtained or negotiated. If it is presented at a bank for payment, the bank will usually insist upon an indorsement in order to know to whom payment has been made and as proof of payment.

Sec. 899. Kinds of Indorsement. 

indorsement in blank, an indorsement may be special, restrictive, qualified, or conditional." (1) A special indorsement specifies the person to whom, or to whose order the instrument is to be further payable.98 If it is payable in the first instance to the order of A, it may be endorsed by A to B or to the order of B. A is likely to endorse specially if the instrument is transferred to B in payment of a debt, and if A wishes to have a written record that B has become a party to the instrument. (2) A restrictive indorsement prohibits the further negotiation of the instrument.99 If it is endorsed by A to B, rather than to the order of B, or if it is endorsed "for deposit," it is no longer negotiable and must be presented for payment. The purpose of a restrictive indorsement is not only to prevent the further negotiation of the instrument, but usually to constitute the transferee the agent of the transferor in presenting the instrument for payment. (3) A qualified indorsement constitutes the endorser a mere assignor of the title to the instrument, without subjecting him to liability for payment in the event of the insolvency of prior parties. It may be made by using the words "without recourse." 100 

There is "nothing in the use of these words that would cause a subsequent holder to suspect that there were any defenses existing between prior parties." 101

Sec. 901. Assignment. The Act of 1806 107 provides that where a note, bond, or other instrument in writing authorizes the confession of judgment, the prothonotary shall, upon application of the original holder, or assignee of such holder, enter judgment against the persons liable in the instrument. For this reason most banks in Pennsylvania rediscount notes under an agree ment by the payee, which is printed on the back, to "sell, assign, transfer and set over" unto the bank all his right, title and interest in the instrument. Such an assignment confers upon the bank the right to have judgment confessed against the maker. An indorsement of this sort, though coupled with an assignment, does not deprive the bank of the rights of a holder in due course, provided the instrument is negotiable. In Peerless 

Heater Company v. Hobson Flatware Co., Inc.,108 a holder in due course instituted an action on a negotiable instrument, alleging that it became the owner "by assignment" from the payee, but it was held that the word "assignment" should be treated as surplusage. 

Farnsworth v. Burdick, 94 Kansas 749 (1915). Wheeler, the payee of a negotiable instrument, executed the following indorsement: "I hereby assine this note over to E. H. Farnsworth, this 

Nov. 1, 1910." The makers denied liability alleging failure of

We are of the opinion that the assignment of this note is an indorsement thereof under the Negotiable Instruments Law; that Farnsworth is a holder in due course; that the makers of the note cannot set up the defense against the note that could have been set up against it in the hands of Wheeler."

Sec. 902. Suretyship. The Negotiable Instruments 

Act imposes a secondary liability upon an endorser, but only upon the endorser of a negotiable instrument, and then only if the requirements as to presentment and notice of dishonor are satisfied. Banks, in making direct loans, seldom use a negotiable instrument. They prefer, for security reasons, to use a note on which judgment may be confessed immediately rather than at maturity. An accommodation indorsement on such an instrument is a nullity. It is meaningless because the instrument does not satisfy the requirements of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and because a signature in blank does not satisfy the Statute of Frauds. For this reason banks, in using the non-negotiable form, usually incorporate on the back of their notes the statement: "I, we, or either of us, hereby guarantee payment of the within note, and all renewals and extensions thereof." 

Such an undertaking is a contract of suretyship, simply because it does not contain in substance the words, "This is not intended to be a contract of suretyship." 109 Occasionally a merchant receives a non-negotiable note from his customer. If a bank rediscounts such a note, an indorsement in blank would merely serve to assign the title to the bank. For this reason banking institutions incorporate a contract of suretyship on the back of a nonnegotiable instrument when it is offered for discount, or furnish forms for use by merchants on which a contract of suretyship is printed on the back. 

100 Act of July 24, 1913, P. L. 971, 8 PS 1.

40

Reardon's Estate, 307 Pa. 350 (1932). The R. C. & K. Beverage 

Company, by S. B. Cunningham, secretary and treasurer, executed a judgment note for $10,000 to the Peoples National Bank of Tarentum. It contained a power of attorney to confess judgment at any time. It was endorsed by Reardon, Cunningham, and Kelley, directors and owners of all the stock of the company. One of the principal questions involved was the liability of the endorser, Reardon. DREW, J. "This note contained a power of attorney to confess judgment at any time, and was therefore non-negotiable. 

Upon the back of the note appear only the signatures of the three endorsers, and it is well settled, under our decisions, that the endorser of a nonnegotiable note is not liable thereon in the absence of a promise in writing to pay the debt of the maker. There was no such agreement by Reardon. The signature itself, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of such contract to satisfy the statute of frauds." 

Part 6. Rights of the Holder Sec. 903. Holder in Due Course. Every holder of a negotiable instrument is deemed prima facie to be a holder in due course.' 110

This is merely a legal assumption. Where the genuineness of the indorsement through which the holder claims title is properly put in issue, he may be required to prove his ownership of the instrument, and if any other defect is shown by the party liable on the instrument, the burden then shifts to him to prove that he is a holder in due course.112

Where the maker shows that the instrument was obtained from him or from some intermediate party by fraud, felony or force, or that it was lost, the holder is called upon to show, not only his lawful possession of the instrument, but also that he acquired it before maturity, for value, and without notice of any defect.¹¹³

One of the most important sections of the Negotiable Instruments Act is that defining the requisites of a holder in due course. It reads:

A holder in due course is a holder who has taken the instrument under the following conditions: (1) That it is complete and reg- 110 56 PS 139.
