Sec. 904. Notice of Infirmity. Notice of infirmity may be actual or constructive.115 If the holder of the instrument has knowledge of such facts that his action in taking it amounts to bad faith, he is not a holder in due course. This principle "is closely analogous to the equitable doctrine of clean hands. Where the instrument is purchased for value and prior to maturity, the fact that interest may be in arrear,118 or that an installment is overdue,119 is not alone sufficient to charge the purchaser with notice of any irregularity. The purchase of the instrument at a considerable discount may be some evidence of irregularity, depending upon the circumstances. 

McNamara v. Jose, 28 Wash. 461 (1902). The payee obtained a promissory note in the sum of $1,000 through fraudulent representation. He sold it to the plaintiff, three months prior to maturity, for one-half that amount. This occurred in the State of 

Washington. The note was payable at Nome, Alaska. The maker had advertised his defense, but this had not come to the attention of the plaintiff. In deciding that the purchase price, in conjunction with payment at Nome, Alaska, was not sufficient to put the plaintiff on inquiry, it was said by FULLERTON, J. "It certainly would not be sought by investors in commercial paper so long as there was a possibility of their being compelled to enforce its payment at that place."

Sec. 906. Rights of H. D. C. "A holder in due course holds the instrument free from any defect of title of prior parties, and free from defenses available to prior parties among themselves, and may enforce payment of the instrument for the full amount thereof against all parties liable thereon." 121 

Cochran v. Fox Chase Bank, 209 Pa. 34 (1904). Certain negotiable coupon bonds belonging to Cochran were stolen by Douglas and pledged with the Fox Chase Bank as collateral for a loan. 

The question involved was: "Whether or not a bank, to which stolen coupon bonds payable to bearer have been pledged as collateral security for a loan by the thief in the ordinary course of business, without notice to the bank of any infirmity in the title, and without any circumstances to put the bank on inquiry, takes a good title thereto as against him from whom they were stolen." 

DEAN, J. "It is . . . settled that a bona fide holder of such an instrument for value before maturity, taken in the usual course of business, acquires a good title thereto, even as against him from whom it was stolen." 

Sec. 907. Title through H. D. C. A holder in due course may delegate another with all the rights that he has in the instrument. Some instruments do not mature for a considerable period of time, and it would be unjust to compel him to personally retain an instrument until it matures merely because he learns of some infirmity after he has acquired it. For this reason if a subsequent holder or assignee "derives his title through a holder in due course," and "is not himself a party to 

121 56 PS 137.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

617 any fraud or illegality affecting the instrument," he "has all the rights of such former holder in respect to all parties prior to the latter." 122 The following problems should make this clear. (1) A executed a negotiable instrument to B without consideration. B negotiated it to C, who qualified as a holder in due course. C negotiated it to D without consideration. Under these circumstances D, having derived his title through a holder in due course, could enforce payment against A or against B. A would be primarily liable, and B would be secondarily liable. In this illustration D could not enforce payment against C because of the failure of consideration as between these immediate parties. (2) A was induced through fraudulent representation to execute a negotiable instrument to B. He was told that the proceeds were to be used for a charitable purpose when such was not the case. 

B negotiated the instrument to C, who qualified as a holder in due course. C negotiated the note to D, but D had notice of the fraud when he took the instrument. Under these circumstances 

D, although he could not qualify as a holder in due course, nevertheless has all the rights of the holder in due course from whom he took the instrument. (3) A purchased a negotiable coupon bond. He sold it to B. 

B deposited it in a safe deposit box, but the bank was burglarized, the bond was stolen, and was subsequently purchased by C, who qualified as a holder in due course. C then sold the bond back to A. Under these circumstances A could enforce payment of the instrument, notwithstanding his knowledge that it had been stolen, inasmuch as he acquired his title through a holder in due course. 123 (4) A was induced through fraudulent representation to execute a negotiable instrument to B. B negotiated the instrument to C, who qualified as a holder in due course. C thereafter negotiated the note back to B. Under these circumstances B could not rely on the fact that he acquired the note from a holder in due course, since he was the person guilty of the fraud.12 124

His transfer to the plaintiff company, though subsequent to maturity, vested in the latter his rights which could not be defeated on the ground that the note was accommodation paper." ..

Link v. Bergdoll, 35 Pa. Superior Ct. 155 (1907). HEAD, J. 

“A contract of indorsement, when made, is neither a primary nor an absolute one. It is secondary and conditional. It is but an agreement for a future liability upon and after the happening of certain contingencies. These are nowhere described in the body of the instrument indorsed, but inhere, ex lege, in the contract created by the simple act of indorsement. They are (a) presentment for payment at the time and place designated by the parties or the law for that purpose; (b) refusal to pay by the party or parties primarily bound; (c) prompt notice of such refusal to the indorser, whose liability then, but not until then, becomes fixed." 

Sec. 910. Implied Warranties. It has been observed that the maker or drawer of a negotiable instrument may assert an absolute defense against any one. The existence of such a defense, however, does not accrue to the advantage of an endorser. A transfer by indorsement is an independent undertaking. The code provides that every person negotiating an instrument by delivery or by qualified indorsement may be held to the following warranties: (1) That the instrument is genuine and in all respects what it purports to be. (2) That he has a good title to it. (3) That all prior parties had capacity to contract. (4) That he has no knowledge of any fact which would impair the validity of the instrument or render it valueless. But when the negotiation is by delivery only, the warranty extends in favor of no holder other than the immediate transferee.131

These warranties considerably enhance the responsibility of an endorser. The instrument as originally executed may have been forged or procured by fraud, or it may have been executed without authority, or it may be the obligation of an infant or a lunatic. These are all defenses which would relieve the principal debtor. The existence of such a defense would not relieve an endorser. An indorsement without recourse will excuse the endorser if non-payment results from the insolvency of the maker, but not from any of the above warranties. 131 56 PS 156.

Sec. 911. Order of Liability. "In the case of ordi nary commercial paper, parties are liable to each other in succession as their names appear on the instrument, the maker being the principal debtor and the endorsers being severally liable in the order in which their names are written." This rule applies to accommodation parties. Thus, an accommodation maker is liable to an accommodation endorser, "unless a cosuretyship was agreed upon." 132

If an endorser is compelled to pay the instrument, he may recover from a prior party, but not from a subsequent party in the absence of an agreement to that effect.133 The right of contribution between parties jointly liable on negotiable instruments arises indedependently of the statute. This right, as said in the cases, is bottomed and fixed on general principles of justice. A joint relation, unless otherwise agreed, imposes an equality of burden.134 

Part 8. Presentment for Payment 

Sec. 912. Manner of Presentment. Presentment for payment is not necessary in order to charge the person primarily liable on the instrument, but it is necessary in order to charge persons secondarily liable.135 It may, however, be waived by contract, express or implied.136

If the instrument is not payable on demand, presentment must be made on the day it falls due.17 It should be presented by the holder, at a reasonable hour on a business day, at a proper place, and to the person primarily liable.138 The place of presentment may be designated in the instrument, but if not, then it should be presented, alternately, at the address of the person to make payment, or his usual place of business or residence, or at his last known place of business or residence or wherever he can be found.139 Presentment is excused if he

Sec. 913. Date of Maturity. Where the date of an instrument is fixed at a certain number of days after date, the maturity date is determined by excluding the date of the instrument and including the date of payment. The code provides that when the day of maturity falls upon Sunday or a holiday, the instrument is payable on the next succeeding business day.143 The act of

Day, Armistice Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, and also every Saturday after twelve o'clock noon. 

Whenever these days fall on Sunday, except Good Friday, Labor Day, Election Day, or Thanksgiving Day, the following Monday is a legal holiday. Saturday morning is a secular or business day, but with the following distinctions: (1) Checks, drafts, bills of exchange, and promissory notes, payable at sight or on demand, which would otherwise be payable on any half holiday Saturday, shall be deemed to be payable at or before twelve o'clock noon.

Sec. 914. Payable at Bank. "Where the instrument is made payable at a bank, it is equivalent to an order to the bank to pay the same for the account of the principal debtor thereon." 145 If the instrument is held by the bank, the bank should appropriate the funds of the maker to the discharge of the obligation, otherwise an endorser will be relieved of liability. 

Franklin Savings & Trust Co. v. Clark, 283 Pa. 212 (1925).

Plaintiff bank held a promissory note of one Garland, which had been endorsed by the defendant. On the day of maturity the bank held credits of the maker sufficient to pay the note, and had been advised to make collection on the day of maturity by the defendant, who said that he would not endorse any further renewal. The bank protested the note on the day of maturity, but failed to appropriate the deposit of the maker in satisfaction of the note. 

On the following two days practically all of the deposit was checked out. The bank then instituted this action against the defendant. 

KEPHART, J. "Where a bank is the holder of a note payable at the banking house, and has on its maturity a cash deposit of the maker exceeding the sum due, the bank is bound to apply this credit of the maker in discharge of the note, unless it has been specifically appropriated by the maker to a particular purpose."

Part 9. Notice of Dishonor 

Sec. 916. Manner of Notice. Whenever a negotiable instrument has been dishonored by non-payment or nonacceptance, notice of dishonor must be given to the parties secondarily liable, otherwise such parties are discharged from liability.155 Notice may be written or oral, and may be given in person or through the mails.158 

Mere knowledge that the instrument has not been paid by the maker is not notice of dishonor. 

Marshall v. Sonneman, 216 Pa. 65 (1906). Sonneman and Marshall were both endorsers on a promissory note. The note having been dishonored by the maker, Marshall, the second endorser, 148 56 PS 324.

A notary public was called and testified that he delivered notices of protest to both Sonneman and Marshall, but apparently the notice addressed to Sonneman had been delivered to Marshall, and the notice addressed to Marshall had been delivered to Sonneman. At any rate the notice produced by Sonneman as having been received by him was addressed to Marshall, as was also the envelope in which it was contained. MESTREZAT, J. "Why should the defendant accept this as a notice of dishonor to him and take care of the note? There is no intimation in the paper that the holder intended to look to him for payment. On the contrary, the notice is that the holder will look to Marshall, his immediate prior indorser, for payment." 157 

Sec. 917. Time of Notice. Where the parties reside in the same place notice should be given either before the close of business hours on the following day, or if given at the residence of the person to receive it, then before the usual hours of rest. If sent by mail, it must be deposited in the post office in time to reach him on the day following. Where the parties reside in different places, notice of dishonor must be deposited in the post office in time to go by mail the day following, and if the mail is not used, then within the same length of time in which a letter posted as above would have been received.158 Notice by mail, properly addressed, is ef fective, notwithstanding any miscarriage in the mails.159 

The party receiving the notice has the same length of time for giving notice to antecedent parties.160 "Notice of dishonor is dispensed with when, after the exercise of reasonable diligence, it cannot be given to or does not reach the parties to be charged." 181 Delay is excused when caused by circumstances beyond the control of the holder, and when it is not imputable to his default, misconduct, or negligence.' 162

Sec. 918. Place of Notice. Where the mail is used and the party entitled to notice has added an address to his signature, notice must be sent to that address. 

Otherwise it may be sent to the post office nearest to his place of residence or where he is accustomed to receive his letters. If he lives in one place and has his place of business in another, it may be sent to either place. 

If he is sojourning in another place, notice may be sent there. 163

If no address has been given and the endorser lives in a city, a letter addressed to that city, without more, will be sufficient.164 Nothing should be added, however, that would lead the carrier to deliver it to a wrong address.

Harr v. Edsall, 121 Pa. Superior Ct. 19 (1936). Defendant endorsed the note of a Philadelphia laundry company, of which he was vice president and secretary. His own place of business was in an office building in a different location in the city. His home was at Haverford. On the due date the note was presented for payment, and notice of dishonor was mailed to him at the address of the laundry company. Three years later a second notice was addressed to his home at Haverford. In deciding that such notice was inadequate, it was said by PARKER, J. "We are of the opinion that the phrase 'his place of business' as used in this statute does not comprehend every place a person may transact any business or a place which he may occasionally visit to transact business. 

It connotes more and refers to a place where he carries on a business in which he is personally engaged as a merchant, tradesman, professional man, or similar trade or calling."

Sec. 922. Presentment. A check must be presented for payment within a reasonable time after its issue, or the drawer will be discharged from liability thereon to the extent caused by the delay." Where the parties all reside in the same place, the holder should present the check on the day it is received, or the following day. When it is payable at a different place from that in which it is negotiated, it should be forwarded by mail on the same or the next day for payment.175 This rule is restricted in its operation to a check received during banking hours and a sufficient time before the close of the bank to enable the payee either to present it for payment or to deposit it for collection on the day on which it is received. Consequently, if it is received after the close of banking hours and is deposited by the payee in

Wendkos v. Scranton Life Ins. Co., 340 Pa. 550 (1941). Plain tiff was the beneficiary of a $5,000 life insurance policy. A payment of $25 fell due on Sunday, April 3. On Saturday the insured mailed his employer's check to the insurance company's office in the same city. The check was received on Monday, April 4, and was deposited in a collecting bank on Tuesday, April 5. The check was presented for payment on Wednesday, April 6, at about 2 P. M.

One hour earlier the funds of the maker (insured's employer) were withdrawn from the bank by a receiver in bankruptcy, and the check was dishonored. The insurance company claimed the policy lapsed for non-payment, but offered to reinstate it on proof of insurability. The insured was unable to furnish such evidence, and died on October 30. In deciding that the insurance company had waited an unreasonable time in presenting the check for payment, it was said by SCHAFFER, C. J. "Where all the parties, as here, are in the same city diligence requires that the check be presented for payment on the day of its receipt or on the following day." 

Sec. 923. Acceptance. The drawee of a bank check or bill of exchange is not liable thereon until he accepts it. A bank check is a bill of exchange, and acceptance by the drawee bank carries with it the same obligation as would the acceptance of a bill of exchange. A telegram promising to honor a check is an acceptance. The payment of a check is the equivalent of an acceptance, and for this reason the bank should ascertain the depositor's account before paying it.

Sec. 924. Certification. "Where a check is certified by the bank on which it is drawn, the certification is equivalent to an acceptance." 179 When the maker causes it to be certified, the payment of it is conditional, and is defeasible upon non-payment or dishonor. Thus, if the bank fails before it can be presented for payment, the maker must bear the loss.180 "Where the holder of a check procures it to be accepted or certified, the drawer and all endorsers are discharged from liability thereon."

Sec. 925. Stop Order. A check is not an assignment of any part of the funds to the credit of the drawer with the bank.183 For this reason the maker is entitled to stop payment.184 If payment has been stopped, the holder may not institute an action against the bank. 

His cause of action, if any, is against the maker. 185 

Knowledge that payment has been stopped is not conclusive of bad faith on the part of a subsequent holder. 

He may still be a holder in due course." 186 

Sec. 926. Death of Maker. In some states the payee of a check is allowed a short period of time, usually ten days, two weeks, or thirty days, in which to present a check for payment after the death of the maker. In 

Pennsylvania an unpaid check is revoked by the death of the maker,187 although it will operate as an equitable assignment when drawn for the full and exact amount in the bank. A signed check, left blank as to payee and amount, is not an assignment of the fund.188 

Mellier's Estate, 320 Pa. 150 (1936). Desirous of having the body of her husband removed from a cemetery in Asbury Park, N. J., and brought to West Laurel Hill Cemetery for reinterment, Etta Mellier, four days prior to her death, delivered a check to the claimant in the sum of $5,000. The check was not paid because of insufficient funds, and this claim was presented at the audit of her estate. MAXEY, J. "In the instant case claimant never received the money the check ordered to be paid her, and the death of decedent revoked the incompleted gift in trust. The delivery of a check is not an executed gift of the money and will be revoked by the death of the drawer before actual payment, except where the check is drawn for the exact amount in the bank, in which case it will be sustained as an equitable assignment of the fund."

Sec. 928. Account Stated. A bank book settled, balance struck, and checks returned to the depositor, will become an account stated if not promptly examined and errors of amount pointed out for correction. As to items not protested it is binding, and as to contested items, the burden of proving error rests upon the disputant.191 It is the duty of the depositor to examine the returned checks promptly and notify the bank of alterations on the face of the checks, or forgeries of his signature as a drawer, but not of forgeries of indorsements upon the checks.192 He may assume that the bank has ascertained the genuineness of the indorsements.193 The Act of 1941194 provides that a bank shall not be liable to its depositor for the amount charged to his account or paid upon a forged, altered or raised check or draft, unless a proper claim is made within six months after notice that his cancelled checks or drafts are ready for delivery, or within six months after the return of the cancelled checks or drafts. The same act also provides that a stop-payment order on a check or draft shall be effective for a period of one year only, unless renewed in writing.

Sec. 929. Worthless Checks. The Penal Code 195 

provides that whoever, with intent to defraud, makes or negotiates any check or draft upon any banking institution, knowing at the time that he has not sufficient funds or credit arrangement with the bank for the payment of the instrument, although no express representation is made in reference thereto, shall be punished by fine not exceeding $1,000 or imprisonment not exceeding two years, or both. Non-payment because of lack of funds or credit constitutes prima facie evidence of intent to defraud, unless the maker makes good the instrument within ten days after receiving notice of non-payment.

Sec. 930. Kinds of Discharge. A negotiable instru ment is discharged by payment, or intentional cancellation, or by any other act which will discharge a simple contract for the payment of money, or when the principal debtor acquires the instrument in his own right.'

A person secondarily liable is discharged when the instrument itself is discharged as above, or by the intentional cancellation of his signature by the holder, or by the discharge of a prior party, or by a valid tender of payment by a prior party, or by release of the principal debtor unless the holder's right of recourse is expressly reserved.197 The holder may expressly renounce his rights against any party to the instrument. Such renunciation must be in writing, unless the instrument is delivered up to the person primarily liable thereon.198 

Sec. 931. Surrender of Collateral. It is well settled that the surrender of collateral security by the holder without the knowledge or consent of an endorser, will relieve the latter from liability to the former. Sec. 932. Extension of Payment. An agreement be tween the holder and the primary debtor to extend the time of payment will discharge an endorser, unless made with the assent of the endorser, or unless the right of recourse against an endorser is expressly reserved.200

Many banking institutions incorporate a contract on the back of their credit instruments, under which an endorser or surety agrees to all renewals or extensions of the principal obligation. Such an agreement is valid, even though a surety has given notice that he would not be liable for the obligation.201 A waiver of due diligence in collecting the note or enforcing its payment is also enforceable.202 203

Part 12. Notes of Banking Institutions 

Sec. 934. Banking Practice. Nearly all banking institutions in Pennsylvania employ the judgment note to the exclusion of the simple promissory note.

A ma- jority of these banks also incorporate a contract of suretyship on the back of their credit instruments, and authorize the confession of judgment therein against the endorser or surety. In banking practice a number of different kinds of judgment notes are used, each one suited to the nature of the undertaking. The following observations are based on a study of 1,788 forms, as submitted by 910 banks, representing nearly all the commercial banking institutions in the commonwealth. 

The detailed characteristics of these obligations are reported in the law reviews.207 (1) Negotiable Judgment Note. This instrument is intended primarily for the use of merchants in extending credit to their customers, and is then rediscounted by the bank. It is a negotiable instrument, as it must be, in order that the bank might qualify as a holder in due course, otherwise the bank would be subject to all the personal defenses that the maker might have. against the merchant. The distinguishable characteristic of this form is the provision that the judgment may be entered only at the maturity of the obligation. (2) Non-negotiable Judgment Note. This instrument is used almost exclusively by banks in making direct loans to borrowers. 

It provides that judgment may be entered at any time, or as it

Notes in Pennsylvania," Vol. XLIV, 

Dick. Law Rev., March, 1940; and 

"Judgment Notes of Banking Institu tions," Vol. IX, American Law School

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS 

635 1 is frequently expressed, "as of any term," in order that the bank might enjoy an immediate lien upon the real estate of the maker during the continuance of the loan. Such a provision destroys the negotiability of the instrument. (3) Judgment Bond. This instrument is designed expressly to serve as collateral security for a separate loan or for a series of credit transactions. Where this device is employed, the borrower signs the judgment bond upon which judgment is to be entered, and an additional negotiable promissory note. 

The bond may cover future advances, and in this respect is similar to a mortgage which is designed to cover future extensions of credit. (4) Renewal Note. This instrument is designed to protect the continuity of the judgment entered on an original judgment note or judgment bond, and to negative any suggestion or understanding that the renewal note will discharge the original, otherwise a second judgment when entered on a renewal obligation might be subordinate to an intervening encumbrance which some other person may have obtained against the maker. The language commonly reads: "It is agreed that the original judgment of which this note is a renewal or part renewal shall be used as collateral security for this loan." (5) Memorandum Note. Most banks prefer to use the non-negotiable judgment note, upon which judgment is entered, in conjunction with a simple memorandum showing the amount due under the judgment, or the balance due when payments are made on account. This memorandum serves as a convenient record of the transaction, inasmuch as the original note, when recorded as a judgment, is surrendered to the prothonotary for that purpose. (6) Installment Judgment Note. This instrument is designed to provide for the payment of the obligation in installments. It has become popular in view of the National Housing Act, but it is equally available for other installment loans. Most of them contain an acceleration clause upon the default of the payment of any installment, and for a late charge on installments overdue. 

The most common charge is 5% on an installment fifteen days overdue, subject to a maximum charge of one dollar on any such installment. 

(7) Personal Loan Judgment Note. This is an installment ob ligation, in which a designated savings or other account is assigned to the bank as collateral security. The assignment commonly provides that deposits shall be made in this account, at regular monthly intervals, until they equal the amount of the loan, at which time the account is to be applied to the discharge of the obligation.

(8) Collateral Judgment Note. This instrument is employed when securities and other property are pledged as collateral security. Some banks require the borrower to sign the non-negotiable judgment note on which judgment is entered, and then record the judgment on the collateral note as the security. For the most part, however, the collateral judgment note is used for the pledge of stocks, bonds, and other securities. These notes commonly provide that the holder may call for additional security, and may sell, transfer, assign, exchange, or rehypothecate such securities at any time. 

(9) Married Woman's Judgment Note. This instrument is de signed for use by a married woman, in which she certifies that the obligation is given for her own personal benefit, and that she is not acting as accommodation endorser, maker, guarantor or surety for any other person. These disabilities of a married woman were removed by the Act of 1945.208 

208 Act of May 17, 1945, P. L. 375,48 PS 31.

CHAPTER XXIII  Part 1. Judgment by Confession Sec. 935. Business Practice. Many of the legal rights and privileges of debtor and creditor are established in the course of business practice. The usual forms through which business is conducted are strikingly similar. There is a difference in the use of these forms, as in the judgment note, a lease of real property, the bailment lease, a conditional sale, real and chattel mortgages, and the like, but most of such obligations conform to a single legal pattern. People bargain for the loan of money, for the lease of a dwelling, or for the purchase and sale of property, but at the same time they bargain for many of the privileges of the law involved in the enforcement of these obligations. Sometimes the choice is between the form of the contract, as between the optional use of the bailment lease or conditional sale. More commonly, the choice is in the law itself, insofar as the law will permit such a choice to be made. 

The law is one thing. The functional use of the law is quite another. We are accustomed to think that a trial by jury is an inalienable right. In business practice it is frequently a part of the bargain. In 82% of the credit instruments used by banking institutions, the debtor authorizes the confession of judgment, and in most cases before the maturity of the obligation. A similar provision appears in other business forms in common use. 

Sec. 936. Warrant of Attorney. Judgment by confession was well known at common law,' and this practice still persists in a number of states, notably Colorado, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Wisconsin. Restrictions in some states make 

13 Black. Com. 397. 637

it impractical to employ this device, and in other states the confession of judgment has been prohibited altogether. In Pennsylvania the authority to confess judgment may be conferred by a warrant of attorney, or by a statement in writing. Many years ago it was held by the Supreme Court that written authority was not essential, but in recent years the court has said, "considering the vast increase in such practice," that "it is much safer if not necessary to have the power in writing."

The Act of 1806 provides that a party to an amicable suit may have judgment entered against him by agreement in writing, executed in the presence of two or more witnesses, expressing the amount due. A warrant of attorney is authorized by the Act of 1836.5 It has been held, however, that this is merely a recognition of the common law. Where the parties resort to a warrant of attorney, and such is quite common, judgment may be confessed by an attorney on the warrant." 3 

Sec. 937. Duty of Prothonotary. A much simpler method of obtaining a judgment by confession is authorized by the Act of 1806.8 This act provides that where a note, bond, or other instrument in writing contains a warrant for an attorney to confess judgment, or where judgment is otherwise confessed, the prothonotary shall, upon application of the original holder (or assignee of such holder), enter judgment against the persons liable in the instrument, for the amount appearing from the face of the instrument to be due, without the agency of an attorney, and without payment of a fee to plaintiff's attorney. In such case, the authority to confess the judgment is vested in the prothonotary. The practice has long been sanctioned of allowing a judgment to be confessed on an obligation sounding in contract, whether

Sec. 938. Opening Judgments. Judgment by con fession has been so much encouraged in Pennsylvania as to make this device of the utmost importance in the usual course of business transactions. Such a judgment, properly obtained, has all the qualities of a verdict.18 This method of obtaining a judgment would be intolerable unless the courts exercised wide latitude to control the proceedings to insure substantial justice between the parties. There "is no limit of time to the exercise of this power." 19 Relief, however, is not a matter of right.

A rule to open a judgment is a substitute for a bill in equity.2 The proceeding is "governed by equitable principles and addressed to the sound discretion of the court." 21

Sec. 939. Costs. Most business contracts which authorize the confession of judgment include the costs. In the judgment notes of banking institutions, the percentage is 91%. This is in accord with a long established practice. In 1278 the English Parliament allowed a successful plaintiff to recover costs in certain actions," and in 1531 this privilege was accorded to a defendant who should succeed in the cause.25 With some statutory limitations and qualifications, the rule thus estab lished in England has always been recognized and enforced in Pennsylvania.26 In actions at law the general rule is that costs follow the judgment. The disposition of costs in equity is within the sound discretion of the chancellor.28 27 

Sec. 940. Tender of Settlement. Other than judg ments obtained by confession, it is possible to avoid the payment of costs by making a sufficient legal tender. 

An act passed by the Colonial Assembly in 1705 provides that in all cases where a tender shall be made as the party by contract or agreement ought to do, and the party to whom such tender is made doth refuse the same and yet afterward will sue for the debt or goods so tendered, the plaintiff shall not recover any costs in such suit. Sec. 947. Landlord and Tenant. A tenant is en titled to the exemptions noted above, but not if the exemptions are waived in the contract.5 Such a waiver is generally incorporated in the printed forms for use in the lease of houses, apartments, and other real estate. A wife whose goods have been seized for rent due from her husband to his landlord has no status to claim an exemption or to reserve her property on the premises. This is because the goods of a stranger, with certain exceptions to be noted in a subsequent chapter, are subject to the landlord's warrant of distress.

Swaney v. Doumont, 44 Pa. Superior Ct. 49 (1910). Swaney executed a lease for a house and lot, in which he waived the benefit of all exemption laws, and with his wife took possession and moved into it their household furnishings. He defaulted in the payment of the rent and the landlord issued a distress warrant, levying upon the personal property upon the premises, some of which belonged to the wife. ORLADY, J. "Neither the relation of landlord and tenant, nor of debtor and creditor was established between Mrs. Swaney and the landlord of her husband, and if not a debtor for the rent, she was not entitled to the exemption of the statute. 

That her property was seized was due to the fact of it being found upon the demised premises."

Sec. 948. Exemption Procedure. The exemption law is not self-operating. It may be waived, not only by contract, but by failure to claim the exemption at the time of the levy.51 If the exemption is requested by the debtor, the officer serving the writ must summon three disinterested and competent persons to appraise the property which the debtor may elect to retain. Each appraiser is entitled to the sum of fifty cents. Should the debtor conceal his property, or deny ownership with intent to defraud, or equivocate and deny ownership of that which he cannot hide, or in any other manner avoid 

50 Beatty v. Rankin, 139 Pa. 358 

51 Harlan v. Haines & Co., 126 Pa. 48 (1889).

the process of the writ, he may forfeit his right to the exemption altogether.

Sec. 949. Statutory Exceptions. Some obligations are of such a nature as not to warrant an exemption on behalf of the debtor. These obligations are enumerated in the following statutes: (1) Board. The Act of 1889 52 provides that no exemption of property from levy and sale or attachment shall be allowed on a judgment obtained for board for four weeks or less. (2) Judgment for Wages. The Act of 1887 53 provides that no exemption of property from attachment, levy, or sale upon execution, shall be allowed upon the judgment for $100 or less, obtained for wages for manual labor. 

(3) Taxes. The Local Tax Collection Law of 1945 54 provides that execution may issue on judgments obtained for unpaid taxes, "without any stay or benefit of any exemption law." (4) Wife and Children. The Act of 1921,55 which authorizes a writ of execution for the support of wife or children, provides: "The person against whom such an order, decree or judgment is made shall not be entitled to the benefits of any exemption law now in force or hereafter passed." (5) Illegitimate Child. The Act of 1907 50 provides that where any person has been convicted of fornication and bastardy and sentenced to pay to the mother of any bastard child any sum for its support, "no exemption of any money, rights, or credits attached thereby shall be allowed." 

(6) Judgments of Criminal Courts. The Act of 1901 57 

pro- vides that where the courts of quarter sessions or oyer and terminer have entered judgment for the payment of any moneys, and the judgment is entered in the court of common pleas, the defendant "shall not be entitled to the benefit of any exemption laws."

Sec. 953. Invalid Waiver. Occasionally an attempt is made in business contracts to waive the Act of 1845 exempting wages from attachment. Such a waiver still appears in 1.6% of the judgment notes of banking institutions. The percentage itself is a sufficient indication of its invalidity. Theoretically, it is just as consistent to recognize a waiver of the wage exemption law as it is the property exemption law. If the question were now to be decided for the first time, however, it is not likely that the Supreme Court would sanction a contractual waiver of either one. The following case marks a turning point in the recognition of the right of a creditor to insist that his debtor waive the application of a law which the legislature has deemed appropriate in the interests of social welfare. 

Firmstone v. Mack, 49 Pa. 387 (1865). A note executed by 

Sheehan contained a waiver of the Exemption Law of 1849, and also a waiver of the Act of 1845 exempting wages from attachment. WOODWARD, C. J. "We have never decided that a debtor may repeal the proviso of the Act of 1845, and public policy pleads strongly against such a decision. If we make it, we bring on the litigation which has sprung out of our decision upon the Act of 1849-the inconveniences to employers before adverted to, and the

Act of May 25, 1945, P. L. 1050, 72 PS 5511.1.

temptation to weak debtors to beggar their families in behalf of sharp and grasping creditors. We will not, therefore, strain the proviso to fit it to our construction of the exemption statutes, but will leave it to its natural operation as it is expressed. The legislature having said that justices shall not attach wages, we will say they shall not, though a particular debtor has said they may."

Part 4. Fraudulent Conveyances 

Sec. 954. Statute of Elizabeth. The law is not so indulgent as to sanction a conveyance, made by an insolvent debtor, in an attempt to place his property beyond the reach of his creditors. This much was decided by the Statute of Elizabeth of 1570.78 This was one of the 

British statutes which was incorporated into the laws of the commonwealth by the Report of the Judges in 1808.79 

In speaking of this statute, it was said by Mr. Justice 

DUNCAN: "The laws ought not to be so framed, or so construed, as to lead men into temptation, but so that they should be induced, by affection for their families, to tread the sure and beaten track of business which they understand, rather than to soar aloft in the regions of speculation; and not to venture in specious and hazardous undertakings, of the danger of which they are ignorant, by allowing them, while they are climbing the ladder and their heads grow dizzy, and they find they are falling, to make a feather bed on which they may fall lightly; and under the plea of affection for their wives and children, take away the beds from under the wives and children of their creditors.' 

Sec. 955. Fraudulent Conveyance Act. The Uni form Fraudulent Conveyance Act was adopted in this commonwealth in 1921.80 Following is a summary of its provisions: (1) Every conveyance made or obligation incurred by a person who is or will be thereby rendered insolvent, without a fair consideration; (2) every conveyance made without a fair considera- 

78 13 Elizabeth Chap. 5 (1570). 

79 Robert's Digest of British Stat utes, 295. 

80 Act of May 21, 1921, P. L. 1045, 39 PS 351.

tion when the person is engaged or is about to engage in a business or transaction in which the property remaining in his hands after the conveyance is an unreasonably small capital; (3) every conveyance and every obligation without a fair consideration when the person intends or believes that he will incur debts beyond his ability to pay as they mature; (4) every conveyance made and every obligation with actual intent to defraud either present or future creditors, in addition to such intent presumed in law; and (5) every conveyance of partnership property and every partnership obligation incurred when the partnership is or will be thereby rendered insolvent, whether to a partner with or without a promise by him to pay partnership debts or to a person not a partner without fair consideration to the partnership; shall, in each and every such instance, be deemed fraudulent as to creditors. 

Sec. 956. Equitable Relief. Insolvency, under this statute, is interpreted to mean the fact of insolvency immediately prior to the conveyance, or the immediate effect of the conveyance, and not insolvency which may result from some subsequent misfortune.81 Where the claim of a creditor has matured and is presently payable, he may have a fraudulent conveyance annulled, or disregard the conveyance and attach or levy execution upon the property conveyed, subject to whatever consideration, less than a fair consideration, has been paid to the debtor. A creditor whose claim has not yet matured may, with leave of court, restrain the debtor from disposing of his property, or have a receiver appointed to take charge of the property, or set aside the conveyance and annul the obligation, or have such other relief as the case may require. In a typical case before the 

Supreme Court, the opinion of the court begins as follows: "Each of three husbands, debtors of plaintiff, on the same day, through a third party, caused certain land theretofore owned by him to be conveyed to himself and wife as tenants by the entireties. Only a nominal consideration was recited." The decree of the lower court, setting aside the conveyances as having been made in fraud of creditors, was affirmed.82 

81 Angler v. Worrell, 346 Pa. 450 (1943). 

82 Bank of Charleroi & Trust Co. v. 

Renchkowsky, 343 Pa. 444 (1941).

Com. Trust Co. of Pittsburgh v. Cirigliano, 352 Pa. 108 (1945).

Plaintiff loaned $3,000 to defendant, and on default secured a judgment for principal and interest in the sum of $3,650. While the suit was pending, defendant conveyed her farm to her son. 

Plaintiff filed a bill in equity to set aside the conveyance. In granting this relief, it was said by DREW, J. "The testimony of the mother, which was received over objection, was that her son had agreed to pay all her bills and respect her as his mother and support her for the rest of her life. And that for this she had conveyed the property to him. The son corroborated the mother. 

Such a consideration has been held invalid as to creditors." 

Part 5. Imprisonment for Debt Sec. 957. Writ of Arrest. The Act of 1836 83 pro vides that executions shall issue, first, upon the personal estate of the defendant, second, upon his real estate, and third, if he does not have sufficient property in the county to satisfy the judgment, then upon the person of the defendant, except a female. The Act of 

19318* provides that no citizen of the commonwealth shall be arrested or imprisoned in any action, unless the sum due or recovered is more than $100. The arrest is by writ of capias ad satisfaciendum. This writ is directed to the sheriff, commanding him to take the debtor therein named and keep him safely, so that he may have his body in court on the return day of the writ, to satisfy the party who has recovered judgment against him. 

The sheriff is liable to the plaintiff if he fails to perform this duty, or permits the debtor to go at large. 85 

83 Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 755, 12 PS 2111. 

84 Act of June 12, 1931, P. L. 558, 12 PS 2142b. 

Sec. 958. Contract Obligations. "Under the com mon law great abuses and grievous extortions were practiced by jailers upon prisoners in both debtor and criminal apartments." 88 The present constitution provides: "The person of a debtor, where there is not strong presumption of fraud, shall not be continued in prison after delivering up his estate for the benefit of his creditors

in such manner as shall be prescribed by law." 87 The 

Act of 1842 88 exempts a debtor from arrest for the satisfaction of a judgment or decree for the recovery of any money due upon any contract, express or implied, or for the recovery of any damages for the non-performance of any contract. 

Sec. 959. Obligations Excepted. There are impor tant exceptions in the foregoing statute, and other circumstances by reason of which a creditor may apply to the court having jurisdiction, for a warrant of arrest and detention. 

(1) Particular Obligations. The first section of the statute expressly excludes "proceedings as for contempt, to enforce civil remedies, as well as actions for fines or penalties . . or on moneys collected by any public officer, or for any misconduct or neglect in office, or in any professional employment." (2) Fraud. The second and third sections of the statute authorize a warrant of arrest: (a) where the debtor is about to remove any of his property out of the jurisdiction of the court in which suit is brought with intent to defraud his creditors; (b) where he has property which he fraudulently conceals; (c) where he has rights in action, or some interest in any public or corporate stock, money or evidence of debt, which he unjustly refuses to apply to the payment of any such judgment which shall have been rendered against him; (d) where he has assigned, removed, or disposed of, or is about to dispose of, any of his property, with the intent to defraud his creditors; and (e) where he fraudulently contracted the debt or incurred the obligation respecting which suit is brought. (3) Trustees. "The cases relating to trusts are excepted from the operation of the Act of 1842 not only because the basis of the claim is not a contract but a legal duty, but also a breach of trust is something more than a contract. In addition, reasons of expediency have a greater influence upon the conclusion of the court, for unless the trustee could be reached by attachment, he could not be reached at all, if he had no property of his own." 27.89 (4) Decrees in Equity. "Equity courts still have power under the Act of June 16, 1836, P. L. 784, section 24, to enforce their decrees by attachment if necessary, such privilege being expressly 

87 Article I, section 16. 

88 Act of July 12, 1842, P. L. 339, 12 PS 257. 

80 Chew's Appeal, 44 Pa. 247 (1863).

reserved in the Act of 1842, and where it appears that there has been disobedience of a lawfully given direction, other than the payment of money due by reason of a contract, express or implied, this remedy may be resorted to." 90 (5) The Act of 1842 has no application to obligations sounding in tort. 

Sec. 960. Fraudulent Concealment. It will be ob served from the foregoing that a judgment debtor is subject to imprisonment where he has property which he fraudulently conceals, or which he unjustly refuses to apply to the payment of the judgment, notwithstanding the debt is a contract obligation, and also where the debt is fraudulently contracted. 

Ex Parte Crawford, 154 Fed. 769 (1907). Johnson recovered a judgment against Crawford in the U. S. District Court for the 

Middle District of Pennsylvania, in the sum of $27,710.60, in an action of assumpsit for timber sold, and having failed to obtain satisfaction, filed an affidavit charging, in substance, that the defendant had money and property which he fraudulently concealed and refused to apply to the payment of the judgment. He thereupon secured a warrant of arrest under the Act of 1842. The defendant was apprehended and committed to the common jail of Lycoming County, whereupon he was allowed a writ of habeas corpus by the Circuit Court of Appeals, alleging that the Act of 1842 was superseded by the federal bankruptcy act. DALLAS, C. J. "The Pennsylvania statute of July 12, 1842, is not an insolvent law. The proceeding it provides is not designed to effect the distribution of the debtor's assets amongst his creditors. It is a proceeding in aid of execution. Its object is to reach property of a judgment debtor which he fraudulently conceals. . . The order of this court is that (the petitioner) be remanded to the custody of the keeper of the common jail of Lycoming County.

A motion for leave to file a petition for a writ of habeas corpus in the Supreme Court of the United States was denied. 

Sec. 961. Disclosure of Assets. There are two stat utes under which the debtor may obtain his release. 

The first is the Insolvency Act of 1901,91 which authorizes the assignment of property for the benefit of creditors; the second is the Act of 1915.02 The procedure in 

90 Ross v. Dever, 298 Pa. 146 (1929). 

Act of June 4, 1901, P. L. 404, 39 PS 1. 

02 Act of June 1, 1915, P. L. 704, 39 PS 9.

both statutes is much the same. The debtor may present his petition to the court praying for his discharge from confinement, by setting forth the nature of the proceedings, the amount of the judgment, a schedule of all his assets, a list of all creditors with the amounts of their claims, the addresses of his creditors, the nature of the debts owing them, and a statement as to why he is unable to pay the judgment. If it appears that the debtor is without means or property with which to pay the judgment, and that he has not secreted or assigned any of his property so as to avoid payment, the court may discharge the prisoner from further confinement. 

The debtor "shall be discharged at the expiration of sixty days from the date of the commitment, if compliance is had with all the requirements of this act and all other acts of Assembly relating to insolvency."

Sec. 962. Release of Debtor. For some time the courts interpreted the Act of 1915 as being discretionary until the expiration of sixty days. Prior to that time the discharge of the debtor was a matter of grace, but at the expiration of sixty days the discharge was matter of right. In De Turk v. Gackenbach," the prisoner had been arrested on a capias ad satisfaciendum for falsely, fraudulently and knowingly misrepresenting the value of certain shares of stock. The court concluded that he had been the moving spirit in a bald and brazen swindle, and refused the discharge. In Matz v. Haug, the court also refused to act where the plaintiff had obtained judg ment for criminal conversation. The doctrine now approved is, that upon complying with the provisions of the statute, the prisoner is entitled to his release prior to the expiration of sixty days. In Miller's Petition, the defendant had an income from a spendthrift trust, but said he would rather sit in jail than pay the judg ment. The lower court permitted him to sit in jail, but the Superior Court ordered his discharge. 94 95 

95 119 Pa. Superior Ct. 283 (1935). 

93 96 Pa. Superior Ct. 38 (1929). 

94 80 Pa. Superior Ct. 583 (1923).

Bloomington v. Shapiro, 129 Pa. Superior Ct. 218 (1937).

Plaintiff was injured as the result of the negligent operation of an automobile by the defendant, and obtained a judgment in the sum of $400. At the time of the recovery of the verdict, defendant offered to pay $150 in full settlement, but this was evidently refused. A capias ad satisfaciendum was issued and the defendant was taken into custody. He filed a petition for his discharge, and after due publication and notice, the matter was heard in open court. The defendant testified that he was a clothing salesman working on a commission basis, that he had a wife and two children, and that his earnings during the past year averaged $35 per week. He stated that he had no property, and was therefore unable to pay the judgment. He also answered all questions put to him by counsel and the court. No evidence was offered to contradict him. The lower court stated that he did not believe the witness, and recommitted him. Defendant appealed in forma pauperis. In ordering his discharge, it was said by STADTFELD, J. if a debtor is without means or property with which to pay the judgment, has not secreted or assigned any of his property, follows the procedure prescribed by the first three sections of that act, and there is not a strong presumption of fraud growing out of either the transaction which formed the basis of the judgment or the proceedings for discharge, he is entitled under the constitution of this commonwealth to a discharge without waiting sixty days." 66 

Part 6. Insolvency

Sec. 963. Insolvency Act. The federal constitution confers upon Congress the power to establish “uniform laws on the subject of Bankruptcies throughout the United States." 96 The jurisdiction thus conferred excludes the operation of all state bankruptcy laws during the continuance of the federal act. In 1901, three years after the passage of the present federal statute, the legislature of Pennsylvania enacted a comprehensive statute on insolvency. For several years thereafter the lower courts held that this statute was inoperative because of the conflict of state and federal jurisdiction. It is now well settled that this statute is not a bankruptcy act, since it does not provide for a statutory distribution of assets to all creditors of an insol- 

96 Article I, section 8.

vent, or a statutory discharge of all obligations owing by the insolvent. As a result, proceedings under the act, in the nature of assignments and receiverships, are valid until such time as either party invokes the jurisdiction of the federal courts under the federal bankruptcy act, where this may be done by reason of the jurisdiction and provisions of the federal law."7 

Sec. 964. Assignments. The Act of 190198 provides that any person, etc., may make a voluntary assignment of property to an assignee for the benefit of all creditors who prove their claims and accept a dividend. An assignment of a part of such property will be deemed to be an assignment of the whole estate. 

Huff's Estate, 299 Pa. 200 (1930). Huff was the owner of the

United Smokeless Coal Company. During his lifetime he took out a $15,000 policy on his life and named the coal company beneficiary. While insolvent he changed the beneficiary to a trustee in trust for two banks to which he was indebted. The trustee received the insurance money, paid the designated banks in full, and credited the balance, some $2,000, to Huff's estate. At the instance of another creditor, the trustee was surcharged the amounts paid, and subrogated to the rights of the banks. WALL- 

ING, J. "When the coal company, which was Huff, in fact, was made beneficiary of the life insurance, it became an asset of his estate and could not thereafter when he was insolvent be given in trust to secure an existing indebtedness to certain banks. The attempt rendered it an assignment for the benefit of all creditors. 

Had the banks been originally named as the beneficiaries, the rule might be different. True, an insolvent may pay certain of his creditors to the exclusion of others. But placing property in trust for some will operate as an assignment for the benefit of all." 

Sec. 965. Moratorium. If the majority of the creditors in number and amount shall consent in writing, the court may order that the estate and effects which the insolvent may afterwards acquire shall be exempt for a period of seven years from any debt contracted or cause of action existing at the time of the assignment. 

08 Note 91 supra. 

97 Walker v. Emerich, 300 Pa. 9 

---

The claims of assenting creditors are completely discharged, unless such creditors prove fraud on the part of the debtor in any of the contingencies provided by the act.

Sec. 966. Receiverships. Any creditor of an alleged insolvent person, etc., may file a petition for the appointment of a receiver whenever such debtor acknowledges his insolvency, or has absconded or is about to abscond with intent to defraud his creditors, or conceals himself within or remains out of the commonwealth with like intent, or secretes any part of his estate, or has assigned, removed or disposed of any part of his property with intent to defraud his creditors, or for like causes designated in the act. If the facts justify it, the court may appoint a receiver. The receiver acts for the benefit of all creditors, and may institute such legal proceedings as are necessary in the liquidation of the estate. Any preference which has been created in favor of any creditor within a period of four months will be set aside, and will inure to the benefit of all creditors. Proof of claims must be filed within six months, and the property of the debtor will then be distributed among his creditors in proportion to their respective claims. Creditors who do not assent are barred from receiving a dividend, but the act does not discharge an insolvent from liability to such of his creditors as do not choose to exhibit their claims, or who, before the schedule of distribution is filed withdraw their claims.

Part 7. Preferred Creditors 

Sec. 967. Kinds of Creditors. A creditor who has obtained a judgment against his debtor, and who has caused the property of the debtor to be sold at a judicial sale, is not always the first to be paid out of the proceeds of the sale. Creditors are of three sorts, general, preferred, and secured. The rights of a general creditor are subordinate to the rights of preferred or

secured creditors. A peferred creditor is a creditor who has been granted a preference, by the legislature, in the distribution of the debtor's estate. Such a preference is usually supported by a lien on the debtor's property. 

It may generally be asserted, not only at a judicial sale, but also in the distribution of decedents' estates, or of the estate of a debtor who has made an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or of a debtor whose estate is being liquidated in receivership. A statutory preference is a special privilege, and is allowed only in the interests of a sound public policy. Aside from taxes and social insurance, only wage earners and landlords have been granted this privilege, and then only to a limited extent. 

Sec. 968. Preferred Wages. The Act of 18919⁹ pro vides that all moneys due for labor, for any period not exceeding six months preceding the sale or transfer of the real or personal property by execution or otherwise on account of the insolvency of the employer, shall be a lien upon his real or personal property, and shall be preferred and first paid out of the proceeds, but not to exceed $200. In the case of a sale, proof of claim should be filed with the prothonotary, and in the case of an execution, with the officer executing the writ. 

Twenty-five occupations or employments are enumer ated in the code. These are sufficiently comprehensive to protect most employees, but not a traveling salesman, or a member of an orchestra who, through his leader, contracted with the proprietor of a restaurant to play for the entertainment of patrons. As said by the Superior Court on this occasion, "These acts secure to certain claimants rights which are denied other suitors; they confer special favors and, therefore, are to be strictly construed; he who claims the benefit of class legislation must bring himself within its provisions." 101 100 

99 Act of May 12, 1891, P. L. 54, 43 PS 221.

Sec. 969. Preferred Rent. Rent is preferred as a claim upon the goods and chattels of the tenant on the demised premises, not to exceed one year's rent. This preference was granted in 1836 as against an execution creditor.102 The Act of 1919 103 includes the disposition of the tenant's property by assignment, insolvency, receivership, or bankruptcy. The Act of 193110* provides that if a distress for rent is pending when other proceedings intervene, the landlord shall be "paid first out of the proceeds of such sale." The preference of the landlord extends only to the date of receivership. In any other claim for rent, the status of the landlord is the same as that of a general creditor.105 Preferred wages have priority over preferred rent. It has been held, however, that rent accruing after receivership and as a part of the expenses of administration, has priority over wage claims.¹ 106 

Sec. 970. Order of Distribution. 

Pennsylvania has no general statute, such as the federal bankruptcy act, which sets forth the order of distribution on behalf of preferred creditors. The priority of a preference under state law is to be ascertained by reference to the statute in which the preference is granted. There is also a difference in the order of distribution under state laws, and the order of distribution as provided by the federal bankruptcy act, as well as in the obligations preferred. 

In each case, however, the state laws govern the distribution, unless the proceedings are superseded by the federal bankruptcy act. Following is the order of distribution as it appears in the several laws of the commonwealth. Part 8. Liens against Personal Property 

Sec. 971. Nature of Lien. In a technical sense a lien signifies a right to retain possession of a chattel until a particular debt or obligation has been paid or satisfied. 

It is now used in a much broader sense to indicate the right of a creditor to compel the liquidation of real or personal property, or if the property has been liquidated, then to have priority in the distribution of the proceeds. 

A lien is a property right which one creditor enjoys over another. A secured creditor has a lien on particular property which he may enforce as against other creditors. This right is not only preserved and regulated whenever an execution is issued out of a state court, or where an assignment is made for the benefit of

Stern's Appeal, 64 Pa. 447 (1870). Stern recovered a judgment against Lorentz, and issued a fieri facias on the judgment on three occasions, telling the sheriff each time "not to do anything with the writ until further orders." As a result the sheriff made no levy. The court below found that these executions were not bona fide, but with a view to secure the property against other creditors. About a month after the third execution Stern directed the sheriff to proceed, as he was afraid another creditor contemplated doing so. This was on a Sunday. On the following day, before a levy had been made, Lowenstein placed a writ of execution in the hands of the sheriff. The lower court made distribution to Lowenstein, and Stern appealed. In sustaining this decision, it was said by THOMPSON, C. J. "Sunday is dies non juridicus. 

The sheriff was not bound to receive or notice such an order on that day. To hold that he was, would be to hold that he was bound to keep his office open on Sundays to receive directions in regard to his official duties."

The Act of 1923 139 confers upon the foregoing, as well as a municipal authority, the right to perfect liens for municipal improvements and services. The unemployment compensation tax is a lien when entered of record, subject to prior recorded real estate mortgages.140 A lien may also be entered of rec ord for awards under the Workmen's Compensation

Sec. 976. Judgment Liens. The verdict of a jury for any specific sum of money automatically becomes a lien against the real estate of the debtor from the date on which it is rendered.144 A decree in equity for the payment of money has the same effect.145 When a person buys real estate under articles of agreement he is said to have an equitable title to the property. A judg ment or decree operates as an inchoate lien against this equitable title, and as soon as the purchase is complete and the equitable and legal title merge, it becomes a lien against the legal title as of the date on which it was entered.146 The lien operates against the real estate of the defendant which may be located in the county where it is recorded, or transferred.147 A judgment is not a lien on real estate which the debtor may thereafter acquire, but may be made so by issuing an execution against the land in question.148

Sec. 977. Revival of Lien. A judgment lien will terminate at the end of five years unless renewed within that period of time. The owner may sell the land while it is so encumbered, but the buyer would take it subject to the lien. Such a buyer is known as a terre tenant. 

In 1943 the Supreme Court ruled that the lien was binding upon the terre tenant for a period of five years from the date of recording the deed, though the lien against the judgment debtor had not been revived within five years from the entry of the judgment.149 In some cases this would have the effect of almost doubling the original five year period as to the terre tenant. A few months later, however, the legislature repealed the old statutes on the subject and substituted a new enactment.¹ Under the new law, the initial judgment shall continue as a lien as to purchasers, mortgagees and 150

Failure to revive the lien does not impair the judgment, but the judgment creditor would loose the security of the lien to the next senior lien creditor. Without such security the judgment may be worthless. 

Dime Bank of Lansford v. Summit Hill Trust Co., 341 Pa. 424 (1941). Plaintiff obtained a judgment lien against certain land on July 26, 1926, which it revived on July 10, 1931, and again on 

July 21, 1936, five years and eleven days later. Prior to this last revival, defendant had acquired a judgment lien against the same property, which it now claimed was first in priority. PER CURIAM. "The court was clearly right in holding that plaintiff permitted its lien to lapse on July 10, 1936, with the result that the judgments of defendant, even if theretofore subsequent in lien to that of plaintiff, acquired priority."

Sec. 978. Notice to Terre Tenant. A judgment lien may be revived by agreement of the plaintiff, the defendant, and the terre tenant, when properly filed, or by a judicial proceeding which is instituted by writ of scire facias. The Act of 1943 continues in effect the rule that where the judgment lien is revived by a judicial proceeding, the writ shall be served on the terre tenant as well as upon the judgment debtor.

Lusk v. Davidson, 3 P. & W. 229 (1881). On April 5, 1823,

Davidson obtained a judgment against Lusk. On March 3, 1824, Lusk conveyed the land to Carothers. On March 15, 1828, the judgment was revived by amicable scire facias, but without serv ice on Carothers. PER CURIAM. "Every dictate of justice sug gests, that the terre-tenant ought not to be bound by a judgment, whose operation is on the land exclusively, without having had a day in court; and we should strain a principle of construction already carried sufficiently far, were we to take for granted, that the legislature did not mean the provision for his protection to be enforced at all events. It is plain, therefore, that notwithstanding the judgment of revival confessed by the defendant, the lien is gone." 

Sec. 979. Mechanic's Liens. A mechanic's lien is an encumbrance upon real estate. The subject, however, is not as important in Pennsylvania as it is in most of

the states. This is because the Pennsylvania code authorizes a waiver of the right to a lien, which will not only be binding upon the contractor, but sub-contractors as well. The owner and the contractor may agree that no claims shall be filed.151 The owner usually insists upon this agreement, at least in building projects of any importance. This waiver may be made effective as to sub-contractors by proof of actual notice to a subcontractor before any labor or materials have been furnished, or by proof that the agreement has been filed in the office of the prothonotary, (1) prior to the commencement of the work upon the ground, or (2) within ten days after the execution of the principal contract, or (3) not less than ten days prior to the contract with the claimant.152 The Pennsylvania statute is peculiar in another respect. The liability of the owner, assuming that a lien has been perfected, is not measured by the price fixed in the contract between the owner and the contractor, but by the reasonable value of the labor and materials which have been furnished.158 

McCrady-Rodgers Co. v. Nenoff, 155 Pa. Superior Ct. 555 

(1944). The owner of real estate engaged a contractor to construct a dwelling. The contract contained a no-lien clause. 

Plaintiff, at the request of the contractor, made deliveries of building materials on 43 different dates beginning March 27 and ending September 10. During this interval, on May 8, the owner filed the no-lien contract in the prothonotary's office. On December 9, plaintiff served written notice on the owner of its intent to file a mechanic's lien for materials furnished before and after the filing of the contract. In sustaining the right to do so, it was said by BALDRIGE, J. "Subcontractors need not make repeated and continuous examinations of the prothonotary's records. to protect themselves; that would be an unreasonable requirement not intended by the legislature. Furthermore, if that were so the owner and principal contractor would be in a position to perpetrate a fraud upon subcontractors and material men." 

Sec. 980. Mortgage Liens. Mortgages are of two kinds, called advance money mortgage and purchase

money mortgage. Where the owner of land borrows money and executes and delivers a mortgage as security for the loan, the mortgagee takes what is called an advance money mortgage. The Act of 1927 154 provides that the lien of this mortgage shall become effective as of the day and hour on which it is left in the office of the recorder of deeds to be recorded. A subsequent purchaser of the land is bound by this lien, and should make a proper search of the records to discover it.155 Where the purchaser of land is unable to pay the full purchase price, he may be permitted by the grantor to pay part of the consideration in cash and to execute a mortgage for the balance. This is known as a purchase money mortgage. The Act of 1927 provides that this mortgage may be recorded within thirty days from the date of the mortgage. If it is so recorded it becomes effective as of the date of its execution. 

Sec. 981. Failure to Record. Failure to record a mortgage does not affect any right which the mortgagee has against the mortgagor under the terms of the mortgage. The contract is personal as to both of them. 

Furthermore, if the mortgagor decides to sell the mortgaged premises, the mortgagee could, by giving timely notice of his mortgage to the purchaser, retain his right in the property. Such notice at a judicial sale is ineffective.156 The holder of a mortgage must record it if he would preserve his right in the property as against a subsequent mortgagee or grantee without notice, or judgment creditor without notice when the judgment debt was contracted.

Part 10. Rights of Lien Holders Sec. 982. Priority of Liens. The same real estate may become the subject of a number of concurrent liens. 

The substantive and procedural rights of all such lien

créditors may give rise to some complication, and there is some danger in the oversimplification of the rules under which such rights are determined. As a general proposition, liens rank, and are satisfied, in the order of their priority. In other words, where the real estate is sold at the instance of one lien creditor, the proceeds of the sale are not distributed equally or ratably among all the lien creditors as a class, but according to their various priorities, excluding such liens as are not divested by the sale. The balance, if any, is distributed to the owner.157 In the determination of the liens of private creditors, it should be noted that while a mortgage lien speaks as of the minute of the day it is left in the recorder's office for recording, a judgment lien speaks as of the day on which it is recorded. Thus, two judg ment liens which are entered on the same day have equal priority. A distinction is also made between an advance money mortgage and a purchase money mortgage. 

If the holder of a purchase money mortgage records it within thirty days, it speaks as of the date of its execution.158 Two such mortgages have equal priority, though one of necessity appears first in the recording.' This also holds for a mortgage and judgment which are entered on the same day.100 To further complicate the problem, a mortgage lien, though recorded after a judgment lien, has priority in the distribution if the judgment creditor had knowledge of the existence of the mortgage when the judgment debt was contracted.101 It should also be noted that a mechanic's lien, if filed within six months after the completion of the work or the furnishing of the last material, speaks as of the date of the commencement of the work.182 159

Sec. 985. Marshalling of Assets. CHAPTER XXIV BANKRUPTCY 

Part 1. Proceedings in Bankruptcy

Sec. 986. Federal Power. The federal constitution confers upon Congress the power to establish "uniform Laws on the subject of bankruptcies throughout the United States." 1 Such laws have been in effect from 

1800-1803, 1841-1843, 1867-1878, and from 1898 to the present time. Following is a brief abstract from a learned opinion by Mr. Justice SUTHERLAND on the first three of these enactments: 2 (1) Act of 1800. The English law as it existed at the time of the adoption of the constitution, was conceived wholly in the interest of the creditor and proceeded upon the assumption that the debtor was necessarily to be dealt with as an offender. Voluntary bankruptcy was unknown to that system. The persons who were permitted to become bankrupts were traders. The Act of 

1800, like the English law, was conceived in the view that the bankrupt was dishonest. It was one exclusively in the interests of the creditor. The framers of the constitution, however, did not intend to limit the power of Congress to the then existing law of England, and the Act of 1800 so far ignored the English law as to include bankers, brokers, and underwriters. (2) Act of 1841. The Act of 1841 proceeded upon the assumption that the bankrupt might be honest but unfortunate. It took what then must have been regarded as a radical step forward by conferring upon the debtor the right by voluntary petition to surrender his property, with some exceptions, and relieve himself of all future liability in respect of past debts. It also extended the provisions of the law to merchants. Other additions have been made by later acts until now practically all classes of persons and corporations are included. (3) Act of 1867. The Act of 1867, as amended in 1874, permitted the debtor for the first time, either before or after an adjudication, to propose terms of composition to his creditors, to become binding upon their acceptance by a designated majority and confirmation by the judge. 

1 Article I, section 8. 

2 Cont. Ill. Nat. B. & T. Co. v. Chi cago, R. I. & P. Ry. Co., 294 U. S. 

648 (1935). 671

Sec. 987. Act of 1898. The present federal statute on bankruptcy was approved on July 1, 1898. Its continuance suspends all state laws in conflict therewith, but as noted heretofore the Insolvency Act of Pennsylvania "is not a bankruptcy act, but it is in harmony with the policy of the Bankruptcy Act and in aid of its purpose." The purpose of the federal statute and its amendments is to "convert the assets of the bankrupt into cash for distribution among his creditors, and then to relieve the honest debtor from the weight of oppressive indebtedness, and permit him to start afresh free from the obligations and responsibilities consequent upon business misfortune." Amendments in recent years have authorized additional forms of relief by way of compositions, extensions, adjustments, moratoriums, corporate reorganizations, and wage earners' plans. 

Sec. 988. Validity of Waiver. Attempts have been made over the years to oblige debtors to waive all bankrupt laws of the United States. Such a waiver still appears in 8% of the judgment notes of banking institutions in Pennsylvania.5 The validity of this waiver has been denied under past and the present bankruptcy laws, and whatever may have prompted the use of this device in years past, it is no longer regarded as a creditable business practice." 

Sec. 989. Proceedings. The federal Bankruptcy Act contemplates the following procedure: (1) the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, (2) formal adjudication of bankruptcy, (3) appointment of a receiver when neces sary for the preservation of the estate, (4) a reference of the case to a referee, (5) the filing of schedules by the bankrupt, (6) a meeting of creditors, (7) nomination and appointment of a trustee, (8) filing claims $30 Stat. 544 (1898), 11 USCA 1.
