In order to facilitate these proceedings the federal courts have jurisdiction to extradite bankrupts from one district to another, enforce obedience by bankrupts and others, punish persons for contempts committed before referees, and to hear and determine all infractions of the act. 

Cooper v. Dasher, 290 U. S. 106 (1933). Dasher was president, and he and his family owned the shares, of the Wauchula Central Pharmacy, Inc. During the night following the filing of a bankruptcy petition, he withdrew the bulk of the merchandise by stealth and lodged it in hiding places known only to himself. Part had been retrieved; part was still concealed. The value of merchandise withheld was nearly $20,000, of which goods worth but $583.69 had identifying marks or labels. The referee ordered the return of this property. The respondent did not dispute the order as to the goods worth $583.69, but contended that the other items should have been set forth in particular schedules in order that he might understand the order. The Circuit Court of Appeals sustained that contention. CARDOZO, J. "Misunderstanding of the mandate is upon the facts in this record an illusory peril. The order gives the only description that the nature of the case allows. 

The respondent, and no one else, is in a position to supply a better one. The mandate is addressed to him, and to him its meaning is definite, however indefinite to others. If it is clear enough to be understood, it is clear enough to be obeyed. . 

Let the respondent yield obedience to a mandate intelligible to him, and his liberty is then assured. The law will not be overpatient with his protest that if he persists in his defiance, he may be caught in his own snares."

Sec. 990. Jurisdiction. The federal courts have jurisdiction of all formal proceedings in bankruptcy. 

The federal law, however, reserves to the state courts their established jurisdiction in the liquidation of bankrupt estates. As it has been expressed by the Supreme

Part 2. Bankrupts 

Sec. 991. Voluntary Bankruptcy. Any person, except a municipal, railroad, insurance, or banking corporation or a building and loan association, may institute voluntary proceedings in bankruptcy.¹¹ bankruptcy." Insolvency is not a prerequisite. A person may voluntarily relinquish his property for the benefit of his creditors, and compel them to prove their claims under this act. In voluntary proceedings an adjudication of bankruptcy is usually made on the day on which the petition is filed. 

The estate of the bankrupt vests in the trustee as of the date of the filing of the petition.12 The claims of his creditors are also determined as of that date. 

Piper v. Acme Brewing Co., 1 Wash. (Pa.) 188 (1920). BROWN- 

SON, J. "The earnings of the plaintiff by his labor and services performed after the filing of his petition in bankruptcy do not belong to the trustee in bankruptcy, but belong to himself, forming no part of the bankrupt estate. The plaintiff therefore has a right of action, in his own name, and for his own use, to recover from the defendant such moneys as the defendant owes for his services rendered subsequent to June 9, 1919, the date at which he filed his petition and was adjudicated a bankrupt."

As amended in 1938, the act provides that property inherited by a bankrupt within six months after bankruptcy, or an estate by the entireties which vests in the bankrupt within six months after bankruptcy, shall now vest in the trustee for the benefit of his creditors.14

Sec. 993. Involuntary Bankruptcy. Any person, except a wage earner or farmer, and any business corporation, except a building and loan association, a municipal, railroad, insurance, or banking corporation, owing debts to the amount of $1,000 or over, may be adjudged an involuntary bankrupt.15 A wage earner is defined as an individual who works for wages or salary at a rate of compensation not exceeding $1,500 per year. A person whose compensation is in excess of that amount is not exempt. Neither are the professions. A farmer is defined as an individual personally engaged in farming or tillage of the soil, or dairy farming, or in the production of poultry, livestock, or their products in their manufactured state, if the principal part of his income is derived from any one or more of such operations.16 

Rice v. Bordner, 140 Fed. 566 (1905). In an involuntary proceeding in bankruptcy, the respondent disclosed that he owned two farms which he managed himself and which brought in a yearly income of about $600; that he owned a small store which brought in about $60 or $70 a year; and that he sold $200 or $300 worth of fertilizer as agent for a phosphate company. AR- 

CHIBALD, J. "That it was upon the farm that he depended for a livelihood is evident; what is called his store being the merest excuse for one, and yielding him but a pittance. . . . The petition is therefore dismissed at the cost of the petitioning creditor."

Where all the partners are adjudged bankrupt, the partnership shall also be adjudged bankrupt. Sec. 996. Withdrawal of Petition. Creditors may withdraw a petition with the approval of the court, after notice to other creditors.22 Where the debtor acquires property after the date on which the petition is filed, it may be to the interests of the creditors to withdraw their petition. By so doing they could reach the newly acquired property of the debtor, either in a civil action in the state courts, or by a subsequent petition in bankruptey.

In re Weidenfield, 257 Fed. 872 (1919). An involuntary petition had been filed against an alleged bankrupt, to which he answered, denying that he was insolvent. About two years thereafter, and prior to adjudication, his wife died leaving him a considerable estate. His creditors asked leave to withdraw the petition, and on the same day the alleged bankrupt requested leave to withdraw his answer, in order that he might be adjudicated a bankrupt. 

GARVIN, D. J. "It does not seem to me that it was ever the intention of those who enacted the Bankruptcy Law to permit a bankrupt, who has resisted an adjudication for nearly two years, to suddenly change his attitude, and to obtain an adjudication as of the date of filing the petition, upon application, upon securing a substantial property, which cannot be applied to the payment of his debts if his application is granted; such application not having been made until the petitioning creditors applied to withdraw their petition, which they were entitled to do unless some other creditor objected."

Sec. 997. Acts of Bankruptcy. A creditors' petition in bankruptcy is an heroic remedy, and is ordinarily destructive of the debtor's business or professional standing. For this reason the act prescribes that a 21 11 USCA 95.

23 (1) "Conveyed, transferred, concealed, removed, or permitted to be concealed or removed any part of his property, with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud his creditors or any of them." This provision is intended primarily to cover those instances where the debtor attempts to put his property beyond the reach of any of his creditors by concealing his assets, or who absconds, or attempts to remove the property from the jurisdiction. (2) "Transferred, while insolvent, any portion of his property to one or more of his creditors with intent to prefer such creditors over his other creditors." This provision is intended to defeat an attempt on the part of the debtor to discriminate among his creditors by using his assets to pay one or more creditors without a substantial equivalent to the remaining creditors. The courts have not been inclined to construe the payment of ordinary debts as they mature as an intent to prefer one creditor over another, except where the injury to other creditors is substantial. (3) "Suffered or permitted, while insolvent, any creditor to obtain a lien upon any of his property through legal proceedings and not having vacated or discharged such lien within thirty days from the date thereof or at least five days before the date set for any sale or other disposition of such property." Sec. 998. Judicial Liens. The bankruptcy act is not destructive of judgment liens acquired more than four months prior to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy." 

Unless creditors were permitted to act within four months after such liens are obtained, such property would not pass to the trustee, and would not be available to the general creditors of the bankrupt. It is for this reason that failure to discharge a judgment lien against real estate within thirty days after it has been obtained, is deemed to be an admission of insolvency, and an intent to prefer one creditor over another. Failure to discharge an execution lien against personal property, at least five days prior to the sale, is also an act of bankruptcy. It should be noted, however, that a judgment, unexecuted, is not a lien against personal property. Where a debtor does not own real estate, a judg ment is not an act of bankruptcy unless an attempt is made to enforce it by a judicial sale of the debtor's property.27

Part 3. Adjudication 

Sec. 999. Jury Trial. A petition may be filed against an insolvent debtor within four months after he shall have committed an act of bankruptcy. Solvency is a complete defense to the petition, but the burden of proof rests upon the alleged bankrupt.28 He may file a written application for a jury trial, both with respect to his solvency and any act of bankruptcy he is alleged to have committed.20

Sec. 1001. Imprisoned Debtor. A bankrupt is exempt from imprisonment upon civil process, except when in contempt of a court of bankruptcy, and on process issued by a state court upon a debt or claim from which his discharge in bankruptcy would not be a release.³¹ According to the Rules of the Supreme Court, if the bankrupt is imprisoned after a bankruptcy proceeding is instituted, or arrested in any civil action during bankruptcy proceedings, the court may order his appearance upon habeas corpus, and if the commitment is upon a claim provable in bankruptcy, the court shall discharge him from further confinement. If the claim is not provable, the court will remand him to the custody in which he may lawfully be.3 32

Barnes v. Silveus, 114 Pa. Superior Ct. 214 (1934). Plaintiff held a judgment note signed by Silveus and Filtz in the sum of $950. On March 3, 1930, the makers of the note, individually, and the same parties doing business as "Fred Silveus," were adjudicated bankrupts, and received a discharge on March 26, 1931. 

The note was not included in the schedules of creditors of either Filtz or the partnership, but was scheduled in the list of creditors of Silveus. Judgment was confessed on the note against Filtz on August 31, 1931. The chancellor found that the plaintiff did not have knowledge of the bankruptcy of Filtz, and refused to open the judgment. In approving this decision, it was said by 

PARKER, J. "It seems clear to us that where it appears that a bankrupt does not schedule an indebtedness, the burden is upon such bankrupt to show actual knowledge upon the part of the creditor of the bankruptcy proceedings in time to prove his claim. 

The present bankruptcy act uses very emphatic language when, in effect, it says that debts shall not be discharged which have not been scheduled in time for proof and allowance unless the creditor has received actual notice. A method is provided for the giving of the notice, and if that procedure is not followed the burden ought to be upon the one through whose fault the situation arose." 

Sec. 1003. Knowledge of Creditor. Where a cred itor has knowledge of a proceeding in bankruptcy against his debtor, he may if he so desires avail himself of the benefits of the law by filing his claim against the bankrupt's estate, and he is not then prejudiced by the failure of the bankrupt to list the debt. 

McDermott v. Sulkin, 154 Pa. Superior Ct. 81 (1943). Plaintiff sought to recover on a $650 judgment note. Defendant pleaded his discharge in bankruptcy. He had neglected to list the debt in his schedules, but had advised plaintiff of the bankruptcy proceedings. Plaintiff called at the office of the clerk of the referee in bankruptcy to discuss the matter, and there was undisputed testimony that "she did not file her claim due to the fact that she considered it a waste of money to pay for the filing expense." 

Under these circumstances, it was said by RHOADES, J. "It therefore follows that appellee's discharge in bankruptcy was an ab- 

34 11 USCA 35.

solute extinguishment of the obligation, and not a mere bar of the remedy upon it."

Sec. 1004. Examination of Bankrupt. It is the duty of the bankrupt to attend the first meeting of his creditors, and at a hearing upon objections to his discharge. 

He may be required to attend at such other times as the court may direct, upon payment of his actual and necessary traveling expense not in excess of one hundred miles from his residence at the date of bankruptcy. At such hearings he may be examined concerning the conducting of his business, the cause of his bankruptcy, his dealings with his creditors and other persons, the amount, kind, and whereabouts of his property, and all matters which may affect the administration and settlement of his estate or the granting of his discharge.35 

In re Bryant, 188 Fed. 530 (1911). Application was made to be allowed to examine the bankrupt in order to ascertain whether he had made a full disclosure of his assets. There had been several meetings of the creditors, at one of which the bankrupt attended and was examined. The last meeting adjourned without a day. For these reasons the bankrupt demurred to the petition. 

WITMER, D. J. "The vigorous and skillful use of examinations of insolvent bankrupts is often the only means by which creditors are enabled to prevent the bankruptcy act being turned into a shield for dishonesty. If hardship and inconvenience result from such examination, as it sometimes may, it should be remembered that a discharge of the bankrupt from his debts is a great privilege and a prize that will reward the hopest debtor amply for such inconvenience." 

Sec. 1005. Duties of Bankrupt. A number of duties are imposed upon the bankrupt in the liquidation of his estate. He must comply with all lawful orders, examine the correctness of claims, execute such papers as may be ordered by the court, transfer to his trustee all his property in foreign countries, disclose any attempt by his creditors or others to evade the act coming to his knowledge, disclose a false claim of which he has knowledge, file in triplicate, at least five days prior 

35 11 USCA 25.

BANKRUPTCY 

683 to the first meeting of his creditors, a statement of his affairs in such form as may be prescribed by the Supreme Court, and when required to do so, file a detailed inventory showing the cost to him of his merchandise or of such other property as may be designated, as of the date of his bankruptcy.36

Sec. 1006. State Exemptions. A bankrupt is entitled to the exemptions prescribed by the laws of the state in which he had had his domicile for a period of six months, or the greater portion thereof than in any other state, immediately preceding the filing of the petition.³ 

The exemptions allowed a debtor in Pennsylvania are set forth in the preceding chapter.38 A claim for the exemptions is a personal privilege, and a request, if made, must appear in the schedules."⁹ If such claim is made, the property exempt does not pass to the trustee or become a part of the bankruptcy assets. If it has been previously waived by contract in favor of a particular creditor, it may be reached by process issuing from the state court. A creditor holding a waiver must present his claim during bankruptcy proceedings, and utilize the process of the state court to enforce it.

Sec. 1007. Release of Exemption. Where the bank rupt has made claim to his exemption, and then discovers that it is about to be swept away by a creditor holding a waiver, he may withdraw his claim in order that this remnant of his estate will inure to the benefit of all of his creditors.

In re Baughman, 83 Fed. 668 (1910). The bankrupt claimed the exemption. By agreement his estate was sold for $251.60, and the proceeds held by the trustees. A creditor holding a waiver issued an execution against the fund. The bankrupt then asked leave to withdraw the claim. The referee allowed the petition. The creditor appealed. ARCHBALD, C. J. "The $300 exemption is allowed to the unfortunate debtor for the benefit of himself and his dependent family. And if he is authorized to waive the right to it, in favor of one creditor over others, he certainly is authorized to make no claim to it after bankruptcy, so that all may fare alike."

Part 5. Discharge Sec. 1010. Grounds for Refusal. The adjudication of any person, except a corporation, operates as an application for a discharge in bankruptcy. A corporation may file its application for a discharge within six months after its adjudication. The bankrupt is deemed to have forfeited his right to a discharge if he fails to submit to an examination by his creditors when required to do Otherwise the bankrupt is entitled to a discharge, but if reasonable grounds appear, the bankrupt must prove that he has not: So. (1) Committed an offense punishable by imprisonment as provided by the act. (2) Destroyed, mutilated, falsified, concealed, or failed to keep or preserve books of account or records, from which his financial condition and business transactions might be ascertained, unless the court deems such acts or failure to have been justified under all the circumstances of the case. (3) Obtained money or property on credit, or obtained an extension or renewal of credit, by making or publishing or causing to be made or published in any manner whatsoever, a materially false statement in writing respecting his financial conditions. 

44 Cohen v. Samuels, 245 U. S. 50 

(1917). 45 11 USCA 110. 

40 McCahan's Estate, 312 Pa. 515 (1933).

(4) At any time subsequent to the first day of the twelve months immediately preceding the filing of the petition in bankruptcy, transferred, removed, destroyed, or concealed, or permitted to be removed, destroyed, or concealed, any of his property, with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud his creditors. (5) Within six years prior to bankruptcy, been granted a discharge, or had a composition or an arrangement by way of composition or a wage earners' plan by way of composition confirmed under the act. (6) In the course of a proceeding, refused to obey any lawful order of, or to answer any material question approved by the court. (7) Failed to explain satisfactorily any losses of assets or deficiency of assets to meet his liabilities.47 

Sec. 1011. Misrepresentation. Clause three above has been broadly construed to include a materially false statement inducing the execution of a contract under which credit in some form is obtained by the bankrupt. 

Fidelity & Deposit Co. of Maryland v. Arenz, 290 U. S. 66 

(1933). Petitioner had furnished a surety bond to the respondent in order to enable him to procure a contract for the construction of a highway. The respondent failed in this project, and having been adjudged bankrupt, applied for a discharge, including his liability on the surety bond. Petitioner filed an objection to the discharge, showing that the respondent "induced it to become surety by means of materially false written statements in respect of his financial condition." The lower courts overruled the objection and granted the discharge. In deciding that respondent was not entitled to a discharge, it was said by BUTLER, J. "The fraud perpetrated by respondent is of the kind condemned.. 

While clause (3) seems aimed particularly at false pretenses made by borrowers and purchasers to obtain money or goods on credit, it is not limited to such transactions. Respondent's application for discharge should have been denied." 

Sec. 1012. Discharge Revoked. A discharge in bankruptcy may be revoked if application is filed within one year thereafter, where it is made to appear that it was obtained through the fraud of the bankrupt, that the knowledge of the fraud has come to the petitioner since the granting of the discharge, and that the actual facts did not warrant the discharge.48 A bankrupt who

BANKRUPTCY 

687 has concealed his assets, may be indicted at any time within three years from the date of his discharge. The penalty is a fine of not more than $5,000, or imprisonment for not more than five years, or both." 

Sec. 1013. Debts not Discharged. There are a number of obligations which are not dischargeable in bankruptcy. The discharge releases the bankrupt from all provable debts except those which: (1) Are due as a tax levied by the United States, or any State, county, district, or municipality. (2) Are liabilities for obtaining money or property by false pretenses or false representations, or for willful and malicious injuries to the person or property of another, or for alimony due or to become due, or for maintenance or support of wife or child, or for seduction of an unmarried female, or for breach of promise of marriage accompanied by seduction, or for criminal conversation. (3) Have not been duly scheduled in time for proof and allowance, with the name of the creditor, if known to the bankrupt, unless such creditor had notice or actual knowledge of the proceedings in bankruptcy. (4) Were created by his fraud, embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation while acting as an officer or in any fiduciary capacity. (5) Are for wages which have been earned within three months before the date of commencement of the proceedings in bankruptcy due to workmen, servants, clerks, or traveling or city salesmen, on salary or commission basis, whole or part time, whether or not selling exclusively for the bankrupt. (6) Are due for moneys of an employee received or retained by his employer to secure the faithful performance by such employee of the terms of a contract of employment.50

Sec. 1014. Conversion. The conversion of the prop erty of another may constitute a willful or malicious injury within the meaning of the code, but not every technical conversion is willful or malicious. The criterion to be observed in such cases is the quality of the offense, or the circumstances under which it was committed. 

49 11 USCA 52. 

50 11 USCA 35.

Davis v. Aetna Acceptance Co., 293 U. S. 328 (1934). Davis was a dealer in automobiles. He obtained a loan from the Aetna 

Acceptance Company in the sum of $1,181.87, and by adding a small amount, procured title to an Auburn sedan. As security for the loan he gave a promissory note and a chattel mortgage, and also a trust receipt which provided that he should not sell the car without the consent of the Acceptance Company in writing. 

He sold the car without written consent and promised to make a prompt remittance by check, subject to an offset or credit growing out of other dealings. He did not keep his promise. Instead, he filed a petition in bankruptcy, listed the Acceptance Company in his schedules, and obtained his discharge. The Acceptance Company instituted this action in trover for the conversion of the car. 

Davis pleaded his discharge in bankruptcy. The trial court found that while he was not actuated by wilful, malicious or criminal intent in disposing of the car, nevertheless it was a legal conversion, and for this reason the obligation was not discharged. In deciding otherwise, it was said by CARDOZO, J. "There may be a conversion which is innocent or technical, an unauthorized assumption of dominion without willfulness or malice. There may be an honest but mistaken belief, engendered by a course of dealing, that powers have been enlarged or incapacities removed. In these and like cases, what is done is a tort, but not a willful and malicious one. No question as to a cause of action arising from a conversion of the proceeds of the sale with willfulness and malice as distinguished from one arising from the conversion of the car itself is before us on this record." 

Part 6. Creditors Sec. 1015. Meetings. A meeting of creditors must be called not less than ten nor more than thirty days after the adjudication. The judge may, but usually the referee presides. The referee in bankruptcy is the representative of the court. At this meeting claims are allowed or disallowed, and the creditors are given an opportunity to examine the bankrupt. Provision is made in the code for additional meetings when necessary, and for a final meeting, although this may be dispensed with in a no-asset case. 51 At the first meeting the creditors may appoint one or three trustees, other- 51 11 USCA 91.

BANKRUPTCY 

689 wise the court will do so. The creditors may also appoint a committee of not less than three of their number to advise and consult with the trustee."2 The trus tee is a representative of the creditors. It is his duty to set aside the bankrupt's exemptions if claim is made, to liquidate the estate, and to pay dividends when declared by the referee.53

Sec. 1016. Proof of Claims. A proof of claim is a statement under oath, in writing, signed by a creditor, setting forth the nature of the claim, the consideration therefor, and whether any, and if so, what securities are held therefor, and whether any, and if so, what payments have been made thereon, and that the sum claimed is justly owing from the bankrupt to the creditor. Claims must be filed within six months after the first meeting of creditors. The right of infants and insane persons without guardians, without notice of the bankruptcy proceedings, may continue six months longer. Where all claims have been paid in full, a delayed claim may be allowed against any surplus remaining in the bankrupt's estate. 54

In re West Penn Fuel Co., N. S. 4, A. B. R. 780 (1924). DAVIS, 

C. J. "The rights of creditors to prove debts and share in the distribution of the assets of a bankrupt estate are fixed by the status of their claim at the time of the filing of the petition in bankruptcy. A debt contracted after the filing of the petition cannot be proved in bankruptcy, nor is the bankrupt released from such debts by a discharge in bankruptcy. 

The remedy of a creditor whose debt arose subsequent to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy is by a new petition."

Sec. 1017. Secured Creditors. The distinction be tween general and secured creditors was pointed out in the preceding chapter. A secured creditor has a lien on particular property which he may enforce as against other creditors. It has also been pointed out that the security of a lien creditor is not only preserved and regu- 

54 11 USCA 93. www

lated whenever an execution is issued out of a state court, or where an assignment is made for the benefit of creditors, but also in the liquidation of the estate of a bankrupt. Except as to voidable liens and preferences created within a period of four months prior to the filing of the petition in bankruptcy, the statute is not destructive of the rights and priorities of secured or preferred creditors. For this reason, creditors holding claims which are secured, or which have priority, are not entitled to participate in the administration or distribution of the estate of the bankrupt, "unless the amounts of such claims exceed the values of such securities or priorities, and then only for such excess." 55 The claims of creditors whose rights under the statute are void or voidable, may not be allowed unless such rights are surrendered. 50

Sec. 1018. Void Liens. The code provides that every lien against the property of a person obtained by attachment, judgment, levy, or other legal or equitable proceeding within four months before the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, shall be null and void, if at the time when such lien was obtained such person was insolvent, or if such lien was sought and permitted in fraud of the provisions of the act. Statutory liens in favor of employees, contractors, mechanics, landlords, or other classes of persons, and statutory liens for taxes and debts owing to the United States, or any state or subdivision thereof, are excepted.57 It will be observed from the above, that even though a lien is obtained by judicial proceedings within four months prior to bankruptcy, it is not void unless the judgment debtor was insolvent at the time. 

Rush v. 

First National Bank, 324 Pa. 285 (1936). Plaintiff obtained judgment against the defendant on a debt of some years' standing. A writ of fieri facias was issued and levies were made against personal property. This occurred on March 15, 1935, and 57 11 USCA 107. 6511 USCA 92. 56 11 USCA 93.

BANKRUPTCY 

691 the lien began as of that date. Less than four months later, July 

9, 1935, the defendant was adjudicated a bankrupt. The question involved was whether the fund raised at the sheriff's sale should be distributed to the plaintiff or to the trustee in bankruptcy. 

SCHAFFER, J. "From the two dates named it will be seen that the levy was within four months of the institution of the bankruptcy proceedings. Does this alone give the bankruptcy trustee the right to claim the fund? In our opinion, it does not, for the reason that there is no proof that at the time the levy was made the defendant was insolvent."

Sec. 1019. Preferred Creditors. A debtor may make substantial payments, or transfer a considerable part of his estate to some of his creditors during the period of four months preceding the filing of a petition in bankruptcy. The interests of the creditors in general require that all such payments or transfers be avoided by the trustee, in order that these assets might be distributed among them all. This is one of the primary objectives of the bankruptcy act. A person is deemed to have given such a preference if, (1) within four months before the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, and (2) being insolvent, he has (3) transferred any of his property to a creditor for an antecedent debt, (4) the effect of which would be to enable such creditor to obtain a greater percentage of his debt than some other creditor of the same class. Such a preference may be avoided by the trustee, (5) if the creditor receiving it had reasonable cause to believe that the debtor was insolvent when it was made. The code as amended in 

1938 provides that if such a transfer is made prior to the four-month period, it must have become so far perfected that no bona-fide purchaser from the debtor and no other creditor could thereafter have acquired any rights in the property superior to the rights of the creditor to whom it was made, otherwise it will be deemed to have been made immediately before bankruptcy." 

An assignment, for example, is not perfected until the 58

assignee gives notice of his right to the property.59 In such a case the period of four months would be computed from the date such notice was given. If no notice is given the assignment will be set aside as having been made immediately before bankruptcy. 

Sec. 1020. Antecedent Debt. The objectionable feature of a voidable preference is the diminution of the bankrupt's estate. The bankrupt will have discharged an antecedent debt by making such a transfer, but this in itself is a preference of one creditor over other creditors. The code does not invalidate a transfer for a fair equivalent value, though made within four months prior to bankruptcy. Quite the contrary, if a creditor who has received a voidable preference afterwards gives his debtor further credit without security, which augments the debtor's assets, the creditor is entitled to a set-off for such new credit as against the amount recoverable by the trustee. The code also protects innocent purchasers who have acquired such property from a preferred creditor if they have paid a fair equivalent value. 

In either case, what the trustee is entitled to recover is anything less than a fair consideration paid for the property. Whether a transfer made within four months prior to bankruptcy will enable one creditor to obtain a greater percentage of his debt than some other creditor of the same class, is to be determined by the status of the bankrupt's estate as of the date of bankruptcy. 60 

Palmer Clay Products Co. v. Brown, 297 U. S. 227 (1936). The 

Metropolitan Builders' Supply Company made a part payment of an overdue debt to the Palmer Clay Products Company. The latter had reasonable cause to believe that the former was insolvent, and that the payment would effect a preference over other creditors of the same class, but contended that this was not a voidable preference on the ground that the debtor's assets, if then distributed, would have been sufficient to pay all creditors of the same class an equal proportion of their claims. BRANDEIS, J. "Whether a cred- 

60 11 USCA 60. 

Corn Exchange Nat. Bank & Trust 

Co. v. Klauder, 318 U. S. 434 (1943).

BANKRUPTCY 

693 itor has received a preference is to be determined, not by what the situation would have been if the debtor's assets had been liquidated and distributed among his creditors at the time the alleged preferential payment was made, but by the actual effect of the payment as determined when bankruptcy results. The payment on account of say 10 per cent within the four months will necessarily result in such creditor receiving a greater percentage than other creditors, if the distribution in bankruptcy is less than 100 per cent. 

For where the creditor's claim is $10,000, the payment on account $1,000, and the distribution in bankruptcy 50 per cent, the creditor to whom the payment on account is made receives $5,500, while another creditor to whom the same amount was owing and no payment on account was made will receive only $5,000. A payment which enables the creditor 'to obtain a greater percentage of his debt than any other of such creditors of the same class' is a preference." 

Sec. 1021. Knowledge of Insolvency. A transfer while insolvent, made by the bankrupt within four months before bankruptcy proceedings, though without a fair equivalent value, and with intent to prefer a particular creditor, is not in itself a voidable preference. 

It must also be shown that the creditor benefiting from such a transfer had reasonable cause to believe that the debtor was insolvent at the time. Inasmuch as the payment of a debt is reasonable behavior, the burden is on the trustee to show some other circumstance sufficient to put the creditor on notice that his debtor was insolvent at the time. In most cases such proof is obtainable, but sometimes it is not. 

Rudisill's Trustee v. Wildasin, 275 Pa. 255 (1922). Within four months prior to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, Rudisill sold his accounts receivable and an automobile, paying from the sum realized two notes held by the Hanover Trust Company on which the defendant was surety. The effect of this payment was to relieve the defendant as endorser on the notes. The bankrupt may have intended to prefer this particular creditor. The jury found, however, that defendant did not have reasonable cause to believe that such a preference would result. In sustaining the finding of the jury, it was said by KEPHART, J. "To establish a preference it must appear defendant had reasonable cause to believe a preference was intended. The act of Congress forbids a preference, 45

under penalty of repayment. But every payment of money by an insolvent is not necessarily a preference, and the fact that the money is paid and the debtor is an insolvent do not, of themselves, give rise to the claim of preference, nor would they, standing alone, be sufficient to support a concerted action having that end in view. 

Nor will a mere suspicion from such evidence; in addition, there should be some evidence showing concerted action or circumstances enough to put an ordinarily prudent man on inquiry. Whether such reasonable cause to believe existed is a question of fact, and the burden of proof is on the trustee. If, however, a creditor knows of his debtor's insolvency, or has reasonable ground to believe he is insolvent, and taking and enforcing the security or transfer would work a preference, he brings himself within the act." 61 

Sec. 1022. Uniform Fraudulent Conveyance Act. 

The Uniform Fraudulent Conveyance Act, a discussion of which will be found in the preceding chapter, was incorporated into the bankruptcy act in 1938. Under this amendment, a fraudulent conveyance made within one year prior to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy may be avoided by the trustee. There is a difference between a voidable preference and a fraudulent conveyance. A voidable preference has the merit of having been made to discharge an antecedent debt. A fraudulent conveyance is made without a fair consideration when the debtor is either insolvent or will be rendered insolvent as the result of the conveyance. As noted in the preceding chapter, a fraudulent conveyance is usually made without any consideration, and in an attempt to place property beyond the reach of creditors. A person is deemed to be insolvent "when the present fair salable value of his property is less than the amount required to pay his debts." 62

A further addition appears in the amendment of 1938. "Every transfer made and every obligation incurred by a debtor within four months prior to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy," is fraudulent, even though a fair consideration is received for

695 63 the property, if made with intent to use such consideration to effect a voidable preference. The two remedies are cumulative, although the trustee is entitled to but one satisfaction."

Part 7. Bankrupt Estates

Sec. 1023. Vesting of Estate. The bankruptcy act of 1867 provided that the property of the bankrupt should pass to the trustee as of the date on which the petition was filed. This was characterized as "an unjust and cruel law," inasmuch as debtors of the bankrupt, in discharging their obligations to him, frequently did not have actual knowledge of the bankruptcy proceedings. The present act contains necessary safeguards. A transfer other than real estate, made by the bankrupt after bankruptcy but before adjudication or before a receiver takes possession of the property, is valid if made for a fair equivalent value. Debtors of the bankrupt are also protected in discharging their obligations to him in good faith and without knowledge of the petition in bankruptcy.05 

Stone, Trustee, v. Superior Fire Ins. Co., 278 Pa. 400 (1924). 

SCHAFFER, J. "This is the question presented: Where a fire insurance company, in settlement of a loss, has made payment to the insured, after the date of filing an involuntary bankruptcy petition against him, but before the adjudication, without knowledge of the petition, can the trustee, the insured having absconded, compel payment by the insurance company a second time? . .

Our conclusion is that the trustee cannot compel the defendant to again pay the money which it in entire good faith parted with to its insured without knowledge that a petition in bankruptcy had been filed against him."

Sec. 1025. Tort Obligations. It has been observed that a bankrupt is not discharged from most obligations arising in tort. According to the provable debts above, the right to recover damages in any action for negligence is a provable claim. Section 17 of the code provides that a discharge in bankruptcy shall release a bankrupt from all of his provable debts, except, inter alia, willful and malicious injuries to the person or property of another."8 There is a well recognized distinction between damages recoverable in an action for negligence, and damages recoverable for willful and malicious injuries to the person or property of another. 

Negligence is one thing. A willful injury is another.

Under the bankruptcy code, a claim for negligent injury is dischargeable in bankruptcy. A claim for a willful injury is not. It will be observed in the following case that the Supreme Court has apparently deferred to the provisions of a state statute as governing the application of the federal law, although not without good cause. 

Reitz v. Mealey, 314 U. S. 83 (1941). Complainant was found guilty of negligent operation of an automobile, and damages were assessed against him in the sum of $5,138.25. On May 29, 1940, his driver's license was suspended under the laws of the State of New York. This statute declared that a discharge in bankruptcy should not constitute satisfaction of such a judgment. Complainant was adjudicated a bankrupt on June 21, 1940. He challenged the state law as inconsistent with the federal bankruptcy act. In sustaining the state statute, in a five to four decision, it was said by ROBERTS, J. "The scheme of the legislation would be frustrated if the reckless driver were permitted to escape its provisions by the simple expedient of voluntary bankruptcy, and, accordingly, the legislature declared that a discharge in bankruptcy should not interfere with the operation of the statute. Such legislation is not in derogation of the Bankruptcy Act. Rather it is an enforcement of permissible state policy touching highway safety." 

67 11 USCA 103. 

68 11 USCA 35.

Sec. 1026. Set-Offs. Mutual debts and credits as between creditors and the bankrupt's estate may be set off against each other. The balance, only shall be allowed or paid. A set-off may not be allowed unless it is a provable claim against the bankrupt's estate, and not then if it "was purchased by or transferred to (the creditor) after the filing of the petition, or within four months before such filing, with a view to such use and with knowledge or notice that such bankrupt was insolvent, or had committed an act of bankruptcy." " Otherwise, a debtor owing money to a bankrupt estate could purchase a claim from a creditor of the estate and use it as a set-off. One creditor would then be substantially paid, while the remaining creditors would have to be content with an uncertain dividend. Discrimination of this sort is not permitted. 69 

Sec. 1027. Priority of Payment. Before any divi dends are declared and paid to the general creditors of the estate of the bankrupt, the following debts and obligations of the estate must be first satisfied, in the order of priority as follows: 70 (1) Expenses of preserving the estate; filing fees paid by creditors; expenses in the recovery of property for the benefit of the estate; and expenses of administration. (2) "Wages, not to exceed $600 to each claimant, which have been earned within three months before the date of the commencement of the proceeding, due to workmen, servants, clerks, or traveling or city salesmen on salary or commission basis, whole or part time, whether or not selling exclusively for the bankrupt." (3) Expenses incurred by creditors in obtaining a refusal or revocation of an arrangement, or wage-earner's plan, or the bankrupt's discharge. (4) Taxes legally due and owing by the bankrupt to the United States or any State or any subdivision thereof, not in excess of the value of the interest of the bankrupt estate therein as determined by the court. (5) "Debts owing to any person, including the United States, who by the laws of the United States is entitled to priority, and

(1941). The Hamilton-Brown Shoe Company was ordered by the

In sustaining the right of the Board to perfect the claims, and the rights of the employees to second class priority, it was said by JOHNSEN, C. J. "We are of the opinion that a back pay allowance should accordingly be treated the same as any other wage claim, for bankruptcy purposes. . . ."

Part 8. Relief of Debtors Sec. 1028. Other Forms of Relief. The foregoing is a summary of the substantive features of bankruptcy. 

Social experience during the last two decades has indicated more clearly than heretofore the need of other forms of relief short of bankruptcy. The idea of a composition with creditors was first introduced in the bankruptcy act of 1867. Corporate reorganization is the outgrowth of the equity receivership, a procedure initiated by the federal courts in order to prevent creditors from dismembering insolvent railroads. From this beginning there has evolved, as a part of the present bankruptcy act, separate provisions dealing with (1) arrangements, (2) real property arrangements, (3) wage earners' plans, (4) corporate reorganization, (5) relief of farmers, (6) composition of indebtedness of local taxing agencies, (7) Maritime Commission Liens, and (8) railroad adjustments. 

Sec. 1029. Arrangements. An "arrangement" is the outgrowth of the composition agreement. A debtor in Potlat

a pending bankruptcy proceeding, or a debtor who could become a bankrupt, including a partnership or a corporation, may file a petition for relief in a bankruptcy court, and submit for the consideration of his creditors a plan for the settlement, satisfaction, or extension of time of payment of his unsecured debts. He may suggest any terms, but as a practical matter, the terms are either a scaling down of unsecured debts, or an extension of time in which to pay his unsecured debts, or relief from executory contracts. Such a plan may also provide for the continuation of the debtor's business, with or without supervision. Where an unexpired lease is rejected, the claim of the landlord for damages is provable, but not to exceed the rent for three years following the date of the surrender of the premises to the landlord, or the date of reëntry of the landlord, whichever first occurs, plus accrued rent. The proposed plan must be approved by a majority of such creditors, in number and amount of claims, and by the court. If the debtor is not able to obtain such approval, the proceeding in bankruptcy will be reinstated, or if none was pending, the court may adjudge the debtor a bankrupt or dismiss the proceeding, whichever may be in the interest of the creditors. No adjudication, however, may be entered against a wage earner or farmer unless such person file with the court consent to the adjudication." 

Greenberger v. Schwartz, 261 Pa. 265 (1918). On October 7, 1916, judgment was entered on a note. Within one month thereafter the creditors of the maker of the note filed an involuntary petition against him in bankruptcy, and adjudication followed. 

On January 10, 1916, the bankrupt offered a composition to his creditors, which was duly confirmed by the court. The judgment on the note was then opened in order to permit the defense of a discharge in bankruptcy. BROWN, J. "Whether the bankrupt estate is administered by a trustee or there is a composition by the bankrupt with his creditors, the effect of a discharge in bankruptcy is the same, if the composition is confirmed by the court." 

71 11 USCA 301, et seq.

BANKRUPTCY 

701 

Sec. 1030. Real Property Arrangements. The "Real 

Property Arrangement" is a cautious attempt by Congress to authorize approval of a plan "which has for its primary purpose the alteration or modification of the rights of creditors or of any class of them, holding debts secured by real property or a chattel real of which the debtor is the legal or equitable owner." The applicant may be a debtor, other than a corporation, who could become a bankrupt. The proceeding follows the pattern outlined in the preceding paragraph, including the claim for rent, but with one important modification. 

The Congress has always been hostile to any device in the bankruptcy act which would disturb the vested rights of bona fide secured creditors. A "Real Property Arrangement" is a departure from this long established tradition. It may not be approved by the court, however, unless it has been accepted in writing by the creditors of each class, holding two-thirds in amount of the debts of such class affected thereby. Adequate provision must be made for any class of secured creditors which is affected by and does not accept the plan, and for the realization by them of the value of their debts against the property dealt with by the arrangement." 

Relatively few petitioners have sought to avail themselves of this form of relief, and undoubtedly because of the difficulties involved. 

72 11 USCA 801, et seq. 72 

Sec. 1031. Wage Earners' Plans. An individual who works for wages, salary, or hire at a rate of compensation which, when added to all his other income, does not exceed $3,600 per year, may file a petition in a pending bankruptcy proceeding or otherwise to effect a composition, or an extension of time in which to pay his debts, or for the rejection of executory contracts. Where an unexpired lease is rejected, the claim of the landlord is limited to an amount not to exceed the rent for one year. The plan may deal with secured and unsecured

debts. It must provide for the submission of future earnings of the debtor to the supervision and control of the court, and reserve to the court the right from time to time to increase or reduce the amount of any installment, or extend or shorten the time for any such payments, as may be justified by the circumstances. It must be approved in writing by a majority in number of all unsecured creditors whose claims have been proved and allowed, which number must represent a majority in amount of such claims, and by the secured creditors whose claims are affected. If at the expiration of three years after confirmation, the debtor has not completed his payments, and the court is satisfied that the failure of the debtor was due to circumstances for which he could not be justly held accountable, the court may discharge the debtor from all his debts and liabilities provided for in the plan, excluding debts which are not dischargeable in bankruptcy held by creditors who have not accepted the plan. If the debtor fails to secure the approval of a plan, or defaults thereunder, the bankruptcy proceeding will be reinstated, or if none was pending the court may, with the debtor's consent, adjudge him a bankrupt.73 Relief of this sort is not so important in Pennsylvania, where wages are not subject to attachment, as it is in those states in which the wage earner may be constantly harrassed by importunate creditors. 

Sec. 1032. Corporate Reorganization. An insolvent corporation which could become a bankrupt, or three or more of its creditors whose claims aggregate $5,000 or over, or a qualified indenture trustee, may in any bankruptcy proceeding or otherwise, file a petition proposing that a plan of reorganization be effected. Where the liquidated indebtedness of the corporation is $250,- 000 or over, the court shall, upon approval of the peti tion, appoint one or more trustees. 

If the indebtedness 

73 11 USCA 601, et seq.

BANKRUPTCY 

703 is less, the court may appoint one or more trustees or it may continue the debtor in possession. It is the duty of the trustee to endeavor to arrange an acceptable plan of reorganization. For this purpose, the creditors of the corporation and its shareholders are classified according to their respective interests. Considerable latitude is allowed in the adjustment of secured and unsecured debts, and in the adjustment of the capital structure of the corporation. The code provides, however, that a proposed plan of reorganization shall provide, as to any class of creditors which is affected by and does not accept it by two-thirds majority, adequate protection for the realization of the value of their claims, and if the corporation is found to be solvent, the plan must also provide for any class of stockholders affected by the plan if it is not accepted by a majority of such stockholders.

Sec. 1033. Approval of Reorganization. Where the indebtedness of a corporation exceeds $3,000,000, a plan for the reorganization of the corporation must be submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission, although its report is advisory only. If the corporation is a public utility, the plan must also be referred to the appropriate regulatory commission for suggested amendments or objections. Before the proposed plan is approved, it must also be referred to the Secretary of the Treasury. The plan may alter the rights of creditors generally, and of shareholders through the issuance of new securities or otherwise. It may also provide for the rejection of executory contracts, except contracts in the public authority. The claim of the landlord, for damages resulting from the rejection of an unexpired lease, is provable, but not to exceed the rent reserved in such lease for three years. If the proposed reorganization is not approved, or is not consummated, the proceeding in bankruptcy will be reinstated, or if none was pending the court may either adjudge the corporation

a bankrupt, or dismiss the proceeding, whichever may be in the interests of the creditors and stockholders." 

The proceeding authorized for the reorganization of an insolvent corporation is lengthy and cumbersome, and if its affairs are not unduly involved by secured debts, and if its capital structure is relatively simple, it should seek relief by way of an "Arrangement," rather than through the reorganization procedures of the bankruptcy act. 

Relief to Farmers. Relief to farmers is 

Sec. 1034. of two sorts. A farmer as defined may request a composition or an extension of time in which to pay his debts. Such a plan may be approved by a majority of his creditors in number and the amount of their claims, provided it does not impair the lien of a secured creditor below the fair and reasonable market value of the property, although the rate of interest may be reduced. 

A farmer failing to obtain such approval, or if he feels aggrieved by the composition or extension, may request to be adjudged a bankrupt, and he may at the same time request relief in the nature of a moratorium." 

Sec. 1035. Moratorium. The Frazier-Lemke Act of 

1934 provided that any farmer could have an appraisal made of his mortgaged property, and, if the mortgagee consented, could purchase the property at its appraised value, acquiring title and immediate possession, by agreeing to the following schedule of deferred payments: 

212% within two years, 22% within three years; 

5% within four years; 5% within five years; and the balance within six years. Deferred payments were to bear interest at the rate of 1%. If the mortgagee refused, which he was likely to do, the farmer could require the court to stay all proceedings for a period of five years, during which time he could retain possession

705 of his property by paying a reasonable rental, to be fixed by the court. At the end of five years he could purchase the property by paying into court the appraised value of the property. This act was held unconstitutional in 1935.76 Three months later Congress passed the second Frazier-Lemke Act. This act is more cautious in its treatment of the creditor. Immediate purchase is eliminated, and the period of stay is shortened to three years, during which the farmer may pay a reasonable rental to be fixed by the court. At the end of three years, or prior thereto, the farmer is entitled to purchase the property at its appraised value, unless a secured creditor requests the sale of the property at public auction. In such case, the farmer is given ninety days within which to redeem the property by payment of the sale price, plus 5% per annum. This act has been upheld by the Supreme Court." CHAPTER XXV REAL ESTATE Part 1. Interests in Land Sec. 1036. Land Tenure. Land tenure in Pennsyl vania is an outgrowth of the feudal system. Under this system, tenancies in land consisted of a gradation of tenures from the King to the person in possession of the soil, since all lands in England were "holden mediately or immediately of the King." Each overlord in succession exacted certain feudal duties and obligations of his immediate tenant in the nature of rents, aids, fines, relief, guardianship of the heir, and escheat, according to the dignity of the several estates. Tenure of this sort had been considerably modified in England prior to the Revolution, and was for the most part abolished in 

Pennsylvania by the Divesting Act of 1779.2 

This act appropriated the proprietary interests of the Penn heirs, except for private manors and estates, for a consideration of one hundred and thirty thousand pounds sterling. Quit-rents, which had been reserved in some of the early deeds, were annulled. 

A quit-rent was merely a token or badge of feudal subservience. 

It usually consisted of a rose, a penny, or a peppercorn to be paid to the grantor. In the Penn Charter it consisted of two beaver skins to be delivered on the first day of January in every year at the castle of Windsor. 

Sec. 1037. Ground Rents. More substantial payments, or ground rents, have been preserved, but a ground rent is the consideration to be paid for the use of the land. Where the grantee is unable to pay the purchase price he may be permitted by the grantor to pay interest on the value of the land. The Act of 1885 3 provides that an irredeemable rent may not be created, and that if such a rent is reserved, it may be extinguished at the option of the grantee within twenty-one

Sec. 1038. Nature of Land. Blackstone divided all property into two classes which he called things real and things personal. "Things real are such as are permanent, fixed, and immovable, and which cannot be carried out of their place; as lands and tenements; things personal are goods, money, and all other movables; which may attend the owner's person wherever he thinks proper to go." This distinction is still recognized today, except that we more commonly use the expressions "personal property" and "real estate." Land includes not only the surface of the earth, but extends upwards to the heavens above and "downwards, whatever is in a direct line, between the surface of any land and the centre of the earth." It is possible to carve out a number of estates within this broad domain, either above or below the surface of the earth. They are "separately the subjects of possession, enjoyment, encumbrance, and taxation."6 

42 Black. Com. 15. 

Ibid., 18.

Sec. 1039. Lands, Tenements and Hereditaments. 

The phrase "lands, tenements and hereditaments" so 

Norris v. Del. Lack. & Wes. R. R. 

Co., 218 Pa. 88 (1907).

commonly appears in deeds as to justify a brief explanation. Things real are of three kinds, "and are usually said to consist in lands, tenements or hereditaments." 8

When this expression is used, land means the soil. A tenement is now understood to mean a house, building, or other permanent improvement on the land. 

An hereditament is any inheritable interest in the land. 

It may be corporeal, or such as may be seen or handledan heirloom or implement which may descend with the property or incorporeal. Most of the incorporeal hereditaments described by Blackstone' are now obsolete. The most common in modern times, or interests which resemble incorporeal hereditaments, are rents, ground rents, easements, licenses, and building restrictions. Easements are of two sorts, called easements in gross and easements appurtenant. 

Sec. 1040. Easements in Gross. An easement in gross is a mere personal privilege of slightly higher dignity than a license, which may be exercised with respect to the land of another. Being personal, it is neither assignable nor inheritable. Blackstone describes such special privileges "as where the owner of land grants to another a liberty of passing over his grounds, to go to church, to market, or the like; in which case the gift or grant is particular, and confined to the grantee alone; it dies with the person; and if the grantee leaves the country, he can not assign over his right to any other, nor can he justify taking another person in his company." 10

Part 2. Estates in Land Sec. 1042. Estates of Freehold. A freehold estate now means either an estate for life, or an estate in fee simple. A fee simple estate is an estate free of feudal obligations. "This is property in its highest degree. . . . 

And hence it is, that, in the most solemn acts of law, we express the strongest and highest estate that any subject can have by these words: 'he is seised thereof in his demesne, as of fee.'" 18 A fee simple estate is the sum total of all other possible estates in land. 

Sec. 1043. Inclusion of Heirs. The word "heirs" commonly appears in a deed. This was necessary at common law to distinguish a life estate from an estate 

11 Lindenmuth v. Safe Harbor Water Power Corp., 309 Pa. 58 (1932). 

12 Henry V. Eves, 306 Pa. 250 (1932). 

13 2 Black. Com. 105. 46

in fee simple.¹ The practice is a relict of the common law. The Act of 1909 15 provides that the words "grant" or "convey" shall be effective to pass a fee simple title without words of inheritance or of perpetuity. It also provides that the words "release and quit claim," when used in a deed, shall constitute a release of whatever interest the grantor may have in the land. The common law recognized what was called an "estate tail." 

This was an estate in the grantee or devisee and to the heirs of his body forever. Its purpose was to retain the land within the same family for succeeding generations. An estate of this sort is opposed to the free alienation of land, and was abolished in 1799.18 

Sec. 1044. Estates in Reversion. "An estate in reversion is the residue of an estate left in the grantor, to commence in possession after the determination of some particular estate granted out by him." 17 It is a future estate which revests in the grantor at the termination of (1) an estate for years, as for some determinate period, (2) an estate at will, as where an estate is held at the will of the lessor, and (3) an estate at sufferance, as "where one comes into possession of land by lawful title, but keeps it afterwards without any title at all." 18 

The usual relation between the parties is that of lessor and lessee, or landlord and tenant, but an estate for life may revert back to the grantor if there is a failure of remaindermen. An estate at will, or at sufferance, will usually ripen into an estate from month to month or from year to year by the acceptance of rent at such intervals of time.19

Part 3. Deeds Sec. 1046. Common Law Deed. According to Black stone, the execution of a deed is "the most solemn and authentic act that a man can possibly perform, with relation to the disposal of his property." 22 The form of the deed, as he outlined it, is still in common use. It is divided into the following parts: (1) Premises: This sets forth the number and names of the parties, an explanation of the reasons for the transaction, the consideration, the name of the grantor, the name of the grantee, and a description of the estate. (2) Habendum: This defines the nature of the estate granted. (3) Tenendum: This was used to signify the tenure of the grantee, but it is now of very little use. (4) Reddendum: This consists of any reser servation, such as ground rent, reserved by the grantor. (5) Condition: This is to explain any contingency upon the happening of which the estate might terminate or be defeated. (6) Warranty: This is a clause in which the grantor secures the title to the estate granted. (7) 

Covenants: These are stipulations of fact with respect to the right to convey, to bind onesself to perform, or for the grantee's quiet

Sec. 1047. Warranties. Warranties of title are of two kinds, special and general. The first is the most commonly used. Each is defined by statute as follows: (1) Special Warranty: This is a covenant that the grantor "will forever warrant and defend the said property, and every part thereof, unto the grantee, his heirs, personal representatives and assigns," as against the claims of the grantor and those claiming under him. (2) General Warranty: This is a covenant that the grantor and those claiming under him "will forever warrant and defend the said property, and every part thereof, unto the grantee, his heirs, personal representatives and assigns, against the lawful claims and demands of all persons whomsoever." 28

The Act of 1715 29 provides that where no reservations are made otherwise, the grantor of a conveyance in fee simple warrants that he has an indefeasible estate to convey, free of incumbrance, and that the grantee shall have and enjoy quiet possession as against the grantor and those claiming under him. A warranty, whether express or implied, is dependent upon the financial stability of the grantor. This hazard may be avoided by obtaining title insurance.

Sec. 1049. Use of Short Form. The short form of deed is seldom used. There are two reasons for this.

In the first place every word and phrase of the common law deed has been tested in the courts, and the lawyer knows when he uses it that he is protecting his client to the fullest extent. The second reason is suggested in the following note which appears in the TEMPLE LAW QUARTERLY for June, 1935.³¹ 

"The failure to sanction the use of the short deed lies with the lawyer. It is not his conservatism, nor his inertia, but rather his fear of loss of clientele that prompts his disapproval. To simplify the deed to such extent that a layman can easily draw one, will inevitably withdraw a source of income that he has enjoyed for centuries. Much of the business formerly his is today controlled by large corporations, banks and trust companies, and he feels it heavily. As long as the deed looks important, as long as it contains words and phrases that only a lawyer understands, just so long will the public have to go to a lawyer, or one specially trained. 

The longer the deed, the more important in appearance, the more 

30 Act of April 30, 1925, P. L. 404, 21 PS 1. 

31 Vol. IX, No. 4, p. 436, signed,

B. L. B. 

sat La Plagn

secure the client feels, and the more he pays. It is that which adds color, an atmosphere of mystery, to the law. The doctor could just as easily write his prescription in understandable English which his patient could understand, but he adds a certain touch to the entire transaction which would be otherwise lost, by writing illegibly, by calling a commonly known pill a technical name, permitting the phramacist to charge more, and justifying his own fee. If the lawyer wrote out a very simple, short deed, he wouldn't be needed the second time. And he wants to retain that business."

Sec. 1050. Acknowledgment. It is not necessary for the grantor to acknowledge a deed in order to protect the grantee against any claim on the part of the grantor. The Act of 1715 32 provides, however, that a deed must be acknowledged before a person qualified to administer an oath before it may be recorded. The Act of 1909, as amended,33 provides that the acknowledgment may be in the following words: 

On this fore me, a came the above named the foregoing deed to be same to be recorded as such. 

Witness my hand and said.

Sec. 1051. Recording. The purpose of recording the deed is not to protect the purchaser from any claim on the part of the grantor, but rather from any other conveyance which might be made by the grantor, or from any mortgage, judgment, or other lien which might be entered as of record against the grantor. The Act of March 18, 1775, allowed six months in which to record the deed. This was reduced by the Act of May 19, 1893, to ninety days. Sec. 1052. Failure to Record. The statute above excludes from its operation the claims of those persons who have actual or constructive knowledge of the deed, even though it is not recorded. Actual residence upon the premises by the grantee is usually constructive notice of his interest in the land, but not where the grantor and grantee both reside on the premises. In Miners 

Savings Bank of Pittston v. Tracy,35 Mr. and Mrs. Tracy were the record owners of certain real estate which they conveyed, on October 8, 1931, and for a valuable consideration, to Mrs. Toole. Mrs. Toole was Mrs. Tracy's mother, and all the parties continued to reside on the premises. On April 12, 1932, plaintiff bank entered judgment on a bond against Mr. and Mrs. Tracy. On 

May 24, 1935, Mrs. Toole recorded her deed. On June 

14, 1935, the premises were sold at sheriff's sale to the plaintiff bank. It was held that Mrs. Toole's residence on the premises was not constructive notice of her deed, and that the judgment, being first recorded, had priority over the deed. 

Part 4. Mortgages 

Sec. 1053. Nature of Mortgage. A mortgage is a technical conveyance by the mortgagor to the mortgagee, to secure the payment of a debt, with a clause of defeasance which provides that the title is to revest in the 

35 326 Pa. 367 (1937).

36 mortgagor upon discharging the obligation. It is a technical conveyance, however, only as between the mortgagor and the mortgagee. As to all other persons the mortgage is simply security for a debt, and the legal title remains in the mortgagor.37 Two principles should be noted at the outset. In the first place, the mortgage may provide that it shall apply to property subsequently acquired by the mortgagor. Such a clause is binding upon the mortgagor, but it is seldom that it will be extended to a successor or grantee of the mortgagor.38 In the second place, the mortgage may not only cover the amount specified when the mortgage is executed, but also advances to be made in the future.39 

Batten v. Jurist, 306 Pa. 64 (1932). In 1917 Jurist and her husband executed a second mortgage to Sutro. There was already a first mortgage on the premises to secure a loan of $5,000. The second mortgage provided: "Whereas, the said party of the second part may hereafter, during the continuance of these presents, make further advances to the said Louise S. Jurist, one of the parties of the first part, and it is intended that the same, with interest, shall be secured thereby." From 1917 to 1920 Sutro made additional advances aggregating $15,000, making a total indebtedness to him of $20,000. Thereafter Mrs. Jurist borrowed $41,000 from a bank. Judgment was entered on the note and the property was sold on execution. After payment of the first mortgage, a balance of $16,339.76 remained for distribution. The bank claimed that Sutro was not entitled to more than $5,000, the specific amount stated in the mortgage, with interest. The lower court awarded the entire fund to Sutro, and the bank appealed. MAXEY, J. "The judgment of the court below should be affirmed. While much may cogently be said about the impolicy of legally recognizing such mortgages and some states have by statute denied them legal recognition, such mortgages have long received judicial sanction in Pennsylvania." ...

Sec. 1055. Mortgage Bond. Nearly every mortgage in Pennsylvania is accompanied by a judgment bond, although it is perhaps more accurate to say that a judg ment bond given for the loan of money is frequently accompanied by a mortgage. The bond is the contract under which the loan is made. The mortgage serves as collateral security. The bond is usually expressed in a penal sum double the amount of the mortgage indebtedness, but this is merely an historical curiosity. The mortgagor may not be compelled to pay more than the loan with interest and costs, together with taxes and water rent, or such other obligations as are expressed in the instrument. 

Sec. 1056. Sale by Mortgagor. Inasmuch as the mortgagor retains a legal title to the property as to all third persons, he may sell it subject to the lien of the mortgage, but for obvious reasons he may not assign his personal liability under the bond without the consent of the mortgagee. The question then arises as to the liability of the purchaser for the mortgage indebtedness. 

The Act of 1878 40 provides that the purchaser shall not become personally liable to the mortgagee, even though the land is sold "under and subject" to the mortgage, unless there is an express or implied agreement to that effect. Where the purchase price includes both the mortgage loan and the mortgagor's equity, the purchaser will ordinarily insist that so much thereof as may be necessary be applied to the discharge of the mortgage. The land would then be free of the mortgage. 

Sec. 1057. Implied Obligation. Where the purchaser buys nothing but the mortgagor's equity, and 

40 Act of June 12, 1878, P. L. 205, 21 PS 655.

41 permits the mortgage to remain as an incumbrance upon the land, there arises an implied obligation on his part to assume the mortgage indebtedness. Otherwise if the mortgagee compelled payment from the mortgagor under the bond, the purchaser would acquire the land for a fraction of its value. Under such circumstances "the law presumes that the grantee has agreed to apply the money so deducted or retained for the purpose of paying the incumbrance." "2 The mortgagee may proceed against the mortgagor on the bond, or he may proceed against the purchaser in the name of the mortgagor.44 

Where the mortgagor is obliged to discharge the obligation, he is entitled to indemnity from the purchaser. 43 

Heaney v. Riddle, 343 Pa. 453 (1942). Plaintiff placed a mortgage upon certain property owned by him. Thereafter he conveyed the property, under and subject to the mortgage, to The Riddle Company. Default having occurred, plaintiff was compelled to pay the balance of the mortgage debt, and brought this action against The Riddle Company to recover the loss. In discussing the principles applicable to such a situation, it was said. by STERN, J. "When title to the premises was conveyed by plaintiff to The Riddle Company under and subject to the $15,000 mortgage, the amount of the mortgage debt was presumably part of the consideration for the purchase, and there arose an obligation of The Riddle Company to indemnify plaintiff against loss by reason of the encumbrance; as between plaintiff and the company, the latter made the mortgage debt its own and became primarily liable therefor. . . . Upon breach of the implied covenant of indemnity, plaintiff was entitled to recover the amount necessary to restore him to the position in which he would have been if the covenant had been kept; his right was that of complete exoneration from the mortgage debt that The Riddle Company had impliedly agreed to discharge."

Sec. 1059. Foreclosure. The Act of 1705 46 provides that where default is made in the payment of the mortgage, the mortgagee may, at any time after the expiration of one year next ensuing the last day whereon the mortgage money ought to be paid, sue out a writ of scire facias. The mortgagor may appear and show cause why the mortgaged premises ought not to be seized and taken in execution, otherwise a definitive judgment may be entered. Execution is by writ of levari facias.

Sec. 1060. Judgment on the Bond. The mortgagee may enter judgment on the bond, either before or after, and with or without foreclosure proceedings. The Act of 18459 provides that the confession of judgment on the bond shall not in any way affect the lien of the mortgage. It has been held, however, that a sale of the premises in an execution under the judgment will divest the mortgage securing the bond.50 The property may be sold without inquisition.51 If the plaintiff refrains from bidding in the property, the sum realized at the sale is conclusive of the value of the property, and is credited to the amount due under the judgment. The plaintiff is then entitled to a deficiency judgment for the balance, if any, and may proceed against any other property owned by the defendant.

Lomison v. Faust, 145 Pa. 8 (1891). Lomison conveyed a farm to Faust for $7,500, and received $1,000 in cash, together with a bond and mortgage for the balance. Faust went into possession and made improvements on the farm costing about $2,500. The mortgage indebtedness was not paid and Lomison entered judgment on the bond. He first proceeded against the personal property of the defendant and sold it for about $475. He then issued execution against the farm which he had sold to the defendant and bought it in for $100. He next issued execution against another farm owned by the defendant and was about to sell it, when the defendant petitioned the court for a rule to show cause why the judgment should not be opened, with a stay of the proceedings. 

PER CURIAM. "We are glad to say that we are seldom called upon to pass upon such a case as this. If we possessed unlimited power we might perhaps relieve the appellant. But we administer the law by fixed rules, and in accordance with established precedents; and we cannot stay the hands of a creditor, who is merely pursuing his legal remedies, because the case as presented to us may appear to be a hard one. Were we to depart from this rule, the evil we would do would be greater than the particular hardship we sought to remedy."

Sec. 1062. Deficiency Judgment Act. Deficiency judgment acts were enacted by the legislature in 1934, 1935, and in 1937, but all of them were held unconstitutional, primarily as an impairment of contracts. On 

April 28, 1941, in Gelfert v. National City Bank,5 the

Supreme Court of the United States upheld the Defi-

56 ciency Judgment Act of New York. Three months later, on July 16, 1941, the legislature of Pennsylvania enacted a similar measure. This act provides that whenever "any" real property has been or is sold, directly or indirectly, to the plaintiff in execution proceedings, at a price insufficient to satisfy the amount of the judgment, interest and costs, the plaintiff must petition the court having jurisdiction to fix the fair market value of the property. Such a petition must be filed within six months after such sale, or if such sale has already been made, then within six months after July 16, 1941. Upon the determination of the fair market value of the property, any persons liable to the plaintiff for the payment of the debt shall be released and discharged of such liability to the extent of the fair market value of the property. Any waiver of the act, either before or at the time of incurring the debt, is void and unenforceable. 

If no petition is filed within six months, the person bound by the judgment may present a petition to have the judgment marked satisfied." This act applies whether the sale is by foreclosure of mortgaged property, or by execution on the bond accompanying the mortgage, and in all sales of real property whether on judgments in contract or in tort.58

Part 5. Landlord and Tenant
