Sec. 1063. Caveat Emptor. The law governing the relation of landlord and tenant is composed largely of principles of indifference. Much of it is reminiscent of the onerous obligations of feudal tenure. Subject to a few common law and statutory rules—and these may be moulded for the most part to suit the convenience of the parties the maxim caveat emptor applies with all its vigor. If one man would lease the property of another, let him examine it to determine whether it is suitable for his use. There is no duty on the part of the landlord to make it so,50 or to see that it is usable, or even habitable.61 The only responsibility on the part of the landlord is to deliver the premises to the tenant in the same condition as when the contract was made."2 "It is well settled in this Commonwealth that no implied covenant rises out of the relationship of landlord and tenant which requires the landlord to repair." 63 It is the tenant who is legally bound to keep the premises in repair, though he need not make repairs of a substantial nature." This obligation is not imposed upon the landlord, except as to proper means of ingress and egress where a building is occupied by several tenants.6 65 Séc. 1064. Rights of Tenant. There is an implied covenant that the tenant is entitled to the quiet enjoy-

In other words, the rights and obligations of the parties to a lease are governed very largely by whatever agreement they may make. 

Sec. 1065. Contractual Rights. In addition to the above, the landlord may, and usually does, insist upon a few extraordinary privileges, but they grow out of the contract relation and not from any act of the law. The most usual are (1) notice of termination to be given by the tenant, (2) the right to confess judgment for future installments of rent in case of default, (3) the right to confess judgment of amicable ejectment in case of default, (4) waiver of the exemption laws, stay of execution, and release of errors, (5) the right to distrain upon goods removed from the premises whether they have been fraudulently or clandestinely removed or not, and (6) an option to terminate the lease without notice, or at shorter notice than is required by statute.

Sec. 1066. Destruction of Premises. Where a building which is the subject of a lease has been destroyed by fire or otherwise, neither the landlord nor the tenant, in the absence of an agreement between them, is bound to restore it.72 The tenant, however, is not relieved of the duty of paying the stipulated rent for the balance of the term, except where the building is occupied by a number of tenants.73 This is a harsh rule, especially since a lease is generally prepared by the landlord, and usually does not relieve the tenant of this obligation.

Sankey v. Martin, 93 Pa. Superior Ct. 389 (1928). Plaintiffs leased a hotel and furniture therein to the defendants for a term of one year beginning May 15, 1924. The hotel was destroyed by fire on February 10, 1925. Defendants defaulted in the payment of rent from January 15, 1925 to the balance of the term. This was an action to recover it. The lease contained the following covenant: "At the end of said term or any renewal, the demised premises shall be delivered up without further notice in as good condition as at the commencement thereof, ordinary wear and tear and unavoidable damage by fire, tempest and lightning excepted." 

GAWTHROP, J. "There was no covenant that the rent should be extinguished by the destruction of the leased premises by fire. 

The general rule is that it is no defense to the claim for rent that the premises had been destroyed by fire and that the landlord had received the insurance money. 

The covenant that the demised premises shall be delivered up in as good condition as in the beginning of the term 'unavoidable damage by fire' excepted, relieved defendants of any obligation to rebuild the hotel, but was no defense to plaintiff's claim for rent." 

Sec. 1067. Return of Premises. Where the tenant has agreed to return the premises, but excepts nothing but reasonable wear and tear, he becomes in effect an insurer of the premises and is bound to restore buildings destroyed by fire. There are but few tenants who grasp the ordinary significance of the word "return," in conjunction with "reasonable wear and tear." These words are quite likely to be construed by the layman as

Sec. 1068. Tenancy, Year to Year. The term of a lease is governed by the contract and by the conduct of the parties to it. It may be for a term of years, or from year to year, from month to month, from week week, or from day to day. Where a lease is for a term of one or more years and the tenant holds over, the landlord generally has an option to treat him as a trespasser, or as a tenant at sufferance, or to hold him to a tenancy from year to year. 

Hemphill v. Flynn, 2 Pa. 144 (1845). SERGEANT, J. "The tenant knows the time when his lease will determine; it is his duty to move out by that time, and surrender the premises to the landlord; and if he does not, it seems reasonable to consider his conduct as evidence of his assent to continue as tenant for another year, which is the time the law ordinarily implies." 

Sec. 1069. Tenancy for One Year. It is important to note that a tenancy for one year does not include the first day of the succeeding year.

They attempt to obviate the legal consequences of such a holding over by saying they did it under a mistake of law as to the time when their lease would expire; but intended to

Sec. 1070. Tenancy, Month to Month. It has been observed heretofore that an oral lease for a term of more than three years is an estate at will. This estate, as well as an estate at sufferance, may ripen into a tenancy from year to year by acts of the parties indicating that intention.76 Where an annual rent is to be paid, the tenancy is from year to year." Where the term is for an indefinite period at a monthly rental, the tenancy is from month to month.78

Sec. 1071. Notice of Termination. Except as the lease may provide otherwise, a tenant may remove from the demised premises at the end of the current term without prior notice. In the absence of an agreement otherwise, notice which must be given by the landlord in order to terminate the lease, is regulated by various statutes. (1) Definite Term. Where the lease is for a definite term, no notice is necessary. (2) One or More Years. Where the lease is for a term of one or more years, or at will, the landlord must give three months' notice to the tenant prior to the expiration of the term.79 (3) Less than One Year. Where the lease is for any time less than one year, or by the month, or for an indeterminate time, the landlord must give thirty days' written notice prior to the expiration of the term.8 80 (4) Default in Rent. Where the tenant defaults in the payment of rent and there are no goods on the premises sufficient to pay the rent in arrear except such as are exempt from levy and sale, the landlord must give fifteen days' notice to quit the premises if such notice is given between the first of April and the first of September, and thirty days' notice if such notice is given between the first of September and the first of April.81

Sec. 1072. Warrant of Distress. The landlord's warrant of distress is a relict of the feudal system. The goods of the tenant may be seized by the landlord or his agent, or by a sheriff or constable acting as his agent. 

A distress may not be made on Sunday, or between the hours of sunset and sunrise, unless the tenant is habitually away at any other time.82 Force may not be used.

Picking the lock of an outer door is force.83 Some seizure is necessary, although it may be slight.

Furbush v. Chappel, 105 Pa. 187 (1884). PER CURIAM. "As a general rule, to render the distress complete, there must be a seizure of the property distrained upon, but a very slight act is sufficient to constitute a seizure in contemplation of law. It need not be an actual seizure of the particular goods. If the landlord gives notice of his claim for rent, and declares the goods which he names shall not be removed from the premises until the rent is paid, it is a sufficient seizure."

Sec. 1073. Goods of a Stranger. The goods of a stranger on the premises are subject to the landlord's warrant of distress, but only when on the demised premises. 84

Where the goods of the tenant have been fraudulently or clandestinely removed from the premises the landlord may follow them for a period of thirty days, but not after they have reached the hands of a bona fide purchaser for value.85 The landlord has no right to follow the goods when they have not been fraudulently or clandestinely removed, unless the lease provides otherwise. 80

The goods of a stranger, when once removed, are altogether exempt. 86 87

Sec. 1075. Common Law Exemptions. Frequently the tenant is in possession of property belonging to third parties under the terms of a bailment, bailment lease, or conditional sales contract, and which would, unless exempt, be subject to the claims of the landlord. Such goods are exempt at common law only if they are in the possession of the tenant by way of trade or business. 

Manufacturers' Finance Accept. Corp. v. Jordan Distributors, 

Inc., 111 Pa. Superior Ct. 448 (1934). Plaintiff placed a secondhand automobile in a dealer's show room for purposes of sale. It was levied upon by the landlord for arrear of rent. PARKER, J. "While the general principle is well settled that the goods of a stranger in the custody of the tenant on the demised premises are subject to levy and sale in a distress for rent, it is subject to a number of exceptions. 'Valuable things in the way of trade shall not be liable to distress': 3 Blackstone's Com. 7."

CHAPTER XXVI DECEDENTS' ESTATES Part 1. Intestacy 

Sec. 1078. Intestate Act. In 1915 the legislature authorized the Governor to appoint a commission to codify and revise the law of decedents' estates. This commission prepared a number of statutes which were adopted with minor revisions, one of which is called the Intestate Act.2 The primary purpose of this act is to define those persons who are entitled to participate in the distribution of an estate in cases of intestacy, after the debts of the decedent have been paid. The act applies only to the estates of those persons domiciled in Pennsylvania who die intestate, and to the estates of those persons who, because of insanity or otherwise, are incompetent to make a valid will, or to fractional parts of estates not disposed of by will.5 An agreement varying the distribution provided by the act will be given effect, except as to a posthumous child. All the property of an intestate which is located in Pennsylvania will descend in accordance with the provisions of the act, as well as personal property which may be located elsewhere. Real estate descends in accordance with the laws of the state in which it is situated. 

Sec. 1079. Widow's Exemption. The widow of a decedent, unless she has forfeited her rights, may claim an exemption of $500 out of the real or personal property of the estate of her deceased husband, whether he died testate or intestate, or solvent or insolvent. Where the estate does not exceed $500, the court may on petition set aside this exemption without appraisement or

Sec. 1080. Forfeiture of Exemption. A widow who does not "stand in the family relation toward the decedent at the time of his death, but has been voluntarily living apart from him without such reasonable cause as would entitle her to a divorce, has forfeited the right to her exemption. As expressed in some of the cases, the law granting the exemption contemplates the case of a wife who lives with her husband until his death, and faithfully performs all her duties to his family, not one who voluntarily separates herself from him, 'unless the separation was the fault of the husband.' ” 12 A widow may have forfeited the right to her exemption, and yet may be entitled to participate otherwise in the distribution of her husband's estate. The grounds of refusal are not the same.13 Where the widow has lived in adultery in a foreign country, and has given birth to an illegitimate child, she is not entitled either to the exemption or to a share in her husband's estate. In the following case she was denied the exemption, but not her share in the estate. 

Dick's Estate, 102 Pa. Superior Ct. 589 (1981). Testator be queathed his property to his children and grandchildren. His widow filed a petition for the allowance of her exemption of $500, and also an election to take against the will. The parties were married in 1924, and each then had adult children by former marriages. They separated in 1925, under an agreement which provided that each of them should have free disposition and control

Sec. 1081. Children's Exemption. If there be no widow, or if she has forfeited her rights, then children forming part of the family of any decedent are entitled to the exemption of $500 without request being made therefor. The Act of 1883 15 limited the exemption to "children under the age of fourteen years," but the present statute merely describes "children." 18 It follows that an infant or an adult child is entitled to the exemption, if forming a part of the family of the deceased, whether dependent or not.¹ If such a family consists of one infant and one adult child, each is entitled to a pro rata interest.18 An adopted child is entitled to the same privilege.19 The word "decedent" as used in the statute means father or mother. Where a mother dies leaving no husband entitled to share in her estate, either because of desertion,20 or because of articles of separation under which he is not entitled to an interest in her estate,¹¹ her children are entitled to an exemption from her estate, but not where the surviving husband is entitled to share in the estate of his wife and is able to support his children.22

If, after separation, the wife commits adultery, the separation from that time on becomes desertion within the meaning of the act. It deprives her of all interest in the estate The present record shows an adulterous relationship for more than a year prior to the husband's death."

Sec. 1086. Effect on Will. An election to take against the will does not render the will inoperative as to other beneficiaries, although it may have the effect of reducing the legacies to some beneficiaries, and eliminating others altogether. This will be determined by the nature and priority of such gifts as expressed in the will. Quite often in such cases the widow has been given a life estate, with remainder over to other beneficiaries. 

Under these circumstances the election of the widow to take against the will is equivalent to her death, and the remainders will be accelerated, but if this works a hardship, as sometimes happens, "parts of the estate may be sequestrated, in accordance with equitable principles, for the benefit of disappointed legatees and devisees." "⁹ 

A testator may anticipate that the surviving spouse will take against the will, and provide for some alternate plan, provided it does not offend public policy or public decency. 

Alexander's Estate, 341 Pa. 471 (1941). Testator had three sons by a former marriage, and one son, Arthur, by his present wife. He provided that the income from the bulk of his estate should be divided equally among his four sons, but that if his widow was not satisfied and offered any legal proceedings, that her son should receive the sum of $5.00. The widow elected to take against the will, and received one-third interest in the estate. 

Concerning the right of her son, it was said by PARKER, J. "Her election to take under the will was a condition precedent to his participation in the remainder along with his brothers. Arthur was entitled to five dollars and nothing more." 

Sec. 1087. Contest of Will. An election to take against the will, and a contest of the will, are two dif

ferent things. The surviving spouse may not contest the will unless he or she can show that if the contest is successful, the share would be greater than by taking against the will. Where such a contest is successful the contestant will receive the same share of the estate as though the testator died without leaving a will. This would include the $5,000 item where there are no children or descendants of a deceased child.40 But where an election is made to take against the will, the $5,000 item is not allowed, the shares otherwise remaining the same.¹¹ 

This $5,000 item is also omitted where a bequest is to consist of the "minimum," or such share as is "required" by law.¹2

Erk's Estate, 311 Pa. 185 (1983). The will of the testator provided, inter alia, "I give and bequeath to my estranged wife (Christie B.) who has not always been loyal to me, such portion of estate which is required by Pennsylvania Law, but not more." 

The widow contended that under the will she was entitled to the sum of $5,000 absolutely, plus one-half of the remaining real and personal estate. PER CURIAM. "Here, appellant did not elect to take against her husband's will; there is no actual intestacy, or any direction in the will that the provisions of the Intestate Act shall measure the wife's interest, consequently the limit of the wife's share is one-half the value of the real and personal property."

Sec. 1088. Order of Distribution. The share of the surviving spouse having been determined, the remainder of the estate, in case of intestacy, is distributed to the heirs of the decedent. It should be noted, as a principle of distribution, that whenever all persons qualified to inherit are related to the decedent in the same degree, that is, where they are all children, or all grandchildren, or all nephews and nieces, or all cousins, etc., they take per capita-share and share alike. Whenever they are not all related to the decedent in the same degree, they take per stirpes or by representation-whatever share

Following is the order of distribution of the estate of an intestate: 43 (1) Descendants. The remaining estate will be distributed to the descendants of the decedent, per capita or per stirpes, to the remotest degree. If the decedent leaves children, but no descendants of a deceased child, the estate will be distributed per capita among the children.44 If he leaves grandchildren, but no children or descendants of deceased grandchildren, the estate will be distributed per capita among the grandchildren.45 If he leaves children and the descendants of deceased children, the latter will take per stirpes, whatever the deceased children would have taken if living.46 (2) Parents. In default of the above heirs, the estate will be distributed to the parents or to the surviving parent of the decedent,47 or if there be none, then to brothers and sisters,48 or descendants of deceased brothers and sisters, 49 per capita or per stirpes, as the case may be, except that no representation is admitted after the grandchildren of brothers and sisters of the decedent.50 The latter may take only in the absence of other heirs of a nearer degree. (3) Grandparents. In default of the above heirs, the estate will be divided into two parts, and will be distributed to the grandparents of the decedent, or descendants of deceased grandparents,51 per capita or per stirpes as the case may be, except that no representation is admitted after the children of uncles and aunts of the decedent.52 The latter may take only in the absence of other heirs of a nearer degree.

Sec. 1089. Real Estate. It should be noted that real estate, including ground rents, does not vest in the administrator of the estate, although available upon petition for the payment of debts. Title to real estate descends or vests in the heirs, automatically, without being administered in the orphans' court. This is one of the peculiar characteristics of real property. As said by Blackstone: "Descent, or hereditary succession, is the title whereby a man on the death of his ancestor acquires his estate by right of representation, as his heir at law. An heir therefore is he upon whom the law casts the estate immediately on the death of the ancestor: and an estate, so descending to the heir, is in law called the inheritance." 54

M'Coy v. Scott, 2 Rawle 222 (1828). An administrator col lected rents on land after the death of the decedent. The question involved was whether such rents should be paid to the creditors of the estate, or delivered to the heirs. ROGERS, J. "Although lands in Pennsylvania are considered as chattels for the payment of debts, yet in the case of an intestacy, the real estate goes to the heirs, and the personal estate to the legal representatives.. When lands are wanted for the payment of debts, there is a mode pointed out by the act of assembly. . . . Until this proceeding takes place, the administrator has nothing to do with real estate. . . We are of the opinion, the money was received for the benefit of the heirs." 

Sec. 1090. Heirs of the Half-Blood. No distinction is made in Pennsylvania between heirs of the full-blood and heirs of the half-blood.55 Under the common law the succession of lands was restricted to lineal heirs, but this has been changed by statute." The land now descends without regard to the source of the decedent's title.57 

Sec. 1091. Advancements. A settlement made by the decedent in his lifetime, or an advancement if it be intended as such, will be charged against the share of 

54 2 Black. Com. 201.

50 Keen's Estate, 297 Pa. 22 (1929).

741 the person who has received it, in computing the share to which such person is entitled in the distribution of the estate. 58 As said by Mr. Justice STEARNE, “An advancement as defined by this Court is a pure and irrevocable gift, by a parent in his lifetime, to his child, on account of such child's share of the estate, after the parent's decease. It is to be treated as if repayment had been made to the estate, the total divided among the heirs, and the advancement deducted from the share of the one advanced. The whole is placed in hotchpot, the advancement added and the total divided. Advancements do not bear interest. Interest is charged, however, after the legal period for the settlement of the estate, or from the time when the other heirs received the balance due." 59 The doctrine of advancements applies only to cases of intestacy,60 although it may be applied where a will expresses such intent. It has no application as between husband and wife." Whether gift is an advancement depends upon the intention of the intestate. A loan is not an advancement at all. 61 

Brahm's Estate, 269 Pa. 82 (1920). Mrs. Brahm died intestate, leaving to survive her three sons and two daughters, and four minor children of a deceased son. She had made loans to her sons over a period of years. Numerous payments were made on account of this indebtedness by her deceased son, the balance, $7,686.50, except an item of $492.50, being barred by the statute of limitations at the time of her death. The auditing judge treated this indebtedness as an advancement. This was reversed by the court in banc. In approving this conclusion, it was said by FRAZER, J. “In case of advancement the gift is an irrevocable one without expectation of repayment except in the way of deduction from the share of the donee in the estate of the donor. Consequently circumstances which show an expectation of repayment always tend to rebut the inference that the transaction was an advancement."

In response to this situation, the Act of 1917 63 provided that no person adjudged guilty, either as principal or accessory, of murder of the first or second degree, should be qualified to inherit the estate of the person killed. In 1934, however, a father was permitted to inherit the estate of the daughter he had killed, on the ground that he subsequently killed himself before he could be adjudged guilty of the crime. In 1941 it was held that a wife who had killed her husband and who pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter, and who was the beneficiary of life insurance policies issued upon his life, could recover on the policies in her capacity as administratrix. The court noted that the act did not disinherit a person guilty of voluntary manslaughter, and suggested that the act be amended. In response to this suggestion the legislature enacted a comprehensive code in 1941. The general purpose of this statute is to deny to the slayer any personal interest in the estate of the decedent, or in an estate owned jointly by the slayer and the decedent, or any interest in the proceeds of insurance on the life of the decedent. 66 65 64

Sec. 1094. Statute of Limitations. All persons concerned in the estate of an intestate who do not present their claims within seven years of the death of the intestate, are forever barred from so doing, except as to infants, who are allowed seven years after coming of age.70

Part 2. Wills 

Sec. 1095. Gift Inter Vivos. A person may make a valid gift of his property during his lifetime, to take effect when the gift is made, as long as this is not done with intent to defraud his creditors. When not made in contemplation of death it is called a gift inter vivos. "To constitute a valid gift inter vivos, there are two essential elements: (1) an intention or purpose to give, accompanied by (2) a delivery, actual or constructive, of a nature sufficient not only to divest the donor of all dominion over the property, but also to invest the donee with complete control over the subject-matter of the gift." "1 71 

08 20 PS 371. 

09 20 PS 1090. 

70 20 PS 134. 

Rynier Estate, 347 Pa. 471 (1943). Ella Rynier was married at the age of 61. She was survived by her husband, who became administrator of her estate, and by her brother, and the children of a deceased sister. Within a period of five years preceding her death she executed three judgment notes of $2,000 each, payable 

71 Henderson v. Hughes, 320 Pa. 124 (1936).

to her brother, which she left with a person engaged in the insurance and real estate business, to be delivered to her brother after her death. The notes were presented at the audit of her estate. 

In sustaining this claim, it was said by STERN, J. "Decedent had a perfect right to give away all or any of her property, and, if she actually divested herself of ownership and there was no fraud (as to which there is here no claim), it is immaterial that her husband was thereby deprived at her death of his distributive share in her estate. . . . Of course, the delivery need not be made directly to the beneficiary."

Sec. 1096. Gift Causa Mortis. A gift causa mortis differs from a gift inter vivos in that it is made in contemplation of death. Should the person making such a gift subsequently recover his health the gift is revocable and he may require that it be returned to him. Otherwise the essential characteristics of the two gifts are much the same. While delivery of the gift is essential, it may be constructive or symbolical. 

Elliott's Estate, 312 Pa. 493 (1933). Decedent had been employed as an engineer by the West Penn Power Company for about thirty years prior to his death. During the last ten years of his life he lived at a boarding house in Connellsville, which was conducted by Teresa Salandra and her husband. He was survived by distant relatives, with whom he maintained no contact. His last illness was brief and he declined to go to a hospital. When informed by the attending physician that he was going to die he replied, according to the testimony of this physician: "If I am going to die everything I have belongs to this woman,' and he slapped her on the back." He removed his keys from his suspenders and gave them to her. One of the keys gave access to his safe deposit box in which was found property valued at $21,104. The lower court held that this was not a valid gift causa mortis. In deciding otherwise, it was said by DREW, J. "There is not even an inference of fraud suggested by anyone. While a gift of this nature is properly the subject of suspicion, where, as here, there is no fraud and no doubt of the intention of the decedent, there should be no hesitation in giving effect to his dying wish."

Sec. 1098. Testamentary Capacity. It is frequently said that it requires less capacity to make a will than to engage in ordinary business transactions. Despondency to the point of taking one's life is not conclusive of testamentary incapacity," nor is an adjudication of insanity. The requirements of testamentary capacity, as indicated in McNitt's Estate," are (1) that the testator had an intelligent knowledge of the act he is engaged in, (2) of his property, (3) of his relatives, and (4) of the disposition he desires to make of his estate. 75

Sec. 1100. Disinheritance. A parent may disinherit a child, unless lack of testamentary capacity is shown. 

In Thomas v. Carter," the testator, who was in ill health, became suddenly incensed at his daughter because of her decision to marry. His reasons were utterly absurd. Her intended husband, he said, had light hair, and besides, he worked for a salary, which incidentally was $3,000 per year. He also asserted that his daughter was bad, and that her intended husband was a knave, both of which were without the least foundation. It was held that delusions of this sort amounted to insanity. It is not necessary, in disinheriting a child, except a posthumous child," to bequeath to it a shilling or any other amount. 80 (1934).

Emernecker's Estate, 218 Pa. 369 (1907). Decedent was sur vived by children and grandchildren. She executed a will leaving her entire estate to a granddaughter who had lived with her. and who had helped to support her. Acting under the impression that the will was invalid because of the omission of gifts of at least $1.00 to her children, she destroyed her will about three weeks before her death, and died suddenly without having made another one.

A copy of the will was offered for probate, and rejected. PER CURIAM. "This case affords an illustration that may almost be called pathetic, of the persistency of popular error. The notion that to disinherit the heir he must be 'cut off with a shilling' (for the probable origin of which see Newlin's Estate, 209 Pa. 456), started more than 300 years ago, never was the law either in England or Pennsylvania, and yet survives with such potency as to lead to results apparently as unjust as they were unintended. . . . It seems to be a hard case, but there is no remedy without making the bad law which such cases are said to invite." 

Sec. 1101. Gifts for Religious Uses. Gifts for relig ious and charitable uses, made within thirty days prior to the death of the testator, are void. The thirty day period "shall be so computed as to exclude the first and to include the last day thereof." 81 Prior legislation upheld gifts of this sort when witnessed by two persons, but this requirement failed to curb improper influences which are apt to surround the testator during the last few days of his life. Sec. 1102. Form of Will. The form of a will is immaterial. Testamentary gifts have been upheld which have been inscribed in pencil on an old gas bill,82 and on the blank page of a printed notice.88 A letter which read, "I am making out my will leaving securities to you" is not a will,84 but a letter to the trustee of a fund in which the testator had an interest, which stated that, "In case of my death without having made a will it is my wish and desire that all money derived" from said fund be paid to a designated person, is testamentary.85

Sec. 1103. Execution. The signature of the tes tator must appear at the end of the will.87 In Friese's 

Estate 88 it was said: "In decedent's safe deposit box was found a testamentary paper dated December 22, 1930, but it was unsigned at the end thereof. He had written his name in every blank space provided for it in the body of the paper, including the testimonium clause and the attestation clause. Had the paper been signed at its end, it would have been a complete will." As it was, it "became a nullity." In 1888 it was held that a will, in which the testator had added the appointment of an executor after his signature, could not be admitted to probate.89 The present statute now provides that such an appointment, or other dispositive or testamentary words or directions, which are made after the signature, shall not invalidate that which precedes the signature." A will should be signed by the testator, unless prevented from doing so by the extremity of his last sickness. The legal requisites of execution may be expressed as follows: "(1) signing by the testator unless last sickness prevents, if so, then by another by direction; (2) if unable to sign for any reason other than last sickness, then by another by direction accompanied by testator's mark if not unable to make it." 92

Proof by two witnesses in either case is essential.

Sec. 1104. Subscribing Witnesses. Most of the states require two subscribing witnesses, and some states follow the old English statute and require three. 

It would be advisable, in order to dispose of property located in other states, or which might be acquired in other states, to have three witnesses attest the execution of a will, but subscribing witnesses in this commonwealth are not vitally essential. When a will is offered for probate it must be proved by two witnesses, but where there are no subscribing witnesses "a will may be sufficiently proved by two witnesses who are acquainted with the handwriting of the maker." 94 Neither is it necessary for a will to be in the handwriting of the testator.95 As said in Weigel v. Weigel," "The signature of a party is prima facie evidence of execution; and though it is less forcible than if the body of the instrument were also in his handwriting, the difference is but in the degree." Some states recognize a holographic will (a will in the handwriting of the testator) without subscribing witnesses, but inasmuch as no subscribing witnesses are necessary in Pennsylvania, this distinction is unimportant.

Sec. 1105. Nuncupative Will. Personal property may be bequeathed by a nuncupative (oral) will, but subject to the following statutory restrictions: (1) Such will shall in all cases be made during the last sickness of the testator, and in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house. (2) Where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars, it shall be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the bequest, did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; and, in all cases, the foregoing requisites shall be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will.

Sec. 1106. Revocation of Will. A will may be changed by codicil, or it may be revoked altogether. A joint will is ambulatory and subject to the possibility of revocation by any one joining in it.98 A will in writing devising real estate must be altered in writing, or by burning, cancelling, obliterating or destroying the same by the testator himself, or by someone in his presence and by his express direction. A will bequeathing personal property may be altered or revoked in the same manner, or by a nuncupative will which is reduced to writing during the lifetime of the testator and proved by two witnesses.⁹⁹ 

Kepp's Estate, 317 Pa. 253 (1935). Decedent, 72 years of age, tore her will into small pieces and directed her nurse to take the fragments to the cellar and burn them in the furnace. It was not burned as directed, but saved and kept in an envelope without her knowledge. PER CURIAM. "The act of tearing must, of course, be accompanied by the intention to revoke, but when the two elements are present, and the instrument is torn into many pieces, as was done in this case, it would be a strained and unnatural construction to hold that the will was not destroyed." 100 

Sec. 1107. Subsequent Marriage. Whenever person marries or has a child, either by birth or adoption, after having made a will, he will be deemed to have died intestate as to such persons.' A surviving spouse under these circumstances will be entitled to the $5,000 item where there are no children. As said in 

Shestack's Estate: 101 "By the marriage of the testatrix to the appellee her will as to him was annulled. 

There was an actual intestacy as to him and this was the correct view of the court below." Where a will is

In Jones' Estate 108 the testator made a bequest to his "wife Mary Brown Jones." The parties were subsequently divorced. It was held that the word "wife" was merely descriptive, and that Mary Brown Jones was entitled to the legacy. 

Sec. 1108. Lapse of Devise or Legacy. A devise is a gift of real estate. A legacy is a gift of personal property. Ordinarily where a testator makes a devise or bequest, and the beneficiary dies before the testator, the gift will lapse. The Wills Act makes an exception to this rule in favor of a devise or bequest to a lineal descendant, or to a brother or sister, either of whom dies prior to, but leaves issue surviving, the testator."

Hammond's Estate, 108 Pa. Superior Ct. 508 (1931). Testator bequeathed to his brother, David Hammond, a legacy of $6,000. 

The will provided: "In the event of his decease, the bequest is to go to his wife, Frances Hammond, absolutely." Both David and Frances predeceased the testator. David died on November 

10, 1927, and Frances on June 30, 1928. They were survived by three sons. The lower court decided that these sons were not entitled to the bequest, reasoning that when their father died their mother became absolute legatee, and that when she died the gift lapsed, inasmuch as she was neither brother or sister of the testator. In approving this conclusion, it was said by CUNNINGHAM, J. "We may add that under the plain language of the will the legacy, upon the death of testator's brother, became an absolute gift to testator's sister-in-law, she thereupon became a legatee, related to the testator by affinity only, who might, and in fact did, 102 297 Pa. 428 (1929).

Sec. 1109. Rule in Shelly's Case. Until 1935 Penn sylvania followed the "Rule in Shelly's Case." Under this rule, with certain exceptions,105 the devise of a life estate, with remainder to the "heirs" or "heirs of the body" of the life tenant, was construed as an absolute gift to the life tenant, although this rule did not apply where the gift over was to the "children" of the life tenant.106

As amended in 1935, the code now provides that such a gift "shall not operate to give such life tenant an estate in fee." 107 

Sec. 1110. Rule against Perpetuities. Public pol icy is opposed to the tying-up of estates over unreasonably long periods of time. As expressed many years ago by the English Parliament in the Thelusson Act, an executory devise may not be withheld from alienation for a longer period than that of a "life or lives in being, and one-and-twenty years afterwards." 108 This is known as the rule against perpetuities. As expressed in modern times, "the limit, under the rule, for the creation of executory interests to commence, is 'within the period of a life or lives in being and twenty-one years, allowing for the period of gestation." The following distinction has been made between a trust created by the testator, and a trust created under a power of appointment from the testator: 

Warren's Estate, 320 Pa. 112 (1936). STEARNE, J. "Suppose A bequeaths his estate to B for life, and after B's death to B's children for the life of the survivor with provision that upon the death of any of B's children, so possessing a life estate, that their children should take the deceased parent's share until the decease of the surviving child, with remainder over to the issue of all children. Obviously, the substitutionary provision for the dispo-

sition of the income until the death of the surviving child would be void as too remote. It would be possible that one of B's children might die over 21 years after B's death, and then let in a new estate. Therefore, the whole provision as to the substitutionary gift of income would be void, as would the remainder. On the other hand, if A gives his estate to B for life with a general power of appointment, and B gives the estate to her children for life of the survivor (who are all living at the death of A) and under exactly the same provisions as above stated, then the whole disposition is valid. The naming of these children, so living, is but lighting another candle' which is burning during the lives of 

A and B."

Sec. 1111. Restraint against Accumulations. The 

Act of 1853, as amended in 1931,109 restricts the accumulation of rents, issues, interest or profits for a longer term than the lives of the grantor, settler, or testator, and the term of twenty-one years thereafter. An exception is made in favor of any donation, bequest, or devise for any literary, scientific, or charitable or religious purpose. An intermediate bequest will be upheld if it can be separated from a bequest in violation of the rule without defeating the general plan of distribution.110

Sec. 1112. Statute of Uses. Public policy is also opposed to the creation of passive trusts. All such trusts were abolished in England by what is known as the Statute of Uses. A "use," in early English law, corresponds to a modern trust. The statute was provoked by attempts to evade the statutes of mortmain. 

These are explained in section 778 supra. The Statute of Uses abolished all trusts, and provided that the legal title (in the trustee) and the equitable title (in the beneficiary) should merge by operation of law in the beneficiary. As interpreted by courts of equity, however, active trusts were distinguished from passive trusts and removed from the operation of the statute. A trust 100 20 PS 3251. 

110 Quigley's Estate, 329 Pa. 281 (1938). 

111 (1536), 27 Hen. VIII, c. 10.

753 is passive where the trustee has no duties to perform, or where the chief purpose of the trust has failed or has been fulfilled. A trust is active where it is necessary to preserve property for remaindermen, or where it requires the administration of the estate for the sole and separate use of married women, or for the benefit or infants and persons under disability.

Sec. 1113. Spendthrift Trusts. Pennsylvania was probably the first state to recognize the validity of a spendthrift trust.112 Such trusts are now recognized in a great majority of the states. The purpose of such a trust is to deny to the spendthrift the right of alienation, and to place both principal and income beyond the reach of his creditors. The trust may be created by deed or by will. A plan of this sort deprives creditors of a fund out of which they might otherwise satisiy their demands, but as said by the Supreme Court of the United States, when first called upon to pass upon the validity of such a trust, "Why a parent or one who loves another, and wishes to use his own property in securing the object of his affection, as far as property can do it, from the ills of life, the vicissitudes of fortune and even his own improvidence or incapacity for self-protection, should not be permitted to do so, is not readily perceived." 99 113 

Much of the litigation on this subject has been concerned with the rights of the spendthrift's wife by way of support. The early decisions denied her any interest in the fund,114 but this rule has since been abrogated. The Wills Act 118 exempts the income from such a trust from the claim of creditors, but not for the support of the wife and children of the beneficiary. The 

Act of 1921 117 provides that such levy or attachment shall only be for fifty per centum thereof. 115

Lippencott v. Lippencott, 349 Pa. 501 (1944). Defendant was the beneficiary of a spendthrift trust. His first wife secured an absolute divorce, with alimony, in New York. He remarried, but deserted his second wife. She obtained an order of support against him in California. Both of them sought to attach the income of the trust. In deciding in favor of the deserted wife, it was said by DREW, J. "Whether the deserted wife be a resident or nonresident, she may now seize by attachment her husband's interest in a spendthrift trust. . . . The Commonwealth has a vital interest in the maintenance of marriage, because it is the foundation of society. . . . On the other hand, the State has no such interest after a complete severance by law of the relationship of husband and wife. . . A man can have but one wife, and when the word 'wife' is used in statute or decision it means a woman then married to a man in lawful wedlock-not a woman who was his wife before she was divorced." 

Sec. 1114. Cy Pres Doctrine. The Act of 1855,118 

as amended in 1895, provides that no disposition of property for any charitable use shall fail, by reason of the objects ceasing, but that the same shall be carried into effect so far as it can be ascertained consistently with law and equity. "The meaning of the doctrine of cy pres, as received by us, is, that when a definite function or duty is to be performed, and it cannot be done in exact conformity with the scheme of the person or persons who have provided for it, it must be performed with as close approximation to that scheme as reasonably practicable; and so, of course, it must be enforced." 119 

Curran's Estate, 310 Pa. 434 (1933). Dr. William Curran established a trust, the income to be used to promote the higher education of females, "in an institution adapted to that purpose, which shall be located in the City of Philadelphia or adjacent. to it." "The foundation he desired to establish was for the higher education of women along classical lines in an institution providing a deeply religious and cultural background." The fund, amounting to an annual income in excess of $30,000, became available in 1927. Three institutions made application, the Philadelphia School for Christian Workers, the Beaver College for Women at Jenkintown, and Wilson College at Chambersburg. The lower

Sec. 1115. Interpretation of Wills. It has often been said that "no will has a brother." 120 If the intention of the testator is clear from the will, then no rules of construction are necessary. 

This is also true of statutory rules of construction.121 Where the meaning of a devise or bequest is uncertain, the courts will adhere as closely as possible to the general rules of inheritance.122 

The code provides that "Every will shall be construed, with reference to the real and personal estate comprised in it, to speak and take effect as if it had been executed immediately before the death of the testator, unless a contrary intention shall appear by the will." 123 The purpose of this regulation was to avoid the common law rule that after-acquired realty did not pass under the terms of a previously executed will.124 

Sec. 1116. Contradictory Devise. The following rule is applied where a contradiction appears in the nature of an estate which is to vest in the devisee: "Where words sufficient to vest an absolute interest are used in a will, such interest is not to be cut down by subsequent provisions unless the testator had indicated a clear intent to take away the estate previously given." 125 

In a typical case, the testator devised his entire estate to his wife and her heirs and assigns forever, but in a subsequent paragraph he declared that anything left after her death should be divided among his four children, although she was to have full power to

It is true that if he does devise an estate in fee simple he cannot subsequently strip it of attributes which the law regards as inseparable from such an estate, but he certainly can, if he employs language adequate for the purpose, effectively manifest an intention to grant a less estate than might otherwise appear from a preceding portion of his will.”

"The last will of any decedent may be offered for probate at any time:

Sec. 1118. Informal Administration. The formal administration of an estate is not always necessary. "If there be no creditors, the heirs have a complete equity in the property, and, if they choose, instead of taking letters of administration, to distribute it by arrangement made and executed amongst themselves, where is the principle which forbids it?" 128

757 who undertakes to administer an estate without letters of appointment is called an executor de son tort. If there be a creditor, he may insist upon a formal administration in order to prove a claim against the estate. 

A formal administration is advisable where the rights of infants are involved, and it may be necessary in order to transfer corporate stock owned by the estate, or to institute legal actions in behalf of the estate, except in the matter of decedent's wages. The Fiduciaries Act, as amended in 1945,120 provides that the employer of the decedent may, not less than thirty days after the death of decedent, pay all wages due, to the wife, children, father or mother, or sister or brother of the deceased (preference being given in the order named), without the necessity of letters of appointment, where such wages do not exceed $250 in amount. Where none of such persons survive, payment may be made to the undertaker, physician, boarding-house keeper, and nurse, each his or her pro rata share, upon affidavit of the amounts due.

Sec. 1119. Small Estates. The Fiduciaries Act 130 

provides that where the value of an estate does not exceed $200, distribution may be made under general or special rules of court without letters of appointment. 

The code also provides that where the personal estate of a decedent does not exceed $500, the executor or administrator may, six months after his appointment, present his petition for discharge without the expense of proceeding to a formal account.181 These measures are all intended to simplify the settlement of small estates. 120 20 PS 867. 130 20 PS 343. 

Sec. 1120. Letters of Appointment. Letters testa mentary, if the decedent died testate, or letters of administration, if the decedent died intestate, are granted by the Register of Wills of the county in which the decedent had his legal domicile.182 Whenever the decedent • 131 20 PS 863. 132 20 PS 341. 49

has left property in other states it is necessary as a rule to raise an ancillary administration, as distinguished from the domiciliary administration, in the state where the property is located. 133 Such property is subject to the claims of creditors of the state in which it is located. 

The balance, if any, is usually forwarded to the domiciliary administrator in order that it may be available to satisfy the claims of other creditors before being distributed among the beneficiaries.134

Sec. 1121. Kinds of Fiduciaries. A person ap pointed by will to administer an estate is called an executor. Where the testator fails to make such an appointment in the will, the Register of Wills will appoint an administrator cum testamento annexo, or as it is abbreviated, administrator c. t. a. If this officer should die or become disqualified before having fully administered the estate, the Register of Wills will appoint a successor de bonis non administratis (this means goods not fully administered), or as it is abbreviated, administrator d. b. n. c. t. a. Where the decedent died intestate, the Register of Wills will appoint an administrator. Where the appointment of a successor is nec- .essary, his title is administrator d. b. n. A knowledge of these titles is helpful in reading the opinions of the courts.

Sec. 1122. Right to Appointment. Where decedent died intestate, the surviving spouse is first entitled to the appointment of administrator, but the Register of Wills may in his discretion join one or more of those in the nearest degree of consanguinity with decedent, or the latter alone where no application is made by the surviving spouse. Otherwise a creditor is entitled to the appointment, or any fit person. Where the decedent died testate, the person who has been bequeathed

Sec. 1123. Bond of Fiduciaries. A resident executor is not required to furnish a bond unless the will so directs, or unless it is necessary to dispose of real estate in order to satisfy the debts of the estate.187 A nonresident executor, and an administrator, are always required to furnish a bond with two or more sufficient individual sureties, or sufficient corporate security, except that a corporation to which letters are granted may give its own bond.138 The Register of Wills is personally liable to pay all damages resulting from a failure to require this security.' 139 

Sec. 1124. Procedure on Appointment. An execu tor or administrator must advertise his appointment in a newspaper published at or near the place where the decedent resided, and in the legal periodical, if any, designated by rule of court, once a week during at least six successive weeks. Every such notice must request all persons having claims or demands against the estate of the decedent to make known the same, and all persons indebted to the estate to make payment without delay.1 It is the duty of the executor or administrator to make an inventory of all the goods, chattels, and credits of the deceased, and cause an appraisal to be made by two or more appraisers. This must be filed in the register's office within thirty days from the time of the appointment.141 An account should be filed at 140 185 20 PS 343. 136 Friese's (1934). Sec. 1125. Proof of Claims. Claims of creditors should be presented within six months after the advertisement.143 This rule is for the protection of the administrator, and is not an absolute bar. A late claim may be presented at any audit of the estate, and may be allowed out of property then available for distribution.144 It has been held that an "executor or administrator, without the audit or even the filing of an account, may make distribution without liability to any creditor who shall not have given written notice of his claim within six months after the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, provided only that the granting of such letters has been properly advertised in accordance with the requirements of the act. 

Certainly a creditor who has not given such notice within the time specified in the statute or before a distribution is made cannot assert a claim against the distributed assets." 145 

Sec. 1126. Existing Liens. All judgments which at the time of the death of the decedent were liens on real estate owned by the decedent, continue for a period of five years from the date of his death,146 but no execution may issue thereon without first warning the personal representatives by writ of scire facias.147 Mortgage liens are in no way affected.148 Such liens rank in the order of their priority, and should be satisfied out of the proceeds of the sale of such property, without regard to the priorities established for other creditors of the decedent.149

We have observed that real estate automatically passes to the heirs. At common law, lands were not subject to the claims of general creditors. Sec. 1128. Lien for Debts. The Fiduciaries Act pro vides that the liens of general creditors, including judg ments against the decedent which were not liens at the time of his death,154 shall terminate at the expiration of one year from the death of the decedent, unless an action is instituted within that period of time against the estate. As amended in 1945, the court may allow an additional period of six months from the date of the filing of a petition therefor. The action must be properly indexed in the county in which it is brought, and also in the county in which the real estate is situated. 

The liens will then continue for five years after the expiration of one year from the decease of the debtor. unless renewed as in the case of other judgment liens.155 

The failure to establish such liens automatically oper ates as a release of such liens in favor of the heirs. Testamentary authority to sell the real estate in order to pay the debts of the decedent will work an equitable conversion of the estate from real to personal property. Sec. 1131. Liquidation of Estate. The obvious function of an executor or administrator is to liquidate the assets of the estate, discharge the obligations of the estate, and make distribution among the beneficiaries. 

In the exercise of these functions, much will depend upon the circumstances of the estate, and whatever direction or discretion appears in a will. An administrator has no authority to continue the decedent's business, and if he does so he becomes personally liable on all obligations incurred. A testator may authorize his executor to carry on the business. When this is done, the assets of the estate are subject to debts contracted for that purpose.' Fiduciaries may incorporate the business and take and distribute stock in lieu thereof.¹ 165 

Where an estate is devised in trust, the trustee may expend funds of the estate in making necessary repairs, but not for the purpose of enlarging the property.160 

The code defines the actions which may be brought by or against executors or administrators. The statute of limitations against the estate is one year, notwithstanding any other statute whereby such actions would have been sooner barred.167 164

Sec. 1133. Investments. "The duty of an executor generally is not to retain and invest, but to liquidate and terminate. If, however, a valid reason exists for the retention of a fund by the executor, it is incumbent upon him not to permit such fund to remain idle, but to invest it, and if there is a default in this regard he is chargeable with lawful interest thereon." 170 An ex- ecutor may be authorized by the will of the testator to retain or to invest in non-legal securities, and if so he is not required to do more than to exercise common skill, common prudence, and common caution, unless he has greater skill than a man of ordinary prudence. In the absence of such authority, it is the duty of a fiduciary to liquidate non-legal securities within a reasonable time. He is "expected to be ordinarily watchful and to exercise normally good judgment," 172 but if no market can be found, or if the securities are worthless, he "cannot be surcharged for not selling something that nobody would buy." 173 

Lewis' Estate, 344 Pa. 586 (1942). Testator created a life estate for his sister, which included 30 shares of certain stock. A substitute trustee having been appointed, the first account of the latter was confirmed on January 13, 1930. The trust terminated upon the death of the life tenant on July 24, 1938. The stock was a non-legal investment and had never been converted. Because of a decline in the value of the stock, the trustee was surcharged in the sum of $13,104. Sec. 1136. Abatement of Legacies. Legacies are of three sorts, specific, demonstrative, and general. A specific legacy is a gift of a particular chattel. If it is disposed of by the decedent prior to his death it is said to be adeemed. A demonstrative or pecuniary legacy is a gift to be paid from a designated fund. A general legacy is a gift to be paid from the residue of the estate. 

Where the assets of the estate are not sufficient to pay all legacies in full, some of them must abate. Subject to the will of the testator, specific legacies are first paid, and if the estate is insufficient to pay them in full, they will abate in proportion to the legacies so given.' Sec. 1137. Administrator's Fee. Pennsylvania has no statute fixing the fee which should be paid to an executor or administrator. Following are the important features of the inheritance tax: (1) Two Per Centum. Sec. 1141. Death Acts. An action for personal in juries at common law could only be brought by the person injured. Consequently, if death resulted from the injuries, no action could be instituted at all. The Act of 1851200 authorized the widow or personal representative to institute an action, but a recovery, if any, was payable to the estate and hence subject to the claims of creditors. Where the estate was insolvent, little or no benefit was derived by the heirs. The Act of 1855 201 provides that the persons who may recover in such actions are husband, widow, children, or parents of the deceased, without liability to creditors, the sum recov ered to be distributed as in case of intestacy. These are known as the death acts. The statute of limitations is one year after the death. The Act of 1927 202 permits the persons indicated above to recover expenses incurred for medical and surgical care, nursing, and reasonable

201 Act of April 26, 1855, P. L. 309, 12 PS 1602. 

202 Act of May 13, 1927, P. L. 992, 12 PS 1604.

funeral expense. The Act of 1937 208 provides that if none of the designated relatives are left to survive, such damages may be recovered by the personal representative. Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, the personal representative has the exclusive right to institute an action for wrongful death during the first six months following the death of the decedent. If he fails to exercise this right, it is no longer exclusive, and during the next six months any person entitled by law to recover damages may institute the action,204 

Minkin v. Minkin, 336 Pa. 49 (1939). Plaintiff, an eight year old minor, by his next friend, brought suit against his mother to recover for the death of his father, alleged to have resulted from his mother's negligence. The lower court held that the action was contrary to public policy. In deciding that such action was authorized under the death acts, it was said by LINN, J. "If it be shown, as the statement of claim avers, that the cause of the father's death was the defendant-mother's negligence, she, in her own right, can take nothing in the suit; but the fact that she has disabled herself from sharing, will not deprive the other beneficiary-the minor of the benefit of his statutory right to recover." 

Sec. 1142. Survival Act. In addition to the right of the above relatives to institute actions for damages peculiar to them, another act passed in 1937, known as the Survival Act,205 provides that the executor or administrator may institute such action, except for slander and libel, and may be sued in any like action, which the decedent could have instituted, or which could have been maintained against him, if he had lived. CHAPTER XXVII  Part 1. Sherman Act 

Sec. 1143. Restraint of Trade. It has always been the common law of Pennsylvania that a contract, agreement, or combination in general restraint of trade and commerce, is contrary to public policy and void, whether the arrangement be horizontal, as between competitors of the same grade, or vertical, as between manufacturer, wholesaler, and retailer. This policy does not extend to all contracts in restraint of trade. A great many contracts restrain trade or commerce in some technical degree, but it is not the function of the courts to strike down such agreements on grounds of public policy, unless it is shown that a substantial public injury is likely to result.¹ It has recently been held by a majority of the Supreme Court that a union agreement requiring uniform prices throughout the laundry industry in Philadelphia, in order to equalize the terms of competition between the drivers of competing units, constituted an unreasonable restraint of trade, but this probably marks the extreme limit to which the common law doctrine of "unreasonableness" could be applied in modern times."

The rule was originally intended to defeat odious and substantial monopolies. 

Morris Run Coal Co. v. Barclay Coal Co., 68 Pa. 173 (1871).

The referee found the following facts: "These corporations represented almost the entire body of bituminous coal in the northern part of the state. By combination between themselves they had the power to control the entire market in that district. And they did control it by a contract not to ship and sell coal otherwise than as therein provided. And in order to destroy competition they provided for an arrangement with dealers and shippers of anthracite coal. They were thereby prohibited from selling under prices to be fixed by a committee representing each company. And they 

1 Monogahela River C. C. & C. Co. v Jutte, 210 Pa. 288 (1904). 

2 Schwarts v. Laundry & Linen Sup. 

Drivers' Union, 339 Pa. 353 (1940). 772

were obliged to suspend shipments upon notice from an agent that their allotted share of the market had been forwarded or sold." 

AGNEW, J. "The combination is wide in scope, general in its influence, and injurious in effects. These being its features, the contract is against public policy, illegal, and therefore void." 

Sec. 1144. Sherman Act. The federal constitution authorizes the national government to regulate commerce among the several states.³ The first measure adopted by Congress in the exercise of this power, which affected the national economy in a substantial degree, was the Sherman Anti-Trust Act of 1890. This act was directed primarily against combination trusts which had become a matter of public concern at that time. It provides that every contract, trust, or conspiracy in restraint of trade among the several states, shall be illegal, and that any person who shall make such contract, or engage in such combination or conspiracy, or monopolize or attempt to monopolize, or conspire with any other person to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several states, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by fine not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. The act also authorizes the recovery of treble damages by any person injured by a violation of its provisions, as well as injunctive relief. 4 

3 Article I, section 8. 

4 26 Stat. 209 (1890), 15 USCA 1. 

Sec. 1145. Scope of Act. The prohibitions con tained in the Sherman Act are expressed as general propositions, and it has been the function of the Supreme Court to interpret and apply its provisions. It was early decided in the consideration of this statute, that while the jurisdiction of Congress over commerce among the states was full and complete, it had none over that which was wholly within a state." In 1911 the Supreme Court also concluded that not every agreement in restraint of trade constituted a violation of the act, but only such as met the standard of "unreasonableness" 

5 Addyston Pipe & Steel Co. v. U. S., 175 U. S. 211 (1899). 50

as understood at common law." Still later, in the case of the United States Steel Corporation, it was held that the law did not make mere size an offense." 

Sec. 1146. Interpretation. As expressed in the cases as a whole, the Sherman Act is directed against any attempt to fix prices or control production, in either case in unreasonable restraint of interstate commerce. Chronologically, important prosecutions which have been instituted under the act disclose such violations as a rate agreement among competing railroads, an agreement to control production among competing iron pipe manufacturers, a holding company controlling the stock of competing railroad companies,¹º a combination of meat packing companies for the purpose of controlling the market," an agreement among an association of hardwood manufacturers to control production and fix prices,12 combination trusts,13 and the like. The act does not prohibit the creation of an exclusive selling agency,¹¹ or the dissemination of information,15 or even a plan designed to stabilize prices, if not injurious to the

In Hunt v. Crumboch,2º decided in 1945, the plaintiffs, Edward and Robert Hunt, were partners operating a motor freight service in interstate commerce. 

In 1937 a union called a strike for a closed shop, during which a union official was killed. One of the plaintiff partners was tried and acquitted. The union eventually obtained a closed shop, and then refused to admit any of plaintiff's employees to membership, as a result of which plaintiffs were forced out of business. They sought to recover treble damages under the Sherman Act, but it was held that the Sherman Act had no application to such a controversy. 

Apex Hosiery Co. v. Leader, 310 U. S. 469 (1940). Plaintiff was a manufacturer of hosiery at Philadelphia. The company employed about 2,500 persons, and manufactured annually merchandise to the value of about $5,000,000. It shipped more than 

80 per centum of its manufactured products in interstate commerce. On May 4, 1937, when but eight of its employees were members of a hosiery union, the union ordered a strike in an effort to organize the plant. A sit-down strike followed, with the cooperation of union members from other plants, at which time the strikers wilfully wrecked machinery of great value. The strikers also refused to permit the company to use its stock on hand to meet current orders. On June 23, 1937, the strikers were forcibly ejected by order of the circuit court of appeals. In an action against those responsible for the damage, the jury awarded a verdict in the sum of $237,310, which the trial court trebled to $711,932.55 under the provisions of the Sherman Act. In deciding that the remedy of the plaintiff was under appropriate state law rather than the Sherman Act, it was said by STONE, J. "The legislative history of the Sherman Act as well as the decisions of this Court interpreting it, show that it was not aimed at policing interstate transportation or movement of goods and property."

Part 2. Clayton Act Sec. 1148. Labor Unions. Experience under the 

Sherman Act indicated the need for some clarification, and additional measures of control. The Clayton Act of 1914 21 was enacted for this purpose, but as a supplement rather than an amendment to the Sherman Act. 

It declares that the labor of a human being is not a commodity or article of commerce, and that nothing contained in the anti-trust laws should be construed to forbid the existence and operation of a labor organization, or forbid such organization from "lawfully" carrying out the legitimate objects thereof. This section was prompted by the decisions under the Sherman Act, but it did not diminish the power of the courts to restrain "unlawful" acts of labor organizations in restraint of interstate commerce. The act also defined the circumstances under which a restraining order or injunction might be granted, but this has been largely superceded by the Norris-LaGuardia Anti-Injunction Act, infra. 22 Sec. 1149. Tying-In Agreement. In 1912 it was held that a manufacturer of a rotary mimeograph, under letters patent, could restrict the use of the machine to its stencils and ink, not patented, to the exclusion of its competitors.23 The Clayton Act is aimed at this or similar practices, whether by way of lease or sale, where the effect may be to substantially lessen competition or create a monopoly. As interpreted, a manufacturer may not lease certain patented machines for the manufacture of shoes, on condition that the lessee will utilize other equipment of the lessor,24 or require the lessee of tabulating machines to use only tabulating cards manufactured by it,25 nor may a corporation license the manufacture of its patented radio receivers with a restriction as to the use of tubes purchased from

Sec. 1150. Stock of Competitor. The act provides that no corporation engaged in commerce shall acquire, directly or indirectly, the whole or any part of the stock of another corporation, where the effect of such acquisition may be to substantially lessen competition between such corporations, except where such stock is acquired solely for purposes of investment, or where the stock is that of a subsidiary corporation which is organized for the purpose of carrying on the legitimate business of the parent corporation or some extension thereof. It had previously been decided by the Supreme 

Court that the Sherman Act did not require such a construction,20 and this section was intended to supply this defect. It has been held, however, that the act does not prevent one corporation from acquiring the stock of another, even though both are engaged in the same business, except where competition may be lessened in a substantial degree."⁰

Sec. 1151. Price Discrimination. The Clayton Act prohibited discrimination in price as between different purchasers, but with two important exceptions. First, it did not prohibit price discrimination based on the grade, quality, or "quantity" of the commodity sold, or allowance for the difference in the cost of selling or transportation, or discrimination necessary to meet competition. Second, it did not prevent persons from selecting their own customers in bona fide transactions
