Part 3. Price Regulation Sec. 1152. Unequal Competition. The merchandis ing giants (the department store, the chain store, and the mail order house), are generally able to undersell the smaller independent merchant. This is usually made possible through larger purchases at wholesale, and a more rapid turnover. A large part of the public undoubtedly benefits from competition of this sort, although much can be said for the survival of the smaller independent merchant. The Clayton Act of 1914 made some effort to curb price discrimination, but it was held that the act did not prohibit a manufacturer from classifying customers as "wholesalers" and "retailers," and granting uniform discounts to each class,81 nor did it prevent a manufacturer from granting a discount to chain stores, while denying such discount to independent merchants who attempted to pool their purchases in an effort to obtain the same concession.32 The recent price laws, both state and federal, have two main objec- 

31 Mennen Co. v. Fed. Trade Com., 288 Fed. 774 (1923). 

32 National Biscuit Co. v. Fed. Trade 

Com., 299 Fed. 733 (1924).

tives, first, to more nearly equalize the terms of competition between these competitive groups, and second, to eliminate the worst forms of predatory price-cutting.

Sec. 1153. Robinson-Patman Act. In 1936 Con gress amended the Clayton Act by the addition of the 

Robinson-Patman amendment.33 The fundamental purpose of this act is to more nearly equalize wholesale prices. The amendment provides that it shall be unlawful to discriminate between different purchasers of commodities of like grade and quality, where such commodities are sold for use, consumption, or resale, where the effect of such discrimination may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly, or to injure, destroy, or prevent competition with any person who either grants or knowingly receives the benefit of such discrimination. Such discrimination may not be accomplished through the payment of rebates, or the allowance of brokerage fees, or the furnishing of facilities or payment of compensation for handling or processing such merchandise, except upon equal terms to all other customers. The same penalties provided by the 

Sherman Act are imposed against any person who violates any of these provisions, including any person who knowingly receives or participates in such discrimination.

Sec. 1154. Price Differentials. The Robinson-Pat man Act does not require absolute uniformity of price. 

Due allowance may be made for differences in the cost of manufacture, sale, or delivery resulting from the differing methods or quantities in which such commodities are sold or delivered. These provisions will, in many cases, justify a difference in price on the basis of the expense involved in manufacturing, packing, and ship ping larger or smaller quantities. The Federal Trade 

Commission may, however, establish quantity limits as 

33 49 Stat. 1528 (1936), 15 USCA 13.

to particular commodities, where it finds that available purchasers in greater quantities are so few as to render differentials on account thereof unjustly discriminatory. 

Price changes may also be made from time to time in response to changing conditions affecting the market, such as actual or imminent deterioration of perishable goods, obsolescence of seasonable goods, distress sales under court process, or sales in good faith in discontinuance of business in the goods concerned. 

Sec. 1155. Selecting Customers. It should also be noted that none of the anti-trust laws deny to manufacturers or wholesalers the right to select their own customers in bona fide transactions. Many such firms which formerly sold at different prices to the large and small merchandising units, now specialize in sales to one or the other, rather than attempt to justify such differences on the basis of cost, although the decisions of the Federal Trade Commission indicate a rather liberal attitude in the administration of the law. 

Sec. 1156. Predatory Practices. Most of the states have adopted statutes designed to curtail the practice of what is known as "bait selling," or sales of "loss leaders." Such sales were almost always confined to identified merchandise known to the public for its quality, and to well known brand names having an established market price. The price-cutter advertised the sale of such a commodity at a loss, primarily for the purpose of getting people into his store, and then recouped the loss by pushing the sale of unknown goods, usually at higher prices. This was made possible because a purchaser seldom bought a "loss leader" and nothing else. 

That such a practice is immoral is free from doubt, at least to the extent that the public is deceived. It is objectionable for other reasons. The public may be led to believe that the commodity has been cheapened, or that other dealers are demanding an unreasonable price.

It is difficult under these circumstances for a producer

or distributor to build up and maintain the good will of the public. He not only has to break down this prejudice, but he must also overcome the antagonism of dealers who suffer from such a practice and who may refuse to stock his product in any but such amounts as are necessary to satisfy an insistent demand. 34 

Sec. 1157. Fair Trade Act. Prior to 1935 Pennsyl vania adhered to the common law rule that a vertical as well as horizontal price-fixing agreement, of sufficient magnitude, was contrary to public policy and void.³ 

In that year the legislature concluded to validate the vertical agreement by adoption of the Fair Trade Act which had gained favor in most of the states.35 This is, of course, a state and not a federal enactment. Its pur- pose is to make it possible for a manufacturer to require uniform retail prices, and to prevent predatory price practices. In order to eliminate the common law objection, it provides that a contract relating to a commodity which bears a trade-mark or brand (including commodities sold by use of vending machines), shall not be considered in restraint of trade if it establishes resale prices. This arrangement must be vertical, from the producer down, and not horizontal. Exception is made in the case of damaged goods, closing out sales, distress sales under legal process, and the sale of books to libraries. The statute is not mandatory. It does not require the making of such contracts, nor does it provide any criminal punishment for the violation of such a contract. It merely authorizes the making of such contracts, and provides that a person who wilfully and knowingly advertises, offers for sale or sells any such merchandise at less than the stipulated price, whether party to the contract or not, shall be liable in a civil action to any person who may be damaged thereby. 

34 Ford Motor Co. v. Quinn, 70 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 337 (1918). 

35 Act of June 5, 1935, P. L. 266, as amended, 73 PS 7.

Bristol-Myers Co. v. Lit Brothers, 336 Pa. 81 (1939). Plaintiff was the manufacturer of Sal Hepatica and Ipana Tooth Paste. It entered into Fair Trade Contracts with certain retailers in Pennsylvania under the terms of which a small package of Sal Hepatica was to be sold at retail at 25g, and Ipana Tooth Paste at 39c. 

The defendant, Lit Brothers, was not a party to such an agreement, but it nevertheless obtained these products which it sold at the prices stipulated. Defendant, however, gave to such customers who requested them, Yellow Trading Stamps, one stamp for each ten cent purchase. The books were then redeemed by Lit Brothers at the rate of $1.40 per thousand stamps. Plaintiff contended that this practice constituted a violation of the Fair Trade Act. MAXEY, J. "While it is the purpose of the Fair Trade Act to prevent 'cutthroat competition,' it is not the purpose of the Act to prevent all business competition. Competition is still 'the life of trade,' and no public policy is sound which stifles the spirit of enterprise. 

If, for example, merchant A provides orchestral music for his customers at a certain hour of the day, or maintains in his store a salon where works of art are exhibited, or a nursery where children are fed and otherwise cared for while their mothers are shopping in the store, or if he provides his customers free bus service to and from his store, merchant B has no grounds for complaint which the law will heed. Yet all these things confer benefits on the customer and some of these benefits are susceptible of pecuniary measurement. It follows, therefore, that for a merchant to confer pecuniary benefits upon his customers, which benefits some competing merchant does not confer, does not amount to such unfair competition as the Fair Trade Law forbids. Merchant A can extend his customers 30 or 60 days credit on the purchase of a commodity while merchant B refuses to extend any credit on the purchase of the same article. A is not thereby violating the Fair 

Trade Act. A may allow a discount of 1% on all bills paid within ten days after being rendered. B may allow no such discount. A is not thereby violating the Fair Trade Act. What Lit Brothers did in this matter is neither a direct price-cutting of certain commodities nor is it a palpable subterfuge to conceal a law evasion. It is not a 'guise' assumed to cloak 'reality.' The issuing of trading stamps is and long has. been a legitimate means of attracting customers to the store issuing them. It has not met with express legislative condemnation in this Commonwealth and there is nothing in the act invoked to indicate that its provisions were intended to prevent the practice." ... 

Sec. 1158. Miller-Tydings Act. Price-fixing contracts of this sort are not new, either in the country or

36 abroad. They have been enforceable in England for years, and are quite common on the continent. They have also been upheld by many of the state courts in this country, and probably would have found favor in most of the states had it not been for the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in 1911, which decided that a plan of this type, which sought to control prices for sales by all dealers, by fixing the amount which the consumer should pay, amounted to an unlawful restraint of trade, invalid both at common law and under the Sherman Act.38 The Miller-Tydings amendment to the Sherman Act as approved in 1937, removes this obstacle.³7 It provides that where such contracts are lawful in the jurisdiction where a resale is to be made, or to which the commodity is to be transported for resale, they shall no longer be unlawful under the 

Sherman Act, or an unfair method of competition under the Federal Trade Commission Act. Enough has been said to indicate the importance of this change in the law. A plan of this sort is primarily in the interests of the business community, but it will be welcome to the public if it accomplishes a general leveling of prices and a greater equality of treatment. 

Sec. 1159. Fair Sales Act. The Fair Trade Act applies only to goods sold under a brand or trade name. 

In order to accomplish the same purpose with respect to other goods, Pennsylvania, in conjunction with a majority of the states, adopted a companion measure known as the Fair Sales Act, in 1937.38 Unlike the Fair Trade

Act, this is a penal statute. It provided that the sale of any merchandise at less than cost by retailers or wholesalers constituted a misdemeanor. It was loosely drawn, however, and differed somewhat from similar enactments which had been generally upheld in other jurisdictions. It was declared unconstitutional by the 

30 Dr. Miles Medical Co. v. John D. 

Park & Sons Co., 220 U. 

(1911). S. 373 37 50 Stat. 693 (1937), 15 USCA 1. 

38 Act of July 1, 1937, P. L. 2672, 73 PS 201.

Supreme Court in 1940, on the ground that it was arbitrary and grossly out of proportion to the object which it sought to accomplish, and failed as a penal measure to lay down a reasonably ascertainable standard of guilt.""

Mr. Justice STERN pointed out, however, that "if the act confined itself to prohibiting sales below cost when intended to destroy competition, it would undoubtedly be valid, as has been held in various jurisdictions where such acts have been enacted with that qualification."

In order to overcome these objections, the legislature enacted a substitute measure in 1941." 40 

Sec. 1160. Definition of Cost. In order to overcome the objection found to the earlier statute, the new law defines cost as the invoice or replacement cost, whichever is lower, less all trade discounts, except customary discounts for cash, advertising allowance, promotional allowances, display allowances and any other allowances for for services rendered and any other mission or remuneration received for services performed on behalf of any governmental agencies; to which should be added, (a) freight charges not otherwise included in the invoice or the replacement cost of the merchandise, and (b) a mark-up to cover in part the cost of doing business, which mark-up in the absence of proof of a lesser cost, should be not less than four per cent of the total cost at the retail outlet, and not less than two per cent of the total cost at the wholesale establishment. Such provisions are divisible whenever the same firm is engaged in wholesale and retail sales. 

Manufacturers not operating a retail business are not covered by the act.

Sec. 1161. Penalties and Exemptions. After de claring that sales at less than cost, with intent to lessen or destroy competition, to be an unfair method of competition and contrary to public policy, the act provides 

39 Com. V. Zasloff, 338 Pa. 457 (1940). 

40 Act of August 11, 1941, P. L. 

900, 73 PS 211.

that any retailer or wholesaler who shall advertise, offer to sell or sell any item of merchandise at less than cost, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and upon conviction shall pay a fine of from $50 to $200 and costs, or undergo imprisonment not exceeding 30 days. The courts of the state are also empowered to restrain violations of the act, and to grant injunctive relief to any person who may be injured by such a violation. A number of transactions are exempt from the provisions of the law. Such exemptions are made with respect to bona fide clearance sales, perishable merchandise, imperfect, damaged, or discontinued merchandise, the final liquidation of a business, sales for charitable purposes, sales to the government and its departments, prices necessary to meet competition, judicial sales, and tools, equipment and materials sold to employees of the seller. 

Sec. 1162. Employee Discount Act. It has long been a very common practice for retail merchants to sell their regular merchandise to their employees at wholesale prices, or at least at discounts which approximate wholesale prices. In recent years this practice has been widely extended to include other kinds of merchandise not regularly handled by the employer, but through the cooperative effort of the employer and wholesale distributors or manufacturers, a matter which has provoked the resentment of retail merchants who regularly handle such merchandise and who probably lose a good many sales as a consequence. If an employee is able to buy through his employer, or in his employer's name, goods or merchandise at wholesale prices, he will very likely take advantage of the opportunity. The Act of 

1941 "¹ declares that such practice diverts the normal flow of trade and constitutes an unfair method of competition. The statute is aimed at the employer. He may no longer sell or procure for sale to his employees, any article not handled in his regular course of trade or 41 

41 Act of August 11, 1941, P. L. 898, 43 PS 941.

business, or not connected with or related to his trade or business. The act is not penal in its nature. It simply declares that such practice shall constitute unfair competition to any retail operator dealing in such merchandise within the same city or county. A violation is actionable by any person damaged thereby, but "such action shall be in equity by injunction only, and no damages shall be assessed."

Sec. 1163. Chain Store Tax. Prior to the develop ment of the price laws, a number of states resorted to a progressively graduated tax against chain stores and theatres in an effort to more nearly equalize the competitive disadvantage of the independent merchant. 

The Supreme Court of the United States has upheld a number of these laws, though department stores were excluded, 42 or service stations were included, and though the tax on stores within the state was based upon the number of stores in the national chain." The chain store tax appears to have been a temporary expedient, and is gradually being withdrawn. Such a law was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1937.45 The tax increased progressively from $1 per unit to $500 per unit, depending upon the number of units in the chain. The constitution of Pennsylvania, however, declares that all taxes shall be uniform, and the law was accordingly declared unconstitutional. A state income tax law, which was adopted in 1935, was overruled for the same reason.* 

This subject has been fully discussed elsewhere.50 46 49 48

Sec. 1165. Confusion of Goods. A newcomer in a field already occupied by a rival of established reputation, must do something to avoid confusion between his goods and those of his rival. Where a dealer, for example, manufactures and sells cigars which have become widely known by his surname, and he eventually incorporates his business, using his name in the corporate title, the corporation has a standing in equity to enjoin another corporation from using the same name in the designation of its product, even though the newcomer is a brother of the first, bearing the same surname. Sec. 1166. Trade Marks and Names. The Act of 

1941,5* amending earlier legislation, authorizes the registration of distinctive labels, trademarks and tradenames in the office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth. Aside from this statute, a manufacturer has no right to enclose his product in packages in such a way as to deceive a purchaser, or label his product as that of another.55 It has been held that while no one can have a trademark monopoly in color of paper or shape of label, in color of ink or in one of another detail, a general collocation of such details will be protected against an imitation which deceives purchasers and which must be presumed to have been adopted for that purpose. 

It is not unlawful, however, for a tradesman to imitate, manufacture and sell, as his own, an article manufactured by another, not covered by a patent, where the likeness is confined to the goods themselves and where there is no attempt to deceive the public with respect to the manufacturer. 57 50

Sec. 1168. Trend of Opinion. In 1920 the Supreme 

Court placed a restricted interpretation upon the language of the act." In more recent years, however, the court has considerably broadened its point of view. As said in 1934, with all justices concurring, "Competition may be unfair within the meaning of this statute and within the scope of the discretionary powers conferred on the Commission, though the practice condemned does not amount to fraud as understood in courts of law." 60

Still later it was said with equal unanimity: "It would not have been a difficult feat of draftsmanship to have restricted the operation of the Trade Commission Act to those methods of competition in interstate commerce which are forbidden at common law which are likely to grow into violations of the Sherman Act, if that had been the purpose of the legislation." Sec. 1169. Fraudulent Merchandising Act. In 1937 the legislature declared certain forms of fraudulent merchandising to be unlawful.62 This act provides that it shall be unlawful to advertise or hold out by any means that any sale of goods, wares, or merchandise is an insurance, bankruptcy, mortgage, insolvent, assignee's, receiver's, trustee's, removal, or closing out sale, or a sale of goods damaged by fire, smoke, or water, unless a license is first obtained to conduct such sale from the treasurer of the city or borough in which it is to be held. As amended in 1943, it is unlawful to conduct such business after the license has expired. The statute requires full disclosure of the facts necessary to inform the treasurer whether such license should be granted, and if any defect appears in the title to the goods, or any false representation is made in the application, the treasurer may refuse to issue a license. The offense is punishable by a fine not exceeding $100, or imprisonment not exceeding thirty days. The fee for the license is $25. The act does not apply to sales by public officers, or by licensed auctioneers extending over a period not in excess of three days, or to sales conducted by or in behalf of insurance companies. 63 

Sec. 1170. Misleading Advertising Act. The Penal 

Code " provides that persons who engage in untrue, false and misleading advertising by newspaper, book, notice, handbill, poster, sign, bill, circular, pamphlet, letter, or in any other way, shall be punished by fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both. Publications enjoined are statements regarding merchandise, security, investment, service or anything offered to the public or concerning the quantity, quality, value, merit, use, present or former price, cost, reason for price, motive for sale, or concerning the 

62 Act of July 1, 1937, P. L. 2821, 53 PS 2421. as Act of June 24, 1939, P. L. 872, 18 PS 4101.

method or cost of production or manufacture, or the possession of rewards, prizes or distinctions conferred, which are known to be or which by the exercise of reasonable care should be known to be untrue, deceptive, or misleading. The code also declares as deceptive, the publication of "liner ads” in such way as to indicate that a sale is being made by a private party or householder not engaged in such business. Publishers and employees of publishing agencies who have no knowledge of the falsity or deceptive character of the matter published are excluded from the penalties of the act. 

Sec. 1171. Racial Discrimination Act. The Penal 

Code, supra, also makes it unlawful to discriminate on account of race, creed, or color, with respect to public accommodations. Among the agencies enumerated in the code are hotels, restaurants, saloons, ice cream parlors, drug stores, hospitals, theatres, bowling alleys, schools, and colleges and universities. The penalty is a fine not exceeding $100 or imprisonment not exceeding ninety days, or both. In the case of railways or railroads, the penalty is a fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding three months, or both. 

Part 5. Social Security Act 

Sec. 1172. Retirement Annuities. In years past many American industries established pension plans for retired employees. There were three main disadvantages to this general program. First, it was discriminatory against the great body of American workmen for whom no provision had been made; second, the annuities were in many cases inadequate; and third, many companies were compelled, through inadequate earnings during the depression years, or insolvency or bankruptcy, to suspend payments. In 1935 Congress entered the field, by enactment of the Social Security Act, in order to provide a more equitable system of 64 

04 49 Stat. 620 (1935), 42 USCA 301.

retirement annuities. The act is altogether federal in this phase of the social security program. The fund for the payment of such annuities is supplied by equal contributions from both the employer and employee, based upon the employee's wage not in excess of $3,000 per year. Such employments as are exempt are set forth in the footnotes.05 The dual tax was to have been 

1% for 1939, 1940, 1941, and 1942; 2% for 1943, 1944, and 1945; 22% for 1946, 1947, and 1948; and 3% for 

1949 and thereafter. During the war years the tax has been retained at 1%. 

Sec. 1173. Minimum Qualifications. As originally enacted, the Social Security Act provided that an employee might qualify for a retirement annuity by earning not less than $3,000 during a period of five years beginning January 1, 1937, and by reaching the age of 

65 on or after January 1, 1942. By amendment on August 10, 1939, Congress reduced the qualifying period to three years, and made the annuities operative as of January 1, 1940. The benefits of the act were also extended to the dependents of a qualified employee. In order to establish these new standards, the amendment defines a currently insured individual as any employee who has been paid wages of not less than $50 for each of not less than six of the twelve calendar quarters, immediately preceding the quarter in which he died. A fully insured individual is defined as any employee who has had not less than one quarter of coverage for each two of the quarters elapsing after 1936 (or since becom- 05 In summary, employment of agricultural labor; employment of domestics in homes, college clubs and fraternities; employment of casual labor not in the course of the employer's trade or business; employment of children, parents, or spouse; service on non-American vessels when outside the United States; employment with the United States government or instrumentality thereof; employment with a state or political subdivision thereof; service for nonprofit rellgious, charitable, and educational organizations; employment with employers exempt from the federal income tax as defined; service for voluntary employees' beneficiary associations as defined; employment of college student employees up to $45, exclusive of room, board and fees; service for foreign governments or instrumentality thereof as defined; employment of nurses in hospitals or training schools, and internes; catching and cultivating fish or other aquatic forms of life; and the delivery of newspapers by infants under the age of eighteen.

Sec. 1174. Primary Insurance Benefit. The pri mary insurance benefit of an employee is computed as follows: (a) 40% of the average monthly wage, if such average monthly wage does not exceed $50, or (b) if such average monthly wage exceeds $50, then 40% of $50, plus 10% of the amount by which such average monthly wage exceeds $50 and does not exceed $250, and (c) an amount equal to 1% of the amount computed as above, multiplied by the number of years in which $200 or more of wages were paid to such individual. Let us assume, for example, that an employee has been a security holder for the first three years, and that during that time he has earned an average of $100 a month. (In that period he will have contributed $36 to the security fund, at the rate of 1% per month of his salary for 36 months.) His primary benefit would be computed as follows: 

40% of his first $50 of average pay 

10% of the next $50 of average pay .... ... $20.00 5.00

Basic benefit 1% of basic benefit times 3 years of coverage 

Primary insurance benefit $25.75 

Sec. 1175. Benefits to Dependents. A fully insured employee who has attained the age of 65, is entitled to the payment of the primary insurance benefit, per month, until he dies. In addition the following benefits are conferred upon his dependents: 25.00 .75 (1) Wife at age of 65: Every wife, at 65 years of age, who was living with her husband, and who is not entitled to receive an annuity in her own right in equal amount, may receive one-half of

the insurance benefit of her husband until any of the following occurs: she dies, her husband dies, or they are divorced. (2) Child under 18: Every child of an individual entitled to primary insurance benefits, or who died currently insured, who is unmarried, under the age of 18, and dependent upon such individual, may receive one-half of the parent's primary insurance benefit until any of the following occurs: the child dies, marries, or attains the age of eighteen. (3) Widow at age of 65: Every widow of an individual fully insured, who has not remarried, who has attained the age of 65, and who is not entitled to receive an annuity in her own right in equal amount, may receive three-fourths of the primary insurance benefit of her deceased husband until any of the following occurs: she remarries or dies. (4) Widow under 65 with children: Every widow of a fully or currently insured individual, who has not remarried, and is not entitled to receive an annuity in her own right in equal amount, and who was living with such individual at the time of his death, and who has in her care a child of such deceased individual entitled to receive a child's insurance benefit, may receive a benefit of three-fourths of her deceased husband's primary benefit until any of the following occurs: no such child is qualified, or she becomes entitled to receive a widow's insurance benefit, or she remarries or dies. (5) Parents at age of 65: If none of the foregoing qualify, then every wholly dependent parent of a fully insured individual, who has attained the age of 65, and who has not married since such individual's death, and who is not entitled to an annuity in his or her own right in equal amount, may receive a benefit of one-half of the primary benefit of such deceased individual until any of the following occurs: such parent remarries or dies. (6) Lump sum death payments: If none of the foregoing qualify, then upon the death, after December 31, 1939, of an individual who died fully or currently insured, an amount equal to six times a primary insurance benefit shall be paid in a lump sum to the heirs of such individual. 

Sec. 1176. Maximum Benefits. The minimum benefit is $10 per month. Whenever the total benefits payable per month exceed $20, then the total maximum benefits shall be the least of any of the following amounts: (a) $85; (b) an amount equal to twice a primary insurance benefit; or (c) an amount equal to

80% of the average monthly wage. This provision places a ceiling over the total amount that any one family may receive. Where payments include children, the total monthly benefit is reduced proportionately as each child attains the age of 18. The Social Security Board may reduce or suspend payments to which an individual is entitled, where such individual renders services for wages of not less than $15, or where a child from 16 to 18 years of age fails to attend school without reasonable cause, or where a widow does not have a qualified child in her care. Deductions equal to the total benefits are also made from any wife's or child's insurance benefit, for any month in which the individual, with respect to whose wages such benefit was payable, rendered services for wages of not less than $15. 

Part 6. Unemployment Compensation 

Sec. 1177. Federal Unemployment Tax. The Social 

Security Act, supra, also imposes upon every employer of eight or more employees, a tax of three per centum of the wages of each employee, ostensibly for the purpose of providing a fund for the payment of unemployment compensation. No contribution is required of the employee. The federal government, however, does not undertake the payment of unemployment compensation. 

Such compensation must be authorized by each state, subject to the minimum standards prescribed in the federal law. If a particular state does not adopt an acceptable plan for the payment of unemployment compensation, the funds paid into the federal treasury are lost to that state. If the state adopts an acceptable plan and imposes a tax upon employers for that purpose, such employers are entitled to a credit of ninety per centum against the federal tax. Under such circumstances the employer would pay a tax of 2.7% to the state government, and .3% to the federal government, the latter to defray such costs of administration as are incurred by the federal government. The tax paid to

the state is deposited in an "Unemployment Trust Fund" maintained by the federal government, and may be used as requisitioned by the state government for the payment of unemployment benefits. It has been argued that the federal plan is coercive, and compels each state to adopt an unemployment compensation law, but this objection has been overruled.6 ees.

Under the schedules appearing in the act, unemployment compensation ranges from $8 to $20 per week, based upon the claimant's highest quarterly wages during the base year;70 and for periods ranging from 9 to 20 weeks during the benefit year,"¹ based upon the claimant's total base year wages. The maximum amount, however, is reduced to $18 per week for a period of 16 weeks (or $288, whichever is the lesser), if the balance in the unemployment trust fund, at the end of any calendar quarter, is less than one and one-half times the highest amount paid out for compensation during any twelve consecutive months. 

Sec. 1179. Eligibility. Unemployment itself is not grounds for compensation. In order to qualify for this relief a claimant must show that he has, within his base year, been paid wages equal to not less than 30 times his weekly benefit rate; that he has registered for work at an employment office; that he is able to work and is available for suitable work (this provision distinguishes unemployment compensation from sickness insurance); and that he has been unemployed for a waiting period of one week. In the case of unemployment resulting from an industrial dispute, no compensation is payable for a period "beginning with the day on which such suspension occurs and ending with (i) the last day of the fourth calendar week immediately following the calendar 70 The first four of the last five completed calendar quarters immediately preceding the first day of the benefit year. 

71 The "benefit year" is defined as a one-year period beginning with the day on which an application for benefits is filed, or next filed after the termination of the last benefit year.

week in which such suspension occurs, or (ii) the day on which such suspension was terminated, whichever is the earlier." It has been held that this prohibition applies in the case of a sympathetic strike,72 and where a work stoppage resulted from a protest by members of a union against the union.73 

Teicher Unemployment Compensation Case, 154 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 250 (1943). Claimant, whose husband had been inducted into the armed forces, voluntarily quit her employment and moved to a distant state where no employment was available, in order to be with him during his training period. In deciding that while she had quit work with good cause, but had not yet qualified for unemployment compensation because not available for work, it was said by KENWORTHEY, J. "This is not to say that an unemployed person in a particular locality must pull up his roots and travel many hundreds of miles to available employment or suffer ineligibility if he refuses. The community may be said to owe a duty to a member who becomes unemployed through no fault of his own which is not fulfilled by requiring him to leave his established home and residence to take employment elsewhere. But here, the claimant was the actor. In our opinion, the duty of the community is temporarily lost or suspended when the member voluntarily removes to another in which there is no employment available and no reasonable expectation of finding any." 

Sec. 1180. Ineligibility. An employee is ineligible to receive compensation for any week in which his unemployment is due to failure, without good cause, either to apply for suitable work, or to accept suitable work when offered to him by the employment office or by an employer, provided the employer simultaneously notifies the employment office of such offer; or for any week in which his unemployment is due to voluntarily leaving work without good cause; or for any week with respect to which he had received or is seeking unemployment benefits under an unemployment compensation law of any other state; or where his unemployment is due to his discharge or suspension for wilful misconduct connected with his work. An employee is not disquali-

73 Miller v. Unemployment Comp.

The following definition applies where the question of suitable work is involved, and in determining whether an employee has left his work voluntarily without good cause: "Suitable Work" means all work which the employe is capable of performing. In determining whether or not any work is suitable for an individual, the department shall consider the degree of risk involved to his health, safety and morals, his physical fitness, prior training and experience, and the distance of the available work from his residence. The department shall also consider among other factors the length of time he has been unemployed and the reasons therefor, the prospect of obtaining local work in his customary occupation, his previous earnings, the prevailing condition of the labor market generally and particularly in his usual trade or occupation, prevailing wage rates in his usual trade or occupation, and the permanency of his residence. However, notwithstanding any other provisions of this subsection, no work shall be deemed suitable in which (1) the position offered is vacant, due directly to a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute, or (2) the remuneration, hours or other conditions of the work offered are substantially less favorable to the employe than those prevailing for similar work in the locality, or (3) as a condition of being employed, the employe would be required to join a company union, or to resign from, or refrain from joining, any bona fide labor organization. 

Part 7. Labor Relations Sec. 1181. National Labor Relations Act. The Na tional Labor Relations Act was adopted by Congress in 1935.7 The fundamental purpose of this law is to confer upon labor engaged in commerce among the several 74 

74 49 Stat. 452 (1935), 29 USCA 151.

states, or in which such commerce is affected, the right of self-determination, and to prohibit certain unfair labor practices. The Supreme Court has indicated a liberal attitude in the interpretation of this jurisdiction by the federal government. 

National Labor Relations Board v. Jones & Laughlin Steel 

Corp., 301 U. S. 1 (1937). Defendant discharged ten employees because of union activities. All were officers or were active leaders of the union. Two were motor inspectors, one was a tractor driver, three were crane operators, one was a washer in the coke plant, and three were laborers. The NLRB ordered the defendant to reinstate these employees and to make good their losses in pay. 

Defendant challenged the constitutionality of the act. In sustaining the law, it was said by HUGHES, C. J. "It is a familiar principle that acts which directly burden or obstruct interstate or foreign commerce, or its free flow, are within the reach of the congressional power. ... Employees have as clear a right to organize and select their representatives for lawful purposes as the respondent has to organize its business and select its own officers and agents. Discrimination and coercion to prevent the free exercise of the right of employees to self-organization and representation is a proper subject for condemnation by competent legislative authority."

Sec. 1182. Provisions of Federal Law. As expressed in the act, "Employees shall have the right to self-organization, to form, join, or assist labor organizations, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to engage in concerted activities, for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection." The act is administered by a board consisting of three members, appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The board is authorized to adopt rules and regulations; to determine whether, in any case within its jurisdiction, the unit appropriate for the purpose of collective bargaining shall be the employer unit, craft unit, or plant unit; to certify any such unit as the sole bargaining agency for such employees; to prevent any person from engaging in any unfair labor practice as defined in the

act; and to apply to any circuit court of appeals for the enforcement of its orders. This legislation has been criticized for its failure to prescribe what might be deemed unfair employee practices such as are addressed to the employer. It provides, in substance, that it shall be an unfair labor practice for an employer: (1) To interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in the right of self-determination. (2) To dominate or interfere with the formation or administration of any labor organization or contribute financial or other support to it, except that subject to the rules of the board, an employer shall not be prohibited from permitting employees to confer with him during working hours without loss of time or pay. (3) By discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization, although he may enter into an agreement with a properly established labor organization to require membership therein of all employees as a condition of employment. (4) To discharge or otherwise discriminate against an employee because he has filed charges or given testimony under the act. (5) To refuse to bargain collectively with the representatives of his employees, subject to the provisions of the statute. 

Sec. 1183. Application of Federal Law. The na tional law and the state law dealing with this subject do not operate concurrently with respect to the same employments. Either the federal or the state law applies to a particular controversy, the former taking precedence over the latter. The line of demarcation has not yet been clearly drawn. In a decision by the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, involving a dairy company which conducted its business in a number of states, and in which the application of the state law was rejected, it was said: "While all the employees engaged in the present dispute were performing intrastate duties-the local delivery of milk-the dispute had a pronounced effect on the interstate activities of the Dair- -K

ies," 75 Following is the distinction as drawn by the Supreme Court of the United States. 

National Labor Relations Board v. Fainblatt, 306 U. S. 601 

(1939). Respondents were two individuals, both operating small plants in New Jersey for the manufacture of wearing apparel. 

Fainblatt employed some sixty women. He received the material from a New York concern, which he converted into garments, and then sent the finished products back to the firm in New York or directly to its customers. In deciding that the federal law applied to a labor dispute in these plants, it was said by STONE, J. "It has been settled by repeated decisions of this Court that an employer may be subject to the National Labor Relations Act although not himself engaged in commerce. 

The amount of the commerce regulated is of special significance only to the extent that Congress may be taken to have excluded commerce of small volume from the operation of its regulatory measure by express provision or fair implication." 76 

Sec. 1184. State Labor Relations Act. A Labor 

Relations Act was adopted in Pennsylvania in 1937.7 

This act creates a state board of three members, to be appointed by the Governor, with the consent of the Senate. The board is authorized to make rules and regulations for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the act, by and with the approval of the Secre tary of Labor and Industry. The provisions of the act dealing with self-determination, the character of the bargaining unit, and certification by the board, are a substantial reënactment of the federal law, with one exception. As amended in 1945, "if the majority of the employees of a particular craft signify a wish for a craft unit, the board shall designate the craft unit as the unit appropriate for collective bargaining for the employees of that particular craft." The code is more explicit in other respects. It provides for an election upon the petition of the employer, or petition of a labor organization, or petition of thirty per centum of the employees affected. The certification of the board shall be binding for a period of one year, or longer if the contract

These objectives are largely accomplished under the federal law by the rules and regulations which the National Labor Relations Board is authorized to adopt. The Supreme Court has held that the state law applies exclusively to industrial pursuits."

Salvation Army Case, 349 Pa. 105 (1944). The Salvation Army at Pittsburgh conducted an Evangeline Residence for young working girls and out-of-town school girls. Rates were charged to cover costs, but the operation was not conducted for profit. A labor union presented a petition to the board asserting that the Salvation Army employed some 38 employees in this operation, and had declined to bargain collectively. In deciding that the act did not cover such employment, it was said by STEARNE, J. "We do not mean to decide or imply that whenever a non-profit organization does enter an industrial field, even though its profits may be devoted to charity, it is exempted from the taxes and regulations such as the Labor Relations Act to which any other industry or business is subjected." (Cases cited were a Y. M. C. A. which rented commercially part of its premises to lodgers; a private hospital which operated farms for profit; a Sunday School 

Union which conducted a book store for profit; and a university which owned and operated an office building.) 

Sec. 1185. Unfair Practices. Such unfair labor practices as are enumerated in the federal law are incorporated in the state statute, but with the addition that any agreement made between an employer and a labor organization, not in violation of the act shall be entitled to full force and effect; and that whenever any party has engaged in an unfair labor practice upon which a complaint is based, such violation shall constitute a complete defense to the complaint. The distinctive feature of the state law is the addition of the following unfair employee practices, namely: (1) To intimidate, restrain, or coerce any employee by threats of force or violence or harm to said employee or members of his 

77 West. Pa. Hospital v. Lichliter, 340 Pa. 382 (1941).

family or to his property, with intent to compel him to join a labor organization. (2) To become a part of a sit-down strike during a labor dispute, or seize or hold or damage or destroy the plant, equipment, machinery, or other property of the employer, with intent to coerce the employer. (3) To intimidate, restrain, or coerce any employer by threats of force or violence or harm to his person or to members of his family, with intent to compel him to accede to demands, conditions, and terms of employment. 

Sec. 1186. The Check-Off. The state code attempts to regulate the check-off by making it an unfair labor practice for an employer "To deduct, collect, or assist in collecting from the wages of employees any dues, fees, assessments, or other contributions, payable to any labor organization, unless he is authorized so to do by a majority vote of all the employees in the appropriate collective bargaining unit taken by secret ballot, and unless he thereafter receives the written authorization from each employee whose wages are affected." The inclusion of the "bargaining unit," rather than the union, is inconsistent, inasmuch as this matter is of primary interest to a labor union rather than to employees not members of a union. 

Sec. 1187. Back Pay. The state code provides, in addition, that the board may order the reinstatement of an employee, but that no order shall award back pay from a period more than six weeks prior to the filing of a complaint. The Supreme Court has applied the general rule of damages to such cases. In W. T. Grant 

Co., Inc., v. United Retail Employees of America, claimant was an employee of a department store, and was also Chairman of the Grievance Committee of the local union. She was wrongfully discharged because of union activities. She made a dilatory effort to obtain other employment, but was unsuccessful. 

It was conceded as a reasonable inference that her activity in 

78 347 Pa. 224 (1943).

her labor union interfered with her securing employment elsewhere, but it was held, nevertheless, that the award of back pay, prior to her reinstatement with the company, should be dated as of the date on which she made a legitimate effort to obtain employment elsewhere. Aside from this ruling, the necessity of filing a complaint within six weeks is open to some criticism, inasmuch as it operates as a deterrent to mediation and arbitration within that period of time. 

Sec. 1188. Federal Injunction Act. Both the federal and state governments have adopted statutes changing the traditional power of the courts to grant injunctions in labor disputes. The federal statute, known as the Norris-LaGuardia Act of 1932, enumerates a number of specific acts which are usually incident to union organization and collective bargaining and which shall not be the subject of a restraining order. 

The statute then declares that the federal courts shall not otherwise issue an injunction in any matter in which a labor dispute is involved, except after a hearing in open court with an opportunity for cross-examination, and then only upon findings to the effect (a) that unlawful acts have been threatened and will be committed unless restrained, (b) that substantial and irreparable injury to complainant's property will follow, (c) that greater injury will be inflicted by the denial of relief than will be inflicted by the granting of such relief, (d) that complainant has no adequate remedy at law, and (e) that the public officers charged with the duty to protect complainant's property are unable or unwilling to furnish adequate protection. 79 

70 47 Stat. 70 (1932), 29 USCA 101.

Part 8. Wages and Hours Sec. 1190. Fair Labor Standards Act. In 1938 

Congress adopted an act for the establishment of fair labor standards with respect to minimum wages and maximum hours, for employees engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce.82 Other than for employees who are exempt,83 the minimum wage for the first year after the effective date of the act is 25 cents per hour, for the next six years 30 cents per hour, and thereafter 40 cents per hour. Subject to additional exemptions and exceptions,85 the maximum hours of employment for the first year after the effective date of the act are 44 hours, for the second year 42 hours, and thereafter 40 hours, unless time and one-half is paid for overtime. Sec. 1191. Minimum Wage for Women. In 1937 the legislature adopted a minimum wage law for women and children.88 This act, however, does not prescribe minimum wages. It provides that upon petition of fifty or more residents of the commonwealth, on behalf of the women or children in any occupation, the Department of Labor and Industry shall appoint a wage board to report on the establishment of minimum fair wages for such employees. A wage board must be composed of not more than three representatives of employers, three representatives of employees, and an equal number rep- 

80 Act of May 27, 1937, P. L. 917, 43 PS 331a.

resenting the public. The standards to be applied in the determination of a fair minimum wage are (a) the cost of living, (b) the reasonable value of services rendered, and (c) wages paid for work of like character by employers who voluntarily maintain minimum fair wage standards. The report of a wage board is subject to the approval of the Department of Labor and Industry before it becomes effective. A violation of the act is punishable by fine of from $50 to $200, or imprisonment from ten to ninety days, or both. An employee may also recover the full minimum wage in a civil action, less the wage actually paid, with costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. The constitutionality of this act has been sustained by the Supreme Court, in a decision approving an order fixing the minimum wage for women and minors in the laundry business at 27 cents per hour.87

Sec. 1192. Maximum Hours for Women. An act regulating the hours of female employees was adopted in 1913.88 As amended in 1943, this act prohibits the employment of females in any establishment, other than for employments which are exempt," for more than 52 days in any one week, or more than 44 hours in any one week, or more than 8 hours in any one day, except as to females employed in charitable or welfare institutions operated on a nonprofit basis, who are permitted to work for not more than 10 hours in any one day, which 10 hours shall be all within one period of thirteen consecutive hours, and not more than 48 hours in 6 days of any calendar week. During the war period and six months thereafter, the maximum limitations for women generally are 48 hours in any one week, not to exceed 10 hours in any one day, or more than 6 consecutive days in any one week, in employment in furtherance of the war effort. Sec. 1193. Purpose of Act. The Workmen's Com pensation Act of Pennsylvania was adopted in 1915.9¹ 

It has been frequently amended, on the last occasion in 1945.92 The purpose of this legislation is to displace the common law liability of the employer for accidental injuries, and to substitute a method of accident insurance, with respect to which the common law furnished inadequate relief or none at all.95 The schedules of compensation provided by the act may be rejected, without the benefit, however, of the common law defenses which the employer enjoyed at common law-contributory negligence, the voluntary assumption of risk, and negligence of a fellow servant. Unless such rejection is properly made, the obligations of the act are binding upon both employer and employee. The act evidences a contract, or at least it "rests on the theory of contract." 98

The employee loses any right to institute a common law action," and must accept whatever is provided by its terms. A companion measure, designed to provide compensation for disability or death resulting from occupational disease, was adopted in 1937,100 replaced in 1939,101 and substantially amended in 1945.102 

The social theory of this legislation is to shift the burden of industrial accidents and occupational disability to the consumer as a legitimate cost of production, and to protect workmen against the degradation and depend- 96

Sec. 1194. Employees Excluded. The act does not provide compensation for injuries sustained by employers. Nor are all employees covered by its terms. The following are excluded: (a) employees of the United

States; (b) employees engaged in agriculture or domestic service, unless the employers petition to be included;103 (c) employees engaged in maritime or interstate commerce;¹ ;104(d) public officials who exercise some sovereign power;105 (e) corporate officials while acting in a purely corporate capacity;106 106 (f) casual employees not engaged in the regular business of the employer;107 and (g) independent contractors. 108 Business partners are not employees as to each other, or of the partnership. Members of volunteer fire companies or departments are included by supplemental act of assembly." 

The act imposes a duty upon a general contractor to obtain or to require a subcontractor to obtain insurance for the protection of the employees of a subcontractor.110

Subject to these exceptions, all employers are required to obtain workmen's compensation insurance, either from the State Workmen's Compensation Insurance 

Fund or an insurance company, or obtain exemption as self-insurers. The penalty in case of default is a fine of from $100 to $500, or imprisonment not exceeding six months, or both. Every day's violation constitutes a separate offense. Employment situations not covered by the act are still actionable in courts of law.111

Sec. 1196. Going to and from Work. An employee sent on an errand is under the protection of the act from the moment he leaves his home,123 or his employer's place of business,12 and even while temporarily in another state.125 If the employer undertakes to furnish a special conveyance to take him to and from work he is protected while riding in the conveyance,126 but not when furnished a pass on a common carrier.127 In all other cases an employee must reach the premises where his particular work is carried on. If he is employed in a service station and is struck by an automobile while on the sidewalk in front of the station, enroute to work, he is a few inches short of the protection of the law.128 On the other hand, it is sufficient if he leaves the public sidewalk and starts down a private alley leading to the entrance of the store building.129 If employed as a miner, he is not covered by the act while walking over the property of his employer toward his place of work, not even when he reaches the wash house where he is to change his clothes,180 or while walking from the wash house to the entrance of the mine, but otherwise from the moment when he reports at a shanty to obtain his lamp or equipment. 181

It is immaterial that he may arrive a few minutes or a half hour early, as long as he is there for the purpose of going to work.132 If he merely goes upon the premises to ascertain when to report for work, or if his employment is terminated and he goes upon the premises to secure his tools, he does so at his own risk.133

If his clothes are saturated with oil and he rubs a match against his pants to light a cigarette and is consumed by fire, his death is com pensable.134 Course of employment includes all acts essential to his comfort and necessity and covers the time spent on the premises during the lunch hour,185 and even acts of foolishness and what is known as horse play.136 In one case a breaker boy jumped down a chute to take a ride during the noon hour. Unfortunately as he did so, someone outside the building drew coal down the chute and he was suffocated, but such a death is compensable.137 An employee is in the course of his employment notwithstanding he disregards and violates the orders of his employer,138 or is guilty of gross negligence,139 as long as he is engaged in the work that he has been instructed to do. It is only when an employee abandons his employment, by leaving the premises,¹ or when he puts himself in the position of a trespasser, as by going to a distant part of the mine and there causing an explosion of gas,141 or when he violates the laws of the commonwealth governing his work, as by smoking in a safety-locked section of the mine, tamping in a lighted fuse, returning prematurely to a misfire,' or riding on a mine motor,148 or when he engages in criminal misconduct, as by attempting to pilfer the property of his employer,144 that he takes himself out of the protection of the act, although it has been held that a truck driver who permits another person to drive the truck is not covered, though he is present in the cab.145 142

Sec. 1198. Awards for Disability. No compensa tion is payable during the first seven calendar days of

disability.¹ Thereafter the award is two-thirds of the average weekly wage of the injured employee. For total disability this amount (subject to a minimum of $10 and a maximum of $20) is payable for a maximum of 500 weeks, but not to exceed the total sum of $10,000. 

Where the average weekly wage is less than $10, the full wage is payable, but not less than $5 per week. For partial disability compensation is payable for a maximum of 300 weeks, at the rate of two-thirds of the loss of earning power of the injured employee, but not more than $17 per week, less the number of weeks during which compensation has been paid for total disability. 

Such compensation is not payable where the wage exceeds that received prior to the accident, though there may be some disability.17 Where a child is employed in violation of the child labor laws, ten per centum is added to the award as a penalty to be paid by the employer. 146 

Sec. 1199. Specific Injuries. For specific injuries, such as the loss of an eye, arm, hand, fingers, leg, foot, toes, loss of hearing, and disfigurement, or a fraction of such losses, compensation is payable for the number of weeks specified in each case, less the number of weeks during which compensation has been paid for total or partial disability. Where, however, specific losses occur in each of two or more accidents, the periods run consecutively, even though there is some overlapping of time.148

Where two specific injuries result in total disability, compensation for such disability is payable by the employer, but where the employer is liable for but one such specific loss, additional compensation for total dis- ' ability after the cessation of payments by the employer, is payable by the commonwealth.149 Medical and surgical services are payable for 60 days after disability begins, not to exceed $150, although the board on petition

Breaker Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct.

may extend the period for an additional 30 days, not to exceed $75. Hospital treatment is provided for 60 days, subject to an additional grant of 30 days. In fatal cases, $200 is allowed for funeral expense. 

Sec. 1200. Dependents. 

Dependents. Where the injury results in death, compensation is based on the average weekly wage of the decedent, which shall be deemed to be not less than $17 nor more than $30 per week. A widow, if living with the decedent at the time of his death or dependent upon him for support, and a widower if incapable of self-support and dependent upon the deceased spouse, receive 44% of the weekly wage of the decedent, for 300 weeks, not to exceed $12 per week, less the period during which compensation was paid to the decedent in his lifetime. If there is but one child, such child receives 25% of the weekly wage of the deceased parent, not to exceed $7 per week. The schedule is then graduated upward, depending upon the number of children entitled to compensation, until each, respectively, attains the age of sixteen. An adopted child, and a child to whom the decedent stood in loco parentis, are included. Should the widow remarry, such compensation is payable for one-third of the period remaining. In the event of a meretricious relationship, such compensation may be terminated. If none of the foregoing survive, compensation is payable to partially or wholly dependent parents, and if there be none, then to brothers and sisters under the age of sixteen who were actually dependent upon the decedent at the time of his death. 

The procedure authorized by the act for the payment of compensation, and the problems incident thereto, are discussed elsewhere.150
